item.title: 同一动作、不同结局才算懂规则：Stateful Harness 把「执行规则」和「生成像素」拆开，成对正确率 32%→92% ｜ State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels
item.description:
一句话：世界状态交给程序、画面交给冻结的视频模型：50 对反事实孪生测试里，最好的纯提示只有 32% 给出正确结局，加 harness 后到 92%。

要点：

  • 每回合先由 harness 按规则解算用户动作、编译成事件指令，再交给冻结的视频模型渲染，生成的片段反过来更新世界状态给下一回合用
  • 语义状态（背包、进度）与空间状态分开维护；空间与相机由可编辑 3D 场景渲出的预览片段提供指导
  • WorldState-Bench 用 50 对反事实孪生（同初始帧同动作、不同隐藏状态要求不同结局）：11 个视频后端里纯规则提示最好 32%，写明结局 64%，整套 harness 92%

为什么值得看：要把视频模型接进玩法，这篇给出了最小可用的分工边界：规则与状态留在传统代码里，模型只负责把「已经算出的事件」画出来，每回合只喂一段可寻址的空间参考，而不是指望模型自己记住。

中文摘要：现有世界模型能从单张图生成动作条件视频，但多数只做相机漫游；一旦动作后果依赖当前画面里看不见的状态（有没有钥匙、宝箱开没开过），纯视频生成就会失效。作者提出 Stateful Harness：把世界演化和视频渲染彻底分开，harness 维护一份按规则推进的世界状态，每回合把玩家动作解析成事件并编译成指令，用冻结的视频模型渲染该事件，再用渲染片段更新状态；空间与相机则由可编辑 3D 场景的预览片段给指导。为量化规则遵从，作者构建 WorldState-Bench，含 50 对共享初始帧与动作、但隐藏状态与应有结局不同的反事实样本。结果显示纯提示下最好的后端只有 32% 成对正确，明确指定结局可提到 64%，而整套 harness 在同一个冻结模型上达到 92%。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels

Abstract

Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.

††footnotetext: ∗ Equal contribution. † Project leader.

1 Introduction

Video generation has advanced rapidly, with recent models producing visually realistic videos with coherent motion [(Wan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025)]. Building on this progress, interactive video world models condition generation on navigation signals, allowing users to move through and explore generated environments [(Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Wang et al., 2026)].

Navigation control makes a generated scene explorable, but does not determine the consequences of interacting with it [(Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Wang et al., 2026)]. Some video world models support richer interactions by conditioning generation on player or agent actions [(Valevski et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026a)]. However, a responsive video does not by itself ensure that an action has the outcome required by the world state and rules, or that its consequences persist across later interactions [(Ding et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a)]. For example, the same action should open a locked chest only when the player holds a key, even if the initial views are identical (Figure 2). Such distinctions require semantic state to record variables such as inventory and progress, together with an addressable spatial state to preserve scene layout and camera paths across turns. While prior systems incorporate explicit state through programmable engines, learned game variables, or reconstructed NPC state [(Huang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026)], their evaluations focus on selected mechanics and do not establish whether a frozen video model can render outcomes prescribed by newly specified rules involving hidden state. Explicit state alone does not ensure that the consequence required by its rules appears in the generated video. The central challenge is therefore to make state transitions authoritative and render their consequences faithfully.

We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful interaction under specified rules (Figure 1). It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. Given a world description and an initial image, a coding agent defines the world state, available actions, and executable rules, while an editable 3D scene represents the spatial layout. The rules remain fixed as the world state evolves through user actions. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state before rendering. The resolved event is compiled into a VisualScript instruction, and a preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. A frozen video model renders the event from these inputs and a visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. A vision language model then interprets the generated clip and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state based on the observed events. The runtime incorporates updates compatible with the fixed rules, and the resulting state determines the consequences of subsequent actions. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form a closed loop that yields state world models.

To evaluate whether an action yields a visible event consistent with hidden state, we construct WorldState-Bench with a Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether the action produces a discernible event, and Comply assesses whether that event satisfies an executable rule. Each of the 50 cases comprises a counterfactual pair with the same initial frame, action, and rule program but different hidden values that require distinct outcomes. We introduce PairFollow and PairStrict as two metrics for joint evaluation of each counterfactual pair. PairFollow requires both clips to show their required endings, whereas PairStrict additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent from both clips. Among eleven unwrapped video backends, the highest PairFollow score under the Rule-only condition is 32%. For MiniMax-H3, explicitly specifying the required ending increases PairFollow from 32% to 64%, although PairStrict reaches only 4%. With MiniMax-H3, the complete Stateful Harness framework achieves 92% PairFollow and 90% PairStrict on the same cases. Beyond the single-turn probe, the same closed loop carries state across longer episodes, as in the multi-turn duel of Figure 6, and extends training-free to worlds whose custom rules and state are written as a new world definition.

2 Related Work

World Models. World models study action-conditioned predictions [(Micheli et al., 2022; Hafner et al., 2025; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)]. The Genie series introduces latent actions and promptable environments [(Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025)], while Oasis demonstrates interaction in an open world [(Decart and Etched, 2024)]. Other systems expand scene range, streaming, and instruction following [(He et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026; DreamX Team et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)], separate appearance from actions [(Yu et al., 2025b)], use game corpora [(Che et al., 2025; Kanervisto et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024a; Tang et al., 2025)], or address memory and visual consistency [(Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2026; Garcin et al., 2026)]. Building on action-conditioned rendering, Stateful Harness uses executable rules to resolve each action against explicit semantic and spatial state before a frozen video model renders the resulting event.

Geometric Control of Video Generation. Camera-conditioned systems inject trajectories through learned pose or motion representations [(Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; He et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2024; Bahmani et al., 2025)]. Other methods reconstruct geometry for training-free control [(Hou and Chen, 2024)] or use boxes, source videos, and reference clips [(Lin et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025)]. MoGe4D generates trajectories over recovered geometry [(Zhang et al., 2026b)]. The Stateful Harness uses a related interface to carry an editable scene across turns, with rule execution determining which spatial edits and semantic events are sent to the renderer.

Explicit State and Rules. Rules can be searched as generative objects or compiled from language [(Salen and Zimmerman, 2003; Cook et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2026)]. PWM couples an engine and a 3D oriented-box representation with conditioning at the pixel level [(Huang et al., 2026)]. Code World Model compiles a code-maintained state into proxy video and fine-tunes its renderer [(Chen et al., 2026b)]. Other work generates rule code without a video renderer [(Lehrach et al., 2026)], recovers state from generated frames [(Deng et al., 2026)], or conditions generation on selected state variables [(Lin et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a)]. Narrative and character state can also be generated together [(Li et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025)]. We combine a persistent editable scene, a semantic state ledger, and the standard reference inputs of a frozen renderer. This combination is minimal: new rule-governed worlds reduce to a small typed program, no engine or fine-tuning. Table 12 compares these interfaces and evaluation protocols.

World Modeling Evaluation. Most existing benchmarks measure visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and perspective changes [(Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026)]. Camera and geometry states can be tracked or remembered [(Nam et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b)]. These measurements are valuable for navigability and continuity, but they do not directly test whether identical images and actions produce different rule-mandated outcomes when only hidden state changes. Concurrent work tests whether a shell-game arrangement is retained in the model’s internal state across a swap chain [(Shin et al., 2026)]. WorldState-Bench instead keeps the hidden state in an explicit rule program and tests whether the mandated outcome is executed in rendered video. Benchmarks inside executable games can compare behavior with engine state [(Hafner, 2022; Bard et al., 2020; Light et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026)], but require an existing game or simulator. WorldState-Bench supplies an explicit rule program and tests its consequences in generated video.

3 Method: The Stateful Harness

Framework Overview. A video model can depict an interaction, but a generated clip alone does not specify which changes should persist or whether those changes satisfy the rules of the world. Figure 2 shows how identical frames and actions require different outcomes when the hidden state differs. Inspired by the role of LLM harnesses, we place a stateful runtime around a frozen video model to separate rule execution, visual realization, and observation of the generated result.

Given a world description and an initial image, a coding agent constructs an executable game definition containing the state schema, available actions, rules, events, goals, and visual semantics. The harness initializes a semantic ledger and an editable 3D scene, while the game definition remains fixed throughout the episode. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state and rules to determine the event and provisional state. The resolved event is compiled into a VisualScript instruction, and a preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. A frozen video model generates the next clip from these inputs and a visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. A vision language model then interprets the generated events and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state. The runtime checks these proposals against the fixed rules and incorporates compatible updates into the world state used to resolve the next action. The final frame also becomes the visual anchor for the next generation step. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form a closed loop that couples explicit world state with a frozen video model, yielding a state world model. Figure 3 illustrates world construction and the rule to render path.

We represent the evolving world state as sₜ=(zₜ,uₜ)∈Sₛₑₘ×Sₛₚ. The semantic component zₜ records resources, entity attributes, progress, attitudes, and terminal status that may be invisible in the current frame. The spatial component uₜ records an editable entity layout, scale, and camera path. A fixed rule program R determines which events an action permits and which state changes those events require. The harness updates the world state through a closed loop,

sₜ₊₁=H_R(sₜ, aₜ, oₜ₊₁).

(1)

Here oₜ₊₁ denotes observations extracted by a vision language model from the generated clip, and H_R combines rule execution with compatible updates derived from these observations. The next state therefore incorporates both the consequences of the action and feedback from the generated video under the fixed rules R. The visual anchor fₜ is initialized from the supplied image and subsequently updated from the final frame of each clip.

3.1 Stage 0: World Construction

World construction produces an executable game definition, an initial frame, a semantic ledger, and an editable spatial scene. The game definition fixes the rules for an episode, whereas the ledger and scene change as interactions unfold.

Executable Rules. From the world description, a coding agent writes the game definition in a small typed language. Each rule has a guard that reads the current state and action, and an effect that specifies ledger updates, spatial edits, and an event. Goal conditions inspect the ledger to determine whether an episode has ended. The agent validates and freezes the definition before interaction begins. In the counterfactual benchmark, both members of a pair share this definition.

Initial Frame and Spatial State. The benchmark supplies an audited first image shared by each counterfactual pair. For a new world, setup accepts a supplied image. A feed forward geometry model lifts the image into instance boxes and initializes u₀ as an untextured, editable 3D scene with a ground plane and labeled cuboids. We call this scene the clay model. Its explicit geometry supports object edits and procedural camera previews across turns.

Semantic State. The ledger is a serializable record of typed fields for resources, entity attributes, progress counters, attitudes, and terminal status. A twin specification declares the theme, twin identifier, and seeds. The initializer assigns different hidden values z_A≠z_B while preserving the same first frame and spatial layout. The rules therefore require different outcomes for the same visible action, even though rendering remains stochastic.

3.2 Stage 1: State Evolution and Video Generation

A turn begins when the user selects an action aₜ after observing the current scene. In open interaction an intent agent can map a user instruction to a structured action. The runtime first settles the rule governed outcome, then compiles and renders it, and finally observes the generated clip for changes relevant to the next turn. This order gives fixed rules authority over action consequences while allowing generated events to inform the evolving world state.

Rule Settlement. The rule program evaluates its guards against sₜ and aₜ before video generation. It produces a provisional semantic state z̄ₜ₊₁, a rule event eₜ, and a spatial edit script εₜ. The edit script may add, move, or remove a box or change the camera path. The provisional spatial state is obtained by applying these edits to the clay model.

(z̄ₜ₊₁, εₜ, eₜ) = τ_R(sₜ, aₜ), ūₜ₊₁ = apply(uₜ, εₜ), s̄ₜ₊₁ = (z̄ₜ₊₁, ūₜ₊₁).

(2)

An optional neural kernel ρ may propose dialogue or freeform narration for the settled event. Schema validation, value clamping, bounded retry, and fallback to the rule defined default constrain its proposals to the allowed set A_τ(s,a). Thus the gated kernel G∘ρ satisfies

Supp((G∘ρ)(·|s,a)) ⊆ A_τ(s,a).

(3)

The proposal may vary how an allowed event is expressed but cannot change the rule mandated transition in Eq. 2.

Spatial Guidance. The runtime applies εₜ to the clay model before rendering so that the preview represents the provisional spatial state. A procedural camera program renders this into a preview clip rₜ, which is an editable representation of layout and cameras rather than the final appearance.

Instruction Compilation. The VisualScript compiler translates the settled state and event into a typed visual script with slots for actor, action, target, reaction, dialogue, effects, end state, and shots. A fixed compiler maps this record to the text instruction pₜ, so identical inputs produce identical instructions. The text carries semantic facts that an oriented box stream cannot express, while the preview supplies layout and camera guidance. The instruction identifies the preview as a spatial reference to discourage the backend from reproducing its clay appearance.

Frozen Video Rendering. The video model receives the instruction as text, the preview clip as video reference, and the visual anchor fₜ as image reference. It generates a clip vₜ₊₁ depicting the settled event, and the last frame becomes the anchor for the next turn.

(pₜ, rₜ) = ℂ(z̄ₜ₊₁, ūₜ₊₁, eₜ), vₜ₊₁ = V_θ(pₜ, rₜ, fₜ), fₜ₊₁ = last(vₜ₊₁).

(4)

The model weights remain frozen, and the runtime uses the stock text, image, and video reference interfaces of a compatible backend. Normal operation makes one generation request per turn, with bounded retries for transient errors. On a scene change, the anchor chain can be reset and appearance information is carried in the instruction instead.

Visual Observation and State Update. A vision language model examines the generated clip together with the settled event and provisional state. It identifies visible events and proposes changes to semantic or spatial fields that the video makes observable. The runtime admits a proposed change only when it is well formed and compatible with the fixed rule program. A visual detail may therefore become part of the next state, while an apparent event that contradicts the settled outcome is recorded as a rendering inconsistency and cannot overturn that outcome. We express this step as

oₜ₊₁ = O_ψ(vₜ₊₁, s̄ₜ₊₁, eₜ), sₜ₊₁ = U_R(s̄ₜ₊₁, oₜ₊₁),

(5)

where O_ψ proposes observations and U_R validates and incorporates permitted updates. The next action is evaluated against sₜ₊₁, closing the interaction loop without changing the rules R. The counterfactual evaluation in this paper tests rendered compliance.

4 Benchmark: WorldState-Bench

Overview. Existing benchmarks evaluate visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and camera or geometric consistency [(Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026)]. These evaluations do not directly isolate whether a change in hidden state produces the distinct visible consequence prescribed by an executable rule. Benchmarks based on executable games assess behavior conditioned on state provided by existing engines [(Hafner, 2022; Bard et al., 2020; Light et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026)]. Worlds initialized from a description and an image lack this predefined engine state. To evaluate such worlds, WorldState-Bench uses counterfactual pairs with identical visible inputs, different hidden values, and expected outcomes determined by an executable rule before generation. Joint evaluation of each pair tests whether both required outcomes are rendered correctly under the corresponding hidden states.

We formalize this with the Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether an action produces a discernible event beyond camera motion. Comply assesses whether the event satisfies the rule for the specified hidden state. This separates the absence of an event from the generation of an event that contradicts the rule. The primary metrics quantify Comply, while clips with no discernible event or unjudgeable content are recorded as Unclear and receive no credit.

Counterfactual Hidden-State Pairs. Each case contains two counterfactual instances, A and B, that share the same first frame and action script. They differ in one hidden value z_A≠z_B that is not observable in the shared frame. The same rule program requires different visible endings for the two instances. A correct ending in an isolated clip does not establish sensitivity to hidden state, whereas identical endings across a pair necessarily violate the required outcome for at least one instance. We therefore count a pair as compliant only when both clips show their required endings. A stricter criterion additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent throughout both clips.

Case Construction. The benchmark comprises 50 cases drawn from 49 hidden variables and 21 scenario themes. Hidden values select which object, character, or elemental form carries the effect. Each hidden variable must be unobservable in the first frame and must select rule branches with visibly different outcomes. FLUX.2 [(Black Forest Labs, 2025)] generates the shared first frame at 1280×720, and each frame is audited for visual cues that reveal the hidden value. This audit forms part of benchmark construction. Authors specify each case program in a typed language that determines the initial states, required endings, and fixed choice judging questions. The harness executes the same rules used to derive the expected outcomes, so the evaluation measures whether the generated videos depict these outcomes.

We compile two instruction conditions from each case specification. Rule-only provides the original case instruction, hidden value, selected rule branch, and action. Rule+end additionally specifies the required terminal outcome in an explicit final state sentence. Table 1 reports results under these conditions, while the harness uses the VisualScript instruction described in §3.2.

Judging. We use the multimodal Qwen3.8-27B-VL [(Yang and others, 2025)] to answer fixed choice questions from sampled video frames. The questions identify the ending shown and determine whether the forbidden outcome appears at any point in the clip. At the clip level, EndFollow requires the prescribed ending, CntAbsent requires the absence of the forbidden outcome, and Strict requires both conditions. At the pair level, PairFollow and PairStrict require both clips to satisfy EndFollow and Strict, respectively. TwinContrast records whether the judged endings differ between the two clips. The judge receives the expected outcomes for the relevant rule branch, but neither the hidden variable nor the rule text.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experiment Setup

The rule compliance experiments use the 50 counterfactual pairs in WorldState-Bench, with 100 clips for individual evaluation and 50 pairs for joint evaluation (§4). Each backend generates one clip of a few seconds per action at its native resolution and frame rate. Clips contain 77 to 128 frames at 15 to 24 fps, with resolutions from 592×336 to 1280×720. The harness generates clips at 864×480 and 24 fps. We evaluate eleven existing backends without additional training or fine-tuning (Table 1). Four image-to-video generators receive instruction text and the initial frame, namely Wan2.2 [(Wan et al., 2025)], LongCat-Video [(LongCat Team et al., 2025)], HunyuanVideo 1.5 [(Wu et al., 2025)], and MiniMax-H3 [(Chen et al., 2026a)]. Seven interactive world models receive inputs through their standard action interfaces, namely LingBot-World v2 [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)], Echo-WM Flash [(Zhang et al., 2026a)], FantasyWorld [(Dai et al., 2026)], AlayaWorld [(AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026)], InSpatio-World [(InSpatio Team et al., 2026)], Astra [(Zhu et al., 2026b)], and HY-WorldPlay [(Sun et al., 2025)]. The Qwen3.8-27B-VL judge evaluates frames sampled at 3 fps together with the final frame. Generation and judging use eight A800 80 GB GPUs.

5.2 Results on WorldState-Bench

Under Rule-only prompting, MiniMax-H3 achieves 66% EndFollow and 32% PairFollow, while Wan2.2 achieves 65% and 32%, respectively (Table 1). The lower joint accuracy indicates that correct outcomes in individual clips do not imply compliance across both hidden states. Astra, HY-WorldPlay, and InSpatio-World achieve less than 20% EndFollow despite high CntAbsent scores. These results indicate that the absence of forbidden content can coincide with failure to generate the required event. Explicit outcome instructions under the Rule+end probe (Track B) improve EndFollow for several backends but do not establish reliable joint compliance. The highest unwrapped PairStrict score is 26% for Wan2.2, while MiniMax-H3 reaches only 4% PairStrict and 30% CntAbsent. The reported harness condition resolves each action before generation and does not use compliance judgments to select among repeated video samples.

With the same frozen MiniMax-H3 weights, the harness reaches 92% PairFollow, 90% PairStrict, and 96% TwinContrast (Table 1). In the blind human comparison, Stateful Harness is preferred in 98% of pairwise comparisons against four widely-used unwrapped baselines, with no comparison won by a baseline (Figure 5, Appendix C).

A component-chain decomposition on WorldState-Bench attributes the gain to outcome specification (+32 points) and to executed state with compiled references (+28 points), with both increments significant under paired exact McNemar tests over the 50 pairs.

5.3 Qualitative Results

Figure 4 shows counterfactual pairs in which unwrapped baselines include the forbidden outcome or reproduce an ending across both hidden states. Appendix Figures 13 and 14 show more pairs. The harness generates the distinct outcomes specified by the rules. Figure 6 illustrates how settled state changes condition subsequent generation, using three real harness episodes read through their HUDs. The three episodes span 15, 29, and 11 turns respectively, showing that Stateful Harness sustains multi-turn interaction on the same frozen weights. The episodes are also three genres: town exploration, dating narrative, and turn-based duel, each with its own state transitions and rules. Each genre is a new executable game definition on the same runtime and video model, instantiated training-free. Appendix Figures 15, 16, and 17 unroll all turns of the three episodes.

5.4 Additional Experiments

Abstract

Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.

††footnotetext: ∗ Equal contribution. † Project leader.

1 Introduction

Video generation has advanced rapidly, with recent models producing visually realistic videos with coherent motion [(Wan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025)]. Building on this progress, interactive video world models condition generation on navigation signals, allowing users to move through and explore generated environments [(Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Wang et al., 2026)].

Navigation control makes a generated scene explorable, but does not determine the consequences of interacting with it [(Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Wang et al., 2026)]. Some video world models support richer interactions by conditioning generation on player or agent actions [(Valevski et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026a)]. However, a responsive video does not by itself ensure that an action has the outcome required by the world state and rules, or that its consequences persist across later interactions [(Ding et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a)]. For example, the same action should open a locked chest only when the player holds a key, even if the initial views are identical (Figure 2). Such distinctions require semantic state to record variables such as inventory and progress, together with an addressable spatial state to preserve scene layout and camera paths across turns. While prior systems incorporate explicit state through programmable engines, learned game variables, or reconstructed NPC state [(Huang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2026)], their evaluations focus on selected mechanics and do not establish whether a frozen video model can render outcomes prescribed by newly specified rules involving hidden state. Explicit state alone does not ensure that the consequence required by its rules appears in the generated video. The central challenge is therefore to make state transitions authoritative and render their consequences faithfully.

We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful interaction under specified rules (Figure 1). It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. Given a world description and an initial image, a coding agent defines the world state, available actions, and executable rules, while an editable 3D scene represents the spatial layout. The rules remain fixed as the world state evolves through user actions. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state before rendering. The resolved event is compiled into a VisualScript instruction, and a preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. A frozen video model renders the event from these inputs and a visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. A vision language model then interprets the generated clip and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state based on the observed events. The runtime incorporates updates compatible with the fixed rules, and the resulting state determines the consequences of subsequent actions. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form a closed loop that yields state world models.

To evaluate whether an action yields a visible event consistent with hidden state, we construct WorldState-Bench with a Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether the action produces a discernible event, and Comply assesses whether that event satisfies an executable rule. Each of the 50 cases comprises a counterfactual pair with the same initial frame, action, and rule program but different hidden values that require distinct outcomes. We introduce PairFollow and PairStrict as two metrics for joint evaluation of each counterfactual pair. PairFollow requires both clips to show their required endings, whereas PairStrict additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent from both clips. Among eleven unwrapped video backends, the highest PairFollow score under the Rule-only condition is 32%. For MiniMax-H3, explicitly specifying the required ending increases PairFollow from 32% to 64%, although PairStrict reaches only 4%. With MiniMax-H3, the complete Stateful Harness framework achieves 92% PairFollow and 90% PairStrict on the same cases. Beyond the single-turn probe, the same closed loop carries state across longer episodes, as in the multi-turn duel of Figure 6, and extends training-free to worlds whose custom rules and state are written as a new world definition.

2 Related Work

World Models. World models study action-conditioned predictions [(Micheli et al., 2022; Hafner et al., 2025; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)]. The Genie series introduces latent actions and promptable environments [(Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025)], while Oasis demonstrates interaction in an open world [(Decart and Etched, 2024)]. Other systems expand scene range, streaming, and instruction following [(He et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026; DreamX Team et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a)], separate appearance from actions [(Yu et al., 2025b)], use game corpora [(Che et al., 2025; Kanervisto et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024a; Tang et al., 2025)], or address memory and visual consistency [(Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b; Hu et al., 2026; Garcin et al., 2026)]. Building on action-conditioned rendering, Stateful Harness uses executable rules to resolve each action against explicit semantic and spatial state before a frozen video model renders the resulting event.

Geometric Control of Video Generation. Camera-conditioned systems inject trajectories through learned pose or motion representations [(Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; He et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2024; Bahmani et al., 2025)]. Other methods reconstruct geometry for training-free control [(Hou and Chen, 2024)] or use boxes, source videos, and reference clips [(Lin et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025)]. MoGe4D generates trajectories over recovered geometry [(Zhang et al., 2026b)]. The Stateful Harness uses a related interface to carry an editable scene across turns, with rule execution determining which spatial edits and semantic events are sent to the renderer.

Explicit State and Rules. Rules can be searched as generative objects or compiled from language [(Salen and Zimmerman, 2003; Cook et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2026)]. PWM couples an engine and a 3D oriented-box representation with conditioning at the pixel level [(Huang et al., 2026)]. Code World Model compiles a code-maintained state into proxy video and fine-tunes its renderer [(Chen et al., 2026b)]. Other work generates rule code without a video renderer [(Lehrach et al., 2026)], recovers state from generated frames [(Deng et al., 2026)], or conditions generation on selected state variables [(Lin et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026a)]. Narrative and character state can also be generated together [(Li et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025)]. We combine a persistent editable scene, a semantic state ledger, and the standard reference inputs of a frozen renderer. This combination is minimal: new rule-governed worlds reduce to a small typed program, no engine or fine-tuning. Table 12 compares these interfaces and evaluation protocols.

World Modeling Evaluation. Most existing benchmarks measure visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and perspective changes [(Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026)]. Camera and geometry states can be tracked or remembered [(Nam et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025b)]. These measurements are valuable for navigability and continuity, but they do not directly test whether identical images and actions produce different rule-mandated outcomes when only hidden state changes. Concurrent work tests whether a shell-game arrangement is retained in the model’s internal state across a swap chain [(Shin et al., 2026)]. WorldState-Bench instead keeps the hidden state in an explicit rule program and tests whether the mandated outcome is executed in rendered video. Benchmarks inside executable games can compare behavior with engine state [(Hafner, 2022; Bard et al., 2020; Light et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026)], but require an existing game or simulator. WorldState-Bench supplies an explicit rule program and tests its consequences in generated video.

3 Method: The Stateful Harness

Framework Overview. A video model can depict an interaction, but a generated clip alone does not specify which changes should persist or whether those changes satisfy the rules of the world. Figure 2 shows how identical frames and actions require different outcomes when the hidden state differs. Inspired by the role of LLM harnesses, we place a stateful runtime around a frozen video model to separate rule execution, visual realization, and observation of the generated result.

Given a world description and an initial image, a coding agent constructs an executable game definition containing the state schema, available actions, rules, events, goals, and visual semantics. The harness initializes a semantic ledger and an editable 3D scene, while the game definition remains fixed throughout the episode. At each turn, the user observes the current scene and selects an action, which the runtime resolves against the current state and rules to determine the event and provisional state. The resolved event is compiled into a VisualScript instruction, and a preview clip from the updated 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. A frozen video model generates the next clip from these inputs and a visual anchor drawn from the initial image or preceding clip. A vision language model then interprets the generated events and proposes updates to the semantic and spatial state. The runtime checks these proposals against the fixed rules and incorporates compatible updates into the world state used to resolve the next action. The final frame also becomes the visual anchor for the next generation step. Together, rule execution, video generation, and visual observation form a closed loop that couples explicit world state with a frozen video model, yielding a state world model. Figure 3 illustrates world construction and the rule to render path.

We represent the evolving world state as sₜ=(zₜ,uₜ)∈Sₛₑₘ×Sₛₚ. The semantic component zₜ records resources, entity attributes, progress, attitudes, and terminal status that may be invisible in the current frame. The spatial component uₜ records an editable entity layout, scale, and camera path. A fixed rule program R determines which events an action permits and which state changes those events require. The harness updates the world state through a closed loop,

sₜ₊₁=H_R(sₜ, aₜ, oₜ₊₁).

(1)

Here oₜ₊₁ denotes observations extracted by a vision language model from the generated clip, and H_R combines rule execution with compatible updates derived from these observations. The next state therefore incorporates both the consequences of the action and feedback from the generated video under the fixed rules R. The visual anchor fₜ is initialized from the supplied image and subsequently updated from the final frame of each clip.

3.1 Stage 0: World Construction

World construction produces an executable game definition, an initial frame, a semantic ledger, and an editable spatial scene. The game definition fixes the rules for an episode, whereas the ledger and scene change as interactions unfold.

Executable Rules. From the world description, a coding agent writes the game definition in a small typed language. Each rule has a guard that reads the current state and action, and an effect that specifies ledger updates, spatial edits, and an event. Goal conditions inspect the ledger to determine whether an episode has ended. The agent validates and freezes the definition before interaction begins. In the counterfactual benchmark, both members of a pair share this definition.

Initial Frame and Spatial State. The benchmark supplies an audited first image shared by each counterfactual pair. For a new world, setup accepts a supplied image. A feed forward geometry model lifts the image into instance boxes and initializes u₀ as an untextured, editable 3D scene with a ground plane and labeled cuboids. We call this scene the clay model. Its explicit geometry supports object edits and procedural camera previews across turns.

Semantic State. The ledger is a serializable record of typed fields for resources, entity attributes, progress counters, attitudes, and terminal status. A twin specification declares the theme, twin identifier, and seeds. The initializer assigns different hidden values z_A≠z_B while preserving the same first frame and spatial layout. The rules therefore require different outcomes for the same visible action, even though rendering remains stochastic.

3.2 Stage 1: State Evolution and Video Generation

A turn begins when the user selects an action aₜ after observing the current scene. In open interaction an intent agent can map a user instruction to a structured action. The runtime first settles the rule governed outcome, then compiles and renders it, and finally observes the generated clip for changes relevant to the next turn. This order gives fixed rules authority over action consequences while allowing generated events to inform the evolving world state.

Rule Settlement. The rule program evaluates its guards against sₜ and aₜ before video generation. It produces a provisional semantic state z̄ₜ₊₁, a rule event eₜ, and a spatial edit script εₜ. The edit script may add, move, or remove a box or change the camera path. The provisional spatial state is obtained by applying these edits to the clay model.

(z̄ₜ₊₁, εₜ, eₜ) = τ_R(sₜ, aₜ), ūₜ₊₁ = apply(uₜ, εₜ), s̄ₜ₊₁ = (z̄ₜ₊₁, ūₜ₊₁).

(2)

An optional neural kernel ρ may propose dialogue or freeform narration for the settled event. Schema validation, value clamping, bounded retry, and fallback to the rule defined default constrain its proposals to the allowed set A_τ(s,a). Thus the gated kernel G∘ρ satisfies

Supp((G∘ρ)(·|s,a)) ⊆ A_τ(s,a).

(3)

The proposal may vary how an allowed event is expressed but cannot change the rule mandated transition in Eq. 2.

Spatial Guidance. The runtime applies εₜ to the clay model before rendering so that the preview represents the provisional spatial state. A procedural camera program renders this into a preview clip rₜ, which is an editable representation of layout and cameras rather than the final appearance.

Instruction Compilation. The VisualScript compiler translates the settled state and event into a typed visual script with slots for actor, action, target, reaction, dialogue, effects, end state, and shots. A fixed compiler maps this record to the text instruction pₜ, so identical inputs produce identical instructions. The text carries semantic facts that an oriented box stream cannot express, while the preview supplies layout and camera guidance. The instruction identifies the preview as a spatial reference to discourage the backend from reproducing its clay appearance.

Frozen Video Rendering. The video model receives the instruction as text, the preview clip as video reference, and the visual anchor fₜ as image reference. It generates a clip vₜ₊₁ depicting the settled event, and the last frame becomes the anchor for the next turn.

(pₜ, rₜ) = ℂ(z̄ₜ₊₁, ūₜ₊₁, eₜ), vₜ₊₁ = V_θ(pₜ, rₜ, fₜ), fₜ₊₁ = last(vₜ₊₁).

(4)

The model weights remain frozen, and the runtime uses the stock text, image, and video reference interfaces of a compatible backend. Normal operation makes one generation request per turn, with bounded retries for transient errors. On a scene change, the anchor chain can be reset and appearance information is carried in the instruction instead.

Visual Observation and State Update. A vision language model examines the generated clip together with the settled event and provisional state. It identifies visible events and proposes changes to semantic or spatial fields that the video makes observable. The runtime admits a proposed change only when it is well formed and compatible with the fixed rule program. A visual detail may therefore become part of the next state, while an apparent event that contradicts the settled outcome is recorded as a rendering inconsistency and cannot overturn that outcome. We express this step as

oₜ₊₁ = O_ψ(vₜ₊₁, s̄ₜ₊₁, eₜ), sₜ₊₁ = U_R(s̄ₜ₊₁, oₜ₊₁),

(5)

where O_ψ proposes observations and U_R validates and incorporates permitted updates. The next action is evaluated against sₜ₊₁, closing the interaction loop without changing the rules R. The counterfactual evaluation in this paper tests rendered compliance.

4 Benchmark: WorldState-Bench

Overview. Existing benchmarks evaluate visual quality, prompt adherence, navigation, subject actions, event editing, and camera or geometric consistency [(Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b; Xu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Nam et al., 2026)]. These evaluations do not directly isolate whether a change in hidden state produces the distinct visible consequence prescribed by an executable rule. Benchmarks based on executable games assess behavior conditioned on state provided by existing engines [(Hafner, 2022; Bard et al., 2020; Light et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2026; La et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026)]. Worlds initialized from a description and an image lack this predefined engine state. To evaluate such worlds, WorldState-Bench uses counterfactual pairs with identical visible inputs, different hidden values, and expected outcomes determined by an executable rule before generation. Joint evaluation of each pair tests whether both required outcomes are rendered correctly under the corresponding hidden states.

We formalize this with the Change-to-Comply protocol. Change assesses whether an action produces a discernible event beyond camera motion. Comply assesses whether the event satisfies the rule for the specified hidden state. This separates the absence of an event from the generation of an event that contradicts the rule. The primary metrics quantify Comply, while clips with no discernible event or unjudgeable content are recorded as Unclear and receive no credit.

Counterfactual Hidden-State Pairs. Each case contains two counterfactual instances, A and B, that share the same first frame and action script. They differ in one hidden value z_A≠z_B that is not observable in the shared frame. The same rule program requires different visible endings for the two instances. A correct ending in an isolated clip does not establish sensitivity to hidden state, whereas identical endings across a pair necessarily violate the required outcome for at least one instance. We therefore count a pair as compliant only when both clips show their required endings. A stricter criterion additionally requires the forbidden ending to be absent throughout both clips.

Case Construction. The benchmark comprises 50 cases drawn from 49 hidden variables and 21 scenario themes. Hidden values select which object, character, or elemental form carries the effect. Each hidden variable must be unobservable in the first frame and must select rule branches with visibly different outcomes. FLUX.2 [(Black Forest Labs, 2025)] generates the shared first frame at 1280×720, and each frame is audited for visual cues that reveal the hidden value. This audit forms part of benchmark construction. Authors specify each case program in a typed language that determines the initial states, required endings, and fixed choice judging questions. The harness executes the same rules used to derive the expected outcomes, so the evaluation measures whether the generated videos depict these outcomes.

We compile two instruction conditions from each case specification. Rule-only provides the original case instruction, hidden value, selected rule branch, and action. Rule+end additionally specifies the required terminal outcome in an explicit final state sentence. Table 1 reports results under these conditions, while the harness uses the VisualScript instruction described in §3.2.

Judging. We use the multimodal Qwen3.8-27B-VL [(Yang and others, 2025)] to answer fixed choice questions from sampled video frames. The questions identify the ending shown and determine whether the forbidden outcome appears at any point in the clip. At the clip level, EndFollow requires the prescribed ending, CntAbsent requires the absence of the forbidden outcome, and Strict requires both conditions. At the pair level, PairFollow and PairStrict require both clips to satisfy EndFollow and Strict, respectively. TwinContrast records whether the judged endings differ between the two clips. The judge receives the expected outcomes for the relevant rule branch, but neither the hidden variable nor the rule text.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experiment Setup

The rule compliance experiments use the 50 counterfactual pairs in WorldState-Bench, with 100 clips for individual evaluation and 50 pairs for joint evaluation (§4). Each backend generates one clip of a few seconds per action at its native resolution and frame rate. Clips contain 77 to 128 frames at 15 to 24 fps, with resolutions from 592×336 to 1280×720. The harness generates clips at 864×480 and 24 fps. We evaluate eleven existing backends without additional training or fine-tuning (Table 1). Four image-to-video generators receive instruction text and the initial frame, namely Wan2.2 [(Wan et al., 2025)], LongCat-Video [(LongCat Team et al., 2025)], HunyuanVideo 1.5 [(Wu et al., 2025)], and MiniMax-H3 [(Chen et al., 2026a)]. Seven interactive world models receive inputs through their standard action interfaces, namely LingBot-World v2 [(Robbyant Team et al., 2026)], Echo-WM Flash [(Zhang et al., 2026a)], FantasyWorld [(Dai et al., 2026)], AlayaWorld [(AlayaWorld Team et al., 2026)], InSpatio-World [(InSpatio Team et al., 2026)], Astra [(Zhu et al., 2026b)], and HY-WorldPlay [(Sun et al., 2025)]. The Qwen3.8-27B-VL judge evaluates frames sampled at 3 fps together with the final frame. Generation and judging use eight A800 80 GB GPUs.

5.2 Results on WorldState-Bench

Under Rule-only prompting, MiniMax-H3 achieves 66% EndFollow and 32% PairFollow, while Wan2.2 achieves 65% and 32%, respectively (Table 1). The lower joint accuracy indicates that correct outcomes in individual clips do not imply compliance across both hidden states. Astra, HY-WorldPlay, and InSpatio-World achieve less than 20% EndFollow despite high CntAbsent scores. These results indicate that the absence of forbidden content can coincide with failure to generate the required event. Explicit outcome instructions under the Rule+end probe (Track B) improve EndFollow for several backends but do not establish reliable joint compliance. The highest unwrapped PairStrict score is 26% for Wan2.2, while MiniMax-H3 reaches only 4% PairStrict and 30% CntAbsent. The reported harness condition resolves each action before generation and does not use compliance judgments to select among repeated video samples.

With the same frozen MiniMax-H3 weights, the harness reaches 92% PairFollow, 90% PairStrict, and 96% TwinContrast (Table 1). In the blind human comparison, Stateful Harness is preferred in 98% of pairwise comparisons against four widely-used unwrapped baselines, with no comparison won by a baseline (Figure 5, Appendix C).

A component-chain decomposition on WorldState-Bench attributes the gain to outcome specification (+32 points) and to executed state with compiled references (+28 points), with both increments significant under paired exact McNemar tests over the 50 pairs.

5.3 Qualitative Results

Figure 4 shows counterfactual pairs in which unwrapped baselines include the forbidden outcome or reproduce an ending across both hidden states. Appendix Figures 13 and 14 show more pairs. The harness generates the distinct outcomes specified by the rules. Figure 6 illustrates how settled state changes condition subsequent generation, using three real harness episodes read through their HUDs. The three episodes span 15, 29, and 11 turns respectively, showing that Stateful Harness sustains multi-turn interaction on the same frozen weights. The episodes are also three genres: town exploration, dating narrative, and turn-based duel, each with its own state transitions and rules. Each genre is a new executable game definition on the same runtime and video model, instantiated training-free. Appendix Figures 15, 16, and 17 unroll all turns of the three episodes.

5.4 Additional Experiments

item.title: 五个生产级引擎、从空项目造完整游戏：agent 拿满集成分却只拿到一半玩法分，只有 16% 的 run 真能玩到结局 ｜ From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
item.description:
一句话：「能 build」不等于「能玩」：50 个任务横跨 Defold/Godot/Roblox/Unity/UE，隐藏评测器只认真实输入试玩，agent 的游戏仅 16% 能走到结局。

要点：

  • 50 个任务，每个引擎 10 个，agent 从空项目 + 设计文档起步；设计文档同时是契约，规定可检查规则与必需的状态接口
  • 单次 run 平均最多 295 步、6500 万 token；隐藏评测器不编译不看代码，只用真实输入把游戏从头玩到结局、退出、再确认存档
  • 四个 scaffold 下 agent 拿到大部分集成分但玩法分通常不到一半；工程师用编码 agent 做的参考实现接近满分，说明差距在 agent 侧；同一游戏在 Unity/UE 上分数更高（检查更多），引擎间配置排名 Kendall τ 仅 0.14–0.62
  • 配套发布 Game Completion Boost 技能（需求驱动的试玩与修复），把三个模型的执行分提高 14.1–24.3 分

为什么值得看：想让 agent 在自家引擎里造内容，这份基准说明瓶颈不在「生成代码」，而在跨系统一致性（改了战斗不能弄坏重开）与验收方式：只有把验收做成真实输入试玩，指标才有意义。

中文摘要：游戏上线的前提是玩家能启动、打完、再回到存档，而这些都不是「编译成功」能保证的。作者提出 CEGame-Bench：第一个跨五个生产级引擎（Defold、Godot、Roblox Studio、Unity、Unreal Engine）的完整游戏创建长程基准，50 个任务都是「工作室交接」场景，agent 从空项目与一份设计文档出发，文档兼作契约，写清可检查规则与必需状态接口；评测由隐藏评测器用真实输入试玩完成。结果显示 agent 能拿到大部分集成分，但玩法分通常不到一半，只有 16% 的 run 能让游戏走到结局；工程师借助编码 agent 做出的参考实现却接近满分——说明 artifact-to-play 的落差在 agent 而非引擎。不同引擎下的配置排名几乎不一致，同一款游戏在 Unity 与 UE 上通常得分更高。作者同时发布 Game Completion Boost 技能，通过需求驱动的试玩与修复把执行分提高 14.1–24.3 分。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·AI原生（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

From Code to Playable Systems:
CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon
Game Creation Agents

Abstract

A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall’s τ0.14–0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1–24.3 points.

1 Introduction

In a game studio, a build ships only after QA plays it to the ending, quits, and finds the save intact. Coding agents are often shown on one-prompt browser games [(Jiang et al., 2026b)], which rarely test what makes a game complete: interdependent parts, where a combat fix must not break restart. We call the distance between a build and a playable game the artifact-to-play gap (Figure 1).

Beyond entertainment, Unity and Unreal Engine, the most demanding engines to drive, power industrial 3D applications [(La et al., 2026)] and embodied-AI simulators [(Zhong et al., 2025)] that coding agents have begun to build [(Kang et al., 2026)]; making games on them is a step toward building such worlds from specifications. Because studios choose an engine per project, a benchmark must span engines to distinguish game-making skill from fluency in one toolchain.

Existing benchmarks each cover one slice: scoped edits to Godot and Unreal projects [(Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026)], browser games [(Jiang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b)], Godot-to-Unity ports [(Chen et al., 2026c)], or whole games on a single engine [(Luo et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026)]. None asks an agent to turn an empty project into a complete game on several production engines, Unity and Unreal Engine included, or judges all engines by the same rules (Table 1).

We introduce Cross-Engine Game Bench (CEGame-Bench), which holds every engine to one execution-based standard. Its 50 tasks are studio handoffs, ten on each of five production engines, from script-centric Defold, Godot, and Roblox Studio to heavyweight Unity and Unreal Engine. In each task, the agent builds a complete game from an empty project and a design document in a fully logged run. The document is a natural-language contract of checkable rules and a required state interface, so one hidden evaluator accepts any implementation on any engine only by playing it with real input.

The gap is large. Autonomous agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum. The engine is a first-class variable: no two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall’s τ 0.14–0.62), and the same game scores higher on the heavyweight engine in five of six engine pairs, by up to 21.5 points, in line with its stricter checks before play. Nor does effort close the gap: nine in ten runs deliver before the time limit, and neither steps nor tokens track the score. These failures motivate Game Completion Boost (GCB), a lightweight agent skill that maps requirements to player checkpoints, compares state with visible outcomes, and replays affected paths after repair. On high-difficulty games from each track, GCB raises the execution-based F of three models under Codex CLI by 14.1–24.3 points and their overall score by 14.7–25.8.

We contribute (i) CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation on five production engines, with controlled engine variation; (ii) a contract-driven evaluation that turns a natural-language design document into executable checks, accepts a game only by play, and logs its construction; and (iii) a cross-engine study of six frontier models under four scaffolds, motivating reusable GCB.

2 Related Work

Long-horizon software and computer-use agents.

Repository benchmarks cover issue resolution [(Jimenez et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2026)], feature evolution [(Zhou et al., 2026; Le et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026)], and construction from specifications [(Ding et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026)]; coding agents [(Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025)] and computer-use benchmarks [(Xie et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Ai et al., 2026)] add tool use and long workflows. Most score only the final outcome, even though the scaffold alone shifts accuracy and cost [(Kapoor et al., 2026)]. Repository tasks, moreover, involve no engine serialization, player input, or runtime transitions; CEGame-Bench involves all three and logs every construction step alongside the score.

Game-development benchmarks.

Game benchmarks each cover one engine, the browser, or part of a game: multi-agent development [(Chen et al., 2023)], scoped edits [(Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026)], Godot [(Luo et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026)] or Unreal [(Yin et al., 2026)] projects, browser games [(Jiang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b)], generation and repair [(Chen et al., 2026b)], and 3D or cinematic content [(Yang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026)]. SWE-Game alone crosses engines, but its Unity port starts from existing Godot code [(Chen et al., 2026c)]. On Godot, JAMER finds that code agents raise compilation rates without improving runtime behavior [(Sun et al., 2026)]; CEGame-Bench has agents build complete games from empty projects on five engines, measures this gap through full player journeys, and re-issues contracts across engines without porting code.

Executable verification and playability.

Prior work checks artifacts against executable specifications or hidden contracts [(Jia et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026)], tests Unity scenes [(Liu and Tatar, 2026)], and studies GUI play and bug discovery [(Peng et al., 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026a)]. GameASG-Bench declares an evaluation interface for real-input checks [(Zhang et al., 2026b)] and GameCraft-Bench verifies games by replayed gameplay [(Luo et al., 2026)], each on a single runtime, while others still grade play with a multimodal judge [(Jiang et al., 2026b)]. CEGame-Bench carries a declared state interface across five runtimes, scores all but presentation by execution, and adds fresh-process reopening and mutant calibration.

3 Benchmark Design

CEGame-Bench turns the studio request ship this game into a long-horizon task anchored by one document: a game design document (GDD) written as a contract that specifies the game, requires it to expose its state, and yields the checks a hidden evaluator runs during play. One contract language and scorecard span five engines, so the engine is a controlled variable; every task is calibrated on a reference game and its broken variants, and every run is logged from first edit to delivery (Figure 2).

3.1 Engine Tracks

The benchmark includes ten tasks on each of five production engines, which differ in where a game lives (Appendix Table 5). On the script-centric Defold, Godot, and Roblox Studio, a game is mostly Lua, GDScript, or Luau code on a scene or instance tree. On the heavyweight Unity and Unreal Engine, much of it lives in imported assets and editor-serialized state behind an import and compile cycle that is slow but validates the game before it runs; Unreal Engine adds binary uasset files, C++ modules, and build targets. Everything else is fixed across tracks (Appendix 8): the 3/5/2 mix of easy, medium, and hard tasks, the starter and GDD structure, an engine-neutral prompt, the scorecard, and the 3600 s budget. Each track ranks configurations on its own games, and a swap experiment isolates the engine by re-issuing a game’s frozen contract on an engine of the other group.

3.2 Task Formulation

A task comprises (s₀,D,M,G,V). The agent receives a starter project s₀, the GDD D, and a tool manual M; the reference implementation G and evaluator V stay hidden. s₀ is an engine-native project that builds, runs, and bundles licensed assets but implements none of the game, M documents the engine’s build, editor-automation, and capture tools, and D is a fifteen-section GDD from pitch and controls to persistence and acceptance. From these alone, the agent works as a studio engineer would: reading documentation, authoring assets and scripts, compiling, playing, and repairing.

The GDD is a contract.

The normative core of D is an implementation-independent contract

C=(ℕ,Sₐ,Sᵣ (world), A,B,T (rules), I,ℙ,Φ (guarantees)),

whose symbols denote entities, authored and runtime state, player actions, branches, temporal rules, invariants, persistence requirements, and the state interface. D fixes what the player experiences (levels, rules, and constants) and the interface through which the game is observed, and leaves class hierarchy, scene organization, and asset layout free. Every requirement in D becomes one or more leaf checks of V, so the document that specifies the game also defines its rubric. In Driftfolk Chronicle, for example, “a dash spends one charge” becomes a check on player.charges.

Observability is part of the task.

Just as a QA build exposes its state to testers, every game must expose a small state interface Φ: a read accessor OmniState.Get(key) over task-specific keys and two lifecycle commands, OmniFlow.LoadState(id) and OmniFlow.Restart(), built on the game’s own loading path. Φ lets the evaluator observe a game without taking its word: it reads and enters declared states but never acts for the player, every action arrives as real input, and every reading is cross-checked against a frame, a log line, or a second key it constrains. Because hidden probes vary inputs, timing, and rejected actions, a reading stays correct only if the game computes it from play, so an interface that reports constants or scripted values fails its own checks (Appendix 9). With Φ, one evaluator tests any implementation on all five engines without reading its code.

3.3 Evaluation and Scoring

V accepts a game the way QA does, by playing it. Static probes check import, compilation, the entry scene, serialized references, and the asset manifest. Dynamic probes start from a real entry point or a state entered through Φ, send real input through the engine’s input layer, and assert on Φ snapshots, logs, and frames after each action, including rejected actions, restart, and fresh-process reopening. Entering later states directly keeps failures local: a level that never loads costs only its own leaves. A player journey then plays the whole game with public controls alone, executing each contract-level step as a closed-loop policy steered by Φ readings, so differently built games complete the same path. Visual probes score captures at reference states with a vision–language model that agrees with human raters at Spearman ρ=0.81.

A task decomposes into 47.2 atomic leaf checks on average, in six dimensions (Appendix 11): integration (D1), completeness (D2), mechanics (D3), lifecycle (D4), feedback (D5), and presentation (D6). D1–D5 are scored by execution alone and only D6 by model judgment (Appendix 10). Each leaf ℓ has a weight w_ℓ∈{1,2,3} (minor, major, critical) and belongs to a familyf of leaves expressing the same obligation. With L_f the judged leaves of f and y_ℓ the credit of ℓ, 1 for a pass and 0 for a failure (a D6 leaf takes the judge’s normalized rating),

π_f=(∑_ℓ∈L_fw_ℓy_ℓ)/(∑_ℓ∈L_fw_ℓ), S_d=W_d∑_f∈F_dβ_d,fπ_f,

where (W₁,…,W₆)=(10,30,20,20,10,10). Family budgets β_d,f sum to one per dimension and stay fixed when a task moves between engines, so an obligation weighs the same however many leaves it takes on a track. The functional score F=∑_d=1⁵S_d (out of 90) is determined entirely by execution, and its D2–D5 part (out of 80) gives the gameplay points, earned only by a game that works under play. The overall score O=F+S̃₆ (out of 100) takes S̃₆=S₆ when the player journey succeeds and \min(S₆,W₆/2) otherwise, so presentation never outweighs play.

A leaf fails only on evidence: the evaluator observes the violation, or the submission itself blocks a required state, as a missing Φ blocks every leaf that reads it. Evaluator faults are retried through an alternate route and, if unresolved, leave the denominator; these exclusions remove at most 2.9% of leaf weight on any engine. Beyond the scorecard, each run yields three binary flags: a completed journey (J), state that survives restart and reopening (Λ), and a fully solved game, in which both hold and every critical leaf passes. Each run also keeps a full trace of every tool call, build, and play session with its tokens and time, so the benchmark reports what each game cost to build alongside its score.

3.4 Dataset Construction and Statistics

Of the 50 tasks, 33 are adapted from permissively licensed open-source games and 17 are original designs. Each passes four stages (Appendix 12). (i) Specification: two annotators draft and cross-check the GDD in player-visible terms, and a third adjudicates and freezes C. (ii) Independent build: engineers working with coding agents build G from the frozen starter in 6–14 engineer-hours, while V is written from C alone, without access to G. (iii) Acceptance by play: V plays G, an equivalent implementation G^′ with a deliberately different structure, the untouched starter s₀, and four mutants that break compilation, feedback, a transition, or persistence, exactly as it later plays submissions. (iv) Calibration gate: the task is frozen and released only if, on O, G scores at least 90, G^′ lands within 2.5 points of G, s₀ scores at most 6, and every mutant is detected while moving the score by at most 2.0 points outside its dependency subgraph, so a fault may block what depends on it but nothing else; otherwise it is re-authored.

The released references anchor the scale. They average 96.4 on O (minimum 92.5), the equivalence gap averages 2.0, starters score 4.1, all 200 mutants are caught, and repeated evaluations of one artifact differ by at most 1.8 points. Since engineers built each reference with coding agents, these scores mark what agents reach under human direction, the bar for autonomous agents.

Every document is newly written, and adapted games are renamed and re-parameterized (Appendix 12). Upon publication we release the starters, design documents, tool manuals, the evaluator and its adapters, leaf schemas, and run traces, all carrying a canary string; references, equivalent implementations, and mutants stay private.

The tasks span 2D, 2.5D, and 3D puzzle, action, RPG, simulation, and narrative games, with difficulty tiers annotated on four axes (Appendix 13). A task averages 2.6 scenes, 14.4 entities, and a 38.6-step player journey; hard tasks average 71 leaf checks and a 76-step journey.

4 Game Completion Boost

Section 5.2 locates failures in completeness, mechanics, and lifecycle, and Appendix 18 shows unreachable goals, rules that contradict the scene, and cropped or crowded views. Game Completion Boost (GCB) targets these failures by organizing the agent’s playtesting and repair (Figure 3), combining specification-derived checks [(Jia et al., 2026)], file-bound verification records, and reflective repair [(Shinn et al., 2023)].

(1) Requirement-directed checkpoints.

The agent maps public requirements, branches, and lifecycle events to checkpoints with prerequisites, relevant files, and required evidence, and checks with public controls that required states are reachable. A helper schedules checkpoints whose prerequisites pass and recommends repairing failures, gathering missing observations, or replaying stale records.

(2) Action-linked state–view evidence.

For visible transitions, the agent compares before/after images with available state or logs from the same input and session, checking for disagreements such as a trap firing on visibly safe floor. Static image checks cover camera framing and UI overlap. Behavior and its visible presentation both drive repair.

(3) Replay and guarded repair.

After an edit, GCB invalidates checks tied to changed files and their dependents; shared or unmapped changes invalidate all checks, following regression test selection [(Gligoric et al., 2015)]. Before repair, GCB saves the project and protects the passed checkpoints. It retains a candidate only after the target and all protected checks pass again; an observed regression triggers rollback. The agent records a diagnosis to guide its next attempt. Every edit clears final acceptance, requiring a complete journey and any specified fresh-process reopen.

The released GCB consists of fixed, task-agnostic instructions and Python helpers. The agent performs and interprets every check from public inputs within the task budget, and the hidden evaluator alone scores the submitted game (Appendix 14).

5 Experiments

Evaluations of game creation commonly take two shortcuts: they treat a project that builds as a working game, and they measure one engine as if it stood for all. We test both, measure what each game costs to build, and evaluate GCB across engine tracks.

5.1 Setup

We evaluate seven configurations pairing six frontier models from four providers with four scaffolds. Codex CLI runs GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, so contrasts within it isolate the model; DeepSeek-V4-Pro also runs under DeepSeek Harness, isolating the scaffold; and Claude Opus 5 and Kimi K3 run in their providers’ Claude Code and Kimi Code.

In the main study, each game–configuration pair is run three times from the frozen starter of its task, with the GDD, tool manual, 3600 s budget, engine version, tool catalog, model, and reasoning setting fixed (Appendix 15); the native study comprises 1,050 runs. We report D1–D6, F, and O averaged over the three runs, weighting the games of a track equally, and compare configurations on F, which execution alone determines. The standard deviation of F across the three runs of a pair averages 8.4 points, so run-to-run noise moves an engine cell by about 1.5 points.

5.2 Buildable Is Not Playable

Configurations reliably deliver projects that import, compile, and load their entry scene: integration (D1) averages 8.9 to 9.7 of 10 points on every engine (Table 2). Whether the game then works is another matter: three in four cells earn under half of the 80 gameplay points (D2–D5), and only GPT-6 Astra clears that bar on every engine. The evaluator’s player journey reaches the ending in only 16% of runs, with 4% fully solved. Claude Code on Roblox Studio, the median cell in gameplay, earns 9.0 of 10 integration points but only a third of the gameplay points. Because integration barely varies, the spread of F is almost entirely a spread in gameplay; a build check would rank most configurations as near-equals, whereas play separates them by tens of points. Nor is the state interface the obstacle: Φ answers the handshake in 94% of delivered projects. Yet these contracts are within reach of the same technology under human direction: the references that engineers built with coding agents are all solved and average 87.3 of 90 on F (96.4 of 100 on O), against 65.0 for the best autonomous configuration and at most 41.0 for the other six. The gap also varies by track: the share of gameplay points runs from 23% on Godot to 57% on Unity, so the same build success stands for very different amounts of playable game.

The scorecard also shows where games fail, and the answer shifts with capability (Appendix Table 18). We split the cells into thirds by F and find, in each, the gameplay dimension that is weakest relative to its weight. In the lowest third it is most often completeness (D2): much of the game is never built. In the middle third it is mechanics (D3): the game exists, but its rules break under play. In the top third it is lifecycle (D4), ahead of feedback (D5) and mechanics: the game plays, but breaks across transitions, restarts, or reopening, or fails to show the player what happened. Stronger agents thus fail at later stages, a progression that a single pass/fail outcome hides and that motivates replaying complete journeys and checking visible responses during play.

5.3 The Engine Is a First-Class Variable

Every engine separates configurations widely, but not equally and not in the same order. The spread of F across configurations ranges from 29.0 points on Unity to 56.9 on Defold, and no two engines rank the configurations alike: Kendall’s τ between engines ranges from 0.14 to 0.62 (Appendix Table 16). Codex CLI with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, for instance, ranks second of seven on Roblox Studio and last on Unreal Engine. GPT-6 Astra, the strongest configuration, leads by 31.5 points on Unreal Engine and 23.1 on Roblox Studio but by only 6.5 on Unity. An engine track can thus amplify a capability difference that another hides, and a leaderboard built on one engine inherits its bias.

Changing one factor at a time shows what transfers (Appendix Table 18). Within the GPT family the order holds on every engine: GPT-6 Astra leads GPT-5.6 Sol by 6.5 to 41.4 points, and Sol leads GPT-5.6 Terra by 5.1 to 22.5. Across families it does not: under Codex CLI, DeepSeek-V4-Pro trails Sol by 26.7 points on Defold yet leads it by 12.7 on Godot. The scaffold can matter as much as the model: with DeepSeek-V4-Pro fixed, moving from Codex CLI to DeepSeek Harness gains 19.8 points on Unreal Engine but loses 21.9 on Roblox Studio. A single-engine leaderboard therefore ranks configurations for that engine alone.

Same game, different engine.

The swap experiment holds the game fixed and changes only the engine: for each of the six heavyweight–script-centric pairs, the five hardest games of each engine are rebuilt on the other engine, which limits ceiling effects on the heavyweight engines (Appendix 17). The heavyweight engine wins five of the six pairs (Table 3): Unity leads Defold and Godot by 11.6 and 10.4 points, Unreal Engine leads Defold, Godot, and Roblox Studio by 21.2, 21.5, and 8.5, and only Unity against Roblox Studio reverses, by 4.3. Pooling both swap directions offsets any advantage a game draws from its native engine, and with ten games per pair, each of the five leads exceeds its standard deviation over games, hence more than three standard errors.

The ordering matches how much an engine checks before play. Unity and Unreal Engine compile their code, validate serialized scenes and references, and ship test frameworks an agent can drive, so many errors surface as diagnostics during construction; the advantage is widest against Defold and Godot, whose dynamically typed scripts fail only at run time, and narrowest against Roblox Studio, whose editor also analyzes scripts. The native tracks agree. Kimi Code never plays or views its game (Appendix Table 19): on Defold it gets no game running, while on Unity it reaches F=55.7, a gap of 49.9 points against 6.5 to 21.7 for the other configurations across both tracks. An agent that never runs its game depends entirely on checks before play. Heavyweight engines are harder to drive but easier to check.

How much they help still varies by configuration: on one swapped game the gain ranges from 7.0 to 77.9 points, and on another the two scaffolds sharing DeepSeek-V4-Pro trade places (Appendix 17). Engine difficulty is therefore no fixed offset that could be calibrated away.

5.4 Effort Does Not Buy Play

Each construction trace shows what a game cost to build (Figure 4). The checks that favor heavyweight engines are paid for in time: Unreal Engine runs reach the highest step and token counts, averaging up to 295 workflow steps and 65M tokens per configuration, because every build–play–repair iteration passes through a long compile and import cycle.
