At the other end, Godot’s headless checks return short diagnostics, so the context resent with every call grows slowly, and many Godot runs, especially early stoppers, stay under 0.3M tokens.

The time budget rarely binds. About nine in ten runs deliver before the 3600 s limit, and those that reach it stall or loop, averaging only 16.3 points of F. Most runs thus end when the agent judges its game finished, so the 6–14 engineer-hours behind each reference do not explain the gap. That judgment is rarely tested by play: playing and viewing the game take at most 13.3% of any configuration’s steps. Even at that maximum, GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-V4-Pro under Codex CLI differ by 29.9 points, so play frequency alone does not decide F. Nor do steps or tokens track F: games of similar cost score anywhere from near zero to 80, and no game whose runs average more than 200 steps reaches 40 points. The best games sit toward the upper left, where GPT-6 Astra reaches its top scores on moderate budgets, so capability shows up as efficiency, not persistence.

5.5 Effect of Game Completion Boost

We evaluate GCB under Codex CLI with three models on 15 high-difficulty games, three per engine track, fixed before any GCB run (Appendices 13 and 14). Each paired comparison holds the task, native prompt, engine-access and image tools, and budget fixed, and the baseline is the strongest of a game’s three native runs by O, so it sits at or above the game’s three-run mean used in Table 2.

GCB improves F and O for every model (Table 4), raising mean F by 14.1–24.3 points and mean O by 14.7–25.8; Terra more than triples its F. Each gains most in the bottleneck that Section 5.2 finds at its score level. DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the strongest baseline here, gains most in lifecycle (D4, +8.6), while Sol and Terra gain most in completeness and mechanics (D2/D3, +5.3/+4.3 and +8.0/+5.3). D6 gains 0.5–1.5 points and D1 changes by -0.7 to +3.3, so most of the gain is gameplay.

6 Conclusion

CEGame-Bench evaluates complete-game creation on five production engines through real-input play. Agents usually deliver projects that build yet earn under half the gameplay points, and most stop before the time limit, whereas engineers directing coding agents reach near the maximum. No two engines rank configurations alike, and the same game usually scores higher on the heavyweight engines, which are harder to drive but easier to check. GCB turns these findings into a playtest-and-repair workflow that improves every evaluated model. For evaluation practice, the results favor scoring games by play, reporting each engine separately, and logging build cost. The shared evaluation protocol and execution traces support comparisons of functional performance across engine tracks and agent configurations. Game creation thus tests whether an agent can inspect and repair its own work before declaring it done, a capability needed to build simulated worlds from specifications.

Limitations

CEGame-Bench evaluates single-player games built offline from a written design document. It measures whether a game meets its specification and leaves player enjoyment, online multiplayer, live services, and design without a specification outside its scope. The five engines span script-centric and heavyweight production engines; other engines and web frameworks can join as new tracks under the same contract language. Engine and editor versions are frozen, so newer releases enter as new benchmark versions rather than shifting existing scores. GCB is evaluated under one scaffold with three models, excluding GPT-6 Astra, on high-difficulty games from each track; its effect under other scaffolds and on the strongest model remains to be measured. The visual judge shares its model with one evaluated configuration, so configurations are compared on F, which excludes D6. Built by engineers working with coding agents, the references mark what human-directed agents reach rather than unaided human skill. A swap changes the starter and tool manual with the engine, so its effect covers the whole toolchain, not the engine core alone. Finally, the heavyweight tracks need full editors and build toolchains, and one Unreal Engine run can consume tens of millions of tokens, so a complete evaluation is costlier than a browser-based benchmark. This cost also bounds the scale: with ten tasks per engine, seven configurations, and swaps on the five hardest games of each track, engine-level rankings and swap effects carry wide spreads, which we report.

Ethical Considerations

All tasks are adapted from permissively licensed open-source games or written from scratch; adapted games are renamed and re-parameterized, and bundled art and audio are used under their licenses with attribution. The six annotators and engineers who built the tasks were compensated in accordance with applicable labor laws and regulations. Every engine runs locally and no game is published online, so the benchmark involves no personal or player data. As with other code-generating agents, game-creation agents could be misused to clone commercial games; the release contains only newly written documents, licensed assets, and our own evaluator and run traces, and no material from commercial games.

（参考文献见原文。）

7 Engine Tracks and Toolchains

Each track is pinned to the engine build of Table 5, one editor build, and one command-line entry point, and a run that resolves any other version is discarded. Unity tasks use the 2D and 3D core packages and no Asset Store content; Unreal Engine tasks use its C++ toolchain and also permit Blueprint; Godot tasks use GDScript only; and Defold tasks use the stock build server. Roblox Studio submissions are .rbxl place files play-tested in local Studio sessions and never published to a live service. Starters bundle CC0 or CC-BY art and audio, adapted source games are licensed under MIT, Apache-2.0, CC0, or zlib, and per-task attribution ships with the release.

Checks before play.

The tracks differ in how much an engine checks a game before it runs, and the tool manual exposes each engine’s own checks to the agent (Table 5, fifth column). On Unity and Unreal Engine, C# and C++ compilation rejects type and reference errors, the editor validates serialized scenes and assets, and built-in test frameworks run scripted checks inside the engine. Roblox Studio analyzes Luau scripts in the editor. Godot parses GDScript on load, and Defold validates resources and Lua syntax at build time; beyond that, errors in their dynamically typed scripts surface only when the game runs. These checks are the diagnostics an agent can act on before it plays its own game.

Starter and tool manual.

Each starter s₀ opens, builds, and runs on its locked version but implements none of the game. It provides an empty entry scene, the task’s licensed art and audio, naming tables for scenes, entry points, and state keys, and the public smoke checks of Appendix 9. The tool manual M documents command-line build and headless run, editor automation, import and packaging, the checks above, log locations, and tools for capturing and inspecting a running game. Starters and manuals follow a common section structure across tracks (Appendix 8).

8 Cross-Engine Comparability

A Defold score and an Unreal Engine score are comparable only if the scale, not the difficulty, is held fixed. Five controls fix the scale and leave the engine as the variable.

  • 1.

    One contract language. Every track instantiates the same contract symbols and six dimensions, and a task keeps its leaf families on every engine; only the evidence route through the engine adapter differs.

  • 2.

    Fixed family budgets. Within a dimension, budgets β_d,f allocate weight to families and stay fixed across engines, so an obligation weighs the same whether it takes twelve leaves on Unreal Engine or three on Defold.

  • 3.

    Matched intended difficulty. Every track has the same 3/5/2 easy/medium/hard composition under the four-axis annotation of Appendix 13.

  • 4.

    Matched ceilings. A task enters any track only if its reference implementation scores at least 90 on O, and the released references score at least 92.5 on every track (Appendix 12), so the full scale is reachable everywhere and a low track mean reflects the agents.

  • 5.

    Matched inputs and budgets. Starter structure, GDD structure, smoke checks, tool-manual sections, and the 3600 s budget are identical across tracks, and the task prompt (Appendix 16) contains no engine-specific hints.

    • The controls preserve each engine’s scene model, asset pipeline, build cycle, and checks before play (Table 5). These set both what each build–play–repair iteration costs and how many errors surface before the game runs, and they are what the benchmark measures. Since tracks have their own games, results are reported per track, and the cross-group swaps of Appendix 17 isolate the engine on a fixed game.

    9 Game Design Document and State Interface

    This appendix details the two public documents of Section 3.2 that define a task for the agent: the GDD and the state interface it requires.

    Document structure.

    Every task uses the same fifteen GDD sections to make the specification’s scope explicit. Table 6 maps each section to the contract symbol it populates and to the dimensions its leaf checks score.

    From requirement to leaf.

    Each sentence of the normative sections becomes one or more leaf checks, written against the contract rather than any implementation. Table 7 traces an excerpt of Driftfolk Chronicle. A requirement is checked on its positive branch and, where the GDD implies one, on its rejected branch: the dash is tested both when it should fire and when it should not. Every assertion reads only declared Φ keys, HUD elements, logs, or frames, so the same rows apply to any implementation on any engine, and only the adapter that sends the input and collects the evidence changes.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：「能 build」不等于「能玩」：50 个任务横跨 Defold/Godot/Roblox/Unity/UE，隐藏评测器只认真实输入试玩，agent 的游戏仅 16% 能走到结局。

要点：

  • 50 个任务，每个引擎 10 个，agent 从空项目 + 设计文档起步；设计文档同时是契约，规定可检查规则与必需的状态接口
  • 单次 run 平均最多 295 步、6500 万 token；隐藏评测器不编译不看代码，只用真实输入把游戏从头玩到结局、退出、再确认存档
  • 四个 scaffold 下 agent 拿到大部分集成分但玩法分通常不到一半；工程师用编码 agent 做的参考实现接近满分，说明差距在 agent 侧；同一游戏在 Unity/UE 上分数更高（检查更多），引擎间配置排名 Kendall τ 仅 0.14–0.62
  • 配套发布 Game Completion Boost 技能（需求驱动的试玩与修复），把三个模型的执行分提高 14.1–24.3 分

为什么值得看：想让 agent 在自家引擎里造内容，这份基准说明瓶颈不在「生成代码」，而在跨系统一致性（改了战斗不能弄坏重开）与验收方式：只有把验收做成真实输入试玩，指标才有意义。

中文摘要：游戏上线的前提是玩家能启动、打完、再回到存档，而这些都不是「编译成功」能保证的。作者提出 CEGame-Bench：第一个跨五个生产级引擎（Defold、Godot、Roblox Studio、Unity、Unreal Engine）的完整游戏创建长程基准，50 个任务都是「工作室交接」场景，agent 从空项目与一份设计文档出发，文档兼作契约，写清可检查规则与必需状态接口；评测由隐藏评测器用真实输入试玩完成。结果显示 agent 能拿到大部分集成分，但玩法分通常不到一半，只有 16% 的 run 能让游戏走到结局；工程师借助编码 agent 做出的参考实现却接近满分——说明 artifact-to-play 的落差在 agent 而非引擎。不同引擎下的配置排名几乎不一致，同一款游戏在 Unity 与 UE 上通常得分更高。作者同时发布 Game Completion Boost 技能，通过需求驱动的试玩与修复把执行分提高 14.1–24.3 分。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·AI原生（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

From Code to Playable Systems:
CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon
Game Creation Agents

Abstract

A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall’s τ0.14–0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1–24.3 points.

1 Introduction

In a game studio, a build ships only after QA plays it to the ending, quits, and finds the save intact. Coding agents are often shown on one-prompt browser games [(Jiang et al., 2026b)], which rarely test what makes a game complete: interdependent parts, where a combat fix must not break restart. We call the distance between a build and a playable game the artifact-to-play gap (Figure 1).

Beyond entertainment, Unity and Unreal Engine, the most demanding engines to drive, power industrial 3D applications [(La et al., 2026)] and embodied-AI simulators [(Zhong et al., 2025)] that coding agents have begun to build [(Kang et al., 2026)]; making games on them is a step toward building such worlds from specifications. Because studios choose an engine per project, a benchmark must span engines to distinguish game-making skill from fluency in one toolchain.

Existing benchmarks each cover one slice: scoped edits to Godot and Unreal projects [(Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026)], browser games [(Jiang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b)], Godot-to-Unity ports [(Chen et al., 2026c)], or whole games on a single engine [(Luo et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026)]. None asks an agent to turn an empty project into a complete game on several production engines, Unity and Unreal Engine included, or judges all engines by the same rules (Table 1).

We introduce Cross-Engine Game Bench (CEGame-Bench), which holds every engine to one execution-based standard. Its 50 tasks are studio handoffs, ten on each of five production engines, from script-centric Defold, Godot, and Roblox Studio to heavyweight Unity and Unreal Engine. In each task, the agent builds a complete game from an empty project and a design document in a fully logged run. The document is a natural-language contract of checkable rules and a required state interface, so one hidden evaluator accepts any implementation on any engine only by playing it with real input.

The gap is large. Autonomous agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum. The engine is a first-class variable: no two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall’s τ 0.14–0.62), and the same game scores higher on the heavyweight engine in five of six engine pairs, by up to 21.5 points, in line with its stricter checks before play. Nor does effort close the gap: nine in ten runs deliver before the time limit, and neither steps nor tokens track the score. These failures motivate Game Completion Boost (GCB), a lightweight agent skill that maps requirements to player checkpoints, compares state with visible outcomes, and replays affected paths after repair. On high-difficulty games from each track, GCB raises the execution-based F of three models under Codex CLI by 14.1–24.3 points and their overall score by 14.7–25.8.

We contribute (i) CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation on five production engines, with controlled engine variation; (ii) a contract-driven evaluation that turns a natural-language design document into executable checks, accepts a game only by play, and logs its construction; and (iii) a cross-engine study of six frontier models under four scaffolds, motivating reusable GCB.

2 Related Work

Long-horizon software and computer-use agents.

Repository benchmarks cover issue resolution [(Jimenez et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2026)], feature evolution [(Zhou et al., 2026; Le et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026)], and construction from specifications [(Ding et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026)]; coding agents [(Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2025)] and computer-use benchmarks [(Xie et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Ai et al., 2026)] add tool use and long workflows. Most score only the final outcome, even though the scaffold alone shifts accuracy and cost [(Kapoor et al., 2026)]. Repository tasks, moreover, involve no engine serialization, player input, or runtime transitions; CEGame-Bench involves all three and logs every construction step alongside the score.

Game-development benchmarks.

Game benchmarks each cover one engine, the browser, or part of a game: multi-agent development [(Chen et al., 2023)], scoped edits [(Chi et al., 2026; La et al., 2026)], Godot [(Luo et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026)] or Unreal [(Yin et al., 2026)] projects, browser games [(Jiang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b)], generation and repair [(Chen et al., 2026b)], and 3D or cinematic content [(Yang et al., 2026; He et al., 2026)]. SWE-Game alone crosses engines, but its Unity port starts from existing Godot code [(Chen et al., 2026c)]. On Godot, JAMER finds that code agents raise compilation rates without improving runtime behavior [(Sun et al., 2026)]; CEGame-Bench has agents build complete games from empty projects on five engines, measures this gap through full player journeys, and re-issues contracts across engines without porting code.

Executable verification and playability.

Prior work checks artifacts against executable specifications or hidden contracts [(Jia et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026)], tests Unity scenes [(Liu and Tatar, 2026)], and studies GUI play and bug discovery [(Peng et al., 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026a)]. GameASG-Bench declares an evaluation interface for real-input checks [(Zhang et al., 2026b)] and GameCraft-Bench verifies games by replayed gameplay [(Luo et al., 2026)], each on a single runtime, while others still grade play with a multimodal judge [(Jiang et al., 2026b)]. CEGame-Bench carries a declared state interface across five runtimes, scores all but presentation by execution, and adds fresh-process reopening and mutant calibration.

3 Benchmark Design

CEGame-Bench turns the studio request ship this game into a long-horizon task anchored by one document: a game design document (GDD) written as a contract that specifies the game, requires it to expose its state, and yields the checks a hidden evaluator runs during play. One contract language and scorecard span five engines, so the engine is a controlled variable; every task is calibrated on a reference game and its broken variants, and every run is logged from first edit to delivery (Figure 2).

3.1 Engine Tracks

The benchmark includes ten tasks on each of five production engines, which differ in where a game lives (Appendix Table 5). On the script-centric Defold, Godot, and Roblox Studio, a game is mostly Lua, GDScript, or Luau code on a scene or instance tree. On the heavyweight Unity and Unreal Engine, much of it lives in imported assets and editor-serialized state behind an import and compile cycle that is slow but validates the game before it runs; Unreal Engine adds binary uasset files, C++ modules, and build targets. Everything else is fixed across tracks (Appendix 8): the 3/5/2 mix of easy, medium, and hard tasks, the starter and GDD structure, an engine-neutral prompt, the scorecard, and the 3600 s budget. Each track ranks configurations on its own games, and a swap experiment isolates the engine by re-issuing a game’s frozen contract on an engine of the other group.

3.2 Task Formulation

A task comprises (s₀,D,M,G,V). The agent receives a starter project s₀, the GDD D, and a tool manual M; the reference implementation G and evaluator V stay hidden. s₀ is an engine-native project that builds, runs, and bundles licensed assets but implements none of the game, M documents the engine’s build, editor-automation, and capture tools, and D is a fifteen-section GDD from pitch and controls to persistence and acceptance. From these alone, the agent works as a studio engineer would: reading documentation, authoring assets and scripts, compiling, playing, and repairing.

The GDD is a contract.

The normative core of D is an implementation-independent contract

C=(ℕ,Sₐ,Sᵣ (world), A,B,T (rules), I,ℙ,Φ (guarantees)),

whose symbols denote entities, authored and runtime state, player actions, branches, temporal rules, invariants, persistence requirements, and the state interface. D fixes what the player experiences (levels, rules, and constants) and the interface through which the game is observed, and leaves class hierarchy, scene organization, and asset layout free. Every requirement in D becomes one or more leaf checks of V, so the document that specifies the game also defines its rubric. In Driftfolk Chronicle, for example, “a dash spends one charge” becomes a check on player.charges.

Observability is part of the task.

Just as a QA build exposes its state to testers, every game must expose a small state interface Φ: a read accessor OmniState.Get(key) over task-specific keys and two lifecycle commands, OmniFlow.LoadState(id) and OmniFlow.Restart(), built on the game’s own loading path. Φ lets the evaluator observe a game without taking its word: it reads and enters declared states but never acts for the player, every action arrives as real input, and every reading is cross-checked against a frame, a log line, or a second key it constrains. Because hidden probes vary inputs, timing, and rejected actions, a reading stays correct only if the game computes it from play, so an interface that reports constants or scripted values fails its own checks (Appendix 9). With Φ, one evaluator tests any implementation on all five engines without reading its code.

3.3 Evaluation and Scoring

V accepts a game the way QA does, by playing it. Static probes check import, compilation, the entry scene, serialized references, and the asset manifest. Dynamic probes start from a real entry point or a state entered through Φ, send real input through the engine’s input layer, and assert on Φ snapshots, logs, and frames after each action, including rejected actions, restart, and fresh-process reopening. Entering later states directly keeps failures local: a level that never loads costs only its own leaves. A player journey then plays the whole game with public controls alone, executing each contract-level step as a closed-loop policy steered by Φ readings, so differently built games complete the same path. Visual probes score captures at reference states with a vision–language model that agrees with human raters at Spearman ρ=0.81.

A task decomposes into 47.2 atomic leaf checks on average, in six dimensions (Appendix 11): integration (D1), completeness (D2), mechanics (D3), lifecycle (D4), feedback (D5), and presentation (D6). D1–D5 are scored by execution alone and only D6 by model judgment (Appendix 10). Each leaf ℓ has a weight w_ℓ∈{1,2,3} (minor, major, critical) and belongs to a familyf of leaves expressing the same obligation. With L_f the judged leaves of f and y_ℓ the credit of ℓ, 1 for a pass and 0 for a failure (a D6 leaf takes the judge’s normalized rating),

π_f=(∑_ℓ∈L_fw_ℓy_ℓ)/(∑_ℓ∈L_fw_ℓ), S_d=W_d∑_f∈F_dβ_d,fπ_f,

where (W₁,…,W₆)=(10,30,20,20,10,10). Family budgets β_d,f sum to one per dimension and stay fixed when a task moves between engines, so an obligation weighs the same however many leaves it takes on a track. The functional score F=∑_d=1⁵S_d (out of 90) is determined entirely by execution, and its D2–D5 part (out of 80) gives the gameplay points, earned only by a game that works under play. The overall score O=F+S̃₆ (out of 100) takes S̃₆=S₆ when the player journey succeeds and \min(S₆,W₆/2) otherwise, so presentation never outweighs play.

A leaf fails only on evidence: the evaluator observes the violation, or the submission itself blocks a required state, as a missing Φ blocks every leaf that reads it. Evaluator faults are retried through an alternate route and, if unresolved, leave the denominator; these exclusions remove at most 2.9% of leaf weight on any engine. Beyond the scorecard, each run yields three binary flags: a completed journey (J), state that survives restart and reopening (Λ), and a fully solved game, in which both hold and every critical leaf passes. Each run also keeps a full trace of every tool call, build, and play session with its tokens and time, so the benchmark reports what each game cost to build alongside its score.

3.4 Dataset Construction and Statistics

Of the 50 tasks, 33 are adapted from permissively licensed open-source games and 17 are original designs. Each passes four stages (Appendix 12). (i) Specification: two annotators draft and cross-check the GDD in player-visible terms, and a third adjudicates and freezes C. (ii) Independent build: engineers working with coding agents build G from the frozen starter in 6–14 engineer-hours, while V is written from C alone, without access to G. (iii) Acceptance by play: V plays G, an equivalent implementation G^′ with a deliberately different structure, the untouched starter s₀, and four mutants that break compilation, feedback, a transition, or persistence, exactly as it later plays submissions. (iv) Calibration gate: the task is frozen and released only if, on O, G scores at least 90, G^′ lands within 2.5 points of G, s₀ scores at most 6, and every mutant is detected while moving the score by at most 2.0 points outside its dependency subgraph, so a fault may block what depends on it but nothing else; otherwise it is re-authored.

The released references anchor the scale. They average 96.4 on O (minimum 92.5), the equivalence gap averages 2.0, starters score 4.1, all 200 mutants are caught, and repeated evaluations of one artifact differ by at most 1.8 points. Since engineers built each reference with coding agents, these scores mark what agents reach under human direction, the bar for autonomous agents.

Every document is newly written, and adapted games are renamed and re-parameterized (Appendix 12). Upon publication we release the starters, design documents, tool manuals, the evaluator and its adapters, leaf schemas, and run traces, all carrying a canary string; references, equivalent implementations, and mutants stay private.

The tasks span 2D, 2.5D, and 3D puzzle, action, RPG, simulation, and narrative games, with difficulty tiers annotated on four axes (Appendix 13). A task averages 2.6 scenes, 14.4 entities, and a 38.6-step player journey; hard tasks average 71 leaf checks and a 76-step journey.

4 Game Completion Boost

Section 5.2 locates failures in completeness, mechanics, and lifecycle, and Appendix 18 shows unreachable goals, rules that contradict the scene, and cropped or crowded views. Game Completion Boost (GCB) targets these failures by organizing the agent’s playtesting and repair (Figure 3), combining specification-derived checks [(Jia et al., 2026)], file-bound verification records, and reflective repair [(Shinn et al., 2023)].

(1) Requirement-directed checkpoints.

The agent maps public requirements, branches, and lifecycle events to checkpoints with prerequisites, relevant files, and required evidence, and checks with public controls that required states are reachable. A helper schedules checkpoints whose prerequisites pass and recommends repairing failures, gathering missing observations, or replaying stale records.

(2) Action-linked state–view evidence.

For visible transitions, the agent compares before/after images with available state or logs from the same input and session, checking for disagreements such as a trap firing on visibly safe floor. Static image checks cover camera framing and UI overlap. Behavior and its visible presentation both drive repair.

(3) Replay and guarded repair.

After an edit, GCB invalidates checks tied to changed files and their dependents; shared or unmapped changes invalidate all checks, following regression test selection [(Gligoric et al., 2015)]. Before repair, GCB saves the project and protects the passed checkpoints. It retains a candidate only after the target and all protected checks pass again; an observed regression triggers rollback. The agent records a diagnosis to guide its next attempt. Every edit clears final acceptance, requiring a complete journey and any specified fresh-process reopen.

The released GCB consists of fixed, task-agnostic instructions and Python helpers. The agent performs and interprets every check from public inputs within the task budget, and the hidden evaluator alone scores the submitted game (Appendix 14).

5 Experiments

Evaluations of game creation commonly take two shortcuts: they treat a project that builds as a working game, and they measure one engine as if it stood for all. We test both, measure what each game costs to build, and evaluate GCB across engine tracks.

5.1 Setup

We evaluate seven configurations pairing six frontier models from four providers with four scaffolds. Codex CLI runs GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, so contrasts within it isolate the model; DeepSeek-V4-Pro also runs under DeepSeek Harness, isolating the scaffold; and Claude Opus 5 and Kimi K3 run in their providers’ Claude Code and Kimi Code.

In the main study, each game–configuration pair is run three times from the frozen starter of its task, with the GDD, tool manual, 3600 s budget, engine version, tool catalog, model, and reasoning setting fixed (Appendix 15); the native study comprises 1,050 runs. We report D1–D6, F, and O averaged over the three runs, weighting the games of a track equally, and compare configurations on F, which execution alone determines. The standard deviation of F across the three runs of a pair averages 8.4 points, so run-to-run noise moves an engine cell by about 1.5 points.

5.2 Buildable Is Not Playable

Configurations reliably deliver projects that import, compile, and load their entry scene: integration (D1) averages 8.9 to 9.7 of 10 points on every engine (Table 2). Whether the game then works is another matter: three in four cells earn under half of the 80 gameplay points (D2–D5), and only GPT-6 Astra clears that bar on every engine. The evaluator’s player journey reaches the ending in only 16% of runs, with 4% fully solved. Claude Code on Roblox Studio, the median cell in gameplay, earns 9.0 of 10 integration points but only a third of the gameplay points. Because integration barely varies, the spread of F is almost entirely a spread in gameplay; a build check would rank most configurations as near-equals, whereas play separates them by tens of points. Nor is the state interface the obstacle: Φ answers the handshake in 94% of delivered projects. Yet these contracts are within reach of the same technology under human direction: the references that engineers built with coding agents are all solved and average 87.3 of 90 on F (96.4 of 100 on O), against 65.0 for the best autonomous configuration and at most 41.0 for the other six. The gap also varies by track: the share of gameplay points runs from 23% on Godot to 57% on Unity, so the same build success stands for very different amounts of playable game.

The scorecard also shows where games fail, and the answer shifts with capability (Appendix Table 18). We split the cells into thirds by F and find, in each, the gameplay dimension that is weakest relative to its weight. In the lowest third it is most often completeness (D2): much of the game is never built. In the middle third it is mechanics (D3): the game exists, but its rules break under play. In the top third it is lifecycle (D4), ahead of feedback (D5) and mechanics: the game plays, but breaks across transitions, restarts, or reopening, or fails to show the player what happened. Stronger agents thus fail at later stages, a progression that a single pass/fail outcome hides and that motivates replaying complete journeys and checking visible responses during play.

5.3 The Engine Is a First-Class Variable

Every engine separates configurations widely, but not equally and not in the same order. The spread of F across configurations ranges from 29.0 points on Unity to 56.9 on Defold, and no two engines rank the configurations alike: Kendall’s τ between engines ranges from 0.14 to 0.62 (Appendix Table 16). Codex CLI with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, for instance, ranks second of seven on Roblox Studio and last on Unreal Engine. GPT-6 Astra, the strongest configuration, leads by 31.5 points on Unreal Engine and 23.1 on Roblox Studio but by only 6.5 on Unity. An engine track can thus amplify a capability difference that another hides, and a leaderboard built on one engine inherits its bias.

Changing one factor at a time shows what transfers (Appendix Table 18). Within the GPT family the order holds on every engine: GPT-6 Astra leads GPT-5.6 Sol by 6.5 to 41.4 points, and Sol leads GPT-5.6 Terra by 5.1 to 22.5. Across families it does not: under Codex CLI, DeepSeek-V4-Pro trails Sol by 26.7 points on Defold yet leads it by 12.7 on Godot. The scaffold can matter as much as the model: with DeepSeek-V4-Pro fixed, moving from Codex CLI to DeepSeek Harness gains 19.8 points on Unreal Engine but loses 21.9 on Roblox Studio. A single-engine leaderboard therefore ranks configurations for that engine alone.

Same game, different engine.

The swap experiment holds the game fixed and changes only the engine: for each of the six heavyweight–script-centric pairs, the five hardest games of each engine are rebuilt on the other engine, which limits ceiling effects on the heavyweight engines (Appendix 17). The heavyweight engine wins five of the six pairs (Table 3): Unity leads Defold and Godot by 11.6 and 10.4 points, Unreal Engine leads Defold, Godot, and Roblox Studio by 21.2, 21.5, and 8.5, and only Unity against Roblox Studio reverses, by 4.3. Pooling both swap directions offsets any advantage a game draws from its native engine, and with ten games per pair, each of the five leads exceeds its standard deviation over games, hence more than three standard errors.

The ordering matches how much an engine checks before play. Unity and Unreal Engine compile their code, validate serialized scenes and references, and ship test frameworks an agent can drive, so many errors surface as diagnostics during construction; the advantage is widest against Defold and Godot, whose dynamically typed scripts fail only at run time, and narrowest against Roblox Studio, whose editor also analyzes scripts. The native tracks agree. Kimi Code never plays or views its game (Appendix Table 19): on Defold it gets no game running, while on Unity it reaches F=55.7, a gap of 49.9 points against 6.5 to 21.7 for the other configurations across both tracks. An agent that never runs its game depends entirely on checks before play. Heavyweight engines are harder to drive but easier to check.

How much they help still varies by configuration: on one swapped game the gain ranges from 7.0 to 77.9 points, and on another the two scaffolds sharing DeepSeek-V4-Pro trade places (Appendix 17). Engine difficulty is therefore no fixed offset that could be calibrated away.

5.4 Effort Does Not Buy Play

Each construction trace shows what a game cost to build (Figure 4). The checks that favor heavyweight engines are paid for in time: Unreal Engine runs reach the highest step and token counts, averaging up to 295 workflow steps and 65M tokens per configuration, because every build–play–repair iteration passes through a long compile and import cycle. At the other end, Godot’s headless checks return short diagnostics, so the context resent with every call grows slowly, and many Godot runs, especially early stoppers, stay under 0.3M tokens.

The time budget rarely binds. About nine in ten runs deliver before the 3600 s limit, and those that reach it stall or loop, averaging only 16.3 points of F. Most runs thus end when the agent judges its game finished, so the 6–14 engineer-hours behind each reference do not explain the gap. That judgment is rarely tested by play: playing and viewing the game take at most 13.3% of any configuration’s steps. Even at that maximum, GPT-6 Astra and DeepSeek-V4-Pro under Codex CLI differ by 29.9 points, so play frequency alone does not decide F. Nor do steps or tokens track F: games of similar cost score anywhere from near zero to 80, and no game whose runs average more than 200 steps reaches 40 points. The best games sit toward the upper left, where GPT-6 Astra reaches its top scores on moderate budgets, so capability shows up as efficiency, not persistence.

5.5 Effect of Game Completion Boost

We evaluate GCB under Codex CLI with three models on 15 high-difficulty games, three per engine track, fixed before any GCB run (Appendices 13 and 14). Each paired comparison holds the task, native prompt, engine-access and image tools, and budget fixed, and the baseline is the strongest of a game’s three native runs by O, so it sits at or above the game’s three-run mean used in Table 2.

GCB improves F and O for every model (Table 4), raising mean F by 14.1–24.3 points and mean O by 14.7–25.8; Terra more than triples its F. Each gains most in the bottleneck that Section 5.2 finds at its score level. DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the strongest baseline here, gains most in lifecycle (D4, +8.6), while Sol and Terra gain most in completeness and mechanics (D2/D3, +5.3/+4.3 and +8.0/+5.3). D6 gains 0.5–1.5 points and D1 changes by -0.7 to +3.3, so most of the gain is gameplay.

6 Conclusion

CEGame-Bench evaluates complete-game creation on five production engines through real-input play. Agents usually deliver projects that build yet earn under half the gameplay points, and most stop before the time limit, whereas engineers directing coding agents reach near the maximum. No two engines rank configurations alike, and the same game usually scores higher on the heavyweight engines, which are harder to drive but easier to check. GCB turns these findings into a playtest-and-repair workflow that improves every evaluated model. For evaluation practice, the results favor scoring games by play, reporting each engine separately, and logging build cost. The shared evaluation protocol and execution traces support comparisons of functional performance across engine tracks and agent configurations. Game creation thus tests whether an agent can inspect and repair its own work before declaring it done, a capability needed to build simulated worlds from specifications.

Limitations

CEGame-Bench evaluates single-player games built offline from a written design document. It measures whether a game meets its specification and leaves player enjoyment, online multiplayer, live services, and design without a specification outside its scope. The five engines span script-centric and heavyweight production engines; other engines and web frameworks can join as new tracks under the same contract language. Engine and editor versions are frozen, so newer releases enter as new benchmark versions rather than shifting existing scores. GCB is evaluated under one scaffold with three models, excluding GPT-6 Astra, on high-difficulty games from each track; its effect under other scaffolds and on the strongest model remains to be measured. The visual judge shares its model with one evaluated configuration, so configurations are compared on F, which excludes D6. Built by engineers working with coding agents, the references mark what human-directed agents reach rather than unaided human skill. A swap changes the starter and tool manual with the engine, so its effect covers the whole toolchain, not the engine core alone. Finally, the heavyweight tracks need full editors and build toolchains, and one Unreal Engine run can consume tens of millions of tokens, so a complete evaluation is costlier than a browser-based benchmark. This cost also bounds the scale: with ten tasks per engine, seven configurations, and swaps on the five hardest games of each track, engine-level rankings and swap effects carry wide spreads, which we report.

Ethical Considerations

All tasks are adapted from permissively licensed open-source games or written from scratch; adapted games are renamed and re-parameterized, and bundled art and audio are used under their licenses with attribution. The six annotators and engineers who built the tasks were compensated in accordance with applicable labor laws and regulations. Every engine runs locally and no game is published online, so the benchmark involves no personal or player data. As with other code-generating agents, game-creation agents could be misused to clone commercial games; the release contains only newly written documents, licensed assets, and our own evaluator and run traces, and no material from commercial games.

7 Engine Tracks and Toolchains

Each track is pinned to the engine build of Table 5, one editor build, and one command-line entry point, and a run that resolves any other version is discarded. Unity tasks use the 2D and 3D core packages and no Asset Store content; Unreal Engine tasks use its C++ toolchain and also permit Blueprint; Godot tasks use GDScript only; and Defold tasks use the stock build server. Roblox Studio submissions are .rbxl place files play-tested in local Studio sessions and never published to a live service. Starters bundle CC0 or CC-BY art and audio, adapted source games are licensed under MIT, Apache-2.0, CC0, or zlib, and per-task attribution ships with the release.

Checks before play.

The tracks differ in how much an engine checks a game before it runs, and the tool manual exposes each engine’s own checks to the agent (Table 5, fifth column). On Unity and Unreal Engine, C# and C++ compilation rejects type and reference errors, the editor validates serialized scenes and assets, and built-in test frameworks run scripted checks inside the engine. Roblox Studio analyzes Luau scripts in the editor. Godot parses GDScript on load, and Defold validates resources and Lua syntax at build time; beyond that, errors in their dynamically typed scripts surface only when the game runs. These checks are the diagnostics an agent can act on before it plays its own game.

Starter and tool manual.

Each starter s₀ opens, builds, and runs on its locked version but implements none of the game. It provides an empty entry scene, the task’s licensed art and audio, naming tables for scenes, entry points, and state keys, and the public smoke checks of Appendix 9. The tool manual M documents command-line build and headless run, editor automation, import and packaging, the checks above, log locations, and tools for capturing and inspecting a running game. Starters and manuals follow a common section structure across tracks (Appendix 8).

8 Cross-Engine Comparability

A Defold score and an Unreal Engine score are comparable only if the scale, not the difficulty, is held fixed. Five controls fix the scale and leave the engine as the variable.

  • 1.

    One contract language. Every track instantiates the same contract symbols and six dimensions, and a task keeps its leaf families on every engine; only the evidence route through the engine adapter differs.

  • 2.

    Fixed family budgets. Within a dimension, budgets β_d,f allocate weight to families and stay fixed across engines, so an obligation weighs the same whether it takes twelve leaves on Unreal Engine or three on Defold.

  • 3.

    Matched intended difficulty. Every track has the same 3/5/2 easy/medium/hard composition under the four-axis annotation of Appendix 13.

  • 4.

    Matched ceilings. A task enters any track only if its reference implementation scores at least 90 on O, and the released references score at least 92.5 on every track (Appendix 12), so the full scale is reachable everywhere and a low track mean reflects the agents.

  • 5.

    Matched inputs and budgets. Starter structure, GDD structure, smoke checks, tool-manual sections, and the 3600 s budget are identical across tracks, and the task prompt (Appendix 16) contains no engine-specific hints.

    • The controls preserve each engine’s scene model, asset pipeline, build cycle, and checks before play (Table 5). These set both what each build–play–repair iteration costs and how many errors surface before the game runs, and they are what the benchmark measures. Since tracks have their own games, results are reported per track, and the cross-group swaps of Appendix 17 isolate the engine on a fixed game.

    9 Game Design Document and State Interface

    This appendix details the two public documents of Section 3.2 that define a task for the agent: the GDD and the state interface it requires.

    Document structure.

    Every task uses the same fifteen GDD sections to make the specification’s scope explicit. Table 6 maps each section to the contract symbol it populates and to the dimensions its leaf checks score.

    From requirement to leaf.

    Each sentence of the normative sections becomes one or more leaf checks, written against the contract rather than any implementation. Table 7 traces an excerpt of Driftfolk Chronicle. A requirement is checked on its positive branch and, where the GDD implies one, on its rejected branch: the dash is tested both when it should fire and when it should not. Every assertion reads only declared Φ keys, HUD elements, logs, or frames, so the same rows apply to any implementation on any engine, and only the adapter that sends the input and collects the evidence changes.

item.title: 别只调用预制工厂：InfiniDream 让 VLM 在符号约束下改程序化生成器，拼出可编辑的写实 3D 大世界 ｜ InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation
item.description:
一句话：把 VLM 的代码能力关进程序化生成的「符号约束」里，既拿到写实可编辑资产，又保住种子多样性，100 物体 + 20 场景任务全面领先。

要点：

  • 纯 VLM 写 Blender 代码只能产出较简单的 3D 资产，而成熟程序化系统（如 4 万行代码的 Infinigen）需要大量手工开发，两者都没解决开放性问题
  • Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation：用既有程序化算法扩展出新资产品类，同时保留可编辑性与基于种子的多样性，而不是自由写几何
  • 端到端 text-to-world：语义场景规划 + Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement，保证大尺度世界里的物体摆放精确、程序化填充与动画一致
  • 100 个物体生成与 20 个场景生成任务上四项感知指标全面提升，另有多样性分析与人工偏好评测

为什么值得看：对引擎侧最直接的价值是资产仍然「可编辑、可改参数、可重出」：输出不是网格汤而是程序，能进 DCC 与引擎的常规资产流水线。

中文摘要：程序化生成在可控性、可编辑性和多样性上明显优于静态网格，是合成数据与游戏开发的关键手段；但传统方法依赖手工规则与预制资产工厂，而近年用 VLM 直接写代码生成 3D 的方法又只能做出相对简单的资产。作者提出 InfiniDream：先用符号约束的资产生成，把 VLM 的生成能力接到既有程序化算法上，从而在未知资产品类上也能产出写实、可编辑、种子可复现的资产；再搭一条端到端 text-to-world 管线，把语义场景规划与确定性视锥引导的网格摆放结合，生成大规模 3D 世界并保持精确摆放、程序化填充与动画。在 100 个物体与 20 个场景任务上，四项感知指标均优于对比方法，多样性与人工偏好评测同样支持这一结论。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·AI原生（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation

October 20, 2026

Abstract

Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework.

Project page:https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream-page/
Code:https://github.com/yichuanH/InfiniDream
Correspondence:wangzx1994@gmail.com, kaipeng.zhang@shanda.com, yulunliu@cs.nycu.edu.tw

1 Introduction

Procedural generation creates 3D assets and scenes through executable programs, offering editability, diversity, and scalability. These advantages have made it widely applicable to synthetic data generation, game development, and virtual world creation [(70)]. However, conventional procedural generation methods rely heavily on handcrafted rules and predefined asset generators, limiting the variety of generated content and their ability to create novel assets and scenes.

Recent advances in the code generation and tool-use capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled the generation and editing of 3D assets and scenes through executable Blender code [(28, 55, 73, 110, 24, 96)]. However, while existing approaches can construct scenes by composing assets or directly synthesizing geometry through code, generating large-scale 3D scenes with consistently rich geometric details, complex materials, and photorealistic appearance remains challenging.

Infinigen [(70)] is built on over 40,000 lines of code, including carefully handcrafted procedural asset factories, to generate photorealistic, editable 3D scenes. However, its generative capabilities remain constrained by predefined asset categories and procedural rules.

Recent studies have explored using LLMs and VLMs to control sophisticated procedural generation systems through function orchestration, parameter adjustment, and the composition of existing generators [(82, 119, 117)]. While these approaches improve the controllability of procedural scene generation, methods that primarily operate within predefined functions and parameter spaces remain limited in their ability to create novel asset types beyond the capabilities of existing generators.

Another line of research explores large-scale 3D world generation using retrieved or generatively synthesized mesh assets [(23, 92)]. Although these methods support instance-level editing, their mesh-based assets lack the parameterized editability and seed-based diversity of procedural generators. Producing diverse object variations often requires direct mesh manipulation or regeneration.

Figure 2 highlights three limitations: VLM Harness produces less photorealistic scenes, Infinigen is restricted to predefined factories, and Code2Worlds [(117)], a recent VLM-guided Infinigen framework, is limited to function calls and parameter adjustment. These limitations motivate open-ended procedural generation beyond existing factory capabilities.

To address these challenges, we introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation, designed to achieve realism, open-endedness, editability, diversity, and scalability. By employing VLM reasoning to compose and extend sophisticated procedural programs, InfiniDream generates novel assets beyond predefined factories while leveraging existing procedural algorithms. Our framework enables the creation of photorealistic, editable, and diverse large-scale 3D worlds from natural language descriptions.

At the asset level, Fig. 3 further motivates our Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE) strategy, which combines the flexibility of VLM-based code generation with the rich procedural structures of existing factories.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • 1.

    Open-Ended Procedural Asset Generation. We propose Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE) to generate novel, photorealistic procedural assets with rich geometric details beyond predefined factories, while preserving editability and seed-based diversity.

  • 2.

    Scalable Procedural World Generation. We introduce an end-to-end text-to-world framework combining semantic scene planning and deterministic frustum-guided grid placement to generate large-scale, editable 3D worlds.

  • 3.

    Comprehensive Experimental Validation. We conduct extensive object- and scene-level evaluations, diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference studies to validate the effectiveness of InfiniDream.

    • 2 Related Work

    Procedural 3D Asset Generation.

    Procedural modeling encodes 3D content as executable rules, from L-systems [(50, 66)] and shape grammars [(97, 60)] to learned procedural shape and CAD programs [(77, 89, 36, 37, 38, 72, 98, 41)]. Advances in code generation [(4)] and tool use [(75, 109)] now let language models synthesize editable 3D assets as Blender code [(13, 55, 73, 96, 105, 9, 69)], other shape programs [(114, 39, 94, 49)], or CAD scripts for mechanical parts [(2, 93, 74, 57)]. Multimodal reasoning, retrieval augmentation [(43)], and iterative visual feedback [(2, 93, 94, 49)] further improve reconstruction, editing, and visual fidelity [(29, 110, 24, 96)]. Procedural material graphs are likewise generated or inferred from images [(78, 21, 27, 44, 45)], whereas inverse procedural modeling fits predefined procedural generators to targets [(85, 91, 81, 63, 118)] and remains bounded by their categories. Still, reliably synthesizing complex procedural geometry with rich geometric details and photorealistic appearance remains challenging. Benchmarks for 3D code generation [(19, 96, 13, 2, 20, 107, 52)] assess executability, geometric fidelity, and the benefits of execution feedback [(6)] and agentic coding [(106)]. However, 3DCodeBench [(19)] draws its procedural modeling categories from predefined Infinigen factories [(70, 71)], leaving procedural asset generation beyond these categories underexplored.

    3D World Generation.

    Procedural content generation [(80, 25, 76)] has long produced noise-based terrains [(64, 61)] and cities [(62)], and now yields photorealistic natural and indoor scenes [(70, 71, 69)], simulation-ready assets [(40)], and houses for embodied AI [(11)]. Language models have been leveraged for 3D scene planning, spatial reasoning, and executable scene construction [(28, 82, 119, 117, 15, 108, 3, 17, 83, 1, 116, 86, 22)], and one line couples them with existing procedural generators through function orchestration, parameter adjustment, and composition of predefined procedural assets [(82, 119, 67, 117, 115, 53, 87, 54)]. Related approaches [(28, 110, 117)] also explore hierarchical generation [(17, 84, 95)], iterative visual feedback [(51)], physics-aware dynamic simulation [(56)], and looping animation of static 3D scenes [(103)]. However, methods restricted to orchestrating predefined procedural generators remain confined to their asset categories and parameter spaces, while semantically consistent and geometrically precise object placement in complex scenes remains challenging. Another line of work builds large-scale worlds [(23, 92)] from procedural layouts, retrieved assets [(10, 108, 1, 12)], generative 3D models [(65, 26, 113, 101)], and object-level composition [(95, 31, 59)], expanding generatable content and enabling instance-level manipulation. However, these approaches and neural scene generators [(35, 46, 16, 112, 111, 88, 30, 5, 8, 18, 120, 14, 7, 48, 102, 42, 99, 58)] generally lack the reusable procedural structures and high-level parameters needed for procedural editing and seed-based geometric variation. Orthogonally, recent work decouples explicit world states from generative video rendering [(32, 34, 47)] and benchmarks whether video models render what a program specifies [(33)]; such systems still require an explicit world specification, which procedural world generation can supply. InfiniDream addresses these gaps: it enables open-ended procedural asset generation beyond predefined factories and integrates it into scalable, fully procedural 3D world generation, while preserving procedural editability and seed-based diversity.

    3 Method

    We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. Given a text prompt, our framework selects a suitable initial scene and employs a Director to produce a structured Scene Plan specifying asset requirements, semantic placement constraints, and motion. Our framework consists of two core components: Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which creates novel procedural assets through constrained editing, and Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement, which translates semantic constraints into precise 3D object placements. Finally, procedural asset pooling, terrain refinement, and animation enable diverse, large-scale world generation.

    3.1 Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation

    Since directly providing a VLM with the entire Infinigen codebase often leads to imprecise editing (Fig. 3), we propose Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE), which extracts key code structures and explicit editing constraints, transforming a large procedural codebase into a manageable editing space (Fig. 4).

    3.1.1 Factory Mapping and Retrieval

    Given a text description and an optional reference image, the system retrieves the most relevant Infinigen factory and constructs a Factory Brief (Fig. 4(A)). It contains a Code Structure Map identifying key functions and dependencies, an Editable Surface consisting of asset-specific modules dynamically identified through depth-limited dependency analysis, and Linked Infrastructure providing read-only access to shared low-level algorithms (e.g., node graphs) via symbolic links. Together, these components establish explicit code-level constraints that restrict editing while preserving the underlying procedural algorithms. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix 12.

    3.1.2 Structured Planning and Coarse Construction

    The Planner produces a structured Editing Plan specifying the editing strategy (Strategy), target locations (Locate), required modifications (Edit), dependencies (Rely-on), and potential risks (Risks), as shown in Fig. 4(B). The plan also accounts for seed-dependent logic to preserve controllable procedural variation.

    We define three editing strategies: Tweak adjusts existing parameters and high-level logic; Create introduces new procedural functions; and Promote selectively extends editing permissions to protected modules when necessary. These strategies enable controlled expansion of the editing space.

    The Coarse Constructor executes the Editing Plan under these constraints (Fig. 4(C)), preserving the original factory entry points and function signatures to maintain compatibility with the population pipeline and random seed control. It reuses existing algorithms to construct a coarse procedural asset. SCE preserves seed-dependent randomness by adjusting sampling ranges rather than fixing parameters to match the reference image.

    3.1.3 Fine Refinement

    As shown in Fig. 4(D), the Reviser iteratively compares rendered results with the target description and reference image, identifying discrepancies in geometry, materials, and visual details. It then performs targeted code modifications within the established editing boundaries. A Selector identifies the best candidate across refinement iterations.

    Through constrained editing and iterative refinement, SCE generates novel procedural assets while preserving procedural editability and seed-controlled diversity.

    3.2 Semantic Placement Reasoning

    Given a text prompt and current scene information, the Director first formulates a natural-language plan and converts it into a structured Scene Plan specifying editing operations (add, replace, and delete), asset requirements, and semantic placement constraints (Fig. 5(A–B)).

    The Director selects among three placement modes: Hero for semantically significant objects, Scattering for large-area distributions, and Swarm for collective entities. Hero placement supports seven Anchoring types (rooted, upright, tilted, conform, afloat, airborne, and submerged). A Semantic Target and Surface Policy further specify target regions, permissible surface types, slope limits, and support conditions. Scattering and Swarm are controlled by density, coverage, and group size.

    The Director also determines the instance count N, distinct procedural prototypes K, World Motion, and Local Animation. World Motion specifies object trajectories and swept envelopes for collision checking. VLM decisions are restricted to discrete semantic operations and constraints, leaving continuous geometric computations to deterministic placement.

    3.3 Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement

    To avoid repeated VLM-based coordinate prediction and costly render-based verification, we propose Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement, which translates the Director’s semantic constraints into candidate 3D positions (Fig. 5(D)). Candidates are evaluated in a near-to-far order without additional VLM calls or iterative rendering.

    3.3.1 Frustum-based Candidate Generation

    Given the specified placement region, we discretize the camera’s image plane into a 2D grid and generate 3D candidate positions along the corresponding camera rays. For surface-supported objects, candidates are determined by ray intersections with scene geometry. For airborne and submerged objects, candidates are sampled at discrete depth intervals along each ray.

    3.3.2 Constraint-based Filtering and Depth-aware Placement

    Each candidate undergoes five deterministic checks: (1) Visibility, (2) Collision with motion swept envelopes, (3) Inter-instance Spacing, (4) Surface Policy, including surface type, slope limits, and full support, and (5) Projected-area Band, requiring a_\min≤a(p)≤a_\max.

    Given depth-sorted candidates ℂ={p₁,…,pₙ}, where gⱼ(p)∈{0,1} indicates satisfaction of constraint j, we select the nearest valid candidate:

    i^*=\min{i \middle| \bigwedgeⱼ₌₁⁵gⱼ(pᵢ)=1}, p^*=p_i^*.

    		(1)

    Combined with projected-area bounds, near-to-far search enables implicit size-aware placement, favoring closer positions for smaller objects and farther positions for larger ones. For multiple instances, the initial search depth increases progressively, while previously placed objects are included in subsequent collision checks. If no valid position exists, hierarchical constraint relaxation is applied (Appendix 13).

    3.4 Scalable Population and Animation

    We combine the procedural assets generated in Sec. 3.1 with the validated placements from Sec. 3.3 through semantically controlled asset pooling, terrain refinement, and procedural animation (Fig. 5(E)).

    Semantically Budgeted Asset Pooling.

    To reduce the repeated construction cost of complex procedural assets, we extend Infinigen’s asset pooling mechanism to independent object population. The Director determines the number of instances N and distinct procedural prototypes K based on scene requirements. For assets supporting seed-based variation, we generate K prototypes using different factory seeds and create N instances through linked duplication:

    M={Mₖ=G(sₖ)}ₖ₌₁^K, Iᵢ=Clone(M_((i-1)\bmodK)+1).

    		(2)

    Here, G denotes the procedural generator, sₖ is the seed for the k-th prototype, and Iᵢ is the i-th instance. This mechanism reduces expensive asset constructions from N to K while maintaining seed-based diversity across prototypes. Assets unsuitable for pooling are generated independently.

    Population, Terrain Refinement, and Animation.

    Procedural assets are placed according to their Anchoring modes and integrated with Infinigen’s fine terrain pipeline. Animation combines World Motion and Local Animation, with shared motion specifications ensuring consistency between placement constraints and actual trajectories. The final scene is then refined and rendered (Fig. 5(E–F)).

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate InfiniDream at both the object and scene levels, complemented by diversity experiments, ablation studies, and a user study.

    4.1 Evaluation Protocol and Baselines

    Object-level Evaluation.

    We compare InfiniDream against five baselines: VLM (one-shot), VLM (harness), VIGA [(110)], BlenderRAG [(73)], and Infinigen [(70)]. Following 3DCodeBench [(19)], we adopt its codebase for the two VLM baselines, evaluating single-turn code generation and iterative refinement with a native coding-agent harness. The remaining baselines represent visual-feedback refinement, retrieval-augmented generation, and original Infinigen factory outputs, respectively.

    Scene-level Evaluation.

    We compare large-scale world generation against VLM (harness), VIGA [(110)], Infinigen [(70)], and Code2Worlds [(117)], representing agentic code generation, visual-feedback refinement, original procedural scene generation, and LLM-driven hierarchical procedural orchestration, respectively.

    Implementation and Metrics.

    We use Claude Opus 4.8 for InfiniDream and all VLM-based baselines, with Blender 4.x for generation and rendering. We evaluate 100 object-level tasks across six categories and 20 scene-level tasks at resolutions of 1024×1024 and 960×540, respectively.

    We report CLIP [(68)], SigLIP2 [(90)], DINOv3 [(79)], and ImageReward [(104)]. At the object level, CLIP, SigLIP2, and ImageReward are averaged over four fixed views (45^∘, 135^∘, 225^∘, and 315^∘), while DINOv3 compares the front view against four held-out reference images, independently generated from the same text prompt, and reports the mean cosine similarity. We additionally report code executability. Scene-level metrics use each method’s primary camera view. For scene-level DINOv3, each method’s primary camera view is compared against a single per-prompt scene reference image, generated by Gemini 3 Pro Image from the same scene prompt as a photorealistic wide-angle photograph of the entire scene; the same reference is shared by all methods and is never provided to any method during generation. Further details are provided in the Appendix.

    Diversity Evaluation.

    We compare InfiniDream with TRELLIS.2 [(100)] on 15 text prompts. For each prompt, InfiniDream generates five variations using different random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 uses five independently generated reference images. We measure semantic consistency using SigLIP2 and visual diversity using average pairwise DINOv2 feature distance.

    4.2 Experimental Results

    Qualitative Comparisons

    Figures 6 and 7 present qualitative comparisons of InfiniDream with existing methods at the object and scene levels, highlighting differences in geometric detail, photorealism, and scene composition.

    Quantitative Comparisons

    As shown in Tables 2 and 2, InfiniDream achieves the highest scores across all four perceptual metrics at both the object and scene levels.

    Human Preference Study

    We conduct a human preference study with 30 participants across 10 object and 10 scene tasks. Participants compare results from competing methods based on semantic alignment and visual quality. Table 4 reports InfiniDream’s preference rates for each criterion and overall.

    4.3 Diversity Analysis

    For each text prompt, InfiniDream generates five variations using different random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 uses five independently generated reference images. We evaluate semantic consistency using SigLIP2 and visual diversity using average pairwise DINOv2 feature distance. InfiniDream achieves greater visual diversity while maintaining comparable semantic alignment (Fig. 8, Table 4).

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Object-level Ablation

    We evaluate six ablation settings on 25 animal and plant tasks: (1) w/o Ref. Image, (2) Random Factory, (3) w/o Planner, (4) Agent (Infinigen), (5) w/o Refiner, and (6) 3 Rounds. The full pipeline allows up to six refinement rounds. For Agent (Infinigen), Claude Opus 4.8 is given the entire Infinigen codebase and Bash access to autonomously write and edit code, render and inspect results, and determine when to stop within six rounds, without our structured planning or editing constraints. Quantitative and qualitative results are shown in Table 10 and Fig. 10.

    Scene-level Ablation.

    We evaluate four settings on 20 scenes: (1) w/o Grid Search, using direct 3D coordinate prediction; (2) w/o Anchoring, reverting to Infinigen’s grounding; (3) w/o Semantic Target, removing semantic surface constraints; and (4) Agent (Placement), allowing a VLM agent to autonomously place our generated 3D assets in the same selected coarse scene given the text prompt, without our placement pipeline.

    We evaluate three placement metrics: Unreadable Rate, the percentage of objects outside the camera view or occupying less than 0.1% of the image area; Ground-contact Error, the absolute distance between an object’s lowest contact point and its supporting surface, capturing floating or penetration; and Contact Spread, the difference between the maximum and minimum terrain-relative gaps across sampled contact points, capturing uneven grounding and partial suspension (surface-supported objects only; see Appendix 15). We report the 95th percentile (P95) for the latter two metrics. For Contact Spread, P95 is computed over per-object values pooled across all surface-supported requested-add objects in the 20 scenes. Results are shown in Table 5 and Fig. 11.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. By combining Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation with semantic planning and deterministic placement, InfiniDream creates novel, photorealistic, and editable procedural assets and composes them into diverse, large-scale 3D worlds. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness at both the object and scene levels.

    Limitations and Future Work.

    Our current animation pipeline relies on a predefined set of motion types. Future work could explore VLM-generated animation code to support more complex and customized motions. We also aim to extend InfiniDream to indoor environments with more complex spatial relationships and object interactions.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    6 Additional Object-level Comparisons

    We provide additional qualitative comparisons of object-level generation across diverse asset categories in Fig. 12. All methods are evaluated using identical text prompts under the same experimental protocol described in Sec. 4.1. These additional examples further illustrate differences in geometric complexity, material details, and visual fidelity among the compared methods.

    7 Additional Scene-level Comparisons

    We provide additional qualitative comparisons of scene-level generation across diverse environments in Fig. 13. All methods are evaluated using identical text prompts under the same experimental protocol described in Sec. 4.1. These additional results illustrate differences in scene composition, geometric detail, semantic alignment, and visual fidelity across the compared methods.

    8 Additional Qualitative Comparison with GPT-6 Astra

    We provide an additional qualitative comparison with GPT-6 Astra in Fig. 14. This comparison is included as supplementary evidence beyond the main benchmark suite. Importantly, InfiniDream still uses Claude Opus 4.8 as the underlying VLM, while GPT-6 Astra serves as an additional strong proprietary baseline. Under identical text prompts, the results highlight differences in visual fidelity, geometric detail, material richness, and overall semantic composition.

    9 Additional Diversity Results

    We provide additional qualitative diversity comparisons between InfiniDream and TRELLIS.2 in Fig. 15. For each text prompt, InfiniDream generates five procedural variations by changing random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 generates five assets from independently generated reference images. These examples further illustrate the diversity of InfiniDream’s procedural assets while preserving semantic consistency and visual quality.

    10 Object-level Comparison with Code2Worlds

    We further compare InfiniDream with Code2Worlds on the 29 out of 100 object-level tasks supported by Code2Worlds. Due to its limited factory coverage, we report this comparison separately from the main benchmark.

    As shown in Fig. 16 and Table 6, InfiniDream achieves higher scores across all four metrics. Code2Worlds can exploit the parameter space of existing factories, such as adjusting the color of a fish, but cannot introduce novel procedural features beyond predefined generators. In contrast, InfiniDream extends existing procedural code to generate new geometric structures and fine-grained details, enabling more flexible open-ended asset generation.

    11 Man-Made Asset Generation

    Beyond natural assets, InfiniDream can retrieve and extend factories for man-made objects. As shown in Fig. 17, while VIGA performs well on geometric objects, InfiniDream achieves comparable structural quality with rich geometric and material details, demonstrating its versatility across both organic and man-made assets.

    12 Implementation Details of Symbolically Constrained Editing

    Reference Synthesis and Factory Retrieval.

    We use Gemini 3 Pro Image to generate an isolated reference object against a white background. Claude Opus 4.8 retrieves the most relevant Infinigen factory, with deterministic lexical matching as a fallback.

    Factory Brief Construction.

    Starting from the selected factory, we perform AST-based import graph traversal with a maximum depth of two. Asset-specific modules form the Editable Surface, while shared modules remain read-only Linked Infrastructure. Unrelated dependencies are pruned, and a VLM summarizes the remaining code into a cached Code Structure Map.

    Constrained Code Editing.

    The Planner produces an Editing Plan specifying Strategy, Locate, Edits, Rely-on, and Risks. The Constructor can modify existing modules (Tweak), promote protected modules (Promote), or synthesize new procedural modules (Create). Editing is restricted to the working directory, preserving the original factory interface and seed-dependent randomness.

    Iterative Refinement.

    Modified modules are integrated into a symbolic-link overlay of the original Infinigen codebase. A vision-based Reviser guides targeted refinement, while execution failures trigger traceback-based repair. The pipeline supports up to six rounds with early stopping. A vision-based Selector chooses the best successful candidate, whose code snapshot is used to reconstruct the final executable generator.

    13 Implementation Details of Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement

    Candidate Generation.

    We discretize the Director’s screen-space region into a 9×5 grid (17×9 for six or more instances). Surface candidates are obtained through ray-scene intersections, while airborne and submerged candidates are sampled along camera rays using geometric depth intervals (×1.3, up to 80 m). Larger objects are placed first, with deterministic hashing ensuring reproducibility. The entire placement process requires no additional VLM calls.

    Constraints and Relaxation.

    Projected area is estimated from the proxy bounding box, with a preferred minimum of 1.2%, a relaxed minimum of 0.2%, and an absolute maximum of 25%. Collision checks account for motion-dependent swept envelopes, while surface placement additionally enforces slope limits and four-corner footprint support. When no valid candidate is found, constraints are progressively relaxed and the search region is expanded. Water-related constraints remain enforced, and all relaxations are recorded in the resulting placement plan.

    14 Baseline Implementation Details

    Baseline Implementations.

    We adopt the official implementations of all baselines, adding Claude Opus 4.8 API adapters where necessary. The VLM (one-shot) and VLM (harness) baselines follow 3DCodeBench, with the latter supporting autonomous code execution and iterative refinement.

    SigLIP2 Score Computation.

    All SigLIP2 scores in this paper (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) are computed with google/siglip2-base-patch16-224 and reported as the cosine similarity between L2-normalized image and text embeddings, recovered from the model’s image–text logits via \cos=(logit-b)/t, where t=112.67 and b=-16.77 are SigLIP2’s learned temperature and bias. Scores are averaged over the four azimuth views at the object level (Tables 1, 5, 7), the primary camera view at the scene level (Table 2), and the five variations per prompt in the diversity evaluation (Table 4).

    Object-level Baselines.

    All methods receive identical text prompts and reference images, except BlenderRAG, which only supports text inputs. Each task has five Gemini-generated reference images: ref_00 is the conditioning reference provided to the generation methods, while ref_01–ref_04 are held out exclusively for evaluation (DINOv3) and the human study and are never shown to any method; the conditioning reference is never used for scoring. All assets are evaluated under identical camera, lighting, background, and rendering settings. Failed generations are retained as blank renders rather than excluded.

    Scene-level Baselines.

    All scene-level methods receive identical text prompts and follow their respective official scene generation and camera selection pipelines. For InfiniDream, the Scene Picker automatically retrieves the most relevant initial coarse scene based on the input prompt from a library of 70 pre-generated environments (14 biomes with five seeds each), which is then used as the basis for subsequent procedural editing. The library was built before the benchmark prompts were finalized and was not modified afterwards. For reproducibility, the Scene Picker’s selection is made once per task, and the chosen base scene and seed are then fixed across all benchmark and ablation runs. The other baselines do not use this library. Code2Worlds selects from its available procedural factories even when no closely matching category exists.

    Failure Handling.

    We resolve version- and environment-related execution issues wherever possible to ensure that baselines run as intended. We do not report a separate scene-level executability metric.

    15 Ablation Study Details

    Object-level Ablation.

    We provide additional implementation details for the six ablation settings: (1) w/o Ref. Image removes the reference image from the generation pipeline; (2) Random Factory replaces factory retrieval with random selection; (3) w/o Planner removes structured planning and replaces the Editing Plan with empty content; (4) Agent (Infinigen) gives a Claude Opus 4.8 coding-agent harness access to the entire Infinigen codebase and Bash tools, allowing autonomous code generation, rendering, and refinement without SCE constraints, for up to six rounds; (5) w/o Refiner removes fine-level refinement; and (6) 3 Rounds limits the refinement budget to three rounds, compared with six in the full method.

    Scene-level Ablation.

    We evaluate four placement variants: (1) w/o Grid Search removes discrete semantic planning and grid-based placement, allowing the Director to predict continuous 3D coordinates directly; (2) w/o Anchoring replaces our seven anchoring types with Infinigen’s original grounding mechanism; (3) w/o Semantic Target removes semantic surface constraints from grid search, allowing placements on semantically inappropriate surfaces; and (4) Agent (Placement) provides a VLM agent with our generated 3D assets, the text prompt, and the same selected coarse scene, allowing autonomous placement without our placement pipeline.

    Contact Spread.
