    For each object, we select the lowest 12% of sampled points and cluster them into four contact regions using k-means. The lowest point in each region is selected, and its vertical gap to the underlying terrain is computed via ray casting. Contact Spread is defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum gaps, capturing uneven grounding independently of terrain elevation.

    Both contact metrics are computed only for surface-supported objects (rooted, upright, tilted, conform, and afloat; afloat is measured against the water surface); airborne and submerged objects are excluded, while the Unreadable Rate covers all placed objects. Ground-contact Error uses the absolute gap, so floating and penetration both count by magnitude. Objects whose contact rays find no supporting surface, or that failed to populate, are excluded. P95 is the nearest-rank 95th percentile of per-object values pooled across all surface-supported requested-add objects in the 20 scenes. For Agent (Placement), anchoring types are inferred from the full-pipeline runs; objects without a counterpart, and plant assets whose lowest vertices are foliage rather than ground contacts, are excluded from its contact statistics.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把 VLM 的代码能力关进程序化生成的「符号约束」里，既拿到写实可编辑资产，又保住种子多样性，100 物体 + 20 场景任务全面领先。

要点：

  • 纯 VLM 写 Blender 代码只能产出较简单的 3D 资产，而成熟程序化系统（如 4 万行代码的 Infinigen）需要大量手工开发，两者都没解决开放性问题
  • Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation：用既有程序化算法扩展出新资产品类，同时保留可编辑性与基于种子的多样性，而不是自由写几何
  • 端到端 text-to-world：语义场景规划 + Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement，保证大尺度世界里的物体摆放精确、程序化填充与动画一致
  • 100 个物体生成与 20 个场景生成任务上四项感知指标全面提升，另有多样性分析与人工偏好评测

为什么值得看：对引擎侧最直接的价值是资产仍然「可编辑、可改参数、可重出」：输出不是网格汤而是程序，能进 DCC 与引擎的常规资产流水线。

中文摘要：程序化生成在可控性、可编辑性和多样性上明显优于静态网格，是合成数据与游戏开发的关键手段；但传统方法依赖手工规则与预制资产工厂，而近年用 VLM 直接写代码生成 3D 的方法又只能做出相对简单的资产。作者提出 InfiniDream：先用符号约束的资产生成，把 VLM 的生成能力接到既有程序化算法上，从而在未知资产品类上也能产出写实、可编辑、种子可复现的资产；再搭一条端到端 text-to-world 管线，把语义场景规划与确定性视锥引导的网格摆放结合，生成大规模 3D 世界并保持精确摆放、程序化填充与动画。在 100 个物体与 20 个场景任务上，四项感知指标均优于对比方法，多样性与人工偏好评测同样支持这一结论。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·AI原生（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

InfiniDream: Open-Ended Photorealistic 3D Worlds Through Procedural Generation

October 20, 2026

Abstract

Procedural generation plays a key role in synthetic data creation and game development, offering greater controllability, editability, and diversity than static mesh representations. However, VLM-based code generation often produces relatively simple 3D assets, while sophisticated photorealistic procedural systems require extensive manual development. Existing VLM-guided procedural methods remain largely constrained by predefined factories and APIs, limiting their ability to create novel asset types. We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. First, we propose Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which leverages existing procedural algorithms to create novel, photorealistic assets while preserving editability and seed-based diversity. Second, we develop an end-to-end text-to-world pipeline that combines semantic scene planning with Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement to construct large-scale 3D worlds with precise object placement, procedural population, and animation. Extensive evaluations on 100 object and 20 scene generation tasks demonstrate improvements across four perceptual metrics. Diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference evaluations further validate the effectiveness of our framework.

Project page:https://yichuanh.github.io/infinidream-page/
Code:https://github.com/yichuanH/InfiniDream
Correspondence:wangzx1994@gmail.com, kaipeng.zhang@shanda.com, yulunliu@cs.nycu.edu.tw

1 Introduction

Procedural generation creates 3D assets and scenes through executable programs, offering editability, diversity, and scalability. These advantages have made it widely applicable to synthetic data generation, game development, and virtual world creation [(70)]. However, conventional procedural generation methods rely heavily on handcrafted rules and predefined asset generators, limiting the variety of generated content and their ability to create novel assets and scenes.

Recent advances in the code generation and tool-use capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled the generation and editing of 3D assets and scenes through executable Blender code [(28, 55, 73, 110, 24, 96)]. However, while existing approaches can construct scenes by composing assets or directly synthesizing geometry through code, generating large-scale 3D scenes with consistently rich geometric details, complex materials, and photorealistic appearance remains challenging.

Infinigen [(70)] is built on over 40,000 lines of code, including carefully handcrafted procedural asset factories, to generate photorealistic, editable 3D scenes. However, its generative capabilities remain constrained by predefined asset categories and procedural rules.

Recent studies have explored using LLMs and VLMs to control sophisticated procedural generation systems through function orchestration, parameter adjustment, and the composition of existing generators [(82, 119, 117)]. While these approaches improve the controllability of procedural scene generation, methods that primarily operate within predefined functions and parameter spaces remain limited in their ability to create novel asset types beyond the capabilities of existing generators.

Another line of research explores large-scale 3D world generation using retrieved or generatively synthesized mesh assets [(23, 92)]. Although these methods support instance-level editing, their mesh-based assets lack the parameterized editability and seed-based diversity of procedural generators. Producing diverse object variations often requires direct mesh manipulation or regeneration.

Figure 2 highlights three limitations: VLM Harness produces less photorealistic scenes, Infinigen is restricted to predefined factories, and Code2Worlds [(117)], a recent VLM-guided Infinigen framework, is limited to function calls and parameter adjustment. These limitations motivate open-ended procedural generation beyond existing factory capabilities.

To address these challenges, we introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation, designed to achieve realism, open-endedness, editability, diversity, and scalability. By employing VLM reasoning to compose and extend sophisticated procedural programs, InfiniDream generates novel assets beyond predefined factories while leveraging existing procedural algorithms. Our framework enables the creation of photorealistic, editable, and diverse large-scale 3D worlds from natural language descriptions.

At the asset level, Fig. 3 further motivates our Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE) strategy, which combines the flexibility of VLM-based code generation with the rich procedural structures of existing factories.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • 1.

    Open-Ended Procedural Asset Generation. We propose Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE) to generate novel, photorealistic procedural assets with rich geometric details beyond predefined factories, while preserving editability and seed-based diversity.

  • 2.

    Scalable Procedural World Generation. We introduce an end-to-end text-to-world framework combining semantic scene planning and deterministic frustum-guided grid placement to generate large-scale, editable 3D worlds.

  • 3.

    Comprehensive Experimental Validation. We conduct extensive object- and scene-level evaluations, diversity analysis, ablation studies, and human preference studies to validate the effectiveness of InfiniDream.

    • 2 Related Work

    Procedural 3D Asset Generation.

    Procedural modeling encodes 3D content as executable rules, from L-systems [(50, 66)] and shape grammars [(97, 60)] to learned procedural shape and CAD programs [(77, 89, 36, 37, 38, 72, 98, 41)]. Advances in code generation [(4)] and tool use [(75, 109)] now let language models synthesize editable 3D assets as Blender code [(13, 55, 73, 96, 105, 9, 69)], other shape programs [(114, 39, 94, 49)], or CAD scripts for mechanical parts [(2, 93, 74, 57)]. Multimodal reasoning, retrieval augmentation [(43)], and iterative visual feedback [(2, 93, 94, 49)] further improve reconstruction, editing, and visual fidelity [(29, 110, 24, 96)]. Procedural material graphs are likewise generated or inferred from images [(78, 21, 27, 44, 45)], whereas inverse procedural modeling fits predefined procedural generators to targets [(85, 91, 81, 63, 118)] and remains bounded by their categories. Still, reliably synthesizing complex procedural geometry with rich geometric details and photorealistic appearance remains challenging. Benchmarks for 3D code generation [(19, 96, 13, 2, 20, 107, 52)] assess executability, geometric fidelity, and the benefits of execution feedback [(6)] and agentic coding [(106)]. However, 3DCodeBench [(19)] draws its procedural modeling categories from predefined Infinigen factories [(70, 71)], leaving procedural asset generation beyond these categories underexplored.

    3D World Generation.

    Procedural content generation [(80, 25, 76)] has long produced noise-based terrains [(64, 61)] and cities [(62)], and now yields photorealistic natural and indoor scenes [(70, 71, 69)], simulation-ready assets [(40)], and houses for embodied AI [(11)]. Language models have been leveraged for 3D scene planning, spatial reasoning, and executable scene construction [(28, 82, 119, 117, 15, 108, 3, 17, 83, 1, 116, 86, 22)], and one line couples them with existing procedural generators through function orchestration, parameter adjustment, and composition of predefined procedural assets [(82, 119, 67, 117, 115, 53, 87, 54)]. Related approaches [(28, 110, 117)] also explore hierarchical generation [(17, 84, 95)], iterative visual feedback [(51)], physics-aware dynamic simulation [(56)], and looping animation of static 3D scenes [(103)]. However, methods restricted to orchestrating predefined procedural generators remain confined to their asset categories and parameter spaces, while semantically consistent and geometrically precise object placement in complex scenes remains challenging. Another line of work builds large-scale worlds [(23, 92)] from procedural layouts, retrieved assets [(10, 108, 1, 12)], generative 3D models [(65, 26, 113, 101)], and object-level composition [(95, 31, 59)], expanding generatable content and enabling instance-level manipulation. However, these approaches and neural scene generators [(35, 46, 16, 112, 111, 88, 30, 5, 8, 18, 120, 14, 7, 48, 102, 42, 99, 58)] generally lack the reusable procedural structures and high-level parameters needed for procedural editing and seed-based geometric variation. Orthogonally, recent work decouples explicit world states from generative video rendering [(32, 34, 47)] and benchmarks whether video models render what a program specifies [(33)]; such systems still require an explicit world specification, which procedural world generation can supply. InfiniDream addresses these gaps: it enables open-ended procedural asset generation beyond predefined factories and integrates it into scalable, fully procedural 3D world generation, while preserving procedural editability and seed-based diversity.

    3 Method

    We introduce InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. Given a text prompt, our framework selects a suitable initial scene and employs a Director to produce a structured Scene Plan specifying asset requirements, semantic placement constraints, and motion. Our framework consists of two core components: Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation, which creates novel procedural assets through constrained editing, and Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement, which translates semantic constraints into precise 3D object placements. Finally, procedural asset pooling, terrain refinement, and animation enable diverse, large-scale world generation.

    3.1 Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation

    Since directly providing a VLM with the entire Infinigen codebase often leads to imprecise editing (Fig. 3), we propose Symbolically Constrained Editing (SCE), which extracts key code structures and explicit editing constraints, transforming a large procedural codebase into a manageable editing space (Fig. 4).

    3.1.1 Factory Mapping and Retrieval

    Given a text description and an optional reference image, the system retrieves the most relevant Infinigen factory and constructs a Factory Brief (Fig. 4(A)). It contains a Code Structure Map identifying key functions and dependencies, an Editable Surface consisting of asset-specific modules dynamically identified through depth-limited dependency analysis, and Linked Infrastructure providing read-only access to shared low-level algorithms (e.g., node graphs) via symbolic links. Together, these components establish explicit code-level constraints that restrict editing while preserving the underlying procedural algorithms. Further implementation details are provided in Appendix 12.

    3.1.2 Structured Planning and Coarse Construction

    The Planner produces a structured Editing Plan specifying the editing strategy (Strategy), target locations (Locate), required modifications (Edit), dependencies (Rely-on), and potential risks (Risks), as shown in Fig. 4(B). The plan also accounts for seed-dependent logic to preserve controllable procedural variation.

    We define three editing strategies: Tweak adjusts existing parameters and high-level logic; Create introduces new procedural functions; and Promote selectively extends editing permissions to protected modules when necessary. These strategies enable controlled expansion of the editing space.

    The Coarse Constructor executes the Editing Plan under these constraints (Fig. 4(C)), preserving the original factory entry points and function signatures to maintain compatibility with the population pipeline and random seed control. It reuses existing algorithms to construct a coarse procedural asset. SCE preserves seed-dependent randomness by adjusting sampling ranges rather than fixing parameters to match the reference image.

    3.1.3 Fine Refinement

    As shown in Fig. 4(D), the Reviser iteratively compares rendered results with the target description and reference image, identifying discrepancies in geometry, materials, and visual details. It then performs targeted code modifications within the established editing boundaries. A Selector identifies the best candidate across refinement iterations.

    Through constrained editing and iterative refinement, SCE generates novel procedural assets while preserving procedural editability and seed-controlled diversity.

    3.2 Semantic Placement Reasoning

    Given a text prompt and current scene information, the Director first formulates a natural-language plan and converts it into a structured Scene Plan specifying editing operations (add, replace, and delete), asset requirements, and semantic placement constraints (Fig. 5(A–B)).

    The Director selects among three placement modes: Hero for semantically significant objects, Scattering for large-area distributions, and Swarm for collective entities. Hero placement supports seven Anchoring types (rooted, upright, tilted, conform, afloat, airborne, and submerged). A Semantic Target and Surface Policy further specify target regions, permissible surface types, slope limits, and support conditions. Scattering and Swarm are controlled by density, coverage, and group size.

    The Director also determines the instance count N, distinct procedural prototypes K, World Motion, and Local Animation. World Motion specifies object trajectories and swept envelopes for collision checking. VLM decisions are restricted to discrete semantic operations and constraints, leaving continuous geometric computations to deterministic placement.

    3.3 Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement

    To avoid repeated VLM-based coordinate prediction and costly render-based verification, we propose Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement, which translates the Director’s semantic constraints into candidate 3D positions (Fig. 5(D)). Candidates are evaluated in a near-to-far order without additional VLM calls or iterative rendering.

    3.3.1 Frustum-based Candidate Generation

    Given the specified placement region, we discretize the camera’s image plane into a 2D grid and generate 3D candidate positions along the corresponding camera rays. For surface-supported objects, candidates are determined by ray intersections with scene geometry. For airborne and submerged objects, candidates are sampled at discrete depth intervals along each ray.

    3.3.2 Constraint-based Filtering and Depth-aware Placement

    Each candidate undergoes five deterministic checks: (1) Visibility, (2) Collision with motion swept envelopes, (3) Inter-instance Spacing, (4) Surface Policy, including surface type, slope limits, and full support, and (5) Projected-area Band, requiring a_\min≤a(p)≤a_\max.

    Given depth-sorted candidates ℂ={p₁,…,pₙ}, where gⱼ(p)∈{0,1} indicates satisfaction of constraint j, we select the nearest valid candidate:

    i^*=\min{i \middle| \bigwedgeⱼ₌₁⁵gⱼ(pᵢ)=1}, p^*=p_i^*.

    		(1)

    Combined with projected-area bounds, near-to-far search enables implicit size-aware placement, favoring closer positions for smaller objects and farther positions for larger ones. For multiple instances, the initial search depth increases progressively, while previously placed objects are included in subsequent collision checks. If no valid position exists, hierarchical constraint relaxation is applied (Appendix 13).

    3.4 Scalable Population and Animation

    We combine the procedural assets generated in Sec. 3.1 with the validated placements from Sec. 3.3 through semantically controlled asset pooling, terrain refinement, and procedural animation (Fig. 5(E)).

    Semantically Budgeted Asset Pooling.

    To reduce the repeated construction cost of complex procedural assets, we extend Infinigen’s asset pooling mechanism to independent object population. The Director determines the number of instances N and distinct procedural prototypes K based on scene requirements. For assets supporting seed-based variation, we generate K prototypes using different factory seeds and create N instances through linked duplication:

    M={Mₖ=G(sₖ)}ₖ₌₁^K, Iᵢ=Clone(M_((i-1)\bmodK)+1).

    		(2)

    Here, G denotes the procedural generator, sₖ is the seed for the k-th prototype, and Iᵢ is the i-th instance. This mechanism reduces expensive asset constructions from N to K while maintaining seed-based diversity across prototypes. Assets unsuitable for pooling are generated independently.

    Population, Terrain Refinement, and Animation.

    Procedural assets are placed according to their Anchoring modes and integrated with Infinigen’s fine terrain pipeline. Animation combines World Motion and Local Animation, with shared motion specifications ensuring consistency between placement constraints and actual trajectories. The final scene is then refined and rendered (Fig. 5(E–F)).

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate InfiniDream at both the object and scene levels, complemented by diversity experiments, ablation studies, and a user study.

    4.1 Evaluation Protocol and Baselines

    Object-level Evaluation.

    We compare InfiniDream against five baselines: VLM (one-shot), VLM (harness), VIGA [(110)], BlenderRAG [(73)], and Infinigen [(70)]. Following 3DCodeBench [(19)], we adopt its codebase for the two VLM baselines, evaluating single-turn code generation and iterative refinement with a native coding-agent harness. The remaining baselines represent visual-feedback refinement, retrieval-augmented generation, and original Infinigen factory outputs, respectively.

    Scene-level Evaluation.

    We compare large-scale world generation against VLM (harness), VIGA [(110)], Infinigen [(70)], and Code2Worlds [(117)], representing agentic code generation, visual-feedback refinement, original procedural scene generation, and LLM-driven hierarchical procedural orchestration, respectively.

    Implementation and Metrics.

    We use Claude Opus 4.8 for InfiniDream and all VLM-based baselines, with Blender 4.x for generation and rendering. We evaluate 100 object-level tasks across six categories and 20 scene-level tasks at resolutions of 1024×1024 and 960×540, respectively.

    We report CLIP [(68)], SigLIP2 [(90)], DINOv3 [(79)], and ImageReward [(104)]. At the object level, CLIP, SigLIP2, and ImageReward are averaged over four fixed views (45^∘, 135^∘, 225^∘, and 315^∘), while DINOv3 compares the front view against four held-out reference images, independently generated from the same text prompt, and reports the mean cosine similarity. We additionally report code executability. Scene-level metrics use each method’s primary camera view. For scene-level DINOv3, each method’s primary camera view is compared against a single per-prompt scene reference image, generated by Gemini 3 Pro Image from the same scene prompt as a photorealistic wide-angle photograph of the entire scene; the same reference is shared by all methods and is never provided to any method during generation. Further details are provided in the Appendix.

    Diversity Evaluation.

    We compare InfiniDream with TRELLIS.2 [(100)] on 15 text prompts. For each prompt, InfiniDream generates five variations using different random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 uses five independently generated reference images. We measure semantic consistency using SigLIP2 and visual diversity using average pairwise DINOv2 feature distance.

    4.2 Experimental Results

    Qualitative Comparisons

    Figures 6 and 7 present qualitative comparisons of InfiniDream with existing methods at the object and scene levels, highlighting differences in geometric detail, photorealism, and scene composition.

    Quantitative Comparisons

    As shown in Tables 2 and 2, InfiniDream achieves the highest scores across all four perceptual metrics at both the object and scene levels.

    Human Preference Study

    We conduct a human preference study with 30 participants across 10 object and 10 scene tasks. Participants compare results from competing methods based on semantic alignment and visual quality. Table 4 reports InfiniDream’s preference rates for each criterion and overall.

    4.3 Diversity Analysis

    For each text prompt, InfiniDream generates five variations using different random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 uses five independently generated reference images. We evaluate semantic consistency using SigLIP2 and visual diversity using average pairwise DINOv2 feature distance. InfiniDream achieves greater visual diversity while maintaining comparable semantic alignment (Fig. 8, Table 4).

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Object-level Ablation

    We evaluate six ablation settings on 25 animal and plant tasks: (1) w/o Ref. Image, (2) Random Factory, (3) w/o Planner, (4) Agent (Infinigen), (5) w/o Refiner, and (6) 3 Rounds. The full pipeline allows up to six refinement rounds. For Agent (Infinigen), Claude Opus 4.8 is given the entire Infinigen codebase and Bash access to autonomously write and edit code, render and inspect results, and determine when to stop within six rounds, without our structured planning or editing constraints. Quantitative and qualitative results are shown in Table 10 and Fig. 10.

    Scene-level Ablation.

    We evaluate four settings on 20 scenes: (1) w/o Grid Search, using direct 3D coordinate prediction; (2) w/o Anchoring, reverting to Infinigen’s grounding; (3) w/o Semantic Target, removing semantic surface constraints; and (4) Agent (Placement), allowing a VLM agent to autonomously place our generated 3D assets in the same selected coarse scene given the text prompt, without our placement pipeline.

    We evaluate three placement metrics: Unreadable Rate, the percentage of objects outside the camera view or occupying less than 0.1% of the image area; Ground-contact Error, the absolute distance between an object’s lowest contact point and its supporting surface, capturing floating or penetration; and Contact Spread, the difference between the maximum and minimum terrain-relative gaps across sampled contact points, capturing uneven grounding and partial suspension (surface-supported objects only; see Appendix 15). We report the 95th percentile (P95) for the latter two metrics. For Contact Spread, P95 is computed over per-object values pooled across all surface-supported requested-add objects in the 20 scenes. Results are shown in Table 5 and Fig. 11.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented InfiniDream, a VLM-driven framework for open-ended procedural 3D world generation. By combining Symbolically Constrained Asset Generation with semantic planning and deterministic placement, InfiniDream creates novel, photorealistic, and editable procedural assets and composes them into diverse, large-scale 3D worlds. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness at both the object and scene levels.

    Limitations and Future Work.

    Our current animation pipeline relies on a predefined set of motion types. Future work could explore VLM-generated animation code to support more complex and customized motions. We also aim to extend InfiniDream to indoor environments with more complex spatial relationships and object interactions.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    6 Additional Object-level Comparisons

    We provide additional qualitative comparisons of object-level generation across diverse asset categories in Fig. 12. All methods are evaluated using identical text prompts under the same experimental protocol described in Sec. 4.1. These additional examples further illustrate differences in geometric complexity, material details, and visual fidelity among the compared methods.

    7 Additional Scene-level Comparisons

    We provide additional qualitative comparisons of scene-level generation across diverse environments in Fig. 13. All methods are evaluated using identical text prompts under the same experimental protocol described in Sec. 4.1. These additional results illustrate differences in scene composition, geometric detail, semantic alignment, and visual fidelity across the compared methods.

    8 Additional Qualitative Comparison with GPT-6 Astra

    We provide an additional qualitative comparison with GPT-6 Astra in Fig. 14. This comparison is included as supplementary evidence beyond the main benchmark suite. Importantly, InfiniDream still uses Claude Opus 4.8 as the underlying VLM, while GPT-6 Astra serves as an additional strong proprietary baseline. Under identical text prompts, the results highlight differences in visual fidelity, geometric detail, material richness, and overall semantic composition.

    9 Additional Diversity Results

    We provide additional qualitative diversity comparisons between InfiniDream and TRELLIS.2 in Fig. 15. For each text prompt, InfiniDream generates five procedural variations by changing random seeds, while TRELLIS.2 generates five assets from independently generated reference images. These examples further illustrate the diversity of InfiniDream’s procedural assets while preserving semantic consistency and visual quality.

    10 Object-level Comparison with Code2Worlds

    We further compare InfiniDream with Code2Worlds on the 29 out of 100 object-level tasks supported by Code2Worlds. Due to its limited factory coverage, we report this comparison separately from the main benchmark.

    As shown in Fig. 16 and Table 6, InfiniDream achieves higher scores across all four metrics. Code2Worlds can exploit the parameter space of existing factories, such as adjusting the color of a fish, but cannot introduce novel procedural features beyond predefined generators. In contrast, InfiniDream extends existing procedural code to generate new geometric structures and fine-grained details, enabling more flexible open-ended asset generation.

    11 Man-Made Asset Generation

    Beyond natural assets, InfiniDream can retrieve and extend factories for man-made objects. As shown in Fig. 17, while VIGA performs well on geometric objects, InfiniDream achieves comparable structural quality with rich geometric and material details, demonstrating its versatility across both organic and man-made assets.

    12 Implementation Details of Symbolically Constrained Editing

    Reference Synthesis and Factory Retrieval.

    We use Gemini 3 Pro Image to generate an isolated reference object against a white background. Claude Opus 4.8 retrieves the most relevant Infinigen factory, with deterministic lexical matching as a fallback.

    Factory Brief Construction.

    Starting from the selected factory, we perform AST-based import graph traversal with a maximum depth of two. Asset-specific modules form the Editable Surface, while shared modules remain read-only Linked Infrastructure. Unrelated dependencies are pruned, and a VLM summarizes the remaining code into a cached Code Structure Map.

    Constrained Code Editing.

    The Planner produces an Editing Plan specifying Strategy, Locate, Edits, Rely-on, and Risks. The Constructor can modify existing modules (Tweak), promote protected modules (Promote), or synthesize new procedural modules (Create). Editing is restricted to the working directory, preserving the original factory interface and seed-dependent randomness.

    Iterative Refinement.

    Modified modules are integrated into a symbolic-link overlay of the original Infinigen codebase. A vision-based Reviser guides targeted refinement, while execution failures trigger traceback-based repair. The pipeline supports up to six rounds with early stopping. A vision-based Selector chooses the best successful candidate, whose code snapshot is used to reconstruct the final executable generator.

    13 Implementation Details of Deterministic Frustum-Guided Grid Placement

    Candidate Generation.

    We discretize the Director’s screen-space region into a 9×5 grid (17×9 for six or more instances). Surface candidates are obtained through ray-scene intersections, while airborne and submerged candidates are sampled along camera rays using geometric depth intervals (×1.3, up to 80 m). Larger objects are placed first, with deterministic hashing ensuring reproducibility. The entire placement process requires no additional VLM calls.

    Constraints and Relaxation.

    Projected area is estimated from the proxy bounding box, with a preferred minimum of 1.2%, a relaxed minimum of 0.2%, and an absolute maximum of 25%. Collision checks account for motion-dependent swept envelopes, while surface placement additionally enforces slope limits and four-corner footprint support. When no valid candidate is found, constraints are progressively relaxed and the search region is expanded. Water-related constraints remain enforced, and all relaxations are recorded in the resulting placement plan.

    14 Baseline Implementation Details

    Baseline Implementations.

    We adopt the official implementations of all baselines, adding Claude Opus 4.8 API adapters where necessary. The VLM (one-shot) and VLM (harness) baselines follow 3DCodeBench, with the latter supporting autonomous code execution and iterative refinement.

    SigLIP2 Score Computation.

    All SigLIP2 scores in this paper (Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, 7) are computed with google/siglip2-base-patch16-224 and reported as the cosine similarity between L2-normalized image and text embeddings, recovered from the model’s image–text logits via \cos=(logit-b)/t, where t=112.67 and b=-16.77 are SigLIP2’s learned temperature and bias. Scores are averaged over the four azimuth views at the object level (Tables 1, 5, 7), the primary camera view at the scene level (Table 2), and the five variations per prompt in the diversity evaluation (Table 4).

    Object-level Baselines.

    All methods receive identical text prompts and reference images, except BlenderRAG, which only supports text inputs. Each task has five Gemini-generated reference images: ref_00 is the conditioning reference provided to the generation methods, while ref_01–ref_04 are held out exclusively for evaluation (DINOv3) and the human study and are never shown to any method; the conditioning reference is never used for scoring. All assets are evaluated under identical camera, lighting, background, and rendering settings. Failed generations are retained as blank renders rather than excluded.

    Scene-level Baselines.

    All scene-level methods receive identical text prompts and follow their respective official scene generation and camera selection pipelines. For InfiniDream, the Scene Picker automatically retrieves the most relevant initial coarse scene based on the input prompt from a library of 70 pre-generated environments (14 biomes with five seeds each), which is then used as the basis for subsequent procedural editing. The library was built before the benchmark prompts were finalized and was not modified afterwards. For reproducibility, the Scene Picker’s selection is made once per task, and the chosen base scene and seed are then fixed across all benchmark and ablation runs. The other baselines do not use this library. Code2Worlds selects from its available procedural factories even when no closely matching category exists.

    Failure Handling.

    We resolve version- and environment-related execution issues wherever possible to ensure that baselines run as intended. We do not report a separate scene-level executability metric.

    15 Ablation Study Details

    Object-level Ablation.

    We provide additional implementation details for the six ablation settings: (1) w/o Ref. Image removes the reference image from the generation pipeline; (2) Random Factory replaces factory retrieval with random selection; (3) w/o Planner removes structured planning and replaces the Editing Plan with empty content; (4) Agent (Infinigen) gives a Claude Opus 4.8 coding-agent harness access to the entire Infinigen codebase and Bash tools, allowing autonomous code generation, rendering, and refinement without SCE constraints, for up to six rounds; (5) w/o Refiner removes fine-level refinement; and (6) 3 Rounds limits the refinement budget to three rounds, compared with six in the full method.

    Scene-level Ablation.

    We evaluate four placement variants: (1) w/o Grid Search removes discrete semantic planning and grid-based placement, allowing the Director to predict continuous 3D coordinates directly; (2) w/o Anchoring replaces our seven anchoring types with Infinigen’s original grounding mechanism; (3) w/o Semantic Target removes semantic surface constraints from grid search, allowing placements on semantically inappropriate surfaces; and (4) Agent (Placement) provides a VLM agent with our generated 3D assets, the text prompt, and the same selected coarse scene, allowing autonomous placement without our placement pipeline.

    Contact Spread.

    For each object, we select the lowest 12% of sampled points and cluster them into four contact regions using k-means. The lowest point in each region is selected, and its vertical gap to the underlying terrain is computed via ray casting. Contact Spread is defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum gaps, capturing uneven grounding independently of terrain elevation.

    Both contact metrics are computed only for surface-supported objects (rooted, upright, tilted, conform, and afloat; afloat is measured against the water surface); airborne and submerged objects are excluded, while the Unreadable Rate covers all placed objects. Ground-contact Error uses the absolute gap, so floating and penetration both count by magnitude. Objects whose contact rays find no supporting surface, or that failed to populate, are excluded. P95 is the nearest-rank 95th percentile of per-object values pooled across all surface-supported requested-add objects in the 20 scenes. For Agent (Placement), anchoring types are inferred from the full-pipeline runs; objects without a counterpart, and plant assets whose lowest vertices are foliage rather than ground contacts, are excluded from its contact statistics.

item.title: 让视频世界模型直接吐出 4D 高斯：AEON 在视频潜空间里生成，输出可渲染可编辑的 4DGS 世界 ｜ Aeon: Unifying Video and 3D World Models
item.description:
一句话：视频模型好看但不保 3D 一致、3D 模型一致却静态：AEON 在视频 latent 空间生成，落地成 4DGS 显式表示，两头都要。

要点：

  • 生成发生在文/图条件化的视频潜空间里，但输出是 4D Gaussian Splatting 这一可渲染的显式世界表示
  • 先用单目视频训一个 4D 重建模型（同时预测 4DGS 与相机位姿）作为初始化好的 4D 解码器
  • domain adapter 通过在视频 VAE 上蒸馏，把生成 latent 翻译成重建 latent，把两条范式接起来
  • 渲染 4DGS 即可按预测相机轨迹做视频式世界建模，同时得到带动力学、可编辑、可实时探索的持久 4D 环境

为什么值得看：生成式引擎若要「可回看、可编辑、可实时重渲」，输出必须是显式表示而不是像素流；4DGS 目前是最现实的中转格式，这条路线值得对照自己引擎的资产与相机管线。

中文摘要：显式世界模拟目前分成两条互斥路线：视频生成模型（如 Sora）外观真实但保不住 3D 一致；3D 生成模型（如 Marble）几何一致却往往产静态、欠真实的观测。AEON 试图统一两者：生成发生在文/图条件化的视频潜空间里，产出的却是有空间局域性的显式图元——4D Gaussian Splatting，从而同时具备写实外观、动态演化、3D 一致、场景持久与实时探索五点。实现上先训一个从单目视频预测 4DGS 与相机位姿的 4D 重建模型作为 4D 解码器，再设计 domain adapter，在视频 VAE 上做蒸馏把生成潜变量转成重建潜变量。这样渲染 4DGS 就能按预测轨迹做视频式世界建模，同时得到一个可编辑、可仿真的持久 4D 场景，在标准基准上取得最优结果。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

Aeon: Unifying Video and 3D World Models

Abstract

Current world models for explicit world simulation typically follow two distinct pathways: (1) video generative models (e.g., Sora), which simulate realistic appearances but fail to preserve 3D consistency; and (2) 3D generative models (e.g., Marble), which generate geometrically consistent scenes but often yield static, less realistic observations. We present AEON, a unified framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based world models and combines the benefits of both. The key insight of AEON lies in a generative model that operates within the text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing renderable 4D graphics primitives—specifically, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)—as the explicit world representation. We train a 4D reconstruction model to predict both 4DGS and camera poses from monocular videos, serving as our initialized 4D decoder. Furthermore, we design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into reconstructive 4D latents through a distillation process on the video VAE. AEON naturally supports video-based world modeling by rendering 4DGS at predicted camera trajectories, and constructs a persistent 4D environment with scene dynamics for realistic world simulation. Consequently, AEON empowers a diverse range of world modeling applications and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON.

22footnotetext: The corresponding authors are Yu-Shen Liu and Junsheng Zhou.

1 Introduction

World modeling has rapidly advanced to the forefront of AI research, driven by its immense potential in embodied AI, autonomous driving, and game design. Despite this progress, there remains a lack of consensus on the optimal representation for explicit world simulation, leaving the field divided between two dominant paradigms: video-based [26, 38] and 3D-based world models [45, 14]. As highlighted in Table 1, these approaches possess orthogonal strengths and suffer from fundamental, paradigm-specific bottlenecks. Consequently, a more powerful and unified representation is imperative to achieve comprehensive world modeling.

We begin by asking a fundamental question: What constitutes a good world model? To train robots to understand physical laws and perceive scenes, a world model should exhibit the following properties: (1) generating realistic appearances that align with real-world domains; (2) modeling dynamic scene evolution (e.g., fire, waves) and moving objects; (3) maintaining 3D consistent environments free from geometric ambiguity; (4) ensuring scene persistence for continuous and repeatable simulation; and (5) supporting real-time exploration to facilitate efficient interaction. We argue that a representation unifying video- and 3D-based world models, thereby benefiting from their complementary strengths, is the key to achieving such an ideal world model.

We present AEON, a generative world model that introduces 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) [41, 53] as its foundational representation, unifying video and 3D models to benefit from both paradigms. 4DGS represents scenes as a set of explicit graphics primitives localized in spatial geometry, and models scene dynamics through the velocity-driven movement and time-varying visibility of these primitives. Consequently, a learned 4DGS representation provides two independent yet crucial capabilities: it models world appearances through direct rendering along user-defined camera trajectories, and it establishes a persistent 4D environment that supports highly controllable 3D simulations. Additionally, it enables explicit modeling of world geometry and physical states, including depth, normals, motion, and optical flow.

Despite the comprehensive capabilities inherent to the 4DGS representation, most existing approaches restrict its application to reconstruction tasks, and generating a persistent 4DGS world directly from text or image conditions remains largely unexplored. In AEON, we propose a novel framework that integrates the generative latent space of a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [38, 29] with the reconstructive latent space of a 4D reconstruction model. Specifically, we train a 4D Gaussian Reconstruction Model (4DRM) to jointly predict 4DGS attributes and camera poses from monocular videos. By utilizing a large-scale annotated 4D video dataset and pretrained geometric priors from MapAnything [17], a scalable geometry model, the 4DRM develops robust reconstructive capabilities to recover world geometry and dynamics. A primary challenge, however, is the significant domain gap between the video and 4DRM latent spaces. We address this by introducing a domain adapter that seamlessly bridges the two. Finally, we employ a multi-stage training pipeline that optimizes the adapter and fine-tunes the reconstruction model through end-to-end distillation from the video model, supervised by video VAE-decoded outputs.

Consequently, AEON unlocks an extensive array of world modeling applications, including text/image/video-to-4DGS generation, 3D world generation, robotics simulation, physical state estimation (e.g., depth, normals, and optical flow), scene editing, and novel view and timestep synthesis.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce AEON, a unified world modeling framework that represents worlds as explicit 4D Gaussians, effectively bridging video-based and 3D-based models to benefit from their complementary strengths.

  • •

    We propose a novel methodology that integrates the generative latent space of a pretrained video DiT with the reconstructive latent space of a 4D Gaussian reconstruction model. To achieve this, we train a specialized domain adapter through an end-to-end distillation of the video model.

  • •

    AEON demonstrates comprehensive versatility, natively supporting a diverse spectrum of world modeling tasks, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video and 3D World Models

    World modeling aims to generate explorable and realistic environments from conditional inputs (e.g., text or images), serving as a foundation for embodied AI and autonomous systems. Current paradigms primarily rely on video-based [26, 11, 32, 19, 52, 38] or 3D-based [45, 35, 51, 14, 33, 3, 10] approaches. Within the video-centric domain, JEPA-style methods [2, 1] excel at forecasting future latent states but lack explicit visual synthesis. Conversely, video world models [26, 38, 19] and their action-conditioned variants [5, 44, 36, 37] can synthesize photorealistic frames, yet they struggle with 3D consistency and incur heavy computational costs due to massive per-frame token generation.

    Alternatively, 3D world models [45, 14] construct explicit environments for simulation. Recent works have explored panoramic generation [35, 51], progressive expansion [14], or leveraging video priors [3]. However, these methods typically employ static representations such as 3DGS [18] or meshes, precluding the modeling of world dynamics and limiting their ability to scale on dynamic internet video datasets. The same holds for 3D generation and reconstruction more broadly, which mostly build on static Gaussians [62, 59, 58, 56, 47] or distance fields [63, 64, 25, 24]. To bridge this gap, we propose AEON, a framework that generates renderable 4D Gaussian Splatting [53, 41] (4DGS) primitives as an explicit world representation. AEON effectively unifies the strengths of both paradigms, achieving dynamic modeling with 3D consistency while overcoming their respective limitations.

    2.2 4D Gaussian Splatting from Videos

    4D Gaussian Splatting [53, 41] advances the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting [18] for modeling scene dynamics. 4DGS learns from multi-view videos to predict Gaussian primitives with explicit temporal attributes such as lifespan, velocity, and time-varying opacity, allowing Gaussians to appear, move, and vanish independently. However, predicting 4DGS from monocular videos remains significantly more challenging due to limited observational data. While optimization-based methods [39, 20, 34] can achieve faithful visual appearances, they require lengthy fitting processes and struggle to generalize or scale. More recently, feed-forward frameworks [31, 48, 50, 22, 60] have been proposed for fast and scalable video-to-4DGS reconstruction, including bullet-time reconstruction at arbitrary timestamps [21] and online reconstruction from uncalibrated video streams [46]. Some of these works predict deformable 3DGS [22, 28] as their foundational representation, which often falls short when modeling complex and diverse dynamics. Related feed-forward models also recover dynamic geometry and camera poses from monocular videos [8]. All of these methods reconstruct scenes from observed videos. Native 4DGS generation has also been explored for animated objects [57]. Closer to our setting, Diff4Splat [28] and Lyra [3] build Gaussian scenes on top of video diffusion priors, but both require a camera trajectory as input and represent dynamics with deformable 3DGS and per-frame 3DGS, respectively. AEON differs in both respects: it generates a world from a text prompt or a single image without camera input, and it represents the world as one persistent set of 4D primitives, each with its own reference time, duration, and velocity, so that content can appear, move, and vanish independently and can be rendered at any continuous timestep.

    3 Method

    We present AEON, a generative world model that operates within the latent space of a pretrained video diffusion model while producing explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) as the world representation. Given a text prompt or conditioning image, our goal is to generate a set of 4D Gaussians encoding both appearance and dynamics, enabling photorealistic rendering and persistent 3D simulation. The overview of AEON is shown in Fig. 2. We begin by introducing the 4DGS representation in Sec. 3.1, which models dynamic scenes through velocity-driven motion and time-varying visibility. In Sec. 3.2, we present the 4D Gaussian Reconstruction Model, whose four task-specific heads jointly predict depth, Gaussian appearance, dynamic evolution, and camera poses from monocular videos. We then describe our domain adapter in Sec. 3.3, which bridges the generative video latent space and the reconstructive 4D latent space through distillation. Finally, Sec. 3.4 details our multi-stage training strategy that optimizes the full pipeline end-to-end.

    3.1 4D Gaussian Splatting as the World Representation

    An ideal world model should jointly capture realistic appearances, scene dynamics, and 3D-consistent geometry within a persistent and efficiently renderable representation. To this end, AEON adopts 4D Gaussian primitives [41, 53, 60] as its foundational scene representation, where each primitive simultaneously encodes geometry, appearance, and temporal evolution. Formally, a single primitive gᵢ is characterized by the following parameter set

    gᵢ={xᵢ,sᵢ,rᵢ,oᵢ,cᵢ,tᵢ,lᵢ,vᵢ,ωᵢ}.

    		(1)

    Specifically, xᵢ∈ℝ³ denotes the spatial center, sᵢ∈ℝ² parameterizes anisotropic scaling along the principal axes, and rᵢ∈ℝ⁴ encodes the orientation as a unit quaternion. The base opacity oᵢ∈[0,1] together with the color cᵢ∈ℝ³ jointly determine the visual appearance of each primitive.

    In addition to these spatial attributes, four temporal parameters govern the dynamic behavior of each primitive. The reference timestep tᵢ∈[0,T] specifies the moment of peak activation, while the duration lᵢ∈ℝ⁺ controls the temporal extent over which the primitive remains visible. The linear velocity vᵢ∈ℝ³ and the angular velocity ωᵢ∈ℝ³ in axis-angle form capture translational and rotational motion, respectively. This decomposition into explicit spatial and temporal components enables AEON to model both persistent scene structure and transient dynamic phenomena within a unified representation.

    3.2 4D Gaussian Reconstruction Model

    While 4DGS offers an ideal world representation, directly generating 4D Gaussians from diverse conditions is highly challenging without proper guidance and geometric initialization. To address this, we first train a 4D Gaussian Reconstruction Model (4DRM) as a foundation, focusing on the more tractable task of world recovery from monocular videos. In a single feed-forward pass, 4DRM uses four task-specific heads to jointly predict depth, camera poses, and 4D Gaussian attributes of appearance and evolution. The model is trained end-to-end via differentiable rendering. Once trained, 4DRM facilitates AEON’s generative world modeling in two ways: (1) it provides a reconstructive foundation to initialize the student 4DRM that recovers the world from video latents, and (2) it acts as a teacher model, guiding the student to acquire 4D Gaussian modeling capabilities through distillation.

    Encoding.

    Given an input video V={Iₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ of T frames, we extract per-frame dense features Fₜ∈ℝ^H/p×W/p×D using a pretrained DINOv2 encoder [27]. To inject temporal identity, we add a sinusoidal positional embedding of the timestep index t to each spatial feature map. The resulting per-frame tokens are concatenated across all frames and processed by a transformer backbone of L layers that alternate between intra-frame and cross-frame self-attention, balancing computational efficiency with long-range temporal modeling. The output features F^S∈ℝ^THW/p²×D encode holistic spatio-temporal context for subsequent decoding. We initialize 4DRM from the pretrained weights of MapAnything [17], a feed-forward metric 3D reconstruction model.

    Decoding.

    We decode the shared spatio-temporal representation F^Sₜ through four task-specific heads, each responsible for a complementary component of the 4DGS world. The Depth Head predicts dense per-frame depth maps Dₜ∈ℝ^H×W, while the Camera Head regresses the intrinsics Kₜ together with per-frame rotations Rₜ (unit quaternions) and translations tₜ. The predicted depths are unprojected via Kₜ into the Gaussian centers xᵢ, anchoring all downstream predictions in a metrically grounded 3D space. Conditioned on these centers, the Gaussian Head predicts the appearance attributes {sᵢ,rᵢ,oᵢ,cᵢ} (scale, orientation, opacity, and color), and the Evolution Head predicts the dynamic attributes {tᵢ,lᵢ,vᵢ,ωᵢ} (temporal reference, duration, and linear and angular velocities) that govern how each primitive moves and fades over time. This decomposition lets the Gaussian and Evolution Heads focus exclusively on appearance and dynamics, while the Camera Head’s joint pose estimation enables 4DRM to operate directly on raw monocular videos, removing the dependency on pre-estimated poses or external Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines required by prior work [48, 22]. As a result, 4DRM recovers a complete dynamic world state from a single monocular video and establishes a robust reconstructive latent space for the subsequent generative integration.

    3.3 Generative World Modeling

    Overview.

    AEON is designed to generate persistent and explorable 4D worlds from diverse conditions, such as text prompts and images. The complete pipeline is illustrated in the lower portion of Fig. 2. Given a condition (e.g., a text prompt), we leverage a pretrained video diffusion model (e.g., Wan 2.2) as the generative foundation to produce a video latent, z_video. Given that z_video encapsulates profound world-modeling priors capable of decoding into realistic, high-quality videos, we aim to unlock its full potential by recovering an explicit and persistent 4DGS world. We introduce a Domain Adapter that performs latent translation, mapping the generative video latent z_video to a reconstructive 4D latent z_4D. A learnable student 4DRM then utilizes z_4D to explicitly recover the 4DGS world. A simpler alternative would decode z_video into frames with the VAE and pass them to the Stage-1 4DRM. We avoid this cascade because the 4DRM is trained on real videos, whereas decoded generations carry VAE and generation artifacts outside that distribution, so decoding errors would compound with reconstruction errors.

    A primary challenge in connecting the video generative model to the 4D reconstruction model is the significant domain gap between their latent representations. The video latent is optimized for generative denoising, while the 4DRM consumes DINOv2 [27] tokens that are trained for geometric and semantic understanding. These two feature spaces therefore occupy fundamentally different distributions. Naively replacing the DINOv2 patch embedding with a randomly initialized projection would forfeit the geometric prior carried by the pretrained backbone and force the student 4DRM to relearn its feature distribution from scratch. To avoid this, we introduce a learnable domain adapter that bridges the two latent spaces while preserving the geometric capabilities of the pretrained 4DRM backbone layers.

    Dual-Path Domain Adapter.

    We implement the domain adapter as a dual-path architecture that couples a linearly initialized convolutional branch with an expressive Perceiver Bridge. To establish a robust baseline, we first solve a closed-form ridge regression to map the video latents to the target DINOv2 activations at each candidate insertion depth ℓ. This linear mapping already recovers a coarse alignment, which makes it a good initialization, although on its own it falls well short of the full adapter (Sec. 4.4). Motivated by this, our dual-path design employs a linear branch to provide a stable foundation, while an expressive residual branch captures complex nonlinear transformations. Specifically, the linear branch L is instantiated as a strided 3D convolution initialized with the closed-form ridge solution. The residual branch ℕ comprises a Perceiver Bridge module, detailed below. A learnable scalar gate γ fuses the two branches as:

    Z=L(z_video)+γ·ℕ(z_video),

    		(2)

    where γ is initialized to zero. Consequently, the adapter’s optimization begins entirely from the stable linear solution and progressively incorporates the nonlinear residual branch as γ updates via gradient descent, ensuring stable optimization from the outset.

    Perceiver Bridge.

    Implementing the residual branch with standard convolutions inherently dilutes fine-grained geometric information due to their restricted local receptive fields. Instead, we design a highly expressive Perceiver [15] Bridge module that leverages a learned token-to-token retrieval with a global receptive field. The video latent is first projected into the target feature dimension by a spatio-temporal Conv3D. An asymmetric temporal upsampler then restores the original temporal resolution by bypassing the independently encoded first frame and applying sub-pixel shuffle to the remaining compressed tokens so that the output length matches the original video exactly. The upsampled tokens are passed into a stack of Perceiver-style cross-attention blocks, where a set of learnable spatial queries attend to the projected video tokens as key-value pairs. Both queries and keys carry fixed 2D sinusoidal positional embeddings, enabling explicit spatial alignment without any resolution-specific learned parameters. Each frame is processed independently through the stack, confining the attention cost to the two-dimensional spatial grid while temporal modeling is handled by the preceding Conv3D and upsampler. A final LayerNorm aligns the output distribution with that of the DINOv2 tokens.

    Token-Level Injection.

    The adapter output Z is integrated into the DINOv2 backbone at layer ℓ by bypassing the patch embedding and the initial ℓ transformer blocks, utilizing Z as the input tokens for the remaining blocks. Notably, these subsequent DINOv2 transformer blocks are fused into the 4DRM as part of the learnable spatio-temporal ViT. The selection of ℓ requires a careful trade-off: integrating the features too early imposes an excessive optimization burden on the adapter, whereas a late integration sacrifices essential geometric features relied upon by the downstream heads. Therefore, we set ℓ to the shallowest layer where the linear branch yields a reliable initialization. This strategy maximizes the number of retained upper blocks, effectively incorporating DINOv2’s geometric knowledge into the 4DRM.

    We train the student 4DRM and the domain adapter with both distillation losses and end-to-end rendering supervisions. The full training procedure is detailed in Sec. 3.4.

    3.4 Training Strategy

    We adopt a multi-stage pipeline that first builds a strong reconstructive backbone and then bridges the generative video latent space through generative distillation and end-to-end rendering refinement.

    Stage 1: Reconstruction Model Training. The 4DRM learns to map monocular video to 4D Gaussian primitives through large-scale training on posed videos. From each training clip of T frames, we select K frames as network input and predict a unified set of 4D Gaussians. These Gaussians are rendered back to all T frames via the differentiable rasterizer, yielding dense photometric supervision that extends well beyond the temporal coverage of the input. Our objective consists of three complementary terms that respectively enforce appearance fidelity, geometric grounding, and dynamic disentanglement.

    Appearance fidelity. We supervise rendered frames Ĩₜ against ground-truth observations Iₜ with a composite loss that balances pixel accuracy and perceptual quality:

    Lₐₚₚ=1/T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(∥Iₜ-Ĩₜ∥₂²+α·LPIPS(Iₜ,Ĩₜ)+β·(1-SSIM(Iₜ,Ĩₜ))).

    		(3)

    The perceptual and structural terms prevent convergence to overly smooth solutions and encourage sharp, realistic textures in the rendered output.

    Geometric grounding. Monocular video alone cannot resolve metric depth ambiguity. We therefore supervise predicted geometry directly with ground-truth depth and normal annotations from our training dataset. Specifically, we render per-frame depth d̃ₜ and normals ñₜ from the predicted 4DGS and minimize their discrepancy with the annotated counterparts dₜ^* and nₜ^*:

    L_geo=1/T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(μ∥dₜ^*-d̃ₜ∥₂²+ν∥nₜ^*-ñₜ∥₂²).

    		(4)

    Unlike prior methods that rely on pseudo labels from monocular expert models, training against metric ground truth provides an unambiguous supervisory signal and anchors all predictions in a consistent world-scale coordinate frame.

    Dynamic disentanglement. Without multi-view constraints, the network may collapse to a degenerate solution where every primitive is assigned a short lifespan, leading the representation to per-frame point clouds. To encourage proper separation of static structure from dynamic content, we penalize unnecessary motion and favor long-lived primitives:

    L_dyn=1/M∑ᵢ₌₁^M(η₁∥vᵢ∥₁+η₂∥ωᵢ∥₁+η₃ lᵢ⁻¹),

    		(5)

    where M is the total number of predicted Gaussians. These penalties ensure that non-trivial velocity and short lifespans are assigned only to genuinely dynamic elements, enabling the model to learn meaningful motion decomposition without explicit motion labels.

    The complete Stage 1 objective combines all three components:

    Lₛ₁=Lₐₚₚ+L_geo+L_dyn.

    		(6)

    Stage 2: Generative Distillation. In the second stage, we connect the generative video latent space to the reconstructive 4D space through end-to-end distillation. We freeze the pretrained 4DRM as a teacher and train the domain adapter alongside a student 4DRM. The teacher takes ground-truth RGB frames as input, while the domain adapter and student 4DRM operate solely on video latents. The training objective drives the student to reproduce the teacher’s 4DGS world reconstruction in a generative manner from the video latents. The overall distillation loss combines three complementary terms:

    L_distill=L_4DGS+L_geom+λ(t) L_feat.

    		(7)

    4D Gaussian attribute alignment.L_4DGS applies a weighted L1 loss between the per-primitive attributes predicted by the teacher and the student, covering spatial position, anisotropic scale, rotation, opacity, color, velocity, and lifespan. This term provides the most direct form of knowledge transfer by enforcing primitive-level correspondence in attribute space.

    Dense geometric alignment. Attribute-space supervision alone is insufficient since distinct sets of Gaussian attributes can produce visually equivalent renderings, while small attribute deviations may cause large visual discrepancies. To address this ambiguity, L_geom supervises the per-view dense geometric predictions from the student 4DRM heads, combining a robust log-depth regression loss, a multi-scale depth gradient term for boundary sharpness, and an L1 penalty on predicted camera parameters. We apply a global scale normalization before computing this loss to eliminate the trivial scale ambiguity between the two models.

    Feature alignment.L_feat regularizes the domain adapter by aligning the student’s intermediate features at the bridge output with the corresponding teacher activations through an L1 loss. Its weight λ(t) follows a cosine decay schedule that imposes strong regularization in early training to prevent catastrophic drift of the adapter and gradually relaxes to let the task-specific losses dominate.

    Together, these objectives supervise the distillation process at complementary granularities. The attribute loss effectively instills the teacher’s 4D reconstruction capabilities into the student, while the geometric and feature losses simultaneously drive domain adaptation by forcing the adapter to project the video latent space onto the reconstructive 4D latent space.

    Stage 3: End-to-End Rendering Refinement. Distillation losses operate in attribute and feature space and do not directly reflect final rendering quality. We therefore fine-tune the domain adapter and student 4DRM with an end-to-end rendering loss, where pseudo ground-truth frames are obtained by decoding z_video through the frozen VAE decoder and compared against the rasterized 4DGS output using the same appearance objective as Stage 1. Gradients flow through the differentiable rasterizer into the full pipeline, so the student is optimized for rendering quality directly rather than only imitating the teacher. A linearly decayed distillation regularizer preserves the geometric structure acquired in Stage 2.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 4D Generation

    We evaluate AEON against 4DNex [7] and Lyra [3] for 4D generation. Unlike 4DNex (per-frame point clouds) and Lyra (per-frame 3DGS), AEON predicts a unified 4DGS representation for real-time exploration. We evaluate on 30 scenes, each specified by an image-text prompt. Evaluation videos, rendered along shared camera trajectories from identical image-text prompts, are assessed via VBench [13] metrics: I2V Subject, Subject Consistency, Motion Smoothness, and Aesthetic Quality. As shown in Table 2, AEON outperforms all baselines. While per-frame reconstruction lacks cross-frame coherence, AEON models scenes via persistent 4D Gaussians with explicit velocity and duration, naturally ensuring temporal consistency. Additionally, AEON generalizes across backbones (Wan 2.1 and Wan 2.2) without architectural modifications, yielding consistently strong results.

    4.2 Video-to-4D Reconstruction

    We evaluate AEON for 4D reconstruction on Dycheck [9] and DaVis [30] against SOTA baselines: L4GM [31], 4DGT [48], MoVies [22], NeoVerse [50], and StreamSplat [46]. Unlike 4DGT and MoVies, which rely on external poses (from GT or π³[42]), AEON’s integrated camera head jointly predicts camera parameters and 4DGS attributes from monocular RGB. StreamSplat additionally requires monocular depth from Depth Anything V2 [49], which AEON does not need. For Dycheck’s novel view synthesis, we assess our video-to-4DGS pipeline by encoding input video into the VAE latent space and decoding it via the domain adapter and student reconstruction model.

    As summarized in Table 3, AEON achieves superior PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS across both benchmarks. Despite operating through the video VAE latent bottleneck, AEON’s domain adapter effectively preserves the geometric details necessary for high-fidelity reconstruction, with especially pronounced gains on complex DaVis sequences. Furthermore, AEON needs neither camera poses nor depth at inference, and only Stage 1 uses annotated videos, so the later training stages can scale to raw videos. Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 3 further corroborate these quantitative trends.

    4.3 Novel Trajectory Rendering

    We collect 30 in-the-wild videos unseen during training and render each scene along several novel camera trajectories. We compare against TrajectoryCrafter [54], RecamMaster [4], and NeoVerse [50], reporting six VBench [13] metrics in Table 4. AEON achieves the best scores on four out of six metrics while remaining competitive on the other two. Since rendering a new trajectory from 4DGS is geometrically exact rasterization rather than learned hallucination, AEON naturally maintains strong consistency and visual quality across viewpoint changes.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    We ablate three key design choices of AEON under the Dycheck and DaVis benchmarks in Table 5. Conv3D projection replaces the full dual-path domain adapter with a single Conv3D layer, showing that the expressive Perceiver Bridge branch is essential for capturing the complex mapping between the two latent spaces. W/o Distill removes the distillation losses and trains the adapter with rendering supervision alone, resulting in a significant performance drop, especially on DaVis, which highlights the importance of the teacher 4DRM as a geometric foundation. W/o Duration disables the temporal opacity evolution of 4DGS, forcing all primitives to remain visible throughout the sequence; the degradation shows that explicit duration modeling of 4DGS representation is critical for handling transient dynamics. The full model combines all components and achieves the best performance on every metric.

    5 Conclusion

    We present AEON, a unified world modeling framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based paradigms and combines the benefits of both. The core of AEON is a generative model that operates within the latent space of a pretrained video diffusion model while producing explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting as the world representation. We train a 4DRM for robust geometric guidance and design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into the reconstructive 4D latents through end-to-end distillation. Experiments across 4D generation, dynamic-scene reconstruction, and novel trajectory rendering demonstrate that AEON achieves state-of-the-art performance while supporting a broad spectrum of world modeling applications within a single unified framework.

    Limitations and future work.

    The temporal extent of generated 4D scenes is currently bounded by the video diffusion model’s sequence length. Because AEON stores the world as a persistent 4DGS rather than as frames, it offers a natural path beyond this window: render conditioning frames from the current 4DGS at the latest camera pose, generate the next window, decode it into new primitives, and fuse them with the existing world where they overlap. Since each step is anchored to explicit geometry rather than extrapolated from previous frames, drift should accumulate more slowly than in video-only autoregression. In addition, regions never observed in the generated video cannot be recovered, so very large viewpoint changes may reveal holes that a generative completion module could fill.

    Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding

    This work was partially supported by Deep Earth Probe and Mineral Resources Exploration – National Science and Technology Major Project (2024ZD1003405) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62272263).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    The 4DRM encoder is built on DINOv2-Large [27] with 24 transformer blocks of dimension 1024. The 4DRM is initialized from the pretrained MapAnything weights [17]. The domain adapter is injected at layer ℓ=4, retaining the upper 20 pretrained transformer blocks as a geometric foundation for the 4DRM. The Linear branch projects the 16-channel Wan video latent to 1024 channels, initialized via closed-form ridge regression against the fourth-layer DINOv2 activations. The Perceiver Bridge employs 4 cross-attention blocks with 16 heads and 1024 learnable queries, and a temporal interleave of factor 4 inverts the video VAE’s temporal compression. All three stages are optimized with AdamW using a weight decay of 10⁻⁴, a cosine schedule with 2 000 linear warmup steps, a base learning rate of 5×10⁻⁶, and gradient clipping at a global norm of 1.0.

    Stage 1 trains the full 4DRM for 20 epochs on video clips with ground-truth camera poses and depth annotations. The appearance loss weights are α=2.0 and β=0.2, the geometry weights are μ=1.0 and ν=0.5, and the dynamic regularization coefficients are η₁=η₂=η₃=0.3. Stage 2 freezes the Stage-1 model as the teacher and trains the domain adapter and the student 4DRM for 30 additional epochs with a 10× learning rate multiplier on the adapter parameters. Since the frozen teacher provides all supervisory signals through distillation, Stage 2 requires only raw RGB videos as input, removing the dependency on pose and depth annotations and enabling training on large-scale unannotated data. The feature alignment weight λ decays from 1.0 to 0 following a cosine schedule. All experiments are conducted on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The Stage-1 training corpus combines DynamicReplica [16], SAILVOS3D [12], Spring [23], TartanAir [40], PointOdyssey [61], and OmniWorld [65], each providing ground-truth camera poses and depth. Because these datasets differ in size by orders of magnitude, we resample the smaller ones by the factors listed in Table 6, so that every source contributes to geometric supervision. In Stage 2, we further incorporate Panda-70M [6] to expand the training distribution beyond annotated domains; it supplies real-world appearance diversity without geometric labels. Stage 3 continues to train the domain adapter and student 4DRM for 10 additional epochs with the end-to-end rendering loss, using the same optimizer configuration as Stage 2. The distillation regularization weight λ_reg is initialized to 0.5 and linearly decayed to zero over the course of training.

    Appendix B Applications

    Text/Image-to-world generation.

    As illustrated in Fig. 1, AEON synthesizes high-quality 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) environments from text or image prompts. This is achieved by first generating video latents using Wan-DiT conditioned on the input prompts. These latents are subsequently translated into 4D spatial-temporal latents and decoded to reconstruct the final 4DGS world.

    Video-to-world reconstruction.

    For video-to-world reconstruction, input videos are encoded into video latents using Wan-VAE. These latents are then processed to generate 4DGS scenes, following the same pipeline as our text/image-to-world generation.

    Novel view synthesis.

    The generated 4DGS representations inherently support real-time novel view synthesis across arbitrary viewpoints and timesteps.

    Physical status estimation.

    The generated 4DGS encapsulates rich geometric and physical properties, which can be directly extracted to derive depth maps, normal maps, motion masks, and optical flow. Specifically, motion masks are obtained by filtering the lifespans of the Gaussians, as dynamic elements typically correspond to Gaussians with shorter lifespans.

    3D world generation.

    Beyond dynamic scene generation, AEON is also highly effective for static 3D world generation. An example of this capability is provided in the third row of Fig. 1.

    Scene editing and simulation.

    Because AEON generates explicit 4D representations, it inherently facilitates seamless scene editing and structural decomposition for downstream simulations (shown in the bottom row of Fig. 1). By leveraging the motion masks derived from Gaussian lifespan filtering, we can cleanly separate a generated scene into its static and dynamic components. These isolated parts from various generated 4DGS worlds can then be freely recomposed to simulate novel scenarios. The same explicit structure is what embodied simulation needs. The metric geometry of the static component can supply occupancy and free space for an agent, the dynamic primitives move according to their own velocities, and real-time rasterization renders egocentric observations at every step. An agent can therefore be placed in a generated world, roll out its actions, and receive rendered observations in a closed loop, and because the world is persistent, the same scenario can be replayed for repeatable evaluation.

    Appendix C Evolution of 4DGS Representation

    Temporal opacity evolution.

    To faithfully represent the appearance and disappearance of scene elements over time, the opacity of each primitive is modulated by a Gaussian kernel centered at its reference timestep tᵢ. Given a query time t, the effective opacity is computed as

    σᵢ=√((lᵢ/2)²)/(-2\log(ε)), oᵢ(t)=oᵢ·\exp (-(t-tᵢ)²/2σᵢ²),

    		(8)

    where ε=0.05 serves as the activation threshold at the duration boundary. This temporal gating mechanism ensures full visibility near the reference timestep while producing smooth fade-in and fade-out transitions. As a result, the representation can naturally accommodate transient phenomena such as fire, splashes, and object entrances without resorting to explicit per-object tracking.

    Velocity-driven spatial evolution.

    The position and orientation of each primitive evolve over time according to a constant-velocity motion model. At query time t, the updated position and rotation are given by

    xᵢ(t)=xᵢ+vᵢ·(t-tᵢ),

    		(9)

    rᵢ(t)=rᵢ⊗AxisAngle2Quat(ωᵢ·(t-tᵢ)),

    		(10)

    where ⊗ denotes quaternion multiplication. The scaling sᵢ remains fixed across time, ensuring that each primitive preserves its intrinsic shape throughout the sequence. Factoring translational and rotational dynamics into independent velocity terms yields a compact yet expressive motion parameterization that supports rigid-body motion while incurring minimal per-primitive overhead. Combined with the temporal opacity mechanism above, the full 4DGS representation enables AEON to unify the photorealistic rendering capability of video models with the geometric consistency and persistence of 3D models.

    Appendix D Evaluation Metrics

    We describe all evaluation metrics used in the main paper. Our experiments rely on two families of metrics: per-frame reconstruction metrics that measure pixel-level fidelity and VBench metrics that assess perceptual video quality along multiple complementary dimensions.

    Reconstruction metrics.

    We evaluate dynamic scene reconstruction with three standard metrics that operate at increasing levels of perceptual abstraction. Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) measures per-pixel reconstruction accuracy in decibels:

    PSNR=10·\log₁₀(R²)/(1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N(Iᵢ-Ĩᵢ)²),

    		(11)

    where R is the maximum pixel intensity, N is the total number of pixels, and I, Ĩ denote the ground-truth and rendered frames respectively. Higher values indicate less distortion. Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) [43] moves beyond pixel-level comparison by jointly evaluating local luminance, contrast, and structural patterns:

    SSIM(I,Ĩ)=((2μ_Iμ_Ĩ+C₁)(2σ_IĨ+C₂))/((μ_I²+μ_Ĩ²+C₁)(σ_I²+σ_Ĩ²+C₂)),

    		(12)

    where μ and σ denote the local mean and standard deviation computed over sliding windows, σ_IĨ is the local cross-covariance, and C₁, C₂ are small stability constants. SSIM ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater structural agreement. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [55] further captures high-level perceptual differences by comparing deep features extracted from a pretrained network:

    LPIPS(I,Ĩ)=∑ₗwₗ∥φₗ(I)-φₗ(Ĩ)∥₂²,

    		(13)

    where φₗ denotes the normalized activations at layer l and wₗ are learned linear weights. Lower LPIPS values indicate higher perceptual similarity.

    VBench video quality metrics.

    For 4D generation and novel trajectory rendering we adopt six metrics from the VBench [13] benchmark, each targeting a distinct aspect of video quality. I2V Subject measures the visual fidelity between the conditioning image and the generated subject, quantifying how faithfully the output preserves the identity of the input. Subject Consistency evaluates the temporal coherence of the foreground subject across frames by computing pairwise feature similarity over the video. Background Consistency similarly measures the stability of background regions to detect unwanted scene drift. Temporal Flickering captures high-frequency luminance and color variations between consecutive frames, where higher scores correspond to smoother transitions. Motion Smoothness assesses whether object trajectories follow physically plausible paths without abrupt jumps. Aesthetic Quality and Imaging Quality respectively evaluate the overall visual appeal and the low-level image attributes such as sharpness and color fidelity. All VBench metrics are reported on a scale where higher values indicate better performance.

    Appendix E Additional Ablation Studies

    Table 7 reports additional ablations on Dycheck and DaVis, where each variant changes one component of the full model.

    Adapter.

    Conv3D projection replaces the dual-path adapter with a single Conv3D projection, while Conv branch only and Perceiver branch only use only a convolutional branch or only the Perceiver branch, respectively. All three variants lower DaVis PSNR to 12.8–15.4 dB, so no single path can bridge the two latent spaces on its own.

    Training.

    W/o Stage 3 stops after Stage 2 and keeps Stages 1 and 2 unchanged. Skipping Stage 3 reduces DaVis PSNR by 1.7 dB, demonstrating the benefit of end-to-end rendering refinement.

    4DRM.
