    Appendix A Error analysis and scene complexity

    Remaining errors. In Fig. 3, the errors of RADIANT concentrate on thin structures, which the rasterizer’s 7×7 dilation renders slightly thicker than in the reference, and on the boundary between an object and its cast shadow, where the hit channels and the routing bias change discontinuously.

    Performance breakdown by scene complexity. The gap measured over the whole held-out split is consistent across subsets of scenes. Tab. 3 splits the same 4,112 images by the number of entities the renderer sees, from the sparsest bucket (at most 7 entities, 796 images) to the most crowded. At matched step 600k, RADIANT’s lead over RenderFormer is 3.1–3.5 dB in every bucket, and its lead over RenderFormer-V2 is 7.3–7.9 dB, confirming that the performance hierarchy of Tab. 2 is not an artifact of scene complexity. Absolute PSNR varies by at most 1.1 dB with the entity count for all three models, which is expected: the corpus holds one to six foreground objects in a template room, so the buckets differ in how much of the image is occupied rather than in the difficulty of the transport. The perceptual metric does separate them: from the sparsest to the most crowded bucket LPIPS rises by 37% for RADIANT, 47% for RenderFormer, and 31% for RenderFormer-V2; the fixed budget of surface-patch tokens per object does not make crowded scenes disproportionately harder. This is a statement about rendering quality only, as the inference cost of RADIANT and RenderFormer at large object counts is measured separately in Tab. 11.

    Appendix B Properties of the geometric mechanisms

    B.1 Statements

    Proposition 1(Object-permutation equivariance).

    The scene transformer is equivariant to permutations of the object set, and the predictor’s output is invariant to them: for any permutation π of {1,…,N}, applying π to the objects permutes the scene-transformer token blocks by π and, provided the rasterization selects the same surface at every pixel under relabeling (no depth ties between different objects), leaves the rendered image unchanged.

    Proposition 2(Relative-pose dependence).

    For the rotary block, the attention logit between patch tokens i and j depends on x⁽ⁱ⁾ and x⁽ʲ⁾ only through their difference: q̃ᵢ^⊤k̃ⱼ=qᵢ^⊤R(x⁽ʲ⁾-x⁽ⁱ⁾) kⱼ for a block-diagonal rotation R determined by the frequencies, for fixed pre-rotation vectors qᵢ,kⱼ. In particular, a common translation of all centroids leaves the rotary-block logits between patch tokens unchanged.

    Proposition 3(Angular alignment).

    For a ray with normalized image-plane coordinates (u,v) and an object at camera-space position (X,Y,Z) with Z<0, the first two spherical coordinates coincide exactly when the ray passes through the object’s centroid, and their difference is the pair of view angles between the ray and the centroid direction. The angular coordinates are therefore invariant to reparameterizations of the intrinsics and resolution that leave the physical rays unchanged.

    Proposition 4(Invariant form-factor attention).

    Let xᵢ=(cᵢ-c̄)/ρ be the token centroids normalized per scene (c̄ the mean and ρ the root-mean-square radius of the scene’s patch centroids), let Gᵢⱼ be as in Eq. 1 with Δᵢⱼ=xⱼ-xᵢ, and let ℓᵢⱼ=∑ₜaₜ(i) bₜ(j) G_ij,t be the geometric term of the logit.

  • 1.

    Each G_ij,t equals ⟨φₜ(i),ψₜ(j)⟩ for per-token features φₜ,ψₜ of total width 16.

  • 2.

    ℓᵢⱼ is unchanged when every centroid is mapped to Rc+t and every normal to Rm, for any R∈O(3) and t∈ℝ³. Gᵢⱼ is moreover unchanged under a uniform scaling c↦sc, s>0, and ℓ permutes with the tokens.

  • 3.

    Every O(3)-invariant polynomial in (Δᵢⱼ,mᵢ,mⱼ) that is homogeneous of degree two is a linear combination of the four entries of Gᵢⱼ, ∥mᵢ∥², and ∥mⱼ∥².

    • B.2 Proofs

    Proof of Proposition 1.

    The encoder of Sec. 3.2 is applied independently to each object, so permuting the objects permutes its outputs. The OBB descriptor x⁽ⁱ⁾, the radiosity encodings δqᵢ,δkᵢ, and the FiLM statistics are each functions of object i alone, so they permute with the tokens; the register tokens’ position is the mean patch centroid, which is permutation-invariant. Self-attention with per-token positional terms is permutation-equivariant, hence so is the scene transformer. In the predictor, ray tokens attend to the set of patch tokens through a softmax over the set, which is permutation-invariant. The rasterizer channels depend on the union of the objects’ surfaces and, under the hypothesis that no two objects tie for the nearest depth at a pixel, select the same surface after relabeling. The routing bias attaches to each object’s tokens by identity. The rendered image is therefore invariant. ∎

    Proof of Proposition 2.

    Write the rotary block as q̃ᵢ=R(x⁽ⁱ⁾)qᵢ and k̃ⱼ=R(x⁽ʲ⁾)kⱼ, where R(x) is block-diagonal with 2×2 rotations by angles ω_fx_d for coordinate d and frequency ω_f. Then q̃ᵢ^⊤k̃ⱼ=qᵢ^⊤R(x⁽ⁱ⁾)^⊤R(x⁽ʲ⁾)kⱼ=qᵢ^⊤R(x⁽ʲ⁾-x⁽ⁱ⁾)kⱼ because planar rotations commute and compose additively. A common translation t of all centroids adds t to the first three coordinates of every patch descriptor and leaves their differences, hence the rotary-block logits between patch tokens, unchanged. The content vectors are translation-invariant because the encoder sees centered samples and the FiLM and radiosity statistics are translation-invariant. ∎

    Proof of Proposition 3.

    A ray with normalized image-plane coordinates (u,v) has camera-space direction proportional to (u,v,-1), so its horizontal and vertical view angles are \arctanu and \arctanv. An object centroid at (X,Y,Z) with Z<0 has view angles atan2(X,-Z) and atan2(Y,-Z). The two pairs coincide exactly when (X,Y)/(-Z)=(u,v), i.e., when the ray passes through the centroid, and their differences are the angular offsets between the ray and the centroid direction. Both quantities are defined from camera-space geometry and the corresponding unnormalized camera-space ray, so a change of focal length or resolution that leaves the physical ray unchanged leaves the coordinates unchanged. ∎

    Proof of Proposition 4.

    1. By expansion,

    -∥xⱼ-xᵢ∥²=⟨[2xᵢ,-∥xᵢ∥²,-1],[xⱼ,1,∥xⱼ∥²]⟩,
    mᵢ^⊤(xⱼ-xᵢ)=⟨[mᵢ,-mᵢ^⊤xᵢ],[xⱼ,1]⟩,
    -mⱼ^⊤(xⱼ-xᵢ)=⟨[xᵢ,1],[mⱼ,-mⱼ^⊤xⱼ]⟩,
    mᵢ^⊤mⱼ=⟨mᵢ,mⱼ⟩,

    of widths 5+4+4+3=16; scaling the query features of term t by aₜ(i) and the key features by bₜ(j) makes ℓᵢⱼ their inner product.

    2. Under c↦Rc+t the mean maps to Rc̄+t and ρ is unchanged, so x↦Rx; with m↦Rm, every entry of Gᵢⱼ is an inner product of Δᵢⱼ, mᵢ, mⱼ and is preserved because R^⊤R=I. Under c↦sc, ρ scales by s, so x is unchanged, and the normals do not change. The gains are functions of per-object statistics (log area, albedo, emission, specular reflectance) that are invariant to rigid motions, though the log area is not invariant to scaling. Hence ℓᵢⱼ is invariant to rigid motions. Every quantity is a function of its own token and of permutation-invariant scene statistics (c̄, ρ), so ℓ permutes with the tokens.

    3. By the first fundamental theorem of invariant theory for O(3)[(Weyl, 1946)], used for equivariant networks by [Villar et al. (2021)], every O(3)-invariant polynomial in vectors v₁,…,vₖ is a polynomial in their inner products ⟨vₐ,v_b⟩. Those homogeneous of degree two are linear combinations of the inner products themselves, which for (Δᵢⱼ,mᵢ,mⱼ) are the four entries of Gᵢⱼ up to sign, ∥mᵢ∥², and ∥mⱼ∥². The last two depend on one token alone: a query-only term cancels in the softmax, and a key-only term is a per-key offset. ∎

    Appendix C Training details

    Tab. 7 summarizes the training configuration and hyperparameters in our experiments. All models are trained from scratch at 512² on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with a global batch size of 24 (without data augmentation). We optimize using AdamW [(Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019)] with β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, weight decay of 0.01 applied to matrix weights, and gradient clipping at a global norm of 1.0. To train RenderFormer, we use its released model code, Base configuration, and training initialization within the training loop shared with RADIANT. RenderFormer-V2 is trained also with its released training loop, with the data loader replaced to read our scenes and the LPIPS backbone set to AlexNet–this loop applies the weight decay to all parameters, warms up from zero, anneals to 5×10⁻⁷, and casts the targets to bfloat16. Both baselines keep their view-dependent stage in TF32, as in their authors’ code.

    The learning rate warms up linearly over 8,000 steps to a peak of 5×10⁻⁵, followed by cosine annealing to a minimum of 10⁻⁶ at 100k steps. Longer runs continue from the 100k checkpoint on the tail of a 200k-step cosine schedule, from the 200k checkpoint on that of a 300k-step one, and from the 300k checkpoint on that of a 600k-step one (same warm-up, peak, and minimum; model and optimizer state carried over), so the learning rate rises at each continuation, for example to 2.6×10⁻⁵ at step 300k; the main comparison is at step 600k. Training uses bfloat16 mixed precision with FP32 master weights.

    Every saved checkpoint is evaluated on the full held-out split of 4,112 images with identical metric definitions (one evaluator for RADIANT and RenderFormer, a port of it to RenderFormer-V2’s released code); the best checkpoint of each model (Tab. 2) is the one with the highest per-image PSNR on this split, selected identically for the three models. Choosing each model’s checkpoint on a random half of the held-out scenes and scoring it on the other half (1,000 halvings) selects the 600k checkpoint in every halving for both RenderFormer generations and in 99.9% of the choices for RADIANT (otherwise its 575k checkpoint) among the regular evaluations from 100k steps on, and the best checkpoints of Tab. 2 exceed these choices by at most 0.02 dB.

    Appendix D Data statistics

    Tab. 9 summarizes the corpus. Scenes follow the RenderFormer protocol: one to six foreground objects from a pool of 18,085 curated Objaverse meshes, placed in a template room whose walls are randomly pruned, with randomized area lights, materials assigned per shading group, and meshes simplified by quadric edge collapse. Each scene is path traced in Blender Cycles from four cameras at 512² with 512 samples per pixel, and a second corpus generated by the same procedure is rendered at 256² with 256 samples per pixel. Both corpora use the Cycles defaults of Blender 4.2: adaptive sampling (noise threshold 0.01), an indirect-light clamp of 10, and denoising with Intel Open Image Denoise. Every entity the renderer sees (foreground objects, walls, and lights) is one object of the model, which is why the entity count exceeds the foreground count. The held-out split is the last 0.1% of scenes in a fixed order, and we verify that the point-sampled and triangle representations carry identical scene sets in identical order and that the split boundary falls on the same scene. The held-out scenes share the curated pool of 18,085 Objaverse meshes with the training set, but they are distinct scenes: their compositions, arrangements, material assignments, emitters, and camera viewpoints are sampled independently of the training scenes. Per-scene statistics are measured on a random sample of 40,000 training scenes (40 data files of 1,000 scenes).

    Appendix E Runtime analysis

    Complexity. With N objects, M=32 patch tokens per object, and 16 register tokens, the scene transformer attends over S=32N+16 tokens at cost O(S²) per layer; the predictor attends Q=HW/16 ray tokens over the scene tokens at cost O(QS) and over themselves at cost O(Q²) (Q=16,384 at 512²); the rasterization is one splat pass over the NP point inputs (P=2,048) with a 7×7 dilation; the DPT head is linear in HW. None of these terms depends on the triangle count of the input meshes. A triangle-level model attends over T tokens at cost O(T²) in its first stage.

    Protocol. Tabs. 11 and 14: the two 206M models of Tab. 2 with random weights, synthetic scenes (2,048 point inputs per object sampled on spheres, with analytic normals, for RADIANT; random small triangles for RenderFormer; surface sampling is not timed), bf16 autocast, batch size 1, one NVIDIA H100 GPU (80 GB; PyTorch 2.7.1, CUDA 12.6), five warm-up and up to twenty timed forward passes per configuration (median reported). Tab. 16: the same models evaluated on eight-object scenes (512 triangles per object for RenderFormer, 2,048 points per object for RADIANT), with five warm-up and twenty timed passes, excluding host-to-device transfers. Fig. 5 plots the latencies of Tab. 11 against the number of objects, together with the latency of a training step. Complete benchmarking scripts and profiling configurations are included in the supplementary materials.

    Breakdown of the forward pass. Tab. 10 splits the forward pass into its components. The view-dependent part dominates RADIANT at 10 and 50 objects (68% and 58% of the time) and grows only from 50 to 75 ms up to 200 objects, while the point encoder and the scene transformer, whose attention runs in float32 (Sec. 3.4), grow with the number of objects (7.3 to 48.0 ms and 9.0 to 104.0 ms). RenderFormer’s triangle transformer grows from 19 ms to 1.20 s with FlashAttention over the same range and takes 94% of the forward pass at 200 objects (96% with PyTorch attention).

    Crossover. Measured between 10 and 50 objects with the settings of Tab. 11, RenderFormer with SDPA is faster at 512² up to 20 objects (70.9 versus 77.2 ms at 20), and RADIANT is faster from 25 objects on; against FlashAttention the crossover lies between 30 and 35 objects. At 128² and 256², RADIANT is faster from 15 objects on (at 128² from 10 against FlashAttention).

    Tessellation. Tab. 12 keeps ten objects and varies only their tessellation. RenderFormer’s time grows with the triangle count, while RADIANT’s input (2,048 points per object) and time do not change: from 2,048 triangles per object on, RADIANT is faster (1.5–2.5×), and at 32,768 triangles per object by 155× (FlashAttention) to 412× (SDPA).

    Cost at the scale of the training scenes.

    On the small scenes of the corpus the balance reverses (Tab. 13, one A100): a single-view forward of RADIANT takes 130 ms against RenderFormer’s 42–49 ms, and for a training step it runs 1.09 s against 0.72–0.91 s. With 5× fewer steps taken to 25 dB, RADIANT still reaches it in 4.8 h of training against 15.9–20.3 h.

    Batched throughput. On small scenes the batched regime (Tab. 16) favors RADIANT at 128² and 256² from batch size 8 on, where object-centric tokens allow efficient parallel processing; at 512², ray tokens dominate per-image overhead.

    Multi-view amortization. Both models compute a view-independent scene representation once and replay only the view-dependent part per view. Tab. 17 times the two parts separately: the split reproduces the output of the unmodified forward pass to within bf16 rounding, and the sum of the two parts matches one end-to-end forward within 0.9%. RADIANT’s view-independent part is the cheaper one from 50 objects on (38 versus 118 ms under FlashAttention, 38 versus 227 ms under the shared backend), and the gap grows with the object count as in Tab. 11. Its view-dependent part, however, costs 52–58 ms at 512², 2.1–3.3 times RenderFormer’s view transformer, because it decodes 16,384 ray tokens through the DPT head. At 512² the amortized per-view cost therefore favors RenderFormer on these 8- and 50-object scenes (16.0 and 29.6 versus 52.6 and 58.5 ms per view at 64 views). At 256² the view-dependent parts are comparable (13–21 ms) and the view-independent part decides: the two models are within a millisecond per view at eight objects and RADIANT is ahead at fifty (16.1 versus 22.4 ms at 64 views).

    Appendix F Architecture

    Tab. 18 lists the modules of RADIANT with their parameter counts (205,942,972 in total). The scene transformer uses QK-LayerNorm, rotary frequencies 1,5^1/3,5^2/3,5 over the 12 descriptor coordinates (96 rotated channels, 32 pass-through, rotate-half convention), 16 register tokens positioned at the mean patch centroid, and the receiver/sender radiosity encodings of Sec. 3.3. The predictor fuses the last three scene-transformer layers into its context, uses rotary frequencies 1,3^1/3,3^2/3,3 over the spherical ray/object coordinates, adds the routing bias with one learned gate per layer, and decodes the ray tokens of the 4×4 pixel patches with a DPT head (256 features, output channels 128/256/512/1,024) that also receives the 14 rasterized surface channels through a zero-initialized 1×1 convolution.

    RenderFormer (205.2M): the released Base configuration, 12 view-independent and 6 view-dependent layers, width 768, 6 heads, feed-forward 3,072, DPT decoder, 8×8 ray patches.

    RenderFormer-V2 (207.6M): the released 200M configuration, which orders tokens along a Hilbert curve and restricts attention among them to a sliding window of ±256 tokens (FlexAttention) with attention sinks (16 register tokens and one summary token per 64 geometry tokens), uses a Swin-style view transformer, and encodes 32×32 material patches into 4×4×80 VAE latents projected to the token width; frozen pretrained encoders of its released input pipeline (a material-to-latent mapper and an image VAE) produce these latents and that of the empty environment map.

    Implementation details omitted from Sec. 3. OBB-RoPE: each patch token i carries x⁽ⁱ⁾=[c⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ e₁⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ e₂⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ e₃⁽ⁱ⁾]∈ℝ¹², its patch centroid and the principal axes of its parent object’s samples (covariance eigendecomposition) scaled by the standard deviations along them, shared by the object’s tokens; each coordinate is mapped through F=4 logarithmically spaced frequencies to phases a⁽ⁱ⁾, and queries and keys are split into a 96-dimensional rotary block and a 32-dimensional pass-through block, q̃=[qᵣ⊙\cosa⁽ⁱ⁾+rot(qᵣ)⊙\sina⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ qₚ] with the rotate-half pairing rot(·).

    Register tokens are positioned at the masked mean of the scene’s patch centroids (with a small numerical epsilon). Eigendecompositions and camera transforms of the descriptor are evaluated in single precision; in the predictor, centroids receive the full rigid camera transform and axes the rotation only. The rotate-half convention pairs each channel of the first half of the rotary block with its partner in the second half, with a sign flip.

    The receiver/sender MLPs of the radiosity encodings (Sec. 3.3) are 8→256→1,024. The intrinsic-complexity FiLM reads covariance spectra, radial moments, and convexity of the object’s samples. CamRay assumes square images with a centered principal point; the ray-token projection is followed by a LayerNorm. Patches without rasterized hits carry a depth coordinate of zero in the spherical frame.

    Invariant form-factor attention (Sec. 3.4). The receiver and sender gains are two MLPs 8→64→12·8·4 over the eight radiosity statistics of Sec. 3.3, one gain per layer, head, and term; the last layer of the sender MLP is initialized at zero, so the invariant terms start at exactly zero. The 16 features per head are appended to the queries and keys after the rotary rotation, the values are padded with zeros, and the attention of these layers is computed in float32 with the softmax scale of the 128-dimensional heads. Centroids are centered at the mean of the scene’s patch centroids and divided by their root-mean-square radius (Prop. 4), which keeps the float32 expansion well conditioned; each mean normal averages, without normalization, the normals of the 128 samples nearest to the patch centroid, the neighborhood of the point encoder, so a patch whose normals cancel carries a short vector rather than an arbitrary direction; register tokens carry a zero normal. The gradients of the gain MLPs are clipped separately from the rest of the model. The extension adds 0.05M parameters (the two gain MLPs, 8→64→384; Tab. 18).

    Appendix G Seed replicates of the ablations

    Rasterizer controls. Tab. 20 separates the rasterizer channels from the scene representation under the 100k-step schedule of Tab. 19, over seeds 42–44, on the model without invariant form-factor attention (row “No invariant form-factor attention” of Tab. 19). Removing the rasterized splat into the output head leaves PSNR unchanged (+0.01±0.07 dB). Removing the scene tokens from the view decoder while keeping every rasterizer channel and the splat costs 5.66±0.06 dB and triples the log-radiance error (0.062 against 0.021), more than removing the rasterizer channels (3.12±0.05 dB). Removing the rasterizer channels and the splat together costs 3.09±0.20 dB. The rasterizer channels identify the surface each ray meets, and the scene tokens provide the global 3D scene context needed to shade it: neither suffices alone.

    Tab. 19 reports the mean of seeds 42, 43, and 44 (42–47 without inter-object attention) under the same 100k-step schedule, and Tab. 21 lists every seed. Each replicate changes both the initialization and the data order; all runs are scored by the same evaluator on the same 2,948 held-out images. The full model’s seed-to-seed standard deviation is 0.01 dB. Paired within seeds, removing the rasterizer channels costs 3.12±0.08 dB and removing invariant form-factor attention 0.52±0.08 dB; removing FiLM costs 0.15±0.02 dB and removing the register tokens costs 0.13±0.01 dB, with the same sign in every seed. Without inter-object attention the loss depends on the seed, from 1.41 to 3.03 dB, so this row reports seeds 42–47; seeds 45–47 have no full-model run of their own and are compared with its three-seed mean. The rasterized splat into the output head (Sec. 3.5) is kept in every row. The result is thus carried by the rasterizer channels, the attention between objects, and invariant form-factor attention, not by the auxiliary conditioning.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：宏观光传输由物体排布而不是网格密度决定，所以按物体而不是按三角形 tokenize：注意力长度与多边形数彻底解耦，500 物体前向 0.83 秒。

要点：

  • 现有 transformer 渲染器逐三角形 tokenize，自注意力随网格分辨率平方增长；更细的细分只会推高 token 数而不改变传输物理
  • 每个物体固定 32 个表面面片 token（PointNet 式编码 + 16 个可学习 register token 吸收多余注意力权重 + 两条 FiLM 通路注入旋转不变形状统计）
  • 场景 transformer 12 层、宽 1024、8 头、97.0M 参数建模物体间辐射交换；视角解码器 96.1M 参数交叉注意相机光线 token，DPT head 上采样回全分辨率 HDR
  • 1.03M 场景基准、同容量（约 206M 参数）下到 25 dB 只需 16k 步（RenderFormer 80k），600k 步达 32.2 dB（+3.3 dB / 对 V2 +7.6 dB）；500 物体前向 0.83 s，比开 FlashAttention 的 RenderFormer 快 8.5×

为什么值得看：如果要在引擎里做前馈 GI，关键取舍是「表示跟谁走」：跟着视觉重要性/物体走，注意力开销才不会随美术把模型越做越细而爆炸。

中文摘要：前馈神经渲染器希望不做逐场景优化、也不做运行时追迹就把全局光照算出来，但现有基于 transformer 的做法按单个三角形 tokenize，自注意力开销随网格分辨率平方增长。作者指出宏观辐射传输由底层表面几何与物体排布决定，而不是某个具体的网格离散方式，更细的细分只是推高 token 数。于是提出 RADIANT（RADiance-based Inter-Actor Neural Transformer）：以物体为中心，每个物体只用 32 个表面面片 token 表示，把注意力序列长度与多边形数量解耦；单个网络里，物体间场景 transformer 负责 3D 辐射交换，视角解码器按目标相机位姿出图，不必显式物化 O(N²) 的偏置矩阵。在 1.03M 场景、同参数容量、同数据集的对照协议下，RADIANT 用 5 倍更少的优化步数达到 25 dB，600k 步收敛到 32.2 dB，500 物体场景前向 0.83 秒，明显优于对照方法。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-10-26

RADIANT: Object-Centric
Feed-Forward Global Illumination

Abstract

Feed-forward neural renderers synthesize global illumination across novel 3D scenes without per-scene optimization or runtime ray tracing. Existing transformer-based renderers tokenize individual triangles, so self-attention scales quadratically with mesh resolution. Yet macroscopic radiative transport is governed by the underlying surface geometry and object arrangements rather than a particular mesh discretization; finer tessellation can thus inflate token counts without changing the underlying transport physics, motivating a discretization-agnostic and object-centric representation. We introduce RADIANT (RADiance-based Inter-Actor Neural Transformer), an object-centric architecture for feed-forward global illumination from point inputs. By representing each object with a compact budget of 32 surface-patch tokens, RADIANT decouples attention sequence length from polygon counts. In a single network, an inter-object scene transformer models 3D radiative exchange and a view decoder renders images at target camera poses. To capture light transport without materializing O(N²) bias matrices, invariant form-factor attention embeds geometric distances and surface orientations directly into query-key dot products as SE(3)-invariant inner products weighted by learned area and material gains. For primary visibility without mesh connectivity, camera rays cross-attend scene tokens guided by depth-tested point splats in a shared spherical frame. Across a 1.03M-scene benchmark under matched model capacity, RADIANT reaches 25 dB tone-mapped PSNR in 5× fewer training steps than RenderFormer, and achieves 32.2 dB at 600k steps (+3.3 dB over RenderFormer and +7.6 dB over RenderFormer-V2). We further demonstrate the scalability of RADIANT, which completes a 512² forward pass of a 500-object scene in 0.83 s, with computational cost scaling with the number of objects rather than polygons. We will release our code and dataset upon publication.

1 Introduction

Global illumination effects (such as soft contact shadows, diffuse interreflections, and color bleeding) provide visual cues for spatial depth and surface geometry, governed by the rendering equation [(Kajiya, 1986)]. Classical Monte Carlo path tracing [(Kajiya, 1986)] and radiosity [(Goral et al., 1984)] compute physically accurate light transport from surface meshes and material definitions, but tracing rays at runtime remains computationally expensive. Per-scene methods such as neural radiance fields and 3D Gaussian splatting [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Kerbl et al., 2023; Hadadan et al., 2021)] avoid runtime path tracing by fitting scene-specific representations, but cannot generalize across new environments. Feed-forward neural renderers [(Zeng et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026)] instead predict radiance across unseen scenes in a single forward pass without test-time optimization.

Existing feed-forward renderers such as RenderFormer [(Zeng et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2026)] tokenize explicit triangle meshes, running self-attention over individual primitives (T triangles). Because full attention scales as O(T²), latency and GPU memory grow rapidly with mesh resolution. Subsequent variants introduce windowed attention [(Zeng et al., 2026)] or object-level pooling [(Du et al., 2026)], but still require explicit triangle-based geometry and compute primitive-level attention during encoding. Point clouds, by contrast, are topology-free and interface directly with depth sensors and 3D generative models. Prior work has learned light transport on point-based scene representations for static and dynamic indoor scenes [(Sanzenbacher et al., 2020)], as a direct-to-indirect illumination operator on 3D point clouds [(Hermosilla et al., 2019)], and as generalizable 3D embeddings for diffuse global illumination [(Xu et al., 2026)]. Building on these point-based light-transport methods, we investigate an object-centric formulation that combines compact surface-patch tokens, scene-level transport, and camera-ray HDR decoding guided by mesh-free primary visibility.

We introduce RADIANT (RADiance-based Inter-Actor Neural Transformer), an object-centric architecture that learns feed-forward global illumination directly from point inputs. In radiosity and radiative heat transfer [(Goral et al., 1984)], energy exchange occurs between finite surface regions and objects regardless of surface tessellation. For fixed surface geometry and materials, macroscopic light transport is the same whether a surface is represented by 50 or 50,000 triangles. By defining attention tokens over a compact set of surface patches per object rather than individual polygons, RADIANT decouples transport sequence length from geometric discretization, providing a unified pipeline for meshes and point clouds.

RADIANT divides computation into 3D scene transport and 2D view decoding. A point encoder first extracts 32 surface-patch tokens per object via point set abstraction, bounding global transport to O(N²) attention over 32N tokens for N scene entities without requiring manifold meshes. An inter-object scene transformer then models radiative transfer among these patch tokens. To incorporate geometric distance and surface orientation without the quadratic memory overhead of explicit pairwise bias matrices, we introduce invariant form-factor attention (Sec. 3.4). Pairwise Euclidean distance and surface-facing angles enter query-key dot products as exact SE(3)-invariant inner products, modulated by learned area and material gains. For novel views, a view decoder cross-attends camera rays to the scene tokens (Sec. 3.5). A lightweight point-splat rasterizer supplies primary hit depth, surface normals, and materials, allowing the cross-attention layers to focus on multi-bounce interreflections, soft contact shadows, and color bleeding.

Under matched parameter capacity (≈206M parameters) and an identical 1.03M-scene dataset (Tab. 1), RADIANT reaches 25 dB tone-mapped PSNR in 5× fewer optimizer steps than RenderFormer (16k vs. 80k) and finishes 600k steps at 32.2 dB (+3.3 dB over RenderFormer, +7.6 dB over RenderFormer-V2). Because sequence length scales with object count rather than polygon count (32N tokens vs. T triangles), a forward pass of RADIANT on a synthetic 500-object scene takes 0.83 s in a runtime-only benchmark, 8.5× faster than RenderFormer with FlashAttention (Sec. 4.4); rendering quality is evaluated on scenes with up to 50 entities.

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce RADIANT, a mesh-free transformer that renders feed-forward global illumination directly from point inputs, decoupling transport complexity from polygon tessellation (O(N²) vs. O(T²) for N scene entities and T triangles, reducing median token counts from 3,205 to 320; Tab. 9).

  • •

    We formulate invariant form-factor attention, exactly factorizing selected geometric invariants motivated by radiative transfer into query-key dot products without pairwise bias tables, paired with a rasterizer-guided view decoder that resolves primary visibility without mesh connectivity.

  • •

    On our 1.03M-scene benchmark under matched training budgets, RADIANT reaches 25 dB in 5× fewer optimizer steps than RenderFormer at the same global batch size, improves final fidelity by +3.3 dB, and runs a forward pass on 500-object scenes in 0.83 s in a runtime-only benchmark.

    • 2 Related Work

    Per-scene neural rendering. Neural radiance fields [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Müller et al., 2022)], 3D Gaussian splatting [(Kerbl et al., 2023)], and Neural Radiosity [(Hadadan et al., 2021)] optimize continuous representations for a single scene by minimizing photometric loss or the rendering equation’s residual [(Kajiya, 1986)]. Although these methods avoid path tracing once trained, they require per-scene fitting and cannot generalize to novel geometric arrangements. In contrast, our goal is feed-forward synthesis: predicting global illumination across novel scenes in a single forward pass without test-time optimization.

    Feed-forward rendering of explicit geometry. RenderFormer [(Zeng et al., 2025)] showed that transformers [(Vaswani et al., 2017)] can learn light transport over triangle meshes by tokenizing triangles with their material attributes. RenderFormer-V2 [(Zeng et al., 2026)] adds environment lighting and participating media with windowed attention, but still relies on triangle primitives. Concurrently, RenderFormer++ [(Du et al., 2026)] pools triangle tokens into object queries, yet still executes full self-attention over each object’s triangles before pooling, which incurs O(∑ᵢTᵢ²) cost. RenderFormer++ is concurrent and has not released code; it requires triangle-based geometry and triangle-level attention, whereas RADIANT operates directly on point inputs via set abstraction [(Qi et al., 2017b)] without computing primitive attention. Other object-centric representations model scattering functions [(Guo et al., 2020)], object-oriented transfer [(Zheng et al., 2023)], superposed fields [(Zheng et al., 2024)], or light probes [(Deng et al., 2025)]. In our framework, surface patches represent the physical scale of macroscopic light exchange directly.

    Point-based and alternative representations for global illumination. Meshless representations have long decoupled illumination from surface tessellation [(Lehtinen et al., 2008)]. [Hermosilla et al. (2019)] learn a direct-to-indirect illumination operator on 3D point clouds and propagate its features to image pixels, while [Xu et al. (2026)] map point clouds to continuous 3D shading queries for diffuse transport. Related approaches aggregate virtual point lights via pixel-light cross-attention [(Ren et al., 2024)] or predict screen-space shading from G-buffers [(Nalbach et al., 2017)]. Here, RADIANT pools point inputs into 32 surface-patch tokens per object, models multi-bounce transfer in 3D self-attention, and decodes HDR radiance along camera rays guided by a point-splat G-buffer (Appendix K).

    Rotary embeddings and attention biases. Spatial geometry and surface orientation determine radiative transfer. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) [(Su et al., 2024)] encode relative offsets into query-key dot products, maintaining compatibility with fused attention kernels [(Dao et al., 2022)]. PRoPE [(Li et al., 2025)] extends rotary embeddings to camera frustums for view synthesis, from which we adopt the CamRay parameterization. Rather than storing explicit O(N²) pairwise bias matrices, low-rank factorizations [(Wu et al., 2025)] decompose spatial biases into inner products. Invariant form-factor attention adopts this principle: Euclidean distance and surface-facing angles enter as exact inner products of per-token vectors, weighted by gains predicted from surface area and material attributes. We additionally incorporate feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) [(Perez et al., 2018)] and register tokens [(Darcet et al., 2024)] to condition on shape statistics and prevent attention sinks.

    3 Method

    Problem setup. A scene is defined as a set of N objects {Oᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, each specified by surface geometry with spatially varying material attributes (diffuse albedo, specular reflectance, roughness, and emission; emissive objects serve as light sources), together with a query camera with intrinsics K and pose [R | t]. The goal is to synthesize, in a single forward pass for novel scenes, the HDR radiance image L∈ℝ^H×W×3 that a reference path tracer would produce. We represent each object by P=2,048 surface point samples, each carrying a 16-dimensional attribute vector comprising position, normal, and ten material parameters. RADIANT is natively mesh-free. Polygonal meshes undergo uniform surface sampling, while raw point clouds with normals and materials are ingested directly without surface reconstruction. Our primary benchmarks evaluate mesh-derived samples, while Sec. 4.2 and Appendix J also evaluate simulated single-view partial point clouds.

    3.1 Architecture

    Fig. 1 illustrates the network architecture. First, a point encoder maps each object’s point inputs to M=32 surface-patch tokens (Sec. 3.2). Global radiative transfer is modeled by a scene transformer (12 self-attention layers, width 1,024, 8 heads, feed-forward width 1,890, 97.0M parameters) with rotary encodings of object pose (Sec. 3.2) and invariant form-factor attention (Sec. 3.4). Next, for each viewpoint, the view decoder (or predictor, 6 layers with alternating cross- and self-attention, 96.1M parameters) renders the image by cross-attending camera ray tokens (constructed from CamRay geometry and point-splat rasterization; Sec. 3.5) to the scene tokens. Finally, a dense prediction transformer (DPT) head [(Ranftl et al., 2021)] upsamples the decoded ray tokens from 4×4 pixel patches to full-resolution HDR radiance.

    3.2 Object tokenization

    A PointNet-style encoder [(Qi et al., 2017a)] (10.0M parameters) embeds P point inputs per object in the object’s centered, scale-normalized coordinate frame. Using PointNet++ set abstraction [(Qi et al., 2017b)], farthest-point sampling (FPS) selects M=32 centroids per object with 128 nearest neighbors, where local max-pooling and linear projection yield 32 patch tokens of width 1,024 per object. Sixteen learnable register tokens [(Darcet et al., 2024)] absorb extraneous attention weight (-0.13±0.01 dB when removed; Tab. 19). By construction, the scene transformer is equivariant to object permutations, ensuring that rendered imagery is invariant to object input ordering (Prop. 1, Appendix B).

    To express relative 3D geometry, we inject object pose into attention queries and keys via an object-centric rotary embedding (OBB-RoPE). Each token is assigned a 12-dimensional oriented bounding box (OBB) descriptor x⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ¹², concatenating the patch centroid with the object’s three principal axes scaled by their standard deviations (computed in world space for the scene transformer and camera space for the predictor; Appendix F). The rotations of queries and keys compose into a function R(x⁽ʲ⁾-x⁽ⁱ⁾) of the relative descriptor (Prop. 2).

    3.3 Radiosity statistics and conditioning

    Each object carries eight radiosity statistics shared by its tokens: a log area proxy (1), mean diffuse albedo (3), mean emission (3), and scalar mean specular reflectance (1). Learned receiver and sender encodings δqᵢ and δkⱼ of these statistics are added to the queries and keys of the scene transformer before rotary encoding (Appendix F), and the same statistics determine the gains of invariant form-factor attention (Sec. 3.4). Two FiLM pathways [(Perez et al., 2018)] (2.1M parameters each) further condition each object’s tokens on rotation-invariant shape statistics of its point inputs and, in the view-dependent part, on its pose relative to the query camera.

    3.4 Invariant form-factor attention

    Although rotary position embeddings capture relative positions, they do not directly expose the geometric invariants that govern radiative exchange, namely pairwise Euclidean distance rᵢⱼ and the angle θᵢ between the receiver normal and the inter-patch displacement vector Δᵢⱼ=cⱼ-cᵢ, and the angle θⱼ between the sender normal and -Δᵢⱼ. Patch centroids are centered at the scene mean and normalized by its root-mean-square radius (Prop. 4). We formulate an exact inner-product factorization that embeds these O(3)-invariant geometric terms directly into query-key dot products. Each patch token carries its centroid cᵢ and unnormalized mean normal mᵢ (averaged over the 128 point inputs of its patch). We construct a 4-dimensional geometric invariant vector Gᵢⱼ∈ℝ⁴ capturing the primary terms of radiative transfer (embedded via a 16-dimensional factored query-key representation):

    Gᵢⱼ=(-∥Δᵢⱼ∥² (distance kernel), mᵢ^⊤Δᵢⱼ (receiver-facing), -mⱼ^⊤Δᵢⱼ (sender-facing), mᵢ^⊤mⱼ (mutual orientation)).

    		(1)

    Each of these four invariant scalar terms expands as an exact inner product between receiver and sender features. For example, the negative squared distance expands as -∥Δᵢⱼ∥²=⟨[2cᵢ,-∥cᵢ∥²,-1],[cⱼ,1,∥cⱼ∥²]⟩. Appending these factored features directly to the scene transformer queries and keys injects a learned form-factor prior without materializing a pairwise bias matrix. Across layers and attention heads, these terms are modulated by receiver and sender gains aₜ(i) and bₜ(j) predicted from radiosity statistics (Sec. 3.3). This contributes a learned scalar bias ∑ₜ₌₁⁴aₜ(i)bₜ(j)G_ij,t to each attention logit without materializing the scene-space geometric bias matrix. Further, this bias is a material-dependent function of distance and orientation; when the product of the distance gains is positive, its squared-distance term contributes a Gaussian-shaped multiplicative factor to the unnormalized attention weights.

    Theoretical properties and scope. These terms provide the exact O(3)-invariant quadratic arguments of the differential radiative form factor dFᵢⱼ=\cosθᵢ\cosθⱼ dAⱼ/(πrᵢⱼ²)[(Goral et al., 1984)] (Prop. 4). Non-quadratic physical phenomena (specifically non-negative cosine clamping [\cosθ]₊, inverse-square distance attenuation 1/rᵢⱼ², and mutual visibility occlusion) are not explicitly represented by this factorization and are left to the learned transformer layers. All main experiments (Sec. 4.2) evaluate RADIANT with this formulation, and we isolate and measure its contribution in the ablation study (Sec. 4.3).

    3.5 View-dependent decoding: ray tokens, rasterizer channels, and spherical cross-attention

    Ray tokens. We tokenize camera rays by adopting an unnormalized variant of the CamRay parameterization [(Li et al., 2025)]. Each pixel’s CamRay, obtained from K⁻¹[uₚᵢₓ,vₚᵢₓ,1]^⊤ and converted to the OpenGL camera frame, preserves the linearity of the image plane. Pixels are grouped into 4×4 patches. For each patch, the CamRay map and per-pixel channels described below are linearly projected and layer-normalized into a single ray token positioned at the patch’s CamRay centroid.

    Rasterizer channels. To avoid burdening cross-attention with geometric ray casting, we separate primary surface visibility from global light transport. A depth-tested point-splat rasterization of the point inputs for the query camera (7×7 dilation) provides a mesh-free primary G-buffer with visible object identity, depth, normal, and material per pixel. The buffer does not explicitly encode incident illumination or shadows; cross-attention to the 3D scene tokens supplies global context for predicting direct and indirect illumination. Besides reflectance, the buffer’s material channels carry only the emission of directly visible emitters. The resulting log-depth, camera-space normal, and hit mask are patchified alongside the CamRay map, ensuring each ray token carries its primary hit geometry. Object identities enter cross-attention as a routing bias: the attention logit between a ray patch and an object’s tokens receives an additive bias proportional to the fraction of patch pixels rasterized to that object, scaled by a learned per-layer signed gate (initialized to zero). For output generation, rasterized normal, materials, and depth (14 channels) are added to full-resolution DPT features via a zero-initialized 1×1 convolution.

    Spherical cross-attention RoPE. Cross-attention requires comparing 3D object positions against 2D image-plane coordinates under a unified relative encoding. We project both into a spherical coordinate frame consisting of two angles in [-π,π] and a depth coordinate: an object at camera-space position (X,Y,Z) maps to (atan2(X,-Z),atan2(Y,-Z),-Z), whereas a ray with normalized image-plane coordinates (u,v), i.e., OpenGL camera-space direction proportional to (u,v,-1), maps to (\arctanu,\arctanv,d̄), where d̄ denotes the mean rasterized hit depth of the patch (or 0 for missed rays). Under RoPE subtraction, the difference in the first two coordinates directly measures the angular offset between the ray and the object from the camera viewpoint, while the third coordinate provides explicit depth information for occlusion reasoning. These angular coordinates coincide exactly when a ray points toward the object’s centroid (Prop. 3).

    3.6 Training objective

    The network is trained end-to-end. Following [Zeng et al. (2025)], the model predicts log radiance ŷ=\log(1+L). The loss L combines mean absolute error in log space with a perceptual term [(Zhang et al., 2018)] on tone-mapped images τ(L)=clip_[0,1](\log₂(1+L)):

    L=∥ŷ-\log(1+L^⋆)∥₁+0.05 LPIPS(τ(L̂),τ(L^⋆)),

    		(2)

    where the first term is averaged over all pixels and color channels, L^⋆ denotes ground-truth radiance, and L̂=\exp(\min(ŷ,10))-1. We optimize using AdamW [(Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019)] with a peak learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵, 8,000 warmup steps, cosine learning rate decay to 10⁻⁶, and a global batch size of 24. All models share this loss, tone map, LPIPS backbone, and optimizer setup, except where RenderFormer-V2’s released training loop differs (Appendix C).

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental setup

    Data. Following the RenderFormer protocol [(Zeng et al., 2025)], we construct procedural scenes with 1–6 Objaverse objects [(Deitke et al., 2023)] drawn from 18,085 meshes in a template room with randomized wall pruning, area lights (1–8 emitters per scene, mean 4.5; Tab. 9), and per-shading-group materials. Four views per scene are rendered with Blender Cycles at 512² resolution (512 samples per pixel, denoised via Intel Open Image Denoise; Appendix D). All models are trained from scratch on our 1.03M-scene corpus without external pre-rendered data. Apart from the frozen LPIPS backbone in the loss, the only pretrained components are the frozen encoders in RenderFormer-V2’s released input pipeline (Appendix F). The held-out evaluation split comprises 1,028 scenes (4,112 images) featuring novel object compositions, materials, emitters, and camera viewpoints. Each model ingests identical scenes in its native format (surface point samples for RADIANT, triangle meshes for baselines).

    Matched-budget protocol. We benchmark three models of matched parameter capacity: RADIANT (205.9M), RenderFormer-Base [(Zeng et al., 2025)] (205.2M), and RenderFormer-V2 (207.6M; Appendix F), retrained under our unified protocol at 512² resolution on NVIDIA A100 GPUs (batch size 24, AdamW, bfloat16 mixed precision with FP32 master weights; Sec. 3.6). Training runs for 600k steps, starting with a 100k-step schedule and extended across successive cosine decays with periodic checkpoint evaluations (Sec. 4.2, Appendix C). Under the 256² protocol, seed-to-seed standard deviation is 0.01 dB, and paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals confirm that our +3.3 dB and +7.6 dB performance margins are statistically significant (Appendix G).

    Metrics. Models are evaluated on the 4,112 held-out images using three complementary metrics: (1) PSNR following Reinhard tone mapping [(Reinhard et al., 2002)] and sRGB conversion, computed both per-image and pooled across all pixels prior to logarithmic compression, (2) LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] with an AlexNet backbone, and (3) mean absolute error in log radiance ℓ₁(\log) (the regression term of the loss).

    4.2 Rendering quality

    RADIANT consistently outperforms both RenderFormer baselines across training, converging in substantially fewer optimizer steps. Learning curves (Fig. 2) and evaluation checkpoints (Tab. 8) show that by step 6k, RADIANT leads RenderFormer by +7.30 dB (23.45 vs. 16.15 dB) and cuts perceptual error by more than half (LPIPS 0.156 vs. 0.350). By step 16k, RADIANT reaches 25.91 dB, surpassing RenderFormer at step 50k (23.25 dB) and reaching 25 dB in five times fewer optimizer steps at the same global batch size (16k vs. 80k).

    Upon completing the 600k-step schedule, RADIANT achieves 32.21 dB per-image PSNR (27.65 dB pooled), outperforming RenderFormer by +3.26 dB (+1.85 dB pooled) and RenderFormer-V2 by +7.63 dB, while reducing LPIPS by 45% and 64%, respectively (0.042 vs. 0.077 and 0.117; Tab. 8). Across training, the margin over RenderFormer remains substantial (+5.4 dB at 50k, +4.4 dB at 100k, +3.5 dB at 300k, and +3.3 dB at 600k). RenderFormer-V2, retrained with its authors’ released implementation under our matched budget, trails both models across all checkpoints. Across all evaluated checkpoints on the held-out split (Tab. 2; Appendix C), the best checkpoints are RADIANT at 596k (32.22 dB), RenderFormer at 600k (28.95 dB), and RenderFormer-V2 at 599k (24.60 dB).

    RADIANT maintains a 3.1–3.5 dB margin over RenderFormer across all entity counts (Tab. 3; Appendix A). On an independent test set of 500 novel Objaverse assets (Tab. 4; Appendix I), RADIANT still leads RenderFormer and RenderFormer-V2 by +3.2 dB and +7.7 dB at training scene scales, and by +2.8 dB and +5.3 dB on crowded scenes with 25–50 entities.

    On crowded held-out scenes (Fig. 3, step 600k), RADIANT resolves contact shadows, fine silhouettes, and color bleeding between nearby surfaces. In contrast, both RenderFormer baselines exhibit blurring and blocking artifacts across planar and curved geometry (detailed error breakdown in Appendix A).

    The mesh-free formulation also handles incomplete point inputs without surface meshing. On novel viewpoints, RADIANT achieves 26.33 dB zero-shot from simulated single-view partial point clouds missing 52%–72% of each foreground object’s point inputs, compared to 34.24 dB from complete geometry (Tab. 5). Fine-tuning for 400 steps on four reference views raises novel-view PSNR to 30.30 dB, recovering half of the missing-geometry gap (Fig. 4, Appendix J).

    4.3 Ablations

    Tab. 6 evaluates individual architectural components under a controlled 100k-step schedule at 256² resolution across 2,948 held-out images.

    3D light transport modeling. Restricting scene attention to intra-object tokens degrades PSNR by 2.46±0.66 dB across six random seeds and nearly doubles log-radiance error from 0.019 to 0.036 (Appendix G): the view decoder’s cross-attention to each object cannot replace global radiative exchange within the scene transformer. Removing invariant form-factor attention (Sec. 3.4) costs 0.52±0.08 dB and raises LPIPS by 7%. A precision control confirms that float32 attention alone does not account for this gain: setting the invariant geometric terms to zero while retaining float32 attention degrades quality by 0.53±0.02 dB (Tab. 19).

    Explicit visibility grounding. Removing the rasterizer channels (hit geometry and routing bias) lowers PSNR by 3.12±0.08 dB and increases LPIPS by 56% (Tab. 6), even though these channels carry only unshaded geometry (depth, normal, and hit mask). This shows providing explicit primary surface hits relieves cross-attention from having to reconstruct visibility. Conversely, on the model without invariant form-factor attention, decoding the rasterized G-buffer without 3D scene tokens lowers PSNR by 5.66±0.06 dB (Tab. 20), demonstrating the importance of global 3D scene context beyond the view-local rasterized buffer.

    Token efficiency and auxiliary modules. On the model without invariant form-factor attention, varying the patch token budget eightfold (M∈{8,16,32,64}) alters PSNR by at most 0.04 dB (Tab. 15): allocating 16 patch tokens achieves 29.47 dB (matching 32 tokens at 29.43 dB) while reducing training step time by 17%, showing that compact patch sets reliably capture macroscopic transport. Conversely, pooling RenderFormer’s triangle tokens into 32 tokens per object lowers its PSNR by 0.38±0.09 dB (Appendix G), indicating that architectural formulation rather than token budget accounts for RADIANT’s performance. Removing FiLM conditioning lowers PSNR by 0.15±0.02 dB, while removing register tokens costs 0.13±0.01 dB (Tab. 19).

    4.4 Inference efficiency and scaling with scene complexity

    Because RADIANT’s sequence length scales with object count (32N) rather than surface primitives, scene self-attention requires O(N²) operations regardless of geometric tessellation. On small scenes (up to 20 objects at 512²), RenderFormer is faster because RADIANT’s runtime is dominated by decoding 16,384 ray tokens. Beyond 25 objects (35 with FlashAttention), RADIANT becomes faster. In a runtime-only benchmark with random weights on synthetic 500-object scenes, RADIANT runs 8.5× faster than RenderFormer with FlashAttention and 22.2× faster than standard PyTorch SDPA (benchmarks across tessellation levels, memory footprints, training costs, and throughput in Appendix E). In crowded regimes with 25–50 entities beyond the training distribution, rendering quality drops for all evaluated models (Tab. 4).

    5 Conclusion

    RADIANT shows that feed-forward global illumination can be learned directly from point inputs without mesh connectivity or per-scene optimization. By grouping point geometry into compact object-centric surface patches, the architecture decouples attention sequence length from polygon counts, while invariant form-factor attention factorizes geometric invariants of radiative transfer into query-key inner products without explicit pairwise bias tables. On a 1.03M-scene benchmark, RADIANT trains to 25 dB in one-fifth the steps of RenderFormer, achieves 32.2 dB at 600k steps, and, in a runtime-only benchmark with 500 objects, runs 8.5× faster than RenderFormer.

    Limitations and future work.

    Our formulation uses a uniform budget of 32 patch tokens per object. While effective for typical assets, this choice can over-allocate tokens to simple planar walls and under-sample geometrically complex objects. Allocating tokens adaptively based on surface area or curvature is left to future work. In addition, full self-attention over ray tokens in the view decoder limits scaling beyond 1024² resolution, which windowed or hierarchical ray attention could alleviate. Our point-splat rasterizer currently handles only direct surface intersections, leaving volumetric media such as smoke or fog to future work. Finally, high-frequency noise in input normals can propagate into rendered planar surfaces (Tab. 24). Pre-filtering normals with learned or bilateral smoothing could improve robustness on noisy real-world scans.

    Appendix A Error analysis and scene complexity

    Remaining errors. In Fig. 3, the errors of RADIANT concentrate on thin structures, which the rasterizer’s 7×7 dilation renders slightly thicker than in the reference, and on the boundary between an object and its cast shadow, where the hit channels and the routing bias change discontinuously.

    Performance breakdown by scene complexity. The gap measured over the whole held-out split is consistent across subsets of scenes. Tab. 3 splits the same 4,112 images by the number of entities the renderer sees, from the sparsest bucket (at most 7 entities, 796 images) to the most crowded. At matched step 600k, RADIANT’s lead over RenderFormer is 3.1–3.5 dB in every bucket, and its lead over RenderFormer-V2 is 7.3–7.9 dB, confirming that the performance hierarchy of Tab. 2 is not an artifact of scene complexity. Absolute PSNR varies by at most 1.1 dB with the entity count for all three models, which is expected: the corpus holds one to six foreground objects in a template room, so the buckets differ in how much of the image is occupied rather than in the difficulty of the transport. The perceptual metric does separate them: from the sparsest to the most crowded bucket LPIPS rises by 37% for RADIANT, 47% for RenderFormer, and 31% for RenderFormer-V2; the fixed budget of surface-patch tokens per object does not make crowded scenes disproportionately harder. This is a statement about rendering quality only, as the inference cost of RADIANT and RenderFormer at large object counts is measured separately in Tab. 11.

    Appendix B Properties of the geometric mechanisms

    B.1 Statements

    Proposition 1(Object-permutation equivariance).

    The scene transformer is equivariant to permutations of the object set, and the predictor’s output is invariant to them: for any permutation π of {1,…,N}, applying π to the objects permutes the scene-transformer token blocks by π and, provided the rasterization selects the same surface at every pixel under relabeling (no depth ties between different objects), leaves the rendered image unchanged.

    Proposition 2(Relative-pose dependence).

    For the rotary block, the attention logit between patch tokens i and j depends on x⁽ⁱ⁾ and x⁽ʲ⁾ only through their difference: q̃ᵢ^⊤k̃ⱼ=qᵢ^⊤R(x⁽ʲ⁾-x⁽ⁱ⁾) kⱼ for a block-diagonal rotation R determined by the frequencies, for fixed pre-rotation vectors qᵢ,kⱼ. In particular, a common translation of all centroids leaves the rotary-block logits between patch tokens unchanged.

    Proposition 3(Angular alignment).

    For a ray with normalized image-plane coordinates (u,v) and an object at camera-space position (X,Y,Z) with Z<0, the first two spherical coordinates coincide exactly when the ray passes through the object’s centroid, and their difference is the pair of view angles between the ray and the centroid direction. The angular coordinates are therefore invariant to reparameterizations of the intrinsics and resolution that leave the physical rays unchanged.

    Proposition 4(Invariant form-factor attention).

    Let xᵢ=(cᵢ-c̄)/ρ be the token centroids normalized per scene (c̄ the mean and ρ the root-mean-square radius of the scene’s patch centroids), let Gᵢⱼ be as in Eq. 1 with Δᵢⱼ=xⱼ-xᵢ, and let ℓᵢⱼ=∑ₜaₜ(i) bₜ(j) G_ij,t be the geometric term of the logit.

  • 1.

    Each G_ij,t equals ⟨φₜ(i),ψₜ(j)⟩ for per-token features φₜ,ψₜ of total width 16.

  • 2.

    ℓᵢⱼ is unchanged when every centroid is mapped to Rc+t and every normal to Rm, for any R∈O(3) and t∈ℝ³. Gᵢⱼ is moreover unchanged under a uniform scaling c↦sc, s>0, and ℓ permutes with the tokens.

  • 3.

    Every O(3)-invariant polynomial in (Δᵢⱼ,mᵢ,mⱼ) that is homogeneous of degree two is a linear combination of the four entries of Gᵢⱼ, ∥mᵢ∥², and ∥mⱼ∥².

    • B.2 Proofs

    Proof of Proposition 1.

    The encoder of Sec. 3.2 is applied independently to each object, so permuting the objects permutes its outputs. The OBB descriptor x⁽ⁱ⁾, the radiosity encodings δqᵢ,δkᵢ, and the FiLM statistics are each functions of object i alone, so they permute with the tokens; the register tokens’ position is the mean patch centroid, which is permutation-invariant. Self-attention with per-token positional terms is permutation-equivariant, hence so is the scene transformer. In the predictor, ray tokens attend to the set of patch tokens through a softmax over the set, which is permutation-invariant. The rasterizer channels depend on the union of the objects’ surfaces and, under the hypothesis that no two objects tie for the nearest depth at a pixel, select the same surface after relabeling. The routing bias attaches to each object’s tokens by identity. The rendered image is therefore invariant. ∎

    Proof of Proposition 2.

    Write the rotary block as q̃ᵢ=R(x⁽ⁱ⁾)qᵢ and k̃ⱼ=R(x⁽ʲ⁾)kⱼ, where R(x) is block-diagonal with 2×2 rotations by angles ω_fx_d for coordinate d and frequency ω_f. Then q̃ᵢ^⊤k̃ⱼ=qᵢ^⊤R(x⁽ⁱ⁾)^⊤R(x⁽ʲ⁾)kⱼ=qᵢ^⊤R(x⁽ʲ⁾-x⁽ⁱ⁾)kⱼ because planar rotations commute and compose additively. A common translation t of all centroids adds t to the first three coordinates of every patch descriptor and leaves their differences, hence the rotary-block logits between patch tokens, unchanged. The content vectors are translation-invariant because the encoder sees centered samples and the FiLM and radiosity statistics are translation-invariant. ∎

    Proof of Proposition 3.

    A ray with normalized image-plane coordinates (u,v) has camera-space direction proportional to (u,v,-1), so its horizontal and vertical view angles are \arctanu and \arctanv. An object centroid at (X,Y,Z) with Z<0 has view angles atan2(X,-Z) and atan2(Y,-Z). The two pairs coincide exactly when (X,Y)/(-Z)=(u,v), i.e., when the ray passes through the centroid, and their differences are the angular offsets between the ray and the centroid direction. Both quantities are defined from camera-space geometry and the corresponding unnormalized camera-space ray, so a change of focal length or resolution that leaves the physical ray unchanged leaves the coordinates unchanged. ∎

    Proof of Proposition 4.

    1. By expansion,

    -∥xⱼ-xᵢ∥²=⟨[2xᵢ,-∥xᵢ∥²,-1],[xⱼ,1,∥xⱼ∥²]⟩,
    mᵢ^⊤(xⱼ-xᵢ)=⟨[mᵢ,-mᵢ^⊤xᵢ],[xⱼ,1]⟩,
    -mⱼ^⊤(xⱼ-xᵢ)=⟨[xᵢ,1],[mⱼ,-mⱼ^⊤xⱼ]⟩,
    mᵢ^⊤mⱼ=⟨mᵢ,mⱼ⟩,

    of widths 5+4+4+3=16; scaling the query features of term t by aₜ(i) and the key features by bₜ(j) makes ℓᵢⱼ their inner product.

    2. Under c↦Rc+t the mean maps to Rc̄+t and ρ is unchanged, so x↦Rx; with m↦Rm, every entry of Gᵢⱼ is an inner product of Δᵢⱼ, mᵢ, mⱼ and is preserved because R^⊤R=I. Under c↦sc, ρ scales by s, so x is unchanged, and the normals do not change. The gains are functions of per-object statistics (log area, albedo, emission, specular reflectance) that are invariant to rigid motions, though the log area is not invariant to scaling. Hence ℓᵢⱼ is invariant to rigid motions. Every quantity is a function of its own token and of permutation-invariant scene statistics (c̄, ρ), so ℓ permutes with the tokens.

    3. By the first fundamental theorem of invariant theory for O(3)[(Weyl, 1946)], used for equivariant networks by [Villar et al. (2021)], every O(3)-invariant polynomial in vectors v₁,…,vₖ is a polynomial in their inner products ⟨vₐ,v_b⟩. Those homogeneous of degree two are linear combinations of the inner products themselves, which for (Δᵢⱼ,mᵢ,mⱼ) are the four entries of Gᵢⱼ up to sign, ∥mᵢ∥², and ∥mⱼ∥². The last two depend on one token alone: a query-only term cancels in the softmax, and a key-only term is a per-key offset. ∎

    Appendix C Training details

    Tab. 7 summarizes the training configuration and hyperparameters in our experiments. All models are trained from scratch at 512² on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with a global batch size of 24 (without data augmentation). We optimize using AdamW [(Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019)] with β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, weight decay of 0.01 applied to matrix weights, and gradient clipping at a global norm of 1.0. To train RenderFormer, we use its released model code, Base configuration, and training initialization within the training loop shared with RADIANT. RenderFormer-V2 is trained also with its released training loop, with the data loader replaced to read our scenes and the LPIPS backbone set to AlexNet–this loop applies the weight decay to all parameters, warms up from zero, anneals to 5×10⁻⁷, and casts the targets to bfloat16. Both baselines keep their view-dependent stage in TF32, as in their authors’ code.

    The learning rate warms up linearly over 8,000 steps to a peak of 5×10⁻⁵, followed by cosine annealing to a minimum of 10⁻⁶ at 100k steps. Longer runs continue from the 100k checkpoint on the tail of a 200k-step cosine schedule, from the 200k checkpoint on that of a 300k-step one, and from the 300k checkpoint on that of a 600k-step one (same warm-up, peak, and minimum; model and optimizer state carried over), so the learning rate rises at each continuation, for example to 2.6×10⁻⁵ at step 300k; the main comparison is at step 600k. Training uses bfloat16 mixed precision with FP32 master weights.

    Every saved checkpoint is evaluated on the full held-out split of 4,112 images with identical metric definitions (one evaluator for RADIANT and RenderFormer, a port of it to RenderFormer-V2’s released code); the best checkpoint of each model (Tab. 2) is the one with the highest per-image PSNR on this split, selected identically for the three models. Choosing each model’s checkpoint on a random half of the held-out scenes and scoring it on the other half (1,000 halvings) selects the 600k checkpoint in every halving for both RenderFormer generations and in 99.9% of the choices for RADIANT (otherwise its 575k checkpoint) among the regular evaluations from 100k steps on, and the best checkpoints of Tab. 2 exceed these choices by at most 0.02 dB.

    Appendix D Data statistics

    Tab. 9 summarizes the corpus. Scenes follow the RenderFormer protocol: one to six foreground objects from a pool of 18,085 curated Objaverse meshes, placed in a template room whose walls are randomly pruned, with randomized area lights, materials assigned per shading group, and meshes simplified by quadric edge collapse. Each scene is path traced in Blender Cycles from four cameras at 512² with 512 samples per pixel, and a second corpus generated by the same procedure is rendered at 256² with 256 samples per pixel. Both corpora use the Cycles defaults of Blender 4.2: adaptive sampling (noise threshold 0.01), an indirect-light clamp of 10, and denoising with Intel Open Image Denoise. Every entity the renderer sees (foreground objects, walls, and lights) is one object of the model, which is why the entity count exceeds the foreground count. The held-out split is the last 0.1% of scenes in a fixed order, and we verify that the point-sampled and triangle representations carry identical scene sets in identical order and that the split boundary falls on the same scene. The held-out scenes share the curated pool of 18,085 Objaverse meshes with the training set, but they are distinct scenes: their compositions, arrangements, material assignments, emitters, and camera viewpoints are sampled independently of the training scenes. Per-scene statistics are measured on a random sample of 40,000 training scenes (40 data files of 1,000 scenes).

    Appendix E Runtime analysis

    Complexity. With N objects, M=32 patch tokens per object, and 16 register tokens, the scene transformer attends over S=32N+16 tokens at cost O(S²) per layer; the predictor attends Q=HW/16 ray tokens over the scene tokens at cost O(QS) and over themselves at cost O(Q²) (Q=16,384 at 512²); the rasterization is one splat pass over the NP point inputs (P=2,048) with a 7×7 dilation; the DPT head is linear in HW. None of these terms depends on the triangle count of the input meshes. A triangle-level model attends over T tokens at cost O(T²) in its first stage.

    Protocol. Tabs. 11 and 14: the two 206M models of Tab. 2 with random weights, synthetic scenes (2,048 point inputs per object sampled on spheres, with analytic normals, for RADIANT; random small triangles for RenderFormer; surface sampling is not timed), bf16 autocast, batch size 1, one NVIDIA H100 GPU (80 GB; PyTorch 2.7.1, CUDA 12.6), five warm-up and up to twenty timed forward passes per configuration (median reported). Tab. 16: the same models evaluated on eight-object scenes (512 triangles per object for RenderFormer, 2,048 points per object for RADIANT), with five warm-up and twenty timed passes, excluding host-to-device transfers. Fig. 5 plots the latencies of Tab. 11 against the number of objects, together with the latency of a training step. Complete benchmarking scripts and profiling configurations are included in the supplementary materials.

    Breakdown of the forward pass. Tab. 10 splits the forward pass into its components. The view-dependent part dominates RADIANT at 10 and 50 objects (68% and 58% of the time) and grows only from 50 to 75 ms up to 200 objects, while the point encoder and the scene transformer, whose attention runs in float32 (Sec. 3.4), grow with the number of objects (7.3 to 48.0 ms and 9.0 to 104.0 ms). RenderFormer’s triangle transformer grows from 19 ms to 1.20 s with FlashAttention over the same range and takes 94% of the forward pass at 200 objects (96% with PyTorch attention).

    Crossover. Measured between 10 and 50 objects with the settings of Tab. 11, RenderFormer with SDPA is faster at 512² up to 20 objects (70.9 versus 77.2 ms at 20), and RADIANT is faster from 25 objects on; against FlashAttention the crossover lies between 30 and 35 objects. At 128² and 256², RADIANT is faster from 15 objects on (at 128² from 10 against FlashAttention).

    Tessellation. Tab. 12 keeps ten objects and varies only their tessellation. RenderFormer’s time grows with the triangle count, while RADIANT’s input (2,048 points per object) and time do not change: from 2,048 triangles per object on, RADIANT is faster (1.5–2.5×), and at 32,768 triangles per object by 155× (FlashAttention) to 412× (SDPA).

    Cost at the scale of the training scenes.

    On the small scenes of the corpus the balance reverses (Tab. 13, one A100): a single-view forward of RADIANT takes 130 ms against RenderFormer’s 42–49 ms, and for a training step it runs 1.09 s against 0.72–0.91 s. With 5× fewer steps taken to 25 dB, RADIANT still reaches it in 4.8 h of training against 15.9–20.3 h.

    Batched throughput. On small scenes the batched regime (Tab. 16) favors RADIANT at 128² and 256² from batch size 8 on, where object-centric tokens allow efficient parallel processing; at 512², ray tokens dominate per-image overhead.

    Multi-view amortization. Both models compute a view-independent scene representation once and replay only the view-dependent part per view. Tab. 17 times the two parts separately: the split reproduces the output of the unmodified forward pass to within bf16 rounding, and the sum of the two parts matches one end-to-end forward within 0.9%. RADIANT’s view-independent part is the cheaper one from 50 objects on (38 versus 118 ms under FlashAttention, 38 versus 227 ms under the shared backend), and the gap grows with the object count as in Tab. 11. Its view-dependent part, however, costs 52–58 ms at 512², 2.1–3.3 times RenderFormer’s view transformer, because it decodes 16,384 ray tokens through the DPT head. At 512² the amortized per-view cost therefore favors RenderFormer on these 8- and 50-object scenes (16.0 and 29.6 versus 52.6 and 58.5 ms per view at 64 views). At 256² the view-dependent parts are comparable (13–21 ms) and the view-independent part decides: the two models are within a millisecond per view at eight objects and RADIANT is ahead at fifty (16.1 versus 22.4 ms at 64 views).

    Appendix F Architecture

    Tab. 18 lists the modules of RADIANT with their parameter counts (205,942,972 in total). The scene transformer uses QK-LayerNorm, rotary frequencies 1,5^1/3,5^2/3,5 over the 12 descriptor coordinates (96 rotated channels, 32 pass-through, rotate-half convention), 16 register tokens positioned at the mean patch centroid, and the receiver/sender radiosity encodings of Sec. 3.3. The predictor fuses the last three scene-transformer layers into its context, uses rotary frequencies 1,3^1/3,3^2/3,3 over the spherical ray/object coordinates, adds the routing bias with one learned gate per layer, and decodes the ray tokens of the 4×4 pixel patches with a DPT head (256 features, output channels 128/256/512/1,024) that also receives the 14 rasterized surface channels through a zero-initialized 1×1 convolution.

    RenderFormer (205.2M): the released Base configuration, 12 view-independent and 6 view-dependent layers, width 768, 6 heads, feed-forward 3,072, DPT decoder, 8×8 ray patches.

    RenderFormer-V2 (207.6M): the released 200M configuration, which orders tokens along a Hilbert curve and restricts attention among them to a sliding window of ±256 tokens (FlexAttention) with attention sinks (16 register tokens and one summary token per 64 geometry tokens), uses a Swin-style view transformer, and encodes 32×32 material patches into 4×4×80 VAE latents projected to the token width; frozen pretrained encoders of its released input pipeline (a material-to-latent mapper and an image VAE) produce these latents and that of the empty environment map.

    Implementation details omitted from Sec. 3. OBB-RoPE: each patch token i carries x⁽ⁱ⁾=[c⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ e₁⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ e₂⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ e₃⁽ⁱ⁾]∈ℝ¹², its patch centroid and the principal axes of its parent object’s samples (covariance eigendecomposition) scaled by the standard deviations along them, shared by the object’s tokens; each coordinate is mapped through F=4 logarithmically spaced frequencies to phases a⁽ⁱ⁾, and queries and keys are split into a 96-dimensional rotary block and a 32-dimensional pass-through block, q̃=[qᵣ⊙\cosa⁽ⁱ⁾+rot(qᵣ)⊙\sina⁽ⁱ⁾ ∥ qₚ] with the rotate-half pairing rot(·).

    Register tokens are positioned at the masked mean of the scene’s patch centroids (with a small numerical epsilon). Eigendecompositions and camera transforms of the descriptor are evaluated in single precision; in the predictor, centroids receive the full rigid camera transform and axes the rotation only. The rotate-half convention pairs each channel of the first half of the rotary block with its partner in the second half, with a sign flip.

    The receiver/sender MLPs of the radiosity encodings (Sec. 3.3) are 8→256→1,024. The intrinsic-complexity FiLM reads covariance spectra, radial moments, and convexity of the object’s samples. CamRay assumes square images with a centered principal point; the ray-token projection is followed by a LayerNorm. Patches without rasterized hits carry a depth coordinate of zero in the spherical frame.

    Invariant form-factor attention (Sec. 3.4). The receiver and sender gains are two MLPs 8→64→12·8·4 over the eight radiosity statistics of Sec. 3.3, one gain per layer, head, and term; the last layer of the sender MLP is initialized at zero, so the invariant terms start at exactly zero. The 16 features per head are appended to the queries and keys after the rotary rotation, the values are padded with zeros, and the attention of these layers is computed in float32 with the softmax scale of the 128-dimensional heads. Centroids are centered at the mean of the scene’s patch centroids and divided by their root-mean-square radius (Prop. 4), which keeps the float32 expansion well conditioned; each mean normal averages, without normalization, the normals of the 128 samples nearest to the patch centroid, the neighborhood of the point encoder, so a patch whose normals cancel carries a short vector rather than an arbitrary direction; register tokens carry a zero normal. The gradients of the gain MLPs are clipped separately from the rest of the model. The extension adds 0.05M parameters (the two gain MLPs, 8→64→384; Tab. 18).

    Appendix G Seed replicates of the ablations

    Rasterizer controls. Tab. 20 separates the rasterizer channels from the scene representation under the 100k-step schedule of Tab. 19, over seeds 42–44, on the model without invariant form-factor attention (row “No invariant form-factor attention” of Tab. 19). Removing the rasterized splat into the output head leaves PSNR unchanged (+0.01±0.07 dB). Removing the scene tokens from the view decoder while keeping every rasterizer channel and the splat costs 5.66±0.06 dB and triples the log-radiance error (0.062 against 0.021), more than removing the rasterizer channels (3.12±0.05 dB). Removing the rasterizer channels and the splat together costs 3.09±0.20 dB. The rasterizer channels identify the surface each ray meets, and the scene tokens provide the global 3D scene context needed to shade it: neither suffices alone.

    Tab. 19 reports the mean of seeds 42, 43, and 44 (42–47 without inter-object attention) under the same 100k-step schedule, and Tab. 21 lists every seed. Each replicate changes both the initialization and the data order; all runs are scored by the same evaluator on the same 2,948 held-out images. The full model’s seed-to-seed standard deviation is 0.01 dB. Paired within seeds, removing the rasterizer channels costs 3.12±0.08 dB and removing invariant form-factor attention 0.52±0.08 dB; removing FiLM costs 0.15±0.02 dB and removing the register tokens costs 0.13±0.01 dB, with the same sign in every seed. Without inter-object attention the loss depends on the seed, from 1.41 to 3.03 dB, so this row reports seeds 42–47; seeds 45–47 have no full-model run of their own and are compared with its three-seed mean. The rasterized splat into the output head (Sec. 3.5) is kept in every row. The result is thus carried by the rasterizer channels, the attention between objects, and invariant form-factor attention, not by the auxiliary conditioning.

item.title: 预算调小推理也该变便宜：RLSplat 用分配策略直接生成目标数量高斯，2K 预算下显存省 9.6 倍 ｜ RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：现有「预算可控」的前馈 3DGS 先猜一大坨再剪枝，延迟与峰值显存几乎不随预算下来；RLSplat 让表示、延迟、显存三者一起线性下降。

要点：

  • 对照 F4Splat：2K 高斯预算下 PSNR 高 0.9 dB，同时峰值显存少 9.6×、速度快 4.1×；预算越低差距越大
  • 8 个上下文视角时，相对 F4Splat 的 PSNR 优势从 4K 的 0.74 dB 增到 2K 的 0.99 dB、1K 的 1.22 dB
  • 24 个视角下只用 24K 高斯拿 25.58 dB，而 SPFSplat 用 1536K 高斯才 25.00 dB，高斯数少 64×
  • 做法是学一个高斯分配策略，把预算按局部区域分下去，直接生成正好所需数量的高斯，而不是先稠密预测再裁剪

为什么值得看：移动端/VR 场景里，「预算可调」必须同时控制推理成本，否则调低预算只省了渲染不省生成；把分配策略和预算绑在一起，才能做成真正的档位表。

中文摘要：前馈 3D Gaussian Splatting 一次前向就能从图像重建 3D 场景，适合资源受限的场合；近年的预算可控方法允许在推理时调整高斯数量以匹配存储上限或渲染延迟。但这些方法忽略推理本身的成本：为了得到目标数量的高斯，它们先预测一个稠密集合再裁剪或选择，导致延迟与峰值内存几乎与预算无关。作者提出 RLSplat：学一个高斯分配策略，把预算分配到各个局部场景区域，直接生成恰好请求数量的高斯，于是表示大小、推理延迟和峰值内存都随预算线性下降。在零样本评测里，每个预算档位上 RLSplat 都优于先前的预算可控方法，低预算下甚至用 4 倍更少的高斯超过最强基线，速度最高快 4.1 倍、峰值显存少 9.6 倍。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-10-26

RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4× fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1× faster with 9.6× less peak memory at low budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/RLSplat.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has become a leading representation for photorealistic, real-time novel view synthesis, supporting applications from AR/VR [(Qian et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024)] to robotics [(Keetha et al., 2024; Matsuki et al., 2024)] and digital content creation [(Tang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b)]. Its explicit form further allows it to serve as a 3D scene representation for downstream models, such as 3D vision-language models [(Li et al., 2025; Thai et al., 2025)]. Since per-scene optimization of 3DGS takes minutes to hours and requires many calibrated views, feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in a single forward pass [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a)], and recent variants even operate directly on uncalibrated images [(Jiang et al., 2025)]. Owing to this fast and readily available reconstruction, FF3DGS has become a practical choice for applications that build 3D scene representations on the fly.

Early FF3DGS methods [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Ye et al., 2025)] simplify the problem by allocating a fixed number of Gaussians to each input pixel, which allows the feed-forward network to be trained effectively. However, this pixel-aligned design produces many redundant Gaussians, since Gaussians from overlapping views become increasingly redundant as more views are added. To address this redundancy, query-based methods [(An et al., 2026; Itkin et al., 2026)] decode a fixed set of learnable query tokens into Gaussians. Yet neither approach can adjust the number of Gaussians without retraining. This lack of controllability makes it difficult to adapt to the diverse resource budgets encountered in real-world deployment.
