To address this, recent works have proposed Gaussian budget-controllable methods. Given a Gaussian budget B, EcoSplat [(Park et al., 2026)] first predicts one Gaussian per pixel and keeps the B Gaussians with the highest opacity. F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)] instead predicts Gaussians at multiple scales and selects the B Gaussians. However, these methods overlook the computational cost of inference itself. Both methods first predict a much larger set of candidate Gaussians before reducing them to B, so their inference latency and peak memory remain nearly constant regardless of the budget, as shown in Fig.1(b) and (c).

We therefore propose RLSplat, a budget-controllable FF3DGS framework that is resource-linear: both its representation size and inference cost scale linearly with the budget B. Given uncalibrated images and a budget B, a geometry backbone encodes the images into anchor tokens, each representing a local 3D region of the scene. To obtain a compact representation, we formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem rather than pruning or selection: we predict how many Gaussians to assign to each anchor’s region, summing to B. Since these discrete allocations are non-differentiable and can only be evaluated by rendering the resulting Gaussians, we model this prediction as a Gaussian allocation policy and train it with policy optimization, using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [(Zheng et al., 2025)] with rendering quality as the reward. Given the allocation, each anchor token spawns as many Gaussian tokens as its allocated count, yielding a total of B Gaussian tokens. To efficiently decode these tokens into the final Gaussians, we introduce a resource-linear decoder. It refines each Gaussian token through local cross-attention over its K_\rmgs nearest Gaussian tokens, which we find with an efficient hierarchical neighbor search. Whereas global self-attention over all B tokens costs O(B²), each token here attends to only K_\rmgs neighbors, so the decoding cost is O(BK_\rmgs) and scales linearly with the Gaussian budget (Fig.1(c)). As a result, RLSplat achieves higher quality than prior budget-controllable methods at every budget (Fig.1(a)), while its peak memory and latency decrease with the budget. At 2K Gaussians, it achieves higher PSNR than F4Splat while using 9.6× less peak memory (Fig.1(b)) and running 4.1× faster (Fig.1(c)).

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify that existing budget-controllable FF3DGS methods control only the size of the output, not the cost of producing it, and introduce RLSplat, a resource-linear FF3DGS framework in which the number of Gaussians, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the budget B is reduced.

  • •

    We formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem and learn a Gaussian allocation policy via policy optimization that places exactly B Gaussians where the scene needs them, together with a resource-linear decoder whose cost decreases linearly as the budget decreases through local cross-attention and an efficient hierarchical neighbor search.

  • •

    RLSplat consistently outperforms prior budget-controllable methods across all budgets. At a budget of 2K Gaussians, it improves PSNR by 0.9 dB over F4Splat while using 9.6× less peak memory and running 4.1× faster.

    • 2 Related Work

    Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] represents a scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and achieves real-time rendering, but requires time-consuming per-scene optimization from many calibrated views. Feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in a single forward pass, from a single image [(Szymanowicz et al., 2024)] or from a few posed views [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024)]. Building on 3D foundation models [(Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025)], recent methods further remove the need for known camera poses [(Ye et al., 2025; Smart et al., 2024; Huang and Mikolajczyk, 2025; Jiang et al., 2025)]. Most of these methods predict one Gaussian per pixel or per voxel, so the number of Gaussians is determined by the input resolution and the number of views rather than by the scene content. This leads to redundant Gaussians in overlapping and textureless regions, and the number of Gaussians cannot be specified directly.

    Compact and Gaussian budget-controllable FF3DGS. For per-scene 3DGS, many works aim to represent a scene with fewer Gaussians without sacrificing quality, either by pruning redundant Gaussians [(Fan et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Papantonakis et al., 2024)] or by deciding where to place Gaussians under a fixed or constrained budget during densification [(Fang and Wang, 2024; Mallick et al., 2024; Kheradmand et al., 2024)]. These methods, however, rely on iterative per-scene optimization. In FF3DGS, C3G [(An et al., 2026)] and GlobalSplat [(Itkin et al., 2026)] decode a fixed set of learnable query tokens into compact sets of Gaussians, whose size is determined by the architecture. EcoSplat [(Park et al., 2026)] and F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)] instead accept a target count at inference, by keeping the Gaussians with the highest budget-conditioned opacity and by selecting one of multiple scales per region, respectively; both derive the output from a dense set of candidates. ZipSplat [(Veicht et al., 2026)], developed concurrently with our work, controls the number of Gaussians by clustering visual tokens at inference. In contrast, we learn to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians and decode only those, so that our inference cost scales with the budget.

    Policy optimization. Policy gradient methods [(Williams, 1992; Schulman et al., 2017)] optimize non-differentiable, discrete decisions from a scalar reward, and have been applied to generative vision models, e.g., to align diffusion models with reward functions [(Black et al., 2024)]. Group-relative variants such as GRPO [(Shao et al., 2024)] and GSPO [(Zheng et al., 2025)] remove the need for a learned value function by normalizing rewards within a group of samples, and have become standard for fine-tuning large language models. In particular, GSPO defines the importance ratio from the likelihood of the whole sequence rather than of individual tokens, and clips it at the sequence level. We adopt this approach to learn Gaussian allocation, treating an allocation as a sequence of B Gaussians and using rendering quality as the reward.

    3 Method

    We present RLSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework whose Gaussian count and inference cost are both controlled by a single budget B. Rather than pruning or selecting from a dense set of Gaussians, RLSplat formulates Gaussian generation as allocation: a Gaussian allocation policy decides how many Gaussians each local region of the scene receives (Sec.3.2), and a resource-linear decoder generates the allocated Gaussians and efficiently refines them with local cross-attention (Sec.3.3). We begin with an overview (Sec.3.1) and conclude with the training procedure (Sec.3.4).

    3.1 Overview of RLSplat

    Given V uncalibrated context images {Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V and a target Gaussian budget B, RLSplat F_θ predicts a set of 3D Gaussians G along with the context camera parameters {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V:

    (G,{Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V)=F_θ({Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V,B), G={g_b}_b=1^B.

    		(1)

    Here, the 3DGS attribute g_b consists of a 3D center, opacity, scale, rotation, and color coefficients.

    As illustrated in Fig.2, a geometry backbone [(Burzio et al., 2026)] encodes the images into N anchor tokens {aₙ}ₙ₌₁^N. These anchors serve as the foundational sites from which the 3D Gaussians are spawned. To use the limited budget effectively, RLSplat adaptively distributes the B Gaussians across these anchors. Specifically, a Gaussian allocation policy assesses the local significance of each anchor to predict a discrete allocation k∈ℤ_≥0^N that strictly sums to the budget (∑kₙ=B), and we optimize this policy via reinforcement learning (Sec.3.2). Next, a resource-linear decoder instantiates exactly kₙ Gaussian tokens at each anchor. It predicts an initial state for each Gaussian and efficiently processes them via a refinement module to produce the final set of B Gaussians. This decoder’s computational footprint scales linearly with the requested budget, as described in Sec.3.3.

    3.2 Gaussian Allocation Policy

    To achieve a compact and high-fidelity representation, Gaussians must be densely allocated to the anchors that encode geometrically complex local 3D regions. We formulate this discrete allocation task as a reinforcement learning problem, parameterizing a policy π_ψ(k|{aₙ}ₙ₌₁^N,B) that maps the anchor tokens and target budget to a discrete allocation k={kₙ}ₙ₌₁^N. Specifically, the policy model predicts allocation proportions p={pₙ}^Nₙ₌₁, where pₙ represents the expected fraction of the Gaussian budget assigned to anchor n. The allocation process is modeled as drawing trials from a multinomial distribution, such that k∼Mult(B,p).

    To optimize π_ψ over these non-differentiable discrete allocations, we leverage Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [(Zheng et al., 2025)]. At each training step, we draw a group of C rollouts, i.e., candidate allocations k⁽ᶜ⁾∼π_old=Mult(B,sg(p)) for c∈{1,…,C}, from the current policy with gradients stopped by sg(·). For each rollout c, we first generate the 3DGS representation G⁽ᶜ⁾. We then render an image Î⁽ᶜ⁾ from G⁽ᶜ⁾ at novel target views, computing the reconstruction loss L_recon⁽ᶜ⁾ against the ground-truth I without gradient tracking. This loss directly serves as the reward signal for rendering quality, defined as R_c=-L_recon⁽ᶜ⁾. Thanks to the highly efficient rasterization of 3DGS, evaluating multiple rollouts introduces minimal training overhead. We then compute the group-relative advantage Â_c by standardizing the rewards within the group:

    Â_c=(R_c-mean({R_c^′}_c^′=1^C))/(std({R_c^′}_c^′=1^C)).

    		(2)

    Following the GSPO framework, we view the allocation of Gaussians as a sequence of length B and compute a length-normalized importance ratio s_c for each rollout:

    s_c=((π_ψ(k⁽ᶜ⁾))/(π_old(k⁽ᶜ⁾)))^1/B=\exp(1/B∑ₙ₌₁^Nk⁽ᶜ⁾ₙ\logpₙ/sg(pₙ)).

    		(3)

    The policy is then updated by maximizing the clipped objective

    J_policy=𝔼[1/C∑_c=1^C\min(s_cÂ_c, clip(s_c,1-ε,1+ε)Â_c)],

    		(4)

    where ε is the clipping range, and the expectation is taken over scenes, budgets, and rollout groups. At inference time, we bypass stochastic sampling and deterministically convert the expected counts Bp into an integer allocation whose counts sum exactly to B. Details of the rounding procedure are provided in appendixB.

    3.3 Resource-Linear Gaussian Decoding

    Given a Gaussian allocation k={kₙ}ₙ₌₁^N, the resource-linear decoder spawns exactly B Gaussian tokens from the anchors and decodes them into the final Gaussians at a cost linear in B. We describe the token spawning, the local refinement with hierarchical neighbor search, and the regularizers that keep this search accurate.

    Gaussian token spawning. For each anchor aₙ, a token generator instantiates kₙ distinct Gaussian tokens, each conditioned on its slot index within the anchor (appendixD):

    {t_b}_b=1^B=TokenGen({(aₙ,kₙ)}ₙ₌₁^N).

    		(5)

    We denote by n_b the anchor that spawned token b. A head then predicts an initial Gaussian g_b⁰=Head(t_b) from each token, including its initial center μ⁰_b.

    Local refinement with hierarchical neighbor search. Since the initial tokens lack spatial context, they must attend to neighboring Gaussians to refine their parameters. To avoid the prohibitive O(B²) cost of global attention, we employ a local cross-attention mechanism over L layers. Anchors with kₙ=0 are excluded from the hierarchical neighbor search. For each remaining anchor n, we compute the centroid μ̄ₙ of its initial Gaussians:

    μ̄ₙ=1/kₙ∑_b: n_b=nμ⁰_b.

    		(6)

    To find neighbors efficiently, we search hierarchically: we find the K_\rmanc nearest anchors, and then search for the K_\rmgs nearest Gaussian tokens only among the Gaussians belonging to these local anchors:

    ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n)=KNN_K_\rmanc(μ̄ₙ;{μ̄ₘ:kₘ>0}),(7)
    ℕᵍˢ(b)=KNN_K_\rmgs(μ⁰_b;{μ⁰ⱼ:nⱼ∈ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b)}).

    By restricting the search space, we keep the neighbor querying highly efficient. Both neighbor sets are computed once using the detached initial positions and shared across all L layers. Each token t_b is then refined by L layers of cross-attention over its neighbors, each followed by a feed-forward layer:

    t_b←t_b+CrossAttn(t_b, {tⱼ}_j∈ℕᵍˢ(b)).

    		(8)

    Finally, a residual head predicts a correction Δg_b from t_b, giving g_b=g_b⁰+Δg_b.

    Locality regularizers. For this hierarchical search to be valid, a Gaussian’s true spatial neighbors must actually reside within its parent’s anchor neighborhood ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b). We enforce this using two regularizers. First, a Voronoi loss keeps each Gaussian closer to its own parent anchor’s centroid μ̄_n_b than to any neighboring anchor’s centroid μ̄ₘ:

    Lᵥₒᵣ=1/B∑_b=1^B∑_m∈ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b)\max(0, ∥μ⁰_b-μ̄_n_b∥-∥μ⁰_b-μ̄ₘ∥).

    		(9)

    Second, an offset loss constrains the residual correction Δμ_b to limit Gaussian drift:

    L_offset=1/B∑_b=1^B\max(0, (∥Δμ_b∥)/(d_n_b)-δ)²,

    		(10)

    where dₙ is the local anchor spacing, defined as the median distance from μ̄n to its K\rmanc nearest anchors, and δ=0.5 is a margin limiting Gaussian movement relative to the local anchor scale.

    3.4 Training

    We train RLSplat in two stages: base training trains the geometry backbone and decoder with random allocations, and policy training introduces the Gaussian allocation policy and fine-tunes the entire model with policy optimization.

    Objectives. To supervise view synthesis, we apply a reconstruction loss L_recon, combining pixel-wise MSE and LPIPS between the rendered and ground-truth target views. For geometric alignment, a camera loss L_cam supervises the translation, rotation, and field-of-view of the predicted context cameras. Additionally, a projection loss Lₚᵣₒⱼ reprojects each anchor’s Gaussians toward their source image patch. Incorporating a cheirality penalty to prevent Gaussians from landing behind the camera, Lₚᵣₒⱼ effectively ties an anchor’s allocation to a specific scene region and prevents arbitrary drift. These terms are combined with the locality regularizers (Lᵥₒᵣ and L_offset) previously introduced in Sec.3.3. Finally, during the policy training stage, we activate the policy loss L_policy=-J_policy (Eq.4) to optimize the discrete allocations via GSPO. The overall training objectives are detailed in appendixE.

    Two-stage training. We train RLSplat in two stages. In base training, we train the encoder and decoder with random allocations, and sample budgets over the full supported range. This exposes the decoder to widely varying per-anchor counts, so that it learns to render diverse allocations before the policy is introduced. In policy training, we add the policy head, initialized to output uniform probabilities (appendixB), and fine-tune the entire model with the policy loss L_policy. Since base training involves no policy, there is no reference policy to regularize toward, and unlike typical RL fine-tuning, we do not apply a KL penalty. During this stage, budgets are sampled with a skew toward the lower end of the range, where the choice of allocation matters most for rendering quality.

    4 Experiments

    Datasets and evaluation. We train on RealEstate10K (RE10K) [(Zhou et al., 2018)] with V∈{2,3,4,6,8,12,24} uncalibrated context views. To assess generalization, we evaluate the RE10K-trained model zero-shot on ACID [(Liu et al., 2021)] (249 test scenes), which consists of aerial footage of coastal and natural scenes. We follow the evaluation protocol of F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)] at a resolution of 256×256 and report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS together with the number of Gaussians (#GS). To measure inference cost, we report the latency and peak VRAM of Gaussian generation, excluding data loading, pose alignment, and rendering. All methods are run on a single RTX A6000 with a batch size of one. For each budget, we discard the first scene as warm-up, reset the peak-memory counter before each timed run, and report the mean over the test scenes.

    Baselines. We mainly compare with budget-controllable methods, EcoSplat [(Park et al., 2026)] and F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)], which take a target Gaussian count as input at inference time. We evaluate all methods at the same requested Gaussian budgets, with particular focus on the low-budget regime. For a broader comparison, we also include budget-fixed methods, which place Gaussians uniformly, either one per pixel (NoPoSplat [(Ye et al., 2025)], SPFSplat [(Huang and Mikolajczyk, 2025)]) or one per voxel (AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)]). Their Gaussian count is therefore determined by the input resolution and the number of views, or by the voxel size, rather than chosen by the user.

    Implementation details. In the base training stage, we train the geometry backbone and Gaussian decoder with random allocations for 40,000 steps. In the subsequent policy training stage, we train for an additional 5,000 steps. During training, the Gaussian budget is sampled from [2048,16384V], where V is the number of input views. Unless otherwise noted, we use K_\rmanc=K_\rmgs=16 for Gaussian decoding in all experiments. Details are provided in appendicesE and F.

    4.1 Novel-view Synthesis Results

    Table1 compares RLSplat with budget-controllable methods at matched budgets of 1K, 2K, and 4K Gaussians per context view. RLSplat achieves the best LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR at every budget and view count. Importantly, its advantage becomes increasingly pronounced as the Gaussian budget decreases. For example, with 8 context views, the PSNR advantage over F4Splat grows from 0.74 dB at 4K Gaussians per view to 0.99 dB at 2K and 1.22 dB at 1K. This trend is consistent across 16 and 24 context views, demonstrating that RLSplat preserves reconstruction quality particularly well under tight representation budgets. This robustness is consistent with how the final B Gaussians are decoded: the baselines predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, whereas RLSplat directly decodes the requested number of Gaussians and refines them through resource-linear decoding.

    For a broader comparison, Table2 includes budget-fixed methods whose output size is determined by the input. Despite using substantially fewer Gaussians, RLSplat outperforms all of these methods on LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR across all view counts. In particular, with 24 context views, RLSplat achieves 25.58 dB PSNR using only 24K Gaussians, compared with 25.00 dB for SPFSplat using 1536K Gaussians, corresponding to 64× fewer Gaussians.

    Fig.4 shows how each method uses the same total budget of 8K Gaussians on RE10K. In the highlighted stair region, EcoSplat and F4Splat retain 2,521 and 3,026 Gaussians, respectively, whereas RLSplat allocates 5,388 Gaussians to the thin, high-frequency structure. The tile-wise allocation maps further show that RLSplat concentrates its budget around the stair balusters while spending fewer Gaussians on the comparatively smooth wall. This targeted allocation leads to substantially better reconstruction of the thin structures: the local PSNR of the highlighted region increases from 17.79 dB for EcoSplat and 20.00 dB for F4Splat to 23.51 dB for RLSplat . The improvement is also reflected in the full-view PSNR (21.82, 23.42, and 26.51 dB, respectively). These results illustrate that the learned allocation policy uses a fixed Gaussian budget more effectively by concentrating capacity where fine geometric and appearance details require it.

    4.2 Ablation Studies and Analysis

    Unless otherwise noted, all experiments in this section are evaluated on ACID with 8 views at a total budget of B=8,192 (1,024 Gaussians per view). Ablations that require retraining use the shortened schedules in appendixF.

    Architecture and objectives.Table3 ablates the locality regularizers, the projection loss, and the local refinement module. These variants change the base training; each is trained from scratch with the shortened pretraining schedule of appendixF. Removing the offset loss lowers PSNR by 0.53 dB, as refinement then moves Gaussians far from the initial positions from which their neighborhoods are computed. Removing the Voronoi loss as well causes a much larger drop of 2.51 dB, since Gaussians also leave their anchor’s cell and the hierarchical search no longer retrieves their true neighbors. Without the projection loss, training fails entirely, since nothing ties an anchor’s Gaussians to the image region it was encoded from. Removing the local refinement module lowers PSNR by 0.96 dB, since each Gaussian is then predicted from its own token alone and cannot be made consistent with its neighbors.

    Allocation policy.Table4 compares our Gaussian allocation policy with learning-free alternatives, all fine-tuned from the same base-trained model: a uniform split and an edge-based heuristic that allocates Gaussians in proportion to the Sobel gradient magnitude of the image. The policy-based allocation achieves the best result on all three metrics. Figure6 shows where this gain comes from. At the same total budget, the policy places fewer Gaussians than uniform allocation in a low-texture wall region with comparable rendering quality, and spends the saved budget on the textured floor, where it recovers the checkerboard pattern that uniform allocation blurs. Figure6 visualizes the learned allocation over whole views. Across views, the policy moves budget away from the near-textureless view; within a view, it concentrates Gaussians on complex structures such as the bed and the building facade, while nearly emptying flat walls, floor, and water.

    Gaussian local refinement.Table5 compares our hierarchical neighbor search with an exact search over all B Gaussians at 65,536 Gaussians, using K_\rmanc=16 anchor neighbors and K_\rmgs=16 Gaussian neighbors. The hierarchical search is 27× faster (8.1 ms vs. 219.6 ms) and reduces the end-to-end latency from 595.0 ms to 388.0 ms. With the Voronoi loss, the hierarchical search retrieves exactly the same K_\rmgs nearest neighbors as the exact search for 99.0% of the Gaussians, whereas without it this rate drops to 60.2%, as Gaussians drift out of their anchor’s cell. Table5 varies the number of neighbors K_\rmgs at inference while keeping K_\rmanc fixed. For every K_\rmgs, peak VRAM decreases linearly with B, and a larger K_\rmgs improves quality at the cost of memory. As the budget grows, the quality gap between different K_\rmgs narrows, while the memory cost of a larger K_\rmgs increases. Since K_\rmgs can be changed without retraining, users can choose a smaller value at large budgets to save memory with little loss in quality, and a larger K_\rmgs at small budgets where it matters most.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented RLSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward 3DGS framework whose inference cost scales linearly with the requested number of Gaussians B. A Gaussian allocation policy, trained with GSPO, distributes exactly B Gaussians across anchors, and a resource-linear decoder refines them through local cross-attention with a hierarchical neighbor search. On ACID, RLSplat achieves the best rendering quality among budget-controllable methods at every tested budget. Its latency and peak memory decrease linearly with B, and it matches or exceeds the quality of the baselines at a fraction of their memory and latency.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

    Image encoding remains a fixed cost independent of B, which bounds the achievable speed-up at small budgets. We also evaluate at a resolution of 256×256 and in a single cross-dataset setting. RLSplat controls both the size of the representation and the cost of producing it. It can therefore serve as a 3D scene representation for downstream tasks that have their own resource limits, such as 3D vision-language models and robot learning. Evaluating it on such tasks is a natural next step.

    Appendix B Allocation Policy Details

    Policy head.

    The policy head predicts a logit lₙ for each anchor token, and the allocation probabilities are obtained as p=softmax(l) with l={lₙ}ₙ₌₁^N. The head is LN(d)→Linear(d,h)→SiLU→Linear(h,1), applied per anchor token. The last linear layer is zero-initialized, so p starts uniform.

    Budget conditioning.

    The head is modulated by FiLM parameters (γ,η). They are predicted from a single scalar, the log-ratio of the requested budget to the number of anchors, u=\log₂(B/N), by Linear(1,h)→SiLU→Linear(h,2d). The modulation is applied after the layer norm: hidden←hidden⊙(1+\tanhγ(u))+η(u). The last layer of the FiLM generator is also zero-initialized. The ratio B/N is floored at 1/64 so that u stays finite for very small budgets.

    Policy initialization at the start of policy training.

    The policy head does not exist during base training. It is created with zero-initialized output layers when policy training begins, so it outputs exactly 0 for every anchor and p is uniform at the first policy-training step. Base training’s random allocation already covers this regime, so the transition introduces no distribution shift for the decoder.

    Deterministic integer allocation.

    At inference, and for the reconstruction loss during policy training, the expected counts Bp are converted into an integer allocation k^⋆ by systematic rounding with a fixed phase. Anchors are laid out on a line in a fixed (view, patch-raster) order, anchor n owning the interval [BPₙ₋₁, BPₙ) with Pₙ=∑_m≤npₘ and P₀=0. We place B points at φ,φ+1,…,φ+B-1 with φ=\tfrac12 and count those that fall inside each interval:

    k^⋆ₙ = ⌈BPₙ-φ⌉-⌈BPₙ₋₁-φ⌉.

    		(11)

    This rule has three properties we rely on: (i) the counts sum to exactly B, since the telescoping sum equals ⌈B-\tfrac12⌉-⌈-\tfrac12⌉=B; (ii) every count is either ⌊Bpₙ⌋ or ⌈Bpₙ⌉, since an interval of length Bpₙ contains that many unit-spaced points; and (iii) an anchor with pₙ=0 receives no Gaussian. With a uniformly random phase, Eq.11 is systematic resampling and satisfies 𝔼[kₙ]=Bpₙ, the mean of the multinomial rollouts. Fixing φ makes it deterministic. It needs a single cumulative sum, so it takes O(N) time, involves no sorting and has no ties to break. We compute it in double precision and renormalize P_N to one.

    Appendix C GSPO Training Details

    GSPO hyperparameters.

    Table6 ablates the two hyperparameters of the rollouts: the group size C and the rollout temperature τ. With τ≠1, the rollouts are drawn from the tempered proposal q rather than from p, and the ratio is no longer one. The policy is robust to both hyperparameters: all settings are within 0.11 dB PSNR of each other. C=5 performs best, and τ=1.0, which samples from the policy itself, outperforms both tempered variants. We use C=5 and τ=1.0 throughout.

    Settled hyperparameters.

    Policy training uses C=5 rollouts and policy loss weight λ_policy=1.0; the entropy and KL weights are both 0, and no minimum per-anchor count is enforced. Base training (Sec.3.4) trains the encoder and decoder without an allocation head at all, so there is no pretrained policy to serve as a KL reference at the start of policy training. The policy instead starts from the zero-initialized, uniform head described above.

    Appendix D Decoder Details

    Gaussian token construction.

    For anchor n with kₙ allocated Gaussians, token r∈{0,…,kₙ-1} has relative position ρ_n,r=(r+\tfrac12)/kₙ∈(0,1), so the tokens of any anchor tile the unit interval regardless of kₙ. We use a mip-NeRF-style [(Barron et al., 2021)] integrated positional encoding PE(ρ,k) that averages Fourier features over the token’s bin of width 1/kₙ, which suppresses the frequencies that would otherwise alias between nearby values of kₙ. The token is

    t⁰_n,r=aₙ+(1+\tanhαₙ)⊙MLP(PE(ρ_n,r,kₙ))+βₙ, (αₙ,βₙ)=Linear(LN(aₙ)),

    		(12)

    with the FiLM layer zero-initialized. All B tokens across a batch are packed into one sequence, so no computation is spent on padding.

    Neighbor search.

    Anchor centroids μ̄ₙ are the mean initial centers of each anchor’s tokens. ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n), the K_\rmanc=16 nearest anchors to n (including n itself), is found once by a K-nearest-neighbor search over the detached centroids and shared by all L=2 decoder layers. A Gaussian’s neighbor set ℕᵍˢ(b) is the K_\rmgs nearest Gaussian tokens, by detached Euclidean distance, among the tokens belonging to ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b).

    Residual head.

    The initial-Gaussian head and the residual head share the same architecture, LN→Linear(d,256)→SiLU→Linear(256,11+3dₛₕ), predicting a center offset (3), an opacity logit (1), scales (3), a quaternion (4), and spherical-harmonic color coefficients. The residual head is zero-initialized, and its center output is scaled by α_μ.

    Appendix E Training Details

    Context views are loaded at 256×256 and bilinearly upsampled to 504×504 immediately before the backbone, while target views, losses, and evaluation remain at 256×256. The DVLT [(Burzio et al., 2026)] backbone runs 12 inference steps. Each training step draws the number of context views V from the divisors of 24, V∈{2,3,4,6,8,12,24}, and sets the batch size to 24/V, so that every step processes 24 context views in total regardless of V.

    Base training.

    The encoder and decoder are trained for 40K steps with allocations drawn uniformly at random, which exposes the decoder to a wide range of per-anchor counts before any policy is learned. The per-sample budget is sampled from a Beta distribution over [2048,16384V]. We use AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ (0.1× for the backbone), 1,000 warm-up steps, and cosine decay on 4 GPUs. The loss weights are 1.0 for MSE, 0.05 for VGG-LPIPS, 0.1 for the reprojection term and 0.05 for the cheirality term of Lₚᵣₒⱼ, and 1.0 for Lᵥₒᵣ. The offset loss L_offset is weighted λ_offset=0.01.

    Policy training.

    Starting from the pretrained model, all parameters are fine-tuned for 5K steps with C=5 rollouts per step and a rollout temperature of τ=1.0; the render used for the reconstruction loss is produced from the deterministic allocation of Sec.3.2. The learning rate is reduced to 10⁻⁵, with a 30× multiplier on the allocation head, and L_offset is disabled. The policy loss L_policy is weighted 1.0. Each sample’s budget is drawn independently from Beta(1,4) over the same range, which biases training toward low budgets where allocation matters most. The total budget of a step is capped, so that peak memory is bounded independently of the per-sample maximum.

    Appendix F Ablation Protocol

    Each ablation changes a single component relative to its reference, except for the variant that removes both locality regularizers. Pretraining ablations (Table3) are trained from scratch for 5K steps, one eighth of the full schedule, with all step-dependent schedules (cosine horizon, optimizer warm-up, view-sampler warm-up, and validation and checkpoint intervals) scaled by the same factor. We compare the full recipe with variants that remove the local refinement module, the projection loss (both its reprojection and cheirality terms), the offset loss, or both the offset and Voronoi losses. The neighbor match rate without the Voronoi loss is measured with the same schedule. Allocation ablations (Tables4 and 6) fine-tune for 1K steps from a single shared pretrained checkpoint and vary the group size C∈{3,5,7}, the temperature τ∈{0.8,1.0,1.2}, and the allocation rule, replacing the learned policy with a uniform split or a learning-free Sobel-energy heuristic. Since a shorter run anneals on its own cosine schedule, each variant is trained for its own horizon rather than truncated from a longer run. All ablations are evaluated on ACID with 8 context views (249 scenes). Allocation ablations are evaluated at B/V=1024.

    Appendix G Allocation Policy Visualizations

    Figs.8, 9 and 10 extend Fig.6 to twelve RE10K two-view test scenes, all at an average of 1024 Gaussians per view. For each anchor we show its expected allocation relative to a uniform split, pₙN, where N is the number of anchors over both views; 1× corresponds to about 0.8 Gaussians per anchor at this budget. This is the policy’s output before the budget is rounded to integer counts. The corner label is the fraction of the total budget that goes to that view. We show the raw per-anchor maps next to the smoothed maps used in the main paper (Gaussian filter, σ=1 anchor, applied to \log₂ of the map), so the smoothing can be checked for artifacts: it only removes anchor-level noise and leaves the spatial pattern unchanged.

    Appendix H Additional Qualitative Comparison

    Figs.11, 12 and 13 compare RLSplat with F4Splat and EcoSplat as the Gaussian budget is reduced from 128K to 32K. As the budget decreases, the baselines progressively blur or lose thin, high-frequency structures such as stair balusters, railings, window frames, and foliage, while RLSplat retains these details at every budget. This is consistent with Table1, where RLSplat exhibits substantially less quality degradation than the baselines as the budget decreases. Unlike the baselines, which reduce a dense set of candidates, RLSplat allocates the budget where the scene needs it and decodes only those Gaussians, preserving fine details even under the tightest budgets.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有「预算可控」的前馈 3DGS 先猜一大坨再剪枝，延迟与峰值显存几乎不随预算下来；RLSplat 让表示、延迟、显存三者一起线性下降。

要点：

  • 对照 F4Splat：2K 高斯预算下 PSNR 高 0.9 dB，同时峰值显存少 9.6×、速度快 4.1×；预算越低差距越大
  • 8 个上下文视角时，相对 F4Splat 的 PSNR 优势从 4K 的 0.74 dB 增到 2K 的 0.99 dB、1K 的 1.22 dB
  • 24 个视角下只用 24K 高斯拿 25.58 dB，而 SPFSplat 用 1536K 高斯才 25.00 dB，高斯数少 64×
  • 做法是学一个高斯分配策略，把预算按局部区域分下去，直接生成正好所需数量的高斯，而不是先稠密预测再裁剪

为什么值得看：移动端/VR 场景里，「预算可调」必须同时控制推理成本，否则调低预算只省了渲染不省生成；把分配策略和预算绑在一起，才能做成真正的档位表。

中文摘要：前馈 3D Gaussian Splatting 一次前向就能从图像重建 3D 场景，适合资源受限的场合；近年的预算可控方法允许在推理时调整高斯数量以匹配存储上限或渲染延迟。但这些方法忽略推理本身的成本：为了得到目标数量的高斯，它们先预测一个稠密集合再裁剪或选择，导致延迟与峰值内存几乎与预算无关。作者提出 RLSplat：学一个高斯分配策略，把预算分配到各个局部场景区域，直接生成恰好请求数量的高斯，于是表示大小、推理延迟和峰值内存都随预算线性下降。在零样本评测里，每个预算档位上 RLSplat 都优于先前的预算可控方法，低预算下甚至用 4 倍更少的高斯超过最强基线，速度最高快 4.1 倍、峰值显存少 9.6 倍。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-10-26

RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4× fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1× faster with 9.6× less peak memory at low budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/RLSplat.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] has become a leading representation for photorealistic, real-time novel view synthesis, supporting applications from AR/VR [(Qian et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024)] to robotics [(Keetha et al., 2024; Matsuki et al., 2024)] and digital content creation [(Tang et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b)]. Its explicit form further allows it to serve as a 3D scene representation for downstream models, such as 3D vision-language models [(Li et al., 2025; Thai et al., 2025)]. Since per-scene optimization of 3DGS takes minutes to hours and requires many calibrated views, feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in a single forward pass [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a)], and recent variants even operate directly on uncalibrated images [(Jiang et al., 2025)]. Owing to this fast and readily available reconstruction, FF3DGS has become a practical choice for applications that build 3D scene representations on the fly.

Early FF3DGS methods [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Ye et al., 2025)] simplify the problem by allocating a fixed number of Gaussians to each input pixel, which allows the feed-forward network to be trained effectively. However, this pixel-aligned design produces many redundant Gaussians, since Gaussians from overlapping views become increasingly redundant as more views are added. To address this redundancy, query-based methods [(An et al., 2026; Itkin et al., 2026)] decode a fixed set of learnable query tokens into Gaussians. Yet neither approach can adjust the number of Gaussians without retraining. This lack of controllability makes it difficult to adapt to the diverse resource budgets encountered in real-world deployment. To address this, recent works have proposed Gaussian budget-controllable methods. Given a Gaussian budget B, EcoSplat [(Park et al., 2026)] first predicts one Gaussian per pixel and keeps the B Gaussians with the highest opacity. F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)] instead predicts Gaussians at multiple scales and selects the B Gaussians. However, these methods overlook the computational cost of inference itself. Both methods first predict a much larger set of candidate Gaussians before reducing them to B, so their inference latency and peak memory remain nearly constant regardless of the budget, as shown in Fig.1(b) and (c).

We therefore propose RLSplat, a budget-controllable FF3DGS framework that is resource-linear: both its representation size and inference cost scale linearly with the budget B. Given uncalibrated images and a budget B, a geometry backbone encodes the images into anchor tokens, each representing a local 3D region of the scene. To obtain a compact representation, we formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem rather than pruning or selection: we predict how many Gaussians to assign to each anchor’s region, summing to B. Since these discrete allocations are non-differentiable and can only be evaluated by rendering the resulting Gaussians, we model this prediction as a Gaussian allocation policy and train it with policy optimization, using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [(Zheng et al., 2025)] with rendering quality as the reward. Given the allocation, each anchor token spawns as many Gaussian tokens as its allocated count, yielding a total of B Gaussian tokens. To efficiently decode these tokens into the final Gaussians, we introduce a resource-linear decoder. It refines each Gaussian token through local cross-attention over its K_\rmgs nearest Gaussian tokens, which we find with an efficient hierarchical neighbor search. Whereas global self-attention over all B tokens costs O(B²), each token here attends to only K_\rmgs neighbors, so the decoding cost is O(BK_\rmgs) and scales linearly with the Gaussian budget (Fig.1(c)). As a result, RLSplat achieves higher quality than prior budget-controllable methods at every budget (Fig.1(a)), while its peak memory and latency decrease with the budget. At 2K Gaussians, it achieves higher PSNR than F4Splat while using 9.6× less peak memory (Fig.1(b)) and running 4.1× faster (Fig.1(c)).

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify that existing budget-controllable FF3DGS methods control only the size of the output, not the cost of producing it, and introduce RLSplat, a resource-linear FF3DGS framework in which the number of Gaussians, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the budget B is reduced.

  • •

    We formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem and learn a Gaussian allocation policy via policy optimization that places exactly B Gaussians where the scene needs them, together with a resource-linear decoder whose cost decreases linearly as the budget decreases through local cross-attention and an efficient hierarchical neighbor search.

  • •

    RLSplat consistently outperforms prior budget-controllable methods across all budgets. At a budget of 2K Gaussians, it improves PSNR by 0.9 dB over F4Splat while using 9.6× less peak memory and running 4.1× faster.

    • 2 Related Work

    Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] represents a scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and achieves real-time rendering, but requires time-consuming per-scene optimization from many calibrated views. Feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in a single forward pass, from a single image [(Szymanowicz et al., 2024)] or from a few posed views [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024)]. Building on 3D foundation models [(Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025)], recent methods further remove the need for known camera poses [(Ye et al., 2025; Smart et al., 2024; Huang and Mikolajczyk, 2025; Jiang et al., 2025)]. Most of these methods predict one Gaussian per pixel or per voxel, so the number of Gaussians is determined by the input resolution and the number of views rather than by the scene content. This leads to redundant Gaussians in overlapping and textureless regions, and the number of Gaussians cannot be specified directly.

    Compact and Gaussian budget-controllable FF3DGS. For per-scene 3DGS, many works aim to represent a scene with fewer Gaussians without sacrificing quality, either by pruning redundant Gaussians [(Fan et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2024; Papantonakis et al., 2024)] or by deciding where to place Gaussians under a fixed or constrained budget during densification [(Fang and Wang, 2024; Mallick et al., 2024; Kheradmand et al., 2024)]. These methods, however, rely on iterative per-scene optimization. In FF3DGS, C3G [(An et al., 2026)] and GlobalSplat [(Itkin et al., 2026)] decode a fixed set of learnable query tokens into compact sets of Gaussians, whose size is determined by the architecture. EcoSplat [(Park et al., 2026)] and F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)] instead accept a target count at inference, by keeping the Gaussians with the highest budget-conditioned opacity and by selecting one of multiple scales per region, respectively; both derive the output from a dense set of candidates. ZipSplat [(Veicht et al., 2026)], developed concurrently with our work, controls the number of Gaussians by clustering visual tokens at inference. In contrast, we learn to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians and decode only those, so that our inference cost scales with the budget.

    Policy optimization. Policy gradient methods [(Williams, 1992; Schulman et al., 2017)] optimize non-differentiable, discrete decisions from a scalar reward, and have been applied to generative vision models, e.g., to align diffusion models with reward functions [(Black et al., 2024)]. Group-relative variants such as GRPO [(Shao et al., 2024)] and GSPO [(Zheng et al., 2025)] remove the need for a learned value function by normalizing rewards within a group of samples, and have become standard for fine-tuning large language models. In particular, GSPO defines the importance ratio from the likelihood of the whole sequence rather than of individual tokens, and clips it at the sequence level. We adopt this approach to learn Gaussian allocation, treating an allocation as a sequence of B Gaussians and using rendering quality as the reward.

    3 Method

    We present RLSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework whose Gaussian count and inference cost are both controlled by a single budget B. Rather than pruning or selecting from a dense set of Gaussians, RLSplat formulates Gaussian generation as allocation: a Gaussian allocation policy decides how many Gaussians each local region of the scene receives (Sec.3.2), and a resource-linear decoder generates the allocated Gaussians and efficiently refines them with local cross-attention (Sec.3.3). We begin with an overview (Sec.3.1) and conclude with the training procedure (Sec.3.4).

    3.1 Overview of RLSplat

    Given V uncalibrated context images {Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V and a target Gaussian budget B, RLSplat F_θ predicts a set of 3D Gaussians G along with the context camera parameters {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V:

    (G,{Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V)=F_θ({Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^V,B), G={g_b}_b=1^B.

    		(1)

    Here, the 3DGS attribute g_b consists of a 3D center, opacity, scale, rotation, and color coefficients.

    As illustrated in Fig.2, a geometry backbone [(Burzio et al., 2026)] encodes the images into N anchor tokens {aₙ}ₙ₌₁^N. These anchors serve as the foundational sites from which the 3D Gaussians are spawned. To use the limited budget effectively, RLSplat adaptively distributes the B Gaussians across these anchors. Specifically, a Gaussian allocation policy assesses the local significance of each anchor to predict a discrete allocation k∈ℤ_≥0^N that strictly sums to the budget (∑kₙ=B), and we optimize this policy via reinforcement learning (Sec.3.2). Next, a resource-linear decoder instantiates exactly kₙ Gaussian tokens at each anchor. It predicts an initial state for each Gaussian and efficiently processes them via a refinement module to produce the final set of B Gaussians. This decoder’s computational footprint scales linearly with the requested budget, as described in Sec.3.3.

    3.2 Gaussian Allocation Policy

    To achieve a compact and high-fidelity representation, Gaussians must be densely allocated to the anchors that encode geometrically complex local 3D regions. We formulate this discrete allocation task as a reinforcement learning problem, parameterizing a policy π_ψ(k|{aₙ}ₙ₌₁^N,B) that maps the anchor tokens and target budget to a discrete allocation k={kₙ}ₙ₌₁^N. Specifically, the policy model predicts allocation proportions p={pₙ}^Nₙ₌₁, where pₙ represents the expected fraction of the Gaussian budget assigned to anchor n. The allocation process is modeled as drawing trials from a multinomial distribution, such that k∼Mult(B,p).

    To optimize π_ψ over these non-differentiable discrete allocations, we leverage Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) [(Zheng et al., 2025)]. At each training step, we draw a group of C rollouts, i.e., candidate allocations k⁽ᶜ⁾∼π_old=Mult(B,sg(p)) for c∈{1,…,C}, from the current policy with gradients stopped by sg(·). For each rollout c, we first generate the 3DGS representation G⁽ᶜ⁾. We then render an image Î⁽ᶜ⁾ from G⁽ᶜ⁾ at novel target views, computing the reconstruction loss L_recon⁽ᶜ⁾ against the ground-truth I without gradient tracking. This loss directly serves as the reward signal for rendering quality, defined as R_c=-L_recon⁽ᶜ⁾. Thanks to the highly efficient rasterization of 3DGS, evaluating multiple rollouts introduces minimal training overhead. We then compute the group-relative advantage Â_c by standardizing the rewards within the group:

    Â_c=(R_c-mean({R_c^′}_c^′=1^C))/(std({R_c^′}_c^′=1^C)).

    		(2)

    Following the GSPO framework, we view the allocation of Gaussians as a sequence of length B and compute a length-normalized importance ratio s_c for each rollout:

    s_c=((π_ψ(k⁽ᶜ⁾))/(π_old(k⁽ᶜ⁾)))^1/B=\exp(1/B∑ₙ₌₁^Nk⁽ᶜ⁾ₙ\logpₙ/sg(pₙ)).

    		(3)

    The policy is then updated by maximizing the clipped objective

    J_policy=𝔼[1/C∑_c=1^C\min(s_cÂ_c, clip(s_c,1-ε,1+ε)Â_c)],

    		(4)

    where ε is the clipping range, and the expectation is taken over scenes, budgets, and rollout groups. At inference time, we bypass stochastic sampling and deterministically convert the expected counts Bp into an integer allocation whose counts sum exactly to B. Details of the rounding procedure are provided in appendixB.

    3.3 Resource-Linear Gaussian Decoding

    Given a Gaussian allocation k={kₙ}ₙ₌₁^N, the resource-linear decoder spawns exactly B Gaussian tokens from the anchors and decodes them into the final Gaussians at a cost linear in B. We describe the token spawning, the local refinement with hierarchical neighbor search, and the regularizers that keep this search accurate.

    Gaussian token spawning. For each anchor aₙ, a token generator instantiates kₙ distinct Gaussian tokens, each conditioned on its slot index within the anchor (appendixD):

    {t_b}_b=1^B=TokenGen({(aₙ,kₙ)}ₙ₌₁^N).

    		(5)

    We denote by n_b the anchor that spawned token b. A head then predicts an initial Gaussian g_b⁰=Head(t_b) from each token, including its initial center μ⁰_b.

    Local refinement with hierarchical neighbor search. Since the initial tokens lack spatial context, they must attend to neighboring Gaussians to refine their parameters. To avoid the prohibitive O(B²) cost of global attention, we employ a local cross-attention mechanism over L layers. Anchors with kₙ=0 are excluded from the hierarchical neighbor search. For each remaining anchor n, we compute the centroid μ̄ₙ of its initial Gaussians:

    μ̄ₙ=1/kₙ∑_b: n_b=nμ⁰_b.

    		(6)

    To find neighbors efficiently, we search hierarchically: we find the K_\rmanc nearest anchors, and then search for the K_\rmgs nearest Gaussian tokens only among the Gaussians belonging to these local anchors:

    ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n)=KNN_K_\rmanc(μ̄ₙ;{μ̄ₘ:kₘ>0}),(7)
    ℕᵍˢ(b)=KNN_K_\rmgs(μ⁰_b;{μ⁰ⱼ:nⱼ∈ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b)}).

    By restricting the search space, we keep the neighbor querying highly efficient. Both neighbor sets are computed once using the detached initial positions and shared across all L layers. Each token t_b is then refined by L layers of cross-attention over its neighbors, each followed by a feed-forward layer:

    t_b←t_b+CrossAttn(t_b, {tⱼ}_j∈ℕᵍˢ(b)).

    		(8)

    Finally, a residual head predicts a correction Δg_b from t_b, giving g_b=g_b⁰+Δg_b.

    Locality regularizers. For this hierarchical search to be valid, a Gaussian’s true spatial neighbors must actually reside within its parent’s anchor neighborhood ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b). We enforce this using two regularizers. First, a Voronoi loss keeps each Gaussian closer to its own parent anchor’s centroid μ̄_n_b than to any neighboring anchor’s centroid μ̄ₘ:

    Lᵥₒᵣ=1/B∑_b=1^B∑_m∈ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b)\max(0, ∥μ⁰_b-μ̄_n_b∥-∥μ⁰_b-μ̄ₘ∥).

    		(9)

    Second, an offset loss constrains the residual correction Δμ_b to limit Gaussian drift:

    L_offset=1/B∑_b=1^B\max(0, (∥Δμ_b∥)/(d_n_b)-δ)²,

    		(10)

    where dₙ is the local anchor spacing, defined as the median distance from μ̄n to its K\rmanc nearest anchors, and δ=0.5 is a margin limiting Gaussian movement relative to the local anchor scale.

    3.4 Training

    We train RLSplat in two stages: base training trains the geometry backbone and decoder with random allocations, and policy training introduces the Gaussian allocation policy and fine-tunes the entire model with policy optimization.

    Objectives. To supervise view synthesis, we apply a reconstruction loss L_recon, combining pixel-wise MSE and LPIPS between the rendered and ground-truth target views. For geometric alignment, a camera loss L_cam supervises the translation, rotation, and field-of-view of the predicted context cameras. Additionally, a projection loss Lₚᵣₒⱼ reprojects each anchor’s Gaussians toward their source image patch. Incorporating a cheirality penalty to prevent Gaussians from landing behind the camera, Lₚᵣₒⱼ effectively ties an anchor’s allocation to a specific scene region and prevents arbitrary drift. These terms are combined with the locality regularizers (Lᵥₒᵣ and L_offset) previously introduced in Sec.3.3. Finally, during the policy training stage, we activate the policy loss L_policy=-J_policy (Eq.4) to optimize the discrete allocations via GSPO. The overall training objectives are detailed in appendixE.

    Two-stage training. We train RLSplat in two stages. In base training, we train the encoder and decoder with random allocations, and sample budgets over the full supported range. This exposes the decoder to widely varying per-anchor counts, so that it learns to render diverse allocations before the policy is introduced. In policy training, we add the policy head, initialized to output uniform probabilities (appendixB), and fine-tune the entire model with the policy loss L_policy. Since base training involves no policy, there is no reference policy to regularize toward, and unlike typical RL fine-tuning, we do not apply a KL penalty. During this stage, budgets are sampled with a skew toward the lower end of the range, where the choice of allocation matters most for rendering quality.

    4 Experiments

    Datasets and evaluation. We train on RealEstate10K (RE10K) [(Zhou et al., 2018)] with V∈{2,3,4,6,8,12,24} uncalibrated context views. To assess generalization, we evaluate the RE10K-trained model zero-shot on ACID [(Liu et al., 2021)] (249 test scenes), which consists of aerial footage of coastal and natural scenes. We follow the evaluation protocol of F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)] at a resolution of 256×256 and report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS together with the number of Gaussians (#GS). To measure inference cost, we report the latency and peak VRAM of Gaussian generation, excluding data loading, pose alignment, and rendering. All methods are run on a single RTX A6000 with a batch size of one. For each budget, we discard the first scene as warm-up, reset the peak-memory counter before each timed run, and report the mean over the test scenes.

    Baselines. We mainly compare with budget-controllable methods, EcoSplat [(Park et al., 2026)] and F⁴Splat [(Kim et al., 2026)], which take a target Gaussian count as input at inference time. We evaluate all methods at the same requested Gaussian budgets, with particular focus on the low-budget regime. For a broader comparison, we also include budget-fixed methods, which place Gaussians uniformly, either one per pixel (NoPoSplat [(Ye et al., 2025)], SPFSplat [(Huang and Mikolajczyk, 2025)]) or one per voxel (AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)]). Their Gaussian count is therefore determined by the input resolution and the number of views, or by the voxel size, rather than chosen by the user.

    Implementation details. In the base training stage, we train the geometry backbone and Gaussian decoder with random allocations for 40,000 steps. In the subsequent policy training stage, we train for an additional 5,000 steps. During training, the Gaussian budget is sampled from [2048,16384V], where V is the number of input views. Unless otherwise noted, we use K_\rmanc=K_\rmgs=16 for Gaussian decoding in all experiments. Details are provided in appendicesE and F.

    4.1 Novel-view Synthesis Results

    Table1 compares RLSplat with budget-controllable methods at matched budgets of 1K, 2K, and 4K Gaussians per context view. RLSplat achieves the best LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR at every budget and view count. Importantly, its advantage becomes increasingly pronounced as the Gaussian budget decreases. For example, with 8 context views, the PSNR advantage over F4Splat grows from 0.74 dB at 4K Gaussians per view to 0.99 dB at 2K and 1.22 dB at 1K. This trend is consistent across 16 and 24 context views, demonstrating that RLSplat preserves reconstruction quality particularly well under tight representation budgets. This robustness is consistent with how the final B Gaussians are decoded: the baselines predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, whereas RLSplat directly decodes the requested number of Gaussians and refines them through resource-linear decoding.

    For a broader comparison, Table2 includes budget-fixed methods whose output size is determined by the input. Despite using substantially fewer Gaussians, RLSplat outperforms all of these methods on LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR across all view counts. In particular, with 24 context views, RLSplat achieves 25.58 dB PSNR using only 24K Gaussians, compared with 25.00 dB for SPFSplat using 1536K Gaussians, corresponding to 64× fewer Gaussians.

    Fig.4 shows how each method uses the same total budget of 8K Gaussians on RE10K. In the highlighted stair region, EcoSplat and F4Splat retain 2,521 and 3,026 Gaussians, respectively, whereas RLSplat allocates 5,388 Gaussians to the thin, high-frequency structure. The tile-wise allocation maps further show that RLSplat concentrates its budget around the stair balusters while spending fewer Gaussians on the comparatively smooth wall. This targeted allocation leads to substantially better reconstruction of the thin structures: the local PSNR of the highlighted region increases from 17.79 dB for EcoSplat and 20.00 dB for F4Splat to 23.51 dB for RLSplat . The improvement is also reflected in the full-view PSNR (21.82, 23.42, and 26.51 dB, respectively). These results illustrate that the learned allocation policy uses a fixed Gaussian budget more effectively by concentrating capacity where fine geometric and appearance details require it.

    4.2 Ablation Studies and Analysis

    Unless otherwise noted, all experiments in this section are evaluated on ACID with 8 views at a total budget of B=8,192 (1,024 Gaussians per view). Ablations that require retraining use the shortened schedules in appendixF.

    Architecture and objectives.Table3 ablates the locality regularizers, the projection loss, and the local refinement module. These variants change the base training; each is trained from scratch with the shortened pretraining schedule of appendixF. Removing the offset loss lowers PSNR by 0.53 dB, as refinement then moves Gaussians far from the initial positions from which their neighborhoods are computed. Removing the Voronoi loss as well causes a much larger drop of 2.51 dB, since Gaussians also leave their anchor’s cell and the hierarchical search no longer retrieves their true neighbors. Without the projection loss, training fails entirely, since nothing ties an anchor’s Gaussians to the image region it was encoded from. Removing the local refinement module lowers PSNR by 0.96 dB, since each Gaussian is then predicted from its own token alone and cannot be made consistent with its neighbors.

    Allocation policy.Table4 compares our Gaussian allocation policy with learning-free alternatives, all fine-tuned from the same base-trained model: a uniform split and an edge-based heuristic that allocates Gaussians in proportion to the Sobel gradient magnitude of the image. The policy-based allocation achieves the best result on all three metrics. Figure6 shows where this gain comes from. At the same total budget, the policy places fewer Gaussians than uniform allocation in a low-texture wall region with comparable rendering quality, and spends the saved budget on the textured floor, where it recovers the checkerboard pattern that uniform allocation blurs. Figure6 visualizes the learned allocation over whole views. Across views, the policy moves budget away from the near-textureless view; within a view, it concentrates Gaussians on complex structures such as the bed and the building facade, while nearly emptying flat walls, floor, and water.

    Gaussian local refinement.Table5 compares our hierarchical neighbor search with an exact search over all B Gaussians at 65,536 Gaussians, using K_\rmanc=16 anchor neighbors and K_\rmgs=16 Gaussian neighbors. The hierarchical search is 27× faster (8.1 ms vs. 219.6 ms) and reduces the end-to-end latency from 595.0 ms to 388.0 ms. With the Voronoi loss, the hierarchical search retrieves exactly the same K_\rmgs nearest neighbors as the exact search for 99.0% of the Gaussians, whereas without it this rate drops to 60.2%, as Gaussians drift out of their anchor’s cell. Table5 varies the number of neighbors K_\rmgs at inference while keeping K_\rmanc fixed. For every K_\rmgs, peak VRAM decreases linearly with B, and a larger K_\rmgs improves quality at the cost of memory. As the budget grows, the quality gap between different K_\rmgs narrows, while the memory cost of a larger K_\rmgs increases. Since K_\rmgs can be changed without retraining, users can choose a smaller value at large budgets to save memory with little loss in quality, and a larger K_\rmgs at small budgets where it matters most.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented RLSplat, a budget-controllable feed-forward 3DGS framework whose inference cost scales linearly with the requested number of Gaussians B. A Gaussian allocation policy, trained with GSPO, distributes exactly B Gaussians across anchors, and a resource-linear decoder refines them through local cross-attention with a hierarchical neighbor search. On ACID, RLSplat achieves the best rendering quality among budget-controllable methods at every tested budget. Its latency and peak memory decrease linearly with B, and it matches or exceeds the quality of the baselines at a fraction of their memory and latency.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

    Image encoding remains a fixed cost independent of B, which bounds the achievable speed-up at small budgets. We also evaluate at a resolution of 256×256 and in a single cross-dataset setting. RLSplat controls both the size of the representation and the cost of producing it. It can therefore serve as a 3D scene representation for downstream tasks that have their own resource limits, such as 3D vision-language models and robot learning. Evaluating it on such tasks is a natural next step.

    Appendix B Allocation Policy Details

    Policy head.

    The policy head predicts a logit lₙ for each anchor token, and the allocation probabilities are obtained as p=softmax(l) with l={lₙ}ₙ₌₁^N. The head is LN(d)→Linear(d,h)→SiLU→Linear(h,1), applied per anchor token. The last linear layer is zero-initialized, so p starts uniform.

    Budget conditioning.

    The head is modulated by FiLM parameters (γ,η). They are predicted from a single scalar, the log-ratio of the requested budget to the number of anchors, u=\log₂(B/N), by Linear(1,h)→SiLU→Linear(h,2d). The modulation is applied after the layer norm: hidden←hidden⊙(1+\tanhγ(u))+η(u). The last layer of the FiLM generator is also zero-initialized. The ratio B/N is floored at 1/64 so that u stays finite for very small budgets.

    Policy initialization at the start of policy training.

    The policy head does not exist during base training. It is created with zero-initialized output layers when policy training begins, so it outputs exactly 0 for every anchor and p is uniform at the first policy-training step. Base training’s random allocation already covers this regime, so the transition introduces no distribution shift for the decoder.

    Deterministic integer allocation.

    At inference, and for the reconstruction loss during policy training, the expected counts Bp are converted into an integer allocation k^⋆ by systematic rounding with a fixed phase. Anchors are laid out on a line in a fixed (view, patch-raster) order, anchor n owning the interval [BPₙ₋₁, BPₙ) with Pₙ=∑_m≤npₘ and P₀=0. We place B points at φ,φ+1,…,φ+B-1 with φ=\tfrac12 and count those that fall inside each interval:

    k^⋆ₙ = ⌈BPₙ-φ⌉-⌈BPₙ₋₁-φ⌉.

    		(11)

    This rule has three properties we rely on: (i) the counts sum to exactly B, since the telescoping sum equals ⌈B-\tfrac12⌉-⌈-\tfrac12⌉=B; (ii) every count is either ⌊Bpₙ⌋ or ⌈Bpₙ⌉, since an interval of length Bpₙ contains that many unit-spaced points; and (iii) an anchor with pₙ=0 receives no Gaussian. With a uniformly random phase, Eq.11 is systematic resampling and satisfies 𝔼[kₙ]=Bpₙ, the mean of the multinomial rollouts. Fixing φ makes it deterministic. It needs a single cumulative sum, so it takes O(N) time, involves no sorting and has no ties to break. We compute it in double precision and renormalize P_N to one.

    Appendix C GSPO Training Details

    GSPO hyperparameters.

    Table6 ablates the two hyperparameters of the rollouts: the group size C and the rollout temperature τ. With τ≠1, the rollouts are drawn from the tempered proposal q rather than from p, and the ratio is no longer one. The policy is robust to both hyperparameters: all settings are within 0.11 dB PSNR of each other. C=5 performs best, and τ=1.0, which samples from the policy itself, outperforms both tempered variants. We use C=5 and τ=1.0 throughout.

    Settled hyperparameters.

    Policy training uses C=5 rollouts and policy loss weight λ_policy=1.0; the entropy and KL weights are both 0, and no minimum per-anchor count is enforced. Base training (Sec.3.4) trains the encoder and decoder without an allocation head at all, so there is no pretrained policy to serve as a KL reference at the start of policy training. The policy instead starts from the zero-initialized, uniform head described above.

    Appendix D Decoder Details

    Gaussian token construction.

    For anchor n with kₙ allocated Gaussians, token r∈{0,…,kₙ-1} has relative position ρ_n,r=(r+\tfrac12)/kₙ∈(0,1), so the tokens of any anchor tile the unit interval regardless of kₙ. We use a mip-NeRF-style [(Barron et al., 2021)] integrated positional encoding PE(ρ,k) that averages Fourier features over the token’s bin of width 1/kₙ, which suppresses the frequencies that would otherwise alias between nearby values of kₙ. The token is

    t⁰_n,r=aₙ+(1+\tanhαₙ)⊙MLP(PE(ρ_n,r,kₙ))+βₙ, (αₙ,βₙ)=Linear(LN(aₙ)),

    		(12)

    with the FiLM layer zero-initialized. All B tokens across a batch are packed into one sequence, so no computation is spent on padding.

    Neighbor search.

    Anchor centroids μ̄ₙ are the mean initial centers of each anchor’s tokens. ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n), the K_\rmanc=16 nearest anchors to n (including n itself), is found once by a K-nearest-neighbor search over the detached centroids and shared by all L=2 decoder layers. A Gaussian’s neighbor set ℕᵍˢ(b) is the K_\rmgs nearest Gaussian tokens, by detached Euclidean distance, among the tokens belonging to ℕᵃⁿᶜ(n_b).

    Residual head.

    The initial-Gaussian head and the residual head share the same architecture, LN→Linear(d,256)→SiLU→Linear(256,11+3dₛₕ), predicting a center offset (3), an opacity logit (1), scales (3), a quaternion (4), and spherical-harmonic color coefficients. The residual head is zero-initialized, and its center output is scaled by α_μ.

    Appendix E Training Details

    Context views are loaded at 256×256 and bilinearly upsampled to 504×504 immediately before the backbone, while target views, losses, and evaluation remain at 256×256. The DVLT [(Burzio et al., 2026)] backbone runs 12 inference steps. Each training step draws the number of context views V from the divisors of 24, V∈{2,3,4,6,8,12,24}, and sets the batch size to 24/V, so that every step processes 24 context views in total regardless of V.

    Base training.

    The encoder and decoder are trained for 40K steps with allocations drawn uniformly at random, which exposes the decoder to a wide range of per-anchor counts before any policy is learned. The per-sample budget is sampled from a Beta distribution over [2048,16384V]. We use AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ (0.1× for the backbone), 1,000 warm-up steps, and cosine decay on 4 GPUs. The loss weights are 1.0 for MSE, 0.05 for VGG-LPIPS, 0.1 for the reprojection term and 0.05 for the cheirality term of Lₚᵣₒⱼ, and 1.0 for Lᵥₒᵣ. The offset loss L_offset is weighted λ_offset=0.01.

    Policy training.

    Starting from the pretrained model, all parameters are fine-tuned for 5K steps with C=5 rollouts per step and a rollout temperature of τ=1.0; the render used for the reconstruction loss is produced from the deterministic allocation of Sec.3.2. The learning rate is reduced to 10⁻⁵, with a 30× multiplier on the allocation head, and L_offset is disabled. The policy loss L_policy is weighted 1.0. Each sample’s budget is drawn independently from Beta(1,4) over the same range, which biases training toward low budgets where allocation matters most. The total budget of a step is capped, so that peak memory is bounded independently of the per-sample maximum.

    Appendix F Ablation Protocol

    Each ablation changes a single component relative to its reference, except for the variant that removes both locality regularizers. Pretraining ablations (Table3) are trained from scratch for 5K steps, one eighth of the full schedule, with all step-dependent schedules (cosine horizon, optimizer warm-up, view-sampler warm-up, and validation and checkpoint intervals) scaled by the same factor. We compare the full recipe with variants that remove the local refinement module, the projection loss (both its reprojection and cheirality terms), the offset loss, or both the offset and Voronoi losses. The neighbor match rate without the Voronoi loss is measured with the same schedule. Allocation ablations (Tables4 and 6) fine-tune for 1K steps from a single shared pretrained checkpoint and vary the group size C∈{3,5,7}, the temperature τ∈{0.8,1.0,1.2}, and the allocation rule, replacing the learned policy with a uniform split or a learning-free Sobel-energy heuristic. Since a shorter run anneals on its own cosine schedule, each variant is trained for its own horizon rather than truncated from a longer run. All ablations are evaluated on ACID with 8 context views (249 scenes). Allocation ablations are evaluated at B/V=1024.

    Appendix G Allocation Policy Visualizations

    Figs.8, 9 and 10 extend Fig.6 to twelve RE10K two-view test scenes, all at an average of 1024 Gaussians per view. For each anchor we show its expected allocation relative to a uniform split, pₙN, where N is the number of anchors over both views; 1× corresponds to about 0.8 Gaussians per anchor at this budget. This is the policy’s output before the budget is rounded to integer counts. The corner label is the fraction of the total budget that goes to that view. We show the raw per-anchor maps next to the smoothed maps used in the main paper (Gaussian filter, σ=1 anchor, applied to \log₂ of the map), so the smoothing can be checked for artifacts: it only removes anchor-level noise and leaves the spatial pattern unchanged.

    Appendix H Additional Qualitative Comparison

    Figs.11, 12 and 13 compare RLSplat with F4Splat and EcoSplat as the Gaussian budget is reduced from 128K to 32K. As the budget decreases, the baselines progressively blur or lose thin, high-frequency structures such as stair balusters, railings, window frames, and foliage, while RLSplat retains these details at every budget. This is consistent with Table1, where RLSplat exhibits substantially less quality degradation than the baselines as the budget decreases. Unlike the baselines, which reduce a dense set of candidates, RLSplat allocates the budget where the scene needs it and decodes only those Gaussians, preserving fine details even under the tightest budgets.

item.title: 连续 LoD 该留谁？KoalaGS 把输入视图的画面复杂度当先验，1% 以下预算才不塌 ｜ KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting
item.description:
一句话：降预算时复杂区和简单区掉得几乎一样多（-62% vs -58%），说明简单区的高斯本来就太多；用重建前的视图复杂度先验做重定位，整个预算谱系都更平滑。

要点：

  • 连续 LoD 的要求是一套图元在「只渲染前缀」时仍然有效，核心问题变成：预算下降时哪些高斯该保留容量
  • 在 3DGS-MCMC 重建上做 pilot 研究：图像复杂度（在优化前从输入视图算）能预测重建误差在图像与 3D 空间里集中到哪里
  • 训练期用这个复杂度先验把高斯向重建差的区域重定位，同时保证跨 LoD 平滑降级；推理期按重要性分数截断即可
  • 按 28 个操作点算分段 AUC：全容量追平最强基线，整个预算谱系优于所有连续 LoD 基线，在 0.1%–1% 极低预算段领先最多

为什么值得看：引擎做 LoD 通常靠距离/屏幕占比；3DGS 的 LoD 更该按「这个视角下重建得准不准」来排，这篇给出了一个不需要额外渲染就能算的复杂度代理。

中文摘要：把训练好的 3D Gaussian Splatting 场景部署到算力不断缩小的设备上，需要同一套图元在「只渲染前 k 个」时仍然可用，这就是连续 LoD：难点在于预算下降时决定哪些高斯保留容量。作者先在 3DGS-MCMC 重建上做 pilot 研究，发现用输入视图在优化前算出的图像复杂度，可以预测重建误差在图像与 3D 空间中的集中位置；同时发现简单区域里高斯过多，降预算时它们的退化幅度和复杂区域几乎一样（约 -62% 对 -58%），尽管这些区域本该更容易表示。据此提出 KoalaGS：训练时以该复杂度为先验，把高斯容量向重建较差处偏置，同时约束跨 LoD 的平滑退化；推理时用一个图元重要性分数在低容量下截断，仍保住场景结构。作者在三个数据集、28 个操作点上按分段 AUC 评估，全容量下与最强基线持平，整个预算区间明显优于所有连续 LoD 基线。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous
Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

Deploying a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene under shrinking compute budgets requires one primitive set to remain effective when rendered at smaller prefixes. In this continuous level of detail (LoD) setting, the challenge is to decide which Gaussians should retain capacity as the budget decreases. A pilot study on 3DGS-MCMC reconstructions shows that image complexity, computed from the input views before optimization, predicts where reconstruction error concentrates in image and 3D space. It also reveals that simple regions contain too many Gaussians and degrade as much as complex ones at lower budgets, despite being inherently cheaper to represent. Subsequently, in KoalaGS, during training we use this complexity prior to bias relocation toward poorly reconstructed areas while ensuring smooth degradation across LoDs. A primitive importance score then enables inference at low-capacity, while preserving the scene structure. Tested across three datasets, KoalaGS maintains competitive full-capacity quality while significantly improving quality across the budget spectrum, yielding smoother transitions across LoDs, and enabling faster progressive streaming.

https://rdbch.github.io/koalags

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting [1] (3DGS) has made neural scene representations practical for novel view synthesis in real time. As the representation has matured, deployment under heterogeneous bandwidth and compute budgets has motivated a growing line of work on continuous level of detail (LoD) for 3DGS, where a single Gaussian set must remain useful when only a leading prefix of its primitives is retained [2, 3, 4]. The central problem in this setting is determining which primitives should retain capacity as the budget shrinks. Existing methods answer it implicitly, ranking primitives by opacity [2] or by learned importance scores [5]. A structural property of the representation suggests a complementary signal. A Gaussian does not contribute equally throughout a scene, as a single primitive may account for a broad region of nearly uniform appearance yet resolve only a fraction of a visually intricate one. We contend that this spatial variation in the value of capacity is what a continuous LoD policy should exploit, and we show that it can be anticipated from the input views alone.

We investigate this claim through a pilot study. Prior work already showed that global image complexity predicts reconstruction error in neural scene representations [6]; however, continuous LoD requires a localized signal that identifies not only which views are difficult, but where that difficulty lies within the scene. We therefore measure the correlation between local image complexity and reconstruction quality in the 2D image plane and, after multiview projection, on the Gaussian primitives. The correlation persists across DL3DV [7] and multiple complexity functionals in both domains, supporting complexity as a spatial prior for reconstruction difficulty that is available before optimization. We then examine how 3DGS-MCMC allocates capacity with respect to this structure. Gaussian density increases with complexity, approximately exponentially in regions of high complexity, yet even visually simple regions are represented by many low-opacity Gaussians. Under truncation according to opacity, quality degrades at comparable rates in simple and complex regions, showing that opacity alone does not expose the spatial redundancy required for robust continuous LoD. Together, these observations expose a mismatch between how 3DGS-MCMC allocates capacity at full budget and how effectively that allocation is preserved under truncation.

Our continuous LoD method for Gaussian Splatting addresses this mismatch. The key insight is that image complexity, which is predictive of reconstruction error, provides an inexpensive spatial prior for allocating capacity and selecting primitives as the budget shrinks. During optimization, a relocation rule biased by complexity steers primitives toward difficult regions, while at inference an importance score modulated by complexity preserves broad primitives in simple regions and relies primarily on opacity in complex ones. A residual variance objective further discourages an abrupt degradation as the budget shrinks. We evaluate the resulting representation along three complementary axes. Our method matches the best baselines at full capacity, while outperforming all continuous LoD baselines across the budget spectrum, even in extremely low budget (<1%). We show that this has great practical implication in streaming context, where our method improves drastically the time-to-quality performance.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    A pilot study on 140 DL3DV scenes showing image complexity predicts where reconstruction error concentrates, while capacity is allocated in a form that truncation cannot preserve.

  • •

    A continuous LoD method combining relocation biased by complexity during training, importance scoring modulated by complexity at inference, and a residual variance objective that discourages localized degradation across budgets.

  • •

    An evaluation of fixed budget quality, integrated spectrum quality, and transition variance, together with a streaming study showing a better time-to-quality tradeoff.

    • 2 Related Work

    Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting transformed neural rendering by using an explicit set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized for visibility-aware rasterization, enabling high-fidelity novel view synthesis at real-time frame rates [1]. A large body of literature focuses on making this representation more stable, efficient, and deployable. On the optimization side, [8] reformulates densification as probabilistic sampling over primitives, [9] introduces structured view-adaptive anchors, [10] incorporates radiance-field-informed optimization for robust high-speed rendering, while [11, 12, 13] reduce training cost or remove expensive densification mechanisms under constrained budgets. A complementary [14, 15] line compresses the trained representation itself, reducing memory footprint and rendering cost to make Gaussian scenes practical on resource-constrained devices. In parallel, other works [16, 17, 18] revisit the primitive parameterization, replacing or constraining 3DGS with 2D variants to improve geometric fidelity and compatibility with classical graphics pipelines. The flexibility of this representation also enables applications beyond static novel view synthesis, including dynamic scene modeling [19, 20], progressive and adaptive streaming [21, 22], mesh reconstruction [23], or higher-level scene understanding through language grounding, segmentation, and editing [24, 25]. Altogether, these works establish 3DGS as a general explicit scene representation.
