Our work employs 3DGS for deployment under heterogeneous primitive budgets, exposing image complexity as a spatial prior over both densification and ranking.

    Level of Detail in Gaussian Splatting. A growing body of work ports classical Level of Detail [26] into the splatting pipeline. A first category imposes explicit hierarchies over the primitive set and exposes a small number of discrete operating points [27, 28, 29], with spatial divide and conquer variants scaling to kilometer sized captures [30, 31, 32]. A second category approximates multi budget behavior through compression and importance pruning at varying targets [12, 15], where each operating point is optimized independently and a new model must be retrained for every budget. A third category pursues continuous LoD over a single primitive set: [3, 4] learn per Gaussian distance dependent opacity decay, while FlexGS [5] learns a differentiable budget conditioned selector that achieves strong quality at targeted budgets but requires a fresh forward pass at every LoD change, precluding progressive streaming. Closer to our setting, Matryoshka-GS [2] introduces a nested prefix renderable ordering trained via stochastic budget sampling, so that any leading slice yields a coherent reconstruction. Our work belongs to this last category but departs from prior approaches in how the ordering is determined: we introduce image complexity as a scene side spatial prior over both densification and ranking, and train for spatial uniformity of the residual between full capacity and prefix renders.

    3 Pilot Study

    This section studies image complexity as a predictor of 3DGS reconstruction quality, computed from the input views before any optimization. The outcomes will shape our method, which must decide where to spend capacity at the moment when reconstruction error, the signal that would otherwise guide it, is not yet available. The intuition is that deploying under a primitive budget is a spatial decision. As primitives are withdrawn, some regions tolerate the loss while others do not, so the capacity that remains should sit where reconstruction error concentrates. Image complexity addresses this, since prior work [6] shows that it predicts reconstruction error and is read from the input images before optimization rather than recovered after training. What that work leaves open is whether the signal is spatial, since an image level score ranks views by difficulty but not where the error lies within them. We therefore investigate two questions: (i) Does complexity localize reconstruction error in space, across the image plane and the 3D world? (ii) Are trained models already allocating capacity where complexity predicts it should? For experimental details we refer to Sec. B.1.

    Does complexity spatially correlate with reconstruction error?

    To address this, we first analyze the spatial distribution of complexity with respect to the reconstruction quality metrics, seeking to study how the two correlate both in the 2D image space and 3D space. The overall methodology is shown in Fig. 1(a). Specifically, we define two spatially indexed fields over image patches. Let Îᵢ=ℝ_θ(Πᵢ) denotes the rendering of a trained 3DGS-MCMC model under camera Πᵢ, and let R(u)⊂Ω be a receptive field centered at pixel u. For 2D, we define the quality map and complexity map as:

    Q^2Dᵢ(u)=(1)/(|R(u)|)∑_v∈R(u)q (Iᵢ(v),Îᵢ(v)), C^2Dᵢ(u)=H (Iᵢ|_R(u)),

    		(1)

    where H is a local complexity functional and q is a local quality measure, with higher values indicating better reconstruction. To obtain their 3D counterparts, we project all quality maps Q^2Dᵢ and complexity maps C^2Dᵢ onto the Gaussian particles under multiview aggregation, obtaining a single quality field Q^3D and complexity field C^3D per scene. To do so, we define the contributing view set as I(x)={ i:πᵢ(x)∈Ω and x visible in view i }, the views in which x projects inside the image domain and is not occluded, so that each point aggregates evidence only from views that observe it. Considering all 3D Gaussian positions x, we then define the 3D fields via direct projection such that:

    Q^3D(x)=(1)/(|I|)∑_i∈IQ^2Dᵢ (πᵢ(x)) and C^3D(x)=(1)/(|I|)∑_i∈IC^2Dᵢ (πᵢ(x)).

    		(2)

    In Fig. 1(b) we report qualitative visuals on bounded and unbounded scenes. They highlight that regardless of the scene type, the complexity and quality fields generally correlate visually. This is very much noticeable on the outdoor pathway which are low complexity regions that also exhibit a low reconstruction error (high quality score).

    We further measure quantitatively the statistical correlations of quality and complexity using the Pearson correlation ρ which denotes the linear association, and the Spearman rank correlation rₛ. For 2D, correlation is observed on paired observations {(C^2Dᵢ(u), Q^2Dᵢ(u))} over all patches and views, while for 3D metrics we evaluate {C^3D(x), Q^3D(x)} over all Gaussian locations. Regardless of the measure used, results in Tab. 1 show consistently high correlation, with large negative values indicating that highly complex regions consistently lead to low reconstruction quality. In the 2D image plane, all three measures exhibit a consistent negative association with patch level quality across scenes and views. The effect is stronger under PSNR (|ρ|,|rₛ| in the range 0.55–0.65) than SSIM (0.21–0.50). Among the functionals, delentropy exhibits the strongest correlation, and we adopt it in our method. In the 3D object space, the picture refines rather than uniformly attenuates. Compared to the 2D metrics, aggregation reduces view dependent appearance noise and recovers a clearer linear relationship (i.e., stronger Pearson correlation), whereas the rank correlations lower substantially (|rₛ|≈0.17–0.39). The interpretation is that multi view averaging preserves the gross magnitude relationship between complexity and quality but compresses the tails of both fields, degrading the fine ordering even where the linear association strengthens. This empirical evidence supports that image complexity provides a spatial cue about where reconstruction errors emerge, both within a view and within a scene. To further establish complexity as a usable spatial prior over reconstruction difficulty, we study how Gaussians are allocated with respect to complexity.

    Does complexity correlate with Gaussian density?

    Since complexity correlates with the reconstruction error, it is reasonable to expect that the optimal ‘per region number of Gaussians’ is already achieved. Indeed, density control mechanism (pruning, cloning, relocation) for 3DGS are designed to increase Gaussian density where reconstruction error is higher. To relate density to complexity at the scene level, we voxelize each scene at a fixed edge length of 0.1 in normalized scene coordinates and, within every voxel, record the mean complexity, the mean reconstruction quality, and the number of Gaussians whose centers fall inside. The fixed scale is well defined because DL3DV test scenes are released in a comparable spatial scale across scenes.

    Reporting the resulting Gaussian counts across complexity intervals in Fig. 2(a), we observe that more complex voxels hold more Gaussians, generally following an exponential trend. At the 90th percentile, the ratio between the least and most complex voxels (13 vs. 119 Gaussians per voxel) is surprising, since the simplest voxels typically depict uniform color and are expected to be reconstructed with only a few Gaussians. We therefore question whether the Gaussian budget is correctly utilized across regions of varying complexity.

    To verify this, we implement a naive LoD strategy which preserves only the top X% of Gaussians by opacity. Varying LoD from 100% (i.e., full capacity) to 0.1%, in Fig. 2(b) we report the PSNR across complexity for a representative scene. While overall PSNR decreases expectedly with complexity and LoD, the study reveals another intriguing characteristic. Decreasing LoD from 100% to 0.1% lowers quality nearly equally in complex regions (≈-62% PSNR) and in simple regions (≈-58% PSNR). This indicates that, even in the simplest regions, 3DGS-MCMC favors decomposing visual signals into multiple lower-opacity Gaussians. Moreover, PSNR fluctuations across complexity reveal uneven Gaussian opacities. Altogether, these observations show that while 3DGS-MCMC reconstructions are denser in complex regions, Gaussians remain suboptimally distributed across complexities. We further analyze how Gaussians are allocated and retained across complexity levels in Sec. D.4.

    4 Method

    We consider the continuous level of detail setting for 3DGS. Given a posed training set D={(Iᵢ,Πᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^M, the goal is to learn a single Gaussian representation G={gⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^N that can be rendered under a variable primitive budget τ∈(0,1], such that

    G_τ⊆G with |G_τ|=⌈τN⌉. At every budgeted representation, our aim is that G_τ remains spatially coherent and degrades gracefully as τ decreases. Following our pilot study (Sec. 3) which demonstrates that image complexity is a surrogate of the reconstruction error, our aim is to benefit from the image complexity signal, readily accessible at training time. Specifically, we apply two simple modifications to the optimization process of state-of-the-art 3DGS-MCMC [8]. First, we utilize complexity to foster (re)allocation of the Gaussians in regions with higher complexity (Sec. 4.1). Second, we introduce a content-aware importance score that retains simple regions at low budgets (Sec. 4.2). We complement them with a residual variance objective that encourages stable reconstruction error across space and LoDs. Experiments show that our simple modification boost performance and efficiency. The proposed LoD is global and view independent, rather than conditioned on camera distance or screen resolution. The implications are further discussed in Sec. B.2.

    Preliminaries.

    A 3DGS representation encodes a scene as a set of Gaussian primitives, where each Gaussian gⱼ=(μⱼ,αⱼ,Σⱼ,cⱼ) is parameterized by its position μⱼ, opacity αⱼ, covariance Σⱼ, and color coefficients cⱼ. To expose complexity to the optimization process, we augment each primitive with a scalar variable Cⱼ, which stores the local image complexity associated with the current Gaussian. This relates to the complexity field in Eq. 2, but differs from the post-hoc analysis in our pilot study since, during training, Gaussian positions and supports change, and therefore their complexity values must be updated online.

    To address this, after each full-capacity training render of a view Πᵢ, we project the means of the contributing Gaussians into the image plane, and update each particle’s complexity via an exponential moving average, using the complexity map C^2Dᵢ(u) from Eq. 1, computed with delentropy. So that:

    Cⱼ ← (1-η) Cⱼ + η C^2Dᵢ (πᵢ(μⱼ)), η∈(0,1].

    		(3)

    Only particles whose centers project in the current view’s frustum are updated. Over the course of training each particle’s Cⱼ converges to the multi-view average similar to those in Eq. (2). At last, Sⱼ is the importance score of a particle used for prefix sorting computed using the scoring function S(·).

    4.1 Complexity-aware Adaptive density control

    In practice, 3DGS variants rely on opacity as a proxy for this error signal: during optimization new primitives are concentrated where opacity has accumulated, and regions the optimizer has not yet resolved remain under-served precisely because they have not been resolved. In 3DGS-MCMC [8], the probability p to relocate at the coordinate of μⱼ writes: p(gⱼ)=αⱼ. Given that complexity is a surrogate of reconstruction errors (cf., Tab. 1), we simply bias this sampling weight towards more complex regions. We therefore sample relocation destinations with:

    p(gⱼ)=αⱼ·\exp (C̃ⱼ) ,

    		(4)

    where C̃ⱼ∈[0,1] is the min-max normalized Cⱼ. Note that we utilize \exp(·) to mimic the exponential growing behavior of particles count with complexity, as in the 90th percentile in Fig. 2(a). Importantly, the multiplicative form keeps opacity in the loop since a primitive that has earned its keep should not be evicted for exploring other regions. To prevent collapse onto fixed complex regions, we apply complexity dropout, setting C̃ⱼ=0 with probability δ=0.2 (ablated in Sec. D.2) and thus scoring that fraction of relocation candidates by opacity alone (δ=0: none; δ=1: all).

    4.2 Complexity-aware Level of Details

    As mentioned in Sec. 3, under a limited budget (i.e., τ<1), only Gaussians with the highest importance score S(·) are preserved. In the literature, this typically resolves to using opacity [2], i.e., S(gⱼ)=αⱼ. As shown in Fig. 2(b), this degrades low-complexity regions as much as complex ones, although they should be the cheapest to retain, because opacity captures learned contribution but not the total spatial footprint over which a primitive contributes. We therefore rank primitives by combining three complementary signals: opacity, scale, and complexity:

    S(gⱼ)=αⱼ+λ·(s(gⱼ))/(\exp(C̃ⱼ(μⱼ))),

    		(5)

    where s(gⱼ) is the max-normalized scale of gⱼ and λ=2 is a fixed scalar weight. The three components play distinct, complementary roles. Opacity captures the importance learned through the photometric objective, allowing a small high-opacity Gaussian to outrank a moderate-opacity one that covers a broader region. Scale supplies this missing spatial footprint, while complexity controls where it should influence the score. In high-complexity regions, \exp(C) attenuates the scale term, avoiding preference for large, potentially blurring primitives and reducing the score toward opacity, which is most reliable where optimization pressure is concentrated. In low-complexity regions, where preserving broad spatial support matters more, the second term reduces to λ·s as \exp(C)→1, restoring weight to large primitives that efficiently cover simple areas despite their moderate opacity.

    We note that LoD-awareness requires the optimizer to vary LoD (i.e., τ) during training. However, the scoring alone does not guarantee that the resulting render degrades uniformly since the optimization support varies with τ. Namely, at full-capacity (τ=1) the optimizer has access to all primitives to fit the image, while at lower LODs (τ<1) the optimizer only accesses the surviving primitives (according to Eq. 5) and may push the latter away from their full-capacity solution. To keep the resulting deviation spatially uniform, we consider the residual of the reconstruction error between full-capacity render and lower LODs render, and minimize it’s variance.

    Formally, at each step we compute the residual of the reconstruction error 𝔼(·) at τ and at full-capacity: Δᵢ=𝔼(Iᵢ^full)-𝔼(Iᵢ^τ), and minimize its spatial variance:

    Lᵥₐᵣ = Var_u∈Ω (Δᵢ(u)).

    		(6)

    Training objectives.

    We use the L1+D-SSIM loss of 3DGS-MCMC on the full (τ=1) and budgeted (τ<1) renders, add λᵥₐᵣLᵥₐᵣ, and average them. Training details are given in Sec. B.2.

    5 Experimental Results

    We evaluate our method on three datasets [33, 34, 35] and compare its performance against five baselines [2, 5, 15, 27, 8]. Since performance of LoD-aware 3DGS may vary across LoD, it is not possible to characterize its performance by a single metric. We therefore assess our method along three complementary axes: quality at predefined LoD targets (Sec. 5.1), spectrum quality as the per-metric area under the curve over the full LoD sweep (Sec. 5.2), and intra- and inter-LOD transition variance (Sec. 5.3), which together capture whether quality is high, whether it is sustained across the spectrum, and whether it degrades gracefully rather than abruptly. We further conduct an ablation in Sec. 5.4 to isolate the contribution of each component of our method. We refer the reader to Sec. C for the experimental setup description and Sec. D for additional experiments. In all tables, best results are in bold and second best are underlined.

    5.1 Quality at Predefined LOD Targets

    We first ask whether our method delivers high quality at the operating points a user is most likely to deploy, therefore evaluating at four log-spaced budgets chosen to probe each decade of the spectrum: 100% reflects full-capacity quality, 10% a moderate compression regime relevant to deployment, 1% an aggressive reduction where ranking quality dominates and an extreme 0.1%, [typically used when initialising a streaming]. Quantitative results are reported in Tab. 2, while separating partial-LoD methods (OctreeGS, FlexGS) as they can only be evaluated at some intervals. Qualitatives are presented in Fig. 3, and curves are visualized in Fig. 4. A consistent picture emerges across datasets. At full capacity, all methods are competitive (Fig. 3, top row), with our method performing generally on par with the strongest baseline on every dataset and confirming that content-aware modifications introduce no penalty at peak fidelity. As the budget shrinks, the field separates sharply. 3DGS MCMC degrades rapidly and has already collapsed by the 1% threshold, confirming that opacity-based ranking alone cannot sustain quality under reduction. LightGaussian retains more quality than opacity-based pruning in most cases, but falls behind both MGS and ours at every reduced budget across all three datasets. OctreeGS cannot operate below its native discrete levels and it remains competitive only on the indoor Deep Blending scenes and falls behind on outdoor scenes. FlexGS, which is not prefix renderable, trades this property for higher quality near the specific operating points it was optimised for, but degrades unpredictably between them. MGS, our closest competitor, follows the same trend as our method but consistently lags behind it. Altogether, content-aware ranking yields a more robust quality versus quantity trade-off than any single-family representative, both quantitatively and visually. We report the rendering speeds in Sec. D.3 and further investigate how our importance score and densification behave jointly in Sec. D.4.

    5.2 Quality Across the LoD Spectrum

    The previous section leaves open how quality evolves across the full LoD spectrum. To address this, we sample 28 operating points in [0.1%,100%], ten linearly spaced per interval ([0.1%,1%], [1%,10%], [10%,100%]) with shared endpoints, and integrate per-metric curves with the trapezoidal rule to compute interval-wise area-under-the-curve (AUC) score, rescaled per interval for direct comparison. Since discrete methods cannot operate across the full spectrum, we focus on prefix-renderable continuous LoD methods. From results in Tab. 3, our method consistently achieves the highest AUC. Since the total AUC is dominated by high budgets where all methods cluster, the sub-interval breakdown is more informative. 3DGS MCMC collapses below 10% capacity, yielding the lowest sub-interval AUC across datasets and confirming that opacity-based ranking alone fails as the budget shrinks. LightGaussian improves PSNR and generally SSIM over opacity-based pruning, but remains behind MGS and ours across all metrics in the two lower-budget intervals. Our largest gain over MGS occurs precisely in the low-budget [0.1%,1%] regime where ranking quality dominates. FlexGS performs better at [1%,10%], but it does not allow full LoD coverage. Besides, FlexGS is outperformed by ours in other intervals, which directly results from its design as it trained for specific operating points at the cost of global consistency, producing the irregular degradation curves visible in Fig. 4. Overall, these results indicate that our method offers the most balanced quality versus quantity trade-off across the LoD spectrum.

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous
Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting

Abstract

Deploying a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene under shrinking compute budgets requires one primitive set to remain effective when rendered at smaller prefixes. Subsequently, in KoalaGS, during training we use this complexity prior to bias relocation toward poorly reconstructed areas while ensuring smooth degradation across LoDs. A primitive importance score then enables inference at low-capacity, while preserving the scene structure. Tested across three datasets, KoalaGS maintains competitive full-capacity quality while significantly improving quality across the budget spectrum, yielding smoother transitions across LoDs, and enabling faster progressive streaming.

https://rdbch.github.io/koalags

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting [1] (3DGS) has made neural scene representations practical for novel view synthesis in real time. As the representation has matured, deployment under heterogeneous bandwidth and compute budgets has motivated a growing line of work on continuous level of detail (LoD) for 3DGS, where a single Gaussian set must remain useful when only a leading prefix of its primitives is retained [2, 3, 4]. The central problem in this setting is determining which primitives should retain capacity as the budget shrinks. Existing methods answer it implicitly, ranking primitives by opacity [2] or by learned importance scores [5]. A structural property of the representation suggests a complementary signal. A Gaussian does not contribute equally throughout a scene, as a single primitive may account for a broad region of nearly uniform appearance yet resolve only a fraction of a visually intricate one. We contend that this spatial variation in the value of capacity is what a continuous LoD policy should exploit, and we show that it can be anticipated from the input views alone.

We investigate this claim through a pilot study. Prior work already showed that global image complexity predicts reconstruction error in neural scene representations [6]; however, continuous LoD requires a localized signal that identifies not only which views are difficult, but where that difficulty lies within the scene. We therefore measure the correlation between local image complexity and reconstruction quality in the 2D image plane and, after multiview projection, on the Gaussian primitives. The correlation persists across DL3DV [7] and multiple complexity functionals in both domains, supporting complexity as a spatial prior for reconstruction difficulty that is available before optimization. We then examine how 3DGS-MCMC allocates capacity with respect to this structure. Gaussian density increases with complexity, approximately exponentially in regions of high complexity, yet even visually simple regions are represented by many low-opacity Gaussians. Under truncation according to opacity, quality degrades at comparable rates in simple and complex regions, showing that opacity alone does not expose the spatial redundancy required for robust continuous LoD. Together, these observations expose a mismatch between how 3DGS-MCMC allocates capacity at full budget and how effectively that allocation is preserved under truncation.

Our continuous LoD method for Gaussian Splatting addresses this mismatch. The key insight is that image complexity, which is predictive of reconstruction error, provides an inexpensive spatial prior for allocating capacity and selecting primitives as the budget shrinks. During optimization, a relocation rule biased by complexity steers primitives toward difficult regions, while at inference an importance score modulated by complexity preserves broad primitives in simple regions and relies primarily on opacity in complex ones. A residual variance objective further discourages an abrupt degradation as the budget shrinks. We evaluate the resulting representation along three complementary axes. Our method matches the best baselines at full capacity, while outperforming all continuous LoD baselines across the budget spectrum, even in extremely low budget (<1%). We show that this has great practical implication in streaming context, where our method improves drastically the time-to-quality performance.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    A pilot study on 140 DL3DV scenes showing image complexity predicts where reconstruction error concentrates, while capacity is allocated in a form that truncation cannot preserve.

  • •

    A continuous LoD method combining relocation biased by complexity during training, importance scoring modulated by complexity at inference, and a residual variance objective that discourages localized degradation across budgets.

  • •

    An evaluation of fixed budget quality, integrated spectrum quality, and transition variance, together with a streaming study showing a better time-to-quality tradeoff.

    • 2 Related Work

    Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting transformed neural rendering by using an explicit set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized for visibility-aware rasterization, enabling high-fidelity novel view synthesis at real-time frame rates [1]. A large body of literature focuses on making this representation more stable, efficient, and deployable. On the optimization side, [8] reformulates densification as probabilistic sampling over primitives, [9] introduces structured view-adaptive anchors, [10] incorporates radiance-field-informed optimization for robust high-speed rendering, while [11, 12, 13] reduce training cost or remove expensive densification mechanisms under constrained budgets. A complementary [14, 15] line compresses the trained representation itself, reducing memory footprint and rendering cost to make Gaussian scenes practical on resource-constrained devices. In parallel, other works [16, 17, 18] revisit the primitive parameterization, replacing or constraining 3DGS with 2D variants to improve geometric fidelity and compatibility with classical graphics pipelines. The flexibility of this representation also enables applications beyond static novel view synthesis, including dynamic scene modeling [19, 20], progressive and adaptive streaming [21, 22], mesh reconstruction [23], or higher-level scene understanding through language grounding, segmentation, and editing [24, 25]. Altogether, these works establish 3DGS as a general explicit scene representation. Our work employs 3DGS for deployment under heterogeneous primitive budgets, exposing image complexity as a spatial prior over both densification and ranking.

    Level of Detail in Gaussian Splatting. A growing body of work ports classical Level of Detail [26] into the splatting pipeline. A first category imposes explicit hierarchies over the primitive set and exposes a small number of discrete operating points [27, 28, 29], with spatial divide and conquer variants scaling to kilometer sized captures [30, 31, 32]. A second category approximates multi budget behavior through compression and importance pruning at varying targets [12, 15], where each operating point is optimized independently and a new model must be retrained for every budget. A third category pursues continuous LoD over a single primitive set: [3, 4] learn per Gaussian distance dependent opacity decay, while FlexGS [5] learns a differentiable budget conditioned selector that achieves strong quality at targeted budgets but requires a fresh forward pass at every LoD change, precluding progressive streaming. Closer to our setting, Matryoshka-GS [2] introduces a nested prefix renderable ordering trained via stochastic budget sampling, so that any leading slice yields a coherent reconstruction. Our work belongs to this last category but departs from prior approaches in how the ordering is determined: we introduce image complexity as a scene side spatial prior over both densification and ranking, and train for spatial uniformity of the residual between full capacity and prefix renders.

    3 Pilot Study

    This section studies image complexity as a predictor of 3DGS reconstruction quality, computed from the input views before any optimization. The outcomes will shape our method, which must decide where to spend capacity at the moment when reconstruction error, the signal that would otherwise guide it, is not yet available. The intuition is that deploying under a primitive budget is a spatial decision. As primitives are withdrawn, some regions tolerate the loss while others do not, so the capacity that remains should sit where reconstruction error concentrates. Image complexity addresses this, since prior work [6] shows that it predicts reconstruction error and is read from the input images before optimization rather than recovered after training. What that work leaves open is whether the signal is spatial, since an image level score ranks views by difficulty but not where the error lies within them. We therefore investigate two questions: (i) Does complexity localize reconstruction error in space, across the image plane and the 3D world? (ii) Are trained models already allocating capacity where complexity predicts it should? For experimental details we refer to Sec. B.1.

    Does complexity spatially correlate with reconstruction error?

    To address this, we first analyze the spatial distribution of complexity with respect to the reconstruction quality metrics, seeking to study how the two correlate both in the 2D image space and 3D space. The overall methodology is shown in Fig. 1(a). Specifically, we define two spatially indexed fields over image patches. Let Îᵢ=ℝ_θ(Πᵢ) denotes the rendering of a trained 3DGS-MCMC model under camera Πᵢ, and let R(u)⊂Ω be a receptive field centered at pixel u. For 2D, we define the quality map and complexity map as:

    Q^2Dᵢ(u)=(1)/(|R(u)|)∑_v∈R(u)q (Iᵢ(v),Îᵢ(v)), C^2Dᵢ(u)=H (Iᵢ|_R(u)),

    		(1)

    where H is a local complexity functional and q is a local quality measure, with higher values indicating better reconstruction. To obtain their 3D counterparts, we project all quality maps Q^2Dᵢ and complexity maps C^2Dᵢ onto the Gaussian particles under multiview aggregation, obtaining a single quality field Q^3D and complexity field C^3D per scene. To do so, we define the contributing view set as I(x)={ i:πᵢ(x)∈Ω and x visible in view i }, the views in which x projects inside the image domain and is not occluded, so that each point aggregates evidence only from views that observe it. Considering all 3D Gaussian positions x, we then define the 3D fields via direct projection such that:

    Q^3D(x)=(1)/(|I|)∑_i∈IQ^2Dᵢ (πᵢ(x)) and C^3D(x)=(1)/(|I|)∑_i∈IC^2Dᵢ (πᵢ(x)).

    		(2)

    In Fig. 1(b) we report qualitative visuals on bounded and unbounded scenes. They highlight that regardless of the scene type, the complexity and quality fields generally correlate visually. This is very much noticeable on the outdoor pathway which are low complexity regions that also exhibit a low reconstruction error (high quality score).

    We further measure quantitatively the statistical correlations of quality and complexity using the Pearson correlation ρ which denotes the linear association, and the Spearman rank correlation rₛ. For 2D, correlation is observed on paired observations {(C^2Dᵢ(u), Q^2Dᵢ(u))} over all patches and views, while for 3D metrics we evaluate {C^3D(x), Q^3D(x)} over all Gaussian locations. Regardless of the measure used, results in Tab. 1 show consistently high correlation, with large negative values indicating that highly complex regions consistently lead to low reconstruction quality. In the 2D image plane, all three measures exhibit a consistent negative association with patch level quality across scenes and views. The effect is stronger under PSNR (|ρ|,|rₛ| in the range 0.55–0.65) than SSIM (0.21–0.50). Among the functionals, delentropy exhibits the strongest correlation, and we adopt it in our method. In the 3D object space, the picture refines rather than uniformly attenuates. Compared to the 2D metrics, aggregation reduces view dependent appearance noise and recovers a clearer linear relationship (i.e., stronger Pearson correlation), whereas the rank correlations lower substantially (|rₛ|≈0.17–0.39). The interpretation is that multi view averaging preserves the gross magnitude relationship between complexity and quality but compresses the tails of both fields, degrading the fine ordering even where the linear association strengthens. This empirical evidence supports that image complexity provides a spatial cue about where reconstruction errors emerge, both within a view and within a scene. To further establish complexity as a usable spatial prior over reconstruction difficulty, we study how Gaussians are allocated with respect to complexity.

    Does complexity correlate with Gaussian density?

    Since complexity correlates with the reconstruction error, it is reasonable to expect that the optimal ‘per region number of Gaussians’ is already achieved. Indeed, density control mechanism (pruning, cloning, relocation) for 3DGS are designed to increase Gaussian density where reconstruction error is higher. To relate density to complexity at the scene level, we voxelize each scene at a fixed edge length of 0.1 in normalized scene coordinates and, within every voxel, record the mean complexity, the mean reconstruction quality, and the number of Gaussians whose centers fall inside. The fixed scale is well defined because DL3DV test scenes are released in a comparable spatial scale across scenes.

    Reporting the resulting Gaussian counts across complexity intervals in Fig. 2(a), we observe that more complex voxels hold more Gaussians, generally following an exponential trend. At the 90th percentile, the ratio between the least and most complex voxels (13 vs. 119 Gaussians per voxel) is surprising, since the simplest voxels typically depict uniform color and are expected to be reconstructed with only a few Gaussians. We therefore question whether the Gaussian budget is correctly utilized across regions of varying complexity.

    To verify this, we implement a naive LoD strategy which preserves only the top X% of Gaussians by opacity. Varying LoD from 100% (i.e., full capacity) to 0.1%, in Fig. 2(b) we report the PSNR across complexity for a representative scene. While overall PSNR decreases expectedly with complexity and LoD, the study reveals another intriguing characteristic. Decreasing LoD from 100% to 0.1% lowers quality nearly equally in complex regions (≈-62% PSNR) and in simple regions (≈-58% PSNR). This indicates that, even in the simplest regions, 3DGS-MCMC favors decomposing visual signals into multiple lower-opacity Gaussians. Moreover, PSNR fluctuations across complexity reveal uneven Gaussian opacities. Altogether, these observations show that while 3DGS-MCMC reconstructions are denser in complex regions, Gaussians remain suboptimally distributed across complexities. We further analyze how Gaussians are allocated and retained across complexity levels in Sec. D.4.

    4 Method

    We consider the continuous level of detail setting for 3DGS. Given a posed training set D={(Iᵢ,Πᵢ)}ᵢ₌₁^M, the goal is to learn a single Gaussian representation G={gⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^N that can be rendered under a variable primitive budget τ∈(0,1], such that

    G_τ⊆G with |G_τ|=⌈τN⌉. At every budgeted representation, our aim is that G_τ remains spatially coherent and degrades gracefully as τ decreases. Following our pilot study (Sec. 3) which demonstrates that image complexity is a surrogate of the reconstruction error, our aim is to benefit from the image complexity signal, readily accessible at training time. Specifically, we apply two simple modifications to the optimization process of state-of-the-art 3DGS-MCMC [8]. First, we utilize complexity to foster (re)allocation of the Gaussians in regions with higher complexity (Sec. 4.1). Second, we introduce a content-aware importance score that retains simple regions at low budgets (Sec. 4.2). We complement them with a residual variance objective that encourages stable reconstruction error across space and LoDs. Experiments show that our simple modification boost performance and efficiency. The proposed LoD is global and view independent, rather than conditioned on camera distance or screen resolution. The implications are further discussed in Sec. B.2.

    Preliminaries.

    A 3DGS representation encodes a scene as a set of Gaussian primitives, where each Gaussian gⱼ=(μⱼ,αⱼ,Σⱼ,cⱼ) is parameterized by its position μⱼ, opacity αⱼ, covariance Σⱼ, and color coefficients cⱼ. To expose complexity to the optimization process, we augment each primitive with a scalar variable Cⱼ, which stores the local image complexity associated with the current Gaussian. This relates to the complexity field in Eq. 2, but differs from the post-hoc analysis in our pilot study since, during training, Gaussian positions and supports change, and therefore their complexity values must be updated online.

    To address this, after each full-capacity training render of a view Πᵢ, we project the means of the contributing Gaussians into the image plane, and update each particle’s complexity via an exponential moving average, using the complexity map C^2Dᵢ(u) from Eq. 1, computed with delentropy. So that:

    Cⱼ ← (1-η) Cⱼ + η C^2Dᵢ (πᵢ(μⱼ)), η∈(0,1].

    		(3)

    Only particles whose centers project in the current view’s frustum are updated. Over the course of training each particle’s Cⱼ converges to the multi-view average similar to those in Eq. (2). At last, Sⱼ is the importance score of a particle used for prefix sorting computed using the scoring function S(·).

    4.1 Complexity-aware Adaptive density control

    In practice, 3DGS variants rely on opacity as a proxy for this error signal: during optimization new primitives are concentrated where opacity has accumulated, and regions the optimizer has not yet resolved remain under-served precisely because they have not been resolved. In 3DGS-MCMC [8], the probability p to relocate at the coordinate of μⱼ writes: p(gⱼ)=αⱼ. Given that complexity is a surrogate of reconstruction errors (cf., Tab. 1), we simply bias this sampling weight towards more complex regions. We therefore sample relocation destinations with:

    p(gⱼ)=αⱼ·\exp (C̃ⱼ) ,

    		(4)

    where C̃ⱼ∈[0,1] is the min-max normalized Cⱼ. Note that we utilize \exp(·) to mimic the exponential growing behavior of particles count with complexity, as in the 90th percentile in Fig. 2(a). Importantly, the multiplicative form keeps opacity in the loop since a primitive that has earned its keep should not be evicted for exploring other regions. To prevent collapse onto fixed complex regions, we apply complexity dropout, setting C̃ⱼ=0 with probability δ=0.2 (ablated in Sec. D.2) and thus scoring that fraction of relocation candidates by opacity alone (δ=0: none; δ=1: all).

    4.2 Complexity-aware Level of Details

    As mentioned in Sec. 3, under a limited budget (i.e., τ<1), only Gaussians with the highest importance score S(·) are preserved. In the literature, this typically resolves to using opacity [2], i.e., S(gⱼ)=αⱼ. As shown in Fig. 2(b), this degrades low-complexity regions as much as complex ones, although they should be the cheapest to retain, because opacity captures learned contribution but not the total spatial footprint over which a primitive contributes. We therefore rank primitives by combining three complementary signals: opacity, scale, and complexity:

    S(gⱼ)=αⱼ+λ·(s(gⱼ))/(\exp(C̃ⱼ(μⱼ))),

    		(5)

    where s(gⱼ) is the max-normalized scale of gⱼ and λ=2 is a fixed scalar weight. The three components play distinct, complementary roles. Opacity captures the importance learned through the photometric objective, allowing a small high-opacity Gaussian to outrank a moderate-opacity one that covers a broader region. Scale supplies this missing spatial footprint, while complexity controls where it should influence the score. In high-complexity regions, \exp(C) attenuates the scale term, avoiding preference for large, potentially blurring primitives and reducing the score toward opacity, which is most reliable where optimization pressure is concentrated. In low-complexity regions, where preserving broad spatial support matters more, the second term reduces to λ·s as \exp(C)→1, restoring weight to large primitives that efficiently cover simple areas despite their moderate opacity.

    We note that LoD-awareness requires the optimizer to vary LoD (i.e., τ) during training. However, the scoring alone does not guarantee that the resulting render degrades uniformly since the optimization support varies with τ. Namely, at full-capacity (τ=1) the optimizer has access to all primitives to fit the image, while at lower LODs (τ<1) the optimizer only accesses the surviving primitives (according to Eq. 5) and may push the latter away from their full-capacity solution. To keep the resulting deviation spatially uniform, we consider the residual of the reconstruction error between full-capacity render and lower LODs render, and minimize it’s variance.

    Formally, at each step we compute the residual of the reconstruction error 𝔼(·) at τ and at full-capacity: Δᵢ=𝔼(Iᵢ^full)-𝔼(Iᵢ^τ), and minimize its spatial variance:

    Lᵥₐᵣ = Var_u∈Ω (Δᵢ(u)).

    		(6)

    Training objectives.

    We use the L1+D-SSIM loss of 3DGS-MCMC on the full (τ=1) and budgeted (τ<1) renders, add λᵥₐᵣLᵥₐᵣ, and average them. Training details are given in Sec. B.2.

    5 Experimental Results

    We evaluate our method on three datasets [33, 34, 35] and compare its performance against five baselines [2, 5, 15, 27, 8]. Since performance of LoD-aware 3DGS may vary across LoD, it is not possible to characterize its performance by a single metric. We therefore assess our method along three complementary axes: quality at predefined LoD targets (Sec. 5.1), spectrum quality as the per-metric area under the curve over the full LoD sweep (Sec. 5.2), and intra- and inter-LOD transition variance (Sec. 5.3), which together capture whether quality is high, whether it is sustained across the spectrum, and whether it degrades gracefully rather than abruptly. We further conduct an ablation in Sec. 5.4 to isolate the contribution of each component of our method. We refer the reader to Sec. C for the experimental setup description and Sec. D for additional experiments. In all tables, best results are in bold and second best are underlined.

    5.1 Quality at Predefined LOD Targets

    We first ask whether our method delivers high quality at the operating points a user is most likely to deploy, therefore evaluating at four log-spaced budgets chosen to probe each decade of the spectrum: 100% reflects full-capacity quality, 10% a moderate compression regime relevant to deployment, 1% an aggressive reduction where ranking quality dominates and an extreme 0.1%, [typically used when initialising a streaming]. Quantitative results are reported in Tab. 2, while separating partial-LoD methods (OctreeGS, FlexGS) as they can only be evaluated at some intervals. Qualitatives are presented in Fig. 3, and curves are visualized in Fig. 4. A consistent picture emerges across datasets. At full capacity, all methods are competitive (Fig. 3, top row), with our method performing generally on par with the strongest baseline on every dataset and confirming that content-aware modifications introduce no penalty at peak fidelity. As the budget shrinks, the field separates sharply. 3DGS MCMC degrades rapidly and has already collapsed by the 1% threshold, confirming that opacity-based ranking alone cannot sustain quality under reduction. LightGaussian retains more quality than opacity-based pruning in most cases, but falls behind both MGS and ours at every reduced budget across all three datasets. OctreeGS cannot operate below its native discrete levels and it remains competitive only on the indoor Deep Blending scenes and falls behind on outdoor scenes. FlexGS, which is not prefix renderable, trades this property for higher quality near the specific operating points it was optimised for, but degrades unpredictably between them. MGS, our closest competitor, follows the same trend as our method but consistently lags behind it. Altogether, content-aware ranking yields a more robust quality versus quantity trade-off than any single-family representative, both quantitatively and visually. We report the rendering speeds in Sec. D.3 and further investigate how our importance score and densification behave jointly in Sec. D.4.

    5.2 Quality Across the LoD Spectrum

    The previous section leaves open how quality evolves across the full LoD spectrum. To address this, we sample 28 operating points in [0.1%,100%], ten linearly spaced per interval ([0.1%,1%], [1%,10%], [10%,100%]) with shared endpoints, and integrate per-metric curves with the trapezoidal rule to compute interval-wise area-under-the-curve (AUC) score, rescaled per interval for direct comparison. Since discrete methods cannot operate across the full spectrum, we focus on prefix-renderable continuous LoD methods. From results in Tab. 3, our method consistently achieves the highest AUC. Since the total AUC is dominated by high budgets where all methods cluster, the sub-interval breakdown is more informative. 3DGS MCMC collapses below 10% capacity, yielding the lowest sub-interval AUC across datasets and confirming that opacity-based ranking alone fails as the budget shrinks. LightGaussian improves PSNR and generally SSIM over opacity-based pruning, but remains behind MGS and ours across all metrics in the two lower-budget intervals. Our largest gain over MGS occurs precisely in the low-budget [0.1%,1%] regime where ranking quality dominates. FlexGS performs better at [1%,10%], but it does not allow full LoD coverage. Besides, FlexGS is outperformed by ours in other intervals, which directly results from its design as it trained for specific operating points at the cost of global consistency, producing the irregular degradation curves visible in Fig. 4. Overall, these results indicate that our method offers the most balanced quality versus quantity trade-off across the LoD spectrum.

item.title: DiT 把每个 token 都算一遍太浪费：MoDDiT 让 MLP 与自注意力各自路由，12.5% 的 token 也能打 ｜ MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers
item.description:
一句话：背景 token 对去噪贡献很小，DiT 却静态均匀地全算一遍；把 MLP 与自注意力各自路由后，12.5% 容量下视频预测 PSNR 更高、去噪 FLOPs 少 36.92%。

要点：

  • 自然图像本身稀疏，大片背景容易去噪；DiT 却对所有 token 施加同样的计算，没有利用这层稀疏
  • 让 token 分别通过 MLP 与自注意力两条路径的独立路由，于是 MLP 侧的算力分配可以随 token、图像与去噪时间步动态变化
  • ImageNet 从零训：50% 容量在与 DiT 对齐 FLOPs 时 FID/sFID/precision/IS 全面更好；25% 容量 FLOPs 少 22% 仍更优；12.5% 容量在约 33% 更少 FLOPs 下与 DiT 相当
  • 视频侧在 1X World Modeling Challenge 上，12.5% 容量路由既提高视频预测 PSNR，又把计入的去噪 FLOPs 压低 36.92%

为什么值得看：生成式渲染的成本瓶颈已经从采样步数转到 backbone 吞吐；这类「不改结构、只改路由」的改动对现有 DiT 管线最友好，适合先做推理侧降本。

中文摘要：实时视频生成、交互式世界模型与端侧图像合成都快成为现实，Diffusion Transformer 的采样质量已经够好，瓶颈转到模型自身吞吐。自然图像天然稀疏：大片背景几乎不承载内容，也容易去噪，但 DiT 对所有图像 token 一视同仁地处理，浪费了这层稀疏性。作者提出 MoDDiT：一个很简单的架构改动，让 token 分别路由通过 MLP 与自注意力，从而让 MLP 的算力分配可以随 token、图像和去噪时间步变化。从零训练时，MoDDiT 显著降低训练与推理成本，最多只用 12.5% 的 token；随着稀疏度与深度增加，成本下降的同时生成质量还优于未路由基线。在视频生成（1X World Modeling Challenge）上，12.5% 容量路由在提高预测 PSNR 的同时把计入的去噪 FLOPs 减少 36.92%。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

Abstract

Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly.

We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.

††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution

1 Introduction

Recent advancements in real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis promise numerous new applications for generative models, and a new frontier of synthetic data. Diffusion models are at the forefront of this progress but are bottlenecked by their iterative generation procedure, which requires multiple model evaluations to generate samples. The resulting latency is often reduced by distilling models into smaller students or subsampling diffusion timesteps. A complementary axis of improvement is given by architecture modifications that reduce the cost of each inference step of the denoising process.

A promising route is exploiting sparsity, inspired by the observation that images and videos are information-sparse modalities where few patches per frame contain a large amount of information. For example, in many images the background is much simpler than the foreground and is therefore easier to denoise. This effect is magnified in videos, where patches containing static objects can be simply copied over from the previous frame. Ideally, diffusion would focus computation on more relevant patches, reducing overall latency. However, predominant diffusion architectures such as diffusion transformers [(Peebles and Xie, 2023, DiT,)] fail to exploit this property, instead applying all operations to every token, thereby allocating compute uniformly over images and videos.

In this work, we introduce MoDDiT, a simple mechanism for routing tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations (section3). While routing through self-attention uses fixed capacity, routing through MLPs enables dynamic compute allocation across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps (section3.2). This allows the model to devote more computation to regions that are visually complex and difficult to denoise.

Unlike prior methods, MoDDiT reduces FLOPs during both training and inference, requires no auxiliary routing loss or post-processing, and enables efficient training on parallel GPU hardware without ragged batches. As illustrated in fig.1, the resulting allocation is interpretable, with computation varying across image regions, samples, and denoising timesteps.

We evaluate MoDDiT across three settings: image generation, video generation, and video distillation. On ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)] (section4), MoDDiT improves the quality–compute tradeoff over vanilla DiT across a range of routing capacities and sampling lengths. For video generation, we evaluate on the 1X World Modeling Challenge [(1X, 2025)] (section5), where routing at 12.5% capacity improves video-prediction PSNR while requiring 36.92% fewer counted denoiser FLOPs on the profiled clip than the DiT baseline. Finally, we integrate sparse feedforward routing into the distillation of pretrained Wan2.1 [(Wan et al., 2025)], converting a dense bidirectional model into a sparse, few-step autoregressive generator (section6). Compared with a matched dense autoregressive student, the sparse model almost matches the dense baseline with a 5% overall reduction in score on the VBench benchmark [(Huang et al., 2023)], while reducing inference FLOPs by 24%. We further analyze the learned routing behavior (figs.4 and 5), showing how computation varies with denoising stage, image and patch class, and temporal change in video.

In summary, MoDDiT provides a simple, efficient mechanism for dynamic token routing, exploiting token-level sparsity in diffusion transformers. By increasing model size and sparsity, it can increase performance while reducing training- and inference-time FLOPs. We compare routing choices and ablations on ImageNet, and give intuitive explanations for allocation across image content and time steps. On 1X, we test action-conditioned video generation and show that learned allocation varies with temporal change. Distilling Wan2.1 tests whether MoDDiT can be combined with distillation and few-step denoising, where the reduction in inference FLOPs comes with a modest reduction in VBench score.

2 Background

2.1 Diffusion Models

Diffusion models [(Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021)] generate images by iteratively removing noise from samples drawn from a known noisy distribution. Specifically, they consist of two complementary Markov processes: a forward noising process and a reverse denoising process. In the forward process, an initial clean image x₀ is progressively corrupted into a purely noisy image x_T across a discrete sequence of timesteps t=1,…,T, following the Gaussian conditional distribution q(xₜ|xₜ₋₁)=ℕ(xₜ;√1-βₜ xₜ₋₁,βₜI), where βₜ∈(0,1) defines the noise schedule at timestep t. Equivalently, this forward process can be expressed as xₜ=√ᾱₜ x₀+√1-ᾱₜ ε, with ε∼ℕ(0,I) and ᾱₜ=∏ᵢ₌₁ᵗ(1-βᵢ). The reverse process, parameterized by a neural network, gradually reconstructs the original clean image from x_T to x₀ by approximating the conditional distributions p_θ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ)=ℕ(xₜ₋₁;μ_θ(xₜ,t),Σ_θ(xₜ,t)). Model training involves minimizing the discrepancy between the predicted and actual noise at each timestep, enabling accurate modeling of the underlying data distribution.

2.2 Vision- and Diffusion Transformers

Following their success in language modeling, transformers [(Vaswani et al., 2017)] have been successfully applied to vision tasks. Vision transformer [(Dosovitskiy et al., 2020, ViT)] achieves this by constructing a flattened token sequence from pixel patches. Similar to transformers, ViT models consist of alternating self-attention [(Bahdanau et al., 2014)] and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) blocks, with intermediate layer normalization [(Ba et al., 2016)]. In these models, self-attention distributes information across the sample, in this case passing information between image patches, while the MLP processes tokens independently. Diffusion transformers [(Peebles and Xie, 2023, DiT, )] adapt ViT models for image diffusion with adaptive layer normalization (adaLN), which conditions the normalization operation on the diffusion timestep and image class.

In addition to image generation, DiTs are the predominant architecture for video generation. Here, bidirectional video models such as Wan2.1 [(Wan et al., 2025)], which generate entire videos at once without causal constraints, are at the forefront of generation quality. To accelerate inference and allow for long-horizon generation, they are often finetuned into autoregressive models with fewer denoising steps [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026)]. MoDDiT is independent of, and compatible with these techniques.

Outside of diffusion, various extensions to ViT have been proposed. [Darcet et al. (2023)] analyse the attention map of ViT models and find attention sinks: low-information image patches with anomalously high attention weights that pool global information. Therefore, the authors propose register tokens with learned embedding values that are appended to the image sequence and discarded at the end of the forward pass. We extend our models to use register tokens to improve compute allocation, inspired by [Darcet et al. (2023)], who demonstrate that removing the attention sinks from the image improves the performance and alignment of saliency maps with semantic features.

2.3 Mixture-of-Experts Models

Mixture-of-experts [(Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022, MoE,)] approaches improve transformer scaling by dividing the transformer’s MLP blocks into multiple expert MLPs, with each token typically routed to only a single expert, as determined by a routing module, a small MLP that computes scalar scores for each token-expert pair. These scores determine the assignment of tokens to experts via (potentially stochastic) top-K selection.

While earlier approaches directly optimize stochastic routing decisions to minimize the expected loss using REINFORCE-style objectives [(Bengio et al., 2015)], recent work instead uses learned gating functions as the router, using the gate as a heuristic proxy for expert utility [(Shazeer et al., 2017)]. [(Raposo et al., 2024)] use such a routing mechanism for sparse token processing in language processing, and we propose combining it with dynamic MLP sparsity for image patches.

3 Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

MoDDiT combines a token bypass [(Krause et al., 2025)] with separate routing for attention and MLPs [(Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026)], allowing for dynamic allocation in MLPs without ragged batches [(Shi et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025)].

3.1 Learning to Route Tokens

At the core of our method is a simple routing mechanism (see fig.2), similar to an MoE routing module as used in [(Raposo et al., 2024; You et al., 2025)]. Each of our router blocks consists of a tiny, two-layer MLP R_φ applied independently to each token tᵢ with i∈1,…,N to compute a scalar routing logit R_φ(tᵢ). During training, we apply stochastic Gumbel top-K[(Jang et al., 2016; Kool et al., 2019)] routing to encourage exploratory routing decisions. Specifically, for each token we sample gᵢ∼Gumbel(0,1) and select the K tokens with the highest perturbed score,

r̃ᵢ=R_φ(tᵢ)+τgᵢ,

where τ is a temperature parameter. By annealing τ→0, we encourage exploration during early training while recovering increasingly deterministic top-K routing from the unperturbed logits.

As in MoE models, the router receives gradients by simultaneously acting as a gating mechanism. Similarly to [Raposo et al. (2024)], we multiply the output of the routed block for each token by its routing weight,

rᵢ=σ(R_φ(tᵢ)).

(1)

3.2 Dynamic Allocation in MLP Routing

MLPs process each token independently, allowing for a simple way to introduce dynamic sparsity.

During training, instead of selecting the top-K tokens per sample, we can merge the batch and token dimensions and select the top-(B·K) tokens across the whole batch on each GPU [(Shi et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025)]. Since samples in each batch belong to different classes and diffusion steps, the model can learn to dynamically allocate compute based on image class and diffusion step (section4).

At inference, however, we might want to generate a single sample (B=1). Selecting the top-(1·K) tokens would lose the dynamic allocation based on class and noise level, thereby introducing a distribution shift in the number of selected tokens. Instead, we can approximate the global top-(B·K) operation applied during training by tracking a logit threshold T at training time, such that p(R_φ(tᵢ)≥T)=c. Here c=K/N is the model capacity, i.e., the targeted fraction of tokens we route on average. We initialize at T=0 and update T←T+α(r̂-c), where α is a learning rate and r̂ is the fraction of tokens with a clean score R_φ(tᵢ)≥T.

This differs from Expert Race [(Yuan et al., 2025)], which averages the cutoff value to the top-K.

3.3 Fixed-Capacity Routing for Self-Attention

In self-attention, the number of tokens in an example determines the dimensions of its attention matrix. For efficient parallel processing on GPUs, all examples in the same batch must use attention matrices with the same dimensions. Therefore, we cannot simply give each example a different number of tokens, because this would produce differently sized matrices and prevent efficient vectorized computation. We subsequently route a fixed number of K tokens for each example.

Additionally, tokens have two distinct roles, each producing an output value and serving as context for other tokens to attend to. This opens up a design space for routing context (keys and values) and output (queries) independently, or routing based on relevance as context. We elaborate and show results for possible setups in sectionA.3.1, and find that the simple method in section3.1 is among the best, so we select it for its simplicity.

4 Results on ImageNet

Experimental Setup

We perform experiments on ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)], using the Face-blurred ILSVRC 2012–2017 variant [(Yang et al., 2022)] at 256×256 resolution. We train all models from scratch for 1M steps using the DiT-L/2 configuration and all hyperparameters from [Peebles and Xie (2023)] without further tuning. This includes using the same pre-trained variational autoencoder [(Kingma et al., 2013, VAE)] from Stable Diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)], with an 8× downsample factor. To make MoDDiT comparable in FLOPs with DiT, we construct MoDDiT by replacing alternate DiT blocks with two MoDDiT blocks, approximately matching DiT FLOPs for a 50% capacity model with the same configuration. For more details, see sectionA.1.

Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate the performance of image generation using standard evaluation metrics of generative models: Fréchet Inception Distance [(Heusel et al., 2017, FID)], spatial FID [(Nash et al., 2021, sFID)], Inception Score [(Salimans et al., 2016, IS)], and Precision/Recall [(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019)], each using 50k samples.

Results

Figure3 and sectionA.2 show the FLOPs-normalized performance of 50%, 25%, and 12.5% MoDDiT models, as well as a dense DiT baseline. The 50% MoDDiT model, which we constructed to match the baseline FLOPs, consistently outperforms the DiT baseline in FID, sFID, precision, and IS. Notably, the 25% model achieves better FID, sFID, and IS, at a 22% reduction in training and inference FLOPs. Furthermore, the 12.5% model is competitive with DiT on all metrics, despite using 33% less FLOPs.

Ablations

We experiment with multiple attention gating methods (see section3.3), and present full results in sectionA.3.1. Our evaluations show that no method uniformly performs best. We thus settle for the simplest possible attention gating setup, as visualized in fig.2. Furthermore, sectionA.3.2 shows that learned token routing substantially improves over random token selection, while independent routing does not uniformly beat coupled routing. Coupled routing has better FID, while the full method has better sFID.

Compute Allocation over Noise Levels

fig.4 shows the compute allocation of samples over denoising steps, as well as the difference in diffusion loss of MoDDiT models with different capacity levels. Again, we show only the MLP routing proportion since the self-attention capacity is constant across samples. We see increased compute allocation at lower noise levels (smaller timesteps) for all models, as well as a greater difference in allocated capacity between models, validating the qualitative example in fig.1. The difference in loss between MoDDiT models is roughly proportional to the difference in compute allocation between them, suggesting models spend their increased capacity at low noise levels to decrease loss.

Compute Allocation over Classes

We analyze compute allocation of MoDDiT models, and find that the variance within each image’s latent representation is a strong predictor of allocation (fig.4). We hypothesize that classes with high-variance latent patches require more iterative refinement throughout the whole denoising process, for example, to update boundaries and relationships to surrounding patches. A uniform patch’s representation contains relatively less information, so additional computation adds little bonus. We find that lower-capacity models have weaker correlation, full results can be found in fig.8.

5 Results on 1X

Experimental Setup

We use the raw video dataset from the 1X World Modeling Challenge [(1X, 2025)], containing approximately 100 hours of humanoid robot POV video at 30 frames per second and 512×512 resolution, as well as continuous controller actions for the robot at every frame. To embed these videos for latent diffusion, we use the pre-trained Cosmos Tokenizer [(NVIDIA, 2025)], selecting the continuous variant with an 8× spatial and temporal downsample factor. This embeds 8 contiguous video frames with dimension 8×512×512×3 into a latent frame with dimension 1×64×64×16. During training, we condition models on two latent context frames, equivalent to 16 image frames, as well as the next 8 robot actions (corresponding to 1 latent frame). We train models to denoise the next latent frame conditioned on this context, and autoregressively sample latent frames during evaluation.

In order to support efficient training on video data, we also introduce spatio-temporal (ST) variants of DiT and MoDDiT, ST-DiT and ST-MoDDiT. These separate the self-attention operation into separate spatial and temporal attention operations, in which tokens attend to other tokens in the same frame or other tokens in the same position in previous frames, respectively. We compare ST-DiT and ST-MoDDiT using the DiT-L/2 configuration at 200,000 optimizer updates (sectionB.1).

Results

We evaluate the 200k EMA checkpoints on 400 paired validation clips, measuring PSNR at 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 seconds after the observed context (table1). ST-MoDDiT at 12.5% capacity improves PSNR by 0.677, 0.376 and 0.213 dB, respectively; all three pointwise 95% paired segment-bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero. It uses 36.92% fewer counted denoiser FLOPs on the profiled clip. Sparse and dense models use training batches of 256 and 217, respectively, so equal optimizer-update counts do not imply equal training-data exposure.

Compute Allocation over Temporal Pixel Difference

Video generation models are conditioned on previous frames, making it trivial to denoise future tokens corresponding to static objects; they can just be copied over. We therefore hypothesise that dynamic objects with high optical flow should benefit from increased compute allocation in MoDDiT models. To evaluate this, we measure the allocation percentage and absolute pixel difference in 8 consecutive frames (corresponding to the temporal downsampling factor of the video tokenizer). We visualise the result in fig.5, which shows a strong positive correlation between a token’s frame difference and allocation frequency, confirming that MoDDiT uses more FLOPs to generate frames with many dynamic objects (sectionB.2).

6 Sparse Distillation with Self-Forcing

Experimental Setup

We investigate the distillation of pretrained Wan2.1-T2V-14B [(Wan et al., 2025)] into a sparse, autoregressive few-step student initialized from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, following Self Forcing [(Huang et al., 2025)]. Our student retains the native 30-block architecture and generates 81-frame videos at 832×480 resolution, processing chunks of three latent frames with four denoising steps per chunk.

We apply MoDDiT routing to MLP sublayers and self-attention queries, retaining dense keys, values, and text cross-attention. We found that decreasing capacity throughout the model’s blocks helped preserve both global structure and fine details; see sectionC.1. We train two models, Funnel50 and Funnel20, which respectively decrease each block’s capacity from 100% to 50% and 20%. Both models use sparse attention and MLP routing. To control stochastic exploration, we adapt the routing-noise temperature to attain a target replacement rate within the top-K. The student weights and routers are jointly optimized. We gradually introduce sparsity during adaptation and use straight-through router gates to preserve the scale of pretrained updates. Training uses AdamW with gradient accumulation to obtain an effective batch size of 64. More details can be found in sectionC.1.

Results

We find that sparse MoDDiT models perform similarly to the dense Self Forcing baseline on the VBench benchmark, with modest reductions in most evaluation categories. The sparse models struggle particularly in generating spatial relations and multiple objects, which require compute to be distributed across the image. Overall, MoDDiT achieves a total VBench score that is 5.35% lower than the dense baseline, at a 23.98% reduction in transformer FLOPs (sectionC.2).

7 Related Work

Transformers have become the predominant architecture for flow-based generative modeling, in both image generation with models such as DiT [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], DALL-E 3 [(Goh et al., 2023)], and Latte [(Ma et al., 2024)], as well as video generation in GAIA-2 [(Russell et al., 2025)], Genie 2 [(Parker-Holder et al., 2024)], Mochi [(GenmoAI, 2024)], Sora [(Brooks et al., 2024)], MovieGen [(Polyak et al., 2024)], and Wan2.1 [(Wan et al., 2025)]. This paradigm naturally invites adaptive compute allocation, since denoising difficulty varies across noise levels and spatio-temporal regions. Furthermore, many of the downstream applications of these models, such as large-scale image generation and real-time video generation, have strict constraints on latency that require fast inference. Despite this, adaptive computation techniques have not yet been adopted in state-of-the-art models.

However, interest in this research area has recently increased. [Wang et al. (2024)] learn sparsity masks for pre-trained diffusion models without content-dependent selection, while [Xi et al. (2025)] use online profiling to sparsify spatial-temporal attention connections while retaining all tokens. Token compression methods reduce the sequence length through token merging in ToMeSD [(Bolya and Hoffman, 2023)]. ToCa [(Zou et al., 2025)] and RAS [(Liu et al., 2026)] reuse computation across denoising timesteps through cached token features and noise predictions for inactive regions, respectively. DiffCR [(You et al., 2025)] routes tokens through or around whole transformer blocks and learns layer- and timestep-specific capacities with an auxiliary budget loss, evaluated by fine-tuning pretrained diffusion models.

More closely related, DyDiT [(Zhao et al., 2025)] and DyDiT++ [(Zhao et al., 2026)] combine timestep-conditioned width reduction with content-dependent token bypass in MLP blocks, using an auxiliary loss to control overall FLOPs. They require full self-attention during training, so sparsity is only introduced in inference. TREAD [(Krause et al., 2025)] accelerates training by randomly selecting tokens to bypass sequences of transformer blocks, while retaining dense computation at inference. Our method learns separate token routers for attention and MLP blocks jointly with the diffusion model from scratch, without auxiliary losses, while preserving tensor shapes for efficient batch inference with per-sample flexibility in the MLP blocks.

Mixture-of-experts mechanisms [(Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022, MoE)] allocate computation by routing tokens among multiple MLP experts, as in EC-DiT [(Sun et al., 2025)]. DiffMoE [(Shi et al., 2025)] pools tokens across examples and learns a capacity predictor for adaptive inference; Expert Race [(Yuan et al., 2025)] combines global token–expert competition with tracked-threshold inference. MoDDiT shares these allocation principles but applies them to a single MLP branch, combines them with independently routed sparse attention, and trains the model from scratch without a separately supervised capacity predictor or auxiliary routing objectives.

Outside of diffusion modeling, adaptive computation has become increasingly prevalent in transformer models, in order to allocate resources efficiently based on input complexity. [Xin et al. (2020)] propose a language model architecture with adaptive depth via an early exiting mechanism. Inspiring this work, mixture-of-depths [(Raposo et al., 2024)] uses a routing mechanism to limit the capacity of transformer layers in autoregressive language models. While this method shows improvements in the FLOPs-normalized performance frontier of such models, we find diffusion to be an even more suitable paradigm for this architecture, as the models avoid causal structure interfering with the top-K operation.

8 Conclusion

Summary

MoDDiT represents a significant advancement in efficient generative modeling, effectively addressing a computational inefficiency inherent in existing diffusion models by dynamically allocating compute across tokens, samples, and noise levels. By employing a minimal yet powerful routing mechanism, MoDDiT demonstrates considerable performance improvements at the same level of compute, on both image and video generation tasks. Our evaluation also provides an intuitive understanding of the learned routing mechanism, highlighting MoDDiT’s capability to align computational effort with semantic importance and temporal dynamics. Our work thus provides a step towards unlocking generative modeling in latency- and hardware-constrained settings and offers insights into the distribution of computational resources within diffusion models.

Limitations and Future Work

While our work provides an extensive evaluation, it is ultimately limited by our computational resources, providing the opportunity for further evaluation with alternate datasets, architectures, and generative algorithms. Namely, image generation datasets such as ArtBench [(Liao et al., 2022)] and Food [(Bossard et al., 2014)], as well as video generation datasets such as Taichi-HD [(Siarohin et al., 2019)] and Minecraft VPT [(Baker et al., 2022)], would strengthen confidence in the performance of MoDDiT.

While MoDDiT can substantially reduce training and inference FLOPs, this reduction does not automatically translate into wall clock time savings. Even though we observe throughput gains at larger batch sizes 111 At batch size 32, we measure 1.64 images/sec for a 50% MoDDiT model, vs. 1.55 images/sec for a DiT., generating few images in parallel is slower. This is likely due to a combination of the additional overhead of the gather and scatter operations, and the fact that dense matrix multiplication is already highly optimized itself. Future work can explore the development of optimized kernels for sparse MoDDiT blocks, which have proven to lead to significant performance increases for attention blocks [(Dao, 2024)].

Finally, MoDDiT introduces a capacity hyperparameter for the MLP and self-attention blocks, providing a range of promising avenues for further investigation. While our method avoids auxiliary losses, the addition of such a loss could enable automatic tuning of this capacity, with a regularization penalty against high compute budgets. Furthermore, we use the same capacity for both MLP and self-attention blocks. Visual inspection suggests that they have distinct allocation dynamics (fig.1), meaning their optimal capacities likely differ and should be investigated.
