Appendix A ImageNet experiments

A.1 Training and evaluation

Dataset

We perform experiments on ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)], using the Face-blurred ILSVRC 2012–2017 variant [(Yang et al., 2022)] at 256×256 resolution.

Model Architecture

We train latent diffusion models using the pre-trained variational autoencoder [(Kingma et al., 2013, VAE)] from Stable Diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)], with an 8× downsample factor, giving a latent embedding with dimensions 32×32×4. Our baseline is the DiT-L/2 architecture from [Peebles and Xie (2023)]. To make MoDDiT comparable in FLOPs with DiT, we construct MoDDiT by replacing alternate DiT blocks with two MoDDiT blocks, approximately matching DiT FLOPs for a 50% capacity model with the same configuration. Finally, MoDDiT models append every latent image with 16 register tokens [(Darcet et al., 2023)], as we found this to help with aligning allocation masks with semantic features, giving a total embedding length of 272. We initialize the final router layer at zero, such that the output is constant 0.5. We use a cosine decay for router Gumbel noise, decaying from 5 to 0 over training.

Training

We train all models from scratch for 1M steps (requiring approximately 6 days on 4 L40S GPUs) using hyperparameters from [Peebles and Xie (2023)] without further tuning. This includes using a global batch size of 256 with AdamW using a learning rate of 10⁻⁴, β=(0.9,0.999), and no weight decay. We use an EMA value of 0.9999 throughout training.

Evaluation

We evaluate all models using 50,000 generated images at 64,128,256, and 512 denoising steps and a classifier-free guidance scale of 1.5. We measure FLOPs on the first 1024 generated images, including both classifier-free guidance branches, excluding the VAE decoder.

A.2 Additional results

A.3 Routing design studies

A.3.1 Attention-routing alternatives

Gating values serve as a proxy for token selection. But what form of gating produces the most useful proxy? Multiplying the attention output by the router score incentivises retaining tokens whose outputs reduce loss. However, there is no incentive to increase the scores of tokens that serve as useful context for others to attend to. To provide such a signal, we may additionally gate the attention values using the routing scores. Let A=softmax(QKᵀ/√d) and R=diag(r). While standard output gating computes Rattn(x)=RAV, additionally gating the attention value yields

RARV=(rr^⊤⊙A)V where (rr^⊤⊙A)ᵢⱼ=rᵢaᵢⱼrⱼ.

This formulation introduces complementary incentives to increase the score R_φ(tᵢ) of a token tᵢ:

  • •

    Output gating: Does tᵢ reduce downstream loss by attending to other tokens?

  • •

    Value gating: Do other tokens decrease downstream loss by attending to tᵢ?

    • Disentangling both incentives by producing two routing scores opens a substantial design space. For example, consolidating both scores for top-K selection can be done as a sum, product, or harmonic mean. Additionally, instead of consolidating scores, one may select two different top-K subsets of tokens for Q and K/V, and compute cross-attention, or implement sparsity only in keys and values.

    We test four of these configurations:

  • •

    Output-only: the default MoDDiT, gating only the self-attention output via RAV.

  • •

    Shared value/output: gating the output and value by the same routing score via RARV.

  • •

    Separate routers: two routers per attention operation, producing R_O and R_V, and selecting tokens independently, then gating as R_OAR_VV.

  • •

    Sparse Q/dense KV: All tokens enter attention as context, but only selected tokens contribute to the output.

    • A.3.2 Selection and capacity ablations

    Appendix B 1X video prediction

    B.1 Training and evaluation

    Dataset

    We use the 1X World Modeling Dataset [(1X, 2025)], with 512×512 video at 30 Hz and 25-dimensional robot states.

    Model architecture

    We use the 12.5%-capacity DiT-L/2, block-replacement scheme and register count from sectionA.1. The frozen Cosmos CV8x8x8 tokenizer [(NVIDIA, 2025)] produces 64×64×16 latent frames. Each frame contains 1024 spatial tokens and eight state tokens in addition to the registers. We adopt spatiotemporal attention from [(Russell et al., 2025)], in which a token at a fixed spatial position and timestep attends to all tokens at the same timestep, and all tokens at the same spatial position in the past.

    Training

    We train from scratch with seed 0, using the AdamW settings and weight EMA from sectionA.1. Global batch sizes are 256 for ST-MoDDiT and 217 for ST-DiT. The learning rate warms up for 5,000 steps, then follows a cosine schedule towards 10⁻⁵ at 1M steps. Routing uses Gumbel-sigmoid temperature 5.

    Inference

    We encode the first 17 frames, then autoregressively predict eight latents (64 frames), retaining three context latents and conditioning on the next eight recorded robot states. Sampling uses 128 DDPM steps per latent and the classifier-free guidance scale from sectionA.1.

    Evaluation

    For table1, we evaluate both models’ EMA checkpoints at exactly 200,000 optimizer updates on 400 paired, non-overlapping 81-frame windows from 249 segments in one video from the raw validation v2.0 split. Clip identities and sampling seeds are shared across models. PSNR is computed against raw RGB frames at 0.5, 1 and 2 seconds after the observed context, averaging squared error across pixels and channels before conversion to dB. We report the clip-weighted mean and paired sparse-minus-dense gains. Pointwise 95% percentile confidence intervals use 20,000 paired bootstrap draws over segments, with seed 20261011, retaining all windows within each sampled segment. These intervals reflect evaluation variability, not training-seed variability. The temporal-change analysis in sectionB.2 uses its separately saved 300k, 100-clip cohort.

    We count denoiser FLOPs over the first clip’s complete eight-latent rollout (128 DDPM calls per latent, CFG 1.5), including both guidance branches and all dense and routed blocks. Registered matrix, convolution and attention operations count a multiply-add as two FLOPs; tokenizer, scalar/nonlinear, normalization, selection and I/O work are excluded. The table reports total rollout TFLOPs, not per-call GFLOPs or measured throughput.

    B.2 Temporal change and allocation

    Using the setup in sectionB.1, we measure temporal change by averaging absolute adjacent-frame grayscale differences over each latent’s temporal interval and spatial token footprint, including interval boundaries. For each spatial patch, allocation is the mean of its binary selection mask over attention and MLP branches, routed blocks, and denoising steps, expressed as a percentage. We use only the conditional guidance branch and exclude state/register tokens and dense blocks.

    For fig.5, we clip frame differences at the global 99th percentile and group them into 100 equal-width bins. The line shows mean allocation; shading spans the within-bin 12.5th–87.5th percentiles, describing observed variation rather than uncertainty in the mean. Higher temporal change is associated with greater allocation, but frame difference is not optical flow, and this association does not establish a causal benefit from routing.

    Appendix C Self-Forcing adaptation

    C.1 Sparse architecture and adaptation

    We follow the chunk-wise Self-Forcing DMD protocol [(Huang et al., 2025)], including its prompt data, optimization settings, and inference procedure, with the following sparse adaptation details.

    Model architecture

    Starting from the released ODE checkpoint, we keep every third block dense and add separate routers of hidden width 256 for self-attention queries and MLP tokens in the remaining blocks. Keys, values, and text cross-attention remain dense, and we use straight-through gates to keep the output magnitude of the pretrained model. Attention uses fixed-count selection; MLP selection is fixed-count for Funnel20 and threshold-based for Funnel50 (sectionC.1).

    Capacity schedules

    We experiment with two MoDDiT models with capacity schedules we call Funnel20 and Funnel50. Across the 30 blocks, target capacity decreases linearly from 100% at block 1 to 20% or 50% at block 30, respectively. Blocks 1, 4, 7, …, 28 override this schedule and remain fully dense. The names are chosen as the final-block targets, not the average model-wide capacity.

    Initial qualitative experiments showed that increasing capacity in early blocks could recover structure that was otherwise lost under aggressive sparsity. We also retain dense keys and values, including cached context, so selected queries can attend to all available tokens, including tokens that receive no attention update.

    Training

    We jointly adapt the student and routers for 3,000 ODE updates, reducing capacity to the target with a cosine schedule over the first 600 updates. Trajectories use 48 sampling steps and guidance scale 6, retaining five states each. We then run 25 critic warmup iterations and 1,000 DMD iterations, starting student EMA at iteration 200.

    Evaluation

    We compare the final student EMA with the released dense EMA checkpoint from Self Forcing. VBench and compute protocols are in sectionC.2; qualitative comparisons are in sectionC.3.

    C.2 VBench evaluation and compute accounting

    Evaluation

    We evaluate the released dense Self-Forcing EMA checkpoint and the Funnel50/Funnel20 EMA checkpoints after 1,000 DMD iterations using the sampling settings in sectionC.1. We use the original English VBench prompts [(Huang et al., 2023)], with five samples per prompt and reproducible seeds derived from the prompt and sample index. We apply the official category normalization and weights, and the total score weights quality and semantic scores 4:1. The separate motion and instruction scores in fig.6 use 100 Causal-Forcing motion prompts, one sample each: motion is the percentage classified as dynamic, and instruction following is 100 times the mean VisionReward yes/no judgment, encoded as 1 or -1.

    Scores

    Table3 gives the category scores and aggregates. Relative to dense Self-Forcing, Funnel50 and Funnel20 reduce the total score by 4.93% and 5.35%, respectively, while decreasing inference FLOPs by 16.8% and 24.0%. Both lose more on multiple objects and spatial relationships than on imaging quality. This could be because they concentrate compute on a single part of the image, not capturing relationships between different image parts.

    Compute

    We count matrix-operation FLOPs for one matched 81-frame raccoon-guitar clip at 832×480, seed 0 and batch size 1, including 28 denoising calls and six KV-cache updates. A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs. Dense Self-Forcing and Funnel20 use runtime operator shapes; Funnel50 uses recorded query and realized MLP token counts. Transformer costs are 950.39, 789.93 and 722.53 TFLOPs for dense, Funnel50 and Funnel20, giving reductions of 16.88% and 23.98%. Adding the shared text-encoder and VAE matrix/convolution cost of 289.39 TFLOPs reduces these savings to 12.94% and 18.38%. Counts exclude scalar/nonlinear operations, indexing, memory transfers and hardware padding. They describe arithmetic for this clip, not benchmark-wide averages or measured speedups; dynamic MLP allocation varies with the input.

    C.3 Qualitative comparisons

一句话：背景 token 对去噪贡献很小，DiT 却静态均匀地全算一遍；把 MLP 与自注意力各自路由后，12.5% 容量下视频预测 PSNR 更高、去噪 FLOPs 少 36.92%。

要点：

  • 自然图像本身稀疏，大片背景容易去噪；DiT 却对所有 token 施加同样的计算，没有利用这层稀疏
  • 让 token 分别通过 MLP 与自注意力两条路径的独立路由，于是 MLP 侧的算力分配可以随 token、图像与去噪时间步动态变化
  • ImageNet 从零训：50% 容量在与 DiT 对齐 FLOPs 时 FID/sFID/precision/IS 全面更好；25% 容量 FLOPs 少 22% 仍更优；12.5% 容量在约 33% 更少 FLOPs 下与 DiT 相当
  • 视频侧在 1X World Modeling Challenge 上，12.5% 容量路由既提高视频预测 PSNR，又把计入的去噪 FLOPs 压低 36.92%

为什么值得看：生成式渲染的成本瓶颈已经从采样步数转到 backbone 吞吐；这类「不改结构、只改路由」的改动对现有 DiT 管线最友好，适合先做推理侧降本。

中文摘要：实时视频生成、交互式世界模型与端侧图像合成都快成为现实，Diffusion Transformer 的采样质量已经够好，瓶颈转到模型自身吞吐。自然图像天然稀疏：大片背景几乎不承载内容，也容易去噪，但 DiT 对所有图像 token 一视同仁地处理，浪费了这层稀疏性。作者提出 MoDDiT：一个很简单的架构改动，让 token 分别路由通过 MLP 与自注意力，从而让 MLP 的算力分配可以随 token、图像和去噪时间步变化。从零训练时，MoDDiT 显著降低训练与推理成本，最多只用 12.5% 的 token；随着稀疏度与深度增加，成本下降的同时生成质量还优于未路由基线。在视频生成（1X World Modeling Challenge）上，12.5% 容量路由在提高预测 PSNR 的同时把计入的去噪 FLOPs 减少 36.92%。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

MoDDiT: Simple Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

Abstract

Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly.

We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.

††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution

1 Introduction

Recent advancements in real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis promise numerous new applications for generative models, and a new frontier of synthetic data. Diffusion models are at the forefront of this progress but are bottlenecked by their iterative generation procedure, which requires multiple model evaluations to generate samples. The resulting latency is often reduced by distilling models into smaller students or subsampling diffusion timesteps. A complementary axis of improvement is given by architecture modifications that reduce the cost of each inference step of the denoising process.

A promising route is exploiting sparsity, inspired by the observation that images and videos are information-sparse modalities where few patches per frame contain a large amount of information. For example, in many images the background is much simpler than the foreground and is therefore easier to denoise. This effect is magnified in videos, where patches containing static objects can be simply copied over from the previous frame. Ideally, diffusion would focus computation on more relevant patches, reducing overall latency. However, predominant diffusion architectures such as diffusion transformers [(Peebles and Xie, 2023, DiT,)] fail to exploit this property, instead applying all operations to every token, thereby allocating compute uniformly over images and videos.

In this work, we introduce MoDDiT, a simple mechanism for routing tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations (section3). While routing through self-attention uses fixed capacity, routing through MLPs enables dynamic compute allocation across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps (section3.2). This allows the model to devote more computation to regions that are visually complex and difficult to denoise.

Unlike prior methods, MoDDiT reduces FLOPs during both training and inference, requires no auxiliary routing loss or post-processing, and enables efficient training on parallel GPU hardware without ragged batches. As illustrated in fig.1, the resulting allocation is interpretable, with computation varying across image regions, samples, and denoising timesteps.

We evaluate MoDDiT across three settings: image generation, video generation, and video distillation. On ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)] (section4), MoDDiT improves the quality–compute tradeoff over vanilla DiT across a range of routing capacities and sampling lengths. For video generation, we evaluate on the 1X World Modeling Challenge [(1X, 2025)] (section5), where routing at 12.5% capacity improves video-prediction PSNR while requiring 36.92% fewer counted denoiser FLOPs on the profiled clip than the DiT baseline. Finally, we integrate sparse feedforward routing into the distillation of pretrained Wan2.1 [(Wan et al., 2025)], converting a dense bidirectional model into a sparse, few-step autoregressive generator (section6). Compared with a matched dense autoregressive student, the sparse model almost matches the dense baseline with a 5% overall reduction in score on the VBench benchmark [(Huang et al., 2023)], while reducing inference FLOPs by 24%. We further analyze the learned routing behavior (figs.4 and 5), showing how computation varies with denoising stage, image and patch class, and temporal change in video.

In summary, MoDDiT provides a simple, efficient mechanism for dynamic token routing, exploiting token-level sparsity in diffusion transformers. By increasing model size and sparsity, it can increase performance while reducing training- and inference-time FLOPs. We compare routing choices and ablations on ImageNet, and give intuitive explanations for allocation across image content and time steps. On 1X, we test action-conditioned video generation and show that learned allocation varies with temporal change. Distilling Wan2.1 tests whether MoDDiT can be combined with distillation and few-step denoising, where the reduction in inference FLOPs comes with a modest reduction in VBench score.

2 Background

2.1 Diffusion Models

Diffusion models [(Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021)] generate images by iteratively removing noise from samples drawn from a known noisy distribution. Specifically, they consist of two complementary Markov processes: a forward noising process and a reverse denoising process. In the forward process, an initial clean image x₀ is progressively corrupted into a purely noisy image x_T across a discrete sequence of timesteps t=1,…,T, following the Gaussian conditional distribution q(xₜ|xₜ₋₁)=ℕ(xₜ;√1-βₜ xₜ₋₁,βₜI), where βₜ∈(0,1) defines the noise schedule at timestep t. Equivalently, this forward process can be expressed as xₜ=√ᾱₜ x₀+√1-ᾱₜ ε, with ε∼ℕ(0,I) and ᾱₜ=∏ᵢ₌₁ᵗ(1-βᵢ). The reverse process, parameterized by a neural network, gradually reconstructs the original clean image from x_T to x₀ by approximating the conditional distributions p_θ(xₜ₋₁|xₜ)=ℕ(xₜ₋₁;μ_θ(xₜ,t),Σ_θ(xₜ,t)). Model training involves minimizing the discrepancy between the predicted and actual noise at each timestep, enabling accurate modeling of the underlying data distribution.

2.2 Vision- and Diffusion Transformers

Following their success in language modeling, transformers [(Vaswani et al., 2017)] have been successfully applied to vision tasks. Vision transformer [(Dosovitskiy et al., 2020, ViT)] achieves this by constructing a flattened token sequence from pixel patches. Similar to transformers, ViT models consist of alternating self-attention [(Bahdanau et al., 2014)] and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) blocks, with intermediate layer normalization [(Ba et al., 2016)]. In these models, self-attention distributes information across the sample, in this case passing information between image patches, while the MLP processes tokens independently. Diffusion transformers [(Peebles and Xie, 2023, DiT, )] adapt ViT models for image diffusion with adaptive layer normalization (adaLN), which conditions the normalization operation on the diffusion timestep and image class.

In addition to image generation, DiTs are the predominant architecture for video generation. Here, bidirectional video models such as Wan2.1 [(Wan et al., 2025)], which generate entire videos at once without causal constraints, are at the forefront of generation quality. To accelerate inference and allow for long-horizon generation, they are often finetuned into autoregressive models with fewer denoising steps [(Yin et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026)]. MoDDiT is independent of, and compatible with these techniques.

Outside of diffusion, various extensions to ViT have been proposed. [Darcet et al. (2023)] analyse the attention map of ViT models and find attention sinks: low-information image patches with anomalously high attention weights that pool global information. Therefore, the authors propose register tokens with learned embedding values that are appended to the image sequence and discarded at the end of the forward pass. We extend our models to use register tokens to improve compute allocation, inspired by [Darcet et al. (2023)], who demonstrate that removing the attention sinks from the image improves the performance and alignment of saliency maps with semantic features.

2.3 Mixture-of-Experts Models

Mixture-of-experts [(Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022, MoE,)] approaches improve transformer scaling by dividing the transformer’s MLP blocks into multiple expert MLPs, with each token typically routed to only a single expert, as determined by a routing module, a small MLP that computes scalar scores for each token-expert pair. These scores determine the assignment of tokens to experts via (potentially stochastic) top-K selection.

While earlier approaches directly optimize stochastic routing decisions to minimize the expected loss using REINFORCE-style objectives [(Bengio et al., 2015)], recent work instead uses learned gating functions as the router, using the gate as a heuristic proxy for expert utility [(Shazeer et al., 2017)]. [(Raposo et al., 2024)] use such a routing mechanism for sparse token processing in language processing, and we propose combining it with dynamic MLP sparsity for image patches.

3 Token Routing in Diffusion Transformers

MoDDiT combines a token bypass [(Krause et al., 2025)] with separate routing for attention and MLPs [(Zhao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026)], allowing for dynamic allocation in MLPs without ragged batches [(Shi et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025)].

3.1 Learning to Route Tokens

At the core of our method is a simple routing mechanism (see fig.2), similar to an MoE routing module as used in [(Raposo et al., 2024; You et al., 2025)]. Each of our router blocks consists of a tiny, two-layer MLP R_φ applied independently to each token tᵢ with i∈1,…,N to compute a scalar routing logit R_φ(tᵢ). During training, we apply stochastic Gumbel top-K[(Jang et al., 2016; Kool et al., 2019)] routing to encourage exploratory routing decisions. Specifically, for each token we sample gᵢ∼Gumbel(0,1) and select the K tokens with the highest perturbed score,

r̃ᵢ=R_φ(tᵢ)+τgᵢ,

where τ is a temperature parameter. By annealing τ→0, we encourage exploration during early training while recovering increasingly deterministic top-K routing from the unperturbed logits.

As in MoE models, the router receives gradients by simultaneously acting as a gating mechanism. Similarly to [Raposo et al. (2024)], we multiply the output of the routed block for each token by its routing weight,

rᵢ=σ(R_φ(tᵢ)).

(1)

3.2 Dynamic Allocation in MLP Routing

MLPs process each token independently, allowing for a simple way to introduce dynamic sparsity.

During training, instead of selecting the top-K tokens per sample, we can merge the batch and token dimensions and select the top-(B·K) tokens across the whole batch on each GPU [(Shi et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025)]. Since samples in each batch belong to different classes and diffusion steps, the model can learn to dynamically allocate compute based on image class and diffusion step (section4).

At inference, however, we might want to generate a single sample (B=1). Selecting the top-(1·K) tokens would lose the dynamic allocation based on class and noise level, thereby introducing a distribution shift in the number of selected tokens. Instead, we can approximate the global top-(B·K) operation applied during training by tracking a logit threshold T at training time, such that p(R_φ(tᵢ)≥T)=c. Here c=K/N is the model capacity, i.e., the targeted fraction of tokens we route on average. We initialize at T=0 and update T←T+α(r̂-c), where α is a learning rate and r̂ is the fraction of tokens with a clean score R_φ(tᵢ)≥T.

This differs from Expert Race [(Yuan et al., 2025)], which averages the cutoff value to the top-K.

3.3 Fixed-Capacity Routing for Self-Attention

In self-attention, the number of tokens in an example determines the dimensions of its attention matrix. For efficient parallel processing on GPUs, all examples in the same batch must use attention matrices with the same dimensions. Therefore, we cannot simply give each example a different number of tokens, because this would produce differently sized matrices and prevent efficient vectorized computation. We subsequently route a fixed number of K tokens for each example.

Additionally, tokens have two distinct roles, each producing an output value and serving as context for other tokens to attend to. This opens up a design space for routing context (keys and values) and output (queries) independently, or routing based on relevance as context. We elaborate and show results for possible setups in sectionA.3.1, and find that the simple method in section3.1 is among the best, so we select it for its simplicity.

4 Results on ImageNet

Experimental Setup

We perform experiments on ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)], using the Face-blurred ILSVRC 2012–2017 variant [(Yang et al., 2022)] at 256×256 resolution. We train all models from scratch for 1M steps using the DiT-L/2 configuration and all hyperparameters from [Peebles and Xie (2023)] without further tuning. This includes using the same pre-trained variational autoencoder [(Kingma et al., 2013, VAE)] from Stable Diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)], with an 8× downsample factor. To make MoDDiT comparable in FLOPs with DiT, we construct MoDDiT by replacing alternate DiT blocks with two MoDDiT blocks, approximately matching DiT FLOPs for a 50% capacity model with the same configuration. For more details, see sectionA.1.

Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate the performance of image generation using standard evaluation metrics of generative models: Fréchet Inception Distance [(Heusel et al., 2017, FID)], spatial FID [(Nash et al., 2021, sFID)], Inception Score [(Salimans et al., 2016, IS)], and Precision/Recall [(Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019)], each using 50k samples.

Results

Figure3 and sectionA.2 show the FLOPs-normalized performance of 50%, 25%, and 12.5% MoDDiT models, as well as a dense DiT baseline. The 50% MoDDiT model, which we constructed to match the baseline FLOPs, consistently outperforms the DiT baseline in FID, sFID, precision, and IS. Notably, the 25% model achieves better FID, sFID, and IS, at a 22% reduction in training and inference FLOPs. Furthermore, the 12.5% model is competitive with DiT on all metrics, despite using 33% less FLOPs.

Ablations

We experiment with multiple attention gating methods (see section3.3), and present full results in sectionA.3.1. Our evaluations show that no method uniformly performs best. We thus settle for the simplest possible attention gating setup, as visualized in fig.2. Furthermore, sectionA.3.2 shows that learned token routing substantially improves over random token selection, while independent routing does not uniformly beat coupled routing. Coupled routing has better FID, while the full method has better sFID.

Compute Allocation over Noise Levels

fig.4 shows the compute allocation of samples over denoising steps, as well as the difference in diffusion loss of MoDDiT models with different capacity levels. Again, we show only the MLP routing proportion since the self-attention capacity is constant across samples. We see increased compute allocation at lower noise levels (smaller timesteps) for all models, as well as a greater difference in allocated capacity between models, validating the qualitative example in fig.1. The difference in loss between MoDDiT models is roughly proportional to the difference in compute allocation between them, suggesting models spend their increased capacity at low noise levels to decrease loss.

Compute Allocation over Classes

We analyze compute allocation of MoDDiT models, and find that the variance within each image’s latent representation is a strong predictor of allocation (fig.4). We hypothesize that classes with high-variance latent patches require more iterative refinement throughout the whole denoising process, for example, to update boundaries and relationships to surrounding patches. A uniform patch’s representation contains relatively less information, so additional computation adds little bonus. We find that lower-capacity models have weaker correlation, full results can be found in fig.8.

5 Results on 1X

Experimental Setup

We use the raw video dataset from the 1X World Modeling Challenge [(1X, 2025)], containing approximately 100 hours of humanoid robot POV video at 30 frames per second and 512×512 resolution, as well as continuous controller actions for the robot at every frame. To embed these videos for latent diffusion, we use the pre-trained Cosmos Tokenizer [(NVIDIA, 2025)], selecting the continuous variant with an 8× spatial and temporal downsample factor. This embeds 8 contiguous video frames with dimension 8×512×512×3 into a latent frame with dimension 1×64×64×16. During training, we condition models on two latent context frames, equivalent to 16 image frames, as well as the next 8 robot actions (corresponding to 1 latent frame). We train models to denoise the next latent frame conditioned on this context, and autoregressively sample latent frames during evaluation.

In order to support efficient training on video data, we also introduce spatio-temporal (ST) variants of DiT and MoDDiT, ST-DiT and ST-MoDDiT. These separate the self-attention operation into separate spatial and temporal attention operations, in which tokens attend to other tokens in the same frame or other tokens in the same position in previous frames, respectively. We compare ST-DiT and ST-MoDDiT using the DiT-L/2 configuration at 200,000 optimizer updates (sectionB.1).

Results

We evaluate the 200k EMA checkpoints on 400 paired validation clips, measuring PSNR at 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 seconds after the observed context (table1). ST-MoDDiT at 12.5% capacity improves PSNR by 0.677, 0.376 and 0.213 dB, respectively; all three pointwise 95% paired segment-bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero. It uses 36.92% fewer counted denoiser FLOPs on the profiled clip. Sparse and dense models use training batches of 256 and 217, respectively, so equal optimizer-update counts do not imply equal training-data exposure.

Compute Allocation over Temporal Pixel Difference

Video generation models are conditioned on previous frames, making it trivial to denoise future tokens corresponding to static objects; they can just be copied over. We therefore hypothesise that dynamic objects with high optical flow should benefit from increased compute allocation in MoDDiT models. To evaluate this, we measure the allocation percentage and absolute pixel difference in 8 consecutive frames (corresponding to the temporal downsampling factor of the video tokenizer). We visualise the result in fig.5, which shows a strong positive correlation between a token’s frame difference and allocation frequency, confirming that MoDDiT uses more FLOPs to generate frames with many dynamic objects (sectionB.2).

6 Sparse Distillation with Self-Forcing

Experimental Setup

We investigate the distillation of pretrained Wan2.1-T2V-14B [(Wan et al., 2025)] into a sparse, autoregressive few-step student initialized from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, following Self Forcing [(Huang et al., 2025)]. Our student retains the native 30-block architecture and generates 81-frame videos at 832×480 resolution, processing chunks of three latent frames with four denoising steps per chunk.

We apply MoDDiT routing to MLP sublayers and self-attention queries, retaining dense keys, values, and text cross-attention. We found that decreasing capacity throughout the model’s blocks helped preserve both global structure and fine details; see sectionC.1. We train two models, Funnel50 and Funnel20, which respectively decrease each block’s capacity from 100% to 50% and 20%. Both models use sparse attention and MLP routing. To control stochastic exploration, we adapt the routing-noise temperature to attain a target replacement rate within the top-K. The student weights and routers are jointly optimized. We gradually introduce sparsity during adaptation and use straight-through router gates to preserve the scale of pretrained updates. Training uses AdamW with gradient accumulation to obtain an effective batch size of 64. More details can be found in sectionC.1.

Results

We find that sparse MoDDiT models perform similarly to the dense Self Forcing baseline on the VBench benchmark, with modest reductions in most evaluation categories. The sparse models struggle particularly in generating spatial relations and multiple objects, which require compute to be distributed across the image. Overall, MoDDiT achieves a total VBench score that is 5.35% lower than the dense baseline, at a 23.98% reduction in transformer FLOPs (sectionC.2).

7 Related Work

Transformers have become the predominant architecture for flow-based generative modeling, in both image generation with models such as DiT [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)], DALL-E 3 [(Goh et al., 2023)], and Latte [(Ma et al., 2024)], as well as video generation in GAIA-2 [(Russell et al., 2025)], Genie 2 [(Parker-Holder et al., 2024)], Mochi [(GenmoAI, 2024)], Sora [(Brooks et al., 2024)], MovieGen [(Polyak et al., 2024)], and Wan2.1 [(Wan et al., 2025)]. This paradigm naturally invites adaptive compute allocation, since denoising difficulty varies across noise levels and spatio-temporal regions. Furthermore, many of the downstream applications of these models, such as large-scale image generation and real-time video generation, have strict constraints on latency that require fast inference. Despite this, adaptive computation techniques have not yet been adopted in state-of-the-art models.

However, interest in this research area has recently increased. [Wang et al. (2024)] learn sparsity masks for pre-trained diffusion models without content-dependent selection, while [Xi et al. (2025)] use online profiling to sparsify spatial-temporal attention connections while retaining all tokens. Token compression methods reduce the sequence length through token merging in ToMeSD [(Bolya and Hoffman, 2023)]. ToCa [(Zou et al., 2025)] and RAS [(Liu et al., 2026)] reuse computation across denoising timesteps through cached token features and noise predictions for inactive regions, respectively. DiffCR [(You et al., 2025)] routes tokens through or around whole transformer blocks and learns layer- and timestep-specific capacities with an auxiliary budget loss, evaluated by fine-tuning pretrained diffusion models.

More closely related, DyDiT [(Zhao et al., 2025)] and DyDiT++ [(Zhao et al., 2026)] combine timestep-conditioned width reduction with content-dependent token bypass in MLP blocks, using an auxiliary loss to control overall FLOPs. They require full self-attention during training, so sparsity is only introduced in inference. TREAD [(Krause et al., 2025)] accelerates training by randomly selecting tokens to bypass sequences of transformer blocks, while retaining dense computation at inference. Our method learns separate token routers for attention and MLP blocks jointly with the diffusion model from scratch, without auxiliary losses, while preserving tensor shapes for efficient batch inference with per-sample flexibility in the MLP blocks.

Mixture-of-experts mechanisms [(Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022, MoE)] allocate computation by routing tokens among multiple MLP experts, as in EC-DiT [(Sun et al., 2025)]. DiffMoE [(Shi et al., 2025)] pools tokens across examples and learns a capacity predictor for adaptive inference; Expert Race [(Yuan et al., 2025)] combines global token–expert competition with tracked-threshold inference. MoDDiT shares these allocation principles but applies them to a single MLP branch, combines them with independently routed sparse attention, and trains the model from scratch without a separately supervised capacity predictor or auxiliary routing objectives.

Outside of diffusion modeling, adaptive computation has become increasingly prevalent in transformer models, in order to allocate resources efficiently based on input complexity. [Xin et al. (2020)] propose a language model architecture with adaptive depth via an early exiting mechanism. Inspiring this work, mixture-of-depths [(Raposo et al., 2024)] uses a routing mechanism to limit the capacity of transformer layers in autoregressive language models. While this method shows improvements in the FLOPs-normalized performance frontier of such models, we find diffusion to be an even more suitable paradigm for this architecture, as the models avoid causal structure interfering with the top-K operation.

8 Conclusion

Summary

MoDDiT represents a significant advancement in efficient generative modeling, effectively addressing a computational inefficiency inherent in existing diffusion models by dynamically allocating compute across tokens, samples, and noise levels. By employing a minimal yet powerful routing mechanism, MoDDiT demonstrates considerable performance improvements at the same level of compute, on both image and video generation tasks. Our evaluation also provides an intuitive understanding of the learned routing mechanism, highlighting MoDDiT’s capability to align computational effort with semantic importance and temporal dynamics. Our work thus provides a step towards unlocking generative modeling in latency- and hardware-constrained settings and offers insights into the distribution of computational resources within diffusion models.

Limitations and Future Work

While our work provides an extensive evaluation, it is ultimately limited by our computational resources, providing the opportunity for further evaluation with alternate datasets, architectures, and generative algorithms. Namely, image generation datasets such as ArtBench [(Liao et al., 2022)] and Food [(Bossard et al., 2014)], as well as video generation datasets such as Taichi-HD [(Siarohin et al., 2019)] and Minecraft VPT [(Baker et al., 2022)], would strengthen confidence in the performance of MoDDiT.

While MoDDiT can substantially reduce training and inference FLOPs, this reduction does not automatically translate into wall clock time savings. Even though we observe throughput gains at larger batch sizes 111 At batch size 32, we measure 1.64 images/sec for a 50% MoDDiT model, vs. 1.55 images/sec for a DiT., generating few images in parallel is slower. This is likely due to a combination of the additional overhead of the gather and scatter operations, and the fact that dense matrix multiplication is already highly optimized itself. Future work can explore the development of optimized kernels for sparse MoDDiT blocks, which have proven to lead to significant performance increases for attention blocks [(Dao, 2024)].

Finally, MoDDiT introduces a capacity hyperparameter for the MLP and self-attention blocks, providing a range of promising avenues for further investigation. While our method avoids auxiliary losses, the addition of such a loss could enable automatic tuning of this capacity, with a regularization penalty against high compute budgets. Furthermore, we use the same capacity for both MLP and self-attention blocks. Visual inspection suggests that they have distinct allocation dynamics (fig.1), meaning their optimal capacities likely differ and should be investigated.

Contributions

JL and MJ co-led the project. MJ developed and implemented the initial method, ran experiments on ImageNet and 1X, and wrote the first version of the paper (May 2025). JL ran extensive ablations, modified and extended the method, added experiments including sparse distillation, and polished the manuscript. JF, SW, and BE co-supervised the project.

Appendix A ImageNet experiments

A.1 Training and evaluation

Dataset

We perform experiments on ImageNet [(Deng et al., 2009)], using the Face-blurred ILSVRC 2012–2017 variant [(Yang et al., 2022)] at 256×256 resolution.

Model Architecture

We train latent diffusion models using the pre-trained variational autoencoder [(Kingma et al., 2013, VAE)] from Stable Diffusion [(Rombach et al., 2022)], with an 8× downsample factor, giving a latent embedding with dimensions 32×32×4. Our baseline is the DiT-L/2 architecture from [Peebles and Xie (2023)]. To make MoDDiT comparable in FLOPs with DiT, we construct MoDDiT by replacing alternate DiT blocks with two MoDDiT blocks, approximately matching DiT FLOPs for a 50% capacity model with the same configuration. Finally, MoDDiT models append every latent image with 16 register tokens [(Darcet et al., 2023)], as we found this to help with aligning allocation masks with semantic features, giving a total embedding length of 272. We initialize the final router layer at zero, such that the output is constant 0.5. We use a cosine decay for router Gumbel noise, decaying from 5 to 0 over training.

Training

We train all models from scratch for 1M steps (requiring approximately 6 days on 4 L40S GPUs) using hyperparameters from [Peebles and Xie (2023)] without further tuning. This includes using a global batch size of 256 with AdamW using a learning rate of 10⁻⁴, β=(0.9,0.999), and no weight decay. We use an EMA value of 0.9999 throughout training.

Evaluation

We evaluate all models using 50,000 generated images at 64,128,256, and 512 denoising steps and a classifier-free guidance scale of 1.5. We measure FLOPs on the first 1024 generated images, including both classifier-free guidance branches, excluding the VAE decoder.

A.2 Additional results

A.3 Routing design studies

A.3.1 Attention-routing alternatives

Gating values serve as a proxy for token selection. But what form of gating produces the most useful proxy? Multiplying the attention output by the router score incentivises retaining tokens whose outputs reduce loss. However, there is no incentive to increase the scores of tokens that serve as useful context for others to attend to. To provide such a signal, we may additionally gate the attention values using the routing scores. Let A=softmax(QKᵀ/√d) and R=diag(r). While standard output gating computes Rattn(x)=RAV, additionally gating the attention value yields

RARV=(rr^⊤⊙A)V where (rr^⊤⊙A)ᵢⱼ=rᵢaᵢⱼrⱼ.

This formulation introduces complementary incentives to increase the score R_φ(tᵢ) of a token tᵢ:

  • •

    Output gating: Does tᵢ reduce downstream loss by attending to other tokens?

  • •

    Value gating: Do other tokens decrease downstream loss by attending to tᵢ?

    • Disentangling both incentives by producing two routing scores opens a substantial design space. For example, consolidating both scores for top-K selection can be done as a sum, product, or harmonic mean. Additionally, instead of consolidating scores, one may select two different top-K subsets of tokens for Q and K/V, and compute cross-attention, or implement sparsity only in keys and values.

    We test four of these configurations:

  • •

    Output-only: the default MoDDiT, gating only the self-attention output via RAV.

  • •

    Shared value/output: gating the output and value by the same routing score via RARV.

  • •

    Separate routers: two routers per attention operation, producing R_O and R_V, and selecting tokens independently, then gating as R_OAR_VV.

  • •

    Sparse Q/dense KV: All tokens enter attention as context, but only selected tokens contribute to the output.

    • A.3.2 Selection and capacity ablations

    Appendix B 1X video prediction

    B.1 Training and evaluation

    Dataset

    We use the 1X World Modeling Dataset [(1X, 2025)], with 512×512 video at 30 Hz and 25-dimensional robot states.

    Model architecture

    We use the 12.5%-capacity DiT-L/2, block-replacement scheme and register count from sectionA.1. The frozen Cosmos CV8x8x8 tokenizer [(NVIDIA, 2025)] produces 64×64×16 latent frames. Each frame contains 1024 spatial tokens and eight state tokens in addition to the registers. We adopt spatiotemporal attention from [(Russell et al., 2025)], in which a token at a fixed spatial position and timestep attends to all tokens at the same timestep, and all tokens at the same spatial position in the past.

    Training

    We train from scratch with seed 0, using the AdamW settings and weight EMA from sectionA.1. Global batch sizes are 256 for ST-MoDDiT and 217 for ST-DiT. The learning rate warms up for 5,000 steps, then follows a cosine schedule towards 10⁻⁵ at 1M steps. Routing uses Gumbel-sigmoid temperature 5.

    Inference

    We encode the first 17 frames, then autoregressively predict eight latents (64 frames), retaining three context latents and conditioning on the next eight recorded robot states. Sampling uses 128 DDPM steps per latent and the classifier-free guidance scale from sectionA.1.

    Evaluation

    For table1, we evaluate both models’ EMA checkpoints at exactly 200,000 optimizer updates on 400 paired, non-overlapping 81-frame windows from 249 segments in one video from the raw validation v2.0 split. Clip identities and sampling seeds are shared across models. PSNR is computed against raw RGB frames at 0.5, 1 and 2 seconds after the observed context, averaging squared error across pixels and channels before conversion to dB. We report the clip-weighted mean and paired sparse-minus-dense gains. Pointwise 95% percentile confidence intervals use 20,000 paired bootstrap draws over segments, with seed 20261011, retaining all windows within each sampled segment. These intervals reflect evaluation variability, not training-seed variability. The temporal-change analysis in sectionB.2 uses its separately saved 300k, 100-clip cohort.

    We count denoiser FLOPs over the first clip’s complete eight-latent rollout (128 DDPM calls per latent, CFG 1.5), including both guidance branches and all dense and routed blocks. Registered matrix, convolution and attention operations count a multiply-add as two FLOPs; tokenizer, scalar/nonlinear, normalization, selection and I/O work are excluded. The table reports total rollout TFLOPs, not per-call GFLOPs or measured throughput.

    B.2 Temporal change and allocation

    Using the setup in sectionB.1, we measure temporal change by averaging absolute adjacent-frame grayscale differences over each latent’s temporal interval and spatial token footprint, including interval boundaries. For each spatial patch, allocation is the mean of its binary selection mask over attention and MLP branches, routed blocks, and denoising steps, expressed as a percentage. We use only the conditional guidance branch and exclude state/register tokens and dense blocks.

    For fig.5, we clip frame differences at the global 99th percentile and group them into 100 equal-width bins. The line shows mean allocation; shading spans the within-bin 12.5th–87.5th percentiles, describing observed variation rather than uncertainty in the mean. Higher temporal change is associated with greater allocation, but frame difference is not optical flow, and this association does not establish a causal benefit from routing.

    Appendix C Self-Forcing adaptation

    C.1 Sparse architecture and adaptation

    We follow the chunk-wise Self-Forcing DMD protocol [(Huang et al., 2025)], including its prompt data, optimization settings, and inference procedure, with the following sparse adaptation details.

    Model architecture

    Starting from the released ODE checkpoint, we keep every third block dense and add separate routers of hidden width 256 for self-attention queries and MLP tokens in the remaining blocks. Keys, values, and text cross-attention remain dense, and we use straight-through gates to keep the output magnitude of the pretrained model. Attention uses fixed-count selection; MLP selection is fixed-count for Funnel20 and threshold-based for Funnel50 (sectionC.1).

    Capacity schedules

    We experiment with two MoDDiT models with capacity schedules we call Funnel20 and Funnel50. Across the 30 blocks, target capacity decreases linearly from 100% at block 1 to 20% or 50% at block 30, respectively. Blocks 1, 4, 7, …, 28 override this schedule and remain fully dense. The names are chosen as the final-block targets, not the average model-wide capacity.

    Initial qualitative experiments showed that increasing capacity in early blocks could recover structure that was otherwise lost under aggressive sparsity. We also retain dense keys and values, including cached context, so selected queries can attend to all available tokens, including tokens that receive no attention update.

    Training

    We jointly adapt the student and routers for 3,000 ODE updates, reducing capacity to the target with a cosine schedule over the first 600 updates. Trajectories use 48 sampling steps and guidance scale 6, retaining five states each. We then run 25 critic warmup iterations and 1,000 DMD iterations, starting student EMA at iteration 200.

    Evaluation

    We compare the final student EMA with the released dense EMA checkpoint from Self Forcing. VBench and compute protocols are in sectionC.2; qualitative comparisons are in sectionC.3.

    C.2 VBench evaluation and compute accounting

    Evaluation

    We evaluate the released dense Self-Forcing EMA checkpoint and the Funnel50/Funnel20 EMA checkpoints after 1,000 DMD iterations using the sampling settings in sectionC.1. We use the original English VBench prompts [(Huang et al., 2023)], with five samples per prompt and reproducible seeds derived from the prompt and sample index. We apply the official category normalization and weights, and the total score weights quality and semantic scores 4:1. The separate motion and instruction scores in fig.6 use 100 Causal-Forcing motion prompts, one sample each: motion is the percentage classified as dynamic, and instruction following is 100 times the mean VisionReward yes/no judgment, encoded as 1 or -1.

    Scores

    Table3 gives the category scores and aggregates. Relative to dense Self-Forcing, Funnel50 and Funnel20 reduce the total score by 4.93% and 5.35%, respectively, while decreasing inference FLOPs by 16.8% and 24.0%. Both lose more on multiple objects and spatial relationships than on imaging quality. This could be because they concentrate compute on a single part of the image, not capturing relationships between different image parts.

    Compute

    We count matrix-operation FLOPs for one matched 81-frame raccoon-guitar clip at 832×480, seed 0 and batch size 1, including 28 denoising calls and six KV-cache updates. A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs. Dense Self-Forcing and Funnel20 use runtime operator shapes; Funnel50 uses recorded query and realized MLP token counts. Transformer costs are 950.39, 789.93 and 722.53 TFLOPs for dense, Funnel50 and Funnel20, giving reductions of 16.88% and 23.98%. Adding the shared text-encoder and VAE matrix/convolution cost of 289.39 TFLOPs reduces these savings to 12.94% and 18.38%. Counts exclude scalar/nonlinear operations, indexing, memory transfers and hardware padding. They describe arithmetic for this clip, not benchmark-wide averages or measured speedups; dynamic MLP allocation varies with the input.

    C.3 Qualitative comparisons

item.title: 头部重打光进实时档：GSHeadRelight 用统一神经辐射传输表示，单卡 240 FPS、比前作快 12 倍 ｜ GSHeadRelight: Fast Relightability for 3D Gaussian Head Synthesis
item.description:
一句话：不用光 stage 数据，只靠 in-the-wild 图像：给每个高斯配反照率与传输向量，光照响应变成线性，H800 上跑到 240 FPS。

要点：

  • 在 3D Gaussian GAN 框架上，给每个高斯点额外的反照率与一个传输向量（形状 3×n²），替换原来与视角无关的颜色
  • 传输表示对入射光线性响应，于是重打光只需换光照系数，不必重跑生成网络
  • 只用 FFHQ 在 4 张 H800 上训练 1500 万图；单张 H800 上约 240 FPS，比之前的 3D-aware portrait relighting 至少快 12 倍
  • FID 5.71 / KID 0.151，与 GSGAN 的 5.60 / 0.161 基本持平，但后者不具备重打光能力

为什么值得看：实时角色管线里，重打光通常意味着多一套材质与光照模型；把「与光无关的反照率」和「线性传输」拆出来存，就能让生成式头部资产跟着场景灯光走。

中文摘要：人像的重打光与新视角合成在摄影、VR、AR 里都关键，但 3D 感知的人像重打光要同时满足写实、实时与对未见被试的泛化。已有方法要么依赖昂贵的光 stage 采集数据做监督，要么效果欠佳；不少工作基于生成式 NeRF，3D 一致性与实时性都差。作者转向生成式 3D Gaussian，并设计一个基于统一神经辐射传输表示的光照模型，对入射光线性响应：每个高斯除颜色外还带反照率与一个传输向量，取代原来与视角无关的颜色。只用 in-the-wild 图像训练，就在重打光效果上达到当前最优，并把渲染速度提到约 240 FPS（单张 H800），相对既有 3D-aware portrait relighting 方法至少快 12 倍。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

GSHeadRelight: Fast Relightability for 3D Gaussian Head Synthesis

© cc

Abstract.

Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits are essential in applications such as portrait photography, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR). Despite recent progress, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains challenging due to the demands for photorealistic rendering, real-time performance, and generalization to unseen subjects. Existing works either rely on supervision from limited and expensive light stage captured data or produce suboptimal results. Moreover, many works are based on generative NeRFs, which suffer from poor 3D consistency and low real-time performance. We resort to recent progress on generative 3D Gaussians and design a lighting model based on a unified neural radiance transfer representation, which responds linearly to incident light. Using only in-the-wild images, our method achieves state-of-the-art relighting results and a significantly faster rendering speed (×12) compared to previous 3D-aware portrait relighting research. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/GSHeadRelight/.

Keywords:

3D portrait relighting, 3D Gaussian splitting, radiance transfer ††cc-license: by-nc

1. Introduction

Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits have always been two fundamental demands in various applications. In portrait photography, finding the ideal lighting and viewpoint often requires intensive expert knowledge and extensive trial and error. In virtual reality and augmented reality, virtual avatars need to be rendered under different lighting conditions and viewpoints in real-time and high fidelity. These demands drive the rapid development of the emerging field of 3D-aware portrait relighting.

However, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains highly challenging due to its three demands: photorealistic appearance, real-time rendering, and one-shot generalization to unseen subjects. Human heads consist of highly intricate and varied materials that display different scattering and reflectance properties, making them among the most challenging objects to model accurately. The demand for real-time rendering significantly constrains algorithm design and model capabilities, and the requirement for sparse data input (single image or video) in many real-world applications brings the ambiguity between lighting and materials. Solving this under-constrained problem inevitably requires leveraging the powerful visual prior from pre-trained generative models.

It has been proven that Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] can provide such a prior. When incorporated with 3D representations, GANs can even learn 3D geometries from mere image datasets. Among them, generative NeRF [(Chan et al., 2022; Mildenhall et al., 2021)] find the balance between photorealism and 3D consistency. The 3D head priors have enabled 3D-aware manipulation over human portraits such as attribute editing [(Gao et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2025)], style transfer [(Yuan et al., 2024)] and relighting [(Jiang et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024a)]. To resolve the ambiguity between lighting and materials, some works [(Mei et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2024)] employ light stage data as ground truth for supervision. Nevertheless, light-stage captured data are expensive and usually closed source, so they are not accessible to common researchers. For better generalization and scalability, learning from casual image datasets is preferred. [Jiang et al. (2023)] distill albedo from weakly labeled image datasets at the cost of handling only white light. [Deng et al. (2024)] propose an inverse rendering framework that models radiance transfer for the diffuse term and uses a simple BRDF for the specular term. Impressive as these works are, most of them are based on generative NeRF, which is prone to limited rendering speed and 3D inconsistencies because of volume rendering and upsampling. More importantly, these works rely on neural rendering and need network evaluation for each lighting, which further limits the real-time performance of relighting.

We introduce GSHeadRelight, a relightable 3D head generative model with the latest generative 3D Gaussian backbone [(Hyun and Heo, 2024; Kirschstein et al., 2024)]. Inspired by precomputed radiance transfer [(Sloan et al., 2002)], we design a lighting model based on Unified Neural Radiance Transfer. We assign spherical harmonics coefficients for each 3D Gaussian ellipsoid to model the radiance transfer, which handles visibility and global illumination, including self-occlusion and subsurface scattering. By making radiance transfer coefficients a function of view directions, our method can model both diffuse terms and low-frequency reflections. However, without explicit supervision of albedo, the ambiguity between albedo and lighting severely affects relighting quality. Since most in-the-wild images are under white illumination, we make a simple white-light assumption during training to mitigate the ambiguity, which provides plausible albedo decoupling. One desirable feature of radiance transfer is that the outgoing radiance, i.e. irradiance, responds to incident light linearly. Although our model is trained solely on white light, it can generalize well to colored illumination during test time. Moreover, since all components are organized as Gaussian attributes independent of lighting, only one forward inference is needed for head synthesis, and relighting can be performed without further generator evaluations. As a result, our method is extremely efficient and significantly reduces hardware requirements.

To summarize, we present three main contributions:

  • •

    A relightable 3D Gaussian head generative model based on unified radiance transfer that supports global illumination.

  • •

    A regime that distills plausible albedo and light transport functions from in-the-wild images without a heavy light stage setup.

  • •

    Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art 3D-aware relighting results with extreme efficiency. Our model achieves a rendering speed of ~240 FPS on a single NVIDIA H800, with at least 12× speedup over previous methods.

    • 2. Related Work

    In this section, we review relevant work in the field of 3D-aware portrait synthesis. We then examine deep neural face relighting from two perspectives: studio-captured data and casual image datasets.

    3D-aware Portrait Synthesis

    Despite Diffusion Models (DMs) [(Ho et al., 2020)] being proven to have stronger model capabilities than GANs [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] in synthesizing images [(Rombach et al., 2022)], videos [(Brooks et al., 2024)] and 3D assets [(Zhang et al., 2024d)], GANs excel at 3D-aware portrait synthesis. The sparsity of high-quality 3D head models hinders the training of DMs, whereas 3D-GANs can learn fine geometry from mere image datasets.

    Early 3D-GANs directly render pixels from explicit or implicit 3D representations, such as meshes [(Chen and Zhang, 2019; Henderson et al., 2020; Kanazawa et al., 2018)] and voxels [(Gadelha et al., 2017; Henzler et al., 2019)], or implicit neural radiance fields [(Chan et al., 2021; Schwarz et al., 2020)]. Some works [(Nguyen-Phuoc et al., 2019; Niemeyer and Geiger, 2021; Xue et al., 2022)] append neural rendering on the image side to improve image fidelity and enable high-resolution rendering. Subsequent works [(Gu et al., 2021; Or-El et al., 2022; Chan et al., 2022)] mostly adopt StyleGAN [(Karras, 2019)] as the generator due to its success. Among them, EG3D [(Chan et al., 2022)] proposes a hybrid radiance field representation and applies a super-resolution module to the generated tri-plane features. Despite its high expressiveness, volume rendering is too slow for native high-resolution synthesis, and super-resolution inevitably causes spatial inconsistencies across views.

    Recent works [(Hyun and Heo, 2024; Kirschstein et al., 2024)] utilize 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] as the new explicit representation, allowing for native high-resolution head synthesis in real-time. [Kirschstein et al. (2024)] bind 3D Gaussians to a template mesh and generate UV maps of each Gaussian attribute under the StyleGAN [(Karras, 2019)] backbone. Gaussian ellipsoids are then queried and mapped back onto the template at arbitrary resolution. [Hyun and Heo (2024)] instead explore a hierarchical generative paradigm without a template mesh, where at each layer 3D Gaussians are constrained by anchor points from the previous layer. A new generative architecture is designed to generate multiple-level anchors and Gaussians. Our method is based on the recent progress in generative 3D Gaussian head synthesis. We refer to [(Sun et al., 2024)] for more recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting.

    Deep Neural Face Relighting

    Portrait relighting requires decomposition of appearance, geometry, and lighting. To acquire accurate facial reflectance fields, a line of works resort to meticulously calibrated studio equipment, including the widely adopted light stage [(Debevec et al., 2000)]. Neural networks are incorporated into the light stage processing to enable single image portrait relighting [(Pandey et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Weir et al., 2022; Nestmeyer et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2024; LeGendre et al., 2020)]. Novel view synthesis and animation along with relighting are present with the development of 3D representations such as mesh [(Lombardi et al., 2018; Bi et al., 2021)], volumetric primitive [(Lombardi et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024)], NeRF [(Xu et al., 2023; Sarkar et al., 2023; Rao et al., 2022)] and 3D Gaussian [(Saito et al., 2024; He et al., 2024)]. Inverse rendering is widely used to decouple intrinsics and enable lighting manipulation [(Nestmeyer et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2024; Pandey et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024c)]. Recent development of diffusion models enables more lighting condition interfaces like prompt [(Zhang et al., 2024b)], background [(Ren et al., 2024)], and scribble [(Mei et al., 2023)].

    While the expensive studio-captured data provides ground truth supervision, easily accessible casual image collections offer more diversity and scalability. Deep generative neural networks like GANs are usually adopted to learn the priors of appearance and lighting. Early works explore style transfer [(Abdal et al., 2021; Shih et al., 2014; Shu et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2024)] to transfer lighting, but fail to maintain identity consistency. The quotient image [(Shashua and Riklin-Raviv, 2001; Peers et al., 2007)] decouples albedo from appearance and is widely used for plausible relighting [(Tewari et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023)]. Inverse rendering is also explored [(Deng et al., 2024)] with self-supervised regulation. Relighting with novel view synthesis from casual images [(Sun et al., 2021; Tewari et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021)] is also present with semantic control over GANs. The incorporation of generative NeRF allows for 3D-aware portrait relighting [(Pan et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2024; Mei et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024a; Ranjan et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024b)].

    3. Method

    In the following, we first introduce preliminaries including spherical harmonics, precomputed radiance transfer, and 3D Gaussian head synthesis. Then we discuss design choices in generative 3D-GAN relighting. Finally, we introduce the proposed Unified Neural Radiance Transfer and the loss functions.

    3.1. Preliminaries

    Precomputed Radiance Transfer

    Computing global illumination is costly because it requires iterative path tracing due to multi-bounce reflections, refractions, and scattering of light. [Sloan et al. (2002)] propose to precompute radiance transfer functions, which are applied to actual incident lighting at run-time. Assuming distant illumination Lᵢₙ, exit radiance L_out,p from a point p is computed by the rendering equation with light transport:

    (1)L_out,p(v̂)=∫_ΩLᵢₙ(l̂)Vₚ(l̂)fᵣ(v̂,l̂)\max(0,n̂·l̂) dl̂

    where n̂ is the surface normal at p, l̂ and v̂ are global light direction and viewing direction, fᵣ is Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) and Vₚ is the light transport function considering self-occlusion and interreflection.

    To efficiently compute the integral in Equation 1, lighting and transfer functions are represented using nth-order spherical harmonics (SH). For specular surfaces, a transfer matrix Mₚ including the BRDF and cosine terms describes the radiance transfer via

    (2)

    L_out,p=∑ⱼ₌₁^n²MₚⁱʲLᵢₙʲ.

    Specifically for diffuse surfaces, radiance transfer can be represented by a transfer vector Vₚ producing scalar exit radiance L_out,p by

    (3)

    L_out,p=∑ᵢ₌₁^n²VₚⁱLₚⁱ.

    In modern neural rendering, precomputing transfer functions is often impractical because the geometric and material properties are unknown. Previous works [(Saito et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Xing et al., 2024)] choose to parameterize and learn diffuse radiance transfer vectors, while employing alternative representations for specular terms because the transfer matrix is too large. We instead propose to use a unified representation that models both diffuse terms and low-frequency reflections.

    3D Gaussian Head Synthesis

    3D Gaussian Splatting [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] is recently introduced as a point-based 3D representation that assigns to each point 5 attributes: position μ∈ℝ³, scale s∈ℝ³, rotation quaternion q∈ℝ⁴, opacity α∈ℝ and color c∈ℝ³. A Gaussian ellipsoid is formulated as

    (4)

    G(x)=e^-1/2(x-μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x-μ), with~~Σ=RSSᵀRᵀ,

    where x is the world coordinates, and the scaling matrix S and rotation matrix R are derived from the scaling s and quaternion q. The color C of a pixel in image space is computed by blending N overlapping sorted points:

    (5)

    C=∑ᵢ₌₁^Ncᵢαᵢ∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-αⱼ).

    Recent works in 3D Gaussian head synthesis [(Hyun and Heo, 2024; Kirschstein et al., 2024)] allow for native high-resolution head synthesis in real time. [Kirschstein et al. (2024)] bind 3D Gaussians to a template mesh and use StyleGAN2 [(Karras et al., 2020)] to generate UV maps of each Gaussian attribute. [Hyun and Heo (2024)] instead explore a hierarchical generative paradigm, where the 3D Gaussians at each layer are constrained by anchor points from the previous layer.

    3.2. Unified Neural Radiance Transfer

    Radiance transfer was primarily used to describe the diffuse component of lighting. We show that by incorporating view directions into the generative framework, a Unified Neural Radiance Transfer representation is capable of describing both diffuse and low-frequency specular terms. Revisiting Equation 1, by absorbing the light transport, BRDF, and cosine term into a unified radiance transfer function Tₚ in SH basis, the rendering equation becomes

    (6)

    L_out,p(v̂)=∫_ΩLᵢₙ(l̂)Tₚ(v̂,l̂) dl̂≈∑ᵢ₌₁^n²lᵢₙⁱtⁱₚ(v̂),

    where lⁱᵢₙ and tⁱₚ(v̂) are the nth-order expansion coefficients. Specifically, we disentangle the albedo ρₚ from tⁱₚ(v̂) for disentangling appearance from lighting. With minor notation abuse, the view-dependent exit radiance is formulated as

    (7)

    L_out,p(v̂)=ρₚ∑ᵢ₌₁^n²lᵢₙⁱtⁱₚ(v̂).

    In this way, both diffuse and specular terms can be handled in a unified manner by making radiance transfer coefficients a function of view direction.

    Based on 3D Gaussian GAN framework, we additionally assign each Gaussian point p an albedo ρₚ∈[0,1]³ and a transfer vector tₚ∈ℝ^3×n² to replace the original view-independent color. Specifically, as shown in Figure 2, the generator gives each Gaussian point p an embedding xₚ. The transfer vector tₚ is obtained by concatenating the Gaussian embedding with encoded view direction and sending it to a transfer vector decoder Ψₜ,

    (8)

    tₚ(v̂)=Ψₜ(x^′ₚ||vₚ),

    where x^′ₚ is a shortened embedding transformed linearly from the Gaussian embedding xₚ. It can be stored to perform real-time rendering with standard 3D Gaussian splatting after generation.

    Without explicit supervision of albedo, the ambiguity between albedo and transfer vectors is unavoidable, as demonstrated in Section 4.5. Observing that the illumination in most real images is approximately white light, we propose to train the model under white light conditions. The light and transfer vectors are then reduced to single channel, i.e. l,t∈ℝ^1×n². In this way, the contribution of the transfer vector to the color distribution is discarded, and thus the ambiguity is resolved. We find in the experiment that adversarial training will average out the impact of light color residuals on the albedo. Moreover, due to the linearity of our unified radiance transfer functions, our model can render colored lighting at test-time by channel-wise applying Equation 7.

    4. Experiments

    4.1. Implementation Details

    Our method is based on GSGAN [(Hyun and Heo, 2024)], which follows the same data preparation pipeline as EG3D [(Chan et al., 2022)]. The lighting labels, represented as monochromatic 3rd-order spherical harmonics, are extracted using DPR [(Zhou et al., 2019)], following the approach of [Jiang et al. (2023)]. We use MODNet [(Ke et al., 2022)] to extract foreground components to alleviate background leakage. The transfer vector decoder Ψₜ is implemented as a lightweight MLP with one hidden layer of 64 units. We train the models on the FFHQ dataset [(Karras, 2019)] from scratch for 15M images with four NVIDIA H800 GPUs.

    4.2. Quantitative Comparisons

    Baselines.

    We compare our method with previous publicly accessible works for novel view portrait relighting: ShadeGAN [(Pan et al., 2021)], Volux-GAN [(Tan et al., 2022)], NeRFFaceLighting [(Jiang et al., 2023)]. We also include LumiGAN [(Deng et al., 2024)], which is not accessible, and report results from the original paper if presented.

    Generative quality and rendering speed.

    We follow  [Chan et al. (2022)] and compute Frechnet Inception Distance (FID) [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and Kernel Inception Distance (KID) [(Bińkowski et al., 2018)] between 50k generated images and all training images. From Table 1, we see that EG3D-based methods have a higher FID due to the 2D super-resolution module, which upsamples low-resolution volume rendering results at the cost of losing 3D consistency. Our method achieves similar or even better generative quality than our backbone GSGAN [(Hyun and Heo, 2024)]. Moreover, our method maintains a high rendering speed, surpassing other relighting works by at least 12×. This is attributed to the simple yet effective architecture of our unified radiance transfer relighting framework.

    Lighting quality.

    Following [Jiang et al. (2023)], we measure the relighting performance with an off-the-shelf estimator [(Feng et al., 2021)] using two metrics: the Lighting Error computes the distance between real lighting and estimated lighting in fake images; the Lighting Stability computes the standard deviation of estimated lighting in 100 fake images generated using the same lighting conditions. The metrics are averaged for 1000 samples. Since these metrics can only be applied to methods with lighting conditions estimated from real images, Volux-GAN and LumiGAN are excluded. Instead, StyleFlow [(Abdal et al., 2021)], DisCoFaceGAN [(Deng et al., 2020)], and GAN-Control [(Shoshan et al., 2021)] are included as 2D generative relighting methods for comparison. Table 2 shows that our method is comparable in lighting quality with state-of-the-art 3D-portrait relighting methods. The 2D relighting method DisCoFaceGAN has higher lighting scores at the cost of low generative quality. Moreover, our method can perform RGB relighting, thanks to its linear radiance transfer framework. This is not achievable by other methods based on implicit neural relighting.

    Spatial consistency.

    Following [Hyun and Heo (2024)], we use a surface estimation model NeUS2 [(Wang et al., 2023)] to validate the spatial consistency of 3D-aware relighting models. Specifically, we randomly generate 30 views of a lit subject, fit them to surface estimation, and compute the reconstruction error using standard PSNR and SSIM metrics. We generate 30 subjects and record the average metrics. We also include the identity similarity metric proposed by [Tan et al. (2022)], and report the mean score across 30 views. From Table 3 we see that although EG3D-based methods do not preserve exact 3D consistency due to 2D super resolution, they do not exhibit disadvantages in terms of reconstruction error. This is possibly because EG3D and NeUS2 share a similar implicit representation and volume rendering process. However, in terms of identity similarity, our method achieves the highest score, demonstrating better 3D consistency than other methods. In general, EG3D-based methods suffer from texture flickering when continuously changing viewpoint due to 2D super resolution, while our method renders an explicit 3D Gaussian model and maintains view consistency. We further refer to the video demo for better visual comparison.

    4.3. Qualitative Comparison

    The Lighting Error and Lighting Stability metrics used in Section 4.2 can only evaluate the lighting similarity by an off-the-shelf lighting estimator. To further evaluate lighting quality under colored light conditions and compare the lighting realism under human eyes, we compare our method to previous works in real environment map lighting conditions. We include NeLF [(Sun et al., 2021)], which is trained using a synthetic lightstage dataset and needs multi-view inputs. Figure 3 shows that our method achieves better relighting quality than previous methods. Volux-GAN [(Tan et al., 2022)] uses 2D convolution layers to add shadows and details, leading to view inconsistencies. NeRFFaceLighting [(Jiang et al., 2023)] can only handle white-light conditions and performs poorly on environment map lighting. LumiGAN [(Deng et al., 2024)] relies on inverse rendering, and incorrect geometry decoupling leads to lighting artifacts, like the unnatural lit parts on the cheek and beside the wings of the nose. NeLF shows poor visual quality and loses facial details like wrinkles and pores. In contrast, our method performs well both in visual quality and relighting quality.

    4.4. Visual Relighting Results

    Our model presents overall good photorealism under different light intensity and directions, as shown in Fig 4. Colored illumination can also be handled correctly, as shown in Figure 5. Given an environment map, image-based lighting requires first converting it to spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Specifically, we apply Gaussian blurring before SH sampling with a radius of 0.1× image width to remove high-frequency details. Image-based lighting results are shown in Figure 6. Thanks to the unified radiance transfer framework, our approach responds linearly to incident light and innately satisfies the light transport consistency. Our method maintains 3D consistency in head poses while delivering plausible albedo and relighting results under various environment maps.

    Real portrait relighting

    With the help of the GAN inversion technique, our model can relight real-face images. The basic idea is to project a real-face image into the latent space and manipulate lighting during reconstruction. We implement the inversion similar to Pivotal Tuning [(Roich et al., 2022)] and compare the result with NeRFFaceLighting in Figure 7. Our method produces better photorealism and identity consistency. We also quantitatively evaluate identity consistency using cosine similarity of VGGFace [(Parkhi et al., 2015)] embedding on a subset of the Goliath dataset [(Martinez et al., 2024)], which has 4 sets of light-stage head capture. Our method (0.443) significantly outperforms NeRFFaceLighting (0.298).

    4.5. Other Design Choices and Ablation Study

    Multiple design choices exist for implementing unified radiance transfer in the 3D-GAN framework. First, the model could be trained using RGB lighting labels instead of monochromatic ones. Second, diffuse and specular reflectance could be modeled separately. We discuss these designs and validate their feasibility. We then conduct an ablation study on our proposed unified radiance transfer.

    No white-light assumption

    Some works [(Fei et al., 2023; Phongthawee et al., 2024)] allow extracting estimated RGB lighting conditions from a single image, which makes training on colored illumination possible. We follow the same setting and modify the parameterization of lighting labels and transfer functions from 1 channel to 3 channels. We use [(Fei et al., 2023)] to extract HDRI environment maps and turn them into 3rd-order RGB spherical harmonics coefficients. As shown in Figure 8, without explicit supervision of intrinsics, training under RGB lighting conditions leads to faded albedo. In this case, the contribution to appearance is entirely provided by lighting, and relighting becomes a style transfer process. The model overfits on certain lighting conditions, does not learn a physically consistent lighting model, and fails under unseen lighting.

    diffuse and specular decomposition

    Inverse rendering is widely adopted in portrait relighting [(Saito et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024)] to infer physical properties such as geometry, materials, and lighting. Diffuse and specular terms are often decoupled using different lighting models. We validate this setting in the 3D-GAN framework. We decouple the transfer vector t(v̂) into view-independent diffuse transfer vector t_diffuse and view-dependent specular transfer vector t_specular(v̂). However, without explicit supervision, albedo, diffuse, and specular terms are disentangled incorrectly and exhibit significant inconsistencies, as shown in Figure 9.

    Ablation study

    We validate the effectiveness of unified radiance transfer in Table 4. Without radiance transfer, we assume the color is directly predicted by a decoder that takes in lighting conditions. All models are trained for 3M images before evaluation. We find that radiance transfer provides strong lighting manipulation ability, demonstrated by the significant increase in Lighting Error in the case without radiance transfer. At the same time, without the view condition, the lighting accuracy also drops since the vanilla vector-based radiance transfer cannot model specular effects.
