In this case, the albedo is often observed with specular residuals. In contrast, our complete unified radiance transfer representation achieves the best lighting manipulation accuracy and yields smooth albedos. From Figure 10, view conditioning reduces most highlight residuals in albedo and yields more satisfactory relighting results.

    5. Conclusion, Limitation, and Future Work

    We present GSHeadRelight, a real-time relightable 3D-aware portrait synthesis framework based on a unified radiance transfer representation, addressing the challenging problem of colored lighting manipulation in the 3D-GAN setting. Our model learns the light transport functions under a white-light assumption from casual image datasets, without requiring expensive and inaccessible light-stage captured data. Since our model responds linearly to incident lighting and innately retains light transport consistency, it generalizes well to colored illumination and produces overall high-quality relighting results. The simple model design discards network evaluation for each light condition, adding real-time relightability for 3D head synthesis. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art 3D-aware relighting quality, superior real-time performance, and better spatial consistency compared with previous relighting methods.

    One limitation of our method is that it mainly models low-frequency and diffuse lighting effects due to the nature of radiance transfer in the spherical harmonics basis. Although the view-conditioned radiance transfer decoder models low-frequency view-dependent effects to some extent, our method is still not expressive enough for high-frequency reflections. In some cases, the model incorrectly learns the specular highlight in the albedo. As shown in Figure 11 (A), highlight on the right cheek remains in the albedo and leads to artifacts. In addition, relighting under illumination from below the face region may seem implausible, as shown in Figure 11 (C). This is because such illumination is scarce in in-the-wild images.

    For future work, it is interesting to model high-frequency and largely view-dependent effects on top of this explicit linear lighting model to support more complex lighting conditions other than spherical harmonics. Exploring the adaptation of our method to dynamic human head scenarios is also worth further investigation.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62322210), Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission (No. Z231100005923031), Innovation Funding of ICT, CAS (No. E461020), the Royal Society (IEC \233596), Kuaishou Technology and CCF-Kuaishou Large Model Explorer Fund. We would like to thank Chunshuo Qiu for assisting with the demo video production and Zhongming Chen for assisting with figure making. We would also like to acknowledge the Nanjing Institute of InforSuperBahn OneAiNexus for providing the training and evaluation platform.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：不用光 stage 数据，只靠 in-the-wild 图像：给每个高斯配反照率与传输向量，光照响应变成线性，H800 上跑到 240 FPS。

要点：

  • 在 3D Gaussian GAN 框架上，给每个高斯点额外的反照率与一个传输向量（形状 3×n²），替换原来与视角无关的颜色
  • 传输表示对入射光线性响应，于是重打光只需换光照系数，不必重跑生成网络
  • 只用 FFHQ 在 4 张 H800 上训练 1500 万图；单张 H800 上约 240 FPS，比之前的 3D-aware portrait relighting 至少快 12 倍
  • FID 5.71 / KID 0.151，与 GSGAN 的 5.60 / 0.161 基本持平，但后者不具备重打光能力

为什么值得看：实时角色管线里，重打光通常意味着多一套材质与光照模型；把「与光无关的反照率」和「线性传输」拆出来存，就能让生成式头部资产跟着场景灯光走。

中文摘要：人像的重打光与新视角合成在摄影、VR、AR 里都关键，但 3D 感知的人像重打光要同时满足写实、实时与对未见被试的泛化。已有方法要么依赖昂贵的光 stage 采集数据做监督，要么效果欠佳；不少工作基于生成式 NeRF，3D 一致性与实时性都差。作者转向生成式 3D Gaussian，并设计一个基于统一神经辐射传输表示的光照模型，对入射光线性响应：每个高斯除颜色外还带反照率与一个传输向量，取代原来与视角无关的颜色。只用 in-the-wild 图像训练，就在重打光效果上达到当前最优，并把渲染速度提到约 240 FPS（单张 H800），相对既有 3D-aware portrait relighting 方法至少快 12 倍。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

GSHeadRelight: Fast Relightability for 3D Gaussian Head Synthesis

© cc

Abstract.

Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits are essential in applications such as portrait photography, virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR). Despite recent progress, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains challenging due to the demands for photorealistic rendering, real-time performance, and generalization to unseen subjects. Existing works either rely on supervision from limited and expensive light stage captured data or produce suboptimal results. Moreover, many works are based on generative NeRFs, which suffer from poor 3D consistency and low real-time performance. We resort to recent progress on generative 3D Gaussians and design a lighting model based on a unified neural radiance transfer representation, which responds linearly to incident light. Using only in-the-wild images, our method achieves state-of-the-art relighting results and a significantly faster rendering speed (×12) compared to previous 3D-aware portrait relighting research. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/GSHeadRelight/.

Keywords:

3D portrait relighting, 3D Gaussian splitting, radiance transfer ††cc-license: by-nc

1. Introduction

Relighting and novel view synthesis of human portraits have always been two fundamental demands in various applications. In portrait photography, finding the ideal lighting and viewpoint often requires intensive expert knowledge and extensive trial and error. In virtual reality and augmented reality, virtual avatars need to be rendered under different lighting conditions and viewpoints in real-time and high fidelity. These demands drive the rapid development of the emerging field of 3D-aware portrait relighting.

However, 3D-aware portrait relighting remains highly challenging due to its three demands: photorealistic appearance, real-time rendering, and one-shot generalization to unseen subjects. Human heads consist of highly intricate and varied materials that display different scattering and reflectance properties, making them among the most challenging objects to model accurately. The demand for real-time rendering significantly constrains algorithm design and model capabilities, and the requirement for sparse data input (single image or video) in many real-world applications brings the ambiguity between lighting and materials. Solving this under-constrained problem inevitably requires leveraging the powerful visual prior from pre-trained generative models.

It has been proven that Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] can provide such a prior. When incorporated with 3D representations, GANs can even learn 3D geometries from mere image datasets. Among them, generative NeRF [(Chan et al., 2022; Mildenhall et al., 2021)] find the balance between photorealism and 3D consistency. The 3D head priors have enabled 3D-aware manipulation over human portraits such as attribute editing [(Gao et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2025)], style transfer [(Yuan et al., 2024)] and relighting [(Jiang et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024a)]. To resolve the ambiguity between lighting and materials, some works [(Mei et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2024)] employ light stage data as ground truth for supervision. Nevertheless, light-stage captured data are expensive and usually closed source, so they are not accessible to common researchers. For better generalization and scalability, learning from casual image datasets is preferred. [Jiang et al. (2023)] distill albedo from weakly labeled image datasets at the cost of handling only white light. [Deng et al. (2024)] propose an inverse rendering framework that models radiance transfer for the diffuse term and uses a simple BRDF for the specular term. Impressive as these works are, most of them are based on generative NeRF, which is prone to limited rendering speed and 3D inconsistencies because of volume rendering and upsampling. More importantly, these works rely on neural rendering and need network evaluation for each lighting, which further limits the real-time performance of relighting.

We introduce GSHeadRelight, a relightable 3D head generative model with the latest generative 3D Gaussian backbone [(Hyun and Heo, 2024; Kirschstein et al., 2024)]. Inspired by precomputed radiance transfer [(Sloan et al., 2002)], we design a lighting model based on Unified Neural Radiance Transfer. We assign spherical harmonics coefficients for each 3D Gaussian ellipsoid to model the radiance transfer, which handles visibility and global illumination, including self-occlusion and subsurface scattering. By making radiance transfer coefficients a function of view directions, our method can model both diffuse terms and low-frequency reflections. However, without explicit supervision of albedo, the ambiguity between albedo and lighting severely affects relighting quality. Since most in-the-wild images are under white illumination, we make a simple white-light assumption during training to mitigate the ambiguity, which provides plausible albedo decoupling. One desirable feature of radiance transfer is that the outgoing radiance, i.e. irradiance, responds to incident light linearly. Although our model is trained solely on white light, it can generalize well to colored illumination during test time. Moreover, since all components are organized as Gaussian attributes independent of lighting, only one forward inference is needed for head synthesis, and relighting can be performed without further generator evaluations. As a result, our method is extremely efficient and significantly reduces hardware requirements.

To summarize, we present three main contributions:

  • •

    A relightable 3D Gaussian head generative model based on unified radiance transfer that supports global illumination.

  • •

    A regime that distills plausible albedo and light transport functions from in-the-wild images without a heavy light stage setup.

  • •

    Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art 3D-aware relighting results with extreme efficiency. Our model achieves a rendering speed of ~240 FPS on a single NVIDIA H800, with at least 12× speedup over previous methods.

    • 2. Related Work

    In this section, we review relevant work in the field of 3D-aware portrait synthesis. We then examine deep neural face relighting from two perspectives: studio-captured data and casual image datasets.

    3D-aware Portrait Synthesis

    Despite Diffusion Models (DMs) [(Ho et al., 2020)] being proven to have stronger model capabilities than GANs [(Goodfellow et al., 2014)] in synthesizing images [(Rombach et al., 2022)], videos [(Brooks et al., 2024)] and 3D assets [(Zhang et al., 2024d)], GANs excel at 3D-aware portrait synthesis. The sparsity of high-quality 3D head models hinders the training of DMs, whereas 3D-GANs can learn fine geometry from mere image datasets.

    Early 3D-GANs directly render pixels from explicit or implicit 3D representations, such as meshes [(Chen and Zhang, 2019; Henderson et al., 2020; Kanazawa et al., 2018)] and voxels [(Gadelha et al., 2017; Henzler et al., 2019)], or implicit neural radiance fields [(Chan et al., 2021; Schwarz et al., 2020)]. Some works [(Nguyen-Phuoc et al., 2019; Niemeyer and Geiger, 2021; Xue et al., 2022)] append neural rendering on the image side to improve image fidelity and enable high-resolution rendering. Subsequent works [(Gu et al., 2021; Or-El et al., 2022; Chan et al., 2022)] mostly adopt StyleGAN [(Karras, 2019)] as the generator due to its success. Among them, EG3D [(Chan et al., 2022)] proposes a hybrid radiance field representation and applies a super-resolution module to the generated tri-plane features. Despite its high expressiveness, volume rendering is too slow for native high-resolution synthesis, and super-resolution inevitably causes spatial inconsistencies across views.

    Recent works [(Hyun and Heo, 2024; Kirschstein et al., 2024)] utilize 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] as the new explicit representation, allowing for native high-resolution head synthesis in real-time. [Kirschstein et al. (2024)] bind 3D Gaussians to a template mesh and generate UV maps of each Gaussian attribute under the StyleGAN [(Karras, 2019)] backbone. Gaussian ellipsoids are then queried and mapped back onto the template at arbitrary resolution. [Hyun and Heo (2024)] instead explore a hierarchical generative paradigm without a template mesh, where at each layer 3D Gaussians are constrained by anchor points from the previous layer. A new generative architecture is designed to generate multiple-level anchors and Gaussians. Our method is based on the recent progress in generative 3D Gaussian head synthesis. We refer to [(Sun et al., 2024)] for more recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting.

    Deep Neural Face Relighting

    Portrait relighting requires decomposition of appearance, geometry, and lighting. To acquire accurate facial reflectance fields, a line of works resort to meticulously calibrated studio equipment, including the widely adopted light stage [(Debevec et al., 2000)]. Neural networks are incorporated into the light stage processing to enable single image portrait relighting [(Pandey et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Weir et al., 2022; Nestmeyer et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2024; LeGendre et al., 2020)]. Novel view synthesis and animation along with relighting are present with the development of 3D representations such as mesh [(Lombardi et al., 2018; Bi et al., 2021)], volumetric primitive [(Lombardi et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024)], NeRF [(Xu et al., 2023; Sarkar et al., 2023; Rao et al., 2022)] and 3D Gaussian [(Saito et al., 2024; He et al., 2024)]. Inverse rendering is widely used to decouple intrinsics and enable lighting manipulation [(Nestmeyer et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2024; Pandey et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024c)]. Recent development of diffusion models enables more lighting condition interfaces like prompt [(Zhang et al., 2024b)], background [(Ren et al., 2024)], and scribble [(Mei et al., 2023)].

    While the expensive studio-captured data provides ground truth supervision, easily accessible casual image collections offer more diversity and scalability. Deep generative neural networks like GANs are usually adopted to learn the priors of appearance and lighting. Early works explore style transfer [(Abdal et al., 2021; Shih et al., 2014; Shu et al., 2017; Deng et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2024)] to transfer lighting, but fail to maintain identity consistency. The quotient image [(Shashua and Riklin-Raviv, 2001; Peers et al., 2007)] decouples albedo from appearance and is widely used for plausible relighting [(Tewari et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023)]. Inverse rendering is also explored [(Deng et al., 2024)] with self-supervised regulation. Relighting with novel view synthesis from casual images [(Sun et al., 2021; Tewari et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021)] is also present with semantic control over GANs. The incorporation of generative NeRF allows for 3D-aware portrait relighting [(Pan et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2024; Mei et al., 2024; Rao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024a; Ranjan et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2024b)].

    3. Method

    In the following, we first introduce preliminaries including spherical harmonics, precomputed radiance transfer, and 3D Gaussian head synthesis. Then we discuss design choices in generative 3D-GAN relighting. Finally, we introduce the proposed Unified Neural Radiance Transfer and the loss functions.

    3.1. Preliminaries

    Precomputed Radiance Transfer

    Computing global illumination is costly because it requires iterative path tracing due to multi-bounce reflections, refractions, and scattering of light. [Sloan et al. (2002)] propose to precompute radiance transfer functions, which are applied to actual incident lighting at run-time. Assuming distant illumination Lᵢₙ, exit radiance L_out,p from a point p is computed by the rendering equation with light transport:

    (1)L_out,p(v̂)=∫_ΩLᵢₙ(l̂)Vₚ(l̂)fᵣ(v̂,l̂)\max(0,n̂·l̂) dl̂

    where n̂ is the surface normal at p, l̂ and v̂ are global light direction and viewing direction, fᵣ is Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) and Vₚ is the light transport function considering self-occlusion and interreflection.

    To efficiently compute the integral in Equation 1, lighting and transfer functions are represented using nth-order spherical harmonics (SH). For specular surfaces, a transfer matrix Mₚ including the BRDF and cosine terms describes the radiance transfer via

    (2)

    L_out,p=∑ⱼ₌₁^n²MₚⁱʲLᵢₙʲ.

    Specifically for diffuse surfaces, radiance transfer can be represented by a transfer vector Vₚ producing scalar exit radiance L_out,p by

    (3)

    L_out,p=∑ᵢ₌₁^n²VₚⁱLₚⁱ.

    In modern neural rendering, precomputing transfer functions is often impractical because the geometric and material properties are unknown. Previous works [(Saito et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Xing et al., 2024)] choose to parameterize and learn diffuse radiance transfer vectors, while employing alternative representations for specular terms because the transfer matrix is too large. We instead propose to use a unified representation that models both diffuse terms and low-frequency reflections.

    3D Gaussian Head Synthesis

    3D Gaussian Splatting [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] is recently introduced as a point-based 3D representation that assigns to each point 5 attributes: position μ∈ℝ³, scale s∈ℝ³, rotation quaternion q∈ℝ⁴, opacity α∈ℝ and color c∈ℝ³. A Gaussian ellipsoid is formulated as

    (4)

    G(x)=e^-1/2(x-μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x-μ), with~~Σ=RSSᵀRᵀ,

    where x is the world coordinates, and the scaling matrix S and rotation matrix R are derived from the scaling s and quaternion q. The color C of a pixel in image space is computed by blending N overlapping sorted points:

    (5)

    C=∑ᵢ₌₁^Ncᵢαᵢ∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-αⱼ).

    Recent works in 3D Gaussian head synthesis [(Hyun and Heo, 2024; Kirschstein et al., 2024)] allow for native high-resolution head synthesis in real time. [Kirschstein et al. (2024)] bind 3D Gaussians to a template mesh and use StyleGAN2 [(Karras et al., 2020)] to generate UV maps of each Gaussian attribute. [Hyun and Heo (2024)] instead explore a hierarchical generative paradigm, where the 3D Gaussians at each layer are constrained by anchor points from the previous layer.

    3.2. Unified Neural Radiance Transfer

    Radiance transfer was primarily used to describe the diffuse component of lighting. We show that by incorporating view directions into the generative framework, a Unified Neural Radiance Transfer representation is capable of describing both diffuse and low-frequency specular terms. Revisiting Equation 1, by absorbing the light transport, BRDF, and cosine term into a unified radiance transfer function Tₚ in SH basis, the rendering equation becomes

    (6)

    L_out,p(v̂)=∫_ΩLᵢₙ(l̂)Tₚ(v̂,l̂) dl̂≈∑ᵢ₌₁^n²lᵢₙⁱtⁱₚ(v̂),

    where lⁱᵢₙ and tⁱₚ(v̂) are the nth-order expansion coefficients. Specifically, we disentangle the albedo ρₚ from tⁱₚ(v̂) for disentangling appearance from lighting. With minor notation abuse, the view-dependent exit radiance is formulated as

    (7)

    L_out,p(v̂)=ρₚ∑ᵢ₌₁^n²lᵢₙⁱtⁱₚ(v̂).

    In this way, both diffuse and specular terms can be handled in a unified manner by making radiance transfer coefficients a function of view direction.

    Based on 3D Gaussian GAN framework, we additionally assign each Gaussian point p an albedo ρₚ∈[0,1]³ and a transfer vector tₚ∈ℝ^3×n² to replace the original view-independent color. Specifically, as shown in Figure 2, the generator gives each Gaussian point p an embedding xₚ. The transfer vector tₚ is obtained by concatenating the Gaussian embedding with encoded view direction and sending it to a transfer vector decoder Ψₜ,

    (8)

    tₚ(v̂)=Ψₜ(x^′ₚ||vₚ),

    where x^′ₚ is a shortened embedding transformed linearly from the Gaussian embedding xₚ. It can be stored to perform real-time rendering with standard 3D Gaussian splatting after generation.

    Without explicit supervision of albedo, the ambiguity between albedo and transfer vectors is unavoidable, as demonstrated in Section 4.5. Observing that the illumination in most real images is approximately white light, we propose to train the model under white light conditions. The light and transfer vectors are then reduced to single channel, i.e. l,t∈ℝ^1×n². In this way, the contribution of the transfer vector to the color distribution is discarded, and thus the ambiguity is resolved. We find in the experiment that adversarial training will average out the impact of light color residuals on the albedo. Moreover, due to the linearity of our unified radiance transfer functions, our model can render colored lighting at test-time by channel-wise applying Equation 7.

    4. Experiments

    4.1. Implementation Details

    Our method is based on GSGAN [(Hyun and Heo, 2024)], which follows the same data preparation pipeline as EG3D [(Chan et al., 2022)]. The lighting labels, represented as monochromatic 3rd-order spherical harmonics, are extracted using DPR [(Zhou et al., 2019)], following the approach of [Jiang et al. (2023)]. We use MODNet [(Ke et al., 2022)] to extract foreground components to alleviate background leakage. The transfer vector decoder Ψₜ is implemented as a lightweight MLP with one hidden layer of 64 units. We train the models on the FFHQ dataset [(Karras, 2019)] from scratch for 15M images with four NVIDIA H800 GPUs.

    4.2. Quantitative Comparisons

    Baselines.

    We compare our method with previous publicly accessible works for novel view portrait relighting: ShadeGAN [(Pan et al., 2021)], Volux-GAN [(Tan et al., 2022)], NeRFFaceLighting [(Jiang et al., 2023)]. We also include LumiGAN [(Deng et al., 2024)], which is not accessible, and report results from the original paper if presented.

    Generative quality and rendering speed.

    We follow  [Chan et al. (2022)] and compute Frechnet Inception Distance (FID) [(Heusel et al., 2017)] and Kernel Inception Distance (KID) [(Bińkowski et al., 2018)] between 50k generated images and all training images. From Table 1, we see that EG3D-based methods have a higher FID due to the 2D super-resolution module, which upsamples low-resolution volume rendering results at the cost of losing 3D consistency. Our method achieves similar or even better generative quality than our backbone GSGAN [(Hyun and Heo, 2024)]. Moreover, our method maintains a high rendering speed, surpassing other relighting works by at least 12×. This is attributed to the simple yet effective architecture of our unified radiance transfer relighting framework.

    Lighting quality.

    Following [Jiang et al. (2023)], we measure the relighting performance with an off-the-shelf estimator [(Feng et al., 2021)] using two metrics: the Lighting Error computes the distance between real lighting and estimated lighting in fake images; the Lighting Stability computes the standard deviation of estimated lighting in 100 fake images generated using the same lighting conditions. The metrics are averaged for 1000 samples. Since these metrics can only be applied to methods with lighting conditions estimated from real images, Volux-GAN and LumiGAN are excluded. Instead, StyleFlow [(Abdal et al., 2021)], DisCoFaceGAN [(Deng et al., 2020)], and GAN-Control [(Shoshan et al., 2021)] are included as 2D generative relighting methods for comparison. Table 2 shows that our method is comparable in lighting quality with state-of-the-art 3D-portrait relighting methods. The 2D relighting method DisCoFaceGAN has higher lighting scores at the cost of low generative quality. Moreover, our method can perform RGB relighting, thanks to its linear radiance transfer framework. This is not achievable by other methods based on implicit neural relighting.

    Spatial consistency.

    Following [Hyun and Heo (2024)], we use a surface estimation model NeUS2 [(Wang et al., 2023)] to validate the spatial consistency of 3D-aware relighting models. Specifically, we randomly generate 30 views of a lit subject, fit them to surface estimation, and compute the reconstruction error using standard PSNR and SSIM metrics. We generate 30 subjects and record the average metrics. We also include the identity similarity metric proposed by [Tan et al. (2022)], and report the mean score across 30 views. From Table 3 we see that although EG3D-based methods do not preserve exact 3D consistency due to 2D super resolution, they do not exhibit disadvantages in terms of reconstruction error. This is possibly because EG3D and NeUS2 share a similar implicit representation and volume rendering process. However, in terms of identity similarity, our method achieves the highest score, demonstrating better 3D consistency than other methods. In general, EG3D-based methods suffer from texture flickering when continuously changing viewpoint due to 2D super resolution, while our method renders an explicit 3D Gaussian model and maintains view consistency. We further refer to the video demo for better visual comparison.

    4.3. Qualitative Comparison

    The Lighting Error and Lighting Stability metrics used in Section 4.2 can only evaluate the lighting similarity by an off-the-shelf lighting estimator. To further evaluate lighting quality under colored light conditions and compare the lighting realism under human eyes, we compare our method to previous works in real environment map lighting conditions. We include NeLF [(Sun et al., 2021)], which is trained using a synthetic lightstage dataset and needs multi-view inputs. Figure 3 shows that our method achieves better relighting quality than previous methods. Volux-GAN [(Tan et al., 2022)] uses 2D convolution layers to add shadows and details, leading to view inconsistencies. NeRFFaceLighting [(Jiang et al., 2023)] can only handle white-light conditions and performs poorly on environment map lighting. LumiGAN [(Deng et al., 2024)] relies on inverse rendering, and incorrect geometry decoupling leads to lighting artifacts, like the unnatural lit parts on the cheek and beside the wings of the nose. NeLF shows poor visual quality and loses facial details like wrinkles and pores. In contrast, our method performs well both in visual quality and relighting quality.

    4.4. Visual Relighting Results

    Our model presents overall good photorealism under different light intensity and directions, as shown in Fig 4. Colored illumination can also be handled correctly, as shown in Figure 5. Given an environment map, image-based lighting requires first converting it to spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. Specifically, we apply Gaussian blurring before SH sampling with a radius of 0.1× image width to remove high-frequency details. Image-based lighting results are shown in Figure 6. Thanks to the unified radiance transfer framework, our approach responds linearly to incident light and innately satisfies the light transport consistency. Our method maintains 3D consistency in head poses while delivering plausible albedo and relighting results under various environment maps.

    Real portrait relighting

    With the help of the GAN inversion technique, our model can relight real-face images. The basic idea is to project a real-face image into the latent space and manipulate lighting during reconstruction. We implement the inversion similar to Pivotal Tuning [(Roich et al., 2022)] and compare the result with NeRFFaceLighting in Figure 7. Our method produces better photorealism and identity consistency. We also quantitatively evaluate identity consistency using cosine similarity of VGGFace [(Parkhi et al., 2015)] embedding on a subset of the Goliath dataset [(Martinez et al., 2024)], which has 4 sets of light-stage head capture. Our method (0.443) significantly outperforms NeRFFaceLighting (0.298).

    4.5. Other Design Choices and Ablation Study

    Multiple design choices exist for implementing unified radiance transfer in the 3D-GAN framework. First, the model could be trained using RGB lighting labels instead of monochromatic ones. Second, diffuse and specular reflectance could be modeled separately. We discuss these designs and validate their feasibility. We then conduct an ablation study on our proposed unified radiance transfer.

    No white-light assumption

    Some works [(Fei et al., 2023; Phongthawee et al., 2024)] allow extracting estimated RGB lighting conditions from a single image, which makes training on colored illumination possible. We follow the same setting and modify the parameterization of lighting labels and transfer functions from 1 channel to 3 channels. We use [(Fei et al., 2023)] to extract HDRI environment maps and turn them into 3rd-order RGB spherical harmonics coefficients. As shown in Figure 8, without explicit supervision of intrinsics, training under RGB lighting conditions leads to faded albedo. In this case, the contribution to appearance is entirely provided by lighting, and relighting becomes a style transfer process. The model overfits on certain lighting conditions, does not learn a physically consistent lighting model, and fails under unseen lighting.

    diffuse and specular decomposition

    Inverse rendering is widely adopted in portrait relighting [(Saito et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024)] to infer physical properties such as geometry, materials, and lighting. Diffuse and specular terms are often decoupled using different lighting models. We validate this setting in the 3D-GAN framework. We decouple the transfer vector t(v̂) into view-independent diffuse transfer vector t_diffuse and view-dependent specular transfer vector t_specular(v̂). However, without explicit supervision, albedo, diffuse, and specular terms are disentangled incorrectly and exhibit significant inconsistencies, as shown in Figure 9.

    Ablation study

    We validate the effectiveness of unified radiance transfer in Table 4. Without radiance transfer, we assume the color is directly predicted by a decoder that takes in lighting conditions. All models are trained for 3M images before evaluation. We find that radiance transfer provides strong lighting manipulation ability, demonstrated by the significant increase in Lighting Error in the case without radiance transfer. At the same time, without the view condition, the lighting accuracy also drops since the vanilla vector-based radiance transfer cannot model specular effects. In this case, the albedo is often observed with specular residuals. In contrast, our complete unified radiance transfer representation achieves the best lighting manipulation accuracy and yields smooth albedos. From Figure 10, view conditioning reduces most highlight residuals in albedo and yields more satisfactory relighting results.

    5. Conclusion, Limitation, and Future Work

    We present GSHeadRelight, a real-time relightable 3D-aware portrait synthesis framework based on a unified radiance transfer representation, addressing the challenging problem of colored lighting manipulation in the 3D-GAN setting. Our model learns the light transport functions under a white-light assumption from casual image datasets, without requiring expensive and inaccessible light-stage captured data. Since our model responds linearly to incident lighting and innately retains light transport consistency, it generalizes well to colored illumination and produces overall high-quality relighting results. The simple model design discards network evaluation for each light condition, adding real-time relightability for 3D head synthesis. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art 3D-aware relighting quality, superior real-time performance, and better spatial consistency compared with previous relighting methods.

    One limitation of our method is that it mainly models low-frequency and diffuse lighting effects due to the nature of radiance transfer in the spherical harmonics basis. Although the view-conditioned radiance transfer decoder models low-frequency view-dependent effects to some extent, our method is still not expressive enough for high-frequency reflections. In some cases, the model incorrectly learns the specular highlight in the albedo. As shown in Figure 11 (A), highlight on the right cheek remains in the albedo and leads to artifacts. In addition, relighting under illumination from below the face region may seem implausible, as shown in Figure 11 (C). This is because such illumination is scarce in in-the-wild images.

    For future work, it is interesting to model high-frequency and largely view-dependent effects on top of this explicit linear lighting model to support more complex lighting conditions other than spherical harmonics. Exploring the adaptation of our method to dynamic human head scenarios is also worth further investigation.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62322210), Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission (No. Z231100005923031), Innovation Funding of ICT, CAS (No. E461020), the Royal Society (IEC \233596), Kuaishou Technology and CCF-Kuaishou Large Model Explorer Fund. We would like to thank Chunshuo Qiu for assisting with the demo video production and Zhongming Chen for assisting with figure making. We would also like to acknowledge the Nanjing Institute of InforSuperBahn OneAiNexus for providing the training and evaluation platform.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 风格化别把光照烘进颜色：RxGS 只改反照率场，留下的是能重新打光的高斯场景 ｜ RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization via BRDF Decomposition
item.description:
一句话：常规风格化优化的是「材质+环境光+法线+视角」揉在一起的 RGB，换光照就崩；RxGS 只动逆渲染出来的漫反射反照率。

要点：

  • 基于参考图的 3D 风格化通常优化 RGB 外观表示，单点颜色同时编码了材质反射、环境光与着色，风格化后光照被烘死
  • RxGS 建立在 BRDF 感知的 3D 高斯表示上，只优化逆渲染恢复的漫反射反照率场，粗糙度、法线、光照保持可重打
  • 16 对场景上，直接反照率监督的损失下降 32.2%，随机光照监督下降 20.1%
  • 风格化结果可在不同光照条件下重新渲染，而不是只在一套光下成立

为什么值得看：资产流水线里「风格化一次、后面还要按关卡灯光重打」是常态；把风格化作用域限制在反照率，等于让风格变成可复用的材质层而不是一张烘死的贴图。

中文摘要：基于参考图的 3D 场景风格化要把参考图外观迁移到重建场景上并保持几何。近期方法通过优化 NeRF 或 3DGS 的外观表示完成迁移，但优化的都是 RGB 表示：单个点的颜色同时混入了材质反射率、环境光照、着色和视角的影响。一旦风格化改动这份混合颜色，风格化时的光照就被烘进存储的外观里，场景无法在别的光照下渲染。作者提出 RxGS：基于 BRDF 感知的 3D Gaussian 表示，不修改每点 RGB，而只优化逆渲染得到的漫反射反照率场，粗糙度等其他材质参数保持不变。这样风格化只作用在材质层，光照留在可替换的一侧，风格化后的场景能在新光照下重新渲染。在多个场景对上，该约束使损失相对直接反照率监督下降 32.2%、相对随机光照监督下降 20.1%。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization via BRDF Decomposition

Abstract

Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of a reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while preserving scene geometry. Recent methods perform this transfer by optimizing the appearance representation of neural scene models including Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). These methods optimize an RGB appearance representation, in which a single per-point colour combines the effects of material reflectance, environment illumination, together with the shading it produces, and the viewing direction. When stylization modifies this combined colour, the illumination effects present during stylization are baked into the stored appearance, so the stylized scene cannot be rendered under different illumination. To address this limitation, we present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware 3D Gaussian representation. Rather than modifying a per-point RGB colour, RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field recovered by inverse rendering, while leaving roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and the estimated environment lighting unchanged. As a result, the stylized scene keeps all the components a physically-based renderer needs other than the edited albedo, and can therefore still be relit. RxGS optimizes the albedo field using a nearest-neighbour feature matching loss together with a spatial smoothness prior over Gaussian centres. We evaluate the method using a Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) based on optical-flow warping error. RxGS achieves the lowest GCC on all evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scenes and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while additionally supporting relightable stylization, which existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods do not provide.

1 Introduction

Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of an artistic reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while keeping the rendered result geometrically consistent across viewpoints. Recent neural rendering methods, in particular Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. (2023)], produce high-quality novel views and have prompted a growing body of 3D stylization work. These methods stylize a scene by modifying the RGB appearance representation that the neural scene model has learned. In many applications a scene must be stylized once and then rendered under several different lighting conditions without repeating the stylization. This requires the stylized scene to keep a representation that can be relit after the appearance transfer, a requirement the RGB representation does not meet, as the next paragraph argues.

An RGB appearance representation stores, at each point, one colour that already combines material reflectance, the environment illumination together with the shading it produces, and view-dependent effects. Because these factors are not stored separately, a stylization process that edits this colour necessarily edits the illumination contribution together with the intrinsic material. The illumination present during stylization is thereby written into the stored appearance: when the scene is later rendered under a different illumination, the stored colour does not change, so no new shading or shadows appear. As illustrated in Fig. 1, stylization applied to an RGB appearance representation fixes the artistic appearance and the illumination contribution together, which prevents the result from responding to novel lighting.

To remove this restriction we build on recent inverse rendering methods for 3D Gaussian representations. Such methods [Liang et al. (2024)] recover separate scene attributes, namely diffuse albedo, material properties, and environment illumination, and so support relightable rendering and material editing. These separated representations have not previously been used for reference-based 3D scene stylization.

We present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware Gaussian scene representation. Given a reconstructed scene, RxGS first applies inverse rendering decomposition to recover, per Gaussian, the diffuse albedo aᵢ, the roughness rᵢ, the metallicity mᵢ, the surface normal nᵢ, and one global environment lighting L. Stylization then optimizes only the field of diffuse albedos {aᵢ} and leaves {rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ} and L and all geometry unchanged. Relightability follows from this bookkeeping rather than from any claim that the albedo alone fixes the rendered colour. A physically-based renderer consumes the geometry, the per-Gaussian material attributes {aᵢ,rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ}, and the environment lighting L. RxGS changes only the albedo coefficients {aᵢ^⋆} and holds every other input fixed, so all non-albedo inputs the renderer needs remain intact, and the same renderer can be re-run under any chosen L to produce a relit image of the stylized scene. To optimize the albedo field, RxGS uses a nearest-neighbour feature matching (NNFM) loss in the VGG feature space together with a spatial smoothness term over Gaussian centres.

We evaluate RxGS on synthetic and real-captured scenes, measuring cross-view geometric consistency with the Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) defined in Section 4. RxGS attains the lowest GCC on every evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scene and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while keeping a relightable scene representation after stylization. Our contributions are the following.

  • •

    We present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework based on a BRDF-aware Gaussian scene representation.

  • •

    We formulate stylization as optimization of the diffuse albedo field alone in a logit parameterization, regularized by a smoothness term on a k-nearest-neighbour graph over Gaussian centres, so that artistic appearance transfer leaves the material and illumination parameters required for relighting unchanged.

  • •

    We evaluate on synthetic and real-captured datasets, reporting cross-view geometric consistency (GCC) that is competitive with prior stylization methods together with relightable stylization that prior methods do not provide.

    • 2 Related work

    2.1 3D Scene Representation and Rendering

    A 3D scene representation encodes scene geometry and appearance in a compact, learnable form that supports downstream tasks such as novel view synthesis, scene editing, relighting, and scene understanding. NeRF [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] introduced an implicit neural representation that parameterizes volumetric density and radiance with multilayer perceptrons, achieving novel view synthesis from multi-view observations. NeRF requires dense volumetric sampling during both training and rendering, which is computationally expensive. To reduce this cost, later work introduced voxel grids, tensor factorizations, and multi-resolution encodings, including DVGO [Sun et al. (2022)], Plenoxels [Fridovich-Keil et al. (2022)], TensoRF [Chen et al. (2022a)], and Instant-NGP [Müller et al. (2022)]. As scene editing and stylization tasks developed, several methods adopted surface-based representations that give a more explicit geometric correspondence than a purely volumetric field, including VolSDF [Yariv et al. (2021)], NeuS [Wang et al. (2021)], NeuMesh [Yang et al. (2022)], and NeRF2Mesh [Tang et al. (2023)].

    Among explicit representations, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. (2023)] represents a scene with a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives. Unlike volumetric methods that rely on dense ray sampling, 3DGS renders through differentiable Gaussian rasterization, which is fast enough for real-time rendering while still reconstructing scene geometry and appearance. Following 3DGS, many extensions adapt the representation to downstream tasks, including scene editing, relighting, and inverse rendering. The inverse rendering line, which recovers separate material and lighting attributes for each Gaussian, is the one RxGS builds upon, and we review it next.

    2.2 Inverse Rendering with 3D Gaussian Representations

    Inverse rendering recovers physically meaningful scene properties, namely geometry, material attributes, and illumination, from image observations. Several methods built this decomposition into neural rendering frameworks. NeRFactor [Zhang et al. (2021b)] factorizes scene appearance into geometry, reflectance, visibility, and illumination for relightable rendering. PhySG [Zhang et al. (2021a)] uses spherical Gaussian representations of the BRDF and of the illumination to put physically-based shading into neural rendering. TensorIR [Jin et al. (2023)] introduces a tensor-based inverse rendering framework that makes scene decomposition and relightable rendering more efficient.

    After 3DGS, inverse rendering was extended to Gaussian representations by attaching material, normal, and illumination attributes to the Gaussian primitives. GaussianShader [Jiang et al. (2024)] adds a shading function to Gaussian rendering and estimates geometry-aware normals to improve reflective surfaces. Relightable 3D Gaussian [Gao et al. (2024)] attaches BRDF attributes and incident lighting to each Gaussian and renders through differentiable physically-based rendering. GS-IR [Liang et al. (2024)] formulates inverse rendering on a BRDF-aware Gaussian representation by jointly estimating scene geometry, material properties, and environment illumination from multi-view observations; RxGS takes the decomposition produced by GS-IR as its input.

    2.3 3D Scene Stylization

    Neural style transfer was first developed for images [Gatys et al. (2016); Huang and Belongie (2017); Doyle and Mould (2019); Xu et al. (2024)], where the goal is to synthesize an image that keeps the scene content of one input while matching the appearance of a reference style image. As 3D scene representations matured, stylization was extended from 2D images to 3D scenes. Before neural scene representations, 3D stylization operated on explicit representations such as meshes and point clouds [Höllein et al. (2022); Cao et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2018)], manipulating surface textures, geometric attributes, or rendered appearance directly.

    Neural scene representations let stylization act on a learned appearance representation, so that style is propagated consistently across viewpoints. Early NeRF-based methods modify the appearance field of a reconstructed scene while keeping the geometry fixed [Chiang et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2024); Nguyen-Phuoc et al. (2022); Goel et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2022)]. ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)] optimizes the appearance field of a NeRF with a neural style transfer objective, giving multi-view consistent stylization, and ARF-plus [Li et al. (2025)] improves stylization quality and training stability through stronger appearance representations and optimization strategies. Ref-NPR [Zhang et al. (2023)] improves controllability by transferring appearance from reference images through geometry-aware feature correspondence, which enables localized stylization. LAE-NeRF [Radl et al. (2024)] lets a user mark target regions in a neural scene representation and propagates the edit through neighbouring volumetric regions. SNeRF [Nguyen-Phuoc et al. (2022)] alternates between image-space stylization and scene reconstruction, transferring artistic appearance into the neural scene representation across iterations.

    Because 3DGS associates appearance attributes directly with individual primitives, it makes appearance manipulation explicit. StylizedGS [Zhang et al. (2025)] supports region-specific style transfer through semantic masks. ReGS [Mei et al. (2024)] adapts 3DGS to reference-based stylization with a texture-guided mechanism that adjusts local Gaussian arrangements to reproduce texture detail from the reference. StyleSplat segments individual objects in a Gaussian scene and fine-tunes the selected Gaussians for object-level stylization. Further methods match segmented regions across views before transfer to keep the style consistent over the whole scene [Liu et al. (2025)], geometry-aware texture transfer [Liu et al. (2026b)], diffusion-based stylization and distillation [Yang et al. (2026)], and feed-forward or optimization-free stylization of Gaussian splats [Liu et al. (2026a); Sablon and Hart (2026)]. All of these methods, whether NeRF-based or Gaussian-based, edit a per-point RGB appearance, and so produce a stylized scene that stores one fixed colour per point and cannot be relit.

    A smaller line of work stylizes a decomposed appearance representation rather than RGB colour. TANGO [Chen et al. (2022b)] performs text-driven stylization by editing BRDF attributes on a relightable mesh, which allows appearance editing under varying illumination. RxGS differs from this mesh-based, text-driven setting: it performs reference-image stylization directly on a BRDF-aware Gaussian representation, editing only the diffuse albedo field of the Gaussians and keeping the rest of the decomposition fixed.

    3 Method

    The task is to modify the appearance of a 3D scene, reconstructed from posed multi-view images {Iₖ,Pₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, so that it matches the style of a reference image J, while keeping both the scene geometry and the physical rendering components that are needed to render the scene under novel illumination.

    3.1 Gaussian Representation

    3.1.1 3D Gaussian Splatting

    3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. (2023)] represents a scene with a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives placed in 3D space. Each Gaussian is parameterized by a centre xᵢ∈ℝ³, a scaling vector sᵢ∈ℝ³, a rotation quaternion qᵢ∈ℝ⁴, an opacity αᵢ∈[0,1], and appearance-related attributes. The scaling vector and rotation quaternion together define the Gaussian covariance. The trainable parameters of the i-th Gaussian are

    Gᵢ={xᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ,φᵢ},(1)

    where φᵢ denotes the appearance representation of the Gaussian.

    Because the Gaussian primitives are defined in 3D space, the appearance attributes of a Gaussian are shared by every viewpoint that observes the same spatial region. This gives a fixed correspondence between scene geometry and appearance during rendering, so a change to a Gaussian’s appearance attributes affects all views of that region in the same way, which is useful for keeping a stylization consistent across viewpoints.

    3.1.2 BRDF-aware Gaussian Representation

    GS-IR [Liang et al. (2024)] refines the 3DGS appearance attribute φᵢ into a BRDF-aware decomposition consisting of diffuse albedo, roughness, metallicity, and surface normal, while jointly estimating a global environment lighting L, represented as an environment map, that is, a function on the unit sphere of incident directions giving the incoming radiance from each direction. Specifically,

    φᵢ={aᵢ,rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ},(2)

    where aᵢ∈[0,1]³ is the diffuse albedo of the i-th Gaussian, rᵢ∈[0,1] is the roughness, mᵢ∈[0,1] is the metallicity, and nᵢ∈ℝ³ is the surface normal.

    In an RGB appearance representation a single per-point colour already combines material reflectance, the illumination together with the shading it produces, and view-dependent effects. The decomposition above instead stores the albedo aᵢ as a separate per-Gaussian coefficient, alongside rᵢ, mᵢ, nᵢ, and the global lighting L. Although the diffuse albedo is represented separately, it still influences the colour of specular reflections under the metallic-roughness BRDF when metallicity is non-zero. Therefore, modifying the albedo changes both the diffuse appearance and the tint of specular highlights. However, the remaining BRDF attributes, including roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and environment lighting, remain unchanged throughout stylization. Consequently, the scene retains the complete set of rendering parameters required for relightable rendering.

    3.2 RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization

    RxGS takes as input posed multi-view images {Iₖ,Pₖ}ₖ₌₁^K and a reference style image J. Let the BRDF-aware scene representation be

    S={G,L},

    where G={Gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N is the set of N Gaussian primitives and L is the estimated environment lighting. RxGS optimizes the diffuse albedo field while keeping all remaining BRDF attributes, geometry, and environment lighting fixed.

    We separate the parameters of each Gaussian into geometry-related and appearance-related parts,

    Gᵢ={Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ,φᵢ},(3)

    where Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ={xᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ}. The stylized appearance decomposition is

    φᵢ^⋆={aᵢ^⋆,rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ},(4)

    where only the diffuse albedo aᵢ^⋆ is optimized; the geometry attributes Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ, the roughness rᵢ, the metallicity mᵢ, the surface normal nᵢ, and the environment lighting L are all held fixed. Fig. 2 gives an overview.

    Existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods perform style transfer on rendered RGB images. Given a rendered image I, the stylized result is

    Ĩ=h^J(I),(5)

    where h^J(·) is a style transfer operator conditioned on the reference style image J. Because the rendered RGB image already combines material reflectance, shading, illumination, and view-dependent effects at each pixel, h^J modifies all of these together. The illumination present in I is thereby encoded in Ĩ. When the scene is later rendered under a different illumination, the stored stylized colour does not change, so the result shows no new illumination-dependent variation.

    RxGS instead modifies only the diffuse albedo field {aᵢ^⋆} and leaves {rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ} and L unchanged. Since only the albedo coefficient is changed and rᵢ, mᵢ, nᵢ, L, and the geometry are held fixed, every rendering input required by the physically-based renderer other than the albedo is intact. The same renderer can therefore be run again under any chosen L, and it produces illumination-dependent variation when relit.

    3.2.1 Albedo Parameterization

    Because only the diffuse albedo is optimized, the optimization must keep its value in the valid reflectance range [0,1]³. Optimizing aᵢ^⋆ directly could leave this range. RxGS therefore parameterizes the stylized albedo aᵢ^⋆∈[0,1]³ through an unconstrained latent variable zᵢ∈ℝ³ in logit space. Let a_i,orig denote the original albedo of Gaussian Gᵢ from the BRDF-aware decomposition. The component-wise inverse sigmoid σ⁻¹ diverges at 0 and 1, so before applying it we clamp each channel of a_i,orig to [ε,1-ε] with ε=10⁻⁶. We initialize

    z_i,0=σ⁻¹ (clamp(a_i,orig)),(6)

    and recover the stylized albedo as

    aᵢ^⋆=σ(zᵢ),(7)

    where σ is the component-wise sigmoid function and σ⁻¹ its inverse. With this parameterization aᵢ^⋆ stays in [0,1]³ for every value of zᵢ, and at initialization aᵢ^⋆ equals the clamped recovered albedo.

    3.2.2 Rendering Strategy

    The style supervision is computed on images rendered from the stylized scene. Let

    G^⋆={Gᵢ^⋆}ᵢ₌₁^N, Gᵢ^⋆={Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ,φᵢ^⋆},

    denote the stylized Gaussian scene. The direct strategy renders the stylized albedo field without illumination,

    Îₖ=Rₐ(G^⋆,Pₖ),(8)

    where Rₐ(·) is albedo rendering, which composites the per-Gaussian albedo aᵢ^⋆ along each ray without applying any shading. Style supervision is then applied directly in the albedo domain.

    We additionally consider a randomized-illumination strategy. Here, at optimization step t, a lighting L⁽ᵗ⁾ is randomly sampled and the stylized scene is rendered under it with a Lambertian, that is diffuse-only, shading model,

    Îₖ=R(G^⋆,Pₖ,L⁽ᵗ⁾),(9)

    where R(·) is a renderer that applies the sampled lighting. Section 4.4 compares the two strategies.

    3.2.3 Style Loss

    Following ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)], we use the nearest-neighbour feature matching (NNFM) loss as the style objective. Given a rendered image Îₖ and the reference style image J, the style loss is L_nnfm(Îₖ,J). It extracts feature maps from a pre-trained VGG-16 network for both images, and for each feature vector of Îₖ it finds the most similar feature vector of J by cosine similarity, then penalizes the cosine distance to that match. Following ARF, the features are taken from the conv3 block of the VGG-16 network.

    To control the trade-off between content preservation and stylization strength, RxGS optionally incorporates a content loss. The stylization objective is

    L_style=L_nnfm+λ_cL_content,(10)

    where λ_c weights the content term. Unless stated otherwise we set λ_c=0, so stylization is driven by the NNFM objective alone.

    3.2.4 Spatial Smoothness Prior on the Gaussian Neighbourhood Graph

    To make the stylized albedo vary smoothly over the scene, we add a smoothness term on the optimized albedo field. The albedo is stored on the Gaussian primitives rather than on a regular image grid, so the smoothness prior is defined on a k-nearest-neighbour graph built from the Gaussian centres. For a Gaussian Gᵢ, its neighbourhood ℕₖ(i) is the set of the k Gaussians whose centres have the smallest Euclidean distance to xᵢ. The spatial gradient of the stylized albedo field at Gᵢ is the average, over the neighbourhood, of the albedo difference weighted by the inverse Euclidean distance between Gaussian centres,

    ∇ₛₚₐₜᵢₐₗaᵢ^⋆=(1)/(\lvertℕₖ(i)\rvert)∑_j∈ℕₖ(i)(aᵢ^⋆-aⱼ^⋆)/(\lVertxᵢ-xⱼ\rVert₂+ε),(11)

    where ε=10⁻⁶ avoids division by zero and k=16 in all experiments. The smoothness loss sums the L₁ norm of this gradient over all Gaussians,

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ=∑ᵢ\lVert∇ₛₚₐₜᵢₐₗaᵢ^⋆\rVert₁.(12)

    The final objective combines the style and smoothness terms,

    L=L_style+λₛLₛₘₒₒₜₕ,(13)

    where λₛ=10⁻³.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate RxGS from two angles: cross-view geometric consistency and relightable stylization. We first compare RxGS with existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods using a geometric consistency metric, which measures how well scene structure is preserved across viewpoints after stylization. Because the existing methods do not support relighting, we then evaluate the relightable stylization of RxGS by rendering stylized scenes under different illumination conditions and examining how the appearance responds.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    We use NeRF-Synthetic [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] and NeRF-LLFF [Mildenhall et al. (2019)] for the geometric consistency comparison, and add TensorIR [Jin et al. (2023)] and Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al. (2022)] for the relightable stylization experiments. NeRF-Synthetic [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] is a synthetic multi-view dataset of eight object-centric scenes, each with 100 training images and 200 test images rendered at 800×800, with camera poses and foreground masks. NeRF-LLFF [Mildenhall et al. (2019)] is a real-world forward-facing multi-view dataset captured by handheld cameras with calibrated poses; it contains more complex geometry, occlusions, and appearance variation than NeRF-Synthetic, and we downsample the input images by a factor of four, following prior work [Zhang et al. (2023); Fridovich-Keil et al. (2022); Tang et al. (2023)]. TensorIR [Jin et al. (2023)] is a multi-view dataset for inverse rendering and relighting, with diverse materials and illumination and with ground-truth geometry, material, and lighting; we use its Lego and Hotdog scenes for relightable stylization. Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al. (2022)] is a real-world multi-view dataset of unbounded indoor and outdoor scenes captured over 360-degree viewpoints, with larger extents and more complex structure than NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF; we use its Garden, Kitchen, and Bicycle scenes.

    Implementation Details.

    We take the BRDF-aware Gaussian representation reconstructed by GS-IR [Liang et al. (2024)] as the input to RxGS. Stylization optimizes the diffuse albedo while keeping the estimated geometry, roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and environment lighting fixed. Following ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)], we use the NNFM loss with a pre-trained VGG-16 network and take features from the conv3 block. Each scene is optimized for 1000 iterations.

    Comparison Methods.

    We compare RxGS with ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)], Ref-NPR [Zhang et al. (2023)], and StylizedGS [Zhang et al. (2025)]. Ref-NPR requires a reference image rather than a style image, so we generate its reference images with the AdaIN style transfer model [Huang and Belongie (2017)] from the same style images the other methods use. StylizedGS is included only on the LLFF scenes, because the original paper does not report NeRF-Synthetic results.

    Evaluation Protocol.

    To reduce bias toward a particular artistic appearance, we evaluate each scene with three different reference styles, and for the geometric consistency comparison we average the reported results over the three styles. For relighting, NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF scenes are rendered under several illumination conditions by rotating the estimated environment map while keeping all stylization parameters fixed. We additionally evaluate relightable stylization on TensorIR and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes to examine the behaviour of stylized scenes under varying illumination across different scene types.

    Metric.

    To measure cross-view geometric consistency we use the Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC), a per-pixel optical-flow warping error used in earlier video and 3D stylization work [Ruder et al. (2018); Zhang et al. (2023)]. Given two stylized renderings Îₖ and Îₖ₋₁ from nearby viewpoints, we estimate the optical flow from Îₖ₋₁ to Îₖ with the pre-trained RAFT model [Teed and Deng (2020)], warp Îₖ₋₁ to the viewpoint of Îₖ using this flow, and compute the mean per-pixel error between Îₖ and the warped frame over the pixels that the warp marks as visible. Averaging this error over consecutive frame pairs of a scene gives its GCC; a lower GCC indicates higher cross-view geometric consistency.

    4.2 Cross-view Geometry Consistency

    4.2.1 Quantitative Comparison

    Using the GCC metric above, we evaluate the cross-view geometric consistency of the scenes stylized by RxGS and compare with ARF, Ref-NPR, and StylizedGS. Table 1 and Table 2 report the GCC values on NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF.

    On NeRF-Synthetic, RxGS attains the lowest GCC in every scene. The margin over ARF and Ref-NPR is largest on Lego, Mic, Ficus, and Ship. On LLFF, RxGS has a lower GCC than ARF and is comparable with Ref-NPR and StylizedGS on most scenes. Despite the greater complexity of the real-captured scenes, RxGS stays on par with these methods while also keeping a relightable scene representation, which they do not.

    4.2.2 Qualitative Comparison

    Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 show qualitative stylization results on NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF. On both datasets, RxGS transfers the colour distribution and texture pattern of the reference style image while keeping the scene structure; these results hold on synthetic scenes (Fig. 4) and on real-captured scenes (Fig. 3) alike. The RxGS results are rendered from the optimized albedo field without illumination, which lets the transferred appearance be examined independently of scene lighting. Relightable renderings under varying illumination follow in the next section.

    4.3 Relightable Stylized Rendering

    Fig. 5 shows relighting results on stylized LLFF scenes under different illumination. As the illumination changes, the rendered appearance shows the corresponding shading while keeping the stylized texture and colour distribution. In the Flower scene, rotating the dominant light source moves the shadows across the petals: under the 90-degree rotated lighting, shadows appear on the petals that face away from the incoming light. The Horns scene behaves similarly, with shadow locations shifting as the lighting direction changes; when the illumination rotates toward the right of the scene, shadows appear on the left of the horns, and under back-facing illumination larger shadowed regions appear in the foreground and the overall appearance is darker. The stylized scene therefore remains responsive to illumination changes after stylization, producing different shading under different lighting while preserving the stylized texture and scene structure.

    Fig. 6 shows relighting results on stylized Mip-NeRF 360 scenes under four environment maps. The stylized appearance stays the same, but the four maps produce distinct illumination-dependent appearance. The City environment gives brighter renderings with stronger overall illumination, the Fireplace environment adds warmer colour tones, the Forest environment adds a green tint, and the Sunset environment gives a softer appearance with more moderate lighting transitions. These effects appear across the Bicycle, Garden, and Kitchen scenes: the stylized texture and structural detail stay fixed while the rendered appearance follows the illumination of each environment map. RxGS therefore keeps a relightable scene representation after stylization, so the stylized scene responds to different lighting environments without re-running the stylization.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    4.4.1 Effect of the Style Supervision Strategy

    We compare two supervision strategies. The first renders the stylized albedo without illumination, so style supervision acts in the albedo domain. The second renders the stylized albedo under randomly sampled Lambertian illumination, which adds illumination-dependent shading during optimization.

    The comparison uses eight NeRF-Synthetic scenes and two reference styles, giving 16 scene-style pairs. For one optimization run we define its loss reduction as (Lᵢₙᵢₜ-L_final)/Lᵢₙᵢₜ, where Lᵢₙᵢₜ and L_final are the stylization loss L_style at the first and the last iteration. Direct albedo supervision gives a lower final stylization loss than randomized-illumination supervision on all 16 pairs. Averaged over the 16 pairs, the loss reduction is 32.2% for direct albedo supervision and 20.1% for randomized-illumination supervision.

    We attribute this gap to the extra appearance variation that randomized illumination introduces. Because the lighting direction changes during optimization, the rendered appearance contains illumination-dependent shading that is unrelated to the target style. The style supervision signal is then less stable and feature matching in the VGG space is harder. Direct albedo supervision removes the illumination contribution, so the optimization works only on the intrinsic appearance transfer. We therefore use direct albedo supervision in all experiments unless stated otherwise.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a BRDF-aware Gaussian scene representation. RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field and leaves the roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and environment lighting fixed, so artistic appearance transfer does not alter the material or illumination parameters and the stylized scene keeps a representation that can be relit. RxGS preserves cross-view geometric consistency and produces illumination-dependent appearance under novel lighting.

    6 Statements and Declarations

    6.1 Competing Interests

    The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：常规风格化优化的是「材质+环境光+法线+视角」揉在一起的 RGB，换光照就崩；RxGS 只动逆渲染出来的漫反射反照率。

要点：

  • 基于参考图的 3D 风格化通常优化 RGB 外观表示，单点颜色同时编码了材质反射、环境光与着色，风格化后光照被烘死
  • RxGS 建立在 BRDF 感知的 3D 高斯表示上，只优化逆渲染恢复的漫反射反照率场，粗糙度、法线、光照保持可重打
  • 16 对场景上，直接反照率监督的损失下降 32.2%，随机光照监督下降 20.1%
  • 风格化结果可在不同光照条件下重新渲染，而不是只在一套光下成立

为什么值得看：资产流水线里「风格化一次、后面还要按关卡灯光重打」是常态；把风格化作用域限制在反照率，等于让风格变成可复用的材质层而不是一张烘死的贴图。

中文摘要：基于参考图的 3D 场景风格化要把参考图外观迁移到重建场景上并保持几何。近期方法通过优化 NeRF 或 3DGS 的外观表示完成迁移，但优化的都是 RGB 表示：单个点的颜色同时混入了材质反射率、环境光照、着色和视角的影响。一旦风格化改动这份混合颜色，风格化时的光照就被烘进存储的外观里，场景无法在别的光照下渲染。作者提出 RxGS：基于 BRDF 感知的 3D Gaussian 表示，不修改每点 RGB，而只优化逆渲染得到的漫反射反照率场，粗糙度等其他材质参数保持不变。这样风格化只作用在材质层，光照留在可替换的一侧，风格化后的场景能在新光照下重新渲染。在多个场景对上，该约束使损失相对直接反照率监督下降 32.2%、相对随机光照监督下降 20.1%。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization via BRDF Decomposition

Abstract

Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of a reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while preserving scene geometry. Recent methods perform this transfer by optimizing the appearance representation of neural scene models including Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). These methods optimize an RGB appearance representation, in which a single per-point colour combines the effects of material reflectance, environment illumination, together with the shading it produces, and the viewing direction. When stylization modifies this combined colour, the illumination effects present during stylization are baked into the stored appearance, so the stylized scene cannot be rendered under different illumination. To address this limitation, we present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware 3D Gaussian representation. Rather than modifying a per-point RGB colour, RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field recovered by inverse rendering, while leaving roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and the estimated environment lighting unchanged. As a result, the stylized scene keeps all the components a physically-based renderer needs other than the edited albedo, and can therefore still be relit. RxGS optimizes the albedo field using a nearest-neighbour feature matching loss together with a spatial smoothness prior over Gaussian centres. We evaluate the method using a Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) based on optical-flow warping error. RxGS achieves the lowest GCC on all evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scenes and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while additionally supporting relightable stylization, which existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods do not provide.

1 Introduction

Reference-based 3D scene stylization transfers the appearance of an artistic reference image onto a reconstructed 3D scene while keeping the rendered result geometrically consistent across viewpoints. Recent neural rendering methods, in particular Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. (2023)], produce high-quality novel views and have prompted a growing body of 3D stylization work. These methods stylize a scene by modifying the RGB appearance representation that the neural scene model has learned. In many applications a scene must be stylized once and then rendered under several different lighting conditions without repeating the stylization. This requires the stylized scene to keep a representation that can be relit after the appearance transfer, a requirement the RGB representation does not meet, as the next paragraph argues.

An RGB appearance representation stores, at each point, one colour that already combines material reflectance, the environment illumination together with the shading it produces, and view-dependent effects. Because these factors are not stored separately, a stylization process that edits this colour necessarily edits the illumination contribution together with the intrinsic material. The illumination present during stylization is thereby written into the stored appearance: when the scene is later rendered under a different illumination, the stored colour does not change, so no new shading or shadows appear. As illustrated in Fig. 1, stylization applied to an RGB appearance representation fixes the artistic appearance and the illumination contribution together, which prevents the result from responding to novel lighting.

To remove this restriction we build on recent inverse rendering methods for 3D Gaussian representations. Such methods [Liang et al. (2024)] recover separate scene attributes, namely diffuse albedo, material properties, and environment illumination, and so support relightable rendering and material editing. These separated representations have not previously been used for reference-based 3D scene stylization.

We present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)-aware Gaussian scene representation. Given a reconstructed scene, RxGS first applies inverse rendering decomposition to recover, per Gaussian, the diffuse albedo aᵢ, the roughness rᵢ, the metallicity mᵢ, the surface normal nᵢ, and one global environment lighting L. Stylization then optimizes only the field of diffuse albedos {aᵢ} and leaves {rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ} and L and all geometry unchanged. Relightability follows from this bookkeeping rather than from any claim that the albedo alone fixes the rendered colour. A physically-based renderer consumes the geometry, the per-Gaussian material attributes {aᵢ,rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ}, and the environment lighting L. RxGS changes only the albedo coefficients {aᵢ^⋆} and holds every other input fixed, so all non-albedo inputs the renderer needs remain intact, and the same renderer can be re-run under any chosen L to produce a relit image of the stylized scene. To optimize the albedo field, RxGS uses a nearest-neighbour feature matching (NNFM) loss in the VGG feature space together with a spatial smoothness term over Gaussian centres.

We evaluate RxGS on synthetic and real-captured scenes, measuring cross-view geometric consistency with the Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC) defined in Section 4. RxGS attains the lowest GCC on every evaluated NeRF-Synthetic scene and remains competitive on real-captured scenes, while keeping a relightable scene representation after stylization. Our contributions are the following.

  • •

    We present RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework based on a BRDF-aware Gaussian scene representation.

  • •

    We formulate stylization as optimization of the diffuse albedo field alone in a logit parameterization, regularized by a smoothness term on a k-nearest-neighbour graph over Gaussian centres, so that artistic appearance transfer leaves the material and illumination parameters required for relighting unchanged.

  • •

    We evaluate on synthetic and real-captured datasets, reporting cross-view geometric consistency (GCC) that is competitive with prior stylization methods together with relightable stylization that prior methods do not provide.

    • 2 Related work

    2.1 3D Scene Representation and Rendering

    A 3D scene representation encodes scene geometry and appearance in a compact, learnable form that supports downstream tasks such as novel view synthesis, scene editing, relighting, and scene understanding. NeRF [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] introduced an implicit neural representation that parameterizes volumetric density and radiance with multilayer perceptrons, achieving novel view synthesis from multi-view observations. NeRF requires dense volumetric sampling during both training and rendering, which is computationally expensive. To reduce this cost, later work introduced voxel grids, tensor factorizations, and multi-resolution encodings, including DVGO [Sun et al. (2022)], Plenoxels [Fridovich-Keil et al. (2022)], TensoRF [Chen et al. (2022a)], and Instant-NGP [Müller et al. (2022)]. As scene editing and stylization tasks developed, several methods adopted surface-based representations that give a more explicit geometric correspondence than a purely volumetric field, including VolSDF [Yariv et al. (2021)], NeuS [Wang et al. (2021)], NeuMesh [Yang et al. (2022)], and NeRF2Mesh [Tang et al. (2023)].

    Among explicit representations, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. (2023)] represents a scene with a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives. Unlike volumetric methods that rely on dense ray sampling, 3DGS renders through differentiable Gaussian rasterization, which is fast enough for real-time rendering while still reconstructing scene geometry and appearance. Following 3DGS, many extensions adapt the representation to downstream tasks, including scene editing, relighting, and inverse rendering. The inverse rendering line, which recovers separate material and lighting attributes for each Gaussian, is the one RxGS builds upon, and we review it next.

    2.2 Inverse Rendering with 3D Gaussian Representations

    Inverse rendering recovers physically meaningful scene properties, namely geometry, material attributes, and illumination, from image observations. Several methods built this decomposition into neural rendering frameworks. NeRFactor [Zhang et al. (2021b)] factorizes scene appearance into geometry, reflectance, visibility, and illumination for relightable rendering. PhySG [Zhang et al. (2021a)] uses spherical Gaussian representations of the BRDF and of the illumination to put physically-based shading into neural rendering. TensorIR [Jin et al. (2023)] introduces a tensor-based inverse rendering framework that makes scene decomposition and relightable rendering more efficient.

    After 3DGS, inverse rendering was extended to Gaussian representations by attaching material, normal, and illumination attributes to the Gaussian primitives. GaussianShader [Jiang et al. (2024)] adds a shading function to Gaussian rendering and estimates geometry-aware normals to improve reflective surfaces. Relightable 3D Gaussian [Gao et al. (2024)] attaches BRDF attributes and incident lighting to each Gaussian and renders through differentiable physically-based rendering. GS-IR [Liang et al. (2024)] formulates inverse rendering on a BRDF-aware Gaussian representation by jointly estimating scene geometry, material properties, and environment illumination from multi-view observations; RxGS takes the decomposition produced by GS-IR as its input.

    2.3 3D Scene Stylization

    Neural style transfer was first developed for images [Gatys et al. (2016); Huang and Belongie (2017); Doyle and Mould (2019); Xu et al. (2024)], where the goal is to synthesize an image that keeps the scene content of one input while matching the appearance of a reference style image. As 3D scene representations matured, stylization was extended from 2D images to 3D scenes. Before neural scene representations, 3D stylization operated on explicit representations such as meshes and point clouds [Höllein et al. (2022); Cao et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2018)], manipulating surface textures, geometric attributes, or rendered appearance directly.

    Neural scene representations let stylization act on a learned appearance representation, so that style is propagated consistently across viewpoints. Early NeRF-based methods modify the appearance field of a reconstructed scene while keeping the geometry fixed [Chiang et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2022); Chen et al. (2024); Nguyen-Phuoc et al. (2022); Goel et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2022)]. ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)] optimizes the appearance field of a NeRF with a neural style transfer objective, giving multi-view consistent stylization, and ARF-plus [Li et al. (2025)] improves stylization quality and training stability through stronger appearance representations and optimization strategies. Ref-NPR [Zhang et al. (2023)] improves controllability by transferring appearance from reference images through geometry-aware feature correspondence, which enables localized stylization. LAE-NeRF [Radl et al. (2024)] lets a user mark target regions in a neural scene representation and propagates the edit through neighbouring volumetric regions. SNeRF [Nguyen-Phuoc et al. (2022)] alternates between image-space stylization and scene reconstruction, transferring artistic appearance into the neural scene representation across iterations.

    Because 3DGS associates appearance attributes directly with individual primitives, it makes appearance manipulation explicit. StylizedGS [Zhang et al. (2025)] supports region-specific style transfer through semantic masks. ReGS [Mei et al. (2024)] adapts 3DGS to reference-based stylization with a texture-guided mechanism that adjusts local Gaussian arrangements to reproduce texture detail from the reference. StyleSplat segments individual objects in a Gaussian scene and fine-tunes the selected Gaussians for object-level stylization. Further methods match segmented regions across views before transfer to keep the style consistent over the whole scene [Liu et al. (2025)], geometry-aware texture transfer [Liu et al. (2026b)], diffusion-based stylization and distillation [Yang et al. (2026)], and feed-forward or optimization-free stylization of Gaussian splats [Liu et al. (2026a); Sablon and Hart (2026)]. All of these methods, whether NeRF-based or Gaussian-based, edit a per-point RGB appearance, and so produce a stylized scene that stores one fixed colour per point and cannot be relit.

    A smaller line of work stylizes a decomposed appearance representation rather than RGB colour. TANGO [Chen et al. (2022b)] performs text-driven stylization by editing BRDF attributes on a relightable mesh, which allows appearance editing under varying illumination.
