RxGS differs from this mesh-based, text-driven setting: it performs reference-image stylization directly on a BRDF-aware Gaussian representation, editing only the diffuse albedo field of the Gaussians and keeping the rest of the decomposition fixed.

    3 Method

    The task is to modify the appearance of a 3D scene, reconstructed from posed multi-view images {Iₖ,Pₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, so that it matches the style of a reference image J, while keeping both the scene geometry and the physical rendering components that are needed to render the scene under novel illumination.

    3.1 Gaussian Representation

    3.1.1 3D Gaussian Splatting

    3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. (2023)] represents a scene with a set of anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives placed in 3D space. Each Gaussian is parameterized by a centre xᵢ∈ℝ³, a scaling vector sᵢ∈ℝ³, a rotation quaternion qᵢ∈ℝ⁴, an opacity αᵢ∈[0,1], and appearance-related attributes. The scaling vector and rotation quaternion together define the Gaussian covariance. The trainable parameters of the i-th Gaussian are

    Gᵢ={xᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ,φᵢ},(1)

    where φᵢ denotes the appearance representation of the Gaussian.

    Because the Gaussian primitives are defined in 3D space, the appearance attributes of a Gaussian are shared by every viewpoint that observes the same spatial region. This gives a fixed correspondence between scene geometry and appearance during rendering, so a change to a Gaussian’s appearance attributes affects all views of that region in the same way, which is useful for keeping a stylization consistent across viewpoints.

    3.1.2 BRDF-aware Gaussian Representation

    GS-IR [Liang et al. (2024)] refines the 3DGS appearance attribute φᵢ into a BRDF-aware decomposition consisting of diffuse albedo, roughness, metallicity, and surface normal, while jointly estimating a global environment lighting L, represented as an environment map, that is, a function on the unit sphere of incident directions giving the incoming radiance from each direction. Specifically,

    φᵢ={aᵢ,rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ},(2)

    where aᵢ∈[0,1]³ is the diffuse albedo of the i-th Gaussian, rᵢ∈[0,1] is the roughness, mᵢ∈[0,1] is the metallicity, and nᵢ∈ℝ³ is the surface normal.

    In an RGB appearance representation a single per-point colour already combines material reflectance, the illumination together with the shading it produces, and view-dependent effects. The decomposition above instead stores the albedo aᵢ as a separate per-Gaussian coefficient, alongside rᵢ, mᵢ, nᵢ, and the global lighting L. Although the diffuse albedo is represented separately, it still influences the colour of specular reflections under the metallic-roughness BRDF when metallicity is non-zero. Therefore, modifying the albedo changes both the diffuse appearance and the tint of specular highlights. However, the remaining BRDF attributes, including roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and environment lighting, remain unchanged throughout stylization. Consequently, the scene retains the complete set of rendering parameters required for relightable rendering.

    3.2 RxGS: Relightable Gaussian Stylization

    RxGS takes as input posed multi-view images {Iₖ,Pₖ}ₖ₌₁^K and a reference style image J. Let the BRDF-aware scene representation be

    S={G,L},

    where G={Gᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N is the set of N Gaussian primitives and L is the estimated environment lighting. RxGS optimizes the diffuse albedo field while keeping all remaining BRDF attributes, geometry, and environment lighting fixed.

    We separate the parameters of each Gaussian into geometry-related and appearance-related parts,

    Gᵢ={Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ,φᵢ},(3)

    where Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ={xᵢ,sᵢ,qᵢ,αᵢ}. The stylized appearance decomposition is

    φᵢ^⋆={aᵢ^⋆,rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ},(4)

    where only the diffuse albedo aᵢ^⋆ is optimized; the geometry attributes Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ, the roughness rᵢ, the metallicity mᵢ, the surface normal nᵢ, and the environment lighting L are all held fixed. Fig. 2 gives an overview.

    Existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods perform style transfer on rendered RGB images. Given a rendered image I, the stylized result is

    Ĩ=h^J(I),(5)

    where h^J(·) is a style transfer operator conditioned on the reference style image J. Because the rendered RGB image already combines material reflectance, shading, illumination, and view-dependent effects at each pixel, h^J modifies all of these together. The illumination present in I is thereby encoded in Ĩ. When the scene is later rendered under a different illumination, the stored stylized colour does not change, so the result shows no new illumination-dependent variation.

    RxGS instead modifies only the diffuse albedo field {aᵢ^⋆} and leaves {rᵢ,mᵢ,nᵢ} and L unchanged. Since only the albedo coefficient is changed and rᵢ, mᵢ, nᵢ, L, and the geometry are held fixed, every rendering input required by the physically-based renderer other than the albedo is intact. The same renderer can therefore be run again under any chosen L, and it produces illumination-dependent variation when relit.

    3.2.1 Albedo Parameterization

    Because only the diffuse albedo is optimized, the optimization must keep its value in the valid reflectance range [0,1]³. Optimizing aᵢ^⋆ directly could leave this range. RxGS therefore parameterizes the stylized albedo aᵢ^⋆∈[0,1]³ through an unconstrained latent variable zᵢ∈ℝ³ in logit space. Let a_i,orig denote the original albedo of Gaussian Gᵢ from the BRDF-aware decomposition. The component-wise inverse sigmoid σ⁻¹ diverges at 0 and 1, so before applying it we clamp each channel of a_i,orig to [ε,1-ε] with ε=10⁻⁶. We initialize

    z_i,0=σ⁻¹ (clamp(a_i,orig)),(6)

    and recover the stylized albedo as

    aᵢ^⋆=σ(zᵢ),(7)

    where σ is the component-wise sigmoid function and σ⁻¹ its inverse. With this parameterization aᵢ^⋆ stays in [0,1]³ for every value of zᵢ, and at initialization aᵢ^⋆ equals the clamped recovered albedo.

    3.2.2 Rendering Strategy

    The style supervision is computed on images rendered from the stylized scene. Let

    G^⋆={Gᵢ^⋆}ᵢ₌₁^N, Gᵢ^⋆={Gᵢᵍᵉᵒ,φᵢ^⋆},

    denote the stylized Gaussian scene. The direct strategy renders the stylized albedo field without illumination,

    Îₖ=Rₐ(G^⋆,Pₖ),(8)

    where Rₐ(·) is albedo rendering, which composites the per-Gaussian albedo aᵢ^⋆ along each ray without applying any shading. Style supervision is then applied directly in the albedo domain.

    We additionally consider a randomized-illumination strategy. Here, at optimization step t, a lighting L⁽ᵗ⁾ is randomly sampled and the stylized scene is rendered under it with a Lambertian, that is diffuse-only, shading model,

    Îₖ=R(G^⋆,Pₖ,L⁽ᵗ⁾),(9)

    where R(·) is a renderer that applies the sampled lighting. Section 4.4 compares the two strategies.

    3.2.3 Style Loss

    Following ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)], we use the nearest-neighbour feature matching (NNFM) loss as the style objective. Given a rendered image Îₖ and the reference style image J, the style loss is L_nnfm(Îₖ,J). It extracts feature maps from a pre-trained VGG-16 network for both images, and for each feature vector of Îₖ it finds the most similar feature vector of J by cosine similarity, then penalizes the cosine distance to that match. Following ARF, the features are taken from the conv3 block of the VGG-16 network.

    To control the trade-off between content preservation and stylization strength, RxGS optionally incorporates a content loss. The stylization objective is

    L_style=L_nnfm+λ_cL_content,(10)

    where λ_c weights the content term. Unless stated otherwise we set λ_c=0, so stylization is driven by the NNFM objective alone.

    3.2.4 Spatial Smoothness Prior on the Gaussian Neighbourhood Graph

    To make the stylized albedo vary smoothly over the scene, we add a smoothness term on the optimized albedo field. The albedo is stored on the Gaussian primitives rather than on a regular image grid, so the smoothness prior is defined on a k-nearest-neighbour graph built from the Gaussian centres. For a Gaussian Gᵢ, its neighbourhood ℕₖ(i) is the set of the k Gaussians whose centres have the smallest Euclidean distance to xᵢ. The spatial gradient of the stylized albedo field at Gᵢ is the average, over the neighbourhood, of the albedo difference weighted by the inverse Euclidean distance between Gaussian centres,

    ∇ₛₚₐₜᵢₐₗaᵢ^⋆=(1)/(\lvertℕₖ(i)\rvert)∑_j∈ℕₖ(i)(aᵢ^⋆-aⱼ^⋆)/(\lVertxᵢ-xⱼ\rVert₂+ε),(11)

    where ε=10⁻⁶ avoids division by zero and k=16 in all experiments. The smoothness loss sums the L₁ norm of this gradient over all Gaussians,

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ=∑ᵢ\lVert∇ₛₚₐₜᵢₐₗaᵢ^⋆\rVert₁.(12)

    The final objective combines the style and smoothness terms,

    L=L_style+λₛLₛₘₒₒₜₕ,(13)

    where λₛ=10⁻³.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate RxGS from two angles: cross-view geometric consistency and relightable stylization. We first compare RxGS with existing reference-based 3D scene stylization methods using a geometric consistency metric, which measures how well scene structure is preserved across viewpoints after stylization. Because the existing methods do not support relighting, we then evaluate the relightable stylization of RxGS by rendering stylized scenes under different illumination conditions and examining how the appearance responds.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    We use NeRF-Synthetic [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] and NeRF-LLFF [Mildenhall et al. (2019)] for the geometric consistency comparison, and add TensorIR [Jin et al. (2023)] and Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al. (2022)] for the relightable stylization experiments. NeRF-Synthetic [Mildenhall et al. (2021)] is a synthetic multi-view dataset of eight object-centric scenes, each with 100 training images and 200 test images rendered at 800×800, with camera poses and foreground masks. NeRF-LLFF [Mildenhall et al. (2019)] is a real-world forward-facing multi-view dataset captured by handheld cameras with calibrated poses; it contains more complex geometry, occlusions, and appearance variation than NeRF-Synthetic, and we downsample the input images by a factor of four, following prior work [Zhang et al. (2023); Fridovich-Keil et al. (2022); Tang et al. (2023)]. TensorIR [Jin et al. (2023)] is a multi-view dataset for inverse rendering and relighting, with diverse materials and illumination and with ground-truth geometry, material, and lighting; we use its Lego and Hotdog scenes for relightable stylization. Mip-NeRF 360 [Barron et al. (2022)] is a real-world multi-view dataset of unbounded indoor and outdoor scenes captured over 360-degree viewpoints, with larger extents and more complex structure than NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF; we use its Garden, Kitchen, and Bicycle scenes.

    Implementation Details.

    We take the BRDF-aware Gaussian representation reconstructed by GS-IR [Liang et al. (2024)] as the input to RxGS. Stylization optimizes the diffuse albedo while keeping the estimated geometry, roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and environment lighting fixed. Following ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)], we use the NNFM loss with a pre-trained VGG-16 network and take features from the conv3 block. Each scene is optimized for 1000 iterations.

    Comparison Methods.

    We compare RxGS with ARF [Zhang et al. (2022)], Ref-NPR [Zhang et al. (2023)], and StylizedGS [Zhang et al. (2025)]. Ref-NPR requires a reference image rather than a style image, so we generate its reference images with the AdaIN style transfer model [Huang and Belongie (2017)] from the same style images the other methods use. StylizedGS is included only on the LLFF scenes, because the original paper does not report NeRF-Synthetic results.

    Evaluation Protocol.

    To reduce bias toward a particular artistic appearance, we evaluate each scene with three different reference styles, and for the geometric consistency comparison we average the reported results over the three styles. For relighting, NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF scenes are rendered under several illumination conditions by rotating the estimated environment map while keeping all stylization parameters fixed. We additionally evaluate relightable stylization on TensorIR and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes to examine the behaviour of stylized scenes under varying illumination across different scene types.

    Metric.

    To measure cross-view geometric consistency we use the Geometry Consistency Cost (GCC), a per-pixel optical-flow warping error used in earlier video and 3D stylization work [Ruder et al. (2018); Zhang et al. (2023)]. Given two stylized renderings Îₖ and Îₖ₋₁ from nearby viewpoints, we estimate the optical flow from Îₖ₋₁ to Îₖ with the pre-trained RAFT model [Teed and Deng (2020)], warp Îₖ₋₁ to the viewpoint of Îₖ using this flow, and compute the mean per-pixel error between Îₖ and the warped frame over the pixels that the warp marks as visible. Averaging this error over consecutive frame pairs of a scene gives its GCC; a lower GCC indicates higher cross-view geometric consistency.

    4.2 Cross-view Geometry Consistency

    4.2.1 Quantitative Comparison

    Using the GCC metric above, we evaluate the cross-view geometric consistency of the scenes stylized by RxGS and compare with ARF, Ref-NPR, and StylizedGS. Table 1 and Table 2 report the GCC values on NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF.

    On NeRF-Synthetic, RxGS attains the lowest GCC in every scene. The margin over ARF and Ref-NPR is largest on Lego, Mic, Ficus, and Ship. On LLFF, RxGS has a lower GCC than ARF and is comparable with Ref-NPR and StylizedGS on most scenes. Despite the greater complexity of the real-captured scenes, RxGS stays on par with these methods while also keeping a relightable scene representation, which they do not.

    4.2.2 Qualitative Comparison

    Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 show qualitative stylization results on NeRF-Synthetic and LLFF. On both datasets, RxGS transfers the colour distribution and texture pattern of the reference style image while keeping the scene structure; these results hold on synthetic scenes (Fig. 4) and on real-captured scenes (Fig. 3) alike. The RxGS results are rendered from the optimized albedo field without illumination, which lets the transferred appearance be examined independently of scene lighting. Relightable renderings under varying illumination follow in the next section.

    4.3 Relightable Stylized Rendering

    Fig. 5 shows relighting results on stylized LLFF scenes under different illumination. As the illumination changes, the rendered appearance shows the corresponding shading while keeping the stylized texture and colour distribution. In the Flower scene, rotating the dominant light source moves the shadows across the petals: under the 90-degree rotated lighting, shadows appear on the petals that face away from the incoming light. The Horns scene behaves similarly, with shadow locations shifting as the lighting direction changes; when the illumination rotates toward the right of the scene, shadows appear on the left of the horns, and under back-facing illumination larger shadowed regions appear in the foreground and the overall appearance is darker. The stylized scene therefore remains responsive to illumination changes after stylization, producing different shading under different lighting while preserving the stylized texture and scene structure.

    Fig. 6 shows relighting results on stylized Mip-NeRF 360 scenes under four environment maps. The stylized appearance stays the same, but the four maps produce distinct illumination-dependent appearance. The City environment gives brighter renderings with stronger overall illumination, the Fireplace environment adds warmer colour tones, the Forest environment adds a green tint, and the Sunset environment gives a softer appearance with more moderate lighting transitions. These effects appear across the Bicycle, Garden, and Kitchen scenes: the stylized texture and structural detail stay fixed while the rendered appearance follows the illumination of each environment map. RxGS therefore keeps a relightable scene representation after stylization, so the stylized scene responds to different lighting environments without re-running the stylization.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    4.4.1 Effect of the Style Supervision Strategy

    We compare two supervision strategies. The first renders the stylized albedo without illumination, so style supervision acts in the albedo domain. The second renders the stylized albedo under randomly sampled Lambertian illumination, which adds illumination-dependent shading during optimization.

    The comparison uses eight NeRF-Synthetic scenes and two reference styles, giving 16 scene-style pairs. For one optimization run we define its loss reduction as (Lᵢₙᵢₜ-L_final)/Lᵢₙᵢₜ, where Lᵢₙᵢₜ and L_final are the stylization loss L_style at the first and the last iteration. Direct albedo supervision gives a lower final stylization loss than randomized-illumination supervision on all 16 pairs. Averaged over the 16 pairs, the loss reduction is 32.2% for direct albedo supervision and 20.1% for randomized-illumination supervision.

    We attribute this gap to the extra appearance variation that randomized illumination introduces. Because the lighting direction changes during optimization, the rendered appearance contains illumination-dependent shading that is unrelated to the target style. The style supervision signal is then less stable and feature matching in the VGG space is harder. Direct albedo supervision removes the illumination contribution, so the optimization works only on the intrinsic appearance transfer. We therefore use direct albedo supervision in all experiments unless stated otherwise.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented RxGS, a relightable 3D scene stylization framework built on a BRDF-aware Gaussian scene representation. RxGS optimizes only the diffuse albedo field and leaves the roughness, metallicity, surface normals, and environment lighting fixed, so artistic appearance transfer does not alter the material or illumination parameters and the stylized scene keeps a representation that can be relit. RxGS preserves cross-view geometric consistency and produces illumination-dependent appearance under novel lighting.

    6 Statements and Declarations

    6.1 Competing Interests

    The authors declare that they have no competing interests.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 前馈 3DGS 总丢细节：FineSplat 把 4×4 细粒度 patch 分两组聚合，再用重渲染误差做反馈 ｜ FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats
item.description:
一句话：前馈模型的 patch 分辨率被几何骨干限制在 14×14/16×16，细几何细纹理就糊；改成 4×4 细 patch + 视图与 3D 两组分组，再补一步误差反馈。

要点：

  • Stage 1 把每个上下文视角切成 4×4 细 patch 编码，用 view-wise 分组只让相邻少数视角互相注意，把细粒度多视角推理的成本压住
  • Stage 2 用 3D 空间分组把几何相关、但在视图分组下从未交互过的 token 重新拉到一起；用重渲染误差当显式反馈，迭代 T=4 步
  • 每个 4×4 token 预测 4 个高斯并各绑定一个不重叠的 2×2 子块，保证高斯落在子块内又能连续亚像素定位
  • 在 DL3DV 的姿态未知设置、RE10K 1600 个测试场景（6 视角）与 Mip-NeRF 360（32/64/128 视角）上做零样本评测，22万 4×4 patch 分辨率带来的细节在 PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS 上均体现

为什么值得看：前馈重建的瓶颈往往不在高斯数量而在「感知分辨率」；把 patch 变小、再用 3D 分组把跨视角关系补回来，是提升进引擎资产质量最直接的一条路。

中文摘要：前馈 3D Gaussian Splatting 承诺一次前向就完成重建，但细粒度几何与外观仍难恢复。作者重新审视前馈模型如何表示、聚合与精修细节信息，提出 FineSplat：以细粒度图像 patch 为核心。由于全局多视角注意力在这种 token 分辨率下代价过高，他们设计了双分组策略——view-wise 分组让相邻视角之间高效交互，3D 空间分组则把可能从未在视图分组下相遇的几何相关 token 提升到 3D 场景空间重新连接。此外用重建误差作为直接反馈，给出显式的基于渲染的信号来恢复细结构，突破单次前馈预测的限制；最后用紧凑的高斯生成方案把每个细 patch token 映射成落在指定子块内的高斯。该方法在多个零样本设置下改善了细节与整体重建质量。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-26

FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.

https://hyebinny.github.io/FineSplat/

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.22footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025b)] has emerged as a powerful representation for high-quality and real-time novel view synthesis, combining an explicit 3D scene representation with efficient differentiable rasterization. Since conventional 3DGS relies on iterative per-scene optimization to achieve high reconstruction quality, it typically requires substantial computational resources for every new scene, limiting its scalability and applicability. To overcome these limitations, recent works have explored feed-forward 3DGS, where a single network forward pass directly predicts Gaussian representations from a set of input images. These approaches have rapidly advanced in both posed [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Ziwen et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026a; Kang et al., 2026b)] and pose-free [(Zhang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a; Ye et al., 2026; An et al., 2025)] settings, enabling fast reconstruction with promising generalization. However, replacing iterative per-scene refinement with a single feed-forward prediction places a much greater burden on the network, requiring it to resolve complex multi-view ambiguities and recover fine-grained scene details all at once. As a result, existing feed-forward approaches still exhibit a considerable reconstruction-quality gap compared with per-scene optimization methods, particularly in recovering fine-grained geometry and appearance details.

Many recent feed-forward 3DGS methods build upon powerful 3D foundation models, benefiting from their strong geometric priors and multi-view reasoning capabilities. However, these models commonly inherit the relatively coarse patch resolution of their geometry backbones, typically using 14×14 or 16×16 image patches [(Wang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026d)]. Such large patches provide broader spatial context that supports large-scale geometric reasoning and helps disambiguate cross-view correspondences, particularly when fine patches contain insufficiently distinctive local visual cues. However, compressing a broad image region into a single token can discard the high-frequency cues needed to reconstruct thin structures, sharp boundaries, textures, and other fine-grained details. Moreover, attention between coarse tokens operates at a limited spatial resolution, which can make it more difficult to precisely localize corresponding image regions across views. Finer patch tokens, particularly with attention between them, may therefore offer a promising avenue for preserving richer local visual cues and enabling more spatially precise cross-view interactions.

Yet, finer tokenization introduces a fundamental computational challenge. Most multi-view transformers rely on global self-attention across tokens from multiple input images, whose quadratic complexity quickly becomes prohibitive as the number of views, image resolution, and token density increase. A practical alternative is to restrict the attention scope. For example, MVP [(Kang et al., 2026b)] partitions input views into small groups and performs fine-grained multi-view attention only within each group, substantially improving the efficiency of high-resolution multi-view reconstruction while maintaining strong accuracy. Such view-wise grouping is particularly effective when the inputs are sequentially captured and nearby views are likely to observe overlapping scene regions. However, the restriction is ultimately imposed in view space rather than scene space: tokens corresponding to the same 3D surface may fall into different view groups and therefore never directly interact. Consequently, any fixed view grouping inevitably creates blind spots, excluding potentially relevant correspondences simply because they lie across group boundaries.

In this work, we propose FineSplat, which addresses this challenge through a dual-grouping strategy that exploits two complementary forms of locality. First, we perform fine-grained multi-view interaction within small groups of neighboring views, enabling efficient attention over high-resolution tokens. We then lift the resulting tokens into 3D space using their predicted scene locations and regroup them according to 3D spatial proximity. This allows tokens from different, potentially distant view groups to interact when they correspond to nearby regions of the underlying 3D scene, recovering geometric relationships missed by view-wise grouping alone. By combining view-wise locality with 3D spatial locality, FineSplat enables rich interactions among fine-grained tokens without the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention.

A faithful 3D reconstruction should reproduce the input images when rendered from their viewpoints, which provides a natural signal for assessing its quality. Conventional per-scene optimization repeatedly exploits this signal, comparing rendered and observed images to identify residual errors and progressively correct the scene representation. A one-pass feed-forward model, in contrast, typically produces its reconstruction without an opportunity to inspect and correct its own errors. Motivated by this observation and recent work [(Xu et al., 2026)], we explicitly leverage this readily available feedback as a direct signal in the second stage of our proposed framework. This provides the network with a second chance to recover structures and fine details that were missed in the first stage, without resorting to costly iterative optimization.

We further introduce a compact Gaussian generation scheme that predicts only a small number of Gaussians from each patch token, rather than densely generating pixel-aligned Gaussians. This design allows the model to retain the benefits of fine-grained image features without increasing the number of Gaussian primitives. Together, the fine-grained representation, dual-grouping strategy, reconstruction error-driven correction, and compact Gaussian generation enable substantially improved reconstruction quality while maintaining an efficient and compact 3D representation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality by a substantial margin in both posed and pose-free settings, while using the same or fewer Gaussians than existing methods.

2 Related Works

Feed-forward 3DGS and compact Gaussian representation.

Feed-forward 3DGS methods amortize per-scene optimization [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] by directly predicting Gaussians from input images in a single forward pass. One common design is pixel-aligned prediction, where each pixel is unprojected along its camera ray into one Gaussian, using epipolar attention [(Charatan et al., 2024)], cost volumes [(Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025)], or large transformers [(Zhang et al., 2024; Ziwen et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a)]. This keeps the geometry well-conditioned and helps preserve fine appearance, but the number of Gaussians grows linearly with resolution and view count, often producing many redundant primitives in overlapping regions [(Park et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026)]. In contrast, non-pixel-aligned methods predict a compact set of Gaussians from learnable tokens, clustered scene features, 3D anchors, or voxels [(Ren et al., 2026; An et al., 2025; Veicht et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Moreau et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Itkin et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b)], but lose the explicit pixel-ray correspondence, which tends to hurt fine detail and makes optimization harder. Between these extremes, patch-aligned methods predict Gaussians at a reduced spatial resolution [(Kang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026)]. In our framework, we extend this patch-aligned approach by generating only a small number of Gaussians along the rays of each sub-patch, and further compact the representation by pruning Gaussians according to their rendering contribution to the context views.

Pose-free feed-forward 3DGS and geometry foundation models.

Geometry foundation models [(Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026d; Lin et al., 2025)] estimate camera poses and dense geometry directly from unposed images. Building on such models, pose-free methods jointly predict camera poses and Gaussians [(Ye et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2025)], mostly in a pixel-aligned manner on top of the geometry backbone. However, these backbones operate on relatively coarse image tokens, which are well suited for global geometric reasoning but may discard local appearance cues important for fine-grained Gaussian reconstruction. To compensate, existing methods often fine-tune the backbone end-to-end so that its pretrained features adapt to appearance reconstruction. This adaptation is computationally expensive, and the model still relies on representations shaped by the coarse tokenization, which may limit its ability to recover fine-grained appearance. Recent works instead decouple geometry estimation from appearance modeling [(Zhang et al., 2025; Jeong et al., 2026)]. We follow this decoupled design for pose-free reconstruction, using a 3D foundation model, such as DA3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], to predict the camera poses while FineSplat performs fine-grained Gaussian prediction.

Combining image-space and 3D locality.

Many useful cues for 3D reconstruction, such as dense image features and rendering errors, are naturally defined in image space, where they are grouped by proximity in the image plane rather than in the underlying scene. Several works therefore bring such image-space cues into 3D and process them according to 3D spatial locality. ODIN [(Jain et al., 2024)] alternates 2D within-view layers with 3D cross-view attention over unprojected features, and DITR [(Knaebel et al., 2026)] projects DINOv2 [(Oquab et al., 2023)] features onto 3D points and injects them into a Point Transformer V3 [(Wu et al., 2024)] backbone. MoGe-3 [(Kong et al., 2026)] lifts monocular geometry into a sparse voxel volume guided by image features to recover sharp details near depth boundaries. In feed-forward 3DGS, ATSplat [(Cho et al., 2026)] unprojects patch features into sparse 3D anchors that gather context from their 3D neighbors, and expands them where rendering errors are predicted to be high. Our second stage lifts fine tokens from all views into 3D and applies serialized attention over their 3D neighborhoods, so that tokens separated by view grouping can interact.

Iterative refinement.

Iterative minimization of an objective has long been a standard approach to solving vision problems [(Lucas and Kanade, 1981; Sun et al., 2010)], and learning-based methods have sought to emulate this process by repeatedly updating an initial estimate. Such learned iterative refinement often outperforms single-step regression and has been successfully applied to a broad range of applications, such as optical flow [(Teed and Deng, 2020)], human pose estimation [(Newell et al., 2016; Carreira et al., 2016)], stereo matching [(Lipson et al., 2021)], SLAM [(Teed and Deng, 2021)], structure-from-motion [(Li et al., 2025)], multi-view stereo [(Wang et al., 2022)], and multi-view 3D reconstruction [(Burzio et al., 2026)]. For Gaussian splatting, prior works refine Gaussians with a single-step or multiple-step network [(Chen et al., 2025; Nam et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026a)], learn updates from rendering gradients [(Chen et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Pearl et al., 2026)] or rendering errors [(Xu et al., 2026)], or fine-tune Gaussian tokens for each scene [(Ren et al., 2026)].

3 Method

Given N context views with or without known camera poses, FineSplat predicts a set of 3D Gaussians in a feed-forward manner. Stage 1 divides each context view into fine-grained 4×4 patches and encodes them with attention of varying scope, where group-wise attention over a few views keeps fine-grained multi-view reasoning affordable. Stage 2 decodes these tokens into an initial set of Gaussians, renders them back into the context views, and uses the resulting error maps to update the tokens through 3D spatial grouping, which lets tokens that fall in different view groups interact once they are lifted to 3D. This dual-grouping strategy makes fine-grained encoding tractable, with 3D spatial grouping complementing view-wise grouping by connecting tokens across view groups. Figure 2 gives an overview of the two stages.

3.1 Stage 1: View-wise token grouping

Global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive with fine-grained tokens. In the first stage, we restrict the attention scope and adopt a view-wise token grouping strategy. Specifically, we leverage the multi-view pyramid architecture (MVP) [(Kang et al., 2026b)]. It performs fine-grained attention within small groups of views, while allowing information exchange across all views through coarser global tokens. This balances local detail preservation with global multi-view reasoning. It organizes its encoder as a three-level pyramid, and we denote the feature map of level ℓ∈{1,2,3} as F^ℓ, from the finest (F¹) to the coarsest (F³). In more detail, given N input images I∈ℝ^N×H×W×3 and patch size p, the first stage fuses the three levels of coarse-to-fine features into M=NHW/p² fine-grained tokens z⁽⁰⁾∈ℝ^M×d,

z⁽⁰⁾=fuse(up(fuse(up(F³)+F²))+F¹),

(1)

where up(·) denotes bilinear upsampling and fuse(·) a convolutional fusion block, which are used to match the token resolutions.

The fixed view grouping strategy inevitably leaves blind spots: fine-grained tokens in different groups cannot directly interact, potentially missing relevant observations from other input views. Thus, view-wise grouping alone cannot fully realize fine-grained multi-view reasoning over all input views. To recover these missing interactions, we pass the fine-grained tokens to the subsequent 3D spatial grouping stage.

3.2 Stage 2: 3D spatial token grouping

Starting from the fine-grained tokens z⁽⁰⁾ produced by the first stage, we first decode an initial set of 3D Gaussians. Specifically, a lightweight Gaussian head D, implemented as a linear decoder, maps each token to K Gaussian primitives and their attributes. We then use the predicted Gaussian centers to lift the corresponding tokens into 3D space, where tokens are regrouped according to their spatial proximity in 3D world coordinates. We then perform self-attention within each 3D group, enabling fine-grained interactions between geometrically related tokens even when they originate from different view groups. To further refine the current estimate, we augment this interaction with reconstruction-error information obtained by rendering the input views. The updated tokens are subsequently decoded into a new set of Gaussian primitives, and this process of Gaussian prediction, 3D grouping, error-guided interaction, and token update is repeated for multiple steps.

Lifting tokens to 3D.

To reason about the tokens in a common 3D space, we anchor each token at the mean position of the Gaussians it produces. Given the j-th token at the i-th step, zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝᵈ,

{μⱼₖ⁽ⁱ⁾}ₖ₌₁^K=D(zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾), pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^Kμⱼₖ⁽ⁱ⁾,

(2)

where μⱼₖ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ³ is the position of each predicted Gaussian. Each token is then projected by a linear layer, yielding a point cloud {(pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾,zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾)}ⱼ₌₁^M whose points carry the fine-grained tokens as features.

Error feature maps.

To measure how well the current Gaussians explain the observations, we render them into every input view. For the n-th context view, we define a signed error map between the input image Iₙ and the rendered image Îₙ, computed as Eₙ=Îₙ-Iₙ. To complement this pixel-level discrepancy with structural cues, we additionally compute a feature-level difference Δφₙ=φ(Îₙ)-φ(Iₙ), where φ(·) is a pretrained ResNet-18 [(He et al., 2016)] encoder. These two terms are combined with the finest-scale features from the first stage, F¹ₙ, which provide the image context in which the errors occur. We obtain the error feature map as follows,

Fₙᵉʳʳ=[ 𝔼ₑᵣᵣ(Eₙ,Δφₙ) ; 𝔼_feat(F¹ₙ) ]∈ℝ^H/p×W/p×dₑ,

(3)

where F¹ₙ denotes the finest-scale features from the first stage for an input view n, 𝔼ₑᵣᵣ and 𝔼_feat are linear embedding layers, and [·;·] represents the feature concatenation.

Gathering errors across views.

A Gaussian affects the rendering of every view in which it is visible, not only the view from which it was predicted. We therefore gather error features for each token from both its own view and the other views that observe it. Let πₙ(·) denote the projection onto the error feature map of view n, and let vⱼₙ∈{0,1} indicate whether pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ lies inside the view n’s frustum and passes an occlusion test against the rendered depth. The aggregated error feature is obtained by averaging the bilinearly sampled features over the visible views,

eⱼᵃᵍᵍ=(∑ₙ₌₁^Nvⱼₙ Fₙᵉʳʳ(πₙ(pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾)))/(∑ₙ₌₁^Nvⱼₙ),

(4)

where Fₙᵉʳʳ(·) reads a feature given a projected coordinate. In addition, we take the error feature at the patch from which zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ originates, denoted as eⱼ^self. While eⱼ^self provides a direct signal from the source view, eⱼᵃᵍᵍ summarizes how consistently the token explains the other views. The two are fused into the final error feature eⱼ=Linear([eⱼ^self;eⱼᵃᵍᵍ]).

3D spatial token grouping and update.

Each lifted point is assigned the feature hⱼ=Linear([zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾;eⱼ]). Neighboring tokens in 3D often originate from different views and describe the same surface, so correcting them jointly is more effective than correcting each token independently. We thus exchange information among nearby points using serialized attention [(Wu et al., 2024)], which orders the points along a space-filling curve, partitions them into groups of S consecutive points, and applies self-attention within each group. Compared with explicit k-nearest-neighbor search, this provides local 3D context at a much lower cost and scales favorably with the number of tokens. The updated features are projected to a token residual by a linear layer,

Δzⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾=Linear(SerialAttn(hⱼ)), zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾=zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾+Δzⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾.

(5)

Then, the updated tokens are decoded into Gaussians with the shared Gaussian head D. Our Stage 2 module is applied for T=4 steps, starting from z⁽⁰⁾: each step takes the tokens from the previous one, re-renders the context views, recomputes the error features, and regroups the tokens at their updated 3D positions.

3.3 Patch-aligned Sub-pixel Gaussian Reconstruction

To obtain a dense Gaussian representation while preserving the spatial structure of image features, we predict four Gaussians for each 4×4 fine-grained token, assigning each Gaussian to one of four non-overlapping 2×2 sub-patches. Rather than constraining a Gaussian to the fixed center ray of its assigned sub-patch, we learn a two-dimensional image-space offset Δ=(Δₓ,Δ_y) that adaptively shifts its ray within the corresponding region. Specifically, for a sub-patch with stride s=2, we bound the offset as δₓ=s/2\tanh(Δₓ),δ_y=s/2\tanh(Δ_y), such that δₓ,δ_y∈[-s/2,s/2]. This guarantees that each Gaussian remains within its designated 2×2 sub-patch while allowing continuous sub-pixel localization. Given the center (u_c,v_c) of each sub-patch, the displaced image coordinate is (u,v)=(u_c,v_c)+δ, which is unprojected using the predicted camera intrinsics. We then transform and normalize this direction using the camera-to-world rotation, with the camera translation serving as the corresponding ray origin.

4 Experiments

4.1 Implementation Details

Setup.

We train a single model only on the DL3DV [(Ling et al., 2024)] dataset, sampling the number of input context views from {6,12,24,32} for each training scene, and use this one checkpoint for all evaluations without dataset-specific fine-tuning. On DL3DV, we evaluate on 140 test scenes with N∈{6,12,24} context views, selected via farthest point sampling with maximum temporal frame gaps of 50, 100, and 150, respectively. We further evaluate zero-shot generalization on 1,600 RealEstate10K (RE10K) [(Zhou et al., 2018)] test scenes with N=6, and on Mip-NeRF 360 [(Barron et al., 2022)] with N∈{32,64,128}, following the view indices from [Veicht et al. (2026)]. Mip-NeRF 360 is a demanding target for a model trained on DL3DV: it covers both indoor and outdoor scenes, its scenes are unbounded, its cameras orbit the scene rather than sweep through it, and it uses far more context views than the 32 seen during training. We hold out 8 target views on all three datasets. For a fair comparison, each method encodes and renders at its native training resolution, and all rendered outputs are resized to 224×224 for evaluation, following [Ye et al. (2026)] (252 × 252 results are provided in Appendix B.3). We report PSNR, SSIM [(Wang et al., 2004)], and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)], averaged over all test scenes.

Supervision and scene normalization.

FineSplat is trained without any depth supervision, using only a mean squared error term and a perceptual term on the rendered views. Several of the baselines instead rely on depth: AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)], DepthSplat [(Xu et al., 2025)], NoDrift3R [(Sun et al., 2026)], DA3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], and ZipSplat [(Veicht et al., 2026)] all use a depth objective during training. Since feed-forward reconstruction is scale-ambiguous, we bring each scene to a canonical scale using only the context camera poses: poses are expressed in the mean context camera frame and translations are rescaled so that all context camera centers lie within [-1,1]³. The same transform is applied to the target poses, both ground-truth and DA3-predicted. ZipSplat instead derives the scene scale from depth at evaluation time, unprojecting per-view depth maps predicted by DA3 and taking the median distance of the resulting points to the first context camera. Details of the scene scale normalization are provided in Appendix A.3. Since we evaluate on the same Mip-NeRF 360 scenes and view indices as ZipSplat, the two differ only in how this scale is obtained: its normalization depends on a dense depth prior, whereas ours needs only camera positions and transfers directly to predicted poses.

Baselines.

We compare against the pose-free methods AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)], C3G [(An et al., 2025)], DA3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], YoNoSplat [(Ye et al., 2026)], NoDrift3R [(Sun et al., 2026)], 2Xplat [(Jeong et al., 2026)], and ZipSplat [(Veicht et al., 2026)], as well as NoPoSplat [(Ye et al., 2025a)], which additionally requires ground-truth camera intrinsics. For pose-dependent methods, we compare against DepthSplat [(Xu et al., 2025)] and MVP [(Kang et al., 2026b)].

4.2 Novel view synthesis

Benchmark performance.

一句话：前馈模型的 patch 分辨率被几何骨干限制在 14×14/16×16，细几何细纹理就糊；改成 4×4 细 patch + 视图与 3D 两组分组，再补一步误差反馈。

要点：

  • Stage 1 把每个上下文视角切成 4×4 细 patch 编码，用 view-wise 分组只让相邻少数视角互相注意，把细粒度多视角推理的成本压住
  • Stage 2 用 3D 空间分组把几何相关、但在视图分组下从未交互过的 token 重新拉到一起；用重渲染误差当显式反馈，迭代 T=4 步
  • 每个 4×4 token 预测 4 个高斯并各绑定一个不重叠的 2×2 子块，保证高斯落在子块内又能连续亚像素定位
  • 在 DL3DV 的姿态未知设置、RE10K 1600 个测试场景（6 视角）与 Mip-NeRF 360（32/64/128 视角）上做零样本评测，22万 4×4 patch 分辨率带来的细节在 PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS 上均体现

为什么值得看：前馈重建的瓶颈往往不在高斯数量而在「感知分辨率」；把 patch 变小、再用 3D 分组把跨视角关系补回来，是提升进引擎资产质量最直接的一条路。

中文摘要：前馈 3D Gaussian Splatting 承诺一次前向就完成重建，但细粒度几何与外观仍难恢复。作者重新审视前馈模型如何表示、聚合与精修细节信息，提出 FineSplat：以细粒度图像 patch 为核心。由于全局多视角注意力在这种 token 分辨率下代价过高，他们设计了双分组策略——view-wise 分组让相邻视角之间高效交互，3D 空间分组则把可能从未在视图分组下相遇的几何相关 token 提升到 3D 场景空间重新连接。此外用重建误差作为直接反馈，给出显式的基于渲染的信号来恢复细结构，突破单次前馈预测的限制；最后用紧凑的高斯生成方案把每个细 patch token 映射成落在指定子块内的高斯。该方法在多个零样本设置下改善了细节与整体重建质量。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-26

FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats

Abstract

Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.

https://hyebinny.github.io/FineSplat/

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.22footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025b)] has emerged as a powerful representation for high-quality and real-time novel view synthesis, combining an explicit 3D scene representation with efficient differentiable rasterization. Since conventional 3DGS relies on iterative per-scene optimization to achieve high reconstruction quality, it typically requires substantial computational resources for every new scene, limiting its scalability and applicability. To overcome these limitations, recent works have explored feed-forward 3DGS, where a single network forward pass directly predicts Gaussian representations from a set of input images. These approaches have rapidly advanced in both posed [(Charatan et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024a; Ziwen et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026a; Kang et al., 2026b)] and pose-free [(Zhang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025a; Ye et al., 2026; An et al., 2025)] settings, enabling fast reconstruction with promising generalization. However, replacing iterative per-scene refinement with a single feed-forward prediction places a much greater burden on the network, requiring it to resolve complex multi-view ambiguities and recover fine-grained scene details all at once. As a result, existing feed-forward approaches still exhibit a considerable reconstruction-quality gap compared with per-scene optimization methods, particularly in recovering fine-grained geometry and appearance details.

Many recent feed-forward 3DGS methods build upon powerful 3D foundation models, benefiting from their strong geometric priors and multi-view reasoning capabilities. However, these models commonly inherit the relatively coarse patch resolution of their geometry backbones, typically using 14×14 or 16×16 image patches [(Wang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026d)]. Such large patches provide broader spatial context that supports large-scale geometric reasoning and helps disambiguate cross-view correspondences, particularly when fine patches contain insufficiently distinctive local visual cues. However, compressing a broad image region into a single token can discard the high-frequency cues needed to reconstruct thin structures, sharp boundaries, textures, and other fine-grained details. Moreover, attention between coarse tokens operates at a limited spatial resolution, which can make it more difficult to precisely localize corresponding image regions across views. Finer patch tokens, particularly with attention between them, may therefore offer a promising avenue for preserving richer local visual cues and enabling more spatially precise cross-view interactions.

Yet, finer tokenization introduces a fundamental computational challenge. Most multi-view transformers rely on global self-attention across tokens from multiple input images, whose quadratic complexity quickly becomes prohibitive as the number of views, image resolution, and token density increase. A practical alternative is to restrict the attention scope. For example, MVP [(Kang et al., 2026b)] partitions input views into small groups and performs fine-grained multi-view attention only within each group, substantially improving the efficiency of high-resolution multi-view reconstruction while maintaining strong accuracy. Such view-wise grouping is particularly effective when the inputs are sequentially captured and nearby views are likely to observe overlapping scene regions. However, the restriction is ultimately imposed in view space rather than scene space: tokens corresponding to the same 3D surface may fall into different view groups and therefore never directly interact. Consequently, any fixed view grouping inevitably creates blind spots, excluding potentially relevant correspondences simply because they lie across group boundaries.

In this work, we propose FineSplat, which addresses this challenge through a dual-grouping strategy that exploits two complementary forms of locality. First, we perform fine-grained multi-view interaction within small groups of neighboring views, enabling efficient attention over high-resolution tokens. We then lift the resulting tokens into 3D space using their predicted scene locations and regroup them according to 3D spatial proximity. This allows tokens from different, potentially distant view groups to interact when they correspond to nearby regions of the underlying 3D scene, recovering geometric relationships missed by view-wise grouping alone. By combining view-wise locality with 3D spatial locality, FineSplat enables rich interactions among fine-grained tokens without the prohibitive cost of global multi-view attention.

A faithful 3D reconstruction should reproduce the input images when rendered from their viewpoints, which provides a natural signal for assessing its quality. Conventional per-scene optimization repeatedly exploits this signal, comparing rendered and observed images to identify residual errors and progressively correct the scene representation. A one-pass feed-forward model, in contrast, typically produces its reconstruction without an opportunity to inspect and correct its own errors. Motivated by this observation and recent work [(Xu et al., 2026)], we explicitly leverage this readily available feedback as a direct signal in the second stage of our proposed framework. This provides the network with a second chance to recover structures and fine details that were missed in the first stage, without resorting to costly iterative optimization.

We further introduce a compact Gaussian generation scheme that predicts only a small number of Gaussians from each patch token, rather than densely generating pixel-aligned Gaussians. This design allows the model to retain the benefits of fine-grained image features without increasing the number of Gaussian primitives. Together, the fine-grained representation, dual-grouping strategy, reconstruction error-driven correction, and compact Gaussian generation enable substantially improved reconstruction quality while maintaining an efficient and compact 3D representation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art rendering quality by a substantial margin in both posed and pose-free settings, while using the same or fewer Gaussians than existing methods.

2 Related Works

Feed-forward 3DGS and compact Gaussian representation.

Feed-forward 3DGS methods amortize per-scene optimization [(Kerbl et al., 2023)] by directly predicting Gaussians from input images in a single forward pass. One common design is pixel-aligned prediction, where each pixel is unprojected along its camera ray into one Gaussian, using epipolar attention [(Charatan et al., 2024)], cost volumes [(Chen et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2025)], or large transformers [(Zhang et al., 2024; Ziwen et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026a)]. This keeps the geometry well-conditioned and helps preserve fine appearance, but the number of Gaussians grows linearly with resolution and view count, often producing many redundant primitives in overlapping regions [(Park et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Nguyen et al., 2026)]. In contrast, non-pixel-aligned methods predict a compact set of Gaussians from learnable tokens, clustered scene features, 3D anchors, or voxels [(Ren et al., 2026; An et al., 2025; Veicht et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Moreau et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Itkin et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b)], but lose the explicit pixel-ray correspondence, which tends to hurt fine detail and makes optimization harder. Between these extremes, patch-aligned methods predict Gaussians at a reduced spatial resolution [(Kang et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026)]. In our framework, we extend this patch-aligned approach by generating only a small number of Gaussians along the rays of each sub-patch, and further compact the representation by pruning Gaussians according to their rendering contribution to the context views.

Pose-free feed-forward 3DGS and geometry foundation models.

Geometry foundation models [(Wang et al., 2024; Leroy et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026d; Lin et al., 2025)] estimate camera poses and dense geometry directly from unposed images. Building on such models, pose-free methods jointly predict camera poses and Gaussians [(Ye et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2025)], mostly in a pixel-aligned manner on top of the geometry backbone. However, these backbones operate on relatively coarse image tokens, which are well suited for global geometric reasoning but may discard local appearance cues important for fine-grained Gaussian reconstruction. To compensate, existing methods often fine-tune the backbone end-to-end so that its pretrained features adapt to appearance reconstruction. This adaptation is computationally expensive, and the model still relies on representations shaped by the coarse tokenization, which may limit its ability to recover fine-grained appearance. Recent works instead decouple geometry estimation from appearance modeling [(Zhang et al., 2025; Jeong et al., 2026)]. We follow this decoupled design for pose-free reconstruction, using a 3D foundation model, such as DA3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], to predict the camera poses while FineSplat performs fine-grained Gaussian prediction.

Combining image-space and 3D locality.

Many useful cues for 3D reconstruction, such as dense image features and rendering errors, are naturally defined in image space, where they are grouped by proximity in the image plane rather than in the underlying scene. Several works therefore bring such image-space cues into 3D and process them according to 3D spatial locality. ODIN [(Jain et al., 2024)] alternates 2D within-view layers with 3D cross-view attention over unprojected features, and DITR [(Knaebel et al., 2026)] projects DINOv2 [(Oquab et al., 2023)] features onto 3D points and injects them into a Point Transformer V3 [(Wu et al., 2024)] backbone. MoGe-3 [(Kong et al., 2026)] lifts monocular geometry into a sparse voxel volume guided by image features to recover sharp details near depth boundaries. In feed-forward 3DGS, ATSplat [(Cho et al., 2026)] unprojects patch features into sparse 3D anchors that gather context from their 3D neighbors, and expands them where rendering errors are predicted to be high. Our second stage lifts fine tokens from all views into 3D and applies serialized attention over their 3D neighborhoods, so that tokens separated by view grouping can interact.

Iterative refinement.

Iterative minimization of an objective has long been a standard approach to solving vision problems [(Lucas and Kanade, 1981; Sun et al., 2010)], and learning-based methods have sought to emulate this process by repeatedly updating an initial estimate. Such learned iterative refinement often outperforms single-step regression and has been successfully applied to a broad range of applications, such as optical flow [(Teed and Deng, 2020)], human pose estimation [(Newell et al., 2016; Carreira et al., 2016)], stereo matching [(Lipson et al., 2021)], SLAM [(Teed and Deng, 2021)], structure-from-motion [(Li et al., 2025)], multi-view stereo [(Wang et al., 2022)], and multi-view 3D reconstruction [(Burzio et al., 2026)]. For Gaussian splatting, prior works refine Gaussians with a single-step or multiple-step network [(Chen et al., 2025; Nam et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026a)], learn updates from rendering gradients [(Chen et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Pearl et al., 2026)] or rendering errors [(Xu et al., 2026)], or fine-tune Gaussian tokens for each scene [(Ren et al., 2026)].

3 Method

Given N context views with or without known camera poses, FineSplat predicts a set of 3D Gaussians in a feed-forward manner. Stage 1 divides each context view into fine-grained 4×4 patches and encodes them with attention of varying scope, where group-wise attention over a few views keeps fine-grained multi-view reasoning affordable. Stage 2 decodes these tokens into an initial set of Gaussians, renders them back into the context views, and uses the resulting error maps to update the tokens through 3D spatial grouping, which lets tokens that fall in different view groups interact once they are lifted to 3D. This dual-grouping strategy makes fine-grained encoding tractable, with 3D spatial grouping complementing view-wise grouping by connecting tokens across view groups. Figure 2 gives an overview of the two stages.

3.1 Stage 1: View-wise token grouping

Global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive with fine-grained tokens. In the first stage, we restrict the attention scope and adopt a view-wise token grouping strategy. Specifically, we leverage the multi-view pyramid architecture (MVP) [(Kang et al., 2026b)]. It performs fine-grained attention within small groups of views, while allowing information exchange across all views through coarser global tokens. This balances local detail preservation with global multi-view reasoning. It organizes its encoder as a three-level pyramid, and we denote the feature map of level ℓ∈{1,2,3} as F^ℓ, from the finest (F¹) to the coarsest (F³). In more detail, given N input images I∈ℝ^N×H×W×3 and patch size p, the first stage fuses the three levels of coarse-to-fine features into M=NHW/p² fine-grained tokens z⁽⁰⁾∈ℝ^M×d,

z⁽⁰⁾=fuse(up(fuse(up(F³)+F²))+F¹),

(1)

where up(·) denotes bilinear upsampling and fuse(·) a convolutional fusion block, which are used to match the token resolutions.

The fixed view grouping strategy inevitably leaves blind spots: fine-grained tokens in different groups cannot directly interact, potentially missing relevant observations from other input views. Thus, view-wise grouping alone cannot fully realize fine-grained multi-view reasoning over all input views. To recover these missing interactions, we pass the fine-grained tokens to the subsequent 3D spatial grouping stage.

3.2 Stage 2: 3D spatial token grouping

Starting from the fine-grained tokens z⁽⁰⁾ produced by the first stage, we first decode an initial set of 3D Gaussians. Specifically, a lightweight Gaussian head D, implemented as a linear decoder, maps each token to K Gaussian primitives and their attributes. We then use the predicted Gaussian centers to lift the corresponding tokens into 3D space, where tokens are regrouped according to their spatial proximity in 3D world coordinates. We then perform self-attention within each 3D group, enabling fine-grained interactions between geometrically related tokens even when they originate from different view groups. To further refine the current estimate, we augment this interaction with reconstruction-error information obtained by rendering the input views. The updated tokens are subsequently decoded into a new set of Gaussian primitives, and this process of Gaussian prediction, 3D grouping, error-guided interaction, and token update is repeated for multiple steps.

Lifting tokens to 3D.

To reason about the tokens in a common 3D space, we anchor each token at the mean position of the Gaussians it produces. Given the j-th token at the i-th step, zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝᵈ,

{μⱼₖ⁽ⁱ⁾}ₖ₌₁^K=D(zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾), pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^Kμⱼₖ⁽ⁱ⁾,

(2)

where μⱼₖ⁽ⁱ⁾∈ℝ³ is the position of each predicted Gaussian. Each token is then projected by a linear layer, yielding a point cloud {(pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾,zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾)}ⱼ₌₁^M whose points carry the fine-grained tokens as features.

Error feature maps.

To measure how well the current Gaussians explain the observations, we render them into every input view. For the n-th context view, we define a signed error map between the input image Iₙ and the rendered image Îₙ, computed as Eₙ=Îₙ-Iₙ. To complement this pixel-level discrepancy with structural cues, we additionally compute a feature-level difference Δφₙ=φ(Îₙ)-φ(Iₙ), where φ(·) is a pretrained ResNet-18 [(He et al., 2016)] encoder. These two terms are combined with the finest-scale features from the first stage, F¹ₙ, which provide the image context in which the errors occur. We obtain the error feature map as follows,

Fₙᵉʳʳ=[ 𝔼ₑᵣᵣ(Eₙ,Δφₙ) ; 𝔼_feat(F¹ₙ) ]∈ℝ^H/p×W/p×dₑ,

(3)

where F¹ₙ denotes the finest-scale features from the first stage for an input view n, 𝔼ₑᵣᵣ and 𝔼_feat are linear embedding layers, and [·;·] represents the feature concatenation.

Gathering errors across views.

A Gaussian affects the rendering of every view in which it is visible, not only the view from which it was predicted. We therefore gather error features for each token from both its own view and the other views that observe it. Let πₙ(·) denote the projection onto the error feature map of view n, and let vⱼₙ∈{0,1} indicate whether pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ lies inside the view n’s frustum and passes an occlusion test against the rendered depth. The aggregated error feature is obtained by averaging the bilinearly sampled features over the visible views,

eⱼᵃᵍᵍ=(∑ₙ₌₁^Nvⱼₙ Fₙᵉʳʳ(πₙ(pⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾)))/(∑ₙ₌₁^Nvⱼₙ),

(4)

where Fₙᵉʳʳ(·) reads a feature given a projected coordinate. In addition, we take the error feature at the patch from which zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾ originates, denoted as eⱼ^self. While eⱼ^self provides a direct signal from the source view, eⱼᵃᵍᵍ summarizes how consistently the token explains the other views. The two are fused into the final error feature eⱼ=Linear([eⱼ^self;eⱼᵃᵍᵍ]).

3D spatial token grouping and update.

Each lifted point is assigned the feature hⱼ=Linear([zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾;eⱼ]). Neighboring tokens in 3D often originate from different views and describe the same surface, so correcting them jointly is more effective than correcting each token independently. We thus exchange information among nearby points using serialized attention [(Wu et al., 2024)], which orders the points along a space-filling curve, partitions them into groups of S consecutive points, and applies self-attention within each group. Compared with explicit k-nearest-neighbor search, this provides local 3D context at a much lower cost and scales favorably with the number of tokens. The updated features are projected to a token residual by a linear layer,

Δzⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾=Linear(SerialAttn(hⱼ)), zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁺¹⁾=zⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾+Δzⱼ⁽ⁱ⁾.

(5)

Then, the updated tokens are decoded into Gaussians with the shared Gaussian head D. Our Stage 2 module is applied for T=4 steps, starting from z⁽⁰⁾: each step takes the tokens from the previous one, re-renders the context views, recomputes the error features, and regroups the tokens at their updated 3D positions.

3.3 Patch-aligned Sub-pixel Gaussian Reconstruction

To obtain a dense Gaussian representation while preserving the spatial structure of image features, we predict four Gaussians for each 4×4 fine-grained token, assigning each Gaussian to one of four non-overlapping 2×2 sub-patches. Rather than constraining a Gaussian to the fixed center ray of its assigned sub-patch, we learn a two-dimensional image-space offset Δ=(Δₓ,Δ_y) that adaptively shifts its ray within the corresponding region. Specifically, for a sub-patch with stride s=2, we bound the offset as δₓ=s/2\tanh(Δₓ),δ_y=s/2\tanh(Δ_y), such that δₓ,δ_y∈[-s/2,s/2]. This guarantees that each Gaussian remains within its designated 2×2 sub-patch while allowing continuous sub-pixel localization. Given the center (u_c,v_c) of each sub-patch, the displaced image coordinate is (u,v)=(u_c,v_c)+δ, which is unprojected using the predicted camera intrinsics. We then transform and normalize this direction using the camera-to-world rotation, with the camera translation serving as the corresponding ray origin.

4 Experiments

4.1 Implementation Details

Setup.

We train a single model only on the DL3DV [(Ling et al., 2024)] dataset, sampling the number of input context views from {6,12,24,32} for each training scene, and use this one checkpoint for all evaluations without dataset-specific fine-tuning. On DL3DV, we evaluate on 140 test scenes with N∈{6,12,24} context views, selected via farthest point sampling with maximum temporal frame gaps of 50, 100, and 150, respectively. We further evaluate zero-shot generalization on 1,600 RealEstate10K (RE10K) [(Zhou et al., 2018)] test scenes with N=6, and on Mip-NeRF 360 [(Barron et al., 2022)] with N∈{32,64,128}, following the view indices from [Veicht et al. (2026)]. Mip-NeRF 360 is a demanding target for a model trained on DL3DV: it covers both indoor and outdoor scenes, its scenes are unbounded, its cameras orbit the scene rather than sweep through it, and it uses far more context views than the 32 seen during training. We hold out 8 target views on all three datasets. For a fair comparison, each method encodes and renders at its native training resolution, and all rendered outputs are resized to 224×224 for evaluation, following [Ye et al. (2026)] (252 × 252 results are provided in Appendix B.3). We report PSNR, SSIM [(Wang et al., 2004)], and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)], averaged over all test scenes.

Supervision and scene normalization.

FineSplat is trained without any depth supervision, using only a mean squared error term and a perceptual term on the rendered views. Several of the baselines instead rely on depth: AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)], DepthSplat [(Xu et al., 2025)], NoDrift3R [(Sun et al., 2026)], DA3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], and ZipSplat [(Veicht et al., 2026)] all use a depth objective during training. Since feed-forward reconstruction is scale-ambiguous, we bring each scene to a canonical scale using only the context camera poses: poses are expressed in the mean context camera frame and translations are rescaled so that all context camera centers lie within [-1,1]³. The same transform is applied to the target poses, both ground-truth and DA3-predicted. ZipSplat instead derives the scene scale from depth at evaluation time, unprojecting per-view depth maps predicted by DA3 and taking the median distance of the resulting points to the first context camera. Details of the scene scale normalization are provided in Appendix A.3. Since we evaluate on the same Mip-NeRF 360 scenes and view indices as ZipSplat, the two differ only in how this scale is obtained: its normalization depends on a dense depth prior, whereas ours needs only camera positions and transfers directly to predicted poses.

Baselines.

We compare against the pose-free methods AnySplat [(Jiang et al., 2025)], C3G [(An et al., 2025)], DA3 [(Lin et al., 2025)], YoNoSplat [(Ye et al., 2026)], NoDrift3R [(Sun et al., 2026)], 2Xplat [(Jeong et al., 2026)], and ZipSplat [(Veicht et al., 2026)], as well as NoPoSplat [(Ye et al., 2025a)], which additionally requires ground-truth camera intrinsics. For pose-dependent methods, we compare against DepthSplat [(Xu et al., 2025)] and MVP [(Kang et al., 2026b)].

4.2 Novel view synthesis

Benchmark performance.

item.title: 城市级 3D 纹理不需要城市级 3D 数据：CityPaint 借 2D 扩散先验 + top-K 相机烘焙反投影 ｜ CityPaint: A Free Lunch from 2D Diffusion for City-Scale 3D Texturing
item.description:
一句话：缺的是城市级 3D 训练数据，多的是一望无际的 2D 图像与扩散模型；用几何先验把 2D 先验投上去，再按地形/建筑分开精修。

要点：

  • 现有方法要么把独立生成的资产拼接起来，要么只用合成城市语料学习，真实感与全局一致性都打折
  • CityPaint 把几何先验和 2D 扩散模型的生成能力结合，用 top-K 相机烘焙做迭代纹理投影，得到全局一致的城市级纹理
  • 针对 2D→3D 投影伪影，设计解耦精修机制：地形纹理与建筑纹理分开优化
  • 全局阶段在 8192×8192 UV 图集上从 320 个视角迭代贴图；精修阶段按 1024×1024 UV tile 处理，去噪强度 0.2、共享全局噪声初始化；全部实验在单张 A100 40GB 上完成

为什么值得看：数字孪生与开放世界需要「几百米尺度、全局一致」的贴图；把 2D 扩散当纹理源、把几何当约束，比训练城市级 3D 生成模型便宜得多。

中文摘要：生成高保真城市级 3D 环境对 VR、游戏与城市数字孪生都很关键，但真实城市级 3D 训练数据稀缺，现有方法只能拼接独立生成的资产或依赖合成城市语料，真实感与全局一致性都受限。相比之下 2D 图像及其生成模型极其丰富，编码了很强的视觉先验。CityPaint 因此用 2D 扩散模型生成全局一致的城市级 3D 纹理，完全不依赖城市级 3D 训练数据：它把几何先验与 2D 扩散的生成能力结合，引入稳健的 top-K 相机烘焙策略做迭代纹理投影；针对 2D 到 3D 投影产生的伪影，又设计了把地形与建筑纹理分开优化的解耦精修机制。实验显示该方法能产出全局协调的城市级纹理。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

CityPaint: A Free Lunch from 2D Diffusion for City-Scale 3D Texturing

© cc

Abstract.

Generating high-fidelity, city-scale 3D environments plays a crucial role in applications such as virtual reality, gaming, and urban digital twins. However, the scarcity of real-world city-scale 3D training data forces existing methods to either stitch independently generated assets or learn from synthetic urban corpora, often sacrificing realism and global consistency. In contrast, 2D image data and their corresponding generative models are abundant and encode rich visual priors. To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a novel framework that leverages 2D diffusion models to generate globally consistent city-scale 3D textures without relying on city-scale 3D training data. Specifically, CityPaint integrates geometric priors with the generative power of 2D diffusion models, introducing a robust top-K camera baking strategy for iterative texture projection. To address the artifacts of 2D-to-3D projection, we further propose a decoupled refinement mechanism that separately optimizes terrain and building textures. Extensive experiments show that CityPaint produces globally coherent textures with fine local details and achieves favorable results against strong baselines in both visual quality and cross-view consistency.

Keywords:

Scene Generation, Diffusion Models, Generative Multimedia ††cc-license: by

1. Introduction

The demand for expansive, high-fidelity 3D urban environments has surged in recent years, driven by rapidly expanding applications in virtual reality, immersive gaming, autonomous driving simulation, and urban digital twins [(Kim et al., 2018; González-Medina et al., 2015; Jamei et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2016)]. Traditionally, constructing these large-scale scenes relies on exhaustive manual modeling by technical artists [(Chen et al., 2023b)]. While recent advancements in 3D generative AI have shown remarkable success in synthesizing single objects or constrained indoor scenes [(Poole et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2023)], subsequent feed-forward and texturing-oriented systems have further improved consistency and efficiency [(Long et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025)]. Scaling these capabilities to the magnitude of an entire city nevertheless remains a formidable challenge.

The primary bottleneck in city-scale 3D generation lies in the extreme scarcity of high-quality, real-world urban 3D data. Constrained by this limitation, existing generative approaches are forced into a fundamental trade-off, typically falling into one of two suboptimal paradigms. On one hand, bottom-up instance composition methods synthesize individual buildings and subsequently stitch them into a scene [(Deng et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2025b)]. While scalable, such approaches inevitably break global contextual consistency and compromise stylistic coherence. On the other hand, holistic scene-level models rely on synthetic datasets or low-quality satellite imagery for training [(Lin et al., 2023b; Xie et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025a)], which introduce significant domain gaps and inherit physical artifacts, such as distorted (“melted”) geometries and baked-in shadows. As a result, the generated environments often lack the richness and realism of real-world cities.

In stark contrast, while 3D urban data remains scarce, 2D image data is abundantly available. Modern diffusion models [(Rombach et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2024; Crowson et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2025)] have demonstrated an extraordinary ability to capture globally consistent visual priors, encoding rich semantic structures of urban layouts and architectural styles. This raises a fundamental question: can we leverage these pre-trained 2D priors as a “free lunch” to enable photorealistic 3D city texturing without requiring city-scale 3D supervision?

To bridge this gap, we propose CityPaint, a 3D-data-free framework that reformulates city-scale 3D generation as a geometry-grounded generative reconstruction problem. Instead of synthesizing unconstrained 3D volumes from scratch, CityPaint leverages readily available geographic data, such as OpenStreetMap, to initialize a semantically structured city mesh. As illustrated in Fig. 1, this lightweight geometric scaffold serves as a structural canvas, onto which the generative power of pre-trained 2D diffusion models is projected, enabling diverse textures and stylistic variations directly on 3D surfaces.

However, directly projecting 2D generations onto large-scale 3D geometry introduces significant challenges. Fixed-height camera trajectories either collide with tall structures or drift excessively above low-rise regions, while oblique viewpoints lead to severe texture distortion and cross-view inconsistencies. To address these issues, CityPaint introduces a heightfield-aware camera placement strategy that adapts to local urban geometry, ensuring stable and consistent observations. Furthermore, rather than naively averaging multi-view projections, we propose a robust face-wise top-K camera baking scheme. By explicitly modeling visibility and discarding grazing-angle observations, this strategy enables seamless texture aggregation into a globally coherent UV atlas, effectively avoiding the blurring artifacts common in conventional blending approaches.

To account for the distinct visual characteristics of different urban elements, we introduce a decoupled refinement mechanism. Large-scale top-down renderings often lack sufficient resolution to capture fine-grained facade details, while stitched terrain patches tend to introduce noticeable seams. These observations suggest that a uniform treatment of the entire city is inherently suboptimal. To address this, CityPaint decomposes the refinement process, optimizing each structural component in its most suitable representation.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We propose CityPaint, a novel 3D-data-free framework that leverages the rich visual priors of pre-trained 2D diffusion models to generate high-fidelity and globally consistent city-scale 3D textures.

  • •

    We introduce a heightfield-aware observation policy, coupled with a robust top-K camera baking strategy, which effectively resolves visibility conflicts and mitigates texture distortion in large-scale 2D-to-3D projection.

  • •

    We design a decoupled refinement mechanism that optimizes terrain in UV space and building facades in instance space, significantly improving both global continuity and fine-grained structural details.

  • •

    Extensive experiments show that CityPaint achieves stronger overall performance than the evaluated baselines in visual fidelity, realism, and cross-view consistency, offering a scalable solution for high-quality urban 3D content generation.

    • 2. Related Work

    2.1. 2D-to-3D Generation via Diffusion Priors

    The emergence of large-scale 2D diffusion models has significantly advanced 3D content generation. A dominant line of work leverages Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) [(Poole et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023a; Tang et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024)] to lift 2D diffusion priors into 3D representations, including Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [(Mildenhall et al., 2021)], explicit meshes, and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [(Kerbl et al., 2023)]. In parallel, feed-forward and multi-view diffusion models [(Liu et al., 2023; Höllein et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024)] have been proposed to improve generation efficiency and enforce cross-view consistency. Despite these advances, existing approaches are primarily designed for object-centric scenarios and struggle to scale to unbounded and structurally complex environments. In particular, unconstrained optimization in SDS-based methods often suffers from over-smoothing, mode collapse, and multi-face artifacts, while feed-forward approaches remain limited by their reliance on implicit geometric priors. These limitations become more pronounced in urban scenes, where large spatial extents, intricate structural layouts, and ambiguous text descriptions jointly exacerbate geometric inconsistencies and texture misalignment. Rather than relying on unstable gradient-based distillation, CityPaint grounds the generative process on deterministic geometry derived from semantic maps. This design effectively reduces spatial ambiguity and enables precise, globally consistent texture synthesis at the city scale.

    2.2. Urban Scene Generation

    Recent deep learning approaches for urban scene generation generally follow two paradigms. The first is instance-based composition, which employs object-level asset pipelines [(Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2025b)] to generate individual buildings that are subsequently populated onto layouts sourced from OpenStreetMap [(OpenStreetMap contributors, 2017)], satellite or generative models [(Deng et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024)]. However, this bottom-up assembly naturally neglects the global urban context, resulting in disjointed environments with conflicting architectural styles.

    The second paradigm attempts holistic scene generation by training directly on large-scale 3D urban datasets. These approaches typically rely on either synthetic city corpora [(Li et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2025a; Hua et al., 2025)] or real-world captures such as satellite and Google Earth imagery [(Lin et al., 2023b; Xie et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025)].
