  float weight = sector_weights[k] * radial_gaussian_weight;
  sum_of_weights_of_sectors[k % (number_of_sectors / 2)] += weight;

  int upper_index = k;
  weighted_mean_of_color_of_sectors[upper_index] += upper_color * weight;
  weighted_mean_of_squared_color_of_sectors[upper_index] += upper_color_squared * weight;

  int lower_index = (k + number_of_sectors / 2) % number_of_sectors;
  weighted_mean_of_color_of_sectors[lower_index] += lower_color * weight;
  weighted_mean_of_squared_color_of_sectors[lower_index] += lower_color_squared * weight;
}

    This makes the shader run 10 TIMES faster.

    It was taking 220ms before, and now it runs in 20.4ms. The shader instruction mix went from (12% float math, 87% conditional and integer) to (79% float math, 17% conditional and integer), which feels way more sensible. It still uses 192 registers and spills (64 bytes -> 48 bytes), but that’s a topic for another day. And the (unrolled) inner loops are now all just math instructions:

    Okay, but what about other GPUs?

    Fair question! I only have two GPUs around here, the other one being RTX 3080Ti. Which, funnily enough, is another GPU where the GPU vendor does not easily allow you to see “what is the actual GPU assembly” bit :)

    Nsight Graphics allows me to debug and profile graphics applications, but for example when using Vulkan, it can show me which of the SPIR-V assembly instructions were costly, but how they map into the underlying GPU instructions, is anyone’s guess.

    In this particular case, speedrun of Kuwahara through Nsight (2026.3 version): Start Activity, pick “GPU Trace Profiler” option, turn on “Real-Time Shader Profiler”, launch the application, do a capture. Find the expensive compute shader dispatch in the timeline (it takes 17.8ms here):

    In lower right corner, under 

    Shader Pipelines
    section, it displays some data about this compute pipeline:

    It can run 8 warps, uses 204 registers (198 live registers), average warp latency is 134K, instruction mix: 44% FMA FP32, 36% data movement.

    With unrolled loop, now our compute dispatch takes only 9.5ms:

    And it can run 16 warps, uses 113 registers (103 live registers), average warp latency is 45K, instruction mix: 60% FMA FP32, 13% data movement.

    So yes even on RTX 3080Ti this particular shader gets twice as fast by just unrolling the inner loop. Half the registers results in twice the occupancy here, but TBH I did not dig much deeper into why exactly the register usage has decreased.

    What’s the lesson?

    Yes the loop unrolling should be left to the compiler… except when it should not :) Sometimes, you should unroll it. Some other times, you should absolutely not unroll it (unrolled loop can incur much higher instruction fetch cost, for example). GLHF!

    That by itself is not very useful, so perhaps a better lesson is - it helps to have at least a vague understanding of what sort of performance should be expected. This way you can go “wait a minute, this feels way too slow” and investigate. In this case, I wanted to fix seemingly very bad compute shader performance on an Apple GPU (and sped it up ten times), but a side effect was that on an NVIDIA GPU the shader also got twice as fast.

    It helps if the performance analysis tools can point out some sort of data that makes you go “huh wait, this should not be here”, like in this case, majority of shader instructions being integer compare/selects. It would be even better if these tools could actually show more data; for Apple GPUs in Xcode frame capture and NVIDIA GPUs in Nsight, I’d like to see GPU assembly. One can dream!

    And now I’ll go and ship these Kuwahara node performance improvements in Blender (PR 164617, just merged for upcoming Blender 5.3). There’s probably more work to do in that area, but that’s for later.

item.title: 别再等 domain reload：MethodReload 只热替换你标了属性的方法体，编辑器和真机都能用 ｜ Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature
item.description:

要点：

  • domain reload 来自 Mono 的 AppDomain 模型：拆域、加载新程序集、重新 JIT、同进程继续；粗暴之处在于改一个方法也全量重来，而 IL2CPP 干脆不支持，任何改动都要整包重编

为什么值得看：这条思路可移植：把「热重载」的粒度从程序集降到方法体，量级直接从几十秒变几秒。代价是要在编译期织入、要求方法签名受限，并且必须与其他资产导入策略配合。

中文摘要：Unity 推出实验性包 MethodReload，目标是消掉迭代中最烦的那段等待：改一点玩法代码就要等 Editor 完成 domain reload，上真机更是每次都要整包重编。文章先解释根因——Play Mode 建在 Mono 的 AppDomain 之上，代码改动会拆域、加载新程序集、重新 JIT，改一个方法和改一百个方法代价相同；而 IL2CPP 完全不支持 domain reload，CoreCLR 虽去掉了 domain 概念但仍需重载程序集，因此该方案同样适用。使用方法很简单：给要迭代的方法打 [MethodReload]（必须 public，返回 void 或 IEnumerator，否则编译期告警并跳过），开启 watcher，进入 Play Mode 或连接 development player，之后编辑方法体，运行实例在下一次调用时就用新实现。真机模式下用 player 的预处理宏编译并推送到所有已连接设备，无需重启。限制是较大改动仍走常规编译，watcher 期间 auto-refresh 关闭、其他资产需手动刷新，且 watch 要能跨 domain reload 重放编辑。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

Skipping domain reload: faster iteration using the MethodReload feature

Oct 22, 2026Programming and DevOpsProgramming and DevOps

We've all been there: you tweak some gameplay code and then wait for the Editor to complete a domain reload. The process can slow down your iteration time and really drain your creativity. Not to mention the extra time spent iterating on a device, where each cycle requires a full build.

Our answer to this is MethodReload. We demoed it on stage at Unite Seoul and it is available now as an experimental package. In this post we’ll cover how to use MethodReload, what its limitations are, and how it compares to hot reload tools you may already have in your project.

Why we're stuck reloading

A little history helps here, because the reason domain reload exists is also the reason it's hard to get rid of.

Play Mode was built on Mono's AppDomains where code changes kicked off a familiar process: tear down the domain, load the new assemblies, re-JIT, and then resume in the same process. For years that was a genuine superpower, and it's a big part of why iterating in Unity felt fast compared to building a player.

It's also a blunt instrument, meaning that during the reload everything goes away and everything comes back, whether you changed one method or one hundred. Furthermore, IL2CPP doesn’t support domain reloads at all, so every change requires rebuilding the entire player.

You might be asking yourself, “won't CoreCLR fix this?” and the answer is: Not magically. While CoreCLR does away with domain reloads, it still has to reload assemblies, and MethodReload can help here as well.

How to use MethodReload

As mentioned above, MethodReload is available now and it ships in 

com.unity.pipeline
, currently at 
0.7.0-exp.1
.

The process of using MethodReload is fairly simple. Just tag one or more methods with the 

[MethodReload]
attribute, start the watcher, enter Play Mode or attach a development player, and then edit the body of your methods. The running instance picks up the new body on its next call.

MethodReload doesn't replace domain reloads completely, however. Bigger changes still go through the usual compile. But for the small tweaks that make up most of an iteration loop, it turns a long wait into a matter of seconds, in the Editor and on device alike.

Try it out

The fastest way to understand MethodReload is to run it, so if you’d like to test this out yourself, here are some steps to get you started. Note: since this is an experimental feature, the process may change in the future and be different from what is described here

1. Install the package (Unity 6.0+ required).You can either install it through the Unity CLI or use the Package Manager to add the Pipeline package manually using “Install package by technical name” and this string: 

com.unity.pipeline@0.7.0-exp.1
.

2. Tag the methods you iterate on. The attribute has to be there before you enter Play Mode or build a player, because the dispatch check is woven in at compile time. Tagged methods must be 

public
(instance or static) and return 
void
or 
IEnumerator
; anything else is skipped at build time with a warning.

using Unity.Pipeline.MethodReload;
using UnityEngine;

public class Spinner : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float rotationSpeed = 90f;

    [MethodReload]
    public void Update()
    {
        transform.Rotate(Vector3.up, rotationSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
    }
}

3. Start the watcher.In order for your MethodReload to see your changes live, you will need to start the MethodReload Watcher. Do this by going to Project Settings → Pipeline → Editor, then in the “Method Reload Interpreter Watch” section, click Start Watching.

While the watcher covers the whole Assets tree, a saved 

.cs
only compiles if it contains a 
MethodReload
attribute, so unrelated saves cost you nothing.

4. If testing in the editor: enter Play Mode.Once running, any tagged code change will be compiled and injected in place. Once you leave play mode, your changes will compile and go through the usual domain reload.

5. If testing on device: plug in a device. Build a development player with the runtime Pipeline driver enabled. Connect the device with Autoconnect Profiler, or attach through the Profiler or Console window. From then on, every save compiles in the Editor using the player's preprocessor defines and pushes to every connected player. No restart is needed in either direction.

Two workflow details worth knowing up front:

  • Auto-refresh is off while the watcher runs, so a save reloads instead of triggering a domain reload; other assets won't import until you hit Ctrl/Cmd+R, and Stop Watching puts your settings back.
  • The watch survives domain reloads: it re-applies edits that a Play Mode reload wiped, and re-pushes to a player that reconnects, since a restarted player boots the original compiled code.

    • What about using the CLI?

    If you prefer working in a terminal, want to work through an agent, or want to push every tagged method rather than only what changed since the watch started, the same functionality is exposed as Unity CLI commands:

    # Reload in the Editor through the interpreter
unity command reload_file_editor_interpreter "Assets/Scripts/Spinner.cs"

# Compile in the Editor, push to connected players (folders work too)
unity command reload_file_player_interpreter "Assets/Scripts" --player 2

    Limitations

    There's no way around domain reload without compromises, and the limitations on MethodReload are in three places: what kinds of change it can apply, what C# it can run, and how fast it runs.

    Only tagged method bodies change. A reload never touches call sites, fields, or type layout. No new fields, no new classes. That constraint is what makes it safe to apply to a live instance, and it's the one you plan around: decide which methods you'll be iterating on and tag them. A reload can declare a new method and call it from a reloaded body, but that method can't be a reload entry point, because nothing compiled knows to call it until your next real compile.

    It runs a C# subset. The interpreter is hand-built and has to stay small enough to live inside a player, so it doesn't implement all of C#. Inside a 

    [MethodReload]
    body you cannot use:

  • await
    and 
    Task
    , 
    try
    /
    catch
    /
    finally
    , 
    lock
    , LINQ query syntax, 
    checked
  • decimal
    , 
    dynamic
    , reflection types, threading types
  • ref
    , 
    out
    , and 
    in
    parameters, 
    ref
    returns and locals, multi-dimensional arrays (jagged is fine), generic methods

    • What does work covers most gameplay code : primitives, method calls, loops, delegates, string interpolation, coroutine 

    yield
    , collections. A Roslyn analyzer ships with the package and flags violations in your IDE, on tagged bodies only, so you find out while typing rather than after a push.

    On device, interpreted code can only call what the player exposes. IL2CPP strips code with no references, so a reloaded body that calls a UnityEngine or BCL member your build never used has nothing to call. In the Editor, missing members bind on demand. On a device, the push checks up front and lists missing members as warnings; if the code reaches one anyway, it throws an exception. Rule of thumb: change what a method does, not the set of APIs it depends on.

    Interpreted code is slower than compiled code. That's the nature of an interpreter, whether the comparison is IL2CPP ahead of time or Mono and CoreCLR just in time. It only affects tagged methods in development builds. In release builds there is no prologue and no interpreter; a tagged method just runs its compiled body. Ultimately, it is up to you to decide if the performance hit during iteration is worth the improved iteration speed and convenience.

    Coroutines pick up changes at creation. A 

    [MethodReload] IEnumerator
    method uses the new body the next time 
    StartCoroutine
    runs. Coroutines already in flight keep the body they started with. Pair it with 
    [OnMethodReloaded]
    , a parameterless instance method that fires on every live instance after a reload lands on its type, and you have a domain-reload-free 
    OnEnable
    for restarting long-lived loops:

    [OnMethodReloaded]
void OnMethodReloaded()
{
    StopAllCoroutines();
    StartCoroutine(MainLoop());
}

    How it works under the hood

    It's the combination of two ideas: the first is that compiling C# produces IL bytecode, and IL that stays inside a modest subset can be executed by an interpreter instead of being compiled. That interpreter is itself ordinary C#, so IL2CPP compiles it along with the rest of your game, which is what lets it run on device.

    The second idea is getting into it. Every 

    [MethodReload]
    method has a wired path to the interpreter. Branching to the interpreter is done by weaving a prologue in the tagged methods at compile time. Decompiled, it looks like this:

    [MethodReload]
public void TakeDamage(int amount)
{
    // weaved during compilation
    if (MethodReloadRegistry.HasOverride("Player.TakeDamage") &&
        MethodReloadRegistry.TryInvokeMethodReload(
            "Player.TakeDamage", this, amount))
    {
        return;
    }

    // initial code
    hp -= amount;
}

    The woven check asks the registry whether an override exists for this method. The watcher and the CLI fill that registry with freshly compiled IL. If there's an entry, the interpreter runs it and the original body is skipped. Otherwise the compiled code runs as usual.

    How this compares

    Good tools already exist for iterating on C# without a domain reload, and we'd rather be precise about where each applies than pretend they don't.

    Packages from the Asset Storepatch methods in a running Mono runtime. That gives them an excellent Editor experience, full C# in the reloaded body, no tagging step, and in Hot Reload's case an on-device mode for Mono player builds. All real advantages. It also means that they don’t work with an IL2CPP player because there's no runtime to patch.

    .NET Hot Reload, the feature in Visual Studio and Rider for .NET applications, applies edits through the runtime's edit-and-continue path. It's built for CoreCLR and doesn't target Unity's Mono or IL2CPP runtimes.

    MethodReload sits in a different spot with its interpreter backend trading language coverage for reach: a subset of C#, but running on the same IL2CPP development build you'd otherwise be redeploying to a phone or a console dev kit, over the cable you already have plugged in, with no extra server in the player and no port to open.

    Honest version: if your iteration pain lives in the Editor, the existing tools are mature and you should keep using what works for you. If your iteration pain lives on a device, and especially on IL2CPP, this is the first option that goes there.

    Final tips

    If you're setting up a workflow for a project right now:

  • Tag your hot spots.
    [MethodReload]
    costs nothing in release builds, so tag the 
    Update
    , tuning, and game-feel methods you know you'll be poking at on device.
  • Let the analyzer keep you inside the subset. If a method needs 
    try
    /
    catch
    or 
    await
    , move that part into an untagged helper and reload the logic around it. The analyzer will let you know if you’re doing something wrong.
  • Try it in the Editor first. The watcher, or 
    reload_file_editor_interpreter
    from the CLI, runs your edit through the same interpreter that runs on device. If it works there, it will work on hardware, so you catch subset and missing-API problems without waiting on a build.

    • What's next

    The command reference, the runtime setup page, and the full constraint list are in the 

    com.unity.pipeline
    docs.

    We encourage you to try this out in your projects and let us know how it goes. Feedback is greatly appreciated and experimental packages improve fastest when people push on them.

    Domain reload isn't going anywhere for the changes that require it. For the changes that don't, you can stop waiting.

It only affects tagged methods in development builds. In release builds there is no prologue and no interpreter; a tagged method just runs its compiled body. Ultimately, it is up to you to decide if the performance hit during iteration is worth the improved iteration speed and convenience.

    Coroutines pick up changes at creation. A 

    [MethodReload] IEnumerator
    method uses the new body the next time 
    StartCoroutine
    runs. Coroutines already in flight keep the body they started with. Pair it with 
    [OnMethodReloaded]
    , a parameterless instance method that fires on every live instance after a reload lands on its type, and you have a domain-reload-free 
    OnEnable
    for restarting long-lived loops:

    [OnMethodReloaded]
void OnMethodReloaded()
{
    StopAllCoroutines();
    StartCoroutine(MainLoop());
}

    How it works under the hood

    It's the combination of two ideas: the first is that compiling C# produces IL bytecode, and IL that stays inside a modest subset can be executed by an interpreter instead of being compiled. That interpreter is itself ordinary C#, so IL2CPP compiles it along with the rest of your game, which is what lets it run on device.

    The second idea is getting into it. Every 

    [MethodReload]
    method has a wired path to the interpreter. Branching to the interpreter is done by weaving a prologue in the tagged methods at compile time. Decompiled, it looks like this:

    [MethodReload]
public void TakeDamage(int amount)
{
    // weaved during compilation
    if (MethodReloadRegistry.HasOverride("Player.TakeDamage") &&
        MethodReloadRegistry.TryInvokeMethodReload(
            "Player.TakeDamage", this, amount))
    {
        return;
    }

    // initial code
    hp -= amount;
}

    The woven check asks the registry whether an override exists for this method. The watcher and the CLI fill that registry with freshly compiled IL. If there's an entry, the interpreter runs it and the original body is skipped. Otherwise the compiled code runs as usual.

    How this compares

    Good tools already exist for iterating on C# without a domain reload, and we'd rather be precise about where each applies than pretend they don't.

    Packages from the Asset Storepatch methods in a running Mono runtime. That gives them an excellent Editor experience, full C# in the reloaded body, no tagging step, and in Hot Reload's case an on-device mode for Mono player builds. All real advantages. It also means that they don’t work with an IL2CPP player because there's no runtime to patch.

    .NET Hot Reload, the feature in Visual Studio and Rider for .NET applications, applies edits through the runtime's edit-and-continue path. It's built for CoreCLR and doesn't target Unity's Mono or IL2CPP runtimes.

    MethodReload sits in a different spot with its interpreter backend trading language coverage for reach: a subset of C#, but running on the same IL2CPP development build you'd otherwise be redeploying to a phone or a console dev kit, over the cable you already have plugged in, with no extra server in the player and no port to open.

    Honest version: if your iteration pain lives in the Editor, the existing tools are mature and you should keep using what works for you. If your iteration pain lives on a device, and especially on IL2CPP, this is the first option that goes there.

    Final tips

    If you're setting up a workflow for a project right now:

  • Tag your hot spots.
    [MethodReload]
    costs nothing in release builds, so tag the 
    Update
    , tuning, and game-feel methods you know you'll be poking at on device.
  • Let the analyzer keep you inside the subset. If a method needs 
    try
    /
    catch
    or 
    await
    , move that part into an untagged helper and reload the logic around it. The analyzer will let you know if you’re doing something wrong.
  • Try it in the Editor first. The watcher, or 
    reload_file_editor_interpreter
    from the CLI, runs your edit through the same interpreter that runs on device. If it works there, it will work on hardware, so you catch subset and missing-API problems without waiting on a build.

    • What's next

    The command reference, the runtime setup page, and the full constraint list are in the 

    com.unity.pipeline
    docs.

    We encourage you to try this out in your projects and let us know how it goes. Feedback is greatly appreciated and experimental packages improve fastest when people push on them.

    Domain reload isn't going anywhere for the changes that require it. For the changes that don't, you can stop waiting.

item.title: 《怪物猎人物语 3》的卡通渲染管线：先吃透 PBR 再故意偏离，前向光照验证完才换延迟 ｜ 《怪物猎人物语 3》动画渲染：光影与管线改
item.category: 公众号·游戏AI编程与图形渲染
item.description:
一句话：目标是把画面做成剧场版动画：赛璐璐底子上砍背景信息、给嘴唇下方单独开强制阴影通道，先在 7 帧的前向光照上验证，再切延迟光照。

要点：

  • 不走正传写实路子：抬身高体比、加细节，但保留赛璐璐底子；团队先吃透物理渲染参数，再故意偏离它
  • 草地法线统一朝一个固定方向、树叶呈放射状，背景里的琐碎信息一下就被压掉
  • 角色明暗分区清楚之后再塞细节：脸部法线抹平重映射、去掉鼻子多余投影，嘴唇下方这类指定阴影单独做成强制阴影通道，供后续管线随时读取
  • 完整环境光打上去阴影边缘容易变脏，所以受光面严格保护、环境光只渗进阴影面；后处理再单独调眩光、暗角与影色；该效果最初跑在前向光照上，最差场景掉到 7 帧，验证完才切到延迟光照并用自定义 G-buffer 存数据，美术可在 Substance 与 Maya 里直接预览

为什么值得看：卡通渲染的工程难点通常在「美术预期与光照模型打架」；这里给出的解法是先把风格化规则显式化成通道（强制阴影、法线重映射）与参数（法线方向），让管线各阶段都能读到同一份约定。

中文摘要：卡普空在《怪物猎人物语 3》里没有沿用正传的写实路线，而是要把画面直接做成剧场版动画：角色头身比拉高、细节更密，但赛璐璐的底子保留。团队的做法是先吃透物理渲染参数，再有意偏离它——草地法线统一朝固定方向、树叶呈放射状，背景中的琐碎信息因此大幅减少。角色方面先划分明暗区域再往里塞细节：脸部法线做抹平与重映射，去掉鼻子多余投影；嘴唇下方这类指定阴影单独做成强制阴影通道，让后续管线随时可读。完整的环境光打上去容易让阴影边缘变脏，于是受光面被严格保护、环境光只渗进阴影面，后处理还能单独调眩光、暗角与影色。这套效果最初跑在前向光照上，代价是负载过高、最差场景掉到 7 帧，验证完成后才切换到延迟光照，并用自定义 G-buffer 存储数据，让美术可在 Substance 与 Maya 中直接预览。

主题：游戏引擎

来源：公众号·游戏AI编程与图形渲染（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-25

本期推送：2026-10-26

卡普空这次做《怪物猎人物语3》，没走正传的写实路子。他们想让游戏画面直接变成剧场版动画。

角色头身比拉高，细节密了，但赛璐璐的底子还在。团队先吃透物理渲染参数，再故意偏离它。草地法线统一朝固定方向，树叶呈放射状。背景里的琐碎信息一下就少了。

角色明暗分区清楚后，再往里塞细节。脸部法线被抹平重映射，鼻子多余投影直接去掉。嘴唇下方这种指定阴影，单独做成强制阴影通道。这样后续管线随时都能读取。

完整环境光一打上去，阴影边缘容易变脏。所以受光面被严格保护，环境光只渗进阴影面。后处理还能单独调眩光、暗角和影色。

这套效果最初是用前向光照跑出来的。代价是负载太高，最差场景掉到 7 帧。验证完才切到延迟光照，靠自定义 G-buffer 存数据。美术在 Substance 和 Maya 里就能预览，不用反复切引擎。

item.title: 生成的烟和火没有涡：FluidGen 并联一路速度场输出，再把速度本身当 DPO 奖励 ｜ FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training
item.description:
一句话：视频模型在烟雾、火焰、爆炸碎屑上系统性失败——缺相干的涡结构；把逐帧速度场做成第二条输出流，物理一致性就有可监督、可奖励的量了。

要点：

  • 经典求解器物理保真但需要完整 3D 场景与精细调参，通用视频模型则会把流体塌成「平淡动力学」
  • 在预训练的 14B 图生视频 DiT 上并联一路 velocity head，RGB 与速度潜变量各 16 通道、按通道拼成 32 通道联合潜变量
  • 训练集 3.5 万条以上视频，混合 Houdini 高保真仿真（带速度场真值）与筛选过的真实流体视频（保证外观多样性）
  • 速度场既作为辅助监督把生成拉向物理一致的运动，又作为可解释的物理量当奖励，做 velocity-aware 的直接偏好优化

为什么值得看：对 VFX 与引擎特效来说，这意味着「生成出来的烟」第一次有了可查询的运动学量；要接进引擎的粒子/体积系统，速度场比像素更接近可直接消费的数据。

中文摘要：视频生成模型动作观感不错，但在流体现象上系统性失败：烟雾、火焰、爆炸碎屑往往缺少相干的涡结构，退化成违反真实流体物理的平淡运动。经典求解器物理保真度高，却需要详细三维场景与仔细调参，难以用于真实世界影像与视频生成。作者的做法是把一个数据驱动的流体先验注入预训练视频模型：训练数据混合高保真 Houdini 仿真（带有配对的速度场真值）与筛选过的真实流体视频以保外观多样性；模型采用双流架构，在生成 RGB 的同时逐帧预测速度场，由仿真真值监督。这个辅助信号既把生成约束到物理一致的运动上，又给出一个可解释的物理量，可进一步当作奖励做速度感知的直接偏好优化，从而在保持外观生动的同时产生结构更合理的流体运动。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-26

FluidGen: Physics-Aware Fluid Video Generation via Motion-Guided Post-Training

Abstract

Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Our data, code, and model will be publicly released. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/.

1 Introduction

Realistic fluid phenomena, including billowing smoke, rolling fire, and the dust and ash of an explosion, are among the most important visual elements in film, games, and immersive media, and also among the hardest to make look right. Their motion is driven by complex, turbulent physical dynamics, and humans can notice errors in problematic fluid dynamics immediately: for example a plume that rises too uniformly, a flame that moves in an unnatural direction, or a debris cloud without proper swirling structure. Synthesizing fluid content that holds up under this realism has been a long-standing goal in computer graphics, and despite decades of progress, it still typically requires expert artists, expensive simulation tools, and large amounts of manual effort.

One family of approaches treats fluid dynamics synthesis as a simulation problem. Classical physical solvers solve the Navier–Stokes equations [(Constantin and Foiaş, 1988)] on grids [(Stam, 2023; Bridson, 2015)], particles [(Müller et al., 2003; Zhu and Bridson, 2005)], or hybrid representations [(Macklin and Müller, 2013)], and produce physically faithful results when the scene parameters and boundary conditions are carefully defined. To extend simulation to single- or multi-view videos captured in the wild, more recent works reconstruct a 3D fluid representation from videos with regularization derived from physical priors [(Eckert et al., 2019; Chu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025)] and re-simulating with the reconstructed representation. Another line of work uses neural networks as replacements to accelerate explicit solvers [(Kim et al., 2019; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Ummenhofer et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2021)]. A shared fundamental component of these works is the reliance on manually designed simulation rules (e.g., Navier–Stokes equations) that are themselves only approximations of the highly complex fluid dynamics process. As a result, they remain brittle: small reconstruction errors build up, fluid parameters must be tuned per scene, and the state-of-the-art methods still struggle on the casual images that dominate real-world content.

A new family of approaches turns to large-scale generative models, which now carry remarkably strong priors over both motion and appearance from internet-scale training [(Wan et al., 2025; Brooks et al., 2024; Polyak et al., 2024; Bar-Tal et al., 2024)]. A natural way to use them in physical content creation is as a learned renderer on top of an explicit simulator, leaning on the generator’s appearance prior while leaving the dynamics to the solver. Yet on fluid phenomena specifically, this combination still falls short. On their own, modern video models consistently violate basic physical rules in scenes with complex fluid dynamics [(Motamed et al., 2025)]. Earlier physics-aware generation efforts have focused mostly on rigid [(Liu et al., 2024)] or elastic [(Tan et al., 2024)] objects rather than on volumetric, turbulent fluids. To close this gap on fluid dynamics, very recent works [(Li et al., 2025b; Zhan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026)] explicitly couple a video generator with an underlying simulator that provides fluid dynamics guidance. However, all aforementioned pipelines still depend on the heavy machinery of an authored 3D scene and a configured simulator, which limits their applicability to in-the-wild fluid content synthesis.

We argue that video model itself can learn complex fluid dynamics directly, but RGB supervision alone provides an insufficient training signal: appearance errors dominate the convergence while subtle physical errors are easily ignored. We therefore introduce an internal motion representation, jointly predicted with RGB, that explicitly exposes fluid dynamics to the model. Specifically, we predict a 3D velocity field describing fluid motion over time, providing a more physically meaningful representation than optical flow or trajectories [(Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b)].

This representation enables a clean two-stage post-training pipeline for a pretrained video diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. First, we jointly supervise RGB and velocity prediction using high-fidelity Houdini simulations with ground-truth velocity fields, together with in-the-wild fluid videos for appearance diversity and gives the model the generalization ability for in-the-wild content. Second, we perform velocity-aware DPO [(Rafailov et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025a)], using the model’s own predicted velocity field together with appearance signals to rank samples by physical plausibility. The resulting model produces more coherent vortices, natural advection, and fine-scale turbulent structure and clearly outperforms state-of-the-art strong video-generation and simulation-based baselines.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We propose a dual-head video model architecture that jointly predicts an internal fluid velocity field alongside RGB pixels, providing an explicit and interpretable physical signal that guides dynamics learning.

  • •

    We curate a fluid training corpus that pairs high-quality Houdini simulations with collected in-the-wild smoke, fire, and explosion footage, combining dense physical supervision with the appearance variety needed for real-world generalization.

  • •

    We design a two-stage training pipeline that first jointly supervises RGB and velocity prediction and then aligns the model outputs with a post-training stage using its own predicted velocity field as the reward.

    • 2 Related Work

    Fluid Simulation and Reconstruction. Realistic fluid visual effect synthesis in graphics has long been driven by analytical physical simulation. Classical Eulerian solvers discretize the Navier–Stokes equations on regular grids [(Stam, 2023; Bridson, 2015)], while particle-based formulations [(Müller et al., 2003; Zhu and Bridson, 2005)] represent fluids as collections of moving particles, and hybrid representations such as PBF [(Macklin and Müller, 2013)] balance accuracy with interactivity from both sides. To reduce simulation cost, neural networks have been used as accelerating components for the traditional solvers [(Kim et al., 2019; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020; Ummenhofer et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2021)]. Built on top of existing fluid simulation formulations, a complementary line of work aims to recover fluid representations directly from captured video and re-simulates them [(Eckert et al., 2019; Chu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2025b)]. Combined with differentiable rendering, these works directly build fluid assets from real-world captures instead of requiring manual construction in the simulator. However all of these methods rely on human-defined simulation rules and are bounded by the approximation accuracy. Our work takes the opposite path: we treat fluid dynamics as the learnable property of a video model itself, without the explicit solver at inference time.

    Physics-Aware Video Synthesis. Recent video diffusion models exhibit strong motion priors but are not necessarily physically faithful, and even frontier models still violate basic physical principles in scenes with complex dynamics [(Motamed et al., 2025; Bansal et al., 2025)]. A line of work combines traditional simulation with video generation. PhysGen [(Liu et al., 2024)] couples video generation with rigid-body physics through SDEdit [(Meng et al., 2021)], PhysMotion [(Tan et al., 2024)] extends this into the elastic domain, and PhysDreamer [(Zhang et al., 2024)] distills physical parameters using a video model as prior. These methods focus on solid materials and cannot naturally extend to volumetric, turbulent fluids. A second family [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] instead steers diffusion sampling with LLM-derived physical context. Another line of work fine-tunes video models on labeled synthetic data to emit auxiliary channels alongside RGB, though these channels are appearance properties, e.g., intrinsics [(Zeng et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025)] or weather [(Lin et al., 2025)], rather than the dynamical state we predict.

    To accommodate fluid effect synthesis, a recent line of work [(Li et al., 2025b; Zhan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026)] built the system on top of the multi-physics simulator [(Authors, 2024)], conditioning the video generation model through bi-modal control. Although these hybrid systems improve physical plausibility for fluids and also other materials, they still require an authored 3D scene and a configured simulator, limiting their applicability to generation from in-the-wild content. We share their goal but bake the physics directly into the video model through our model design and the training pipeline, with no manual effort on explicit simulators.

    Preference Optimization Post-Training. Preference optimization, as a post-training stage, has become a standard recipe for aligning generative models with human-defined high-dimensional quality. DPO [(Rafailov et al., 2023)] provides a simple offline formulation for the optimization target, and Diffusion-DPO [(Wallace et al., 2024)] further adapts it to training with diffusion models. VideoDPO [(Liu et al., 2025a)] extends preference alignment to the video diffusion domain with a multi-aspect scoring system, and DenseDPO [(Wu et al., 2026)] introduces fine-grained temporal preference labels to better target motion quality. EpipolarDPO [(Kupyn et al., 2025)] employs epipolar constraints to enhance geometry consistency of video generation. Inspired by these, we further treat physical quality, especially complex fluid effects, as another signal that can be used for preference optimization. In detail, we leverage our model’s native velocity field prediction as part of the reward signal, turning an auxiliary physical output into a physics-grounded preference indicator at the alignment stage.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    Our model is trained to jointly generate a fluid video and a pixel-aligned 3D velocity field video using a single video diffusion model, and subsequently trained with the reward metric computed directly from its own velocity field output. Therefore, velocity and RGB predictions serve two key roles. First, as an auxiliary motion signal that regularizes the appearance stream toward more coherent and consistent dynamics through this joint prediction [(Chefer et al., 2025)]. More importantly, it transforms every generated sample into the physical dynamics that can be evaluated directly, thereby enabling a velocity-based preference optimization stage without requiring any external motion estimator or simulator.

    Concretely, our architecture is a dual-head extension of a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)]) (§3.3) that produces both an RGB stream and a velocity stream from a shared latent. The model is trained in two stages: 1) Joint supervised fine-tuning (§3.4): a flow-matching [(Lipman et al., 2022)] objective over the joint latent trained on a mixed corpus of Houdini simulations with paired ground-truth velocity, and in-the-wild fluid videos. 2) Velocity-aware DPO post-training (§3.5): a DPO objective driven by a velocity-informed reward that evaluates each generated trajectory using its predicted velocity field. Both stages share the same model and output velocity representation, which we introduce first in §3.2.

    3.2 Velocity Field Representation

    At every pixel of each generated frame, we represent the 3D motion of the underlying fluid particles as a velocity vector v=(vₓ,v_y,v_z)∈ℝ³, expressed in the camera coordinate system. To remain compatible with the standard video model latent space and preserve the pretrained VAE encoder without modification, we do not regress v directly. Instead, we encode v into a three-channel color c∈[0,1]³ via a spherical decomposition, as illustrated in Fig. 3, and have the velocity head predict c as an auxiliary RGB-like stream. Let ρ=∥v∥, θ=\arccos(v_z/ρ)∈[0,π], and φ=atan2(v_y,vₓ)∈[-π,π]. The encoding is defined as

    c=(\tfracρS, \tfracθπ, \tfracφ+π2π)∈[0,1]³, S=σ√H²+W²,

    		(1)

    where (H,W) is the image resolution and the global scale σ=10⁻² is chosen such that typical advection magnitudes occupy the middle of the [0,1] range. At inference, the predicted c is decoded back to v by inverting Eq. 1.

    3.3 Dual-Head Joint Diffusion Architecture

    Our model builds upon a pretrained 14B image-to-video Diffusion Transformer [(Wan et al., 2025)], whose VAE encodes a video into a 16-channel spatiotemporal latent zʳᵍᵇ∈ℝ^16×T×h×w. We extend the backbone with a parallel velocity head operating on a velocity latent of identical shape, and concatenate the two along the channel dimension to form a joint latent, following VideoJam [(Chefer et al., 2025)]:

    z̃=[zʳᵍᵇ; zᵛᵉˡ]∈ℝ^32×T×h×w.

    		(2)

    The velocity latent is encoded and decoded using the same VAE as the RGB stream: we simply treat the encoded velocity image (Eq. 1) as an additional RGB clip. This preserves the pretrained perceptual capability of the backbone while avoiding the need to train a separate encoder-decoder latent space. Two transformer components are widened to support the joint latent (Fig. 2):

    Patch Embedding Input. The initial patchify projection is expanded so that its input depth grows from 16+K to 16+16+K, where K denotes the number of conditioning channels (conditional image and binary mask latent). The first 16+K channels reuse the pretrained weights directly, while the additional 16 corresponding to the velocity latent are zero-initialized. So the model can start the training stage without losing the base prediction ability.

    Output Head. The final projection layer mapping tokens back to patch space is widened from an output dimension of 16 to 32. The RGB channels reuse the pretrained weights, while the velocity channels are initialized to zero. This zero initialization scheme preserves the pretrained model behavior at initialization: the RGB branch is initially identical to the original pretrained model, while the velocity branch remains inactive at the beginning of the joint supervised fine-tuning. We empirically explored architectures with separate denoisers and explicit cross-attention bridges, but found that a single shared denoiser sampled along one trajectory already maintains strong causal consistency between RGB and velocity while being substantially simpler for training and inference.

    3.4 Joint Supervised Fine-Tuning

    Training Data. The dual-head model is fine-tuned on two complementary datasets. 1) High-fidelity Houdini simulations of smoke, fire, and explosion scenes rendered together with dense ground-truth Eulerian velocity fields, which provide clean (RGB,v) supervision as illustrated in Fig. 3 and anchor the velocity head to physically plausible fluid behavior. Please refer to §4 and Appendix B.2 for more details on the dataset construction. 2) A curated collection of in-the-wild fluid videos supplies appearance diversity, including lighting, materials, scales, and camera motion, which is difficult to produce in simulation and is critical for generalization to real-world inputs.

    Joint Flow-Matching Objective. Both heads are trained jointly with a single flow-matching objective [(Lipman et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2025)] over the combined 32-channel latent. Let z₁=[z₁ʳᵍᵇ;z₁ᵛᵉˡ] denote the encoded clean target, let z₀∼ℕ(0,I) be the noise sampled from a standard Gaussian distribution, and let zₜ=(1-t)z₀+tz₁ be the linear interpolation. The denoiser v_Θ(zₜ,t,c,y) is trained to predict the conditional flow z₁-z₀ via

    L_SFT=𝔼_t, z₀, z₁[m ∥v_Θ(zₜ,t,c,y)-(z₁-z₀)∥²],

    		(3)

    where c denotes the image-conditioning input and y the text prompt. The per-channel mask m equals 1 for all channels on samples with velocity supervision (the Houdini subset), and equals 0 only on RGB channels for samples without velocity targets (the in-the-wild subset). Consequently, the velocity head is trained exclusively on simulation data, while the RGB head benefits from the full appearance distribution. In practice, the two datasets are interleaved at a fixed mixing ratio during training.

    3.5 Velocity-Aware DPO Post-Training

    First stage fine-tuning yields a model capable of jointly generating an RGB stream and a plausible velocity field stream in a single forward pass. However, the physical quality of generated samples still exhibits suboptimal performance. Many samples will remain visibly degenerate, as it is hard for the model to simply learn the physical process [(Bansal et al., 2025)] – especially for highly unconstrained and complex fluid dynamics. Consequently, we employ a post-training stage to reduce this variability by aligning the generator with the physics-informed reward, through the preference optimization.

    Physics-Informed Reward. We assign each generated sample a scalar reward R(z̃)∈[0,1], defined as a convex combination of thirteen component rewards. Each component acts as a soft indicator of physical plausibility. Eleven components are computed directly from the decoded velocity field and fall into three categories:

    Structural terms: including direction diversity, temporal coherence, and multi-scale gradient detail, which encourage non-trivial and temporally stable flow structure;

    Statistical terms: including activity naturalness, temporal dynamics balance, life-cycle envelope, and radial outflow, which encourage agreement with the empirical distribution of Houdini simulations;

    Physical terms: including advection self-consistency, Q-criterion diversity, direction-field enstrophy [(Hunt et al., 1988)], and Kolmogorov inertial range compliance [(Kraichnan, 1974)], which encourage classical properties of turbulent flow.

    As illustrated in Fig. 4, this composite reward reliably separates faithful fluid dynamics from unrealistic ones, and serves as the criterion for preference pairs in the post-training stage.

    Preference Pairs and Flow-DPO Objective. For each conditioning pair (cᵢ,yᵢ) drawn from the first stage training corpus, we sample N=4 candidates using independent random seeds. Since each sample is itself a 32-channel video latent containing both RGB and velocity streams generated by the same denoiser, the aforementioned reward can be evaluated directly on the model output without any additional motion estimator. Within each candidate set, we construct a preference pair (z̃⁺,z̃⁻) using the highest and lowest reward samples, respectively, and discard pairs whose reward gap is below a threshold δ.

    Given a pair at diffusion time t, let u^⋆ₜ denote the flow-matching target from Eq. 3, and let v_Θ and v_Θ_ref denote the trainable and reference denoisers, respectively. Following the MSE-based Diffusion-DPO formulation [(Wallace et al., 2024)] adapted to flow matching [(Rafailov et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025a)], we define the per-sample preference residual as:

    Δ(z̃)=∥v_Θ(z̃,t)-u^⋆ₜ∥²-∥v_Θ_ref(z̃,t)-u^⋆ₜ∥²,

    		(4)

    and optimize

    L_DPO=-𝔼_(z̃⁺,z̃⁻), t \logσ (-\tfrac12β(Δ(z̃⁺)-Δ(z̃⁻))),

    		(5)

    where σ(·) denotes the logistic sigmoid function and β is a temperature parameter. The objective decreases when the trainable model improves its prediction error on preferred samples more than on dispreferred samples, relative to the reference model. During this stage, we optimize v_Θ using low-rank adaptation (LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)]) applied to attention and FFN linear layers while freezing the backbone parameters. The reference model v_Θ_ref is obtained implicitly by disabling the LoRA adapters during inference.

    4 Experiments and Results

    We evaluate our method’s ability to generate visually compelling and physically plausible fluid phenomena. Our experiments are designed to answer three key questions: 1) Does our dual-head architecture and training pipeline improve the physical fidelity of generated fluids compared to state-of-the-art video models? 2) How do the joint velocity prediction and the subsequent DPO post-training individually contribute to the final performance? Please refer to our project page for more video results and comparisons.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets. As aforementioned in §3.4, our training dataset is consist of two sources. In detail, we constructed 13125 videos from Houdini simulation, 15570 real-world videos from FluidNexus dataset [(Gao et al., 2025)], and curated 6521 videos from the real-world footage. In total resulting in a training set of more than 35K videos. Each video is resized to the desired 480×832 resolution, for portrait videos we equally pad black pixels on left and right to match the size ratio. Each video has 81 frames for training.

    Implementation Details. Our model is initialized from the pretrained Wan-2.1-14B image-to-video diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. During the joint Supervised Fine-Tuning (FT) stage, we train the widened transformer blocks for 7000 iterations with a batch size of 1 and a learning rate of 1e-5. For the Velocity-Aware DPO stage, we freeze the backbone and train LoRA adapters (rank r=64) for 500 iterations using a preference margin threshold δ=0.05 and temperature β=500. Training was conducted on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. The codebase is built on DiffSynth [(ModelScope Community, 2024)] and Epipolar-DPO [(Kupyn et al., 2025)].

    Baselines. We compare our approach against strong foundational video generation models and recent physics-aware methods: 1) Wan-14B[(Wan et al., 2025)]: The state-of-the-art base model our architecture is built upon, serving as the direct baseline for our physical augmentations. This model also stands for the current performance of the latest open-source video model can achieve on fluid dynamics. 2) FluidNexus[(Gao et al., 2025)]: On benchmarks with ground-truth data, we also compare with an upgraded multi-view version of the original FluidNexus model. We directly use applicable multi-view videos to reconstruct the underlying fluid representations. And show that even with the additional multi-view information, the pure physics-based approach still can’t faithfully generate complex fluid dynamics at the desired level.

    Metrics. We evaluate along two axes using two benchmarks. The FluidNexus benchmark [(Gao et al., 2025)] provides multiview captures of real fluids with ground-truth reference frames; on 15 randomly selected sequences, we report PSNR and SSIM for per-frame reconstruction fidelity, LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] for perceptual similarity, and FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] for distributional distance over spatiotemporal features. To evaluate general video quality on in-the-wild image inputs, we additionally report VBench [(Huang et al., 2024)] scores on 20 selected images along three dimensions relevant to fluid synthesis: Imaging Quality (per-frame visual fidelity), Aesthetic Quality (perceptual appeal), and Subject Consistency (temporal stability of foreground content, critical for coherent advection without flickering).

    4.2 Quantitative Evaluation

    Tab. 2 reports results on the FluidNexus benchmark. We note that the FluidNexus baseline used here is an upgraded multi-view variant of the original method, which consumes multiple synchronized views as input and requires several hours of per-scene optimization to reconstruct the underlying fluid representation. Despite this substantially heavier setup, it still fails to recover some fine level turbulent details such as small scale eddies and high-frequency boundary roll-ups, which is reflected in its lower SSIM and notably higher LPIPS and FVD compared to our method. Wan2.1-I2V-14B, on the other hand, struggles to produce faithful fluid dynamics from a single image and frequently introduces appearance artifacts such as color shifting and texture drift over time. In contrast, our model, conditioned on only a single image and run in a single forward pass, achieves the best or on par metrics with the multi-view FluidNexus baseline, indicating that our generated complex fluid dynamics closely match the ground-truth captures.

    To verify that our training stages do not compromise general generative capability on in-the-wild content, we evaluate our method using VBench metrics in Tab. 2. Our final model matches or surpasses the Wan2.1-I2V-14B base model on all three reported dimensions, with clear gains in Imaging Quality and Subject Consistency. The improvement in Subject Consistency is particularly meaningful for fluid scenes: it indicates that the auxiliary velocity stream regularizes the RGB stream toward temporally coherent advection, mitigating the flickering and shifting artifacts observed in the base model. Together, the two benchmarks show that our method substantially improves physical fidelity.

    4.3 Qualitative Results

    Fig. 6 shows visual comparisons against ground-truth captures from the FluidNexus benchmark. The upgraded FluidNexus baseline recovers the coarse shape and trajectory of the smoke plume, but its reconstructions after several hours of optimization still appear overly smooth and lose some fine-scale wisps and turbulent filaments visible in the ground truth, indicating the disadvantage of relying only on the manually defined physical approximation laws. Wan2.1-I2V-14B produces motion that diverges from the reference dynamics and exhibits noticeable color drift and appearance inconsistency over time. In contrast, our method reproduces both the global rising trajectory and fine turbulent structures, including thin tendrils at the plume boundary, while requiring only a single forward pass from a single input image. We further compare against Wan2.1-I2V-14B on in-the-wild inputs in Fig. 5, where our full model produces more vivid and physically realistic fluid dynamics. Finally, our model supports several downstream applications, including fluid-related visual effects (Fig. 1) via keyframe control (images are generated by NanoBanana 2 [(Google DeepMind, 2026)]), velocity field prediction (Fig. 7) from input videos using RePaint-style [(Lugmayr et al., 2022)] conditional sampling, and fluid simulation driven by the generated 3D velocity fields (Fig. 8). More results are provided in Appendix A and on our project page.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    We ablate the two stages of our pipeline against the Wan2.1-I2V-14B base model. Results are reported in Tab. 2 and Tab. 2; qualitative comparisons in Fig. 5.

    Joint Supervised Fine-Tuning. The stage I fine-tuning achieves significant gain compared to the basemodel: FluidGen w/o DPO improves PSNR from 22.50 to 31.52 and reduces FVD from 569.7 to 192.1 over the base model, while improving Subject Consistency on VBench (0.8929→0.9383). We attribute this improvement to our curated training corpus of high-fidelity Houdini simulations and in-the-wild fluid videos, which exposes the model to the turbulent dynamics largely absent from the base model’s pretraining distribution.

    Velocity-Aware DPO. DPO trades a small amount of reconstruction fidelity for noticeably better perceptual quality. FluidNexus metrics remain on par with the FT-only model, while VBench Imaging Quality improves significantly and Aesthetic Quality slightly. The slight drop in Subject Consistency (0.9383→0.9350) is expected: the preference signal favors higher-energy, more turbulent motion. Qualitatively (Fig. 5), the FT+DPO model (FluidGen) produces richer fine-scale details and more vivid fire and smoke motion than FluidGen w/o DPO. Please refer to our project page for better visualization.

    5 Conclusion

    We present FluidGen, a framework for synthesizing physically plausible fluid dynamics directly within a video diffusion model, bridging the gap between the rich appearance priors of generative models and the dynamic constraints of classical fluid solvers. By augmenting a pretrained video diffusion transformer with a dual-head architecture, our model jointly predicts RGB pixels and an underlying 3D velocity field, capturing complex fluid dynamics without authored 3D scenes or explicit simulators at inference.

    Our two-stage training pipeline first jointly fine-tunes the model with dense physical supervision from high-fidelity Houdini simulations alongside the visual diversity of in-the-wild videos, then applies a velocity-aware preference optimization stage that uses the model’s native velocity predictions to compute a physics-informed reward over structural, statistical, and fluid properties, aligning the generator toward turbulent, coherent, and physically sound motion.

    While our method focuses on volumetric fluids such as smoke, fire, and explosions, the core idea of embedding interpretable physical representations into generative latents points toward a broader paradigm for physics-aware synthesis. Future work could extend the dual-head approach to other physical systems such as liquids or elastic materials, or expose the predicted velocity fields as a direct control handle for artists. Our results demonstrate that with the right internal representations and alignment strategies, large-scale video models can natively master complex physical dynamics.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Additional Results

    Fig. 9 shows a keyframe-controlled visual effect generated by FluidGen, and Fig. 10 shows additional qualitative results on smoke, ink, and fire.

    Appendix B More Details

    B.1 Physics-Informed Reward Components

    Notation. Let vₜ(x,y)=(vₓ,v_y,v_z) denote the per-pixel 3D velocity field at frame t decoded from the velocity stream of a generated sample z̃ via the inverse transformation of Eq. 1. We write ρₜ=∥vₜ∥ for the speed magnitude and ûₜ=vₜ/ρₜ for the unit-direction field, and set it to zero when ρₜ falls below a small numerical floor value. At each frame we define an active region Aₜ={(x,y):ρₜ(x,y)>τ_ρ} that filters out near static background pixels, where τ_ρ=αₐS with S the encoding scale of Eq. 1 and αₐ a fixed fraction. We also use the normalized R-channel Rₜ∈[0,1] of the encoded velocity image directly for temporal-difference statistics. The symbols κ_•, μ_•, and σ_• denote scalar hyper-parameters; their values are calibrated once on a small held-out set of Houdini-simulated and curated in-the-wild clips, and are listed at the end of this section.

    Reward components. In total, we compute eleven reward components (Tab. 3), which act on the velocity stream and fall into three groups.

    Structural terms target the spatial and temporal organization of the direction field:

  • •

    R_div penalizes direction collapse via the per-component variance of û,

  • •

    R_tc measures the temporal Pearson correlation of the spatial gradients of û,

  • •

    R_msd rewards consistent gradient richness at scales s∈{1,2,4} so that the flow shows structured detail at all scales rather than blur or pure noise.

    • Statistical terms match the empirical distribution of Houdini simulations:

  • •

    R_act on the mean active-pixel fraction f̄ₐ=𝔼ₜ[|Aₜ|/HW],

  • •

    R_tdb on the mean temporal change of Rₜ,

  • •

    R_lc on the global rise-peak-decay envelope of per-frame energy eₜ=𝔼_x,y[ρₜ] via a weighted combination of peak position, monotone rise, monotone decay, second-derivative smoothness, and contrast sub-scores {sₖ},

  • •

    Rᵣₒ on the speed weighted cosine alignment between the image plane velocity (vₓ,v_z) and the radial direction r from an automatically estimated source, averaged over early frames.

    • Physical terms encode classical criterions of turbulent flow:

  • •

    R_adv checks one-step advection self-consistency through a bilinear warp W of vₜ along (vₓ,v_z),

  • •

    R_Q rewards a spread of the Q-criterion of û, Q_û=Ω₁₂²-(S₁₁²+S₂₂²+2S₁₂²), where S and Ω are the symmetric and antisymmetric parts of ∇û[(Hunt et al., 1988)],

  • •

    Rₑₙₛ rewards the enstrophy of the directional field vorticity ω_û=∂ₓû_z-∂_zûₓ on Aₜ,

  • •

    Rₖ rewards Kolmogorov inertial range scaling of the second order structure function S₂(r)=⟨∥v(x+r)-v(x)∥²⟩_A along r∈{1,2,4,8,16} pixels, fit to a power law S₂(r)∼r^α and scored by closeness of α to 2/3[(Kraichnan, 1974)].

    • The total reward used by the DPO objective in Eq. 5 is the convex combination R(z̃)=∑ᵢwᵢRᵢ with wᵢ≥0 and ∑ᵢwᵢ=1.

    B.2 Houdini Dataset Construction

    We synthesize the training set in SideFX Houdini using its Pyro solver, covering three asset families: rising fire, ambient smoke, and bursting explosions. Each scene is independently randomized in source geometry, solver parameters, wind perturbation, camera placement, and environment lighting, then rendered with the Karma path tracer to obtain RGB frames and a per-pixel velocity AOV. Algorithm. 1 summarizes the per-scene pipeline; Tab. 4 lists the randomization ranges that drive variation between sequences.

    Source emitter. For fire and smoke we instantiate a noisy spherical emitter whose center is sampled from a Gaussian around the world origin. The noise displacement amplitude, pulse duration, fractal octaves and roughness are re-sampled per scene to diversify the initial density and temperature fields. Explosions reuse an authored .hipnc scene built around SideFX’s pyro burst source and the Axiom GPU solver, with the shapeoffset seed randomized so each run starts from a different turbulent pattern.

    Pyro and Axiom solvers. The Pyro solver runs at voxel size Δx = 0.02 for fire and Δx = 0.01 for smoke. Each scene resamples buoyancy lift, turbulence strength, disturbance strength, divergence scale, and dissipation; fire additionally resamples the blackbody intensity. Explosions are driven by the Axiom solver. All scenes simulate T = 90 frames at 24 fps.

    Wind perturbation. With probability of 1/2 we inject one rasterized wind volume into the solver. A box of random extent is scattered with points, each carrying a velocity vector w = s·d̂ where s ∼ U(0,0.8) and the azimuth of d̂ is drawn uniformly on [0,2π); the field is rasterized and connected as an additional velocity source to the Pyro solver.

    Camera and lighting. A single perspective camera is placed at (0, y, z) with z ∼ U(6,10) for fire/smoke and z ∼ U(30,35) for explosions, oriented via a look-at transformation to the emitter center. Lighting combines a random HDR environment map drawn from a library with intensity sampled per scene, and for smoke scenes, two opposing rim point lights to better expose silhouettes.

    Rendering and velocity AOV. We render with Karma renderer at 128 path-traced samples. To export per-pixel velocity, we patch the Pyro shader’s material network with two binded VOPs: the first reads the volume’s vel attribute, the second exports it under the AOV name velocity. This produces a second image in the same EXR whose three channels are the velocity at that pixel.
