一句话：HOI 模型懂手，HSI 模型懂房间，但没人会一整套；用编排把两个专家的输出接起来，关键在接缝处的物理连续性。

要点：

  • HOI 与 HSI 各自在领域内很强，但没有单一模型覆盖需要多种交互技能的任务，而统一训练又受限于稀缺且昂贵的数据
  • World2HOSI 从 3DGS 场景出发，用多专家编排 harness 连续生成 HOSI 数据，绕开统一模型的数据瓶颈
  • 光靠「接近/接触」判据不保物理合理：单靠联合人体-物体生成时完成度尚可，但有 85.44% 的帧出现严重穿模
  • 接缝精修在每段边界 ±0.5 秒内，把关节位移、关节角变化与速度跳变相对基线分别降低 29.4%、67.6%、67.3%

为什么值得看：引擎里做长镜头交互动画（人物坐下、拿物、走过房间）同样面临「不同技能模块拼接」的问题；这篇的重点是接缝处的速度连续性，而不是单段动作质量。

中文摘要：长程的人-物-场景交互是具身智能、动画与游戏的关键问题。现有的 HOI 与 HSI 模型在各自领域很强，但没有一个能覆盖需要多种交互技能的任务，而训练统一模型又受制于数据稀缺与采集成本。作者提出 World2HOSI：一个多专家编排 harness，从 3D Gaussian Splatting 场景出发连续生成 HOSI 数据。他们指出仅靠邻近或接触判据不能保证物理合理——纯联合的人-物生成虽然完成度不低，却有 85.44% 的帧出现严重穿模；因此在专家段落之间做残差精修，在每个接缝边界前后 0.5 秒内显著降低关节位移、关节角度变化与速度跳变（相对基线分别下降 29.4%、67.6%、67.3%），从而在多技能拼接处维持物理连续性。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·图形检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-20

本期推送：2026-10-26

World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for
Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation

Abstract

Long-horizon human–object–scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human–scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action’s effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data. Project Page: nintreesssss.github.io/World2HOSI.

22footnotetext: Corresponding author.

1 Introduction

Human-centric 3D scene understanding connects renderable environments with embodied AI training. Beyond high-fidelity reconstruction, it captures natural interactions with static scenes and their objects, termed human-object-scene interaction (HOSI). Such motion data support training and evaluation in computer graphics, embodied AI, and agent learning, but remain scarce. GRAB [(Taheri et al., 2020)], BEHAVE [(Bhatnagar et al., 2022)], and TRUMANS [(Jiang et al., 2024b)] capture human motion together with objects or scenes to support interaction learning. Yet costly motion capture struggles to cover increasingly diverse indoor layouts, object combinations, and multi-stage tasks. This motivates using existing scene and motion resources to produce richer HOSI data.

Generative models offer an alternative route to data synthesis. BEDLAM [(Black et al., 2023)] shows that networks trained entirely on synthetic data can achieve state-of-the-art human pose and shape estimation. InHabit [(Kister et al., 2026)] leverages interaction priors in image foundation models to synthesize 3D human poses in scenes, benefiting downstream tasks such as contact estimation. For 4D interactions, existing models offer complementary capabilities: human-scene interaction (HSI) models condition motion on static furniture geometry, while human-object interaction (HOI) models coordinate humans and dynamic objects [(Rempe et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025)]. However, individual models lack the full chain of capabilities required for long-horizon HOSI. For example, “move the chair and then sit down” combines dynamic manipulation with static interaction, and requires subsequent motion to reflect the chair’s new location. Either capability alone is insufficient. A unified HOSI generator can broaden this capability coverage, but doing so requires training data spanning diverse combinations of actions, objects, and scenes, which remain scarce. InfBaGel’s hybrid-data training indirectly reflects the scarcity of these data [(Zou et al., 2026)]. If an additional unified generator needs to be trained for data production, this reintroduces dependence on the very data that are extremely scarce. Orchestrating complementary experts through conditioning interfaces is therefore essential to expanding task coverage without additional motion-generator training.

Therefore, our goal is to generate text-guided, long-horizon 4D interactions in realistic reconstructed scenes by coordinating motion experts. We build on 3D Gaussian Splatting(3DGS), whose rich appearance provides renderable worlds for data synthesis [(Kerbl et al., 2023)]. But the central question is not only how to render realistic scenes and simply concatenate expert outputs, but how the scene representation gives each expert the right conditions as earlier actions change the world. A scheduler is required to connect task intent to a shared scene state that persists across expert invocations.

Realizing this goal presents three related challenges. First, native 3DGS is primarily a visual representation, typically static and monolithic, which fails to provide separated object identities required for planning and manipulation, thereby hindering a closed loop scene state update [(Hu et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2024)]. Second, converting natural language into executable actions requires spatial understanding and long-horizon planning. Instructions often leave objects and execution order unspecified, requiring decomposition based on spatial relationships and action preconditions. Third, expert models differ in their capabilities and motion boundaries. A shared textual goal alone is insufficient for them to disambiguate their respective roles and produce a continuous sequence.

We introduce World2HOSI, a stage-based orchestration harness for long-horizon HOSI data synthesis. Its organizing principle is a closed loop between a structured scene state and experts that read and update it. An Interactive Scene Package (ISP) maintains object assets and evolving spatial relationships. We use a large language model (LLM) to decompose instructions into a structured script of ordered actions, compiled into numerical conditions at each stage, thereby enabling task-specific expert models to generate corresponding motion segments. Finally, when physical execution is needed, a physics optimizer applies residual corrections for physical plausibility. Object transformations are written back to the ISP to condition subsequent tasks. Experiments show the highest task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated tasks and greater data diversity. A user study confirms that participants prefer our interactions over existing methods.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

  • 1.

    We present the first multi-expert orchestration harness for long-horizon HOSI data synthesis. This framework resolves stages against this state and compiles expert-specific conditions, enabling complementary capabilities to be used without training an additional unified motion generator.

  • 2.

    We introduce a structured scene-state substrate for 4D HOSI generation, linking renderable scenes, object interaction geometry, and persistent object identities so that heterogeneous experts share a consistent account of the world.

  • 3.

    We establish a closed-loop generation mechanism that carries state across motion boundaries and writes action outcomes back to the world, allowing subsequent targets to follow the environmental changes induced by earlier actions.

    • 2 Related Work

    From Renderable Scenes to Interactive Worlds. 3D Gaussian Splatting supports high-quality reconstruction with an explicit Gaussian representation [(Kerbl et al., 2023)], providing visually realistic 3D environments. Making these visual assets interactive additionally requires object-level editability. WorldAct uses object segmentation and geometry construction to make objects in monolithic 3D worlds independently editable and manipulable [(Hu et al., 2026)]. InteriorGS provides indoor Gaussian scenes with semantic annotations and structural information [(SpatialVerse Research Team, Manycore Tech Inc., 2025)], while SAGE-3D builds on these assets to provide mesh representations [(Miao et al., 2026)]. Together, these efforts supply assets for scene understanding and interaction research. EgoSim [(Hao et al., 2026)] maintains an evolving 3D world state for egocentric interaction video generation. InHabit demonstrates the potential of reusing foundation-model priors for automated scene-related human data synthesis, although its outputs are primarily static poses [(Kister et al., 2026)]. This motivates using generative priors to construct scene-related human data.

    Human Object and Scene Interaction Generation. HSI and HOI methods develop different motion priors. HSI methods use static environments as geometric constraints, progressively combining obstacle-avoiding navigation with furniture interactions such as sitting and lying down. DIMOS [(Zhao et al., 2023)] is a representative example. Complementing this line, MDM [(Tevet et al., 2023)] uses diffusion for text-conditioned human motion generation. OmniControl [(Xie et al., 2024)] and Kimodo [(Rempe et al., 2026)] further support control signals including text, full-body keyframes, and 2D paths, providing priors for diverse motion along specified routes.

    HOI methods focus on coordination between humans and movable objects. OMOMO [(Li et al., 2023)] synthesizes full-body manipulation from object trajectories, using intermediate hand positions to strengthen hand-object contact constraints. CHOIS [(Li et al., 2024)] jointly generates human and object motion from text, initial states, and sparse object waypoints, using sampling guidance to improve contact consistency. HOI-FHLI [(Wu et al., 2025)] further integrates navigation and manipulation generation into a single system, providing more comprehensive priors for long-horizon manipulation. PrimHOI [(Jia et al., 2025)] composes reusable contact primitives for complex HOI.

    These conditioning interfaces allow World2HOSI to treat existing models as an orchestrated capability set. A high-level planner decomposes tasks, invokes models, and coordinates outputs. Compatible experts can introduce new capabilities without requiring one base model to master every locomotion and interaction type.

    Joint Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation. Several methods pursue joint HOSI generation. HOSIG [(Yao et al., 2026)] incorporates scene constraints into navigation and fine-grained manipulation, InteractMove [(Cai et al., 2025)] addresses interactions in scenes with movable objects. InfBaGel [(Zou et al., 2026)] updates dynamic scene perception during generation and mitigates data scarcity through hybrid training on HOI and HSI data. These methods highlight environmental changes and data coverage as central issues. Physical imitation and reference-trajectory refinement [(Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026)] further provide contact-driven execution for kinematic sequences, allowing them to satisfy dynamics constraints. However, these methods all face data scarcity, which also limits the generalization of their learned priors.

    3 Method

    World2HOSI is a multi-model orchestration framework that generates human-object-scene interactions from 3D Gaussian scenes and text instructions, as illustrated in Figure 3.

    3.1 Interactive World Representation

    Representation. Native 3DGS provides a renderable collection of Gaussians [(Kerbl et al., 2023)], but not the object-level structure needed for task planning, interaction, and state memory. So we introduce the Interactive Scene Package (ISP), a unified structure with persistent object identities. Each object has visual assets, local collision geometry, semantic labels, a world transformation, and physical properties. The scene also maintains a static background, support regions, object relationships, and navigable space. Rendering and interaction use separate representations aligned by shared object transformations. Gaussian assets provide appearance, while geometric proxies support collision checking and path planning:

    W={V,B,(idᵢ,Gᵢ,Tᵢ,Aᵢ,Sᵢ)ᵢ₌₁^N,M,R}.

    		(1)

    Here, V denotes visual assets, B scene geometry, idᵢ a unique identifier for each object, Gᵢ local object geometry, and Tᵢ∈SE(3) world transformations. Aᵢ contains manipulability and physical properties such as mass, Sᵢ denotes object-local support regions, M navigation occupancy, and R object and spatial relationships. Movable objects are separated from the static background, with Tᵢ applied consistently to their visual, collision, and semantic geometry.

    Scene Update. Following object pose changes, the ISP updates support regions and navigation occupancy to condition later tasks. Support regions use object-local coordinates, moving or reorienting a chair recomputes its seat’s world coordinates through Tᵢ, enabling subsequent sitting without manually reannotating the support surface. Navigation occupancy separates static-background and object-instance layers. Old object occupancy is removed and geometry inserted at the new pose, so path planning uses the updated obstacles.

    The ISP underlies subsequent generation and exposes interpretable task conditions, object movability, the supporting object associated with a target region, and whether a location can be approached are all queryable before motion generation. Details on constructing the ISP are provided in Appendix  A.1.

    3.2 Task Compiler and Scene Grounding

    Natural language typically describes task intent without exact action orders or spatial coordinates. To let different experts interpret tasks in a shared scene, we separate semantic and numerical representations. At the semantic level, instructions are decomposed into ordered actions in a structured Activity Script, recording each stage’s action type, object identity, target region, and support relationships. For “move the chair next to the table and sit on the seat,” the planner first binds “the chair” to a candidate instance in the ISP using semantic and manipulability information. The later “seat” refers to this same chair’s local support region, rather than to its initial world coordinates. Scripts can be generated by an LLM using predefined prompt templates and ISP information, or specified manually.

    Before each stage, the numerical compiler reads the Activity Script, current ISP, and human state to compute the required conditions. Writing the stage description as aₖ=(cₖ,oₖ,gₖ,ρₖ), with action type cₖ, object identity oₖ, target reference gₖ, and support relations ρₖ, the logical representation of the compilation is

    ℂₖ=Compile(aₖ,Wₖ,hₖ)=(cₖ,oₖ,hₖ,T_oₖ,k,ℙʰₖ,ℙᵒₖ,Gₖ,ηₖ).

    		(2)

    Here, hₖ contains the starting root translation and joint rotations, T_oₖ,k is the selected object’s pose, ℙʰₖ and ℙᵒₖ denote human path and object waypoints, and Gₖ contains world-space target poses or support regions resolved from gₖ. The metadata ηₖ records coordinate frame, units, temporal sampling, and human representation. These form the Motion Intermediate Representation (MotionIR) passed to the expert, standardizing coordinate frames, units, and human identity to reduce cross-model mismatches.

    Compilation thus grounds textual intent in stage-wise numerical conditions. The two intermediate representations unify task semantics and numerical specifications, keeping scene and task understanding from being delegated entirely to motion generators.

    3.3 Multi-Expert Motion Synthesis

    Generation. Once the current stage has been grounded, the planner uses its action type to orchestrate experts from a configured mapping. Experts are defined by capability, independently of specific models. Most HOSI tasks can be decomposed into navigation, dynamic HOI (e.g. carrying, pushing, or pulling), and static HSI (e.g. sitting or lying down). The navigation expert generates scene-constrained locomotion, the HOI expert jointly generates human and object motion, and the HSI expert generates interactions with static scene geometry. All receive conditions through the same upstream interface, decoupling task representation from individual generators. The harness is therefore independent of any model or architecture, experts can be replaced and new capabilities added without redesigning the pipeline.

    Cross-Expert Reconciliation.MotionIR aligns task semantics and spatial targets but does not ensure compatible boundaries between independently generated segments. We therefore introduce a lightweight boundary projection mechanism that reconciles their initial states in the motion space. Specifically, it projects a short prefix of the incoming segment onto the terminal state of the preceding segment, and smoothly relaxes the projection over time. This preserves the expert-generated motion away from the transition while enforcing local positional and rotational continuity. Let p⁻ and Rⱼ⁻ denote the human root position and rotation of joint j in the preceding segment’s final frame, and let p⁺(t) and Rⱼ⁺(t) denote the incoming expert’s original trajectories. We first compute the translational and rotational offsets between the boundary states:

    Δp=p⁻-p⁺(0), ΔRⱼ=Rⱼ⁻(Rⱼ⁺(0))⁻¹.

    		(3)

    The correction is then gradually released over a window of duration τ. Here, t≥0 denotes the elapsed time from the start of the incoming segment, u∈[0,1] is the normalized transition time, and s(u) is a smooth release weight that increases from 0 to 1 over the window. We use the quintic smoothstep function

    s(u)=10u³-15u⁴+6u⁵, u=\min(t/τ,1),

    		(4)

    to obtain the corrected root trajectory p̃⁺(t) and joint rotations R̃ⱼ⁺(t):

    p̃⁺(t)=p⁺(t)+(1-s(u))Δp,(5)
    R̃ⱼ⁺(t)=Slerp (ΔRⱼ,I,s(u))Rⱼ⁺(t).(6)

    Here, Slerp denotes spherical linear interpolation of rotations, and I is the identity rotation. At t=0, the corrected root position and joint pose match the final frame of the preceding segment. The correction decays smoothly within τ and vanishes at the end of the window, after which the incoming expert’s original motion is fully recovered.

    Unlike smoothing both sides of a transition, our adapter has an explicit temporal direction. HOSI tasks follow a semantic stage order, so we enforce continuity with the existing motion state and restrict deviations from the prior to the incoming segment’s initial window. Our ablation measures velocity jumps and joint changes to assess quality.

    3.4 Physics-Based Execution with Bounded Residuals

    Kinematic motion priors do not explicitly enforce gravity, friction, or sustained contact, so even an individual expert’s output may contain physical violations. To address the physical violations in generated motions caused by missing contact physics and joint limits, we introduce an RL-based post-optimization process to yield physically valid outputs. Following residual tracking [(Zhao et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025)], a reinforcement-learning controller makes bounded adjustments to the reference joint targets, executed by proportional-derivative (PD) controllers. Objects move through simulated human contact, their reference trajectories are tracking objectives, not directly replayed motions or frame-by-frame external forces. The controller balances reference tracking with motion smoothness, seeking a nearby executable realization while preserving interaction intent. Its control law, reward terms, and optimization details are provided in Appendix A.5.

    4 Experiments

    We extensively evaluate World2HOSI through quantitative comparisons, a perceptual user study, and component ablations. The evaluation covers interaction generation quality, data diversity, stitching effectiveness, and physical plausibility.

    4.1 Comparison with External Methods on Shared Tasks

    Our harness targets long-horizon HOSI. We assess the generated data through quantitative measures of task completion and geometric quality, together with human perceptual evaluation.

    Dataset and metrics.

    We construct 10 ISP scenes spanning real-world reconstructions and synthetic environments, and design 20 human-level instructions covering daily actions: carrying, pushing, pulling, sitting, lying down, and multi-stage combinations. Each task uses three random seeds, resulting in a total of 60 sequences. We evaluate motion from three perspectives. For task completion, waypoint following errors T_xy[(Wu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024)] measures how the human root trajectory deviates from the planned route during approach, carrying after pickup, and subsequent approaches. The task progress score Sₜ decomposes instructions into ordered stages and continuously scores partial completion. Carrying, pushing, and pulling check final human and object distances to their targets; sitting and lying check target pose changes. Later stages receive credit only after prerequisite actions are observed. The geometry score S_g aggregates geometric quality metrics. The detailed scoring rules are provided in Appendix  A.4. For interaction plausibility, we measure the contact ratio during object motion (OCP, %) [(Zou et al., 2026; Li et al., 2024)], severe-penetration frame ratio (P_f, %) [(Zhao et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2026)], using a penetration-depth threshold of 2 cm. Non-contact object displacement (NCOD, cm), measured as the maximum object-surface displacement before first hand contact, and mean object-scene penetration (Pₒₛ) [(Zhao et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2026)], assessing how plausibly a human could execute the interaction. For human motion quality, we measure mean human-object penetration (Pₕₒ) [(Zou et al., 2026)], foot sliding score (FS) [(Wu et al., 2025; Zou et al., 2026)], and foot-ground deviation (O_feet).

    Baselines.

    Although recent years have witnessed significant advances in motion generation, the complex nature of HOSI poses unique challenges, leaving it supported by only two existing baselines, i.e. InfBaGel [(Zou et al., 2026)] and HOSIG [(Yao et al., 2026)]. Meanwhile, to validate the benefit of our multi-expert orchestration, we also compare against a single-expert variant using HOI-FHLI. For fairness, our harness compiles shared target objects, target regions, approach positions, and navigation paths, ensuring identical task semantics, scenes, and object geometry across methods. Navigation paths are constructed using A* on clearance-inflated occupancy grids, followed by collision-checked simplification and smoothing.

    Table 4 shows the highest task progress and aggregate geometry scores for World2HOSI. Our method follows the planned tasks, completing intermediate operations more fully while approaching targets. InfBaGel reduces foot sliding but has lower progress and contact, indicating that higher-quality human motion alone is insufficient for long-horizon HOSI. HOSIG achieves relatively high completion but 85.44% severe-penetration frames proximity or contact alone does not ensure plausibility, exposing limitations in joint human-object generation. Our balance of completion and geometry supports the benefits of unified closed-loop state update mechanism.

    4.2 Motion Diversity

    Separately from the comparison above, we construct a generation set of 90 sequences with more varied tasks. We compare this set against equally sized random subsets of BEHAVE [(Bhatnagar et al., 2022)], TRUMANS [(Jiang et al., 2024b)], and LINGO [(Jiang et al., 2024a)]. Our set contains 60 interactions with dynamic objects and 30 static interactions across different scenes. For action-semantic diversity [(Kister et al., 2026)], a vision-language model (VLM) extracts action and target-object text labels from each sequence. A shared text encoder [(Reimers and Gurevych, 2019)] maps labels to unit-normalized embeddings, whose average cosine distance measures diversity. For pose diversity, we compute average APD over SMPL-X joints in uniformly sampled frames [(Kister et al., 2026; Pavlakos et al., 2019)]. Table 2 shows that our data achieve the greatest diversity in actions, target objects, and poses.

    4.3 Ablation Study

    Cross-expert reconciliation.

    We compare three strategies for resolving boundary-state mismatches between expert-generated motion segments, using the same pregenerated segments and keeping the human representation and timeline fixed. A0 directly concatenates segments without correction. A1 blends both sides of the boundary using conventional translation interpolation and spherical linear interpolation of rotations. A2 applies our projection adapter: the preceding segment remains fixed, while the incoming segment’s initial state is aligned with the preceding final frame and the correction decays within a local window. A1 and A2 use identical window durations to control the temporal extent of adjustment. Within 0.5 s on either side of each boundary, A2 reduces joint displacement, joint angle change, and velocity jumps relative to A1 by 29.4%, 67.6%, and 67.3%, respectively (Table 4.3). These results support the adapter’s effectiveness in reducing cross-expert boundary discontinuities while preserving the preceding motion segment.

    Bounded residual refinement.

    We evaluate residual refinement on several physics-based clips averaging approximately 10 s and involving objects of different shapes and types. We measure human joint error (Eₕ, cm) and object error (Eₒ, cm) between physical execution under the residual policy and the kinematic reference [(Wu et al., 2025)]. These metrics quantitatively assess how closely the physically executed human and object motions track the kinematic reference. The small tracking errors in Table 4.3 indicate that the policy remains close to the reference trajectories while allowing local adjustments for physical execution.

    Physics-based optimization further improves physical plausibility by reducing reference artifacts, including foot sliding, floating, and interpenetration, as illustrated in Figure 4.3. Contact-driven execution allows local adjustments to the reference motion, helping establish more consistent human-object and foot-ground interactions.

    4.4 Long-Horizon Stateful Interaction

    To evaluate how our closed-loop state-update mechanism supports complex, long-horizon HOSI, we test multi-stage tasks with cross-stage state dependencies. As shown in Figure 4.4, the human first relocates a chair, drinks coffee, puts down the cup, and finally sits on the relocated chair. In the second task, the human carries books, repositions a stool, and sits on it. Both tasks involve subsequent interactions grounded in updated object poses, and our method successfully completes all stages in both cases.

    4.5 User Study

    Since current quantitative metrics often fail to fully capture visual realism and physical plausibility, we conduct a user study to evaluate the true perceptual quality and naturalness of the generated motions from a human perspective. Using each method on the shared tasks, we generate a total of 24 sequences and organize them into eight comparison videos, each containing our method and two baselines with identical rendering and camera settings. An online questionnaire collects responses from 30 participants, who select the method with the highest task completion and best interaction quality for each comparison. Our method substantially leads the baselines in preference rates on both criteria (Figure 6).

    5 Conclusion

    We presented World2HOSI, an orchestration framework for long-horizon HOSI data generation. It transforms static 3D Gaussian scenes into continuously updated interactive worlds. Through the Interactive Scene Package, task compilation, and projection-based stitching, navigation, human-object, and human-scene models generate continuous motion under shared state, with object motion affecting subsequent task conditions. Bounded residual optimization further refines the kinematic reference for physical plausibility. This loop establishes the first systematic multi-expert orchestration framework for complex, long-horizon HOSI tasks, offering a new pathway to alleviate joint interaction data scarcity and a reusable engine for future research and extensions.

    Limitations. While World2HOSI enables long-horizon interactions through state-aware orchestration, its optional physics-based refinement remains dependent on the motion references produced by the selected experts. Bounded-residual control is designed to improve physical plausibility while preserving these references, which limits its ability to correct substantial motion errors or fundamentally infeasible interactions. Addressing these limitations is an important direction for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Appendix

    A.1 ISP Construction Details

    An ISP can be constructed either from annotated scene assets or from a monolithic 3DGS reconstruction [(Kerbl et al., 2023)]. For annotated scenes from ScanNet++ [(Yeshwanth et al., 2023)] and InteriorGS [(SpatialVerse Research Team, Manycore Tech Inc., 2025)], we use the scanned meshes, instance annotations, and initial 3D bounding boxes to select informative views. Text prompts and projected bounding boxes are then provided to SAM3 [(Carion et al., 2025)] to obtain multi-view object masks. These segmentation results are fused using camera poses, scan depth, and Gaussian projection contributions to extract object-level mesh and Gaussian assets.

    For unannotated 3DGS scenes, we adopt a WorldAct-style pipeline [(Hu et al., 2026)]. Qwen3.6-Plus [(Qwen Team, 2026)] is used to identify separable objects and evaluate candidate views, followed by multi-view segmentation with SAM3. We then determine the instance assignment of 3D Gaussians using camera calibration, occlusion relationships, and Gaussian projection contributions, while unassigned Gaussians are retained as the static background. The required meshes are obtained from existing scans when available, or reconstructed using Gaussian Wrapping [(Gomez et al., 2026)].

    Finally, the decoupled visual assets and collision geometry are organized in a shared metric coordinate frame, with persistent object identities, bounding boxes, and initial occupancies recorded for each instance. Support regions are extracted from mesh surfaces and stored in object-local coordinates. Category-level priors provided by an LLM are further used to initialize basic properties such as manipulability, mass, and friction. Before finalizing the ISP, manual inspection and correction can be applied to segmentation, alignment, functional orientation, and support geometry.

    A.2 Complete Task Definitions

    This appendix lists the semantic structure of the tasks used in the main experiments.

    A.2.1 Task Instances and State Dependencies

    Dynamic object manipulation (T01-T06).

    Support-based scene interactions (T07-T10).

    Combined manipulation and support interactions (T11-T14).

    State-dependent tasks (T15-T18).

    Continuous manipulation on multiple objects (T19–T20).

    A.2.2 Shared Conditions and Model Invocation

    Our shared-task implementation uses Kimodo [(Rempe et al., 2026)] for navigation, HOI-FHLI [(Wu et al., 2025)] for dynamic object interactions, and DIMOS [(Zhao et al., 2023)] for static interaction. For the diversity extension, we additionally use LINGO’s scene interaction capability [(Jiang et al., 2024a)]. All outputs are converted to a shared world coordinate frame, metric units, and a common human representation. Each task-seed pair is associated with identical scene and object geometry, initial states, and target conditions across methods.

    InfBaGel and HOSIG use their respective pretrained generators [(Zou et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026)]. Their adaptation layers only perform geometry and coordinate conversion, condition encoding, and output conversion back to the shared representation. To accommodate the baselines’ limitations on long-horizon tasks, the same baseline may be invoked stage by stage for complex tasks, with each stage inheriting the actual generated state of the previous stage and the resulting segments concatenated.

    A.3 More results of Long-Horizon Tasks with State-Update Dependencies

    To further demonstrate the capability of our framework to generate long-horizon tasks involving cross-stage state dependencies, we present two representative scenarios in new environments, as shown in Figure A.3. In the first task, the human must first move an obstacle blocking a doorway and then enter the room through the cleared passage. In the second task, the human is required to move a chair to a designated open area and subsequently sit on the chair at its new location. Both tasks require subsequent actions to depend on scene state changes induced by preceding interactions. By updating the shared world state after each stage, World2HOSI enables subsequent motions to be generated based on the updated object positions and scene, thereby supporting multi-stage human–object–scene interactions with explicit state dependencies.

    A.4 Definitions of Aggregate Metrics for Shared Tasks

    A.4.1 Task Progress Score Sₜ

    For each carrying, pushing, or pulling subtask, we assign weights of 1, 2, 2, and 1 to approach, initiation, movement, and completion, respectively. For sitting or lying down, approach, pose change, and the target pose receive weights of 1, 2, and 2. Observed evidence at each stage is mapped to a partial-completion value in [0,1] and multiplied by the stage weight. The total score is 100× the sum of earned points divided by the sum of available points.

    Stage recognition proceeds in temporal order. Once evidence of a stage is observed, evaluation may advance to the next stage even if the current stage has not received full credit. High scores in later stages cannot compensate for entirely missing prerequisite actions.

    A.4.2 Geometry Score S_g

    The geometry score S_g assesses motion plausibility independently of task completion. It combines contact quality, collision behavior, and foot behavior with equal weights.

    Let OCP, P_f, FS, and O_feet denote these means. The contact score is OCP, and the collision score is 100-P_f, with both percentages expressed on a 0-100 scale. The mean foot sliding FS (cm/frame) and mean foot-ground distance O_feet (cm) are converted to scores as 100/(1+FS) and 100/(1+O_feet/5), respectively. Their average forms the foot score. The final score is

    S_g=(OCP+100-P_f)/(3)+1/6(100/1+FS+(100)/(1+O_feet/5)).

    		(7)

    A.5 Physics-Based Refinement Details

    For tasks requiring physical execution, the generated kinematic sequence supplies a reference for a bounded-residual controller. Objects move solely through physical human contact, the controller neither replays object trajectories nor applies frame-by-frame external forces to reproduce them. It must establish and maintain contacts that drive object motion while preserving interaction intent. Following the residual-tracking paradigm [(Zhao et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025)], the policy predicts residuals around the reference joint state q_ref(t) rather than generating complete joint targets from scratch:

    q_target(t)=clip (q_ref(t)+m⊙b⊙\tanh(a(t)), q_\min,q_\max).

    		(8)

    Here, a(t) is the policy output, m masks correctable joints, b sets per-joint residual bounds, and q_\min,q_\max specify joint limits. The clip operator clamps corrected targets to valid joint ranges. Joint proportional-derivative (PD) controllers execute q_target. Residual bounds and joint limits restrict the search to a neighborhood of the reference, permitting posture adjustments for contact while preserving the overall motion structure as closely as possible.

    The reward combines reference tracking and smoothness terms [(Wu et al., 2025)]:

    rₜ=rₜᵗʳᵃᶜᵏ+λₛrₜᵃᶜᶜ, rₜᵗʳᵃᶜᵏ=λₒᵣᵢrₜᵒʳⁱ+λₚₒₛrₜᵖᵒˢ+λ_handrₜʰᵃⁿᵈ.

    		(9)

    where (λₒᵣᵢ,λₚₒₛ,λ_hand,λₛ)=(0.4,0.4,0.2,0.05). The orientation term rₜᵒʳⁱ measures disagreement between simulated and reference human or object orientations, rₜᵖᵒˢ measures their positional disagreement. The hand-relative term rₜʰᵃⁿᵈ measures disagreement in hand-object geometry in the object’s local frame. The hand-relative term specifies their geometric relationship without explicitly requiring contact, avoiding the imposition of reference penetration or floating artifacts as execution targets. The term rₜᵃᶜᶜ penalizes excessive acceleration to reduce high-frequency jitter. Using proximal policy optimization (PPO) [(Schulman et al., 2017)], we search for a physically executable solution near the reference rather than generate a new interaction. This preserves its overall structure while reducing unintended floating, penetration, and jitter, enabling contact-driven object motion with improved physical executability.

    A.6 User Study

    The questionnaire contains eight tasks. For each task, World2HOSI, InfBaGel, and HOSIG each generate one kinematic video, yielding 24 videos in total. The tasks correspond to T01, T02, T03, T04, T05, T06, T11, and T12 in the evaluated version. Each group of three videos uses identical human appearance, scene conditions, camera settings, and rendering parameters. The videos are randomly ordered and displayed side by side with the labels A, B, and C, without revealing the method names.

    Each task has two independent questions: select the video with the best task completion and select the one with the best interaction quality. The response options are methods A, B, and C, and No Preference.

    With the informed consent of the participants, all 30 participants had answered both questions for all eight tasks. Each evaluation criterion therefore has 30×8=240 responses.

item.title: 互动世界模型该压多少倍？CADRE 扫遍时空压缩率：8× 时间压缩光延迟就 400ms ｜ Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
item.description:
一句话：世界模型直接继承文生视频的 VAE，压多少倍没人管；但 τ=8、20 fps 时单是时间压缩就让动作至少延迟 400ms，而人超过 230ms 就能察觉。

要点：

  • 交互世界模型在视频自编码器的潜空间里生成，压缩倍数直接决定每帧成本与「动作多久才生效」
  • 既有工作多沿用文生视频的 VAE（为离线生成设计，没有 agent 在等），且缺训练数据与代码时无法改压缩率重训
  • 人对自己动作延迟超过约 230ms 即可察觉，要「即时」得低于 100ms；而 τ=8 在 20 fps 下仅时间压缩就带来 400ms，任何裁帧加速都救不回来
  • CADRE 是一族开放的因果扩散表示自编码器，跨多个时空压缩率，成员只差冻结特征上的小瓶颈、共享自蒸馏到一步或少步的扩散解码器；训练后世界模型单 H100 跑 20 fps、反应低于 230ms，占据延迟-质量前沿的大部分

为什么值得看：如果要把世界模型当引擎用，「压缩率」不是工程细节而是交互预算的第一性参数：它先决定延迟，再决定你还有多少算力可以用来提升画质。

中文摘要：视频世界模型从过去帧与动作预测未来帧，可充当 agent 训练、规划、评测的模拟器，也能被人交互控制。它们在视频自编码器的潜空间里生成，而压缩率同时决定每帧成本与动作生效的等待时间；但现有世界模型往往直接复用文生视频的自编码器——那些是为离线生成设计的，没有 agent 在等，且在没有原始训练数据与代码时无法换一个压缩率重训。作者因此系统研究「世界模型该在哪、该压多少」。他们构建 CADRE：一族开放的因果扩散表示自编码器，横跨多种时空压缩，成员之间只在冻结特征上的一个小瓶颈不同，并共享一个自蒸馏到一步或少数步的扩散解码器。在操纵与导航两个域、各两个环境上训练同一世界模型后，CADRE 在单张 H100 上以 20 fps 运行、反应时间低于 230 ms，并在运动保真度与动作跟随两项指标上占据延迟-质量前沿的大部分。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-26

Rethinking Video Autoencoders
for Interactive World Models

Abstract

Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-22-cadre.

1 Introduction

A world model is a learned simulator of an environment [(Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018)]. Given past frames and an agent’s actions, a video world model generates the next frames, and can be used to train agents [(Hafner et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024)], evaluate robot policies [(Yang et al., 2024)], plan the outcome of actions [(Bar et al., 2025)], or simply play a game [(Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026)]. To enable all these applications, two different aspects have to be optimized: the throughput that measures the number of frames generated per second, and the latency that measures the delay between the action and its effect on the output. Throughput limits how fast a simulation can happen, whereas latency limits how reactive and faithful a simulation can be.

Most video world models operate in the latent space of a video autoencoder [(Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025)]. To avoid designing an ad hoc autoencoder, many methods [(He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2026a)] reuse the autoencoder of a text-to-video generator such as LTX-2 [(HaCohen et al., 2026)], Wan 2.2 [(Wan et al., 2025)] or HunyuanVideo [(Kong et al., 2024)]. They thus inherit the throughput and latency that come with it. Yet, such autoencoders were not designed with the throughput-latency trade-off of world models in mind, and often perform massive temporal compression since it has low impact on visual quality. A typical 8× temporal compression delays every action by at least 400 ms at 20 frames per second. Humans notice when their own movement appears more than about 230 ms late [(Shimada et al., 2009)], and interaction feels immediate only below 100 ms [(Miller, 1968; Claypool & Claypool, 2006)]. This raises the question of how other throughput-latency trade-offs affect rollout quality and action following.

To address this question, we propose CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders built for interactive world models. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features, which sets the compression, and share a causal diffusion decoder that needs one or a few steps. To study compression across settings, we train the same world model, a causal diffusion transformer following MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], on each autoencoder, in two domains: manipulation (by a robot and by human hands) and navigation (driving and indoor). We compare CADRE with the autoencoders of Wan 2.2, Cosmos [(NVIDIA et al., 2025)] and LTX-2, the image autoencoder DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025b)] and the MIRA autoencoder retrained on our data. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera (Figure 1).

Interestingly, our study points to four findings. (1) At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression, and a few-step flow model trained by progressive self-distillation is a good fit. (2) In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model: patching inside the world model loses detail, and at eight frames also action following. (3) Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions. In manipulation the camera is still, so temporal compression costs little while spatial compression is costly. In navigation the camera moves and the balance reverses, so it pays to keep frames and compress spatially, the low-latency choice. (4) Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality, and, in robot manipulation, action following too.

Contributions.

  • •

    What compression controls in an interactive world model. We make explicit how an autoencoder’s spatial and temporal compression set a world model’s throughput and action latency, and we separate how much to compress from where to compress (Section 2).

  • •

    CADRE, causal diffusion representation autoencoders for interactive world models. Open models at seven spatio-temporal compressions, whose decoder learns one- or few-step decoding by progressive self-distillation, in a single stage and without an adversarial loss (Section 3).

  • •

    Where, and how much, to compress video for a world model. A controlled study in four environments, judged by rollouts and action following (Sections 4 and 5).

    • 2 What Compression Controls in an Interactive World Model

    Before studying how to compress, we make explicit what compression controls. An interactive world model generates in the latent space of an autoencoder that compresses a clip by τ temporally and s spatially, written τ×s×s: 2×32×32 compresses 2× temporally and 32× spatially. These two factors set the world model’s cost, action latency and throughput. The compression itself can happen in the autoencoder or in the world model (Section 5.1).

    Compression sets the world model’s cost. The world model we study is a causal, space-time-factorized diffusion transformer that predicts the next latent frame from the previous ones and the current action or action chunk (Section 4, Appendix D). Its cost grows with the number of tokens it processes, which only the spatial and temporal compression set: a clip of T frames of size H×W becomes N=(T/τ)(H/s)(W/s) latent tokens for the world model.

    A latent frame waits for all its actions. Every frame registers one action. A latent frame spans τ frames, so the world model can predict it only once all τ conditioning actions are known. It therefore consumes actions in chunks, and the actions of one chunk shape the next (Figure 2). The agent thus commits to τ actions before seeing their effect, as action-chunking policies do [(Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025)]. Causality holds between chunks. Within a chunk, the τ frames decode from the same latent, and their order is learned from real video.

    Temporal compression delays every action. The first action of a chunk waits τ/f for the chunk to close, where f is the frame rate, then t_gen for the world model to generate the latent frame and t_dec for the autoencoder to decode it into τ frames, which sets the throughput:

    latency=τ/f (chunk closes)+\underbracet_gen+t_dec_generate and decode, throughput=(τ)/(t_gen+t_dec).

    		(1)

    No speed-up shortens the first term, which at τ=8 and 20 frames per second is 400 ms, beyond the 230 ms lag humans notice in their own movement [(Shimada et al., 2009)]. In exchange, a larger τ raises the throughput and, at a fixed spatial factor, cuts the token count N.

    3 CADRE: Causal Diffusion Representation Autoencoders

    Studying compression means training the autoencoder at many compression points. The autoencoders of text-to-video generators release their weights but not their training data or code, so they cannot be retrained. We instead design an open family of autoencoders for world models, one per compression point (Figure 3). Its members share one recipe, differ only in their compression and are each trained from scratch, so the world models trained on them differ by compression alone.

    3.1 Architecture

    Frozen features and one trained layer encode the clip. As in MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], the encoder is that of a representation autoencoder [(Zheng et al., 2026)]. A frozen DINOv3 extractor [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] encodes each frame into one feature per p×p patch, aggregating several layers as in RAEv2 [(Singh et al., 2026)]. One trained 3D convolution with kernel (τ,k,k) and stride (τ,s^′,s^′) compresses τ frames of s^′2 patches into a deterministic latent, with s=p s^′ (Appendix B).

    A causal diffusion decoder keeps textures sharp. A strongly compressed latent keeps a scene’s layout and semantics but little texture, so a perceptual regression decoder averages the textures consistent with it into a blur [(Xu et al., 2026)]. We therefore use a diffusion decoder [(Preechakul et al., 2022; Pernías et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025d)], which samples the clip conditioned on the latent. It is a space-time-factorized transformer [(Bertasius et al., 2021; Arnab et al., 2021)] on a q×q patch grid, whose blocks attend over space, then causally over time. Most blocks process one token per latent frame, that is, per τ video frames. A linear map then splits each token into τ tokens, one per frame, so the last blocks resolve motion within a latent frame. The latent conditions the diffusion decoder in three places: (i) lifted by a transposed convolution and summed with the patchified noisy clip, (ii) through a spatial AdaLN [(Park et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020; Dufour et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2026)] in every block, which also receives the flow time t and the jump length d, the size of the denoising step the decoder takes (Section 3.2, Appendix B), and (iii) through a zero-initialized skip into a light convolutional head. The decoder is time-causal, so it streams chunk by chunk.

    3.2 Training

    The decoder learns by flow matching and perceptual losses. The decoder g_θ uses the x-prediction, x-loss form of flow matching [(Li & He, 2026)]. It predicts the clean clip x from the latent z and a noisy clip xₜ=t x+(1-t) ε, with ε∼ℕ(0,I) and t=0 pure noise. As in diffusion forcing [(Chen et al., 2024a)], each chunk of τ frames draws its own t∼U(0,1). The loss is

    L_fm = E_x,ε,t ℓ_rec(g_θ(z, xₜ, t, 0), x),

    		(2)

    where the last argument, the jump length d, is zero here. The term ℓ_rec sums a mean absolute error, two perceptual distances (LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] and its analog in DINO feature space) and a 3D wavelet term as in LTX-Video [(HaCohen et al., 2024)], weighted by gradient balancing. CADRE trains on a 76k-hour mixture of web, robot, driving and camera video (Appendix C).

    Self-distillation makes one or two decoding steps enough. Flow-matching trajectories curve, so following them takes many steps, while an interactive world model needs single- or few-step decoding. Shortcut models [(Frans et al., 2025)] and self-distilled flow maps [(Boffi et al., 2025)] condition the network on its step size and train one large step to agree with two smaller ones. Following them, g_θ(z,xᵣ,r,d) predicts where a jump from r to r+d lands, through x_r+d=xᵣ+\tfracd1-r(x̂-xᵣ) with implied velocity v_θ=(x̂-xᵣ)/(1-r). One jump from r to t is trained to land where two half jumps through u=(r+t)/2 do (dropping z from the notation),

    L_psd = E ∥(1-r)(v_θ(xᵣ,r,t-r)-sg[\tfrac12(v_θ(xᵣ,r,u-r)+v_θ(x̂ᵤ,u,t-u))])∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where sg stops the gradient and x̂ᵤ is the point reached by the first half jump. Unlike the consistency decoder [(OpenAI, 2023)] and SSDD [(Vallaeys et al., 2026)], which distill a decoder in a second stage, the CADRE decoder is its own teacher and learns one- or few-jump decoding in one stage.

    4 Judging an Autoencoder by Its World Model

    An autoencoder is trained to reconstruct its input, yet in latent generation, reconstruction and generation trade off [(Yao et al., 2025; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2025)], and a line of work shapes the latent for the generator instead [(Leng et al., 2025; Kouzelis et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026; Ramanana Rahary et al., 2026b)]. We therefore score rollouts instead of reconstructions (Appendix F). As in MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], we judge each autoencoder by the rollouts of a world model trained on its latents; the world model, clips and actions are shared, so only the latent varies.

    Four environments span manipulation and navigation. We train world models in four environments, two of manipulation and two of navigation (Table 1), so that no conclusion rests on a single environment. In manipulation the view is static for the robot and nearly static for the head-mounted camera of the human, so mainly the arms or hands and the objects they handle move. In navigation the view itself moves, so the whole frame changes; we separate driving, a dynamic scene where other road users move on their own, from indoor navigation in static scenes. Action complexity ranges from 2 dimensions for driving to 102 for two hands. All videos are resampled to 20 frames per second at 288×512. Evaluation uses held-out episodes, and the official split for driving.

    One world model recipe serves every autoencoder. The world model is a 1.2B-parameter causal diffusion transformer conditioned on the τ actions of each latent frame and trained with diffusion forcing [(Chen et al., 2024a)] (Appendix D). Every autoencoder, CADRE included, uses the same recipe from MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], with its latents standardized by their own statistics. Following SD3 [(Esser et al., 2024)] and RAE [(Zheng et al., 2026)], our tuning includes shifting the noise schedule with each autoencoder’s latent size and token count.

    Rollouts are scored on image and motion quality, and on action following. Each world model receives 40 real frames (2 s) with their actions and generates the next 96 (4.8 s) under the recorded actions, on 2048 held-out samples per environment shared across autoencoders. We score the last 16 decoded frames. FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] measures image quality and FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] also penalizes implausible motion and temporal seams. PSNR and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] measure closeness to the recorded future; PSNR should always be accompanied by distributional metrics, as it rewards blur. Action following is measured by the action recoverability ratio (ARR), which extends the inverse dynamics evaluation of MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)]: a frozen probe reads the actions back from the rollout, and their coefficient of determination (R²) is normalized by the probe’s R² on real video, so an ARR of one means real-video recoverability (Appendix E).

    We compare seven CADRE autoencoders with five recent ones. The seven differ only in their compression τ×s×s, and we name each CADRE-τ×s×s (Figure 12, Appendix G). Of the others, four are off the shelf and used at their native compression: Wan 2.2 [(Wan et al., 2025)] (4×16×16), Cosmos [(NVIDIA et al., 2025)] (8×8×8), LTX-2 [(HaCohen et al., 2026)] (8×32×32) and the image autoencoder DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025b)] (1×32×32). The fifth retrains the MIRA recipe [(Hu et al., 2026)] on our data at 2×32×32. The LTX-2 decoder reads future latents, so we decode each prefix and keep its newest frames, as a streaming system would. The generators they come from train on far more video, such as 20M curated hours for Cosmos, likely including many datasets used here.

    4.1 Should the decoder use perceptual regression or diffusion?

    A decoder can regress one video from the latent or sample one by diffusion. MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)] takes the first route: it replaces the adversarial losses used since VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2021)] with perceptual losses (LPIPS and DINO) and works well on Rocket League. It is also the only autoencoder besides CADRE that runs at 20 frames per second within the 230 ms lag humans notice (Figure 1). To test this route beyond games, we retrain the MIRA recipe on our mixture (Appendix C) at 2×32×32 with our extractor and budget (Figure 4a). Against the CADRE decoder, it gives higher PSNR but worse FID and FVD in every environment. In one step, the CADRE decoder lowers FVD by 1.4 to 2.5× with similar action following. A second step lowers FID by up to 23%.

    4.2 How do the autoencoders trade quality for latency?

    To compare the autoencoders on both axes at once, we plot rollout quality against action latency (Figure 4b for robot manipulation, Figure 1 for driving, Figure 14 for all); an autoencoder lies on the Pareto frontier when no other is both faster and better. CADRE autoencoders form most of this frontier in every environment. In 42 of the 48 comparisons with MIRA, Wan 2.2, Cosmos and LTX-2 (four environments; FID, FVD and ARR), a CADRE autoencoder is at least as fast and better by more than 2%; DC-AE, faster than all, is compared below. With two decoding steps, the best FID of every environment belongs to CADRE, most often to CADRE-4×16×16, and so does the best FVD, except in robot manipulation, where CADRE and Cosmos tie. The gap widens with a moving camera: in navigation, all CADRE autoencoders but one beat every other on FID and FVD, while Wan 2.2’s FVD grows from 53 in robot manipulation to 600 or more in navigation and LTX-2’s ARR falls to 0.04 indoors. CADRE also drifts least in 64 s robot manipulation rollouts (Appendix H).

    At the fast end, CADRE-1×48×48 reacts about as fast as DC-AE and beats it in navigation; DC-AE wins in manipulation. Few autoencoders are both fluid and responsive: streaming on one H100 with eight denoising steps, only CADRE-2×32×32, CADRE-2×16×16 and MIRA run at 20 frames per second under the 230 ms lag humans notice [(Shimada et al., 2009)] (Figure 1). The world models of Figure 5 run fluidly, at 29 to 58 frames per second (Appendix D), and, from the same context, follow actions never recorded with it, such as holding still or turning the other way (Figure 22).

    5 How to Compress for Interactive World Models

    We now ask three questions: which component should compress temporally, how many frames one latent should span, and what coarser spatial tokens trade for their speed. Comparisons follow the protocol of Section 4, so arms differ only in how the video is compressed.

    5.1 Should the autoencoder or the world model compress temporally?

    Temporal compression can happen in the autoencoder or in the world model. The alternative to CADRE is an image autoencoder that leaves frames temporally uncompressed, with the world model patching its latent temporally. Both routes give the same token grid, but a different model learns the compression. In robot manipulation, we reach each grid a second time by patching the latent of CADRE-1×16×16 inside the world model (Figure 6). Only the compression changes. Actions and noise levels stay per frame, and a patched token receives the actions of every frame it covers.

    Temporal compression in the autoencoder gives better frames than in the world model. Compressing in the autoencoder gives better FID, FVD, PSNR and LPIPS at every temporal grid, except FVD at 2×32×32, where space is compressed too. The FVD gap grows with the factor, from 9 points when compressing 2 frames to 28 when compressing 8. Decoder capacity does not explain it, since the patched arm decodes with CADRE-1×16×16, the best reconstruction among them (Table 6). We attribute this to the training objectives. The autoencoder is trained to reconstruct pixels, so its compression keeps appearance. The world model is trained to predict latents, so its compression keeps only what helps that prediction. This matches image and video generation, where compressing in the autoencoder beats patching [(Chen et al., 2025b; Gupta et al., 2024)].

    Where temporal compression happens barely changes action following. The exception is 8 frames, where patching drops ARR from 0.72 to 0.56. Action following depends on the motion the actions cause, which the world model’s compression is trained to keep.

    5.2 How many frames should one latent span?

    To separate temporal compression from the cost of coarser tokens, we vary τ in two sweeps (Figure 7). The first holds s=16 and isolates temporal compression. The second holds about 1100 tokens per 16-frame clip, so at a given τ its gap to the first measures the cost of coarser spatial tokens. All world models are matched in training steps and total training frames.

    Latents should span many redundant frames in manipulation and few in navigation. In manipulation, the camera is mostly still, so consecutive frames are redundant and one latent can span many of them at no cost (green curve in Figure 7). In navigation, the camera moves and the view shifts by more than a token within one long latent (Appendix I), so long latents degrade motion, raising FVD by up to 64% over two-frame latents. Action following changes less (Appendix G). Camera motion is our leading explanation, though the domains also differ in actions and scenes.

    In 64 s robot manipulation rollouts, long latents do not make errors accumulate: CADRE-8×16×16 is best from about 13 s on and ends with the lowest FVD (Appendix H). Long latents do leave seams, visible jumps between chunks. A boundary excess compares the frame-to-frame change across chunk boundaries with the change within chunks, relative to real video (Appendix K). It grows with τ in all four environments, to 1.6–1.8 at τ=8 (Table 10). With a moving view, the seams also show in FVD, which grows 1.6 to 2.1× more at τ=8 than at τ=2.

    At a fixed token budget, navigation favors few frames per latent and manipulation many. Along the orange curve of Figure 7, autoencoders give about 1100 tokens per 16-frame clip. In navigation, the low-latency CADRE-2×32×32 is best, with two frames and coarser tokens. In manipulation, CADRE-8×16×16 gives the most plausible motion, with eight frames and fine tokens.

    5.3 What do coarser spatial tokens trade for their speed?

    At a given τ, coarser spatial tokens cut the world model’s cost, and the gap between the two sweeps isolates what they lose in quality and action following.

    Fine spatial tokens matter most when the action is small and stays in view. In robot manipulation, the action shows in a small region that stays in view. At τ=2, coarser spatial tokens multiply FVD by 2.4 and lower action following, with almost no change in FID (orange against green in Figure 7). In navigation, the action moves the whole frame, which coarse tokens already capture, and the gap nearly vanishes (Appendix G). FID may miss errors confined to small regions, but ARR, which reads the motion itself, drops too (Appendix G).

    6 Related Work

    World models and their autoencoders. Video world models serve driving [(Russell et al., 2025)], robotics [(Yang et al., 2024)] and open scenes [(Bruce et al., 2024)]. Interactive ones stream in real time [(Valevski et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024)], often by distilling a text-to-video generator whose autoencoder they inherit [(He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a)]. Few study that autoencoder. SANA-WM [(Zhu et al., 2026a)] swaps two of them offline, and MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)] judges its own through the world model, but only on a single game. We compare twelve autoencoders of varied compression through world models in four environments.

    Latent structure and compression. Generation quality depends on the structure of the latent [(Rombach et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2025)]. Representation autoencoders generate in the space of a frozen self-supervised encoder [(Zheng et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026)], at one compression rate. Video autoencoders mostly compress 8× in space and 4× in time [(Wan et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024)], some far more [(HaCohen et al., 2024; HaCohen et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025b)]. A generator can also compress through its patch size [(Peebles & Xie, 2023; Gupta et al., 2024)]. For images, DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025b)] finds that compressing in the autoencoder beats patching. We test this for video world models and build representation autoencoders that span seven spatio-temporal compressions.

    Few-step diffusion decoders. Diffusion decoders avoid adversarial losses [(Preechakul et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2025d)] but need many steps, or a second stage to reach one [(OpenAI, 2023; Vallaeys et al., 2026)]. Shortcut models and flow maps learn few-step generation in one stage from their own predictions [(Frans et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2025)]. Our causal video decoder learns one- or two-step decoding this way, with no adversarial loss or second stage. Appendix L extends this section.

    7 Conclusion

    An interactive world model inherits its cost per frame, its action latency and much of its quality from its autoencoder, so its compression is a design choice. To study this choice, we build CADRE, an open family spanning seven compressions, and train the same world model on each in manipulation and navigation. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera, and our study points to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression, even in one or two steps. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality, and, in robot manipulation, action following too.

    Our world models each cover one environment; whether these findings carry over to a generalist one, and to policy training and planning, remains open. Our manipulation data use still or nearly still cameras; wrist-mounted cameras move, so our account predicts they favor the compression of navigation. We hope open autoencoders will let practitioners fit a world model’s compression to its scenes and to the latency and throughput its users need.

    • Appendix B Autoencoder implementation details

    Encoder. DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] (p=16) runs at 288×512, and its features average layers 2 and 4 to 11 plus the last layer. The bottleneck convolution maps its 768 channels to 64. In time, its kernel equals its stride τ and it has no padding, so it is causal. In space, the 18×32 grid is zero-padded to a multiple of the stride and cropped back in the decoder. Kernel and stride are 3 for 1×48×48 (6×11 tokens), 2 for 2×32×32 and 1 for s=16. CADRE-4×24×24 uses kernel 5, stride 3 and padding 1, and reshapes 4×64 output channels into a 2×2 block of latents (12×22 tokens).

    Decoder. It has 24 space-time blocks of width 1024 with 16 heads on a 16×16 patch grid; the last 4 form the temporal tail at the native frame rate. Blocks use QK-normalization, gated attention, rotary embeddings in space and time, SwiGLU and LayerScale, with 4 spatial and 1 temporal register tokens. After the unpatchify, a refine head applies two residual blocks of dilated depthwise and causal temporal convolutions. The decoder has about 480M parameters.

    Spatial AdaLN. AdaLN in DiT [(Peebles & Xie, 2023)] modulates all tokens of a sample with one vector. Like SPADE [(Park et al., 2019)], SEAN [(Zhu et al., 2020)], SCAM [(Dufour et al., 2022)] and PixelDiT [(Yu et al., 2026)], spatial AdaLN modulates each token hᵢ from the latent zᵢ at its position. With c the embedding of the flow time t and jump d,

    (γᵢ,βᵢ)=Linear(SiLU(zᵢ+c)), hᵢ←(1+γᵢ)⊙LN(hᵢ)+βᵢ.

    		(4)

    It is applied before space attention, time attention and the MLP, with separate scales and shifts. One head is shared by all blocks, with a learned per-block offset, and is zero-initialized.

    Gradient balancing. Each weight in Equation (6) is set at every step from gradient norms, as in the adaptive weight of VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2021)]:

    λᵢ = sg [(∥∇_Wℓ₁∥₂)/(∥∇_Wℓᵢ∥₂+δ)],

    		(5)

    where W is the weight of the head’s last layer, ℓ₁ the pixel term and ℓᵢ an auxiliary term, with δ=10⁻⁶ and weights clipped at 10⁴.

    Losses. The reconstruction term of Equation (2) is

    ℓ_rec(x̂,x) = ℓ₁(x̂,x) + λₗₚᵢₚₛ ℓₗₚᵢₚₛ(x̂,x) + λ_dino ℓ_dino(x̂,x) + λ_dwt ℓ_dwt(x̂,x),

    		(6)

    where ℓ_dino is the squared distance between normalized DINO features and ℓ_dwt the L₁ distance between two-level 3D Haar coefficients, which weights the high frequencies that pixel losses underweight [(Degeorge et al., 2026)]. LPIPS and DINO use a random quarter of the frames. The wavelet term has an extra factor of 0.25 and weights its low-pass band by 0.25.

    Progressive self-distillation.L_psd has weight 1 on a random quarter of steps. For each latent frame, r and t are two sorted uniform draws, and both half jumps use the current weights without gradients. The reconstruction and perceptual losses supervise only d=0. Table 3 gives the training recipe.

    Released autoencoders. We also release CADRE-2×32×32, 2×16×16, 4×16×16 and 8×16×16 trained beyond our experiments: to 360k steps, with the learning rate decayed from 2×10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻⁵ over the last 70k, then for 40k steps on clips of five resolutions from 256×448 to 384×640. Our results and world models use the 150k-step versions.

    Appendix C Autoencoder training data

    Every CADRE autoencoder and the MIRA-recipe baseline train on the same 23 video sources, about 76k hours (Figure 8, Table 2). A sample is a random 16-frame window from a video of a randomly drawn source, resized to cover 288×512, center-cropped and resampled to 20 frames per second. Videos shorter than 16 frames or below 256 pixels on the short side are dropped.

    Appendix D World model architecture and training

    The world model follows MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], and Figure 9 is redrawn from theirs. Table 3 lists its hyperparameters.

    Blocks. Each block runs bidirectional space attention within a latent frame, then a SwiGLU MLP; blocks 0, 4, 8, 12 and 15 add causal time attention in between. Attention uses 16 query and 4 key/value heads, QK-normalization, a gate and rotary embeddings (2D in space, 1D in time). Blocks are pre-norm, without LayerScale or registers.

    Conditioning. Each latent frame is conditioned on its flow time and on the τ actions that produced it, action aⱼ producing frame j+1. Actions are normalized per environment; their per-frame embeddings are concatenated, projected and passed through an MLP. The flow time gets a sinusoidal embedding and an MLP, and the sum of both embeddings drives AdaLN [(Peebles & Xie, 2023)] before space attention, time attention and the MLP of every block. In human manipulation, each hand contributes the frame-to-frame change in wrist position (3), wrist orientation (3) and 15 finger-joint rotations (45).

    Objective and recipe. Under diffusion forcing [(Chen et al., 2024a)], each latent frame draws its own flow time tᵢ, and the model regresses the velocity z₁-z₀ from z_tᵢ=tᵢz₁+(1-tᵢ)z₀ (Figure 9). PSD-U, the progressive self-distillation of [Boffi et al. (2025)] with a uniformly sampled intermediate time, is added on a fixed quarter of every batch. The recipe (Table 3) is the same for every autoencoder; only the action encoder follows the environment. The world model does not patch the latent further, except in Section 5.1.

    Inference. The context is encoded once. At each chunk boundary, the world model reads the previous latent frame and the τ actions entered during the chunk and predicts the next latent frame in 10 denoising steps. The frame is decoded for display, re-noised to level 0.2 and cached (Figure 11). Since aₜ produces frame t+1, an action first shows τ frames after it is entered. This timing comes from supervision: the architecture only keeps an action from changing frames already shown, and within a latent frame each decoded frame can depend on all τ actions, so frame 5 reflects a₄ and earlier actions such as a₃.

    Latency. Figures 4b and 14 plot the action latency of Equation (1) for the first action of a chunk, the worst case, at f=20 frames per second. We time t_gen, one world model call with its 10 denoising steps and cache pass, and t_dec, the decode of one new latent frame, on one H100 at batch 1 in bf16 with torch.compile, averaged over 32 latent frames after warm-up on the robot-manipulation world models (Table 4). Each decoder runs its most efficient streaming decode: causal decoders decode only the new latent and reuse the context (exactly for Wan 2.2; for CADRE, MIRA and Cosmos we time the decode of the new latent, the cost of a decoder cache), DC-AE decodes each frame alone, and the non-causal LTX-2 re-decodes an 8-latent window. The rollouts of Table 7 are decoded over each decoder’s trained window. The resulting maximum frame rate, τ/(t_gen+t_dec), differs from the displayed rate, which is always 20 frames per second; it only tells whether the world model runs fluidly. Every CADRE autoencoder with τ≥4 does, as does CADRE-2×32×32 with one step; those with τ=1 reach only 7 to 13 frames per second. Raising τ raises both the action latency and the maximum frame rate (Figure 1). With fewer denoising steps, every CADRE autoencoder with τ≥2 runs fluidly, while at τ=1 this needs one decoding step and at most four denoising steps (Figure 10).

    Appendix E Inverse dynamics probes for action recoverability

    A frozen probe, one per environment, reads the actions back from decoded frames, so it scores every autoencoder in the same space.

    Architecture. The probe maps a window of 8 frames to one action per frame. A frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] gives patch features from layers 2, 5, 8 and 11, combined by a learned softmax. Six factorized space-time blocks with bidirectional attention follow, then a per-frame attention pool and a two-layer head (27M trained parameters).

    Training. The probe trains on real clips from the world models’ training split with a smooth L₁ loss on standardized actions and photometric augmentation only. It uses AdamW (learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, batch 384) with cosine decay over 60k steps; we keep the 55k-step checkpoint (60k for human manipulation).

    Score. For each action dimension d, R²_d compares the recovered actions with the commanded ones over the last 16 generated frames of all clips, and ARR averages it normalized by the probe’s R² on the real continuation,

    ARR=(1)/(|D|)∑_d∈D(\max(R²_d, -1))/(R²_d(real)).

    		(7)

    On real video, the probe reaches R² of 0.91 in robot manipulation, 0.93 in driving and 0.83 in indoor navigation. Human manipulation has 102 action dimensions, and the probe barely reads the 90 finger-joint dimensions at 288×512, so D holds only the 12 wrist dimensions there (real-video R² 0.82).

    Control. We also score the recovered actions against the clip’s own commands shifted by 48 frames, which the rollout never received. A world model that ignores its actions scores alike on both, so the gap between the two raw R² values measures action following (Table 5). Every CADRE autoencoder keeps a clear gap in every environment. In driving, the gap of Wan 2.2, Cosmos and LTX-2 is small (0.04 to 0.14), and so is that of Cosmos and LTX-2 in human manipulation (0.24 and 0.12): their rollouts reproduce motion common to the environment, such as forward travel in driving.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：世界模型直接继承文生视频的 VAE，压多少倍没人管；但 τ=8、20 fps 时单是时间压缩就让动作至少延迟 400ms，而人超过 230ms 就能察觉。

要点：

  • 交互世界模型在视频自编码器的潜空间里生成，压缩倍数直接决定每帧成本与「动作多久才生效」
  • 既有工作多沿用文生视频的 VAE（为离线生成设计，没有 agent 在等），且缺训练数据与代码时无法改压缩率重训
  • 人对自己动作延迟超过约 230ms 即可察觉，要「即时」得低于 100ms；而 τ=8 在 20 fps 下仅时间压缩就带来 400ms，任何裁帧加速都救不回来
  • CADRE 是一族开放的因果扩散表示自编码器，跨多个时空压缩率，成员只差冻结特征上的小瓶颈、共享自蒸馏到一步或少步的扩散解码器；训练后世界模型单 H100 跑 20 fps、反应低于 230ms，占据延迟-质量前沿的大部分

为什么值得看：如果要把世界模型当引擎用，「压缩率」不是工程细节而是交互预算的第一性参数：它先决定延迟，再决定你还有多少算力可以用来提升画质。

中文摘要：视频世界模型从过去帧与动作预测未来帧，可充当 agent 训练、规划、评测的模拟器，也能被人交互控制。它们在视频自编码器的潜空间里生成，而压缩率同时决定每帧成本与动作生效的等待时间；但现有世界模型往往直接复用文生视频的自编码器——那些是为离线生成设计的，没有 agent 在等，且在没有原始训练数据与代码时无法换一个压缩率重训。作者因此系统研究「世界模型该在哪、该压多少」。他们构建 CADRE：一族开放的因果扩散表示自编码器，横跨多种时空压缩，成员之间只在冻结特征上的一个小瓶颈不同，并共享一个自蒸馏到一步或少数步的扩散解码器。在操纵与导航两个域、各两个环境上训练同一世界模型后，CADRE 在单张 H100 上以 20 fps 运行、反应时间低于 230 ms，并在运动保真度与动作跟随两项指标上占据延迟-质量前沿的大部分。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-26

Rethinking Video Autoencoders
for Interactive World Models

Abstract

Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-22-cadre.

1 Introduction

A world model is a learned simulator of an environment [(Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018)]. Given past frames and an agent’s actions, a video world model generates the next frames, and can be used to train agents [(Hafner et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024)], evaluate robot policies [(Yang et al., 2024)], plan the outcome of actions [(Bar et al., 2025)], or simply play a game [(Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026)]. To enable all these applications, two different aspects have to be optimized: the throughput that measures the number of frames generated per second, and the latency that measures the delay between the action and its effect on the output. Throughput limits how fast a simulation can happen, whereas latency limits how reactive and faithful a simulation can be.

Most video world models operate in the latent space of a video autoencoder [(Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025)]. To avoid designing an ad hoc autoencoder, many methods [(He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Zhu et al., 2026a)] reuse the autoencoder of a text-to-video generator such as LTX-2 [(HaCohen et al., 2026)], Wan 2.2 [(Wan et al., 2025)] or HunyuanVideo [(Kong et al., 2024)]. They thus inherit the throughput and latency that come with it. Yet, such autoencoders were not designed with the throughput-latency trade-off of world models in mind, and often perform massive temporal compression since it has low impact on visual quality.
