A typical 8× temporal compression delays every action by at least 400 ms at 20 frames per second. Humans notice when their own movement appears more than about 230 ms late [(Shimada et al., 2009)], and interaction feels immediate only below 100 ms [(Miller, 1968; Claypool & Claypool, 2006)]. This raises the question of how other throughput-latency trade-offs affect rollout quality and action following.

To address this question, we propose CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders built for interactive world models. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features, which sets the compression, and share a causal diffusion decoder that needs one or a few steps. To study compression across settings, we train the same world model, a causal diffusion transformer following MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], on each autoencoder, in two domains: manipulation (by a robot and by human hands) and navigation (driving and indoor). We compare CADRE with the autoencoders of Wan 2.2, Cosmos [(NVIDIA et al., 2025)] and LTX-2, the image autoencoder DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025b)] and the MIRA autoencoder retrained on our data. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera (Figure 1).

Interestingly, our study points to four findings. (1) At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression, and a few-step flow model trained by progressive self-distillation is a good fit. (2) In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model: patching inside the world model loses detail, and at eight frames also action following. (3) Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions. In manipulation the camera is still, so temporal compression costs little while spatial compression is costly. In navigation the camera moves and the balance reverses, so it pays to keep frames and compress spatially, the low-latency choice. (4) Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality, and, in robot manipulation, action following too.

Contributions.

  • •

    What compression controls in an interactive world model. We make explicit how an autoencoder’s spatial and temporal compression set a world model’s throughput and action latency, and we separate how much to compress from where to compress (Section 2).

  • •

    CADRE, causal diffusion representation autoencoders for interactive world models. Open models at seven spatio-temporal compressions, whose decoder learns one- or few-step decoding by progressive self-distillation, in a single stage and without an adversarial loss (Section 3).

  • •

    Where, and how much, to compress video for a world model. A controlled study in four environments, judged by rollouts and action following (Sections 4 and 5).

    • 2 What Compression Controls in an Interactive World Model

    Before studying how to compress, we make explicit what compression controls. An interactive world model generates in the latent space of an autoencoder that compresses a clip by τ temporally and s spatially, written τ×s×s: 2×32×32 compresses 2× temporally and 32× spatially. These two factors set the world model’s cost, action latency and throughput. The compression itself can happen in the autoencoder or in the world model (Section 5.1).

    Compression sets the world model’s cost. The world model we study is a causal, space-time-factorized diffusion transformer that predicts the next latent frame from the previous ones and the current action or action chunk (Section 4, Appendix D). Its cost grows with the number of tokens it processes, which only the spatial and temporal compression set: a clip of T frames of size H×W becomes N=(T/τ)(H/s)(W/s) latent tokens for the world model.

    A latent frame waits for all its actions. Every frame registers one action. A latent frame spans τ frames, so the world model can predict it only once all τ conditioning actions are known. It therefore consumes actions in chunks, and the actions of one chunk shape the next (Figure 2). The agent thus commits to τ actions before seeing their effect, as action-chunking policies do [(Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025)]. Causality holds between chunks. Within a chunk, the τ frames decode from the same latent, and their order is learned from real video.

    Temporal compression delays every action. The first action of a chunk waits τ/f for the chunk to close, where f is the frame rate, then t_gen for the world model to generate the latent frame and t_dec for the autoencoder to decode it into τ frames, which sets the throughput:

    latency=τ/f (chunk closes)+\underbracet_gen+t_dec_generate and decode, throughput=(τ)/(t_gen+t_dec).

    		(1)

    No speed-up shortens the first term, which at τ=8 and 20 frames per second is 400 ms, beyond the 230 ms lag humans notice in their own movement [(Shimada et al., 2009)]. In exchange, a larger τ raises the throughput and, at a fixed spatial factor, cuts the token count N.

    3 CADRE: Causal Diffusion Representation Autoencoders

    Studying compression means training the autoencoder at many compression points. The autoencoders of text-to-video generators release their weights but not their training data or code, so they cannot be retrained. We instead design an open family of autoencoders for world models, one per compression point (Figure 3). Its members share one recipe, differ only in their compression and are each trained from scratch, so the world models trained on them differ by compression alone.

    3.1 Architecture

    Frozen features and one trained layer encode the clip. As in MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], the encoder is that of a representation autoencoder [(Zheng et al., 2026)]. A frozen DINOv3 extractor [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] encodes each frame into one feature per p×p patch, aggregating several layers as in RAEv2 [(Singh et al., 2026)]. One trained 3D convolution with kernel (τ,k,k) and stride (τ,s^′,s^′) compresses τ frames of s^′2 patches into a deterministic latent, with s=p s^′ (Appendix B).

    A causal diffusion decoder keeps textures sharp. A strongly compressed latent keeps a scene’s layout and semantics but little texture, so a perceptual regression decoder averages the textures consistent with it into a blur [(Xu et al., 2026)]. We therefore use a diffusion decoder [(Preechakul et al., 2022; Pernías et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025d)], which samples the clip conditioned on the latent. It is a space-time-factorized transformer [(Bertasius et al., 2021; Arnab et al., 2021)] on a q×q patch grid, whose blocks attend over space, then causally over time. Most blocks process one token per latent frame, that is, per τ video frames. A linear map then splits each token into τ tokens, one per frame, so the last blocks resolve motion within a latent frame. The latent conditions the diffusion decoder in three places: (i) lifted by a transposed convolution and summed with the patchified noisy clip, (ii) through a spatial AdaLN [(Park et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2020; Dufour et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2026)] in every block, which also receives the flow time t and the jump length d, the size of the denoising step the decoder takes (Section 3.2, Appendix B), and (iii) through a zero-initialized skip into a light convolutional head. The decoder is time-causal, so it streams chunk by chunk.

    3.2 Training

    The decoder learns by flow matching and perceptual losses. The decoder g_θ uses the x-prediction, x-loss form of flow matching [(Li & He, 2026)]. It predicts the clean clip x from the latent z and a noisy clip xₜ=t x+(1-t) ε, with ε∼ℕ(0,I) and t=0 pure noise. As in diffusion forcing [(Chen et al., 2024a)], each chunk of τ frames draws its own t∼U(0,1). The loss is

    L_fm = E_x,ε,t ℓ_rec(g_θ(z, xₜ, t, 0), x),

    		(2)

    where the last argument, the jump length d, is zero here. The term ℓ_rec sums a mean absolute error, two perceptual distances (LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] and its analog in DINO feature space) and a 3D wavelet term as in LTX-Video [(HaCohen et al., 2024)], weighted by gradient balancing. CADRE trains on a 76k-hour mixture of web, robot, driving and camera video (Appendix C).

    Self-distillation makes one or two decoding steps enough. Flow-matching trajectories curve, so following them takes many steps, while an interactive world model needs single- or few-step decoding. Shortcut models [(Frans et al., 2025)] and self-distilled flow maps [(Boffi et al., 2025)] condition the network on its step size and train one large step to agree with two smaller ones. Following them, g_θ(z,xᵣ,r,d) predicts where a jump from r to r+d lands, through x_r+d=xᵣ+\tfracd1-r(x̂-xᵣ) with implied velocity v_θ=(x̂-xᵣ)/(1-r). One jump from r to t is trained to land where two half jumps through u=(r+t)/2 do (dropping z from the notation),

    L_psd = E ∥(1-r)(v_θ(xᵣ,r,t-r)-sg[\tfrac12(v_θ(xᵣ,r,u-r)+v_θ(x̂ᵤ,u,t-u))])∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where sg stops the gradient and x̂ᵤ is the point reached by the first half jump. Unlike the consistency decoder [(OpenAI, 2023)] and SSDD [(Vallaeys et al., 2026)], which distill a decoder in a second stage, the CADRE decoder is its own teacher and learns one- or few-jump decoding in one stage.

    4 Judging an Autoencoder by Its World Model

    An autoencoder is trained to reconstruct its input, yet in latent generation, reconstruction and generation trade off [(Yao et al., 2025; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2025)], and a line of work shapes the latent for the generator instead [(Leng et al., 2025; Kouzelis et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026; Ramanana Rahary et al., 2026b)]. We therefore score rollouts instead of reconstructions (Appendix F). As in MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], we judge each autoencoder by the rollouts of a world model trained on its latents; the world model, clips and actions are shared, so only the latent varies.

    Four environments span manipulation and navigation. We train world models in four environments, two of manipulation and two of navigation (Table 1), so that no conclusion rests on a single environment. In manipulation the view is static for the robot and nearly static for the head-mounted camera of the human, so mainly the arms or hands and the objects they handle move. In navigation the view itself moves, so the whole frame changes; we separate driving, a dynamic scene where other road users move on their own, from indoor navigation in static scenes. Action complexity ranges from 2 dimensions for driving to 102 for two hands. All videos are resampled to 20 frames per second at 288×512. Evaluation uses held-out episodes, and the official split for driving.

    One world model recipe serves every autoencoder. The world model is a 1.2B-parameter causal diffusion transformer conditioned on the τ actions of each latent frame and trained with diffusion forcing [(Chen et al., 2024a)] (Appendix D). Every autoencoder, CADRE included, uses the same recipe from MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], with its latents standardized by their own statistics. Following SD3 [(Esser et al., 2024)] and RAE [(Zheng et al., 2026)], our tuning includes shifting the noise schedule with each autoencoder’s latent size and token count.

    Rollouts are scored on image and motion quality, and on action following. Each world model receives 40 real frames (2 s) with their actions and generates the next 96 (4.8 s) under the recorded actions, on 2048 held-out samples per environment shared across autoencoders. We score the last 16 decoded frames. FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)] measures image quality and FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)] also penalizes implausible motion and temporal seams. PSNR and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] measure closeness to the recorded future; PSNR should always be accompanied by distributional metrics, as it rewards blur. Action following is measured by the action recoverability ratio (ARR), which extends the inverse dynamics evaluation of MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)]: a frozen probe reads the actions back from the rollout, and their coefficient of determination (R²) is normalized by the probe’s R² on real video, so an ARR of one means real-video recoverability (Appendix E).

    We compare seven CADRE autoencoders with five recent ones. The seven differ only in their compression τ×s×s, and we name each CADRE-τ×s×s (Figure 12, Appendix G). Of the others, four are off the shelf and used at their native compression: Wan 2.2 [(Wan et al., 2025)] (4×16×16), Cosmos [(NVIDIA et al., 2025)] (8×8×8), LTX-2 [(HaCohen et al., 2026)] (8×32×32) and the image autoencoder DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025b)] (1×32×32). The fifth retrains the MIRA recipe [(Hu et al., 2026)] on our data at 2×32×32. The LTX-2 decoder reads future latents, so we decode each prefix and keep its newest frames, as a streaming system would. The generators they come from train on far more video, such as 20M curated hours for Cosmos, likely including many datasets used here.

    4.1 Should the decoder use perceptual regression or diffusion?

    A decoder can regress one video from the latent or sample one by diffusion. MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)] takes the first route: it replaces the adversarial losses used since VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2021)] with perceptual losses (LPIPS and DINO) and works well on Rocket League. It is also the only autoencoder besides CADRE that runs at 20 frames per second within the 230 ms lag humans notice (Figure 1). To test this route beyond games, we retrain the MIRA recipe on our mixture (Appendix C) at 2×32×32 with our extractor and budget (Figure 4a). Against the CADRE decoder, it gives higher PSNR but worse FID and FVD in every environment. In one step, the CADRE decoder lowers FVD by 1.4 to 2.5× with similar action following. A second step lowers FID by up to 23%.

    4.2 How do the autoencoders trade quality for latency?

    To compare the autoencoders on both axes at once, we plot rollout quality against action latency (Figure 4b for robot manipulation, Figure 1 for driving, Figure 14 for all); an autoencoder lies on the Pareto frontier when no other is both faster and better. CADRE autoencoders form most of this frontier in every environment. In 42 of the 48 comparisons with MIRA, Wan 2.2, Cosmos and LTX-2 (four environments; FID, FVD and ARR), a CADRE autoencoder is at least as fast and better by more than 2%; DC-AE, faster than all, is compared below. With two decoding steps, the best FID of every environment belongs to CADRE, most often to CADRE-4×16×16, and so does the best FVD, except in robot manipulation, where CADRE and Cosmos tie. The gap widens with a moving camera: in navigation, all CADRE autoencoders but one beat every other on FID and FVD, while Wan 2.2’s FVD grows from 53 in robot manipulation to 600 or more in navigation and LTX-2’s ARR falls to 0.04 indoors. CADRE also drifts least in 64 s robot manipulation rollouts (Appendix H).

    At the fast end, CADRE-1×48×48 reacts about as fast as DC-AE and beats it in navigation; DC-AE wins in manipulation. Few autoencoders are both fluid and responsive: streaming on one H100 with eight denoising steps, only CADRE-2×32×32, CADRE-2×16×16 and MIRA run at 20 frames per second under the 230 ms lag humans notice [(Shimada et al., 2009)] (Figure 1). The world models of Figure 5 run fluidly, at 29 to 58 frames per second (Appendix D), and, from the same context, follow actions never recorded with it, such as holding still or turning the other way (Figure 22).

    5 How to Compress for Interactive World Models

    We now ask three questions: which component should compress temporally, how many frames one latent should span, and what coarser spatial tokens trade for their speed. Comparisons follow the protocol of Section 4, so arms differ only in how the video is compressed.

    5.1 Should the autoencoder or the world model compress temporally?

    Temporal compression can happen in the autoencoder or in the world model. The alternative to CADRE is an image autoencoder that leaves frames temporally uncompressed, with the world model patching its latent temporally. Both routes give the same token grid, but a different model learns the compression. In robot manipulation, we reach each grid a second time by patching the latent of CADRE-1×16×16 inside the world model (Figure 6). Only the compression changes. Actions and noise levels stay per frame, and a patched token receives the actions of every frame it covers.

    Temporal compression in the autoencoder gives better frames than in the world model. Compressing in the autoencoder gives better FID, FVD, PSNR and LPIPS at every temporal grid, except FVD at 2×32×32, where space is compressed too. The FVD gap grows with the factor, from 9 points when compressing 2 frames to 28 when compressing 8. Decoder capacity does not explain it, since the patched arm decodes with CADRE-1×16×16, the best reconstruction among them (Table 6). We attribute this to the training objectives. The autoencoder is trained to reconstruct pixels, so its compression keeps appearance. The world model is trained to predict latents, so its compression keeps only what helps that prediction. This matches image and video generation, where compressing in the autoencoder beats patching [(Chen et al., 2025b; Gupta et al., 2024)].

    Where temporal compression happens barely changes action following. The exception is 8 frames, where patching drops ARR from 0.72 to 0.56. Action following depends on the motion the actions cause, which the world model’s compression is trained to keep.

    5.2 How many frames should one latent span?

    To separate temporal compression from the cost of coarser tokens, we vary τ in two sweeps (Figure 7). The first holds s=16 and isolates temporal compression. The second holds about 1100 tokens per 16-frame clip, so at a given τ its gap to the first measures the cost of coarser spatial tokens. All world models are matched in training steps and total training frames.

    Latents should span many redundant frames in manipulation and few in navigation. In manipulation, the camera is mostly still, so consecutive frames are redundant and one latent can span many of them at no cost (green curve in Figure 7). In navigation, the camera moves and the view shifts by more than a token within one long latent (Appendix I), so long latents degrade motion, raising FVD by up to 64% over two-frame latents. Action following changes less (Appendix G). Camera motion is our leading explanation, though the domains also differ in actions and scenes.

    In 64 s robot manipulation rollouts, long latents do not make errors accumulate: CADRE-8×16×16 is best from about 13 s on and ends with the lowest FVD (Appendix H). Long latents do leave seams, visible jumps between chunks. A boundary excess compares the frame-to-frame change across chunk boundaries with the change within chunks, relative to real video (Appendix K). It grows with τ in all four environments, to 1.6–1.8 at τ=8 (Table 10). With a moving view, the seams also show in FVD, which grows 1.6 to 2.1× more at τ=8 than at τ=2.

    At a fixed token budget, navigation favors few frames per latent and manipulation many. Along the orange curve of Figure 7, autoencoders give about 1100 tokens per 16-frame clip. In navigation, the low-latency CADRE-2×32×32 is best, with two frames and coarser tokens. In manipulation, CADRE-8×16×16 gives the most plausible motion, with eight frames and fine tokens.

    5.3 What do coarser spatial tokens trade for their speed?

    At a given τ, coarser spatial tokens cut the world model’s cost, and the gap between the two sweeps isolates what they lose in quality and action following.

    Fine spatial tokens matter most when the action is small and stays in view. In robot manipulation, the action shows in a small region that stays in view. At τ=2, coarser spatial tokens multiply FVD by 2.4 and lower action following, with almost no change in FID (orange against green in Figure 7). In navigation, the action moves the whole frame, which coarse tokens already capture, and the gap nearly vanishes (Appendix G). FID may miss errors confined to small regions, but ARR, which reads the motion itself, drops too (Appendix G).

    6 Related Work

    World models and their autoencoders. Video world models serve driving [(Russell et al., 2025)], robotics [(Yang et al., 2024)] and open scenes [(Bruce et al., 2024)]. Interactive ones stream in real time [(Valevski et al., 2025; Alonso et al., 2024)], often by distilling a text-to-video generator whose autoencoder they inherit [(He et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a)]. Few study that autoencoder. SANA-WM [(Zhu et al., 2026a)] swaps two of them offline, and MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)] judges its own through the world model, but only on a single game. We compare twelve autoencoders of varied compression through world models in four environments.

    Latent structure and compression. Generation quality depends on the structure of the latent [(Rombach et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2025)]. Representation autoencoders generate in the space of a frozen self-supervised encoder [(Zheng et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2026)], at one compression rate. Video autoencoders mostly compress 8× in space and 4× in time [(Wan et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024)], some far more [(HaCohen et al., 2024; HaCohen et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025b)]. A generator can also compress through its patch size [(Peebles & Xie, 2023; Gupta et al., 2024)]. For images, DC-AE [(Chen et al., 2025b)] finds that compressing in the autoencoder beats patching. We test this for video world models and build representation autoencoders that span seven spatio-temporal compressions.

    Few-step diffusion decoders. Diffusion decoders avoid adversarial losses [(Preechakul et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2025d)] but need many steps, or a second stage to reach one [(OpenAI, 2023; Vallaeys et al., 2026)]. Shortcut models and flow maps learn few-step generation in one stage from their own predictions [(Frans et al., 2025; Boffi et al., 2025)]. Our causal video decoder learns one- or two-step decoding this way, with no adversarial loss or second stage. Appendix L extends this section.

    7 Conclusion

    An interactive world model inherits its cost per frame, its action latency and much of its quality from its autoencoder, so its compression is a design choice. To study this choice, we build CADRE, an open family spanning seven compressions, and train the same world model on each in manipulation and navigation. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera, and our study points to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression, even in one or two steps. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality, and, in robot manipulation, action following too.

    Our world models each cover one environment; whether these findings carry over to a generalist one, and to policy training and planning, remains open. Our manipulation data use still or nearly still cameras; wrist-mounted cameras move, so our account predicts they favor the compression of navigation. We hope open autoencoders will let practitioners fit a world model’s compression to its scenes and to the latency and throughput its users need.

    Reproducibility statement

    Section 3 and Appendix B describe the autoencoder architecture, losses and training recipe, and Table 3 lists the hyperparameters of both the autoencoders and the world models. Appendix C lists every source of the autoencoder training mixture with its sampling weight, size and preprocessing. Appendix D gives the world model architecture, conditioning, objective, training recipe and inference protocol, and Appendix E specifies the inverse dynamics probes behind action recoverability. Section 4 fixes the evaluation protocol shared by every autoencoder, and Table 7 reports every number behind the figures. We release the code and the checkpoints.

    Ethics statement

    All training and evaluation data come from published datasets, used under their licenses. Some show people, such as the hands in human manipulation and the faces in talking-head and action videos; we use them only to learn video representations and do not identify anyone. Generated video can be misused to fabricate footage. Our world models are specialized to manipulation and navigation, run at 288×512 and follow low-level actions, which limits such use.

    AI use statement

    We used generative AI tools to implement and debug code, including the training, evaluation and plotting scripts; to draft and edit parts of the paper for readability; to create and edit figures; and to search for and format references. We reviewed all AI-assisted work and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Overview

    The supplementary material details how CADRE and its world models are built and scored, reports every autoencoder in every environment and metric, and adds the analyses behind the explanations of Section 5: long rollouts, camera motion, counterfactual actions and seams. It also compares rollouts of every autoencoder.

    Supplementary map.

  • •

    B Autoencoder implementation: encoder layers and bottleneck strides, decoder blocks, spatial AdaLN, gradient balancing, losses and progressive self-distillation (Section 3).

  • •

    C Autoencoder training data: the 23 video sources, about 76k hours, shared by every CADRE autoencoder and the MIRA recipe (Figure 8, Table 2).

  • •

    D World model: architecture, action conditioning and training recipe (Table 3), the streaming inference loop (Figure 11), and the timing behind every latency and frame rate of the paper (Table 4, Figure 10).

  • •

    E Inverse dynamics probes: probe architecture and training, the definition of ARR, and a control against shifted commands (Table 5).

  • •

    F Reconstruction: held-out reconstruction of every autoencoder (Table 6), and why we do not rank autoencoders by it (Section 4).

  • •

    G Full results: every autoencoder in every environment and metric, with one and two decoding steps (Table 7); the compression plane (Figure 12); and Figures 4 and 7 in full (Figures 13, 14 and 15, the last with CADRE-4×24×24).

  • •

    H Long-horizon rollouts: 64 s rollouts on robot manipulation (Figure 17), their drift rates (Table 8) and examples (Figure 16).

  • •

    I Motion in the evaluation sets: how much each environment moves (Table 9), behind the camera-motion explanation of Section 5.2.

  • •

    J Qualitative results: counterfactual rollouts (Figure 22), and rollouts of every autoencoder on the same clip in each environment (Figures 18 to 21).

  • •

    K Boundary excess: the seam metric and its values at τ=2, 4 and 8 (Table 10).

  • •

    L Extended related work.

    • Appendix B Autoencoder implementation details

    Encoder. DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] (p=16) runs at 288×512, and its features average layers 2 and 4 to 11 plus the last layer. The bottleneck convolution maps its 768 channels to 64. In time, its kernel equals its stride τ and it has no padding, so it is causal. In space, the 18×32 grid is zero-padded to a multiple of the stride and cropped back in the decoder. Kernel and stride are 3 for 1×48×48 (6×11 tokens), 2 for 2×32×32 and 1 for s=16. CADRE-4×24×24 uses kernel 5, stride 3 and padding 1, and reshapes 4×64 output channels into a 2×2 block of latents (12×22 tokens).

    Decoder. It has 24 space-time blocks of width 1024 with 16 heads on a 16×16 patch grid; the last 4 form the temporal tail at the native frame rate. Blocks use QK-normalization, gated attention, rotary embeddings in space and time, SwiGLU and LayerScale, with 4 spatial and 1 temporal register tokens. After the unpatchify, a refine head applies two residual blocks of dilated depthwise and causal temporal convolutions. The decoder has about 480M parameters.

    Spatial AdaLN. AdaLN in DiT [(Peebles & Xie, 2023)] modulates all tokens of a sample with one vector. Like SPADE [(Park et al., 2019)], SEAN [(Zhu et al., 2020)], SCAM [(Dufour et al., 2022)] and PixelDiT [(Yu et al., 2026)], spatial AdaLN modulates each token hᵢ from the latent zᵢ at its position. With c the embedding of the flow time t and jump d,

    (γᵢ,βᵢ)=Linear(SiLU(zᵢ+c)), hᵢ←(1+γᵢ)⊙LN(hᵢ)+βᵢ.

    		(4)

    It is applied before space attention, time attention and the MLP, with separate scales and shifts. One head is shared by all blocks, with a learned per-block offset, and is zero-initialized.

    Gradient balancing. Each weight in Equation (6) is set at every step from gradient norms, as in the adaptive weight of VQGAN [(Esser et al., 2021)]:

    λᵢ = sg [(∥∇_Wℓ₁∥₂)/(∥∇_Wℓᵢ∥₂+δ)],

    		(5)

    where W is the weight of the head’s last layer, ℓ₁ the pixel term and ℓᵢ an auxiliary term, with δ=10⁻⁶ and weights clipped at 10⁴.

    Losses. The reconstruction term of Equation (2) is

    ℓ_rec(x̂,x) = ℓ₁(x̂,x) + λₗₚᵢₚₛ ℓₗₚᵢₚₛ(x̂,x) + λ_dino ℓ_dino(x̂,x) + λ_dwt ℓ_dwt(x̂,x),

    		(6)

    where ℓ_dino is the squared distance between normalized DINO features and ℓ_dwt the L₁ distance between two-level 3D Haar coefficients, which weights the high frequencies that pixel losses underweight [(Degeorge et al., 2026)]. LPIPS and DINO use a random quarter of the frames. The wavelet term has an extra factor of 0.25 and weights its low-pass band by 0.25.

    Progressive self-distillation.L_psd has weight 1 on a random quarter of steps. For each latent frame, r and t are two sorted uniform draws, and both half jumps use the current weights without gradients. The reconstruction and perceptual losses supervise only d=0. Table 3 gives the training recipe.

    Released autoencoders. We also release CADRE-2×32×32, 2×16×16, 4×16×16 and 8×16×16 trained beyond our experiments: to 360k steps, with the learning rate decayed from 2×10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻⁵ over the last 70k, then for 40k steps on clips of five resolutions from 256×448 to 384×640. Our results and world models use the 150k-step versions.

    Appendix C Autoencoder training data

    Every CADRE autoencoder and the MIRA-recipe baseline train on the same 23 video sources, about 76k hours (Figure 8, Table 2). A sample is a random 16-frame window from a video of a randomly drawn source, resized to cover 288×512, center-cropped and resampled to 20 frames per second. Videos shorter than 16 frames or below 256 pixels on the short side are dropped.

    Appendix D World model architecture and training

    The world model follows MIRA [(Hu et al., 2026)], and Figure 9 is redrawn from theirs. Table 3 lists its hyperparameters.

    Blocks. Each block runs bidirectional space attention within a latent frame, then a SwiGLU MLP; blocks 0, 4, 8, 12 and 15 add causal time attention in between. Attention uses 16 query and 4 key/value heads, QK-normalization, a gate and rotary embeddings (2D in space, 1D in time). Blocks are pre-norm, without LayerScale or registers.

    Conditioning. Each latent frame is conditioned on its flow time and on the τ actions that produced it, action aⱼ producing frame j+1. Actions are normalized per environment; their per-frame embeddings are concatenated, projected and passed through an MLP. The flow time gets a sinusoidal embedding and an MLP, and the sum of both embeddings drives AdaLN [(Peebles & Xie, 2023)] before space attention, time attention and the MLP of every block. In human manipulation, each hand contributes the frame-to-frame change in wrist position (3), wrist orientation (3) and 15 finger-joint rotations (45).

    Objective and recipe. Under diffusion forcing [(Chen et al., 2024a)], each latent frame draws its own flow time tᵢ, and the model regresses the velocity z₁-z₀ from z_tᵢ=tᵢz₁+(1-tᵢ)z₀ (Figure 9). PSD-U, the progressive self-distillation of [Boffi et al. (2025)] with a uniformly sampled intermediate time, is added on a fixed quarter of every batch. The recipe (Table 3) is the same for every autoencoder; only the action encoder follows the environment. The world model does not patch the latent further, except in Section 5.1.

    Inference. The context is encoded once. At each chunk boundary, the world model reads the previous latent frame and the τ actions entered during the chunk and predicts the next latent frame in 10 denoising steps. The frame is decoded for display, re-noised to level 0.2 and cached (Figure 11). Since aₜ produces frame t+1, an action first shows τ frames after it is entered. This timing comes from supervision: the architecture only keeps an action from changing frames already shown, and within a latent frame each decoded frame can depend on all τ actions, so frame 5 reflects a₄ and earlier actions such as a₃.

    Latency. Figures 4b and 14 plot the action latency of Equation (1) for the first action of a chunk, the worst case, at f=20 frames per second. We time t_gen, one world model call with its 10 denoising steps and cache pass, and t_dec, the decode of one new latent frame, on one H100 at batch 1 in bf16 with torch.compile, averaged over 32 latent frames after warm-up on the robot-manipulation world models (Table 4). Each decoder runs its most efficient streaming decode: causal decoders decode only the new latent and reuse the context (exactly for Wan 2.2; for CADRE, MIRA and Cosmos we time the decode of the new latent, the cost of a decoder cache), DC-AE decodes each frame alone, and the non-causal LTX-2 re-decodes an 8-latent window. The rollouts of Table 7 are decoded over each decoder’s trained window. The resulting maximum frame rate, τ/(t_gen+t_dec), differs from the displayed rate, which is always 20 frames per second; it only tells whether the world model runs fluidly. Every CADRE autoencoder with τ≥4 does, as does CADRE-2×32×32 with one step; those with τ=1 reach only 7 to 13 frames per second. Raising τ raises both the action latency and the maximum frame rate (Figure 1). With fewer denoising steps, every CADRE autoencoder with τ≥2 runs fluidly, while at τ=1 this needs one decoding step and at most four denoising steps (Figure 10).

    Appendix E Inverse dynamics probes for action recoverability

    A frozen probe, one per environment, reads the actions back from decoded frames, so it scores every autoencoder in the same space.

    Architecture. The probe maps a window of 8 frames to one action per frame. A frozen DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [(Siméoni et al., 2026)] gives patch features from layers 2, 5, 8 and 11, combined by a learned softmax. Six factorized space-time blocks with bidirectional attention follow, then a per-frame attention pool and a two-layer head (27M trained parameters).

    Training. The probe trains on real clips from the world models’ training split with a smooth L₁ loss on standardized actions and photometric augmentation only. It uses AdamW (learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, batch 384) with cosine decay over 60k steps; we keep the 55k-step checkpoint (60k for human manipulation).

    Score. For each action dimension d, R²_d compares the recovered actions with the commanded ones over the last 16 generated frames of all clips, and ARR averages it normalized by the probe’s R² on the real continuation,

    ARR=(1)/(|D|)∑_d∈D(\max(R²_d, -1))/(R²_d(real)).

    		(7)

    On real video, the probe reaches R² of 0.91 in robot manipulation, 0.93 in driving and 0.83 in indoor navigation. Human manipulation has 102 action dimensions, and the probe barely reads the 90 finger-joint dimensions at 288×512, so D holds only the 12 wrist dimensions there (real-video R² 0.82).

    Control. We also score the recovered actions against the clip’s own commands shifted by 48 frames, which the rollout never received. A world model that ignores its actions scores alike on both, so the gap between the two raw R² values measures action following (Table 5). Every CADRE autoencoder keeps a clear gap in every environment. In driving, the gap of Wan 2.2, Cosmos and LTX-2 is small (0.04 to 0.14), and so is that of Cosmos and LTX-2 in human manipulation (0.24 and 0.12): their rollouts reproduce motion common to the environment, such as forward travel in driving.

item.title: 世界模型不知道这块橡皮有多软：PhysiCalWorld 用一段探索视频编成物理描述符，不微调也能校准 ｜ PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
item.description:
一句话：质量分布、关节阻尼、摩擦这类决定状态转移的性质，单帧或窄窗口里根本看不到；不校准，预测就会回归先验、在新场景里漂移。

要点：

  • 现有世界模型只从当前帧或很窄的历史窗口感知场景，观察不到决定动力学的物理属性
  • PhysiCalWorld 把测试场景里采集的一小段探索交互编码成一个紧凑的 physics descriptor token，用 in-context prompting 校准，不微调也不建解析物理模型
  • 只用潜预测损失端到端训练，不需要任何物理标签
  • 推理时 descriptor 只提一次，可在多次 rollout 中复用，额外算力几乎可忽略

为什么值得看：「同一套权重，换一个场景就失灵」是世界模型落地最大的坑之一；用一段交互当上下文、而不是给每个场景重训，这个思路对引擎里「运行时自适应」的场景同样适用。

中文摘要：现有世界模型通常只根据当前视觉帧或很窄的历史窗口理解场景，但这些观测往往揭示不出决定状态转移的物理属性，比如物体的质量分布、关节阻尼或表面摩擦。不做这些因素的校准，世界模型的预测就会向经验先验回归，在新测试场景里产生严重漂移。作者提出 PhysiCalWorld：通过在上下文里提示（in-context prompting）把动作条件化的世界模型校准到该实例特有的动力学上，既不需要微调，也不需要解析的物理建模。方法把在测试场景内采集的一段探索性交互编码成紧凑的 physics descriptor token，让后续预测锚定到场景真实的物理行为上；整个模型只用潜空间预测损失端到端训练，不使用物理标签。推理时描述符 token 提取一次即可，可在多次 rollout 中复用，额外计算开销可忽略。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-26

PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models

Abstract

Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object’s mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene’s actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training. Project page at https://physical-world.github.io/.

††footnotetext: *Equal contribution.  †Equal advising.

1 Introduction

World models predict how a scene evolves given its current state and the intended actions of the agents within it. Trained on internet-scale data, video-based world models [(Bruce et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2023; Team et al., 2026; Agarwal et al., 2026)] are now able to generate photorealistic visual predictions of complex scene dynamics that are difficult to model with traditional physics engines. Modeling the world in image space is thus becoming a promising alternative to hand-built physics modeling in such areas as robotics [(Hou et al., 2026)] and autonomous driving [(Feng et al., 2025)].

Existing world models usually generate predictions from the current frame or a short visual history. However, such observations may leave the underlying physical properties unconstrained, forcing the world models to guess a future state among multiple possible ones. For example, an opaque bottle appears identical whether or not it is filled with water, yet it will respond differently under identical actuation. A world model that relies only on empirical priors over object category or appearance will produce incorrect predictions in such scenarios, limiting its applicability in downstream applications that require accurate dynamics [(Zhou et al., 2025; Quevedo et al., 2026)]. This motivates calibrating the world model to the hidden physical properties of each scene.

A natural way to resolve this physics ambiguity is to physically interact with the scene to infer its hidden properties, similar to how we humans would do for an object with unknown properties. Inspired by this, prior system identification methods [(Wu et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2021)] attempt to construct accurate physical models with closed-form equations and fit the predefined physics parameters to the in-situ interaction data. However, real-world systems exhibit complex, coupled physics factors, thus building a geometric model or formulating closed-form equations can be challenging. Hence, to adapt to each deployment setting, existing world models [(Gao et al., 2026)] are typically finetuned on a small set of in-house data, which is computationally expensive.

To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, a method for in-context Physics Calibration for World models. Inspired by the in-context learning capabilities of large sequence models [(Brown et al., 2020; Bar et al., 2022)], we prompt world models with a sequence of observation-action pairs collected in the test environment (i.e., an environment whose physics configuration is unknown) for physics calibration. Our in-context prompting method sidesteps both the need for human effort to build analytical physics simulators for system identification and expensive model finetuning. Our method requires only an exploratory interaction clip without any gradient descent steps. PhysiCalWorld compresses the interaction sequence into a compact physics descriptor token that conditions the world model. The entire system is trained end-to-end with only a video prediction objective, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

At test time, PhysiCalWorld first extracts the descriptor from a few exploratory interactions with the test scene (e.g., via random exploration or scripted policies). This descriptor then conditions all subsequent rollouts in that scene, enabling the world model to generate physically consistent predictions in novel configurations without any test-time weight updates.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

  • •

    In-Context Physics Calibration: We formulate physics calibration of generative world models as in-context conditioning: from a short interaction sequence, the model adapts zero-shot to instance-specific dynamics, with no test-time weight updates.

  • •

    Physics Descriptors Learned from Video Alone: We introduce a physics descriptor token that grounds the world model in hidden physical properties. It is learned end-to-end from video prediction alone, requiring neither ground-truth physics parameters nor a simulator.

  • •

    Performance and Analysis: Across four environments with single and coupled physics variations, PhysiCalWorld consistently improves rollout accuracy and planning success on two world model backbones. Its single-token descriptor matches or exceeds raw-context conditioning at a fraction of the cost. Without physics labels, the descriptors form a physically structured latent space and extrapolate beyond the training parameter range.

    • 2 Related Work

    World Models for Robotics.

    World models predict future states conditioned on current observations and agent actions, serving as an increasingly foundational framework for robotics [(Li et al., 2025c; Hou et al., 2026)]. For example, they are scalable neural simulators, enabling low-cost policy evaluation without real-world execution [(Guo et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026e; Team et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2025)]. Through future imagination, world models can also substantially improve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning [(Hafner et al., 2019; Hansen et al., 2022; Seo et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023)] and facilitate policy learning [(Saxena et al., 2026; Luo & Du, 2025)]. Moreover, optimizing action sequences with world models enables embodied agents to complete novel tasks via visual trajectory planning [(Zhou et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024)]. However, existing methods typically condition only on the current frame or a narrow observation history, assuming that these observations suffice to identify the underlying transition dynamics of the test scene. As a result, predictions tend to suffer from severe drift if latent physical properties vary across test scenes. In this work, we ground model predictions in the actual test-scene dynamics by introducing an additional in-context interaction prompt collected within the test scene as input to the world model, substantially enhancing the prediction accuracy and visual planning performance.

    In-Context Learning in Physical AI.

    Context can serve embodied agents in various forms. For example, it can adapt a robot policy to test-scene dynamics by conditioning directly on execution history or by explicitly recovering physical parameters [(Lee et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025)]. Another role is in-context policy learning, where task demonstrations steer actions either through structured representations such as keypoints and graphs [(Di Palo & Johns, 2024; Vosylius & Johns, 2025; Hwang et al., 2024)] or raw video-action pairs [(Fu et al., 2024; Shah et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2026)], and in-context reinforcement learning [(Lee et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023)]. Most recently, context has been applied to action-conditioned world models by prepending context prefixes to adapt to new camera viewpoints or embodiments [(Yang et al., 2026)]. However, prior works focus on policy adaptation, require privileged physical priors, or prepend raw context frames at high computational cost. In contrast, we use context to enable physics-grounded future prediction in world models, introducing a compact physics descriptor token to minimize computational overhead while maintaining high prediction accuracy and rollout efficiency.

    Physics-Aware Video Generation.

    Video generative models have advanced rapidly [(Yang et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026)], with widespread commercial deployment [(Seedance et al., 2026; Wan et al., 2025)]. However, their adherence to physical laws remains limited [(Motamed et al., 2026; Upadhyay et al., 2026; Bansal et al., 2025; Meng et al., 2024)]. Recent efforts seek to improve physical awareness in video models by incorporating explicit physics equations or parameters in the generation process [(Zhang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b)], coupling with external physics simulators [(Liu et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025; Foo et al., 2026)], leveraging foundation models [(Xue et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b)], or optimizing handcrafted rewards [(Zhang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2025a)]. However, these approaches either rely on analytical formulations and are restricted to a pre-defined set of physics properties, or focus on learning general physics and tend to fail in scenarios that require fine-grained instance-level physics grounding. In comparison, our work focuses on calibrating action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics of a test scene from an exploratory interaction prompt, operating entirely end-to-end without prior assumptions or ground-truth supervision of the environment’s underlying physics.

    3 Method

    We consider an embodied agent interacting with an environment over discrete timesteps t. At each step, the agent receives a high-dimensional visual observation oₜ∈O⊂ℝ^H×W×3 (and an optional proprioceptive state pₜ∈ℝ^dₚ) and executes a control action aₜ∈A⊂ℝ^dₐ. Our objective is to learn an action-conditioned world model that predicts future observations directly in a compact latent space and enables both long-horizon rollout and visual planning.

    Latent World Models.

    While our proposed in-context prompting framework is a plug-and-play module applicable to different world model architectures, we base the proposed method on two recent latent world models, DINO-WM [(Zhou et al., 2025)] and LeWM [(Maes et al., 2026)], due to their efficiency and strong trajectory planning performance. In these latent world models, each input RGB frame oₜ is encoded by a visual encoder Eᵥ into a set of visual tokens zₜ:

    zₜ=Eᵥ(oₜ)∈ℝ^N_z×d_z,

    		(1)

    where N_z denotes the number of visual tokens per frame and d_z is the feature dimension. Meanwhile, actions aₜ are mapped into action embeddings eₜᵃ∈ℝ^dₐ^′ via a learned MLP Eₐ:

    eₜᵃ=Eₐ(aₜ).

    		(2)

    The latent dynamics predictor f_θ (a causal transformer with weights θ) models temporal transitions over a history window of K steps. At step t, the predictor takes a sequence of past visual tokens and action embeddings to predict the next latent tokens:

    ẑₜ₊₁=f_θ({zᵢ,eᵢᵃ}_i=t-K+1ᵗ).

    		(3)

    For visual evaluation and pixel-space rollouts, we train a lightweight convolutional decoder Dᵥ that reconstructs images ôₜ from latent tokens, ôₜ₊₁=Dᵥ(ẑₜ₊₁), while downstream visual planning can be conducted directly within the latent space ℤ.

    3.1 Physics Calibration via Physics Descriptor Token

    Physics Ambiguity in Visual World Models.

    The forward transition function T of an environment depends not only on the current states and actions, but also on a set of underlying physics properties ξ∈X (e.g., mass, surface friction, or joint damping). Because many of these physics properties rarely correlate with surface appearance, a static visual frame oₜ or a brief observation window can hardly identify ξ and hence leaves the true transition dynamics underdetermined.

    Consequently, action-conditioned future prediction becomes an ill-posed, one-to-many problem. Without sufficient interaction data from the test scene to calibrate the future predictor f_θ, its prediction may collapse to the expectation over the training distribution with compounding dynamic drift when the test environment deviates from the nominal mean. While one could explicitly estimate and feed the test-scene physics parameters to f_θ, this usually relies on ad-hoc analytical modeling (as one must know in advance which physics properties determine the dynamics) and also introduces cascading estimation errors. An alternative strategy is to scale up the history window K of world models, so that the future predictor f_θ can directly extract the physical transition dynamics from previous interaction. However, self-attention complexity in transformers scales quadratically with sequence length, making long-history conditioning computationally prohibitive. Furthermore, continuously carrying long raw frame histories (e.g., thousands of tokens) in every inference step introduces substantial redundancy, as the underlying physics configuration can usually be represented far more compactly.

    Physics Descriptor Token.

    To address these challenges, our method calibrates world models through a single compact representation, termed physics descriptor tokenz_phy, which is extracted from an exploratory interaction sequence collected in the test scene. Formally, given an interaction clip ℂ={(oᵢᶜ,aᵢᶜ)}ᵢ₌₁^T_c of length T_c, the context encoder g_φ maps it to a descriptor token z_phy=g_φ(ℂ)∈ℝ^d_phy. Internally, a lightweight visual encoder E_cᵛ extracts per-frame visual features and an action encoder E_cᵃ maps the control actions into action embeddings. At each timestep i, the two are concatenated along the channel dimension into a joint transition token [E_cᵛ(oᵢᶜ)|E_cᵃ(aᵢᶜ)]∈ℝ^dᵥ+dₐ^′. A transformer E_c^fuse then fuses these transition tokens across time and pools them via a learnable query token z_cls:

    z_phy=g_φ(ℂ)\coloneqqE_c^fuse(z_cls, {[ E_cᵛ(oᵢᶜ) | E_cᵃ(aᵢᶜ) ]}ᵢ₌₁^T_c)₀,

    		(4)

    where [ ·|· ] denotes channel-wise concatenation and (·)₀ denotes the output at the query-token position. We use φ to collectively denote the parameters of g_φ, including E_c^fuse, E_cᵛ, E_cᵃ, and z_cls. The world model’s latent dynamics predictor f_θ is subsequently conditioned on z_phy alongside the default observation-action history window K, predicting future latents ẑₜ₊₁ as:

    ẑₜ₊₁=f_θ({(zᵢ,eᵢᵃ)}_i=t-K+1ᵗ, z_phy).\vskip-5.0pt

    		(5)

    Efficiency and Reusability. The design of physics descriptor token provides two practical advantages. (1) minimal rollout overhead: adding a single additional token z_phy into the predictor f_θ introduces only a constant and almost negligible computational cost, circumventing the quadratic attention overhead compared to using longer history or simply prepending raw context frames to f_θ (see +Long-History and +Context-Prefix in Section 4 and Figure 6 for comparison); (2) one-pass extraction and in-context reuse: z_phy is computed via a single forward pass of a lightweight context encoder and can then be cached. If the dynamics of the test scene remain unchanged, the same descriptor can be reused across arbitrarily many future rollouts or planning tasks with no additional encoding cost.

    3.2 Training PhysiCalWorld without Physics Labels

    To enable physics-calibrated predictions, existing models typically rely on pre-specified analytical equations [(Li et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026c)] or train explicit system identification modules using privileged physical parameters [(Yu et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2021)]. However, constructing analytical physics formulations often demands substantial human effort and is often intractable for unstructured scenes with coupled dynamics. Meanwhile, obtaining the ground-truth physics parameters requires instrumented environments and often introduces measurement errors, which would then propagate to model training. As a result, these approaches are typically confined to controlled settings and struggle to scale to novel, uncalibrated in-the-wild scenes governed by unknown physical properties.

    In contrast, PhysiCalWorld requires neither prior physics equations nor the error-prone explicit parameter estimation during both training and evaluation. While deriving analytical formulations or measuring exact physical parameters of in-the-wild scenes is intractable, constructing data groups where each group consists of interaction data collected within the same physical environment is simple and requires minimal additional effort during data collection. Such data grouping alone is sufficient to train PhysiCalWorld and learn an effective physics descriptor token.

    Specifically, the training dataset is categorized into M groups Dₜᵣₐᵢₙ={Gⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^M, where each group Gⱼ comprises episodes that share the same underlying physics configuration ξⱼ. In training, for any transition (oₜ,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼Gⱼ, we independently sample another clip ℂₜᵣʲ={(oₖᶜ,aₖᶜ)}ₖ₌₁^T_c∼Gⱼ from the same group as the interaction prompt. Because both sequences share the identical underlying transition dynamics T_ξⱼ, the context encoder g_φ can learn to distill the scene’s physical characteristics into the compact descriptor token z_phy to synthesize the correct prediction. We jointly optimize the context encoder g_φ and dynamics predictor f_θ end-to-end using the latent prediction objective:

    L(θ,φ)=𝔼_Gⱼ∼Dₜᵣₐᵢₙ, (oₜ,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼Gⱼ, ℂₜᵣʲ∼Gⱼ[ ∥f_θ(zₜ,eₜᵃ,z_phy)-zₜ₊₁∥₂² ],(6)
    where~~zₜ=Eᵥ(oₜ),~~eₜᵃ=Eₐ(aₜ),~~zₜ₊₁=Eᵥ(oₜ₊₁),~~z_phy=g_φ(ℂₜᵣʲ; φ).

    For simplicity, we assume the input window size K of f_θ to be 1 in Equation 6. This formulation enables PhysiCalWorld to extract instance-specific physical dynamics directly from the interaction clip ℂₜᵣ into the compact physics descriptor token z_phy, circumventing the need for ground-truth physics labels as supervision. As in Figure 7, this self-supervised predictive objective can autonomously learn a structured latent space correlated to the underlying physics variations of the scenes.

    3.3 Inference with PhysiCalWorld

    Collecting the Interaction Prompt.

    At test time, PhysiCalWorld enables zero-shot adaptation to environments with novel physics configurations without fine-tuning. To calibrate the world model to an unseen test scene, the agent first executes a sequence of exploratory actions to collect a context prompt ℂₑᵥₐₗ={(oₖᵉ,aₖᵉ)}ₖ₌₁^T_c of length T_c, which consists of the applied actions and the corresponding observations. The actions {aₖᵉ}ₖ₌₁^T_c can be either randomly sampled or generated by a task-agnostic playful policy, as this interaction prompt is only for revealing the physical dynamics of the scene. However, these actions should produce physical contact with the environment since interactions lacking contact or motion cannot reveal the underlying dynamics.

    Physics-grounded Rollout.

    Given ℂₑᵥₐₗ collected in the test scene, the physics descriptor token is computed once by the context encoder g_φ and can be held fixed if the test scene dynamics remain unchanged. Calibrated by descriptor z_phyᵉᵛ, the predictor f_θ can then predict the future latents as:

    ẑₜ₊₁=f_θ({(zᵢ,eᵢᵃ)}_i=t-K+1ᵗ, z_phyᵉᵛ), z_phyᵉᵛ=g_φ(ℂₑᵥₐₗ),

    		(7)

    where predicted latents ẑᵢ can be fed back to f_θ as observation to enable long-horizon open-loop rollout (see Algorithm 2 for pseudocode). If the intrinsic physics of the scene does not change, z_phy can be shared across every rollout step and across every candidate trajectory to be evaluated during visual planning. Therefore, the prompt only needs to be encoded once per scene, regardless of the planning horizon or the number of sampled action sequences. Notably, no physical parameters, analytical models, or task-specific fine-tuning are required at inference: adapting PhysiCalWorld to a new scene only requires collecting a period of in-context interaction.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments evaluate five questions: (1)Physics Calibration: Does conditioning on in-context interaction clips enable effective physics calibration and yield more accurate future predictions? (2)Descriptor Expressiveness and Efficiency: Can PhysiCalWorld learn compact, expressive physics descriptor tokens without analytical physics priors and enable high compute efficiency? (3)Coupled Physics Dynamics: Can PhysiCalWorld scale to complex scenes whose dynamics are jointly governed by multiple physics properties? (4)Backbone Generalization: Can PhysiCalWorld function as an architecture-agnostic, plug-and-play module across diverse world-model backbones? (5)Out-of-Distribution Extrapolation: Can PhysiCalWorld extrapolate to unseen environments whose physics parameters lie outside the training distribution?

    Baselines. Our in-context prompting framework can be integrated into various world model backbones. We use DINO-WM [(Zhou et al., 2025)] and LeWM [(Maes et al., 2026)] as our base world models due to their rollout efficiency and strong trajectory planning performance, alongside Temporal Straightening (TS-WM) [(Wang et al., 2026d)] as a competitive latent world model baseline.

    We train several variants of models for systematic study: (1)+Long History, which takes in a long history window K to investigate if simply extending history memory in world models can enable physics-calibrated predictions; (2)+Context Prefix, which directly prepends the raw context interaction prompt to the input of the world model instead of using the proposed physics descriptor token; (3)+Estimated Physics†, which trains an encoder to predict physics parameters from a context clip and feeds the estimated physics values to the world model (hence this baseline requires additional physics labels for model training). For further analysis, we additionally evaluate (4)+Privileged Physics‡ in Section 4.3, which takes the ground-truth test-scene physics parameters as input, serving as an oracle ceiling rather than a directly comparable baseline. Finally, we compare LeWM against LeWM+PhysiCal to verify that our method generalizes across different world model backbones. See Appendix A.1 for detailed description of each baseline.

    Environments and Evaluation. We illustrate all our environments in Figure 3 and show how different physics configurations will affect the future world states. We train the models on M=135 different configurations and report the results on 15 unseen configurations, with 5 validation episodes per configuration, giving 75 episodes in total. We report four visual metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, IoU) in open-loop rollout, which starts from the initial frame and autoregressively predicts all frames of an episode by recursively feeding the model’s own predictions back as input. We also evaluate on 75 planning tasks per environment and report the success rate (SR). Each task is defined by a start image and a goal image. We execute the planned actions in the environments. The success criterion is whether the target object reaches the goal within a threshold. See Appendix B for details.

    4.1 Environments with Single Physics Variation

    Push-T under Varying Center of Mass.

    The Push-T environment consists of a circular pusher (the agent) and a T-shaped block (see Figure 3). The world model predicts the future latents of the scene alongside the pusher’s proprioception conditioned on the pusher’s actions. In planning, each goal is defined by an image and a target agent state. The block’s center of mass (CoM) is randomly sampled. Different CoMs will not change the block’s appearance but will alter how the block rotates and slides when pushed, hence resulting in significantly different states even under identical push actions.

    As in Table 1, methods without in-context prompts as input (e.g., DINO-WM and TS-WM) generally underperform, showing that in-context interaction prompts can effectively facilitate physics calibration. We observe that compared to other long-context variants (e.g., +Long History and +Context Prefix, see Appendix A.1 for details), +PhysiCal achieves significantly better performance, especially in challenging open-loop rollout, showing that a single descriptor token can stably ground the physics over long-horizon rollout. Our method also outperforms +Estimated Physics† in all open-loop rollout visual metrics without using any physics labels during training. Moreover, compared to +Context Prefix, our compact descriptor token design avoids the quadratic self-attention cost caused by the long context sequence, yielding markedly speedup in both training and inference (Figure 6 and Table A8).

    Reacher Control under Varying Joint Damping.

    This environment consists of a two-link robot arm actuated by continuous joint torques. The damping coefficients of the two joints can affect how much the arm moves under the same applied torques. Each planning task optimizes a torque trajectory to steer the arm toward a target state specified by a goal image. The in-context prompts are randomly sampled actions. We present the quantitative results in Table 1. Our in-context conditioning consistently improves both DINO-WM and LeWM, outperforming all unprivileged baselines and trailing only +Estimated Physics, which requires ground-truth joint damping parameters for model training. While +PhysiCal achieves a similar planning success rate as +Context Prefix, our method surpasses it across all visual prediction metrics by a margin and is more compute efficient. We specify implementation details of the Reacher environment in Appendix B.2.

    BeerPong under Varying Impact Energy Dissipation.

    In BeerPong, a robot arm throws a ball toward a target cup on a tabletop. The ball needs to bounce off the table at least once to enter the cup due to the long distance. We vary impact energy dissipation by changing the table’s contact damping (e.g., higher damping causes greater energy loss, resulting in lower bounce height). The action input to the world models is the end-effector release velocity. The cup location is randomly initialized in each planning task. The planner then optimizes the release velocity so that the ball can land right inside the cup after bounce. The in-context prompts are collected via randomly sampled actions. Please see Appendix B.3 for additional details.

    We present quantitative results in Table 2. Across both world-model backbones, +PhysiCal consistently improves visual prediction accuracy over the uncalibrated baselines. While our method surpasses +Context Prefix across all visual metrics, it achieves a slightly lower planning success rate. This is potentially because the physics variation in BeerPong manifests only when the ball contacts the table, leading to temporally sparse physical cues. Under such observation sparsity, self-attention over the full raw context frames may provide an advantage in identifying collision dynamics.

    4.2 Environments with Multiple Physics Variations

    FetchSlide under Multiple Physics Variations. We next investigate whether PhysiCal can calibrate world models in environments where transition dynamics are simultaneously governed by multiple physics properties. To this end, in FetchSlide, we concurrently vary three physics parameters: puck mass, table surface friction, and aerodynamic drag. In this environment, a robot arm strikes a flat puck across a tabletop, where these three properties jointly determine the puck’s post-strike deceleration and sliding distance. The action space is end-effector delta position, which subsequently defines the striking velocity and angle. In planning, we optimize the strike actions so that the puck can stop at the target position specified by a goal image. The context sequence is collected via random actions.

    Quantitative results are presented in Table 2. Despite the added complexity of coupled physical factors, +PhysiCal effectively calibrates predictions without requiring analytical physics equations,

    yielding significant gains across both backbones. Our method is only surpassed by +Estimated Physics†, which is trained with the ground-truth values of all three physical properties. However, oftentimes finding what physics parameters govern the scene and precisely measuring them are impractical, whereas +PhysiCal is trained directly via the future latent prediction objective without any physics labels. We also provide qualitative results of the final prediction of an open-loop rollout in Figure 6, where uncalibrated DINO-WM deviates from the target position, while +PhysiCal generates predictions that faithfully capture the ground-truth puck state.

    4.3 Analysis

    Physics Calibration vs. Privileged Physics‡. We additionally compare our method against an oracle baseline, +Privileged Physics‡, serving as an upper-bound reference. Specifically, this baseline directly receives ground-truth physics parameters as supplementary inputs during both training and inference (Privileged Physics‡ and Estimated Physics† share the same future predictor f_θ, but at inference, Estimated Physics† uses physics parameters estimated by a neural network). In contrast, +PhysiCal accesses only an unannotated interaction clip from the test scene for calibration, and nevertheless, as shown in Table 3, our method achieves competitive performance across most metrics and even surpasses this privileged baseline in Push-T.

    Generalization to Out-of-Distribution Physics Parameters. We investigate whether PhysiCalWorld can extrapolate to environments where physics parameters lie outside the training distribution (Figure 8). Specifically, in Reacher, we sweep the first joint’s damping coefficient beyond its training range while holding the second joint’s damping fixed. While +Privileged Physics achieves higher accuracy in-distribution, its performance deteriorates sharply when the damping falls below or exceeds the training interval. In particular, its rollout PSNR significantly drops, producing blurry predictions (Figure A6). In contrast, our method demonstrates robust extrapolation over unseen regimes, probably because our model learns latent patterns to infer dynamics rather than overfitting to rigid scalars.

    Interpretability and Latent Structure of the Physics Descriptor z_phy. We analyze whether the physics descriptor learns structured representations of the test-scene physics. Specifically, in Push-T, we collect 10 interaction clips in each of the 8 unseen center of mass (CoM) locations (P₁–P₈) and encode each clip into a physics descriptor token using the context encoder g_φ. We then compute the pairwise cosine similarities between these tokens and average them across each CoM pair. As shown in Figure 7, descriptors from adjacent CoM locations exhibit strong positive correlation, while CoMs that are far apart yield negative similarity values. This indicates that our training objective enables the context encoder to capture meaningful physics properties correlated with the scene dynamics, even without using ground-truth physics labels during training.

    5 Discussion

    Limitations. Our approach has several limitations. First, training PhysiCalWorld requires grouping trajectories by the physics configurations under which they were collected. While partitioning data by environment identity is far less demanding than deriving analytical equations, curating grouped data from in-the-wild video remains non-trivial. One potential direction to relax this is leveraging self-supervised representation learning to automatically cluster latent transition dynamics into environment groups. Moreover, the proposed test-time calibration depends on the quality of the interaction prompt given to the model. While we find that simple playful or even random policies often suffice, future work could explore active or curiosity-driven exploration to collect more informative prompts. Finally, our framework assumes the physics properties are stationary: the dynamics remain unchanged within an episode. Extending this approach to non-stationary environments (e.g., fluctuating wind fields) may require additional techniques such as reactive prompting or online descriptor updates.

    Conclusion. We believe that world models should go beyond generic visual fidelity toward instance-specific physics-grounded prediction. In this work, we take a step toward this goal by introducing an in-context calibration framework that grounds action-conditioned world models in the actual physics dynamics of novel test scenes. We achieve this by prompting the model with an interaction sequence collected within the test scene, enabling zero-shot calibration without finetuning or analytical physics priors. Evaluations across diverse environments demonstrate that our approach substantially improves predictive accuracy and downstream visual planning.
