    Appendix A Implementation Details

    A.1 Baselines

    In this section, we provide a detailed description for each baseline we used in our paper. Please see the description of each method below:

  • a)

    DINO-WM[(Zhou et al., 2025)]: We follow the implementation in the official codebase, using a frozen DINOv2 [(Oquab et al., 2023)] backbone as the visual encoder Eᵥ. The input to the dynamics predictor f_θ is an observation-action sequence of K=3 steps, including K-1 historical transitions alongside the current observation and action. The predictor predicts one-step future observation ôₜ₊₁. Because this baseline receives no in-context interaction prompt, it must infer transition dynamics solely from this local history window. We observe that DINO-WM exhibits severe rollout drift when physical properties vary across test scenes.

  • b)

    DINO-WM + Context Prefix: This baseline uses the same model architecture and training objective as DINO-WM. The only difference is that it additionally feeds the latent embeddings of the whole in-context interaction prompt to the dynamics predictor f_θ. As a result, for this baseline, the total input window size of f_θ is T_c+K. Since transformer self-attention scales quadratically with the number of input tokens, this uncompressed prefix adds substantially more computation to both model training and inference (see Figure 6 and Table A9 for runtime comparisons).

  • c)

    DINO-WM + Long History: This baseline uses the same model architecture and training objective as DINO-WM. The only difference is that it extends the target observation history from 3 to 15 consecutive frames (i.e.,K=15). The goal of this baseline is to study whether extending history can enable effective physics-calibration in world models.

  • d)

    LeWM[(Maes et al., 2026)]: LeWM is a latent world model directly trained from scratch (without using frozen pre-trained models like DINOv2), hence it learns task-specific latent visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics. We follow the implementation in its official codebase. Based on LeWM, we also include LeWM + PhysiCal (Ours), where we integrate the proposed physical calibration module into LeWM, to show that our proposed physics calibration method is a plug-and-play module that can potentially extend to any latent world models.

  • e)

    TC-LeWM[(Liu et al., 2026)]: This method applies SIGReg to temporally centered residuals rather than the full latent distribution, preventing the suppression of fine-grained moving components. We include this to enhance the LeWM baseline, as vanilla LeWM’s latent representations fail to capture the ball in the BeerPong environment (yielding very low IoU and planning success). Similarly, we include TC-LeWM + PhysiCal (Ours) to evaluate whether our proposed method can be applied to this improved LeWM baseline.

  • f)

    Temporal Straightening (TS-WM)[(Wang et al., 2026d)]: we adopt this TS-WM variant: DINOv2 (patch) + proj configuration with 16×16×8 spatial features, as it achieves the strongest overall performance reported in the original paper. Similar to DINO-WM, this variant uses a frozen DINOv2 visual encoder and a causal transformer dynamics predictor, but inserts an additional lightweight projection head between the visual encoder and the predictor. During training, TS-WM introduces a curvature regularizer to enforce a more structured latent representation, and such regularization has demonstrated stronger planning performance. We include this baseline to study whether additional regularization can promote physics grounding in world models.

  • g)

    DINO-WM + Estimated Physics†: This baseline first estimates the physics configurations of the scenes (e.g., the center of mass in Push-T or the joint damping in Reacher) from a context clip and feeds the estimated value as condition for the dynamics predictor f_θ. Specifically, we train a separate physics estimator based on the same context-encoder architecture as our method but use the ground-truth physics labels as supervision. At inference time, the estimated parameters are provided to the dynamics predictor as additional input for conditioning. This baseline compares explicit, supervised physics estimation with our end-to-end in-context calibration method. Note that this baseline requires predefined physics labels for training, while our method does not.

  • h)

    DINO-WM + Privileged Physics‡: This baseline is based on DINO-WM but can access the ground-truth physics configurations of the scenes during both training and inference. Specifically, the dynamics predictor directly receives these true physical parameters as supplementary inputs alongside standard observation and action tokens.

    • A.2 Implementation of PhysiCalWorld

    Software and Hardware.

    Our experiments are implemented in Python 3.10 on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8.10. We train and evaluate our models using NVIDIA L40S GPUs and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs interchangeably.

    Base World Models.

    We implemented PhysiCalWorld on two latent world-model backbones, DINO-WM [(Zhou et al., 2025)] and LeWM [(Maes et al., 2026)], denoted as DINO-WM+PhysiCal and LeWM+PhysiCal, as in Table 1 and Table 2. The base architecture and optimization hyperparameters used for the two backbones are summarized in Table A1.

    Context Encoder.

    For all our experiments, the context encoder g_φ maps a 12-frame (T_c=12) interaction sequence to a 64-dimensional physics descriptor z_phy. Each frame is embedded by a ResNet-based visual encoder E_cᵛ into 64 two-dimensional keypoints via spatial softmax [(Finn et al., 2016)]. The world model’s input action is embedded by a single linear layer E_cᵃ:ℝ^Nₐ×dₐ→ℝ¹⁰, where Nₐ denotes the length of the input action chunk and dₐ denotes the dimension of a single action. For Push-T, the 4D observable pusher state is additionally embedded by E_cᵖ:ℝ⁴→ℝ¹⁰. The resulting per-step features are concatenated channel-wise and mapped to one 512-dimensional latent embedding (i.e., data of each timestep is now represented by one latent embedding). A four-layer Transformer encoder with eight attention heads takes latent embeddings of all T_c timesteps as input and pools them with a learnable token z_cls. Finally, the output corresponding to z_cls is fed to an MLP , whose output is the physics descriptor tokenz_phy. For simplicity, we set the dimension of z_phy to 64 across all our experiments. We summarize the hyperparameters of the context encoder g_φ in Table A2.

    Context Sampling and Backbone Integration.

    For each prediction segment sampled from a physical-configuration group Gⱼ, we independently sample the interaction context from a different episode in the same group. Thus, the context shares the same underlying physical dynamics as the prediction target without containing trajectory-specific future observations. All contexts contain T_c=12 observations sampled at the model prediction gap of the corresponding world model.

    For Push-T and Reacher, we uniformly sample the T_c=12-frame context window within a prompt episode. That 12-frame clip typically spans a few seconds. For BeerPong, we sample the context from the beginning of the episode, such that the context contains both the initial release status and ball-table interaction that reveals the contact damping. Similarly, for FetchSlide, we also start the context from the beginning of each episode to include the initial robot-puck interaction sequence and also because episodes in FetchSlide are relatively short. If the in-context prompt episode has fewer than 12 frames, we pad the context to length T_c by repeating the final available frame.

    For DINO-WM+PhysiCal, z_phy is broadcast across all spatial patches and temporal steps and concatenated with the predictor features along the channel dimension. For LeWM+PhysiCal, the 64-dimensional descriptor is concatenated with the 192-dimensional per-step latent representation before feeding into the causal future predictor f_θ, while action conditioning follows the original LeWM implementation through AdaLN-zero.

    Implementation of the Temporal Straightening (TS-WM) Baseline.

    For Temporal Straightening (TS-WM) [(Wang et al., 2026d)], we follow the original implementation and use the DINOv2 (patch) + projection configuration with the default curvature regularization and optimization settings given by the authors, as it is the best-performing model reported in the original paper. We summarize the corresponding hyperparameters in Table A3.

    A.3 Training and Inference Pseudocode of PhysiCalWorld

    We present the pseudocode for training PhysiCalWorld in Algorithm 1, which is also described in Section 3.2. Training PhysiCalWorld requires neither ground-truth physics labels nor an analytical dynamics model; the only supervision structure it consumes is the group partition of the dataset (where data collected within environments sharing identical physics are grouped together).

    Hence, unlike Estimated Physics† or Privileged Physics‡, PhysiCalWorld learns to calibrate directly from the dynamics patterns in the data: it does not need to know which physics properties actually govern the transition dynamics nor their corresponding values. Because every episode in Gⱼ shares the same underlying transition dynamics T_ξⱼ, if both the context prompt and the train target segment are sampled from the same group, context encoder g_φ can minimize the prediction loss by encoding context-specific physical dynamics ξⱼ from the prompt into z_phy. Note that we draw the interaction prompt from an episode distinct from the trajectory segment used for future prediction so as to prevent the prompt from carrying information about the future.

    During training, the predictor is teacher-forced on the visual encoder representations under causal masking (e.g., z₀ cannot attend to z₁), with prediction loss gradients flowing jointly into both θ and φ. The visual decoder Dᵥ is trained separately using an ℓ₂ reconstruction loss to map predicted latents ẑₜ back to pixel-space images.

    We outline the procedure for open-loop rollout inference with PhysiCalWorld in Algorithm 2, as detailed in Section 3.3. At test time, the descriptor is extracted once prior to the rollout loop and subsequently held fixed. Inside the loop, autoregressive rollout runs similarly to the base world model except for the addition of the conditioning physics descriptor token, preserving per-step latency at the level of the unconditioned base predictor (Appendix C.4). Latent-to-pixel decoding through Dᵥ is only required for visual evaluation; our visual planning directly operates in the latent space, ẑ.

    A.4 Visual Latent Planning with Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)

    Following DINO-WM [(Zhou et al., 2025)], we employ the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) for zero-shot visual latent planning (see Algorithm 3 for pseudocode). Given the current observation o₀ and the goal observation o_g, both represented as RGB images, we first encode them into latent space via the visual encoder Eᵥ, namely z₀ and z_g. We first collect an interaction clip ℂₑᵥₐₗ as the context, either through purely random actions or a task-agnostic policy for ensuring sufficient contacts. We then extract the physics descriptor token of the test scene z_phyᵉᵛ←g_φ(ℂₑᵥₐₗ). As within each planning task, the physics configuration of the scene is constant, we can use the same z_phyᵉᵛ across all the CEM iterations of one task, reducing the planning time.

    At each CEM iteration, we sample N (e.g., N=300) candidate action sequences of horizon T from a Gaussian distribution that is independent across time steps and action dimensions, parameterized by a mean μ∈ℝ^T×dₐ and a standard deviation σ∈ℝ^T×dₐ (initialized to μ=0,σ=1), where dₐ is the action dimension. For each candidate sequence, we unroll the physics-calibrated world model f_θ autoregressively in the latent space and evaluate the corresponding cost C, which we define as the mean squared error (MSE) between the final predicted latent ẑ_T and the goal latent z_g, as in Line 17. We then select the top Mₑₗᵢₜₑ (e.g., Mₑₗᵢₜₑ=30) action sequences with the lowest costs and refit μ and σ to their element-wise mean and standard deviation. After J optimization iterations (e.g., J=30), the planner outputs the updated elite-mean action sequence μ=a_0:T-1^*. We then execute a_0:T-1^* in the environment. See Table A4 for the CEM hyperparameters in each environment.

    Appendix B Environment Training and Evaluation Details

    In this section, we provide detailed descriptions of our experiments in each environment, including environment setup, training and evaluation details. Table A5 summarizes the dataset scale and hyperparameters of the world models in each environment. The resolution of the image observation is 224×224 for all four environments.

    B.1 Push-T

    Task and Physics Variation.

    Push-T is a planar manipulation task in a 512×512 pixel workspace, where a circular pusher of radius 15 pixels moves a rigid T-shaped block toward a goal configuration specified by an RGB image. The block consists of a 120×30 pixel crossbar and a 30×90 pixel stem. We uniformly sample the block’s local center of mass (CoM) inside its T-shaped interior and hold it fixed within each episode. Changing the CoM changes the moment arms of contact forces and the resulting translational and rotational response, while the block appearance remains fixed.

    Dataset and Action Space.

    The dataset contains 150 CoM configurations, with 135 used for training and 15 held out for evaluation, totaling 15,150 episodes with 101 episodes per configuration. We train a CoM-agnostic PPO policy that targets pushing the T-block to the light-green area and use this policy to collect trajectories for training, since a random policy cannot ensure sufficient and meaningful interaction. In theory, any policy that produces sufficient contacts can serve as the data-collection policy. Each raw action specifies an absolute 2D pusher target in simulator pixel coordinates, tracked by a PD controller at a control frequency of 10 Hz. Following [Zhou et al. (2025)], we inject independent Gaussian noise into the output action during policy execution. The noise uses ten different standard deviations: σ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0,2.5,3.0,7.0,15.0} pixels. This online noise injection enhances dataset coverage and generalization, which is particularly essential for downstream planning using CEM, as its initial optimization phase relies heavily on exploring noisy action trajectories. We subsample observations every 5 control steps and concatenate the 5 2D actions in between into a stacked 10D action. We use this 10D action as the input to the world models, yielding a prediction interval of 0.5 seconds. Models receive 224×224 RGB images and a 4D pusher proprioceptive input (x,y,vₓ,v_y), whose velocity entries are zero-filled so that only poisition information is provided.

    Training and evaluation.

    Please see Table A1, Table A2, and Table A3 for detailed model hyperparameters, and Table A8 for training wall-clock durations. Visual prediction IoU is computed on the union of the agent and block foreground masks. Each planning task pairs a single current observation with a goal observation recorded 15 control steps later in the same trajectory. Success requires the Euclidean position error over the concatenated agent and block coordinates to be below 20 pixels and the wrapped block-orientation error to be below π/9 (20^∘). For open-loop execution, we set the planning horizon to 25 control steps (i.e., 5-step future prediction in the world model). In Table 1, we report the success rate under this fixed 25-step budget when directly executing the planned action sequence from the initial observation. To leverage the world model for dynamic planning, we also experiment with model predictive control (MPC), in which the model actively replans if the task has not succeeded. Table A7 evaluates cumulative success rates with at most two replans (i.e., budgets of 25, 50, and 75 control steps). We observe that the success rate of our method consistently increases with larger step budgets, as iterative replanning allows for continuous error correction.

    B.2 Reacher

    Task and physical variation.

    We modify the Reacher environment from the DeepMind Control Suite [(Tassa et al., 2018)], where a planar two-link arm moves toward a goal configuration specified by an RGB image. The proximal and distal links have lengths of 0.12 and 0.10 meters, respectively. We vary the two joint damping coefficients over [0.005,0.020] N·m·s/rad using Latin-hypercube sampling and hold them fixed within each episode. Changing joint damping alters the two-link arm’s resistance to motion without changing the visual appearance.

    Dataset and action space.

    The dataset contains 150 joint-damping configurations, with 135 used for training and 15 held out for evaluation, totaling 3,000 episodes with 20 episodes per configuration. Each episode contains 100 control steps and starts from randomly sampled joint angles with zero initial joint velocities. Unlike Push-T, random torque commands naturally induce diverse joint motions and provide broad coverage of the joint-state and velocity space, so no task-specific data-collection policy is required. Each 2D action is sampled independently from [-1,1]² and specifies normalized motor commands corresponding to joint torques in [-0.05,0.05] N·m. Each command is held for two 0.02-second simulation steps, giving a control frequency of 25 Hz. Similar to Push-T, we subsample observations every 5 control steps and concatenate the five intervening 2D actions into a 10D world-model action, yielding a prediction interval of 0.2 seconds. Unlike Push-T, Reacher does not provide proprioception inputs.

    Training and evaluation.

    Visual prediction IoU is computed on the union of the two arm links’ foreground masks. Each planning task pairs a single current observation with a goal observation recorded 25 control steps later in the same trajectory. Success requires the angular error of each joint to be below 10^∘ (π/18 radians). Similar to Push-T, we use a 25-control-step planning horizon (i.e., 5-step future prediction in the world model), and report the 25-step budget planning result in Table 1. We additionally evaluate MPC with at most two replans, yielding cumulative budgets of 25, 50, and 75 control steps, as reported in Table A7. Note that repeated replanning substantially reduces the effect of accumulated model error in Reacher, allowing even imperfect models to iteratively approach the target and resulting in high MPC success rates. We observed that LeWM-based models perform particularly well on Reacher, which may be attributed to its encoder being task-specific and able to focus on essential structures such as the angles of the joints, whereas DINOv2 is trained as a general-purpose image encoder.

    B.3 BeerPong

    Task and physical variation.

    We modify the BeerPong environment from Fancy Gym [(Otto et al., )], where a simulated Barrett Whole-Arm Manipulator (WAM) throws a ball toward a cup across a table. We omit an explicit gripper and instead kinematically attach the ball to the end effector during the first five control steps, after which it is released with the end effector’s instantaneous velocity. The robot starts from a fixed configuration, while the cup position is sampled along the table’s central axis and remains fixed within each episode. We uniformly sample the ball-contact damping parameter over [10,40),N·s/m and hold it fixed within each episode. This changes energy dissipation during contact and the resulting bounce trajectory without changing visual appearance. We empirically choose the contact-damping range as lower values produce insufficient rebound while higher values lead to excessively unstable ball trajectories. With damping parameter inside this range, most episodes are physically feasible, with some throws capable of making the ball reach the cup after one or two bounces on the table. The table measures approximately 0.90×1.68 meters, the cup has an inner radius of 0.10 meters, and the ball has a radius of 0.049 meters and a mass of 0.10 kilograms.

    Dataset and action space.

    The dataset contains 150 contact-damping configurations, with 135 used for training and 15 held out for evaluation, totaling 9,000 episodes with 60 episodes per configuration. Each episode contains 300 control steps. A 2D throw command is sampled uniformly from [2.5,3.0) m/s for forward end-effector velocity and [6.0,8.0) m/s for upward end-effector velocity. After releasing the ball, the robot arm retracts to a fixed configuration to prevent its post-throw pose from leaking information about the throw command. Each control step spans two 0.005-second simulation steps, giving a control frequency of 100 Hz. We subsample observations every 15 control steps, yielding a prediction interval of 0.15 seconds (the time gap between two predicted frames by the world model). Since the robot actions cannot affect the ball after the robot releases the ball, we provide the normalized 2D throw command as the world model’s action input at every prediction step, both before and after the release. The world models receive 224×224 RGB images without proprioception inputs.

    Training and evaluation.

    Visual prediction IoU is computed on the ball’s foreground mask. Each planning task consists of a single initial observation and a final observation of a successful in-cup throw (i.e., an image in which the ball is inside the cup). The success criterion is that the ball can be thrown inside the cup and stay in the cup. We evaluate each method on 75 shared targets, where all planning tasks share the same initial robot and ball configuration and differ in the randomly sampled cup position and the table contact damping of the held-out configuration. Different from Push-T and Reacher, BeerPong is a one-shot planning task, in which the planner optimizes a single 2D throw command.

    B.4 FetchSlide

    Task and Physics Variation.

    We modify the FetchSlide-v4 environment from Gymnasium Robotics [(de Lazcano et al., 2024)], where a Fetch manipulator strikes a cylindrical puck toward a goal position on a table. The puck has a radius of 0.05 meters and a height of 0.04 meters. We independently sample puck mass m∈[0.04,0.36) kg, surface friction μ∈[0.0305,0.0435), and fluid density ρ∈[0,40) kg/m³ from uniform distributions and hold them fixed within each episode. These numbers are selected under the principles that the environments can remain valid. For example, if we set the upper limit of the surface friction to a very large value, in most of the cases, the puck might simply stop very quickly, resulting in tiny difference between different environments.

    At a high level, the interplay between these physics properties can be described as follows. For the same strike action, lower puck mass results in a higher post-strike velocity. The subsequent puck’s deceleration depends jointly on surface friction and aerodynamic drag, where stronger friction and higher fluid density will increase deceleration rate. In addition, since we do not vary the shape of the puck, given the same air density, a puck of larger mass will decelerate slower compared to a lighter puck.

    Dataset and action space.

    The dataset contains 150 physical configurations, with 135 used for training and 15 held out for evaluation, totaling 36,000 episodes with 240 episodes per configuration. Each strike is specified by a 2D action sampled uniformly from [0.35,0.85)×[-0.8,0.8).

    Following the original setting of FetchSlide-v4 [(de Lazcano et al., 2024)], action is expanded into a 4D Cartesian command (aₓ,a_y,0,0), where the first three components specify end-effector displacement and the final component controls the gripper, which is always closed. The same command is applied for the first two control steps. Each control step spans 0.04 seconds. We subsample observations every five control steps, yielding a prediction interval of 0.2 seconds, and concatenate the two initial 4D commands into a normalized 8D condition provided at every world-model step. After striking the puck, the robot arm moves to a fixed position to prevent information leakage from the post-strike pose. Models receive 224×224 RGB images without proprioception input.

    Training and evaluation.

    Visual prediction IoU is computed on the puck’s foreground mask. All planning tasks share the same initial robot and puck configuration and differ only in the target puck position. Similar to BeerPong, FetchSlide is a one-shot planning task, where the planner optimizes a single 2D strike command, after which the puck will move on the tabletop until it stops, without additional intervention from the robot. We evaluate all methods across a shared benchmark of 75 planning targets, defining the success of one target when the final puck position lies within 0.03m Euclidean distance of the target position on the table.

    Appendix C Additional Quantitative Results

    We first present performance comparison of next-frame prediction in Section C.1, where we conduct teacher-forcing style evaluation (only score the immediate next frame when computing the metrics), complementing the open-loop rollout evaluation presented in the main paper. Then, we show the planning task success rates over more replanning budgets in Section C.2. Following this, we present the training time and inference time comparison of each method in Section C.3 and Section C.4, respectively. Finally, we report how different success thresholds will affect the planning success rate in Section C.5.

    C.1 Next-Frame Prediction Performance

    We provide additional next-frame prediction results on all four environments in Table A6. We report PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and foreground IoU to evaluate both pixel-level reconstruction quality and foreground prediction accuracy. Across all four environments, incorporating PhysiCal consistently improves the next-frame prediction performance of both DINO-WM and LeWM.

    C.2 MPC Results Across Execution Budgets

    Following DINO-WM [(Zhou et al., 2025)], in addition to the open-loop CEM planning, we also evaluate model predictive control (MPC), where the model replans from the newly observed state after executing a sequence of optimized actions. Specifically, in Push-T and Reacher, CEM optimizes an action sequence spanning 25 control steps (i.e., 5 world model steps due to action stacking) using the world model. The full sequence is then executed in the environment. If this action sequence cannot complete the task, we replan an additional 25 control steps. We allow at most two additional replans, corresponding to maximum 25, 50, and 75 control steps.

    The result is shown in Table A7. +PhysiCal consistently improves performance on Push-T under all maximum numbers of control steps, showing that the performance of our method can scale with additional compute. In Reacher, +PhysiCal shows a strong advantage over context-free baselines after the first 25 execution steps. However, the gap narrows after replanning because the task is highly feedback-correctable and the structure of the task is relatively easy (only consisting of two rotary joints), allowing MPC to quickly compensate for systematic model bias.

item.title: 世界模型不是越像越好：DRILL 把训练目标换成「策略收益」，像素 MSE 高 17% 反而策略更强 ｜ DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels
item.description:
一句话：用世界模型给 VLA 做 RL 时，世界模型的成败标准不该是像素，而是「想象出来的 rollout 能不能把策略练好」；两者会系统性地背离。

要点：

  • 现有做法按单步像素预测训练世界模型，但它在 RL 后训练里的作用不是渲染可信视频，而是产出能改进策略的学习信号
  • 更低像素 MSE 可能给出更差的策略梯度；反过来，一个为「策略效用」训练的世界模型虽然下一帧 MSE 高 17%，能训出更好的下游策略
  • DRILL 是双层框架：世界模型按「内层在想象 rollout 上做一次 GRPO 更新后策略的回报」来更新；两个实例分别是闭式代理（DRILL-VWI）与完整 meta-gradient（DRILL-IMG）
  • 五个操纵仿真 + 两个 VLA 主干上，DRILL-IMG 平均成功率比 WMPO 高 13.1 分、比 RLVR-World 高 7.9 分；LIBERO-Long 上随世界模型变大优势从 7.9 分扩到 16.4 分

为什么值得看：如果你的引擎/训练管线用世界模型做 agent 后训练，指标该换成收益而不是重建质量——这条对「用什么评价模型」的影响比对模型结构本身更大。

中文摘要：世界模型越来越多被用于在强化学习后训练视觉-语言-动作策略时减少与环境交互，但它们通常仍按「预测下一步像素」来训练，而在这类场景里世界模型的职责不是渲染视觉上忠实的视频，而是从想象 rollout 中产出能改进策略的学习信号。作者指出这种错配很严重：更低的像素 MSE 可能带来更差的策略梯度；反之，按策略效用训练的世界模型虽然下一帧 MSE 高 17%，仍能得到更好的下游策略。为此他们提出 DRILL，一个双层框架：外层更新世界模型，使其最大化内层在想象 rollout 上做 GRPO 更新之后策略的回报；并给出两个实例——需要额外模拟器 rollout 的闭式代理 DRILL-VWI，以及完整 meta-gradient 的 DRILL-IMG。在五个操纵仿真与两个 VLA 主干上，DRILL-IMG 相比 WMPO 平均成功率高 13.1 分、相比 RLVR-World 高 7.9 分，并能与 RLVR 预训练叠加。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels

Abstract

World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy’s return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.

††footnotetext: †Corresponding Author.

1 Introduction

World models are becoming a practical substitute for robot or simulator interaction in reinforcement-learning post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) policies. In this setting, however, their role is not merely to predict the next video frame: they generate the imagined rollouts from which the policy learns. This distinction creates an objective mismatch. A model optimized for one-step pixel prediction is not necessarily the model that induces the most useful policy-gradient update.

The reason is that pixel fidelity and policy utility weight errors in different places. Pixel MSE penalizes prediction errors uniformly over pixels and time, including backgrounds, robot geometry, and visually salient but task-irrelevant regions. A policy-gradient update instead emphasizes the states the current policy visits and the actions whose advantages are large. A model can therefore be an excellent next-frame predictor while producing weak learning signals, or a worse predictor on average while better supporting the transitions that determine policy improvement. The relevant question is not only whether the imagined video looks right, but whether learning inside it moves the policy in the right direction.

This mismatch matters because recent VLA post-training systems replace expensive robot or simulator interaction with imagined rollouts. At foundation-model scale, reinforcement-learning post-training can require millions of environment steps, so recent methods train a video world model from offline demonstrations and apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [(Shao et al., 2024)] inside the model [(Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2024)]. Yet the world model is still typically optimized as a one-step video predictor. Diagnostic methods such as Policy-Aware WM [(Zhao et al., 2025)] and ESNR [(Zollicoffer et al., 2025)] show that pixel fidelity does not reliably track policy competence, but do not provide a training objective. RLVR-World [(Wu et al., 2025)] post-trains the world model with prediction correctness as the reward, improving it as a predictor rather than directly optimizing the policy update induced by imagined rollouts.

We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that trains video world models by the return of the policy obtained after learning in them. The inner loop performs a GRPO update on imagined rollouts generated by the world model; the outer loop updates the world model so that this post-update policy achieves higher return in the target simulator. The objective is therefore not pixel accuracy under the model’s own rollouts, but downstream return in the environment that defines task success.

DRILL has two operating points. DRILL-VWI (Visitation-Weighted Imagination) is a lightweight signed surrogate that replaces uniform pixel MSE with weights from policy visitation, group-relative advantage, and model confidence, requiring no additional simulator rollouts over a WMPO-style pipeline. DRILL-IMG (Implicit Meta-Gradient) estimates the downstream-return meta-gradient more directly by differentiating through the inner GRPO update with truncated Hessian-vector products and a small simulator-rollout batch. Thus DRILL-VWI is the budget-conscious drop-in update, while DRILL-IMG is the more faithful estimator when limited simulator interaction and BPTT memory are available.

The two variants are connected theoretically: the core DRILL-VWI surrogate is the first-order Taylor approximation of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under standard local assumptions, and DRILL-IMG admits a non-asymptotic convergence rate with truncated backpropagation through the inner update. This explains when a local visitation- and advantage-weighted prediction loss can approximate the more expensive meta-gradient, and when longer-horizon trajectory effects make DRILL-IMG worth the additional cost.

Across five public manipulation simulators [(Liu et al., 2023; Mees et al., 2022; Nasiriany et al., 2024)] and two foundation VLA backbones [(Black et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024)], DRILL-IMG raises mean policy success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, while its world model has 17% higher one-step pixel MSE on the same training data. The gains are consistent across seeds, increase with rollout horizon and out-of-distribution shift, and remain complementary to prediction-correctness pretraining: applying DRILL-IMG to an RLVR-World-pretrained world model yields a further 3.2-point improvement on average. We also introduce the Policy-Utility Residual (PUR), a method-agnostic diagnostic measuring the angular gap between the pixel-MSE gradient and the policy-improvement direction; across the objectives we evaluate, lower PUR tracks higher downstream success.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify and formalize an objective mismatch in VLA world-model post-training: world models are trained for one-step pixel prediction, but used to generate policy-learning signals for imagined-rollout reinforcement learning.

  • •

    We introduce DRILL, a bilevel framework that trains the world model for the downstream return of the policy obtained after an inner GRPO update, and instantiate it as both a no-extra-rollout surrogate (DRILL-VWI) and a simulator-grounded meta-gradient method (DRILL-IMG).

  • •

    We show that DRILL-VWI is a first-order approximation to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient, provide a non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for DRILL-IMG under truncated BPTT, and validate the framework across five simulators and two VLA backbones with higher downstream success despite higher pixel MSE.

  • •

    We introduce PUR as a method-agnostic diagnostic of the angular gap between pixel prediction and policy improvement, and show that it tracks downstream success across objectives.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video world models for VLA post-training. Recent VLA post-training systems use video world models to replace expensive robot or simulator interaction with imagined rollouts. WMPO [(Zhu et al., 2025)], VLAW [(Guo et al., 2026)], WoVR [(Jiang et al., 2026)], SC-VLA [(Li et al., 2024)], Ctrl-World [(Guo et al., 2025)], World4RL [(Jiang et al., 2025)], and World-Gymnast [(Sharma et al., 2026)] pretrain the world model from demonstrations and then update the policy inside the learned dynamics. These methods differ in rollout construction, filtering, and policy optimization details, but the world model is still primarily trained as a next-frame predictor. Policy-Aware WM [(Zhao et al., 2025)] and ESNR [(Zollicoffer et al., 2025)] diagnose the gap between prediction quality and policy competence, while RLVR-World [(Wu et al., 2025)] and WorldCompass [(Wang et al., 2026)] improve the predictor with prediction-correctness rewards. DRILL instead optimizes the world model by the downstream return of the policy after learning from its imagined rollouts; it is therefore complementary to RLVR-style pretraining rather than a replacement for it.

    Policy-aware world-model learning. The idea that a model should be useful for control, not only accurate under a prediction loss, appears in value-aware model learning [(Farahmand et al., 2017; Grimm et al., 2020)] and in neural model-based RL systems such as MuZero [(Schrittwieser et al., 2020)], IRIS [(Micheli et al., 2022)], and DreamerV3 [(Hafner et al., 2023)]. DRILL brings this perspective to VLA post-training with imagined GRPO rollouts. Classical value-aware objectives rely on a learned V_ψ(o) or bootstrapped targets; DRILL uses the group-relative advantage produced online by GRPO as a per-batch surrogate for downstream utility. Proposition 1 shows that the signed advantage weighting in DRILL-VWI is recovered as a first-order approximation to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under a local score-compatibility condition, and Section 5.3 compares this approximation with a direct value-aware adaptation.

    Meta-gradient and implicit differentiation. DRILL-IMG is also related to methods that differentiate through an inner optimization step, including truncated MAML [(Finn et al., 2017)], iMAML [(Rajeswaran et al., 2019)], and implicit-gradient methods for RL [(Nikishin et al., 2022)]. Unlike iMAML-style approaches, DRILL-IMG uses a short unroll of the policy update rather than solving the inner problem to convergence. Our analysis keeps the resulting truncation bias explicit: Theorem 1 expresses the BPTT bias as a function of the truncation length K. The practical distinction is scale and target: DRILL-IMG applies meta-gradients to foundation-scale VLAs paired with >1B-parameter video world models, using a small simulator-rollout batch to train the world model for the post-update return of the policy.

    3 The DRILL Framework

    DRILL couples two updates. The inner update uses the current world model as the environment for one GRPO step in imagination. The outer update evaluates the policy produced by that step in the target environment and assigns credit back to the world model. DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG differ only in how much of this outer gradient they estimate. Figure 1 gives the full training loop and marks where the two estimators enter.

    3.1 Problem setup

    We consider a VLA policy π_θ(a_t:t+Hₐ|o_≤t,ℓ), a video world model W_φ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,aₜ) with predicted next-frame mean ôₜ₊₁(φ), and a frozen vision-language reward model r_ψ(oₜ,ℓ)∈[0,1]. Training uses offline demonstrations D_demo and imagined rollouts of horizon H produced by π_θ under W_φ. We write d_\rmenv^π_θ(oₜ) for the on-policy state visitation in the target environment, which in our experiments is the high-fidelity simulator that defines task return (Section 5.1), and d̃_φ^π_θ(oₜ) for the corresponding imagined-rollout visitation induced by π_θ inside W_φ.

    The standard WMPO recipe [(Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026)] alternates between fitting the world model to demonstration pixels and improving the policy inside the model:

    φ← \argmin_φ \E_(o_≤t,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼D_demo\lVertôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁\rVert₂²,(1)
    θ← θ + η_θ ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ,r_ψ).(2)

    The first update is optimized for pixel fidelity, while the second uses the model through the policy-gradient signal it induces. DRILL replaces the pixel-fitting update with one aligned to this downstream role.

    3.2 The DRILL objective

    Let

    θ⁺(φ) = θ+η_θ ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ)

    		(3)

    be the policy produced by one imagined GRPO step. DRILL trains W_φ so that this updated policy obtains high return in the target environment:

    φ^* = \argmax_φ J (π_θ⁺(φ)), J(π) = \E_τ∼Pₑₙᵥ(π)[∑ₜrₜ].

    		(4)

    The expectation in J is taken under the trajectory distribution of the target environment, not under W_φ: the world model is not asked to evaluate itself. Optimizing (4) requires the meta-gradient ∇_φJ(π_θ⁺(φ)) through the inner update (3). This formulation changes what the world model is optimized for: rather than fitting all demonstrated pixels equally, DRILL rewards model changes that make the imagined policy update improve target-environment return. The useful signal is therefore not frame fidelity alone, but whether the model induces the right policy-gradient direction on states the current policy actually visits.

    DRILL uses two operating points. DRILL-VWI is a local signed surrogate requiring no additional simulator rollouts, while DRILL-IMG estimates the downstream-return meta-gradient more directly with truncated differentiation through the inner update and a small simulator batch for the outer return gradient.

    3.3 DRILL-VWI: Visitation-Weighted Imagination

    DRILL-VWI replaces the pixel-MSE loss (1) with a policy-aware signed local surrogate,

    L_VWI(φ) = \E_(oₜ,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼D_demo[w(oₜ,aₜ)\lVertôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁\rVert₂²],

    		(5)

    with

    w(oₜ,aₜ) = d̃̂_φ^π_θ(oₜ)·Ã_α(oₜ,aₜ)·s(oₜ), Ã_α(oₜ,aₜ)=sgn(Â(oₜ,aₜ)) \lvertÂ(oₜ,aₜ)\rvert^α.

    		(6)

    The three factors are quantities already produced by the imagined GRPO loop: d̃̂_φ^π_θ(oₜ) estimates model-rollout visitation, Â(oₜ,aₜ) is the group-relative GRPO advantage, and s(oₜ)>0 downweights states on which the world model is uncertain. The weight is stopped and clipped in implementation, so (5) is a local update direction, not a globally normalized likelihood objective. Proposition 1 formalizes its first-order connection to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient. Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1 gives the full training loop, including clipping, normalization, and visitation estimation. Since all factors come from imagined rollouts, DRILL-VWI adds no environment interaction over WMPO.

    3.4 DRILL-IMG: Implicit Meta-Gradient

    DRILL-IMG estimates the meta-gradient of (4) by differentiating through the inner update (3):

    ∇_φJ (π_θ⁺(φ)) = η_θ ∇_θ⁺J (π_θ⁺) ∇_φ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ).

    		(7)

    The first factor is a policy-gradient estimate in the target simulator, computed from a small batch of simulator rollouts. The second factor is a mixed derivative through the imagined GRPO update, computed as a Hessian-vector product with K-step truncated BPTT. In the main experiments we use K=2 and Bᵣₑₐₗ=30 simulator rollouts per outer step. DRILL-IMG is therefore a more faithful estimator of the DRILL objective than DRILL-VWI, at the cost of additional simulator interaction and BPTT memory. Algorithm 2 in Appendix D.2 gives the full pseudocode, checkpointing details, and numerical-stability controls.

    4 Theoretical Analysis

    The analysis has three roles. First, it explains when the cheap DRILL-VWI update is a first-order surrogate for the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient. Second, it states the convergence guarantee for DRILL-IMG under truncated BPTT. Third, it defines a diagnostic, PUR, for measuring whether a world-model objective is aligned with policy improvement.

    4.1 First-order meta-gradient and the DRILL-VWI surrogate

    The inner update (3) is a single gradient step, so the outer objective J(π_θ⁺(φ)) can be expanded in the inner step size η_θ. The proposition below keeps only the main statement needed in the paper body; the full proof and residual definitions are given in Appendix B.

    Proposition 1(DRILL-VWI as a first-order local surrogate).

    Suppose (A1) J is C² in θ; (A2) W_φ has a Gaussian observation head with mean ôₜ₊₁(φ) and fixed scale σ_W; and (A3) the imagined-rollout visitation marginal d̃_φ^π_θ is locally stationary over one inner step. Treat the GRPO advantages as stop-gradient quantities when forming ∇_φ∇_θĴ_GRPO. Let L_VWIᶜᵒʳᵉ denote the idealized VWI surrogate with exact imagined-rollout visitation, α=1, s(oₜ)=1, and unclipped signed weights. If the local policy-score contraction is compatible with the signed advantage direction up to residual ε_comp, the omitted multi-step trajectory-score terms have residual R_H, and the demo-anchor transfer has residual R_demo, then for some alignment scalar κ>0,

    ∥∇_φJ (π_θ⁺(φ))+(κη_θ)/(2σ_W²)∇_φL_VWIᶜᵒʳᵉ(φ)∥≤η_θM_Wε_comp+η_θR_H+η_θR_demo+O(η_θ²).

    		(8)

    The result should not be read as an exact identity between DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG. It says that the signed VWI update recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient when the policy-score contraction is approximately scalar on the advantage-weighted support and when trajectory-locality and demo-anchor residuals are small. Intuitively, positive-advantage transitions are sharpened, while negative-advantage transitions may be deliberately deemphasized rather than fit more accurately as pixels.

    The residuals describe when this local approximation is reliable. ε_comp measures whether the world-model score and the policy-gradient contraction agree on which transition changes matter; R_H grows when multi-step consequences dominate local next-frame error; and R_demo captures mismatch between demonstration anchors and on-policy imagined transitions. Thus short-horizon or well-covered tasks favor DRILL-VWI, while large trajectory or demo-anchor residuals motivate the more expensive DRILL-IMG estimator.

    4.2 Convergence rate under truncated BPTT

    DRILL-IMG replaces the exact mixed derivative in (7) by a K-step truncated BPTT estimate. The following theorem analyzes one fixed-policy outer subproblem. Fix current policy parameters θ̄ and define

    J_θ̄(φ):=J (π_θ̄+η_θ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ̄;W_φ)).

    This is a per-outer-subproblem guarantee, not a proof of global convergence for the jointly evolving (θₜ,φₜ) process.

    Theorem 1(DRILL-IMG convergence rate under truncated BPTT).

    Suppose (A4) the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator has conditional variance at most σ_g²; (A5) J_θ̄ is L-smooth in φ and bounded above with J^*:=\sup_φJ_θ̄(φ)<∞; and (A6) the K-step BPTT truncation bias satisfies \lVertbias_K\rVert≤Bρ^K for some ρ∈(0,1). Let J₀:=J_θ̄(φ₀). With step size

    η_φ=\min (1/4L,√(2(J^*-J₀))/(LTσ_g²)),

    the T-step stochastic ascent iterates on J_θ̄ satisfy

    \min_0≤t

    		(9)

    The three terms correspond to optimization error, stochastic-gradient variance, and truncation bias. The guarantee is qualitative at our scale: it shows convergence to a neighborhood of a stationary point and that the squared-gradient contribution from BPTT truncation decays geometrically in K. This supports using a shallow truncation when the extra unroll depth no longer changes the meta-gradient direction much. The practical choice K=2 is therefore made empirically, from the truncation and return-per-compute studies in the appendix, rather than from the worst-case constants in the bound.

    Corollary 1(Truncation depth).

    The truncation contribution in (9) falls below any target ε>0 once K=Θ(\log(1/ε)), with constants determined by B and ρ.

    4.3 Policy-Utility Residual

    The previous results are specific to DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG. To compare arbitrary world-model objectives, we measure whether the pixel-MSE gradient is aligned with the direction that improves the policy after imagined training. We define the Policy-Utility Residual as

    PUR(φ) = 1 - (⟨∇_φL_MSE(φ), -∇_φJ (π_θ⁺(φ))⟩)/(\lVert∇_φL_MSE\rVert \lVert∇_φJ\rVert).

    		(10)

    Equivalently, PUR=1+\cos∠(∇_φL_MSE,∇_φJ) whenever both gradients are nonzero. Thus PUR ≈ 0 means that descending pixel MSE also improves the downstream-return objective, PUR ≈ 1 means the two directions are nearly orthogonal, and PUR ≈ 2 means that descending pixel MSE is anti-aligned with policy improvement.

    We estimate ∇_φJ by finite differences in the simulator rather than by reusing the HVP machinery of DRILL-IMG. This keeps PUR independent of any particular training method, so the same diagnostic applies to WMPO, RLVR-World, DRILL-VWI, DRILL-IMG, and other world-model objectives. Section 5.5 tests whether lower PUR tracks higher downstream success across the methods we evaluate.

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate DRILL on five robot-manipulation simulators, two VLA backbones, and five training baselines, while also reporting diagnostic metrics from policy-aware WM evaluation. The main text keeps the headline comparison, compact diagnostic panels, architectural checks, component-level summaries, and the criterion for choosing DRILL-VWI or DRILL-IMG. Detailed ablations, cross-backbone tables, robustness breakdowns, hyperparameter sweeps, reward-model swaps, and auxiliary diagnostic curves are collected in Appendices D.7–F.6.

    5.1 Setup

    Benchmarks and baselines. We use LIBERO-Long [(Liu et al., 2023)], CALVIN ABC→D [(Mees et al., 2022)], RoboCasa [(Nasiriany et al., 2024)], Meta-World MT50, and SimplerEnv. These simulators define both evaluation and the small real-rollout budget used by DRILL-IMG’s outer gradient, Bᵣₑₐₗ=30 simulator rollouts per outer step; no real-robot results are included. Baselines are Scratch-GRPO, WMPO [(Zhu et al., 2025)], VLAW [(Guo et al., 2026)], RLVR-World [(Wu et al., 2025)], and a simulator-budget-matched model-free PPO control, Sim-PPO. Sim-PPO receives the same simulator episode budget as DRILL-IMG but no imagined rollouts, isolating whether the world model amplifies limited simulator interaction. Policy-Aware WM [(Zhao et al., 2025)] is diagnostic rather than a training method, so we report its ESNR score alongside PUR.

    Protocol. Headline results use five seeds; ablations use three. We report Welch’s t-test p-values and 95% CIs for head-to-head comparisons. The headline run uses about 17k NVIDIA H20-hours, or 24 H20 GPUs for roughly four weeks. Appendix D.9 gives the per-phase breakdown.

    5.2 Main Results

    On π₀-3B, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, averaged across the five benchmarks, while increasing one-step pixel MSE by 17% on the same training data. The gain is largest on long-horizon tasks and smallest on SimplerEnv, where DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG are statistically tied: 64.0 ± 1.9 versus 63.1 ± 2.6. This exception motivates the horizon analysis in Section 5.4.

    The compact diagnostic panels in Figure 3 give three additional views of the same result: DRILL variants break the usual link between lower pixel MSE and higher success, improve faster on LIBERO-Long, and reduce PUR during training. A compute-matched control in Appendix F.1 further shows that extra WMPO updates move LIBERO-Long SR from 64.2 ± 1.6 to at most 65.1 ± 1.9, far below DRILL-IMG’s 81.3 ± 1.3. Together, these checks rule out a pure compute or pixel-fidelity explanation: the methods that improve most are those that better align imagined updates with downstream policy utility. The appendix reports the full breakdowns, while the main text keeps only this recurring trend.

    Backbone and pretraining checks. We repeat the headline comparison on OpenVLA-7B using LIBERO-Long, CALVIN, and RoboCasa. LIBERO-Long and CALVIN preserve the ranking DRILL-IMG > DRILL-VWI > RLVR-World > WMPO. On RoboCasa, DRILL-IMG and DRILL-VWI are statistically tied, 50.8 ± 2.3 versus 48.7 ± 2.1 with p = 0.12, matching that benchmark’s shorter, object-centric episodes. DRILL-IMG reaches 68.9 mean SR on OpenVLA, compared with 53.8 for WMPO, a 15.1-point gain; the full per-benchmark table is in Appendix F.7. This replication changes both the policy backbone and the pretraining mixture, yet preserves the same method ordering on the two longer-horizon benchmarks. We therefore use the appendix tables mainly as robustness evidence for the objective, rather than as a separate architecture claim.

    Orthogonality with RLVR-World. Initializing the WM with RLVR-World pretraining and then applying DRILL-IMG improves mean SR by another roughly 3 points over DRILL-IMG alone. Prediction-correctness pretraining and downstream-return imagination are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable. The stacked variant helps most on SimplerEnv, where the shorter horizon weakens the DRILL-IMG HVP signal and a better pretrained WM matters more.

    A plausible mechanism is that RLVR-World pretraining lowers the variance of the supervised prediction gradient on task-relevant transitions, so that the downstream-return outer gradient is less likely to be drowned out early in training. We treat this as an interpretation of the empirical trend rather than a formal claim, and leave a direct curvature-level test (cf. Appendix D.4) to future work.

    5.3 Ablations and Scaling

    Objective ablations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa, each factor in the signed DRILL-VWI coaching surrogate helps: visitation-only reaches 64.2 mean SR, signed-advantage-only 66.8, and confidence-only 60.1, compared with 58.2 for WMPO. Combining all three gives 69.2. The exponent sweep peaks at α=1, consistent with Proposition 1: the score-compatible local surrogate is linear in the signed advantage, whereas α≠1 deliberately distorts that direction. Increasing to α=2 lowers SR to 67.9, consistent with higher variance from overemphasizing high-magnitude signed-advantage samples. A minimal value-aware baseline, VA-WM, reaches 62.4 mean SR, closing part of the gap to WMPO but remaining 6.8 points below DRILL-VWI and 11.0 below DRILL-IMG; the complete ablation table is in Appendix F.2.

    Scaling and coupling. On LIBERO-Long, the DRILL-IMG margin over WMPO grows with WM size: 7.9 points at 300M parameters, 13.1 at 1.2B, and 16.4 at 7B. DRILL-IMG also transfers across WM backbones: Ctrl-World obtains 81.3 ± 1.3 SR and a matched Cosmos-Predict2-style model obtains 79.6 ± 1.7, a gap within two standard deviations. Finally, freezing the VWI signed coaching multipliers from a GRPO-warmstart policy reaches only 64.9 ± 1.5 mean SR, 4.3 points below DRILL-VWI. The gain therefore comes from tracking the current policy’s signed advantage signal, not from a fixed supervised MSE reweighting.

    5.4 When DRILL-IMG Pays Off over DRILL-VWI

    At the default horizon H=50, DRILL-VWI captures most of the gain on LIBERO-Long: it recovers 11.9 of the 17.1 points between WMPO and DRILL-IMG. DRILL-IMG costs about 1.4× more per outer step and uses Bᵣₑₐₗ=30 simulator rollouts that DRILL-VWI does not require, so the choice should depend on horizon. The residual decomposition suggests this dependence: the one-step DRILL-VWI surrogate omits multi-step trajectory-score terms collected in the trajectory-locality residual R_H, while DRILL-IMG partially recovers these terms through truncated BPTT. If one additionally assumes R_H=O(η_θH²), this residual induces an O(η_θ²H²) horizon-dependent component, but the experiment should be read as testing whether the IMG–VWI gap grows with H, not as isolating a universal H² law.

    The horizon sweep (Figure 3) is consistent with this residual-based criterion. The DRILL-IMG margin over DRILL-VWI grows from 1.8 points at H=20 to 5.2 at H=50, 7.5 at H=100, and 8.1 at H=200. WMPO falls from 67.4 to 49.8 SR as rollout error compounds; DRILL-VWI is more stable but saturates around the mid-70s. DRILL-IMG peaks at H=100 with 83.4 SR and drops to 78.6 at H=200, where imagined trajectories become too noisy. The short-horizon checks point the other way: on LIBERO-Long the IMG-over-VWI gap shrinks to 0.6 at H=10 and becomes a non-significant -0.2 ± 1.1 at H=5; on SimplerEnv, whose effective horizon is below H=20, DRILL-VWI slightly exceeds DRILL-IMG, 64.0 versus 63.1 SR. We recommend DRILL-VWI as the budget-conscious choice for very short horizons or when simulator rollouts are unavailable, and DRILL-IMG when the task horizon is moderate to long or when the extra simulator budget is acceptable. In our default H=50 setting, DRILL-IMG already gives a 5.2-point gain over DRILL-VWI on LIBERO-Long, while SimplerEnv illustrates the short-horizon regime where VWI can be preferable. Full horizon tables and reward-model swaps are in Appendices F.3 and F.8.

    HVP validation. On a 2D gridworld and Meta-World MT10, where the exact meta-gradient is tractable, the K=2 truncated HVP has cosine similarity 0.74 ± 0.04 and 0.71 ± 0.05 to the untruncated target meta-gradient, respectively. The full K-sweep and estimated contraction rate ρ are in Appendix D.4.

    5.5 Diagnostics and Robustness

    Robustness and diagnostics. Under LIBERO zero-shot perturbations, DRILL-IMG has an 18.6% average relative SR drop, compared with 30.2% for WMPO and 25.6% for RLVR-World. The only exception is pose perturbation, where DRILL-VWI slightly wins, again matching a shorter effective horizon; the per-condition breakdown is in Appendix F.9. PUR also tracks policy utility (Figure 3): WMPO drifts upward, RLVR-World plateaus, DRILL-VWI stays bounded, and DRILL-IMG decreases; across the PUR-reporting headline rows, the Spearman correlation with downstream SR is ρ_S=-0.89 with 95% bootstrap CI [-0.97,-0.71]. Two held-out variants give 1.5 points mean absolute error when final SR is predicted from checkpoint-level PUR at step 5k.

    DRILL also improves task-relevant imagination rather than visual fidelity alone. On LIBERO-Long, WMPO reaches lower pixel MSE but plateaus at 0.61 ± 0.02 TRPS, while DRILL-IMG reaches 0.81 ± 0.03 TRPS despite higher MSE. In a forced-choice human study with 120 trials and six blinded raters, visual-quality preferences for WMPO or RLVR-World over DRILL-IMG are not significant, but when task completion is shown, 62% prefer DRILL-IMG over WMPO (p < 0.001). TRPS curves and human-evaluation details are in Appendices F.4 and F.10.

    6 Conclusion

    We introduced DRILL, a bilevel framework for training video world models as policy-improvement environments rather than as standalone next-frame predictors. Its two instantiations expose a practical trade-off: DRILL-VWI provides a lightweight visitation- and advantage-weighted surrogate that can be used in a WMPO-style pipeline, while DRILL-IMG more directly optimizes downstream return by differentiating through imagined policy updates. The theoretical connection between these variants explains when the cheaper local surrogate should be sufficient and when longer-horizon trajectory effects make the meta-gradient worth its extra cost. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL improves policy success even when one-step pixel MSE becomes worse, reinforcing the central claim that visual fidelity is not the right standalone target for world-model post-training. The accompanying PUR diagnostic makes this mismatch measurable, and the gains from combining DRILL with RLVR-World suggest that prediction-correctness pretraining and policy-aware downstream optimization are complementary. More broadly, DRILL shifts the optimization target from making imagined videos look accurate to making learning inside those videos useful.

    Limitations.

    Our evaluation remains simulation-only and uses a small simulator-rollout budget for DRILL-IMG rather than physical robot interaction. This leaves open how sensitive the method is to real-world perception noise, actuation delay, safety constraints, and sim-to-real distribution shift. DRILL-IMG also introduces additional compute and memory overhead through truncated backpropagation and Hessian-vector products, so DRILL-VWI may be the more appropriate choice when interaction, memory, or wall-clock budget is the binding constraint. Extending DRILL to real-robot post-training and reducing the cost of the meta-gradient estimator are therefore important next steps.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Notation and Preliminaries

    This appendix collects the symbols, assumptions, and intermediate definitions used throughout the paper, so that Appendices B–C can be read without re-tracing the main text.

    A.1 Symbol glossary

    A.2 Assumptions

    Six assumptions are used across the proofs in Appendices B–C. We restate them here in compact form; the long-form versions, with remarks on tightness and on the WM-architecture cases they cover, appear inline at first use in each proof.

  • •

    (A1) Outer smoothness in θ.J:Θ→ℝ is C² in a neighborhood of θ with bounded second derivatives, so that

    J(θ+η_θg)=J(θ)+η_θ∇_θJ(θ)^⊤g+O(η_θ²).

  • •

    (A2) Gaussian WM head. For each (o_≤t,aₜ), the WM output distribution is Gaussian with mean ôₜ₊₁(φ) and isotropic covariance σ_W²I, and φ↦ôₜ₊₁(φ) is C¹. Equivalently,

    ∇_φ\logW_φ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,aₜ)=-(1)/(2σ_W²)∇_φ∥ôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁∥₂².

    For diffusion or flow WMs, an analogous score-objective version can be derived, but the simple pixel-MSE identity above is specific to the Gaussian-head presentation; see the remark in Appendix B.1.

  • •

    (A3) One-step on-policy stationarity and stop-gradient advantage. Over one inner update, the imagined-rollout visitation marginal d̃_φ^π_θ is treated as locally fixed. The induced occupancy drift generally carries horizon- and mixing-dependent constants, and is absorbed into the residual terms of Proposition 1. The group-relative GRPO advantage Â(oₜ,aₜ) is treated as a stop-gradient, and the expected inner update is analyzed in the vanilla GRPO regime where the importance-ratio clip is inactive:

    ∇_θĴ_GRPO=\E_oₜ∼d̃_φ^π_θ, aₜ∼π_θ(·|o_≤t)[Â(oₜ,aₜ)∇_θ\logπ_θ(aₜ|o_≤t)].

    In practice, clip activation and advantage-estimation drift are absorbed into the local residuals in Proposition 1; imagined-visitation drift contributes to the trajectory-locality residual R_H, and demo-anchored transfer effects contribute to R_demo.

  • •

    (A4) Bounded truncated meta-gradient variance. For the fixed conditional objective J_θ̄, the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator ĝₜ:=∇̂_φJ_θ̄(φₜ) from Bᵣₑₐₗ simulator rollouts and one truncated HVP satisfies

    \E [∥ĝₜ-\E[ĝₜ|φₜ]∥² \middle| φₜ]≤σ_g²,

    uniformly in t.

  • •

    (A5) L-smoothness in φ. For fixed current policy parameters θ̄, the conditional objective J_θ̄ is L-smooth along the outer optimization trajectory:

    ∥∇_φJ_θ̄(φ^′)-∇_φJ_θ̄(φ)∥≤L∥φ^′-φ∥

    for all φ,φ^′ on that trajectory.

  • •

    (A6) Exponential truncation-bias decay. The bias of the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator satisfies

    ∥\E[ĝₜ|φₜ]-∇_φJ_θ̄(φₜ)∥≤Bρ^K

    for some B>0 and ρ∈(0,1) determined by the spectral radius of the inner-loop Jacobian. This is the standard contraction assumption used for truncated BPTT through unrolled iterative solvers, and parallels the spectral-radius bounds that drive the implicit-MAML rate of Rajeswaran et al. [24]; we estimate ρ directly in Section 5.4.

    • (A1)–(A3) underlie Proposition 1 (Appendix B); (A4)–(A6) underlie Theorem 1 (Appendix C). Appendix F.5 reports how the constants L, σ_g, B, and ρ are estimated in the experiments and gives the numerical ranges used to instantiate the theorem.

    Remark on the score-compatibility residual.

    Proposition 1 does not assume that DRILL-VWI is exactly equal to the target first-order direction underlying DRILL-IMG. Instead, it keeps the local policy-score contraction

    q_θ(oₜ,aₜ)=⟨∇_θ\logπ_θ(aₜ|o_≤t),∇_θJ(π_θ)⟩

    explicit, and measures the quality of the DRILL-VWI substitution q_θ(oₜ,aₜ)≈κ through ε_comp. The DRILL-VWI–DRILL-IMG gap therefore has a compatibility component, a trajectory-locality component R_H, a demo-anchor component R_demo, and a higher-order Taylor component.

    Remark on (A6) and its failure mode.

    The contraction parameter ρ is the spectral radius of the inner-loop Jacobian ∂θ⁺(φ)/∂θ evaluated along the unrolled imagined rollout. For a stable inner-loop optimizer on a well-conditioned WM, ρ<1 holds locally; we measure ρ directly on gridworld and Meta-World MT10 in Section 5.4. The assumption breaks when the inner loop sits near a fixed point of the WM dynamics, so that successive imagined transitions become near-identity in θ: the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator then has ρ→1 and the ρ^2K term in Theorem 1 no longer decays meaningfully in K. Engineering remedies are spectral normalization on the WM head, weight decay on φ, and diagonal damping of the inner Jacobian; we use weight decay throughout (Appendix D.7) and observe no ρ→1 regime in our experiments, but flag the regime explicitly because the convergence guarantee is no longer informative in it.

    A.3 The GRPO surrogate, restated

    For self-containment, we restate the GRPO surrogate [2] used inside the inner update. Given an imagined trajectory τ=(o₀,a₀,r₀,o₁,…,o_H) sampled by π_θ under W_φ,

    Ĵ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ)=\E_τ=(o₀,a₀,…,o_H)∼P_W_φ(π_θ)[1/H∑ₜ₌₀^H-1Â(oₜ,aₜ)\logπ_θ(aₜ|o_≤t)],

    		(11)

    where P_W_φ(π_θ) denotes the imagined trajectory law induced by rolling out π_θ in W_φ, and Â(oₜ,aₜ) is the group-relative advantage formed by sampling a group of G rollouts from π_θ and standardizing their returns within the group. The advantage is treated as a constant in θ and φ for the purposes of differentiation, in line with the stop-gradient GRPO implementation. Residuals from advantage recomputation and policy-ratio clipping are included in the local approximation residuals of Proposition 1; one-step imagined-visitation drift contributes to R_H, and transferring rollout-derived advantages to raw demonstration transitions contributes to R_demo. All other appearances of Ĵ_GRPO in this paper refer to Eq. (11).

    Appendix B Proof of Proposition 1: First-order meta-gradient and the DRILL-VWI surrogate

    This appendix proves Proposition 1 from Section 4.1. The proof derives the target first-order direction underlying DRILL-IMG, keeps the local policy-score contraction explicit, and shows that DRILL-VWI is recovered as a score-compatible closed-form surrogate with explicit residual terms. Thus DRILL-VWI is a principled local gradient surrogate rather than an exact first-order identity in general.

    B.1 Setup and notation

    We recall the bi-level formulation from Section 3.1. The VLA policy π_θ(a_t:t+Hₐ|o_≤t,ℓ) is parameterized by θ, and the video world model (WM) W_φ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,aₜ) is parameterized by φ. The reward model r_ψ is frozen throughout. Given the current (θ,φ), the inner one-step GRPO update on imagined trajectories generated by W_φ is

    θ⁺(φ)=θ+η_θg(φ,θ), g(φ,θ):=∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ),

    		(12)

    where η_θ>0 is the inner learning rate and Ĵ_GRPO is the GRPO surrogate evaluated on rollouts from W_φ. The outer objective is the expected return of the updated policy in the target environment,

    J(π_θ⁺(φ))=\E_τ∼Pₑₙᵥ(π_θ⁺(φ))[∑ₜrₜ].

    		(13)

    DRILL-IMG optimizes φ by differentiating (13) through (12). DRILL-VWI instead uses a signed local coaching surrogate

    L_VWI(φ;w̄)=\E_(oₜ,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼μ_demo[w̄(oₜ,aₜ)∥ôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁∥₂²],

    		(14)

    where the unclipped signed coefficient is

    w(oₜ,aₜ)=d̃_φ^π_θ(oₜ) sgn (Â(oₜ,aₜ))|Â(oₜ,aₜ)|^αs(oₜ),

    		(15)

    and w̄ is the clipped, normalized, stop-gradient version used by the implemented DRILL-VWI objective. The core theoretical case sets α=1, s(oₜ)=1, uses exact imagined-rollout visitation, and removes clipping. We denote this idealized loss by L_VWIᶜᵒʳᵉ(φ).

    To avoid overloading notation, we distinguish the state-visitation marginal from the joint transition distributions. Let μᵣₒₗₗ denote the time-averaged local imagined-rollout transition distribution obtained by sampling a time index t uniformly from the H-step imagined rollout, then sampling oₜ∼d̃_φ^π_θ, aₜ∼π_θ(·|o_≤t), and oₜ₊₁∼W_φ(·|o_≤t,aₜ). Let μ_demo denote the raw demonstration transition distribution before applying VWI weights. In demo-side expectations, Â(oₜ,aₜ) denotes the stop-gradient advantage assigned to the demo transition by the same rollout-derived advantage-transfer rule used by the implemented VWI objective. The mismatch between the local rollout distribution and this raw demo-anchor distribution is kept as the explicit residual R_demo below.

    We work under the following assumptions.

要点：

  • 五个操纵仿真 + 两个 VLA 主干上，DRILL-IMG 平均成功率比 WMPO 高 13.1 分、比 RLVR-World 高 7.9 分；LIBERO-Long 上随世界模型变大优势从 7.9 分扩到 16.4 分

为什么值得看：如果你的引擎/训练管线用世界模型做 agent 后训练，指标该换成收益而不是重建质量——这条对「用什么评价模型」的影响比对模型结构本身更大。

中文摘要：世界模型越来越多被用于在强化学习后训练视觉-语言-动作策略时减少与环境交互，但它们通常仍按「预测下一步像素」来训练，而在这类场景里世界模型的职责不是渲染视觉上忠实的视频，而是从想象 rollout 中产出能改进策略的学习信号。作者指出这种错配很严重：更低的像素 MSE 可能带来更差的策略梯度；反之，按策略效用训练的世界模型虽然下一帧 MSE 高 17%，仍能得到更好的下游策略。为此他们提出 DRILL，一个双层框架：外层更新世界模型，使其最大化内层在想象 rollout 上做 GRPO 更新之后策略的回报；并给出两个实例——需要额外模拟器 rollout 的闭式代理 DRILL-VWI，以及完整 meta-gradient 的 DRILL-IMG。在五个操纵仿真与两个 VLA 主干上，DRILL-IMG 相比 WMPO 平均成功率高 13.1 分、相比 RLVR-World 高 7.9 分，并能与 RLVR 预训练叠加。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

DRILL: Training World Models to Improve Policies, Not Predict Pixels

Abstract

World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy’s return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
