1 Introduction

World models are becoming a practical substitute for robot or simulator interaction in reinforcement-learning post-training of vision-language-action (VLA) policies. In this setting, however, their role is not merely to predict the next video frame: they generate the imagined rollouts from which the policy learns. This distinction creates an objective mismatch. A model optimized for one-step pixel prediction is not necessarily the model that induces the most useful policy-gradient update.

The reason is that pixel fidelity and policy utility weight errors in different places. Pixel MSE penalizes prediction errors uniformly over pixels and time, including backgrounds, robot geometry, and visually salient but task-irrelevant regions. A policy-gradient update instead emphasizes the states the current policy visits and the actions whose advantages are large. A model can therefore be an excellent next-frame predictor while producing weak learning signals, or a worse predictor on average while better supporting the transitions that determine policy improvement. The relevant question is not only whether the imagined video looks right, but whether learning inside it moves the policy in the right direction.

This mismatch matters because recent VLA post-training systems replace expensive robot or simulator interaction with imagined rollouts. At foundation-model scale, reinforcement-learning post-training can require millions of environment steps, so recent methods train a video world model from offline demonstrations and apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [(Shao et al., 2024)] inside the model [(Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2024)]. Yet the world model is still typically optimized as a one-step video predictor. Diagnostic methods such as Policy-Aware WM [(Zhao et al., 2025)] and ESNR [(Zollicoffer et al., 2025)] show that pixel fidelity does not reliably track policy competence, but do not provide a training objective. RLVR-World [(Wu et al., 2025)] post-trains the world model with prediction correctness as the reward, improving it as a predictor rather than directly optimizing the policy update induced by imagined rollouts.

We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that trains video world models by the return of the policy obtained after learning in them. The inner loop performs a GRPO update on imagined rollouts generated by the world model; the outer loop updates the world model so that this post-update policy achieves higher return in the target simulator. The objective is therefore not pixel accuracy under the model’s own rollouts, but downstream return in the environment that defines task success.

DRILL has two operating points. DRILL-VWI (Visitation-Weighted Imagination) is a lightweight signed surrogate that replaces uniform pixel MSE with weights from policy visitation, group-relative advantage, and model confidence, requiring no additional simulator rollouts over a WMPO-style pipeline. DRILL-IMG (Implicit Meta-Gradient) estimates the downstream-return meta-gradient more directly by differentiating through the inner GRPO update with truncated Hessian-vector products and a small simulator-rollout batch. Thus DRILL-VWI is the budget-conscious drop-in update, while DRILL-IMG is the more faithful estimator when limited simulator interaction and BPTT memory are available.

The two variants are connected theoretically: the core DRILL-VWI surrogate is the first-order Taylor approximation of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under standard local assumptions, and DRILL-IMG admits a non-asymptotic convergence rate with truncated backpropagation through the inner update. This explains when a local visitation- and advantage-weighted prediction loss can approximate the more expensive meta-gradient, and when longer-horizon trajectory effects make DRILL-IMG worth the additional cost.

Across five public manipulation simulators [(Liu et al., 2023; Mees et al., 2022; Nasiriany et al., 2024)] and two foundation VLA backbones [(Black et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024)], DRILL-IMG raises mean policy success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, while its world model has 17% higher one-step pixel MSE on the same training data. The gains are consistent across seeds, increase with rollout horizon and out-of-distribution shift, and remain complementary to prediction-correctness pretraining: applying DRILL-IMG to an RLVR-World-pretrained world model yields a further 3.2-point improvement on average. We also introduce the Policy-Utility Residual (PUR), a method-agnostic diagnostic measuring the angular gap between the pixel-MSE gradient and the policy-improvement direction; across the objectives we evaluate, lower PUR tracks higher downstream success.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We identify and formalize an objective mismatch in VLA world-model post-training: world models are trained for one-step pixel prediction, but used to generate policy-learning signals for imagined-rollout reinforcement learning.

  • •

    We introduce DRILL, a bilevel framework that trains the world model for the downstream return of the policy obtained after an inner GRPO update, and instantiate it as both a no-extra-rollout surrogate (DRILL-VWI) and a simulator-grounded meta-gradient method (DRILL-IMG).

  • •

    We show that DRILL-VWI is a first-order approximation to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient, provide a non-asymptotic convergence guarantee for DRILL-IMG under truncated BPTT, and validate the framework across five simulators and two VLA backbones with higher downstream success despite higher pixel MSE.

  • •

    We introduce PUR as a method-agnostic diagnostic of the angular gap between pixel prediction and policy improvement, and show that it tracks downstream success across objectives.

    • 2 Related Work

    Video world models for VLA post-training. Recent VLA post-training systems use video world models to replace expensive robot or simulator interaction with imagined rollouts. WMPO [(Zhu et al., 2025)], VLAW [(Guo et al., 2026)], WoVR [(Jiang et al., 2026)], SC-VLA [(Li et al., 2024)], Ctrl-World [(Guo et al., 2025)], World4RL [(Jiang et al., 2025)], and World-Gymnast [(Sharma et al., 2026)] pretrain the world model from demonstrations and then update the policy inside the learned dynamics. These methods differ in rollout construction, filtering, and policy optimization details, but the world model is still primarily trained as a next-frame predictor. Policy-Aware WM [(Zhao et al., 2025)] and ESNR [(Zollicoffer et al., 2025)] diagnose the gap between prediction quality and policy competence, while RLVR-World [(Wu et al., 2025)] and WorldCompass [(Wang et al., 2026)] improve the predictor with prediction-correctness rewards. DRILL instead optimizes the world model by the downstream return of the policy after learning from its imagined rollouts; it is therefore complementary to RLVR-style pretraining rather than a replacement for it.

    Policy-aware world-model learning. The idea that a model should be useful for control, not only accurate under a prediction loss, appears in value-aware model learning [(Farahmand et al., 2017; Grimm et al., 2020)] and in neural model-based RL systems such as MuZero [(Schrittwieser et al., 2020)], IRIS [(Micheli et al., 2022)], and DreamerV3 [(Hafner et al., 2023)]. DRILL brings this perspective to VLA post-training with imagined GRPO rollouts. Classical value-aware objectives rely on a learned V_ψ(o) or bootstrapped targets; DRILL uses the group-relative advantage produced online by GRPO as a per-batch surrogate for downstream utility. Proposition 1 shows that the signed advantage weighting in DRILL-VWI is recovered as a first-order approximation to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under a local score-compatibility condition, and Section 5.3 compares this approximation with a direct value-aware adaptation.

    Meta-gradient and implicit differentiation. DRILL-IMG is also related to methods that differentiate through an inner optimization step, including truncated MAML [(Finn et al., 2017)], iMAML [(Rajeswaran et al., 2019)], and implicit-gradient methods for RL [(Nikishin et al., 2022)]. Unlike iMAML-style approaches, DRILL-IMG uses a short unroll of the policy update rather than solving the inner problem to convergence. Our analysis keeps the resulting truncation bias explicit: Theorem 1 expresses the BPTT bias as a function of the truncation length K. The practical distinction is scale and target: DRILL-IMG applies meta-gradients to foundation-scale VLAs paired with >1B-parameter video world models, using a small simulator-rollout batch to train the world model for the post-update return of the policy.

    3 The DRILL Framework

    DRILL couples two updates. The inner update uses the current world model as the environment for one GRPO step in imagination. The outer update evaluates the policy produced by that step in the target environment and assigns credit back to the world model. DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG differ only in how much of this outer gradient they estimate. Figure 1 gives the full training loop and marks where the two estimators enter.

    3.1 Problem setup

    We consider a VLA policy π_θ(a_t:t+Hₐ|o_≤t,ℓ), a video world model W_φ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,aₜ) with predicted next-frame mean ôₜ₊₁(φ), and a frozen vision-language reward model r_ψ(oₜ,ℓ)∈[0,1]. Training uses offline demonstrations D_demo and imagined rollouts of horizon H produced by π_θ under W_φ. We write d_\rmenv^π_θ(oₜ) for the on-policy state visitation in the target environment, which in our experiments is the high-fidelity simulator that defines task return (Section 5.1), and d̃_φ^π_θ(oₜ) for the corresponding imagined-rollout visitation induced by π_θ inside W_φ.

    The standard WMPO recipe [(Zhu et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026)] alternates between fitting the world model to demonstration pixels and improving the policy inside the model:

    φ← \argmin_φ \E_(o_≤t,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼D_demo\lVertôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁\rVert₂²,(1)
    θ← θ + η_θ ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ,r_ψ).(2)

    The first update is optimized for pixel fidelity, while the second uses the model through the policy-gradient signal it induces. DRILL replaces the pixel-fitting update with one aligned to this downstream role.

    3.2 The DRILL objective

    Let

    θ⁺(φ) = θ+η_θ ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ)

    		(3)

    be the policy produced by one imagined GRPO step. DRILL trains W_φ so that this updated policy obtains high return in the target environment:

    φ^* = \argmax_φ J (π_θ⁺(φ)), J(π) = \E_τ∼Pₑₙᵥ(π)[∑ₜrₜ].

    		(4)

    The expectation in J is taken under the trajectory distribution of the target environment, not under W_φ: the world model is not asked to evaluate itself. Optimizing (4) requires the meta-gradient ∇_φJ(π_θ⁺(φ)) through the inner update (3). This formulation changes what the world model is optimized for: rather than fitting all demonstrated pixels equally, DRILL rewards model changes that make the imagined policy update improve target-environment return. The useful signal is therefore not frame fidelity alone, but whether the model induces the right policy-gradient direction on states the current policy actually visits.

    DRILL uses two operating points. DRILL-VWI is a local signed surrogate requiring no additional simulator rollouts, while DRILL-IMG estimates the downstream-return meta-gradient more directly with truncated differentiation through the inner update and a small simulator batch for the outer return gradient.

    3.3 DRILL-VWI: Visitation-Weighted Imagination

    DRILL-VWI replaces the pixel-MSE loss (1) with a policy-aware signed local surrogate,

    L_VWI(φ) = \E_(oₜ,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼D_demo[w(oₜ,aₜ)\lVertôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁\rVert₂²],

    		(5)

    with

    w(oₜ,aₜ) = d̃̂_φ^π_θ(oₜ)·Ã_α(oₜ,aₜ)·s(oₜ), Ã_α(oₜ,aₜ)=sgn(Â(oₜ,aₜ)) \lvertÂ(oₜ,aₜ)\rvert^α.

    		(6)

    The three factors are quantities already produced by the imagined GRPO loop: d̃̂_φ^π_θ(oₜ) estimates model-rollout visitation, Â(oₜ,aₜ) is the group-relative GRPO advantage, and s(oₜ)>0 downweights states on which the world model is uncertain. The weight is stopped and clipped in implementation, so (5) is a local update direction, not a globally normalized likelihood objective. Proposition 1 formalizes its first-order connection to the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient. Algorithm 1 in Appendix D.1 gives the full training loop, including clipping, normalization, and visitation estimation. Since all factors come from imagined rollouts, DRILL-VWI adds no environment interaction over WMPO.

    3.4 DRILL-IMG: Implicit Meta-Gradient

    DRILL-IMG estimates the meta-gradient of (4) by differentiating through the inner update (3):

    ∇_φJ (π_θ⁺(φ)) = η_θ ∇_θ⁺J (π_θ⁺) ∇_φ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ).

    		(7)

    The first factor is a policy-gradient estimate in the target simulator, computed from a small batch of simulator rollouts. The second factor is a mixed derivative through the imagined GRPO update, computed as a Hessian-vector product with K-step truncated BPTT. In the main experiments we use K=2 and Bᵣₑₐₗ=30 simulator rollouts per outer step. DRILL-IMG is therefore a more faithful estimator of the DRILL objective than DRILL-VWI, at the cost of additional simulator interaction and BPTT memory. Algorithm 2 in Appendix D.2 gives the full pseudocode, checkpointing details, and numerical-stability controls.

    4 Theoretical Analysis

    The analysis has three roles. First, it explains when the cheap DRILL-VWI update is a first-order surrogate for the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient. Second, it states the convergence guarantee for DRILL-IMG under truncated BPTT. Third, it defines a diagnostic, PUR, for measuring whether a world-model objective is aligned with policy improvement.

    4.1 First-order meta-gradient and the DRILL-VWI surrogate

    The inner update (3) is a single gradient step, so the outer objective J(π_θ⁺(φ)) can be expanded in the inner step size η_θ. The proposition below keeps only the main statement needed in the paper body; the full proof and residual definitions are given in Appendix B.

    Proposition 1(DRILL-VWI as a first-order local surrogate).

    Suppose (A1) J is C² in θ; (A2) W_φ has a Gaussian observation head with mean ôₜ₊₁(φ) and fixed scale σ_W; and (A3) the imagined-rollout visitation marginal d̃_φ^π_θ is locally stationary over one inner step. Treat the GRPO advantages as stop-gradient quantities when forming ∇_φ∇_θĴ_GRPO. Let L_VWIᶜᵒʳᵉ denote the idealized VWI surrogate with exact imagined-rollout visitation, α=1, s(oₜ)=1, and unclipped signed weights. If the local policy-score contraction is compatible with the signed advantage direction up to residual ε_comp, the omitted multi-step trajectory-score terms have residual R_H, and the demo-anchor transfer has residual R_demo, then for some alignment scalar κ>0,

    ∥∇_φJ (π_θ⁺(φ))+(κη_θ)/(2σ_W²)∇_φL_VWIᶜᵒʳᵉ(φ)∥≤η_θM_Wε_comp+η_θR_H+η_θR_demo+O(η_θ²).

    		(8)

    The result should not be read as an exact identity between DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG. It says that the signed VWI update recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient when the policy-score contraction is approximately scalar on the advantage-weighted support and when trajectory-locality and demo-anchor residuals are small. Intuitively, positive-advantage transitions are sharpened, while negative-advantage transitions may be deliberately deemphasized rather than fit more accurately as pixels.

    The residuals describe when this local approximation is reliable. ε_comp measures whether the world-model score and the policy-gradient contraction agree on which transition changes matter; R_H grows when multi-step consequences dominate local next-frame error; and R_demo captures mismatch between demonstration anchors and on-policy imagined transitions. Thus short-horizon or well-covered tasks favor DRILL-VWI, while large trajectory or demo-anchor residuals motivate the more expensive DRILL-IMG estimator.

    4.2 Convergence rate under truncated BPTT

    DRILL-IMG replaces the exact mixed derivative in (7) by a K-step truncated BPTT estimate. The following theorem analyzes one fixed-policy outer subproblem. Fix current policy parameters θ̄ and define

    J_θ̄(φ):=J (π_θ̄+η_θ∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ̄;W_φ)).

    This is a per-outer-subproblem guarantee, not a proof of global convergence for the jointly evolving (θₜ,φₜ) process.

    Theorem 1(DRILL-IMG convergence rate under truncated BPTT).

    Suppose (A4) the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator has conditional variance at most σ_g²; (A5) J_θ̄ is L-smooth in φ and bounded above with J^*:=\sup_φJ_θ̄(φ)<∞; and (A6) the K-step BPTT truncation bias satisfies \lVertbias_K\rVert≤Bρ^K for some ρ∈(0,1). Let J₀:=J_θ̄(φ₀). With step size

    η_φ=\min (1/4L,√(2(J^*-J₀))/(LTσ_g²)),

    the T-step stochastic ascent iterates on J_θ̄ satisfy

    \min_0≤t

    		(9)

    The three terms correspond to optimization error, stochastic-gradient variance, and truncation bias. The guarantee is qualitative at our scale: it shows convergence to a neighborhood of a stationary point and that the squared-gradient contribution from BPTT truncation decays geometrically in K. This supports using a shallow truncation when the extra unroll depth no longer changes the meta-gradient direction much. The practical choice K=2 is therefore made empirically, from the truncation and return-per-compute studies in the appendix, rather than from the worst-case constants in the bound.

    Corollary 1(Truncation depth).

    The truncation contribution in (9) falls below any target ε>0 once K=Θ(\log(1/ε)), with constants determined by B and ρ.

    4.3 Policy-Utility Residual

    The previous results are specific to DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG. To compare arbitrary world-model objectives, we measure whether the pixel-MSE gradient is aligned with the direction that improves the policy after imagined training. We define the Policy-Utility Residual as

    PUR(φ) = 1 - (⟨∇_φL_MSE(φ), -∇_φJ (π_θ⁺(φ))⟩)/(\lVert∇_φL_MSE\rVert \lVert∇_φJ\rVert).

    		(10)

    Equivalently, PUR=1+\cos∠(∇_φL_MSE,∇_φJ) whenever both gradients are nonzero. Thus PUR ≈ 0 means that descending pixel MSE also improves the downstream-return objective, PUR ≈ 1 means the two directions are nearly orthogonal, and PUR ≈ 2 means that descending pixel MSE is anti-aligned with policy improvement.

    We estimate ∇_φJ by finite differences in the simulator rather than by reusing the HVP machinery of DRILL-IMG. This keeps PUR independent of any particular training method, so the same diagnostic applies to WMPO, RLVR-World, DRILL-VWI, DRILL-IMG, and other world-model objectives. Section 5.5 tests whether lower PUR tracks higher downstream success across the methods we evaluate.

    5 Experiments

    We evaluate DRILL on five robot-manipulation simulators, two VLA backbones, and five training baselines, while also reporting diagnostic metrics from policy-aware WM evaluation. The main text keeps the headline comparison, compact diagnostic panels, architectural checks, component-level summaries, and the criterion for choosing DRILL-VWI or DRILL-IMG. Detailed ablations, cross-backbone tables, robustness breakdowns, hyperparameter sweeps, reward-model swaps, and auxiliary diagnostic curves are collected in Appendices D.7–F.6.

    5.1 Setup

    Benchmarks and baselines. We use LIBERO-Long [(Liu et al., 2023)], CALVIN ABC→D [(Mees et al., 2022)], RoboCasa [(Nasiriany et al., 2024)], Meta-World MT50, and SimplerEnv. These simulators define both evaluation and the small real-rollout budget used by DRILL-IMG’s outer gradient, Bᵣₑₐₗ=30 simulator rollouts per outer step; no real-robot results are included. Baselines are Scratch-GRPO, WMPO [(Zhu et al., 2025)], VLAW [(Guo et al., 2026)], RLVR-World [(Wu et al., 2025)], and a simulator-budget-matched model-free PPO control, Sim-PPO. Sim-PPO receives the same simulator episode budget as DRILL-IMG but no imagined rollouts, isolating whether the world model amplifies limited simulator interaction. Policy-Aware WM [(Zhao et al., 2025)] is diagnostic rather than a training method, so we report its ESNR score alongside PUR.

    Protocol. Headline results use five seeds; ablations use three. We report Welch’s t-test p-values and 95% CIs for head-to-head comparisons. The headline run uses about 17k NVIDIA H20-hours, or 24 H20 GPUs for roughly four weeks. Appendix D.9 gives the per-phase breakdown.

    5.2 Main Results

    On π₀-3B, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, averaged across the five benchmarks, while increasing one-step pixel MSE by 17% on the same training data. The gain is largest on long-horizon tasks and smallest on SimplerEnv, where DRILL-VWI and DRILL-IMG are statistically tied: 64.0 ± 1.9 versus 63.1 ± 2.6. This exception motivates the horizon analysis in Section 5.4.

    The compact diagnostic panels in Figure 3 give three additional views of the same result: DRILL variants break the usual link between lower pixel MSE and higher success, improve faster on LIBERO-Long, and reduce PUR during training. A compute-matched control in Appendix F.1 further shows that extra WMPO updates move LIBERO-Long SR from 64.2 ± 1.6 to at most 65.1 ± 1.9, far below DRILL-IMG’s 81.3 ± 1.3. Together, these checks rule out a pure compute or pixel-fidelity explanation: the methods that improve most are those that better align imagined updates with downstream policy utility. The appendix reports the full breakdowns, while the main text keeps only this recurring trend.

    Backbone and pretraining checks. We repeat the headline comparison on OpenVLA-7B using LIBERO-Long, CALVIN, and RoboCasa. LIBERO-Long and CALVIN preserve the ranking DRILL-IMG > DRILL-VWI > RLVR-World > WMPO. On RoboCasa, DRILL-IMG and DRILL-VWI are statistically tied, 50.8 ± 2.3 versus 48.7 ± 2.1 with p = 0.12, matching that benchmark’s shorter, object-centric episodes. DRILL-IMG reaches 68.9 mean SR on OpenVLA, compared with 53.8 for WMPO, a 15.1-point gain; the full per-benchmark table is in Appendix F.7. This replication changes both the policy backbone and the pretraining mixture, yet preserves the same method ordering on the two longer-horizon benchmarks. We therefore use the appendix tables mainly as robustness evidence for the objective, rather than as a separate architecture claim.

    Orthogonality with RLVR-World. Initializing the WM with RLVR-World pretraining and then applying DRILL-IMG improves mean SR by another roughly 3 points over DRILL-IMG alone. Prediction-correctness pretraining and downstream-return imagination are therefore complementary rather than interchangeable. The stacked variant helps most on SimplerEnv, where the shorter horizon weakens the DRILL-IMG HVP signal and a better pretrained WM matters more.

    A plausible mechanism is that RLVR-World pretraining lowers the variance of the supervised prediction gradient on task-relevant transitions, so that the downstream-return outer gradient is less likely to be drowned out early in training. We treat this as an interpretation of the empirical trend rather than a formal claim, and leave a direct curvature-level test (cf. Appendix D.4) to future work.

    5.3 Ablations and Scaling

    Objective ablations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa, each factor in the signed DRILL-VWI coaching surrogate helps: visitation-only reaches 64.2 mean SR, signed-advantage-only 66.8, and confidence-only 60.1, compared with 58.2 for WMPO. Combining all three gives 69.2. The exponent sweep peaks at α=1, consistent with Proposition 1: the score-compatible local surrogate is linear in the signed advantage, whereas α≠1 deliberately distorts that direction. Increasing to α=2 lowers SR to 67.9, consistent with higher variance from overemphasizing high-magnitude signed-advantage samples. A minimal value-aware baseline, VA-WM, reaches 62.4 mean SR, closing part of the gap to WMPO but remaining 6.8 points below DRILL-VWI and 11.0 below DRILL-IMG; the complete ablation table is in Appendix F.2.

    Scaling and coupling. On LIBERO-Long, the DRILL-IMG margin over WMPO grows with WM size: 7.9 points at 300M parameters, 13.1 at 1.2B, and 16.4 at 7B. DRILL-IMG also transfers across WM backbones: Ctrl-World obtains 81.3 ± 1.3 SR and a matched Cosmos-Predict2-style model obtains 79.6 ± 1.7, a gap within two standard deviations. Finally, freezing the VWI signed coaching multipliers from a GRPO-warmstart policy reaches only 64.9 ± 1.5 mean SR, 4.3 points below DRILL-VWI. The gain therefore comes from tracking the current policy’s signed advantage signal, not from a fixed supervised MSE reweighting.

    5.4 When DRILL-IMG Pays Off over DRILL-VWI

    At the default horizon H=50, DRILL-VWI captures most of the gain on LIBERO-Long: it recovers 11.9 of the 17.1 points between WMPO and DRILL-IMG. DRILL-IMG costs about 1.4× more per outer step and uses Bᵣₑₐₗ=30 simulator rollouts that DRILL-VWI does not require, so the choice should depend on horizon. The residual decomposition suggests this dependence: the one-step DRILL-VWI surrogate omits multi-step trajectory-score terms collected in the trajectory-locality residual R_H, while DRILL-IMG partially recovers these terms through truncated BPTT. If one additionally assumes R_H=O(η_θH²), this residual induces an O(η_θ²H²) horizon-dependent component, but the experiment should be read as testing whether the IMG–VWI gap grows with H, not as isolating a universal H² law.

    The horizon sweep (Figure 3) is consistent with this residual-based criterion. The DRILL-IMG margin over DRILL-VWI grows from 1.8 points at H=20 to 5.2 at H=50, 7.5 at H=100, and 8.1 at H=200. WMPO falls from 67.4 to 49.8 SR as rollout error compounds; DRILL-VWI is more stable but saturates around the mid-70s. DRILL-IMG peaks at H=100 with 83.4 SR and drops to 78.6 at H=200, where imagined trajectories become too noisy. The short-horizon checks point the other way: on LIBERO-Long the IMG-over-VWI gap shrinks to 0.6 at H=10 and becomes a non-significant -0.2 ± 1.1 at H=5; on SimplerEnv, whose effective horizon is below H=20, DRILL-VWI slightly exceeds DRILL-IMG, 64.0 versus 63.1 SR. We recommend DRILL-VWI as the budget-conscious choice for very short horizons or when simulator rollouts are unavailable, and DRILL-IMG when the task horizon is moderate to long or when the extra simulator budget is acceptable. In our default H=50 setting, DRILL-IMG already gives a 5.2-point gain over DRILL-VWI on LIBERO-Long, while SimplerEnv illustrates the short-horizon regime where VWI can be preferable. Full horizon tables and reward-model swaps are in Appendices F.3 and F.8.

    HVP validation. On a 2D gridworld and Meta-World MT10, where the exact meta-gradient is tractable, the K=2 truncated HVP has cosine similarity 0.74 ± 0.04 and 0.71 ± 0.05 to the untruncated target meta-gradient, respectively. The full K-sweep and estimated contraction rate ρ are in Appendix D.4.

    5.5 Diagnostics and Robustness

    Robustness and diagnostics. Under LIBERO zero-shot perturbations, DRILL-IMG has an 18.6% average relative SR drop, compared with 30.2% for WMPO and 25.6% for RLVR-World. The only exception is pose perturbation, where DRILL-VWI slightly wins, again matching a shorter effective horizon; the per-condition breakdown is in Appendix F.9. PUR also tracks policy utility (Figure 3): WMPO drifts upward, RLVR-World plateaus, DRILL-VWI stays bounded, and DRILL-IMG decreases; across the PUR-reporting headline rows, the Spearman correlation with downstream SR is ρ_S=-0.89 with 95% bootstrap CI [-0.97,-0.71]. Two held-out variants give 1.5 points mean absolute error when final SR is predicted from checkpoint-level PUR at step 5k.

    DRILL also improves task-relevant imagination rather than visual fidelity alone. On LIBERO-Long, WMPO reaches lower pixel MSE but plateaus at 0.61 ± 0.02 TRPS, while DRILL-IMG reaches 0.81 ± 0.03 TRPS despite higher MSE. In a forced-choice human study with 120 trials and six blinded raters, visual-quality preferences for WMPO or RLVR-World over DRILL-IMG are not significant, but when task completion is shown, 62% prefer DRILL-IMG over WMPO (p < 0.001). TRPS curves and human-evaluation details are in Appendices F.4 and F.10.

    6 Conclusion

    We introduced DRILL, a bilevel framework for training video world models as policy-improvement environments rather than as standalone next-frame predictors. Its two instantiations expose a practical trade-off: DRILL-VWI provides a lightweight visitation- and advantage-weighted surrogate that can be used in a WMPO-style pipeline, while DRILL-IMG more directly optimizes downstream return by differentiating through imagined policy updates. The theoretical connection between these variants explains when the cheaper local surrogate should be sufficient and when longer-horizon trajectory effects make the meta-gradient worth its extra cost. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL improves policy success even when one-step pixel MSE becomes worse, reinforcing the central claim that visual fidelity is not the right standalone target for world-model post-training. The accompanying PUR diagnostic makes this mismatch measurable, and the gains from combining DRILL with RLVR-World suggest that prediction-correctness pretraining and policy-aware downstream optimization are complementary. More broadly, DRILL shifts the optimization target from making imagined videos look accurate to making learning inside those videos useful.

    Limitations.

    Our evaluation remains simulation-only and uses a small simulator-rollout budget for DRILL-IMG rather than physical robot interaction. This leaves open how sensitive the method is to real-world perception noise, actuation delay, safety constraints, and sim-to-real distribution shift. DRILL-IMG also introduces additional compute and memory overhead through truncated backpropagation and Hessian-vector products, so DRILL-VWI may be the more appropriate choice when interaction, memory, or wall-clock budget is the binding constraint. Extending DRILL to real-robot post-training and reducing the cost of the meta-gradient estimator are therefore important next steps.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Notation and Preliminaries

    This appendix collects the symbols, assumptions, and intermediate definitions used throughout the paper, so that Appendices B–C can be read without re-tracing the main text.

    A.1 Symbol glossary

    A.2 Assumptions

    Six assumptions are used across the proofs in Appendices B–C. We restate them here in compact form; the long-form versions, with remarks on tightness and on the WM-architecture cases they cover, appear inline at first use in each proof.

  • •

    (A1) Outer smoothness in θ.J:Θ→ℝ is C² in a neighborhood of θ with bounded second derivatives, so that

    J(θ+η_θg)=J(θ)+η_θ∇_θJ(θ)^⊤g+O(η_θ²).

  • •

    (A2) Gaussian WM head. For each (o_≤t,aₜ), the WM output distribution is Gaussian with mean ôₜ₊₁(φ) and isotropic covariance σ_W²I, and φ↦ôₜ₊₁(φ) is C¹. Equivalently,

    ∇_φ\logW_φ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,aₜ)=-(1)/(2σ_W²)∇_φ∥ôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁∥₂².

    For diffusion or flow WMs, an analogous score-objective version can be derived, but the simple pixel-MSE identity above is specific to the Gaussian-head presentation; see the remark in Appendix B.1.

  • •

    (A3) One-step on-policy stationarity and stop-gradient advantage. Over one inner update, the imagined-rollout visitation marginal d̃_φ^π_θ is treated as locally fixed. The induced occupancy drift generally carries horizon- and mixing-dependent constants, and is absorbed into the residual terms of Proposition 1. The group-relative GRPO advantage Â(oₜ,aₜ) is treated as a stop-gradient, and the expected inner update is analyzed in the vanilla GRPO regime where the importance-ratio clip is inactive:

    ∇_θĴ_GRPO=\E_oₜ∼d̃_φ^π_θ, aₜ∼π_θ(·|o_≤t)[Â(oₜ,aₜ)∇_θ\logπ_θ(aₜ|o_≤t)].

    In practice, clip activation and advantage-estimation drift are absorbed into the local residuals in Proposition 1; imagined-visitation drift contributes to the trajectory-locality residual R_H, and demo-anchored transfer effects contribute to R_demo.

  • •

    (A4) Bounded truncated meta-gradient variance. For the fixed conditional objective J_θ̄, the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator ĝₜ:=∇̂_φJ_θ̄(φₜ) from Bᵣₑₐₗ simulator rollouts and one truncated HVP satisfies

    \E [∥ĝₜ-\E[ĝₜ|φₜ]∥² \middle| φₜ]≤σ_g²,

    uniformly in t.

  • •

    (A5) L-smoothness in φ. For fixed current policy parameters θ̄, the conditional objective J_θ̄ is L-smooth along the outer optimization trajectory:

    ∥∇_φJ_θ̄(φ^′)-∇_φJ_θ̄(φ)∥≤L∥φ^′-φ∥

    for all φ,φ^′ on that trajectory.

  • •

    (A6) Exponential truncation-bias decay. The bias of the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator satisfies

    ∥\E[ĝₜ|φₜ]-∇_φJ_θ̄(φₜ)∥≤Bρ^K

    for some B>0 and ρ∈(0,1) determined by the spectral radius of the inner-loop Jacobian. This is the standard contraction assumption used for truncated BPTT through unrolled iterative solvers, and parallels the spectral-radius bounds that drive the implicit-MAML rate of Rajeswaran et al. [24]; we estimate ρ directly in Section 5.4.

    • (A1)–(A3) underlie Proposition 1 (Appendix B); (A4)–(A6) underlie Theorem 1 (Appendix C). Appendix F.5 reports how the constants L, σ_g, B, and ρ are estimated in the experiments and gives the numerical ranges used to instantiate the theorem.

    Remark on the score-compatibility residual.

    Proposition 1 does not assume that DRILL-VWI is exactly equal to the target first-order direction underlying DRILL-IMG. Instead, it keeps the local policy-score contraction

    q_θ(oₜ,aₜ)=⟨∇_θ\logπ_θ(aₜ|o_≤t),∇_θJ(π_θ)⟩

    explicit, and measures the quality of the DRILL-VWI substitution q_θ(oₜ,aₜ)≈κ through ε_comp. The DRILL-VWI–DRILL-IMG gap therefore has a compatibility component, a trajectory-locality component R_H, a demo-anchor component R_demo, and a higher-order Taylor component.

    Remark on (A6) and its failure mode.

    The contraction parameter ρ is the spectral radius of the inner-loop Jacobian ∂θ⁺(φ)/∂θ evaluated along the unrolled imagined rollout. For a stable inner-loop optimizer on a well-conditioned WM, ρ<1 holds locally; we measure ρ directly on gridworld and Meta-World MT10 in Section 5.4. The assumption breaks when the inner loop sits near a fixed point of the WM dynamics, so that successive imagined transitions become near-identity in θ: the K-truncated meta-gradient estimator then has ρ→1 and the ρ^2K term in Theorem 1 no longer decays meaningfully in K. Engineering remedies are spectral normalization on the WM head, weight decay on φ, and diagonal damping of the inner Jacobian; we use weight decay throughout (Appendix D.7) and observe no ρ→1 regime in our experiments, but flag the regime explicitly because the convergence guarantee is no longer informative in it.

    A.3 The GRPO surrogate, restated

    For self-containment, we restate the GRPO surrogate [2] used inside the inner update. Given an imagined trajectory τ=(o₀,a₀,r₀,o₁,…,o_H) sampled by π_θ under W_φ,

    Ĵ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ)=\E_τ=(o₀,a₀,…,o_H)∼P_W_φ(π_θ)[1/H∑ₜ₌₀^H-1Â(oₜ,aₜ)\logπ_θ(aₜ|o_≤t)],

    		(11)

    where P_W_φ(π_θ) denotes the imagined trajectory law induced by rolling out π_θ in W_φ, and Â(oₜ,aₜ) is the group-relative advantage formed by sampling a group of G rollouts from π_θ and standardizing their returns within the group. The advantage is treated as a constant in θ and φ for the purposes of differentiation, in line with the stop-gradient GRPO implementation. Residuals from advantage recomputation and policy-ratio clipping are included in the local approximation residuals of Proposition 1; one-step imagined-visitation drift contributes to R_H, and transferring rollout-derived advantages to raw demonstration transitions contributes to R_demo. All other appearances of Ĵ_GRPO in this paper refer to Eq. (11).

    Appendix B Proof of Proposition 1: First-order meta-gradient and the DRILL-VWI surrogate

    This appendix proves Proposition 1 from Section 4.1. The proof derives the target first-order direction underlying DRILL-IMG, keeps the local policy-score contraction explicit, and shows that DRILL-VWI is recovered as a score-compatible closed-form surrogate with explicit residual terms. Thus DRILL-VWI is a principled local gradient surrogate rather than an exact first-order identity in general.

    B.1 Setup and notation

    We recall the bi-level formulation from Section 3.1. The VLA policy π_θ(a_t:t+Hₐ|o_≤t,ℓ) is parameterized by θ, and the video world model (WM) W_φ(oₜ₊₁|o_≤t,aₜ) is parameterized by φ. The reward model r_ψ is frozen throughout. Given the current (θ,φ), the inner one-step GRPO update on imagined trajectories generated by W_φ is

    θ⁺(φ)=θ+η_θg(φ,θ), g(φ,θ):=∇_θĴ_GRPO(π_θ;W_φ),

    		(12)

    where η_θ>0 is the inner learning rate and Ĵ_GRPO is the GRPO surrogate evaluated on rollouts from W_φ. The outer objective is the expected return of the updated policy in the target environment,

    J(π_θ⁺(φ))=\E_τ∼Pₑₙᵥ(π_θ⁺(φ))[∑ₜrₜ].

    		(13)

    DRILL-IMG optimizes φ by differentiating (13) through (12). DRILL-VWI instead uses a signed local coaching surrogate

    L_VWI(φ;w̄)=\E_(oₜ,aₜ,oₜ₊₁)∼μ_demo[w̄(oₜ,aₜ)∥ôₜ₊₁(φ)-oₜ₊₁∥₂²],

    		(14)

    where the unclipped signed coefficient is

    w(oₜ,aₜ)=d̃_φ^π_θ(oₜ) sgn (Â(oₜ,aₜ))|Â(oₜ,aₜ)|^αs(oₜ),

    		(15)

    and w̄ is the clipped, normalized, stop-gradient version used by the implemented DRILL-VWI objective. The core theoretical case sets α=1, s(oₜ)=1, uses exact imagined-rollout visitation, and removes clipping. We denote this idealized loss by L_VWIᶜᵒʳᵉ(φ).

    To avoid overloading notation, we distinguish the state-visitation marginal from the joint transition distributions. Let μᵣₒₗₗ denote the time-averaged local imagined-rollout transition distribution obtained by sampling a time index t uniformly from the H-step imagined rollout, then sampling oₜ∼d̃_φ^π_θ, aₜ∼π_θ(·|o_≤t), and oₜ₊₁∼W_φ(·|o_≤t,aₜ). Let μ_demo denote the raw demonstration transition distribution before applying VWI weights. In demo-side expectations, Â(oₜ,aₜ) denotes the stop-gradient advantage assigned to the demo transition by the same rollout-derived advantage-transfer rule used by the implemented VWI objective. The mismatch between the local rollout distribution and this raw demo-anchor distribution is kept as the explicit residual R_demo below.

item.title: 想改物体又想自由换视角：UniState 把空间记忆和编辑合成同一份世界状态表示 ｜ UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation
item.description:
一句话：「物体在动」和「相机在动」在控制信号里老是混在一起；把两者放进同一份世界状态表示，干预才变得可指定、可复用。

要点：

  • 在世界里做干预、并从任意视角观察结果一直很难，因为控制规格里缺少区分「物体运动」与「视点变化」的显式结构
  • UniState 用统一的世界状态表示把空间记忆与用户干预合一：用户在空间记忆里直接指定物体运动，相机轨迹独立选择
  • 指定干预不需要写清所有结果运动——视频模型可以自己合成可控物体内部的额外运动，以及物体与周围环境的合理交互
  • 基于预训练 Cosmos3-Nano 图生视频模型，两阶段课程：先在 DL3DV 上训 20K 步，再在 HM-World 上训 10K 步；输出 81 帧、832×480、16 fps

为什么值得看：这类「记忆 + 编辑」的统一表示，是交互式世界模型能不能被当成关卡编辑器用的分水岭：能指定干预、还能换视角验收，才谈得上迭代内容。

中文摘要：世界模型提供了越来越丰富的可探索环境，但在世界里实施干预、并从自由选择的视角观察后果仍然很难。作者提出 UniState：一个基于统一世界状态表示的可控世界模拟框架，该表示把空间记忆与用户干预合为一体——用户在空间记忆里直接指定物体运动，同时独立选择观察该世界状态的相机轨迹。这种统一让「场景」与「请求的改动」之间的关系变得明确，从而消除控制规格里物体运动与视点变化之间的歧义。关键在于指定干预并不需要把每个结果运动都写清，视频模型可以自己合成可控物体内部的额外运动，以及与周围环境的合理交互。作者还给出训练与采样策略，让生成视频既遵循指定的物体运动与相机轨迹，又保持场景一致，并用预训练的图生视频模型做两阶段课程训练。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-26

UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation

Abstract

World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.

1 Introduction

World simulation models have been built from video models for their increasing performance of producing high-fidelity future predictions given an initial frame and a description of the events occurring in the scene [(Team Wan and others, 2025; NVIDIA, 2026)]. They can be used as explorable environments for training agents, especially with camera controls [(Wang et al., 2025a; Xing et al., 2025)] and object controls [(Wang et al., 2024a; Geng et al., 2025)].

However, using world models for learning agents is limited to viewpoint exploration [(Bar et al., 2025)] even though recent world models cover complex real-world environments, and training agents with physical intervention to the world is limited to restricted configurations such as grippers with a fixed camera [(Du et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026)]. We attribute this gap to recent world models that cover navigation and omit physical intervention.

We suggest that physical intervention beyond navigation is a crucial component for training physical agents, as well as other important requirements including spatio-temporal coherence and free-viewpoint observation. Existing video models exploit persistent spatial memory to support spatio-temporal coherence [(Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026)], camera control to support free-viewpoint observation [(He et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025b)], and dedicated conditions to support object motion [(Wu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)]. However, supporting physical intervention in a persistent world with free-viewpoint observation remains challenging.

We introduce UniState, capable of above three requirements. Briefly, it contains initial spatial memory and user intervention in the same world coordinate system in order to work as a spatio-temporal twin of the world and allow the viewpoint to be separately specified. It removes the ambiguity that the same trajectories can be achieved by either object motion or viewpoint control in previous methods. The initial spatial memory is the latents lifted into 3D from an initial image [(Yu et al., 2026)]. Then users specify motion of a region with a sequence of 6-DoF transformations, enabling 3D object translation and rotation, as illustrated in Fig.1. Finally, a camera trajectory determines the viewpoints from which UniState is rendered. Last but not least, we introduce sampling and training techniques to reflect all the above variables.

This unified state guides video generation while preserving the model’s capacity to synthesize plausible responses to the specified interventions. For example, an intervention in the surrounding environment can lead the model to generate an agent’s evasive maneuver, such as taking a detour to avoid an approaching vehicle (Fig.1(a)). Controlling a bulldozer can similarly induce motion in nearby objects through contact, without explicitly prescribing their trajectories (Fig.1(b)). This flexibility also extends to motion within the controlled object: specifying only the translation of a cat’s torso allows the model to generate the accompanying leg movements for walking (Fig.1(f)).

To guarantee that the video model to faithfully translate the unified representation into observations from the specified viewpoint, we design both sampling and training strategies for coherent joint object and camera control. Our sampling strategy promotes consistent generation from the specified viewpoint during object interventions, while our training strategy reduces the mismatch between training and inference conditions, helping the video model follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while retaining its capacity to generate plausible responses.

Experiments show that UniState achieves more accurate joint object and camera control than the evaluated baselines. Qualitative results demonstrate manipulation of whole objects and selected parts with consistent depth ordering and occlusion, alongside motion and interactions beyond the prescribed transformations. Ablation studies support the benefits of the proposed training and sampling strategies for control accuracy.

Our key contributions are:

  • •

    With UniState, we show that unifying spatial memory and user interventions in a unified world-state representation allows object motion and camera trajectory to be specified independently.

  • •

    We show that using the initial state as a reference during sampling and reducing the mismatch between training and inference conditions improve joint object and camera control.

    • 2 Related work

    Video world models as interactive simulators.

    Video world models simulate the consequences of actions for planning and policy learning, using generated videos as plans for control [(Du et al., 2023)] or as interactive environments for policy training [(Yang et al., 2024)]. Action-conditioned video models further leverage pretrained video priors or learn from latent actions and recorded controls for interactive simulation [(Rigter et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Bruce et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; He et al., 2026)]. Recent methods extend exploration across diverse scenes, using context management and accelerated generation to sustain interaction [(Mao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026; Ball et al., 2025)]. Complementary approaches use predicted observations for navigation planning [(Bar et al., 2025)], incorporate geometric prediction [(Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025)], or ground exploration in geographically indexed street views [(Seo et al., 2026)]. Instruction-driven behaviors and object-directed actions further broaden interaction beyond navigation [(Tang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026)]. UniState extends world exploration with time-varying 6-DoF interventions on selected object regions with the unified representation and world coordinate system as persistent memory, while allowing the camera trajectory to be specified independently.

    Object control and camera control.

    Methods for controlling motion in video generation specify motion through point trajectories [(Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Geng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)] or bounding boxes [(Wang et al., 2024a)]; joint object and camera control further requires coordinating these motion signals with viewpoint conditions [(Wang et al., 2024b; Xing et al., 2025)], often using depth, pose, or 3D guidance [(Wang et al., 2025b; Ji et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026)]. Since viewpoint change and object motion both induce image-space displacement, recent methods disentangle them through cross-view transfer [(Liu et al., 2026)] or dynamic reprojection of world-anchored trajectories [(Gu et al., 2026)]. Methods using explicit 3D representations condition video generation on Gaussians expressed in a shared coordinate frame [(Zheng et al., 2026)] or editable foreground caches [(Wu et al., 2026)], while appearance-aware methods transport latent features along point tracks [(Chu et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026)]. As summarized in Table1, the compared methods encode spatial memory and user intervention in separate representations. This separation leaves generation susceptible to background drift and ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change. UniState grounds both in a shared appearance-bearing 3D representation and world coordinate system, making their spatial relationship explicit.

    Persistent and editable spatial memory.

    While camera conditioning controls the viewpoint [(He et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025b)], scene consistency can be maintained by retrieving spatially relevant observations [(Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026)] or compressing historical context [(Zhang et al., 2025a; Oshima et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2025)]. Retrieval and compression retain scene evidence but do not themselves define geometric operations on entities. Geometry-based approaches render, warp, or retrieve scene information using explicit spatial memories [(Ren et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c; Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b)], with some excluding dynamic objects from persistent memory [(Wang et al., 2026c)]. Other memory-based approaches maintain out-of-view dynamics [(Chen et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026)] or combine coordinated 3D object and camera trajectories with persistent dynamic object memory [(Wang et al., 2026a)]. Spatial patch memories further support relocation, duplication, and deletion, but focus on scene composition rather than prescribed instance-level motion over time [(Yu et al., 2026)]. Explicit spatial representations also support editing through evolving voxel states, but validation of this approach remains limited to game environments [(Garcin et al., 2026)]. UniState applies time-varying 6-DoF transformations to whole or partial object regions within shared 3D spatial memory, while the video prior synthesizes dynamics beyond the prescribed rigid motion.

    3 Method

    UniState generates a video from an initial frame, user-specified interventions, and a camera trajectory. We lift initial-frame latent features into 3D to construct spatial memory, then express user interventions by transforming the geometry of selected regions within this memory. The transformed entities and unchanged scene context thus remain in a single set of 3D latents, which we call a unified world-state representation. Rendering this state along an independently specified camera trajectory provides the conditions for video generation. Fig.2 summarizes the inference and training pipelines.

    We first describe how UniState constructs, manipulates, and renders this unified state (Section3.1). We then introduce Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance (Section3.2) and a training strategy (Section3.3) that help the video model follow the resulting conditions.

    3.1 Unified World-State Representation

    Constructing spatial memory.

    We encode the initial image into VAE latent features and lift them into 3D using the source camera and estimated depth [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. Each resulting 3D latent pair has geometry with its source feature; together, these latents form the initial state S₀. Additional views of the same initial scene can extend S₀ by lifting and registering their latent features in the same world coordinate system. Geometric construction details are provided in Appendix A.1.

    Expressing interventions within the state.

    Source-view segmentation masks, provided by the user or obtained with SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)], identify the latent index set Iₖ for each entity k, which may be a whole object or a selected part. For each entity, the user specifies rigid111 Part-wise rigid transformations can approximate non-rigid motion. transformations {G_t,k∈SE(3)}ₜ₌₁ᵀ in the shared world coordinate system over T subsequent frames. Let X_0,i denote the geometry of the i-th 3D latent in the initial state S₀. At each time t, its geometry is

    X_t,i=\begincasesG_t,kX_0,i,&i∈Iₖ, X_0,i,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(1)

    We construct each intervened state Sₜ directly from S₀ using these transformed geometries, while preserving source latent features and leaving unselected regions unchanged.

    Rendering the state along the camera trajectory.

    Given an independently specified camera trajectory C={Cₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, a visibility-aware renderer ℝ projects the intervened state into each camera view: (Wₜ,Mₜ)=ℝ(Sₜ;Cₜ). Here, Wₜ contains the projected source latent features, and Mₜ marks the visible regions of selected entities. Visibility is resolved against the complete scene; rendering details are provided in Appendix A.1.

    The UniState adapter and intervention-mask adapter independently project the patchified latent condition W={Wₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ and intervention masks M={Mₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ into the video-token dimension. Their outputs are added to the input video tokens once, before the transformer blocks. The camera-conditioning module instead operates in every transformer block: a parallel attention branch uses the relative-ray camera representation and adds its output to the backbone self-attention output. These conditions guide generation while the video model synthesizes the remaining scene content and motion.

    Interaction and state updates.

    User interventions specify the motion of the controlled entity, while the video model synthesizes plausible responses in the surrounding scene. Conditioning scene regions involved in an interaction on their previous configuration can constrain these responses. We therefore temporarily exclude these regions from the memory condition while retaining the prescribed control over the entity. This allows nearby objects to move in response to contact without explicitly prescribing their trajectories.

    After the interaction, we obtain updated geometry and latent features for the affected regions from generated observations, register the geometry to the shared world coordinate system, and update the corresponding state regions. The updated state serves as S₀ for the next rollout, allowing subsequent viewpoint changes and interventions to build on the resulting scene configuration.

    3.2 Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance

    Our conditional video model f_θ is trained with a flow-matching objective and predicts latent velocities during sampling.

    Although the unified state specifies interventions independently of camera viewpoint, the generated video may still entangle their effects, causing background motion to deviate from the prescribed camera trajectory. Our key observation is that this ambiguity can be removed by constructing a camera-only reference: if we render the initial state S₀ under the same camera trajectory but without applying any intervention, the resulting condition should contain scene changes induced by viewpoint change alone. We therefore use the velocity conditioned on the intervention for the intervened region and use the velocity conditioned on the initial state for the background. We spatially route between these two predictions and blend the result with the full joint prediction. We call this procedure Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance (SAJG).

    Scene-anchor and joint predictions.

    Using the same camera trajectory, we render the initial state S₀ without interventions to obtain the scene-anchor condition Wₛ, and the intervened states {Sₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ to obtain the joint condition Wⱼ, corresponding to W in Section3.1.

    Using the same noisy video latent, denoising timestep, camera condition, source observation, and text prompt, we evaluate f_θ under the scene-anchor and joint conditions to obtain the respective velocity predictions Vₛ and Vⱼ. Both predictions use classifier-free guidance; implementation details are provided in Appendix A.2.

    Spatial routing.

    The scene-anchor prediction provides a reference for camera-induced changes in the surrounding scene, while the joint prediction incorporates the requested interventions. We therefore use the joint prediction in regions affected by these transformations, including the entities’ target locations and the regions they vacate. A soft scene mask Gₛ excludes these projected source and target regions, combining the predictions as

    V_routed=Gₛ⊙Vₛ+(1-Gₛ)⊙Vⱼ,

    		(2)

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. Mask construction details are provided in Appendix A.2.

    Joint prediction anchoring.

    To retain the joint prediction’s contribution throughout the video, including scene regions assigned to the scene-anchor prediction, we blend the spatially routed prediction with the full joint prediction:

    V_final=αVⱼ+(1-α)V_routed, α∈[0,1].

    		(3)

    Here, α controls the weight of the full joint prediction in the final blend, ensuring a minimum joint contribution of α at every spatio-temporal location. Setting α=0 uses the spatially routed prediction alone, whereas α=1 uses only the joint prediction. We use α=0.25 unless stated otherwise. At each denoising step, V_final is passed to the flow-matching solver.

    3.3 Training

    Training conditions.

    We train on videos paired with camera conditions C, latent conditions W, and intervention masks M derived from per-frame object masks. We construct W by combining initial-state renders with ground-truth entity latents. The latter preserve alignment with the target video, avoiding misalignment and floating artifacts caused by transporting source features with imperfect geometry (see Fig.10 in the appendix).

    We render the initial state from each target camera and zero out the selected entities’ projected source regions. We then insert ground-truth entity latents at their target locations, retaining the initial-state render elsewhere. Vacated source regions remain zero unless covered by a target entity. The exact compositing formulation is provided in Appendix A.3.

    Transport-Aligned Augmentation.

    The composited conditions introduce a training–inference mismatch: training uses entity latents from each ground-truth target frame, whereas inference transports source latents through the transformed geometry. To reduce this mismatch, we apply Transport-Aligned Augmentation (TAA), which spatially coarsens future-frame entity latents while preserving their target support. TAA modifies only the latent condition; the intervention masks and ground-truth training targets remain unchanged. The augmentation procedure is detailed in Appendix A.3.

    Curriculum training.

    We train UniState in two stages using a flow-matching objective L_FM, keeping the pretrained video backbone, VAE, and text encoder frozen. [(Ling et al., 2024)]. The first stage trains the camera-conditioning module and UniState adapter on DL3DV [(Ling et al., 2024)].

    Starting from these weights, the second stage adds the intervention-mask adapter and jointly trains all three modules on HM-World[(Chen et al., 2026)] using the composited conditions and TAA described above.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation details

    We use a pretrained Cosmos3-Nano I2V model [(NVIDIA, 2026)] and follow the two-stage curriculum in Section3.3, with 20K optimization steps on DL3DV followed by 10K on HM-World. We generate 81-frame videos at 832×480 resolution and 16 fps. Optimization settings and caption construction are detailed in Appendix A.3.

    4.2 Evaluation

    We evaluate all methods on the same 277 scenarios spanning diverse camera trajectories and user interventions. Each method generates two videos per scenario with independent random seeds (554 videos total), using an identical evaluation protocol and averaging metrics across the two seeds.

    Joint control accuracy

    We introduce World-Control Projection Error (WCPE) to evaluate object control specified in world coordinates. Because video models produce 2D observations, an object’s screen-space position alone does not establish whether it follows the specified motion in the world. We therefore assess object motion relative to the surrounding scene, while checking that the scene remains aligned with the specified camera trajectory. WCPE implements this assessment as a 2D proxy, using target projections to evaluate object–background relative positions and background alignment. Requiring both prevents correct screen-space object placement alone from yielding a low error when the surrounding scene is misaligned. The metric formulation and evaluation protocol are detailed in SectionA.4.

    Camera-control accuracy

    We evaluate camera-control accuracy by comparing the camera trajectory recovered from each generated video with its target trajectory. We report Cam-T, the mean translation error between the recovered and target camera positions, and Cam-R, the mean geodesic rotation error between their orientations, measured in degrees. Lower values for both metrics indicate more faithful camera control.

    4.3 Qualitative Results

    Diverse control through user interventions.

    Fig.1(c) and (d) demonstrate depth-axis control and occlusion handling consistent with scene geometry. Interventions can also target selected object parts: in Fig.1(e), the user rotates the excavator’s upper structure independently of its tracks, specifying the rotation direction and angular speed. For non-rigid objects, partial control allows the video model to complete unspecified articulation. In Fig.1(f), the user specifies only the cat’s torso trajectory, while the model generates accompanying limb motion and maintains a coherent body configuration. Fig.1(g) and (h) further demonstrate camera-controlled world exploration and simultaneous control of multiple objects, respectively.

    State persistence and control across rollouts.

    In Fig.3, the controlled bulldozer displaces a passive rock. After the resulting state is incorporated into memory, the camera moves away until the affected region is out of view, then returns. The rock retains its displaced position upon revisitation, providing qualitative evidence of state persistence across rollouts. Fig.3(b) demonstrates continued control of the same world across three successive rollouts. The user first moves the excavator with the camera fixed, then changes the viewpoint while preserving the excavator’s updated world-space pose, and finally controls both the object and camera. Each rollout continues from the preceding state, allowing the user to manipulate an entity, observe the resulting configuration from another viewpoint, and intervene again. This separates control of the entity’s world state from control of the observation viewpoint.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance.

    Fig.4 shows that intermediate values of α outperform both spatial routing alone (α=0) and the joint prediction alone (α=1). We select α=0.25, which achieves the lowest WCPE and Cam-R and nearly the lowest Cam-T. These results support combining a scene-anchor correction with a global joint contribution.

    Transport-Aligned Augmentation.

    We compare three ways of constructing entity latent conditions during training: transporting initial-frame latents using estimated geometry, using aligned ground-truth entity latents from each target frame, and applying TAA to those ground-truth latents.

    All variants share training data, initialization, optimization budgets, inference conditions, and SAJG settings. As shown in Table2, replacing transported initial-frame latents with ground-truth latents reduces WCPE and Cam-T, but slightly increases Cam-R. Applying TAA further reduces all three errors, supporting the combination of spatially aligned training conditions and augmentation that reduces their latent mismatch with inference-time transport.

    Curriculum training.

    Staged training outperforms interleaved training under matched data exposure and computation; details are provided in Appendix B.1.

    4.5 Comparisons

    We compare our method with VerseCrafter [(Zheng et al., 2026)], WorldDirector [(Wang et al., 2026a)], MotionCanvas [(Xing et al., 2025)], SymphoMotion [(Zhang et al., 2026)], and Real2SAM2Real [(Wu et al., 2026)]. We evaluate joint object and camera control using WCPE, Cam-T, and Cam-R. As shown in Table3, our method achieves the lowest WCPE, Cam-T, and Cam-R, demonstrating accurate joint control of object motion and camera viewpoint. Qualitative comparisons in Fig.5 further show these failure modes. In this example, the user keeps the camera static while translating and rotating the ball laterally behind the alphabet blocks. VerseCrafter and Real2SAM2Real often absorb object motion into viewpoint change, resulting in undesired viewpoint change despite the specified static camera condition. This makes the ball appear to move with the camera rather than independently in the scene. WorldDirector and MotionCanvas preserve the static camera more reliably, but fail to reproduce the correct depth ordering and rotation of the ball. In contrast, our method faithfully follows the intended joint object and camera control, capturing object translation and rotation under a static camera while handling occlusion. See AppendixC for additional qualitative comparisons. An additional comparison with MosaicMem is provided in Table7.

    5 Conclusion

    UniState unifies spatial memory and user interventions in a shared world coordinate system for controllable world simulation. This unified world-state representation allows object motion and camera trajectory to be specified independently. It provides spatial constraints for video generation while preserving the video model’s capacity to synthesize plausible responses, so users can specify intended changes without prescribing every resulting motion or interaction. Quantitative comparisons and ablations support our training and sampling strategies for joint object and camera control across diverse camera trajectories and user interventions. Revisitation results further show that generated interaction outcomes can be incorporated into spatial memory and retained across rollouts. Together, these findings support physical intervention in a persistent world with free-viewpoint observation.

    Limitations

    Interaction effects rely on the video model’s generative prior: although controlled object states can be updated outside the camera view, their interactions with surrounding objects cannot be explicitly simulated while out of view. Spatial resolution limits control over small objects, while temporal resolution limits fast motion. The model may also fail to follow physically implausible interventions, such as moving a solid object through a solid wall.

    Acknowledgements

    This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (RS-2026-25497603: Fundamentals of Online 4D Reconstruction with Semantic Viewpoint Control and Generative Priors for Proactive Content Consumption); the IITP grant [RS-2020-II201361, Artificial Intelligence Graduate School Program (Yonsei University)] funded by the Korean government (MSIT); and the “Advanced GPU Utilization Support Program” funded by the Government of the Republic of Korea (Ministry of Science and ICT).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation details

    A.1 UniState Construction

    Geometry and feature alignment.

    Given an initial image I₀ and its camera C₀, we obtain latents z₀=𝔼(I₀) using a VAE encoder and estimate depth D₀ using an off-the-shelf estimator [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. Using D₀ and C₀, we associate each feature z_0,i with 3D geometry X_0,i in the world coordinate system defined by C₀. These geometry–feature pairs form the initial state S₀={ℙ_0,i}ᵢ₌₁^N, where ℙ_0,i=(X_0,i,z_0,i) denotes a 3D latent. Additional views of the same initial scene can extend S₀ by lifting and registering their latent features into this coordinate system.

    Let {Ωᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N denote the initial image patches. We construct the geometric support of patch i as

    X_0,i=Π⁻¹_C₀(Ωᵢ,D₀[Ωᵢ]),

    where Π⁻¹_C₀ denotes unprojection through the source camera. The implementation approximates the resulting local geometry with an oriented planar primitive. Its appearance grid is sampled from the aligned latent coordinates Uᵢ.

    Intervention.

    Entity geometry is transformed according to Eq.1. At each time t, we construct Sₜ={ℙ_t,i}ᵢ₌₁^N directly from S₀, where ℙ_t,i=(X_t,i,z_0,i). Thus, each transformed geometry remains paired with its source latent feature.

    Patch selection.

    Given an entity mask Sₖ, patch i is assigned to entity k when

    (|Ωᵢ∩Sₖ|)/(|Ωᵢ|)>τ_seg.

    We store a control indicator αᵢ=1[i∈\bigcupₖIₖ] separately from the transform. This indicator remains active when the selected entity holds a constant pose.

    Back-face rejection.

    Let n_i,t and x̄_t,i denote the transformed surface normal and patch center. Given target camera center oₜ, patch i is rendered when

    ⟨n_i,t,oₜ-x̄_t,i⟩>0.

    Patches at an angle of 90^∘ or greater relative to the front-facing viewing direction are rejected.

    Intervention support.

    We first rasterize every selected and front-facing patch:

    M̃ₜ=ℝₛᵤₚₚₒᵣₜ({X_t,i}_αᵢ=1;Cₜ).

    A scene-level depth test then produces

    Mₜ=Vis(M̃ₜ;{X_t,i}ᵢ₌₁^N,Cₜ).

    Thus, patches occluded by other scene geometry are absent from Mₜ.

    Adapter injection.

    The latent and intervention-mask conditions are injected at the transformer input, whereas camera conditioning is applied within each transformer block.

    For the input conditions, let h_V,base⁽⁰⁾ denote the backbone’s video-token embeddings after the input projection and timestep embedding, before adding the W and M conditions. We form the conditioned input tokens as

    h_V⁽⁰⁾=h_V,base⁽⁰⁾+P_W (patch(W))+P_M (patch(M)).

    Here, patch arranges each condition into patches aligned with the backbone’s video-token grid. P_W and P_M are separate trainable linear projections without bias, mapping 192-dimensional latent patches and 4-dimensional binary mask patches, respectively, to the 4096-dimensional video-token space. Each mask patch corresponds to a 2×2 spatial region. These residuals are added once before the transformer blocks; the M term is omitted during the first training stage.

    For camera conditioning, each transformer block contains a trainable attention branch parallel to the backbone self-attention. This branch computes queries, keys, and values from the normalized video tokens and applies PRoPE using the relative-ray representation derived from the camera poses and intrinsics. Let a_V,base^(ℓ) denote the backbone self-attention output for the video tokens at block ℓ. The camera-conditioned attention output is

    a_V^(ℓ)=a_V,base^(ℓ)+A_cam^(ℓ) (LN(h_V^(ℓ)),C),

    where A_cam^(ℓ) denotes the parallel camera-aware attention branch. We apply this branch in all 36 transformer blocks with a residual scale of 1. The backbone remains frozen, while the camera branches and the input-condition projections are trained according to the two-stage curriculum.

    Initialization from multiple observations.

    Although a single frame is sufficient to initialize the initial state, patches from additional observations can be lifted into the same world coordinate system to extend its spatial coverage. The long sequence in Fig.3(b) uses an initial state initialized from multiple observations and spans three successive rollouts with object control and camera control.

    A.2 SAJG Construction

    Condition rendering.

    For each target camera Cₜ, the scene-anchor condition renders the initial state without interventions:

    (W_s,t,_)=ℝ(S₀;Cₜ).

    		(4)

    The joint condition renders the intervened state:

    (W_j,t,Mₜ)=ℝ(Sₜ;Cₜ).

    		(5)

    Both conditions use the complete scene for depth testing. The joint branch receives the intervention-mask condition, while the scene-anchor branch omits it.

    Scene-mask construction.

    We construct Gₛ in latent-video coordinates. For each target camera, we project the selected entities at their source and target poses to obtain the binary support volumes E_src and E_tgt. The scene mask is

    Gₛ=F_1,1[1-D₁(E_src∪E_tgt)],

    		(6)

    where D₁ applies one-cell spatial dilation and F_1,1 applies one-cell spatial and temporal feathering. The resulting values lie in [0,1], and the mask is broadcast across latent channels. Unlike the intervention mask M, which marks the visible target entity regions, Gₛ selects scene regions away from both source and target entity supports, with soft transitions at their boundaries.

    The mask is geometry-derived rather than learned. It may vary across video frames, but is computed only once for each input and remains unchanged across denoising steps. All dilation and feathering settings are fixed; only α is varied in the routing ablation.

    Equivalent correction form.

    Substituting Eq.2 into Eq.3 gives

    V_final=Vⱼ+(1-α)Gₛ⊙(Vₛ-Vⱼ)(7)
    =wₛ⊙Vₛ+wⱼ⊙Vⱼ,

    where

    wₛ=(1-α)Gₛ, wⱼ=1-(1-α)Gₛ.

    		(8)

    Thus, wₛ+wⱼ=1 and wⱼ≥α at every spatio-temporal location. The equivalent correction form shows that the scene-anchor prediction modifies the joint prediction only where the scene mask permits. At the default α=0.25, the effective weights are wₛ=0.75Gₛ and wⱼ=1-0.75Gₛ. Setting α=0 applies the maximum scene correction permitted by the mask, while α=1 removes the correction.

    Classifier-free guidance and evaluation cost.

    Given the same noisy latent x_τ at flow-matching time τ and camera condition C, the conditional video model f_θ produces velocity predictions with classifier-free guidance (CFG):

    Vₛ=CFG[f_θ(x_τ,τ;C,Wₛ)],Vⱼ=CFG[f_θ(x_τ,τ;C,Wⱼ)].

    		(9)

    Both predictions share the source observation and text prompt; these and the intervention-mask input are omitted from the notation.

    The main-paper equations use predictions after classifier-free guidance. In implementation, we apply the same spatial weights wₛ and wⱼ separately to the conditional and null-text predictions, and then apply classifier-free guidance to the two mixed predictions. With the same guidance scale for both branches, this is algebraically equivalent to mixing the guided predictions because both operations are linear. The exact computation uses a separate null-text prediction for each branch and requires four transformer evaluations per denoising step.

    We additionally tested an approximation that reuses a single null-text prediction for both branches while retaining their separate conditional predictions. Although the two branch-specific null-text predictions are not necessarily identical, we observed no noticeable differences in the generated results under this approximation in the tested settings. Reusing one null-text prediction reduces the computation to three transformer evaluations per denoising step.

    A.3 Training

    Training settings and captions.

    Both stages use AdamW with a global batch size of 8 and a base learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴. We generate training-video captions using Qwen2.5-VL [(Bai et al., 2025)]. The captions describe scene content while omitting motion and object-location descriptions (e.g., “A is to the left of B”).

    Optimization.

    Both stages use the flow-matching objective

    L_FM=𝔼_x,τ[∥f_θ(x_τ,τ;C,W,M)-V_τᵍᵗ∥₂²],

    		(10)

    with the M condition omitted in the first stage. The first stage trains the C and W conditioning modules on DL3DV for 20K steps. The second stage initializes these modules from the first-stage checkpoint, adds the M module, and jointly trains all three conditioning paths on HM-World for 10K steps. The video backbone, VAE, and text encoder remain frozen.

    Training condition construction.

    We render S₀ from the target camera Cₜ and zero out the selected entities’ projected source regions, obtaining Wₜˢʳᶜ. Let zₜᵉ denote the ground-truth entity latent aligned with the target latent grid, and Bₜ its binary spatial support. We form the training condition as

    Wₜᵗʳᵃⁱⁿ=(1-Bₜ)⊙Wₜˢʳᶜ+Bₜ⊙zₜᵉ,

    		(11)

    with Bₜ broadcast across latent channels. This retains source-scene appearance outside the target entities, while vacated source regions remain zero unless covered by a target entity.

    Conditioning augmentation.

    For a latent grid of size H×W, D_NN reduces the spatial resolution to round(ρH)×round(ρW) using nearest-neighbor sampling. U_NN restores the original resolution using nearest-neighbor upsampling. Given the ground-truth entity latents zₜᵉ and their binary spatial support Bₜ, we define

    z̃ₜᵉ=\begincasesz₀ᵉ,&t=0, (1-Bₜ)⊙zₜᵉ+Bₜ⊙U_NN(D_NN(zₜᵉ)),&t>0.\endcases

    		(12)

    As defined in Eq.12, the resampled values replace the conditioning appearance only within the future-frame entity support Bₜ. The support mask itself is not resampled. The augmented entity latents are then composited with the initial-state renders using Eq.11. Neither the intervention mask M nor the ground-truth training target is modified.

    A.4 WCPE Evaluation

    Motivation and target projections.

    An object’s image-space position alone does not establish whether the prescribed world-space control is realized relative to the scene. WCPE therefore evaluates object–background relative positions together with background alignment. Target trajectories are constructed from the input scene proxy: object points follow the prescribed object transformations, while background points remain fixed in world coordinates. Both are projected using the target camera trajectory. These targets are shared across methods for each evaluation condition.

    Metric formulation.

    We track object queries and background anchors in the generated videos using CoTracker3 [(Karaev et al., 2025)]. For an object query at a given frame, let p̂ and p^* denote its tracked image position and target projection. Similarly, b̂ⱼ and bⱼ^* denote the tracked and target positions of background anchor j. Using the same valid anchor set V, we define

    eᵣₑₗ=median_j∈V(\lVert(p̂-b̂ⱼ)-(p^*-bⱼ^*)\rVert₂)/(D),

    		(13)

    e_bg=median_j∈V(\lVertb̂ⱼ-bⱼ^*\rVert₂)/(D),

    		(14)

    where D=√W²+H² is the image diagonal. The joint error is

    eⱼₒᵢₙₜ=\max(eᵣₑₗ,e_bg).

    		(15)

    A low joint error requires both accurate object–background relative positions and accurate background alignment with the target projection.

    Failure handling and aggregation.

    We report WCPE@5 with an error cap and missing-measurement penalty of τ=0.05, corresponding to 5% of the image diagonal:

    e_score=\begincases\min(eⱼₒᵢₙₜ,τ),&if the measurement is valid, τ,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(16)
