一句话：「物体在动」和「相机在动」在控制信号里老是混在一起；把两者放进同一份世界状态表示，干预才变得可指定、可复用。

要点：

  • 在世界里做干预、并从任意视角观察结果一直很难，因为控制规格里缺少区分「物体运动」与「视点变化」的显式结构
  • UniState 用统一的世界状态表示把空间记忆与用户干预合一：用户在空间记忆里直接指定物体运动，相机轨迹独立选择
  • 指定干预不需要写清所有结果运动——视频模型可以自己合成可控物体内部的额外运动，以及物体与周围环境的合理交互
  • 基于预训练 Cosmos3-Nano 图生视频模型，两阶段课程：先在 DL3DV 上训 20K 步，再在 HM-World 上训 10K 步；输出 81 帧、832×480、16 fps

为什么值得看：这类「记忆 + 编辑」的统一表示，是交互式世界模型能不能被当成关卡编辑器用的分水岭：能指定干预、还能换视角验收，才谈得上迭代内容。

中文摘要：世界模型提供了越来越丰富的可探索环境，但在世界里实施干预、并从自由选择的视角观察后果仍然很难。作者提出 UniState：一个基于统一世界状态表示的可控世界模拟框架，该表示把空间记忆与用户干预合为一体——用户在空间记忆里直接指定物体运动，同时独立选择观察该世界状态的相机轨迹。这种统一让「场景」与「请求的改动」之间的关系变得明确，从而消除控制规格里物体运动与视点变化之间的歧义。关键在于指定干预并不需要把每个结果运动都写清，视频模型可以自己合成可控物体内部的额外运动，以及与周围环境的合理交互。作者还给出训练与采样策略，让生成视频既遵循指定的物体运动与相机轨迹，又保持场景一致，并用预训练的图生视频模型做两阶段课程训练。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-18

本期推送：2026-10-26

UniState: Unifying Memory and Intervention for Controllable World Simulation

Abstract

World models offer increasingly rich environments for exploration, yet intervening in a world while observing the consequences from freely chosen viewpoints remains challenging. We tackle these challenges by introducing UniState, a framework for controllable world simulation built on a unified world-state representation. This representation unifies spatial memory and user interventions. Users specify object motion directly within spatial memory, while independently choosing the camera trajectory from which the resulting world state is observed. This unification makes the relationship between the scene and the requested changes explicit, removing ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change from the control specification. Crucially, specifying an intervention does not require prescribing every resulting movement: the video model can synthesize additional motion within controlled objects and plausible interactions with their surroundings. We develop training and sampling strategies that help generated videos follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while preserving this capacity to generate responses beyond the prescribed transformations. Experiments demonstrate more accurate joint object and camera control than the existing methods, alongside qualitative evidence that intervention-induced scene changes persist across rollouts.

1 Introduction

World simulation models have been built from video models for their increasing performance of producing high-fidelity future predictions given an initial frame and a description of the events occurring in the scene [(Team Wan and others, 2025; NVIDIA, 2026)]. They can be used as explorable environments for training agents, especially with camera controls [(Wang et al., 2025a; Xing et al., 2025)] and object controls [(Wang et al., 2024a; Geng et al., 2025)].

However, using world models for learning agents is limited to viewpoint exploration [(Bar et al., 2025)] even though recent world models cover complex real-world environments, and training agents with physical intervention to the world is limited to restricted configurations such as grippers with a fixed camera [(Du et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026)]. We attribute this gap to recent world models that cover navigation and omit physical intervention.

We suggest that physical intervention beyond navigation is a crucial component for training physical agents, as well as other important requirements including spatio-temporal coherence and free-viewpoint observation. Existing video models exploit persistent spatial memory to support spatio-temporal coherence [(Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026)], camera control to support free-viewpoint observation [(He et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025b)], and dedicated conditions to support object motion [(Wu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)]. However, supporting physical intervention in a persistent world with free-viewpoint observation remains challenging.

We introduce UniState, capable of above three requirements. Briefly, it contains initial spatial memory and user intervention in the same world coordinate system in order to work as a spatio-temporal twin of the world and allow the viewpoint to be separately specified. It removes the ambiguity that the same trajectories can be achieved by either object motion or viewpoint control in previous methods. The initial spatial memory is the latents lifted into 3D from an initial image [(Yu et al., 2026)]. Then users specify motion of a region with a sequence of 6-DoF transformations, enabling 3D object translation and rotation, as illustrated in Fig.1. Finally, a camera trajectory determines the viewpoints from which UniState is rendered. Last but not least, we introduce sampling and training techniques to reflect all the above variables.

This unified state guides video generation while preserving the model’s capacity to synthesize plausible responses to the specified interventions. For example, an intervention in the surrounding environment can lead the model to generate an agent’s evasive maneuver, such as taking a detour to avoid an approaching vehicle (Fig.1(a)). Controlling a bulldozer can similarly induce motion in nearby objects through contact, without explicitly prescribing their trajectories (Fig.1(b)). This flexibility also extends to motion within the controlled object: specifying only the translation of a cat’s torso allows the model to generate the accompanying leg movements for walking (Fig.1(f)).

To guarantee that the video model to faithfully translate the unified representation into observations from the specified viewpoint, we design both sampling and training strategies for coherent joint object and camera control. Our sampling strategy promotes consistent generation from the specified viewpoint during object interventions, while our training strategy reduces the mismatch between training and inference conditions, helping the video model follow the specified object motion and camera trajectory while retaining its capacity to generate plausible responses.

Experiments show that UniState achieves more accurate joint object and camera control than the evaluated baselines. Qualitative results demonstrate manipulation of whole objects and selected parts with consistent depth ordering and occlusion, alongside motion and interactions beyond the prescribed transformations. Ablation studies support the benefits of the proposed training and sampling strategies for control accuracy.

Our key contributions are:

  • •

    With UniState, we show that unifying spatial memory and user interventions in a unified world-state representation allows object motion and camera trajectory to be specified independently.

  • •

    We show that using the initial state as a reference during sampling and reducing the mismatch between training and inference conditions improve joint object and camera control.

    • 2 Related work

    Video world models as interactive simulators.

    Video world models simulate the consequences of actions for planning and policy learning, using generated videos as plans for control [(Du et al., 2023)] or as interactive environments for policy training [(Yang et al., 2024)]. Action-conditioned video models further leverage pretrained video priors or learn from latent actions and recorded controls for interactive simulation [(Rigter et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Bruce et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025a; He et al., 2026)]. Recent methods extend exploration across diverse scenes, using context management and accelerated generation to sustain interaction [(Mao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Team et al., 2026; Ball et al., 2025)]. Complementary approaches use predicted observations for navigation planning [(Bar et al., 2025)], incorporate geometric prediction [(Zhu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025)], or ground exploration in geographically indexed street views [(Seo et al., 2026)]. Instruction-driven behaviors and object-directed actions further broaden interaction beyond navigation [(Tang et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026)]. UniState extends world exploration with time-varying 6-DoF interventions on selected object regions with the unified representation and world coordinate system as persistent memory, while allowing the camera trajectory to be specified independently.

    Object control and camera control.

    Methods for controlling motion in video generation specify motion through point trajectories [(Wu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Geng et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)] or bounding boxes [(Wang et al., 2024a)]; joint object and camera control further requires coordinating these motion signals with viewpoint conditions [(Wang et al., 2024b; Xing et al., 2025)], often using depth, pose, or 3D guidance [(Wang et al., 2025b; Ji et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026)]. Since viewpoint change and object motion both induce image-space displacement, recent methods disentangle them through cross-view transfer [(Liu et al., 2026)] or dynamic reprojection of world-anchored trajectories [(Gu et al., 2026)]. Methods using explicit 3D representations condition video generation on Gaussians expressed in a shared coordinate frame [(Zheng et al., 2026)] or editable foreground caches [(Wu et al., 2026)], while appearance-aware methods transport latent features along point tracks [(Chu et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026)]. As summarized in Table1, the compared methods encode spatial memory and user intervention in separate representations. This separation leaves generation susceptible to background drift and ambiguity between object motion and viewpoint change. UniState grounds both in a shared appearance-bearing 3D representation and world coordinate system, making their spatial relationship explicit.

    Persistent and editable spatial memory.

    While camera conditioning controls the viewpoint [(He et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025b)], scene consistency can be maintained by retrieving spatially relevant observations [(Xiao et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026)] or compressing historical context [(Zhang et al., 2025a; Oshima et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2025)]. Retrieval and compression retain scene evidence but do not themselves define geometric operations on entities. Geometry-based approaches render, warp, or retrieve scene information using explicit spatial memories [(Ren et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c; Zhao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b)], with some excluding dynamic objects from persistent memory [(Wang et al., 2026c)]. Other memory-based approaches maintain out-of-view dynamics [(Chen et al., 2026; Duan et al., 2026)] or combine coordinated 3D object and camera trajectories with persistent dynamic object memory [(Wang et al., 2026a)]. Spatial patch memories further support relocation, duplication, and deletion, but focus on scene composition rather than prescribed instance-level motion over time [(Yu et al., 2026)]. Explicit spatial representations also support editing through evolving voxel states, but validation of this approach remains limited to game environments [(Garcin et al., 2026)]. UniState applies time-varying 6-DoF transformations to whole or partial object regions within shared 3D spatial memory, while the video prior synthesizes dynamics beyond the prescribed rigid motion.

    3 Method

    UniState generates a video from an initial frame, user-specified interventions, and a camera trajectory. We lift initial-frame latent features into 3D to construct spatial memory, then express user interventions by transforming the geometry of selected regions within this memory. The transformed entities and unchanged scene context thus remain in a single set of 3D latents, which we call a unified world-state representation. Rendering this state along an independently specified camera trajectory provides the conditions for video generation. Fig.2 summarizes the inference and training pipelines.

    We first describe how UniState constructs, manipulates, and renders this unified state (Section3.1). We then introduce Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance (Section3.2) and a training strategy (Section3.3) that help the video model follow the resulting conditions.

    3.1 Unified World-State Representation

    Constructing spatial memory.

    We encode the initial image into VAE latent features and lift them into 3D using the source camera and estimated depth [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. Each resulting 3D latent pair has geometry with its source feature; together, these latents form the initial state S₀. Additional views of the same initial scene can extend S₀ by lifting and registering their latent features in the same world coordinate system. Geometric construction details are provided in Appendix A.1.

    Expressing interventions within the state.

    Source-view segmentation masks, provided by the user or obtained with SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)], identify the latent index set Iₖ for each entity k, which may be a whole object or a selected part. For each entity, the user specifies rigid111 Part-wise rigid transformations can approximate non-rigid motion. transformations {G_t,k∈SE(3)}ₜ₌₁ᵀ in the shared world coordinate system over T subsequent frames. Let X_0,i denote the geometry of the i-th 3D latent in the initial state S₀. At each time t, its geometry is

    X_t,i=\begincasesG_t,kX_0,i,&i∈Iₖ, X_0,i,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(1)

    We construct each intervened state Sₜ directly from S₀ using these transformed geometries, while preserving source latent features and leaving unselected regions unchanged.

    Rendering the state along the camera trajectory.

    Given an independently specified camera trajectory C={Cₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, a visibility-aware renderer ℝ projects the intervened state into each camera view: (Wₜ,Mₜ)=ℝ(Sₜ;Cₜ). Here, Wₜ contains the projected source latent features, and Mₜ marks the visible regions of selected entities. Visibility is resolved against the complete scene; rendering details are provided in Appendix A.1.

    The UniState adapter and intervention-mask adapter independently project the patchified latent condition W={Wₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ and intervention masks M={Mₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ into the video-token dimension. Their outputs are added to the input video tokens once, before the transformer blocks. The camera-conditioning module instead operates in every transformer block: a parallel attention branch uses the relative-ray camera representation and adds its output to the backbone self-attention output. These conditions guide generation while the video model synthesizes the remaining scene content and motion.

    Interaction and state updates.

    User interventions specify the motion of the controlled entity, while the video model synthesizes plausible responses in the surrounding scene. Conditioning scene regions involved in an interaction on their previous configuration can constrain these responses. We therefore temporarily exclude these regions from the memory condition while retaining the prescribed control over the entity. This allows nearby objects to move in response to contact without explicitly prescribing their trajectories.

    After the interaction, we obtain updated geometry and latent features for the affected regions from generated observations, register the geometry to the shared world coordinate system, and update the corresponding state regions. The updated state serves as S₀ for the next rollout, allowing subsequent viewpoint changes and interventions to build on the resulting scene configuration.

    3.2 Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance

    Our conditional video model f_θ is trained with a flow-matching objective and predicts latent velocities during sampling.

    Although the unified state specifies interventions independently of camera viewpoint, the generated video may still entangle their effects, causing background motion to deviate from the prescribed camera trajectory. Our key observation is that this ambiguity can be removed by constructing a camera-only reference: if we render the initial state S₀ under the same camera trajectory but without applying any intervention, the resulting condition should contain scene changes induced by viewpoint change alone. We therefore use the velocity conditioned on the intervention for the intervened region and use the velocity conditioned on the initial state for the background. We spatially route between these two predictions and blend the result with the full joint prediction. We call this procedure Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance (SAJG).

    Scene-anchor and joint predictions.

    Using the same camera trajectory, we render the initial state S₀ without interventions to obtain the scene-anchor condition Wₛ, and the intervened states {Sₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ to obtain the joint condition Wⱼ, corresponding to W in Section3.1.

    Using the same noisy video latent, denoising timestep, camera condition, source observation, and text prompt, we evaluate f_θ under the scene-anchor and joint conditions to obtain the respective velocity predictions Vₛ and Vⱼ. Both predictions use classifier-free guidance; implementation details are provided in Appendix A.2.

    Spatial routing.

    The scene-anchor prediction provides a reference for camera-induced changes in the surrounding scene, while the joint prediction incorporates the requested interventions. We therefore use the joint prediction in regions affected by these transformations, including the entities’ target locations and the regions they vacate. A soft scene mask Gₛ excludes these projected source and target regions, combining the predictions as

    V_routed=Gₛ⊙Vₛ+(1-Gₛ)⊙Vⱼ,

    		(2)

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. Mask construction details are provided in Appendix A.2.

    Joint prediction anchoring.

    To retain the joint prediction’s contribution throughout the video, including scene regions assigned to the scene-anchor prediction, we blend the spatially routed prediction with the full joint prediction:

    V_final=αVⱼ+(1-α)V_routed, α∈[0,1].

    		(3)

    Here, α controls the weight of the full joint prediction in the final blend, ensuring a minimum joint contribution of α at every spatio-temporal location. Setting α=0 uses the spatially routed prediction alone, whereas α=1 uses only the joint prediction. We use α=0.25 unless stated otherwise. At each denoising step, V_final is passed to the flow-matching solver.

    3.3 Training

    Training conditions.

    We train on videos paired with camera conditions C, latent conditions W, and intervention masks M derived from per-frame object masks. We construct W by combining initial-state renders with ground-truth entity latents. The latter preserve alignment with the target video, avoiding misalignment and floating artifacts caused by transporting source features with imperfect geometry (see Fig.10 in the appendix).

    We render the initial state from each target camera and zero out the selected entities’ projected source regions. We then insert ground-truth entity latents at their target locations, retaining the initial-state render elsewhere. Vacated source regions remain zero unless covered by a target entity. The exact compositing formulation is provided in Appendix A.3.

    Transport-Aligned Augmentation.

    The composited conditions introduce a training–inference mismatch: training uses entity latents from each ground-truth target frame, whereas inference transports source latents through the transformed geometry. To reduce this mismatch, we apply Transport-Aligned Augmentation (TAA), which spatially coarsens future-frame entity latents while preserving their target support. TAA modifies only the latent condition; the intervention masks and ground-truth training targets remain unchanged. The augmentation procedure is detailed in Appendix A.3.

    Curriculum training.

    We train UniState in two stages using a flow-matching objective L_FM, keeping the pretrained video backbone, VAE, and text encoder frozen. [(Ling et al., 2024)]. The first stage trains the camera-conditioning module and UniState adapter on DL3DV [(Ling et al., 2024)].

    Starting from these weights, the second stage adds the intervention-mask adapter and jointly trains all three modules on HM-World[(Chen et al., 2026)] using the composited conditions and TAA described above.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation details

    We use a pretrained Cosmos3-Nano I2V model [(NVIDIA, 2026)] and follow the two-stage curriculum in Section3.3, with 20K optimization steps on DL3DV followed by 10K on HM-World. We generate 81-frame videos at 832×480 resolution and 16 fps. Optimization settings and caption construction are detailed in Appendix A.3.

    4.2 Evaluation

    We evaluate all methods on the same 277 scenarios spanning diverse camera trajectories and user interventions. Each method generates two videos per scenario with independent random seeds (554 videos total), using an identical evaluation protocol and averaging metrics across the two seeds.

    Joint control accuracy

    We introduce World-Control Projection Error (WCPE) to evaluate object control specified in world coordinates. Because video models produce 2D observations, an object’s screen-space position alone does not establish whether it follows the specified motion in the world. We therefore assess object motion relative to the surrounding scene, while checking that the scene remains aligned with the specified camera trajectory. WCPE implements this assessment as a 2D proxy, using target projections to evaluate object–background relative positions and background alignment. Requiring both prevents correct screen-space object placement alone from yielding a low error when the surrounding scene is misaligned. The metric formulation and evaluation protocol are detailed in SectionA.4.

    Camera-control accuracy

    We evaluate camera-control accuracy by comparing the camera trajectory recovered from each generated video with its target trajectory. We report Cam-T, the mean translation error between the recovered and target camera positions, and Cam-R, the mean geodesic rotation error between their orientations, measured in degrees. Lower values for both metrics indicate more faithful camera control.

    4.3 Qualitative Results

    Diverse control through user interventions.

    Fig.1(c) and (d) demonstrate depth-axis control and occlusion handling consistent with scene geometry. Interventions can also target selected object parts: in Fig.1(e), the user rotates the excavator’s upper structure independently of its tracks, specifying the rotation direction and angular speed. For non-rigid objects, partial control allows the video model to complete unspecified articulation. In Fig.1(f), the user specifies only the cat’s torso trajectory, while the model generates accompanying limb motion and maintains a coherent body configuration. Fig.1(g) and (h) further demonstrate camera-controlled world exploration and simultaneous control of multiple objects, respectively.

    State persistence and control across rollouts.

    In Fig.3, the controlled bulldozer displaces a passive rock. After the resulting state is incorporated into memory, the camera moves away until the affected region is out of view, then returns. The rock retains its displaced position upon revisitation, providing qualitative evidence of state persistence across rollouts. Fig.3(b) demonstrates continued control of the same world across three successive rollouts. The user first moves the excavator with the camera fixed, then changes the viewpoint while preserving the excavator’s updated world-space pose, and finally controls both the object and camera. Each rollout continues from the preceding state, allowing the user to manipulate an entity, observe the resulting configuration from another viewpoint, and intervene again. This separates control of the entity’s world state from control of the observation viewpoint.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    Scene-Anchored Joint Guidance.

    Fig.4 shows that intermediate values of α outperform both spatial routing alone (α=0) and the joint prediction alone (α=1). We select α=0.25, which achieves the lowest WCPE and Cam-R and nearly the lowest Cam-T. These results support combining a scene-anchor correction with a global joint contribution.

    Transport-Aligned Augmentation.

    We compare three ways of constructing entity latent conditions during training: transporting initial-frame latents using estimated geometry, using aligned ground-truth entity latents from each target frame, and applying TAA to those ground-truth latents.

    All variants share training data, initialization, optimization budgets, inference conditions, and SAJG settings. As shown in Table2, replacing transported initial-frame latents with ground-truth latents reduces WCPE and Cam-T, but slightly increases Cam-R. Applying TAA further reduces all three errors, supporting the combination of spatially aligned training conditions and augmentation that reduces their latent mismatch with inference-time transport.

    Curriculum training.

    Staged training outperforms interleaved training under matched data exposure and computation; details are provided in Appendix B.1.

    4.5 Comparisons

    We compare our method with VerseCrafter [(Zheng et al., 2026)], WorldDirector [(Wang et al., 2026a)], MotionCanvas [(Xing et al., 2025)], SymphoMotion [(Zhang et al., 2026)], and Real2SAM2Real [(Wu et al., 2026)]. We evaluate joint object and camera control using WCPE, Cam-T, and Cam-R. As shown in Table3, our method achieves the lowest WCPE, Cam-T, and Cam-R, demonstrating accurate joint control of object motion and camera viewpoint. Qualitative comparisons in Fig.5 further show these failure modes. In this example, the user keeps the camera static while translating and rotating the ball laterally behind the alphabet blocks. VerseCrafter and Real2SAM2Real often absorb object motion into viewpoint change, resulting in undesired viewpoint change despite the specified static camera condition. This makes the ball appear to move with the camera rather than independently in the scene. WorldDirector and MotionCanvas preserve the static camera more reliably, but fail to reproduce the correct depth ordering and rotation of the ball. In contrast, our method faithfully follows the intended joint object and camera control, capturing object translation and rotation under a static camera while handling occlusion. See AppendixC for additional qualitative comparisons. An additional comparison with MosaicMem is provided in Table7.

    5 Conclusion

    UniState unifies spatial memory and user interventions in a shared world coordinate system for controllable world simulation. This unified world-state representation allows object motion and camera trajectory to be specified independently. It provides spatial constraints for video generation while preserving the video model’s capacity to synthesize plausible responses, so users can specify intended changes without prescribing every resulting motion or interaction. Quantitative comparisons and ablations support our training and sampling strategies for joint object and camera control across diverse camera trajectories and user interventions. Revisitation results further show that generated interaction outcomes can be incorporated into spatial memory and retained across rollouts. Together, these findings support physical intervention in a persistent world with free-viewpoint observation.

    Limitations

    Interaction effects rely on the video model’s generative prior: although controlled object states can be updated outside the camera view, their interactions with surrounding objects cannot be explicitly simulated while out of view. Spatial resolution limits control over small objects, while temporal resolution limits fast motion. The model may also fail to follow physically implausible interventions, such as moving a solid object through a solid wall.

    Appendix A Implementation details

    A.1 UniState Construction

    Geometry and feature alignment.

    Given an initial image I₀ and its camera C₀, we obtain latents z₀=𝔼(I₀) using a VAE encoder and estimate depth D₀ using an off-the-shelf estimator [(Wang et al., 2026b)]. Using D₀ and C₀, we associate each feature z_0,i with 3D geometry X_0,i in the world coordinate system defined by C₀. These geometry–feature pairs form the initial state S₀={ℙ_0,i}ᵢ₌₁^N, where ℙ_0,i=(X_0,i,z_0,i) denotes a 3D latent. Additional views of the same initial scene can extend S₀ by lifting and registering their latent features into this coordinate system.

    Let {Ωᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N denote the initial image patches. We construct the geometric support of patch i as

    X_0,i=Π⁻¹_C₀(Ωᵢ,D₀[Ωᵢ]),

    where Π⁻¹_C₀ denotes unprojection through the source camera. The implementation approximates the resulting local geometry with an oriented planar primitive. Its appearance grid is sampled from the aligned latent coordinates Uᵢ.

    Intervention.

    Entity geometry is transformed according to Eq.1. At each time t, we construct Sₜ={ℙ_t,i}ᵢ₌₁^N directly from S₀, where ℙ_t,i=(X_t,i,z_0,i). Thus, each transformed geometry remains paired with its source latent feature.

    Patch selection.

    Given an entity mask Sₖ, patch i is assigned to entity k when

    (|Ωᵢ∩Sₖ|)/(|Ωᵢ|)>τ_seg.

    We store a control indicator αᵢ=1[i∈\bigcupₖIₖ] separately from the transform. This indicator remains active when the selected entity holds a constant pose.

    Back-face rejection.

    Let n_i,t and x̄_t,i denote the transformed surface normal and patch center. Given target camera center oₜ, patch i is rendered when

    ⟨n_i,t,oₜ-x̄_t,i⟩>0.

    Patches at an angle of 90^∘ or greater relative to the front-facing viewing direction are rejected.

    Intervention support.

    We first rasterize every selected and front-facing patch:

    M̃ₜ=ℝₛᵤₚₚₒᵣₜ({X_t,i}_αᵢ=1;Cₜ).

    A scene-level depth test then produces

    Mₜ=Vis(M̃ₜ;{X_t,i}ᵢ₌₁^N,Cₜ).

    Thus, patches occluded by other scene geometry are absent from Mₜ.

    Adapter injection.

    The latent and intervention-mask conditions are injected at the transformer input, whereas camera conditioning is applied within each transformer block.

    For the input conditions, let h_V,base⁽⁰⁾ denote the backbone’s video-token embeddings after the input projection and timestep embedding, before adding the W and M conditions. We form the conditioned input tokens as

    h_V⁽⁰⁾=h_V,base⁽⁰⁾+P_W (patch(W))+P_M (patch(M)).

    Here, patch arranges each condition into patches aligned with the backbone’s video-token grid. P_W and P_M are separate trainable linear projections without bias, mapping 192-dimensional latent patches and 4-dimensional binary mask patches, respectively, to the 4096-dimensional video-token space. Each mask patch corresponds to a 2×2 spatial region. These residuals are added once before the transformer blocks; the M term is omitted during the first training stage.

    For camera conditioning, each transformer block contains a trainable attention branch parallel to the backbone self-attention. This branch computes queries, keys, and values from the normalized video tokens and applies PRoPE using the relative-ray representation derived from the camera poses and intrinsics. Let a_V,base^(ℓ) denote the backbone self-attention output for the video tokens at block ℓ. The camera-conditioned attention output is

    a_V^(ℓ)=a_V,base^(ℓ)+A_cam^(ℓ) (LN(h_V^(ℓ)),C),

    where A_cam^(ℓ) denotes the parallel camera-aware attention branch. We apply this branch in all 36 transformer blocks with a residual scale of 1. The backbone remains frozen, while the camera branches and the input-condition projections are trained according to the two-stage curriculum.

    Initialization from multiple observations.

    Although a single frame is sufficient to initialize the initial state, patches from additional observations can be lifted into the same world coordinate system to extend its spatial coverage. The long sequence in Fig.3(b) uses an initial state initialized from multiple observations and spans three successive rollouts with object control and camera control.

    A.2 SAJG Construction

    Condition rendering.

    For each target camera Cₜ, the scene-anchor condition renders the initial state without interventions:

    (W_s,t,_)=ℝ(S₀;Cₜ).

    		(4)

    The joint condition renders the intervened state:

    (W_j,t,Mₜ)=ℝ(Sₜ;Cₜ).

    		(5)

    Both conditions use the complete scene for depth testing. The joint branch receives the intervention-mask condition, while the scene-anchor branch omits it.

    Scene-mask construction.

    We construct Gₛ in latent-video coordinates. For each target camera, we project the selected entities at their source and target poses to obtain the binary support volumes E_src and E_tgt. The scene mask is

    Gₛ=F_1,1[1-D₁(E_src∪E_tgt)],

    		(6)

    where D₁ applies one-cell spatial dilation and F_1,1 applies one-cell spatial and temporal feathering. The resulting values lie in [0,1], and the mask is broadcast across latent channels. Unlike the intervention mask M, which marks the visible target entity regions, Gₛ selects scene regions away from both source and target entity supports, with soft transitions at their boundaries.

    The mask is geometry-derived rather than learned. It may vary across video frames, but is computed only once for each input and remains unchanged across denoising steps. All dilation and feathering settings are fixed; only α is varied in the routing ablation.

    Equivalent correction form.

    Substituting Eq.2 into Eq.3 gives

    V_final=Vⱼ+(1-α)Gₛ⊙(Vₛ-Vⱼ)(7)
    =wₛ⊙Vₛ+wⱼ⊙Vⱼ,

    where

    wₛ=(1-α)Gₛ, wⱼ=1-(1-α)Gₛ.

    		(8)

    Thus, wₛ+wⱼ=1 and wⱼ≥α at every spatio-temporal location. The equivalent correction form shows that the scene-anchor prediction modifies the joint prediction only where the scene mask permits. At the default α=0.25, the effective weights are wₛ=0.75Gₛ and wⱼ=1-0.75Gₛ. Setting α=0 applies the maximum scene correction permitted by the mask, while α=1 removes the correction.

    Classifier-free guidance and evaluation cost.

    Given the same noisy latent x_τ at flow-matching time τ and camera condition C, the conditional video model f_θ produces velocity predictions with classifier-free guidance (CFG):

    Vₛ=CFG[f_θ(x_τ,τ;C,Wₛ)],Vⱼ=CFG[f_θ(x_τ,τ;C,Wⱼ)].

    		(9)

    Both predictions share the source observation and text prompt; these and the intervention-mask input are omitted from the notation.

    The main-paper equations use predictions after classifier-free guidance. In implementation, we apply the same spatial weights wₛ and wⱼ separately to the conditional and null-text predictions, and then apply classifier-free guidance to the two mixed predictions. With the same guidance scale for both branches, this is algebraically equivalent to mixing the guided predictions because both operations are linear. The exact computation uses a separate null-text prediction for each branch and requires four transformer evaluations per denoising step.

    We additionally tested an approximation that reuses a single null-text prediction for both branches while retaining their separate conditional predictions. Although the two branch-specific null-text predictions are not necessarily identical, we observed no noticeable differences in the generated results under this approximation in the tested settings. Reusing one null-text prediction reduces the computation to three transformer evaluations per denoising step.

    A.3 Training

    Training settings and captions.

    Both stages use AdamW with a global batch size of 8 and a base learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴. We generate training-video captions using Qwen2.5-VL [(Bai et al., 2025)]. The captions describe scene content while omitting motion and object-location descriptions (e.g., “A is to the left of B”).

    Optimization.

    Both stages use the flow-matching objective

    L_FM=𝔼_x,τ[∥f_θ(x_τ,τ;C,W,M)-V_τᵍᵗ∥₂²],

    		(10)

    with the M condition omitted in the first stage. The first stage trains the C and W conditioning modules on DL3DV for 20K steps. The second stage initializes these modules from the first-stage checkpoint, adds the M module, and jointly trains all three conditioning paths on HM-World for 10K steps. The video backbone, VAE, and text encoder remain frozen.

    Training condition construction.

    We render S₀ from the target camera Cₜ and zero out the selected entities’ projected source regions, obtaining Wₜˢʳᶜ. Let zₜᵉ denote the ground-truth entity latent aligned with the target latent grid, and Bₜ its binary spatial support. We form the training condition as

    Wₜᵗʳᵃⁱⁿ=(1-Bₜ)⊙Wₜˢʳᶜ+Bₜ⊙zₜᵉ,

    		(11)

    with Bₜ broadcast across latent channels. This retains source-scene appearance outside the target entities, while vacated source regions remain zero unless covered by a target entity.

    Conditioning augmentation.

    For a latent grid of size H×W, D_NN reduces the spatial resolution to round(ρH)×round(ρW) using nearest-neighbor sampling. U_NN restores the original resolution using nearest-neighbor upsampling. Given the ground-truth entity latents zₜᵉ and their binary spatial support Bₜ, we define

    z̃ₜᵉ=\begincasesz₀ᵉ,&t=0, (1-Bₜ)⊙zₜᵉ+Bₜ⊙U_NN(D_NN(zₜᵉ)),&t>0.\endcases

    		(12)

    As defined in Eq.12, the resampled values replace the conditioning appearance only within the future-frame entity support Bₜ. The support mask itself is not resampled. The augmented entity latents are then composited with the initial-state renders using Eq.11. Neither the intervention mask M nor the ground-truth training target is modified.

    A.4 WCPE Evaluation

    Motivation and target projections.

    An object’s image-space position alone does not establish whether the prescribed world-space control is realized relative to the scene. WCPE therefore evaluates object–background relative positions together with background alignment. Target trajectories are constructed from the input scene proxy: object points follow the prescribed object transformations, while background points remain fixed in world coordinates. Both are projected using the target camera trajectory. These targets are shared across methods for each evaluation condition.

    Metric formulation.

    We track object queries and background anchors in the generated videos using CoTracker3 [(Karaev et al., 2025)]. For an object query at a given frame, let p̂ and p^* denote its tracked image position and target projection. Similarly, b̂ⱼ and bⱼ^* denote the tracked and target positions of background anchor j. Using the same valid anchor set V, we define

    eᵣₑₗ=median_j∈V(\lVert(p̂-b̂ⱼ)-(p^*-bⱼ^*)\rVert₂)/(D),

    		(13)

    e_bg=median_j∈V(\lVertb̂ⱼ-bⱼ^*\rVert₂)/(D),

    		(14)

    where D=√W²+H² is the image diagonal. The joint error is

    eⱼₒᵢₙₜ=\max(eᵣₑₗ,e_bg).

    		(15)

    A low joint error requires both accurate object–background relative positions and accurate background alignment with the target projection.

    Failure handling and aggregation.

    We report WCPE@5 with an error cap and missing-measurement penalty of τ=0.05, corresponding to 5% of the image diagonal:

    e_score=\begincases\min(eⱼₒᵢₙₜ,τ),&if the measurement is valid, τ,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(16)

item.title: 画面好看不等于同一个 3D 世界：Orbia 用受控重访把 720 个用例拆成三个一致性维度 ｜ Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?
item.description:
一句话：评测世界模型不能靠 VLM 打分：要测输入保持、生成内容持久、3D 自一致三件事；测下来世界模型控制力强 24.8 分，视觉质量反而低 5.7 分。

要点：

  • 既有评测要么只看个别几何性质，要么用视觉语言模型判断记忆与一致性，缺少系统的 3D 评测
  • 三个维度：输入保持（用配准 RGB-D 参考与标注锚点测外观、几何、空间稳定性）、生成内容持久性（重访输入图里没有的区域，比对第一次生成观测）、3D 自一致（跨视角深度与特征对应、区域尺度一致、留出高斯渲染）
  • 通过受控探索与重访组织评测：720 个用例、859 个锚点评测目标，含 480 个短用例与 240 对分钟级延长，统一 720p / 16 FPS
  • 世界模型在控制维度平均 57.29，比图生视频模型的 32.48 高 24.80 分；但视觉质量更低（71.80 对 77.53），说明两类能力并不自动同步

为什么值得看：给「世界模型能不能当引擎用」建立可复现的验收标准：不是看生成的片子好不好看，而是回去同一个地方，看它还是不是同一个地方。

中文摘要：视频生成器正被当作可探索、可模拟的交互世界，但画面真实好看并不等于描绘了一个一致的 3D 世界。现有基准要么只评估选定的几何性质，要么用视觉语言模型判断记忆与一致性，缺少系统的 3D 评测。作者提出 Orbia：第一个专门系统、全面评估交互世界模型 3D 一致性的基准。它通过受控探索与重访组织评测，分三个维度：输入保持（用配准的 RGB-D 参考与标注锚点支撑外观、几何与空间稳定性度量）、生成内容持久性（重访输入图像中不存在的区域，与首次生成观测比对，检验模型是否守住自己造出来的内容）、3D 自一致（跨视角深度与特征对应、区域尺度一致、留出高斯渲染）。基准含 720 个用例、859 个锚点目标，统一 720p / 16 FPS。结果显示世界模型在控制维度上明显领先图生视频模型（57.29 对 32.48），但视觉质量反而更低（71.80 对 77.53）。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-14

本期推送：2026-10-26

AOrbia: Do Generated Videos
Form a Consistent 3D World?Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?

October 2026

Abstract

Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce AOrbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our AOrbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.

figureOverview of AOrbia. This work introduces AOrbia, a benchmark for evaluating 3D consistency along three dimensions: 1input preservation, 2generated-content persistence, and 33D self-consistency. Six exploration-and-revisit templates support short and minute-long evaluation across public datasets, self-captured scenes, and UE simulation. We benchmark world models and video generators through text, action, and camera-pose interfaces.

1 Introduction

Video generation is expanding from visual synthesis toward world simulation [Brooks et al., 2024; Wan Team et al., 2025; Google DeepMind, 2025; Gao et al., 2025], supporting interactive games [Bruce et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025], open-domain exploration [Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025; Sun et al., 2025], generative rendering [Yu et al., 2025a; Shen et al., 2026], and embodied simulation [Yang et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025]. This shift is contextualized by [Kong et al., 2025b], which organizes world modeling around video, occupancy, and LiDAR representations. These applications require observations across time and viewpoints to remain compatible with a persistent 3D world. A player should return to the same environment, a renderer should reveal mutually consistent surfaces, and an embodied agent should reuse previously observed spatial relationships. Visually convincing frames alone cannot establish this structural reliability across viewpoints and repeated visits. As generated videos become environments for exploration and interaction, a fundamental question arises: Do generated videos form a consistent 3D world?

Existing benchmarks address different aspects of this question. These protocols assess perceptual quality [Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024], local or scene-level geometric self-coherence [Duan et al., 2025; Ying et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026c; Zhao et al., 2026], or memory and state retention upon revisit using same-view appearance comparisons, point-cloud comparisons, and vision-language judgments [Ye et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2026a]. WorldLens [Liang et al., 2026b] broadens driving-world evaluation to reconstruction, action following, downstream tasks, and human preference. Yet systematic, quantitative evaluation of 3D consistency remains underexplored. Geometric agreement does not guarantee content preservation, nor does a successful return establish consistency throughout exploration. A dedicated benchmark must jointly evaluate 3D structure and the preservation of input and generated content across viewpoints and over time during exploration and repeated revisits.

We introduce AOrbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. We organize evaluation into three dimensions (Figure AOrbia: Do Generated Videos
Form a Consistent 3D World?Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?).

(1) Input preservationassesses whether the model preserves the environment shown in the input as the viewpoint changes. Registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors measure the appearance, geometry, and spatial relationships of observed content. Exploration also reveals regions outside the input, whose appearance the model must generate.

(2) Generated-content persistencecompares newly revealed content across visits, using its first generated appearance as the reference. The model is free to create unseen content, but should preserve what it has created. Beyond content retention, generated views must agree in their underlying 3D structure.

(3) 3D self-consistencytests whether generated views describe the same 3D scene through cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering. These measurements examine both local surface compatibility and scene-level coherence. To assess resistance to temporal drift under longer exploration and more frequent revisits, we extend sequences to one minute and repeatedly return to previously visited regions. This tests whether models maintain scene geometry and content as the exploration history grows. We also examine how control accuracy and visual quality relate to the three consistency dimensions.

Joint evaluation requires cross-view references and controlled revisits. Our construction pipeline prepares registered RGB-D pairs, verifies anchor correspondence and surface support, and synthesizes trajectories connecting the reference poses. We select revisits to newly revealed regions and manually review anchors, reference views, and trajectories. To cover diverse scene distributions, we draw on 1real-world datasets, 2self-captured scenes, and 3simulated environments, spanning indoor and outdoor settings in both real and virtual worlds. Processing over 110k source samples and investing over 300 hours in annotation and curation yields 720 evaluation instances, comprising 480 short cases and 240 paired minute-long extensions. Six exploration-and-revisit protocols cover trajectories with distinct spatial demands. Model-specific adapters translate the trajectories into text instructions, action sequences, or camera conditions for evaluation across control interfaces for the same exploration and revisit tasks.

To summarize, our contributions are fourfold:

  • [itemsep=2pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt]

  • •

    We introduce AOrbia, the first benchmark dedicated to systematic, quantitative evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models across viewpoints and exploration horizons.

  • •

    We decompose 3D consistency into input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency to systematically assess content and geometry.

  • •

    We build a unified annotation pipeline yielding 720 instances with registered evidence and controlled revisits across real and simulated environments.

  • •

    We evaluate 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models, examining how 3D consistency relates to control execution, visual quality, and exploration duration.

item.title: 把视频理解与视频生成放进同一张地图：读、写、共享、交互四种操作 ｜ Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
item.description:
一句话：把观察到的视频看作「潜在时间世界的部分、有损、按时间排序的投影」，视频理解与视频生成其实是同一件事的四个操作。

要点：

  • 视频基础模型在做理解与生成，视频世界模型想抓住画面背后的动力学；两者目标不同，但都关心「视频观测」与「演化中的世界」的关系
  • 以世界建模为统一视角，把文献组织成四种互补操作：读（从观测视频推世界属性）、写（从指定或学到的世界条件合成视频）、共享（用共同建模机制打通理解与生成）、交互（在动作与演化观测下预测并更新世界状态）
  • 核心区分是「序列的时间连贯」与「底层世界状态的一致」——两者常被混为一谈，但后者才是世界模型要的
  • 在任务、表示、模型、数据与基准之间梳理出重心从「片段级」向「状态级」迁移的趋势

为什么值得看：给这个领域建立坐标系用：判断一篇新论文是在解决「读」还是「写」、在保证序列连贯还是状态一致，能避免把生成质量改进误当成世界建模进步。

中文摘要：视频基础模型在理解与生成视觉序列上进步很快，而视频世界模型试图抓住画面背后的动力学。两者目标不同，却都关心视频观测与一个演化中的世界之间的关系，因此作者以世界建模作为统一视角来审视这些进展：把观察到的视频看作潜在时间世界的一个部分、有损、按时间排序的投影，并把文献围绕四种互补操作组织起来——读是从观测视频推断世界属性，写是从指定或学到的世界条件合成视频，共享是通过共同的建模机制把理解与生成整合起来，交互是在动作与不断演化的观测下预测并更新世界状态。这个视角把「观察或生成序列中的时间连贯」与「底层世界状态的一致」明确区分开，并沿任务、表示、模型、数据集与基准，追踪该领域从片段级关注向状态级关注的转移。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·世界模型+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting
with the World through Video

A Survey Toward Unified Video World Models

Abstract

Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.

1
