    L_diff=𝔼_(z₀,c),ε,k [\lVertε_θ(zₖ,k,c)-ε\rVert²].

    		(4)

    Sampling starts from z_K∼ℕ(0,I) and applies denoising updates z_K→…→zₖ→zₖ₋₁→…→z₀, after which z₀ is decoded into video; networks may equivalently predict the clean sample or the velocity. Flow matching instead trains a vector field that transports a simple base distribution to the data along a chosen probability path [Lipman et al., 2023]. Here k is continuous: for the linear path zₖ=(1-k)z₀+kε with k∼U[0,1], the target velocity is ε-z₀:

    L_fm=𝔼_(z₀,c),ε,k [\lVertv_θ(zₖ,k,c)-(ε-z₀)\rVert²].

    		(5)

    Sampling integrates dzₖ/dk=v_θ(zₖ,k,c) from noise at k=1 to data at k=0, in practice over a discrete grid of steps. Diffusion and flow matching can share backbones and samplers. Section 5 uses masked prediction to learn representations, Section 6 covers generators built on these objectives, and Section 8 adapts them to action-conditioned online rollout.

    4.4 Taxonomy of Video World Models

    A video world model performs the interacting operation of Definition  with a video-centered state. Unlike a general video generator, which aims at plausible content, it learns how that state evolves. We exclude models whose primary persistent state is an explicit 3D structure, such as a neural field, 3D Gaussians, or an occupancy grid, as well as purely symbolic or text-based world models; models that keep 3D structure only as auxiliary memory for a video-centered state remain in scope (Section 8.2.2). World models from model-based reinforcement learning are included only when their state is learned from video.

    We classify video world models along two independent axes. On the first axis, the prediction space, observation-space models predict future frames, video tokens, or generative latents decoded to video, as GAIA [Hu et al., 2023; Russell et al., 2025] and EVA [Chi et al., 2024] do. Although VAE latents are not pixels, predicting them for decoding to video still counts as observation-space prediction. Latent-state models instead predict future video-derived features that need not be decoded to video: V-JEPA [Bardes et al., 2024] and V-JEPA 2 [Assran et al., 2025] learn such features by masked feature prediction, which serves as pretraining for latent transition models (Section 8), and DINO-WM [Zhou et al., 2025a] and V-JEPA 2-AC add action-conditioned transitions for planning. The second axis, the transition interface, describes how controls reach the model. Passive models predict from observations alone, while action-conditioned models receive a control sequence fixed before rollout, such as the ego trajectories of Vista [Gao et al., 2024a] or the robot actions of IRASim [Zhu et al., 2025]. Interactive models accept new controls during rollout, so each input can change what follows, as in GameNGen [Valevski et al., 2025], Genie 2 [Parker-Holder et al., 2024], and related playable simulators [Alonso et al., 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025g; He et al., 2025a]. Section 8 reviews each cell of the resulting 2×3 grid (Figure 10).

    5 Video Comprehension: Reading the World

    Video comprehension performs the reading operation V→W of Section 3: given a trace V, the model estimates properties of the latent world W that produced it. From a limited viewpoint and interval, it must recover which entities and events are present, where they are, how they change, which constraints govern that change, and what may have caused it. Occlusion, camera motion, editing, sparse sampling, and missing modalities leave much of this state unobserved, and the viewing scenarios of Section 4.1 change how much evidence must be selected and remembered. Sections 5.1–5.5 cover tasks and benchmarks, encoders, Video-LLMs, agents, and applications in turn. Tang et al. [Tang et al., 2026a] survey Video-LLMs in more detail; here we organize the evaluation of reading by the world properties it tests (Section 5.1) and review Video-LLMs as one stage of the reading pipeline.

    5.1 Tasks, Data, and Evaluation

    We organize video-understanding tasks by the main dimension of world state they require: semantic (entities, actions, events), spatial (location, identity, layout, viewpoint), temporal (order, duration, boundaries, long-range dependencies), physical (contact, gravity, containment, material behavior), and causal (effects, interventions, counterfactuals). The dimensions interact, as when tracking combines identity with temporal continuity, so Table 4 places each benchmark under the dimension it mainly tests, even when the text introduces it elsewhere. Output format is a separate axis: a label, span, mask, or sentence can probe any dimension, and what a benchmark measures depends on the evidence needed to produce its output.

    Aggregate accuracy does not show that a model used the intended evidence, since many questions can be answered from the text, a single frame, or static appearance. Text-only, single-frame, shuffled-order, and restricted-context baselines expose these shortcuts, and TempCore [Ok & Lee, 2025] and Video-Index [Song et al., 2026] use them to filter existing benchmarks down to vision-dependent, order-sensitive subsets. Minimal pairs of near-identical videos with different answers block appearance-only solutions (TimeBlind [Li et al., 2026], MVP [Krojer et al., 2025]).

    5.1.1 Semantic Understanding

    Semantic understanding identifies the entities, actions, events, and relations that make a video meaningful. Action recognition is the most established semantic task: UCF101 [Soomro et al., 2012] and HMDB51 [Kuehne et al., 2011] test closed-set recognition in trimmed clips, Kinetics [Kay et al., 2017] scales up the number and diversity of classes, and Something-Something [Goyal et al., 2017] makes labels depend on how objects change under manipulation. Language moves the output beyond fixed categories through retrieval (MSR-VTT [Xu et al., 2016]), captioning (VATEX [Wang et al., 2019], YouCook2 [Zhou et al., 2018]), and video question answering (VideoQA: ActivityNet-QA [Yu et al., 2019], TVQA [Lei et al., 2018], TGIF-QA [Jang et al., 2017]).

    Recent Video-LLM benchmarks mix semantic questions with temporal, spatial, and knowledge-intensive items (Video-MME and Video-MME-v2 [Fu et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2026], MMVU [Zhao et al., 2025a], Video-MMMU [Hu et al., 2026c; Luo et al., 2026]). Hallucination benchmarks test whether the reported content is supported by the video at all: VideoHallucer [Wang et al., 2024g; Luo et al., 2026c] uses adversarially paired questions, EventHallusion [Zhang et al., 2024] probes events suggested by language priors, and ARGUS [Rawal et al., 2025] scores hallucination and omission in free-form captions.

    5.1.2 Spatial Understanding

    Spatial understanding asks where entities are, how their extent changes, and whether their identity persists as viewpoint and visibility vary. Spatiotemporal grounding links a referring expression to a region tube over an interval (VidSTG [Zhang et al., 2020]). Video object segmentation tracks pixel masks (DAVIS [Pont-Tuset et al., 2017], YouTube-VOS [Xu et al., 2018]), referring variants select the target by language or motion (Ref-YouTube-VOS [Seo et al., 2020], MeViS [Ding et al., 2023]; addressed by ReferFormer [Wu et al., 2022]), and MOTChallenge [Milan et al., 2016] and LaSOT [Fan et al., 2019] test identity across occlusion and reappearance. Memory-based and promptable trackers such as XMem [Cheng & Schwing, 2022], AOT [Yang et al., 2021], DEVA [Cheng et al., 2023], and SAM 2 [Ravi et al., 2025] keep earlier evidence as the target changes appearance or disappears.

    Spatial reasoning benchmarks go beyond masks and tracks: VSI-Bench [Yang et al., 2025b] and MMSI-Video-Bench [Lin et al., 2025a] test relative position, viewpoint, and layout, STI-Bench [Li et al., 2025j] asks for quantitative pose and motion, and DSI-Bench [Zhang et al., 2025i] separates observer motion from object motion. A newer group tests state that is out of view: SCP-Bench [Zhao et al., 2026b] infers unseen past or future layouts, Beyond3D [Ma et al., 2026] asks where relocated objects now are, and OVO-S-Bench [Li et al., 2026i] answers from the video prefix seen so far. These tasks test the object permanence and revisit consistency that world models must maintain (Section 8.2.2).

    5.1.3 Temporal Understanding

    Temporal understanding recovers when an event occurs, how long it lasts, and how evidence at different moments is ordered or connected. Temporal action detection locates predefined actions in untrimmed video (THUMOS [Idrees et al., 2017], ActivityNet [Heilbron et al., 2015]), and moment retrieval returns the segment that matches a language query (Charades-STA [Gao et al., 2017], QVHighlights [Lei et al., 2021], DiDeMo [Hendricks et al., 2017]). Dense event captioning localizes and describes possibly overlapping events (ActivityNet Captions [Krishna et al., 2017], addressed end to end by Vid2Seq [Yang et al., 2023]), and anticipation predicts an action not yet observed (e.g., Ego4D forecasting [Grauman et al., 2022]).

    Fine-grained and long-form benchmarks stress subtle temporal differences and sparse evidence. TemporalBench [Cai et al., 2024] and TempCompass [Liu et al., 2024d] test ordering, speed, and direction, TimeBlind [Li et al., 2026] pairs videos that differ only in temporal structure, and Video-MME-Logical [Kwan et al., 2026] separates logical complexity from scene recognition. MLVU [Zhou et al., 2025b], LVBench [Wang et al., 2025c], and LongVideoBench [Wu et al., 2024] pose heterogeneous questions over long videos, and VideoOdyssey [He et al., 2026] extends this to ultra-long, omni-modal video, measuring how much context stays usable as evidence length grows.

    Streaming benchmarks make state maintenance directly observable. SVCBench [Liu et al., 2026d] asks for running object and event counts at many points in a video, TRACE [Ma et al., 2026a] scores answer quality together with latency, false alarms, and missed responses under causal input, and StreamingEval [Tang et al., 2026] adds encoding throughput, time to first token, and a fixed memory budget.

    5.1.4 Physical Understanding

    Physical understanding concerns how a visible state can change under constraints that are often only partly observed. Plausibility benchmarks ask whether an observed transition is possible: IntPhys [Riochet et al., 2022] and IntPhys 2 [Bordes et al., 2025] test object permanence and intuitive physics, ImplausiBench [Motamed et al., 2025] contains videos that violate expected physical behavior, and Physion [Bear et al., 2021] instead asks whether objects will make contact. Other benchmarks ask for next states, interaction outcomes, or the mechanism behind a change. CLEVRER [Yi et al., 2020] asks descriptive, predictive, and explanatory questions about collisions, while PhysicsMind [Mak et al., 2026], PhysBench [Chow et al., 2025], and PAI-Bench-U [Zhou et al., 2026] broaden coverage to object properties, commonsense constraints, task completion, and next actions. APT [Wu et al., 2026a] further labels timestamped transitions by mechanism (contact, gravity, or friction).

    Two benchmarks check that answers rest on physical evidence rather than priors. MVP [Krojer et al., 2025] pairs near-identical videos that require opposite answers, and VisPhyWorld [Liang et al., 2026a] asks the model to rebuild the scene as executable simulator code so that its physical hypothesis can be checked. Physics benchmarks for generated video, such as Physics-IQ [Motamed et al., 2026] and VideoPhy [Bansal et al., 2025; Bansal et al., 2026], are covered in Sections 6.1.2 and 8.4.

    5.1.5 Causal Understanding

    Causal understanding asks why an observed event occurred and how the outcome would change if an action, object, or condition were different. On synthetic collisions, CLEVRER [Yi et al., 2020] adds counterfactual questions to its explanatory ones. Real-world and procedural benchmarks link actions to effects that may appear much later: NExT-QA [Xiao et al., 2021] and STAR [Wu et al., 2021] ask about event relations and reasons, Video-Holmes [Cheng et al., 2026] and Causal2Needles [Li et al., 2025f] spread the clues far apart, and CaST-Bench [Zhang et al., 2026h] covers more varied settings and causal structures. Counterfactual benchmarks test altered outcomes directly: CausalVQA [Foss et al., 2025] asks counterfactual, hypothetical, and planning questions about real egocentric video, and DMC-CF [Zhang et al., 2026g] pairs such questions about real videos with causal-graph interventions, whose regenerated variants also limit data contamination.

    5.2 Video Representation Learning and Encoding

    Video representation learning maps frames to features that can be reused across recognition, retrieval, grounding, reasoning, and multimodal modeling. Convolutional backbones such as I3D [Carreira & Zisserman, 2017] and SlowFast [Feichtenhofer et al., 2019] established supervised spatiotemporal processing, and TimeSformer [Bertasius et al., 2021], ViViT [Arnab et al., 2021], and Video Swin [Liu et al., 2022] carried the Vision Transformer [Dosovitskiy et al., 2021] to video at different spatial and temporal scales. The pretraining objective decides what these backbones retain, and we group objectives by their dominant supervision signal into the four families of Figure 3. The families overlap: masked feature prediction, for instance, is both masked and predictive. Variational autoencoders and tokenizers built for synthesis are covered in Section 6.

    5.2.1 Contrastive Learning

    Contrastive learning pulls positive pairs together in embedding space and pushes mismatched pairs apart, commonly with an InfoNCE-style objective. In video-only learning, CVRL [Qian et al., 2021] and ρMoCo [Feichtenhofer et al., 2021] draw positives from augmentations or clips of the same video, and the sampling distance sets a trade-off: views too close give little contrast, while views too far apart may show different events.

    Video–text contrastive learning pairs clips with language. Among dual-encoder retrieval models, Frozen in Time [Bain et al., 2021] trains a space–time Transformer jointly on image–text and video–text pairs, and CLIP4Clip [Luo et al., 2022] transfers the CLIP image–text encoder and adds temporal aggregation, while VideoCLIP [Xu et al., 2021], X-CLIP [Ma et al., 2022], ViCLIP [Wang et al., 2024c], and Finsta [Fei et al., 2024b] develop video-specific alignment. Foundation encoders combine contrastive pretraining with masked or generative losses (InternVideo [Wang et al., 2022a], InternVideo2 [Wang et al., 2024d]), distillation into a masked-video student (VideoPrism [Zhao et al., 2024]), or later alignment stages for language and dense prediction (Perception Encoder [Bolya et al., 2025]). Global alignment can drop fine-grained detail: the World Embedding Benchmark [Liu et al., 2026j] shows that alignment and recoverable physical state can diverge, as physics-specific contrastive tuning improves video–text matching but weakens physical-quantity regression from frozen features; the added losses aim to retain it.

    5.2.2 Masked Learning

    Masked learning removes much of the spatiotemporal input and trains the model to recover it, an idea that VideoBERT [Sun et al., 2019] applied early to quantized video tokens and speech transcripts jointly. VideoMAE [Tong et al., 2022] reconstructs pixels behind tube masks, with a high mask ratio that exploits the redundancy of adjacent frames, and VideoMAE-V2 [Wang et al., 2023] scales it with dual masking. Feature targets replace raw pixels: MaskFeat [Wei et al., 2022] reconstructs handcrafted or learned features, and UMT [Li et al., 2023a] distills from an unmasked teacher that sees the full clip. Learned or teacher targets shift capacity from low-level appearance toward the semantics and motion that the teacher encodes, but they also inherit its biases.

    5.2.3 Predictive Learning

    Predictive learning trains a model to predict the latent representation of hidden or future content, without pixel reconstruction or negative examples. V-JEPA [Bardes et al., 2024] predicts the features of masked regions against a slowly updated target encoder, V-JEPA 2 [Assran et al., 2025] scales this to larger and more diverse data, and V-JEPA 2.1 [Mur-Labadia et al., 2026] improves dense features. InternVideo-Next [Wang et al., 2026] bridges the masked and predictive families, combining masked reconstruction with latent prediction of its first-stage targets, without video–text data. Adding an action-conditioned transition model to such a representation yields the action-conditioned latent-state world models of Section 8.

    5.2.4 Generative Learning

    Generative pretraining shapes a representation by requiring it to produce missing or future content. Visual autoregressive objectives [Yan et al., 2021] predict future frames, patches, or tokens, which rewards sensitivity to appearance and motion but can spend capacity on reconstruction detail that recognition does not need. Vision-language generation outputs text instead: GIT-style [Wang et al., 2022] training generates captions or answers from visual features, and VideoCoCa [Yan et al., 2022] combines captioning with contrastive alignment. In both cases, the representation is shaped only by what captions describe. Large video diffusion models offer a third route: Gen4U [King et al., 2026] reuses a frozen generator’s intermediate activations for classification, geometry, and captioning, and GenCeption [Wang et al., 2026c] adapts a diffusion backbone into a text-steered model for depth, normals, pose, segmentation, and keypoints (Section 7.2).

    5.3 Video-Language Foundation Modeling

    Video-LLMs extend language foundation models to video for open-ended description, dialogue, question answering, grounding, and reasoning. They take visual features from encoders such as those in Section 5.2 and must decide which frames to observe, how to encode time, and how many visual tokens the language model can afford. We review their architectures, training, and test-time scaling in turn.

    5.3.1 Architectures

    Visual front end. Many systems apply an image encoder such as CLIP [Radford et al., 2021] or SigLIP [Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025] to sampled frames, a route that is cheap and semantically strong but leaves temporal modeling to later modules. Native-video encoders [Assran et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026] model local motion before fusion, and direct patch or visual-token inputs keep finer spatial detail at a higher context cost. No encoder can recover an event from an unsampled frame.

    Time and position. Frame order may be encoded by temporal embeddings, timestamps, or multidimensional rotary positions. Qwen2.5-VL [Bai et al., 2025a] uses M-RoPE to coordinate temporal and spatial indices, Qwen3-VL [Bai et al., 2025] adds textual timestamps so that answers can cite moments, and the InternVL series [Wang et al., 2025d] advances visual positions in fractional steps so that long sequences stay within the trained positional range. Temporal Transformers and state-space models such as Mamba [Gu & Dao, 2024] can also aggregate frame sequences before they reach the LLM.

    Vision-language connector. The connector maps visual features into the language backbone’s embedding space and token budget. Linear or MLP projectors turn each visual feature into a prefix token, as in LLaVA-style systems [Liu et al., 2023], while Q-Former and resampler designs [Li et al., 2023] extract a fixed number of query tokens, as in early Video-LLaMA [Zhang et al., 2023] and VideoChat [Li et al., 2025e]. Gated cross-attention, as in Flamingo [Alayrac et al., 2022], instead lets language layers consult visual features at selected depths. Structure-preserving compressors downsample while keeping spatial layout, through convolutional abstractors (Honeybee [Cha et al., 2024]), spatial-temporal convolution (VideoLLaMA 2 [Cheng et al., 2024]), or pixel unshuffle (InternVL [Wang et al., 2025d]). Projectors keep the most direct token path, resamplers and cross-attention give the most control over how much visual information enters the LLM, and compressors trade some directness for locality-aware reduction.

    Compression and memory. Video token count grows with both the number of frames and the tokens per frame, and pooling, merging, or resampling reduce it at the risk of erasing small objects, short events, or precise timestamps. Some designs spend tokens unevenly over time: LLaVA-Video [Zhang et al., 2025h] keeps a few frames dense and pools the rest, Keye-VL-1.5 [Yang et al., 2025] routes frames with large visual change to a high-resolution pathway, and LLaVA-OneVision-2 [An et al., 2026a] groups tokens adaptively like a video codec. Others compress each unit: Chat-UniVi [Jin et al., 2024] merges tokens into dynamic multi-scale units, LLaMA-VID [Li et al., 2024c] reduces each frame to as few as two tokens, and Video-LaVIT [Jin et al., 2024a] pairs keyframes with compact motion vectors. For long video, LongVA [Zhang et al., 2025d] and LongVILA [Chen et al., 2025f] rely on long-context transfer and token budgeting, and Video-XL [Shu et al., 2025] adds structured compression. One finding bounds this design space: a few tokens carry most of the discriminative information, but finding them without an oracle is hard [Hao et al., 2025]. Memory solves a different problem from compression: MovieChat [Song et al., 2024] and MA-LMM [He et al., 2024] maintain a memory of past segments, which decides what remains available after the original frames leave the context (agent memory is treated in Section 5.4).

    Language backbone and output. An instruction-following LLM combines the retained evidence with the query and produces dialogue, descriptions, explanations, or structured predictions. Early systems extended image-language models to video with adapters and compressed frame tokens [Zhang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025e; Maaz et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024c], and later open models add larger multimodal mixtures, more efficient video tokens, and grounded or reasoning outputs [Li et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025d; Yan et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026g]. Boxes, timestamps, and masks can be emitted as special tokens or by attached heads, which makes the evidence behind an answer easier to inspect. Closed systems such as Gemini [Team et al., 2024] show strong long-context video and audio results but disclose few design details. Table 5 lists the encoder, connector, and LLM of representative open systems and what each training stage updates.

    Streaming and audio-visual input. Streaming models must answer from the evidence seen so far and bound their state with windows, recurrent memory, or key–value (KV) caches. VideoLLM-online [Chen et al., 2024b] introduced real-time dialogue over a continuously advancing stream, StreamingVLM [Xu et al., 2026a] keeps a compact KV cache for unbounded streams, and OneStreamer [Zeng et al., 2026a] writes timestamped caption memory and learns when to record and when to respond. For audio-video input, Qwen2.5-Omni [Xu et al., 2025] and Qwen3-Omni [Xu et al., 2025a] place both modalities on one timeline with time-aligned multimodal rotary positions.

    5.3.2 Learning Paradigms

    Video-LLMs are usually trained in stages because the encoder, connector, and language backbone start from different representations. In alignment pretraining, the encoder and LLM are often frozen while the connector learns from caption pairs, video–text matching, and grounding data, following the visual instruction tuning recipe for images [Liu et al., 2023]. Table 6 lists pair corpora and instruction datasets for this stage and the next.

item.title: 用键鼠在《我的世界》里像人一样玩：HiSTEVE 分层 VLA + 能力感知 harness，原子任务 85% ｜ HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA Agents for Open-World Games
item.description:
一句话：上层用 VLM 规划、下层用一个只吃画面只发键鼠的 VLA 执行，再用策略耦合的完成判定器切任务，能从零做出一把铁镐。

要点：

  • 既有 agent 要么只做短程视动控制、没有长程自主性，要么靠环境 API 或预制技能做高层规划，两者都不像人
  • orchestration 层：harness 带结构化记忆追踪进度，VLM planner 只在 VLA 能力范围内选子任务；control 层：单个 VLA 只用视觉感知、只发原生键鼠动作
  • 用「策略耦合的任务完成判定器」判断子任务是否完成：输入查询前 800/600/400/200 ms 的历史帧，与 VLA 共享图像编码器与自注意力流
  • MineStudio Bench 严格 pass@1 平均 85.0%（Mine 93.3 / Kill 86.7 / Craft 66.7 / Smelt 93.3），比最强基线高 20.0 个百分点；OpenHA 平均 37.4%；长程任务如从零合成铁镐可完成

为什么值得看：游戏作为 agent 训练环境的价值在于「没有 API 可走」；这套分层 harness 与完成判定器的设计，反过来也提示引擎侧可以提供哪些最小观测与状态接口来提升可评测性。

中文摘要：在《我的世界》这类开放式游戏里构建像人类玩家一样行动的虚拟具身智能体，需要长程自主性与可靠的原生界面控制两者兼备。已有 agent 往往只具备其一：要么有原生视动控制但没有长程自主性，要么靠环境 API 或预定义技能来执行高层规划。作者提出 HiSTEVE：一个带能力感知 agent harness 的分层 VLA 智能体。编排层为 harness 配备结构化记忆以追踪进度，并用 VLM 规划器在 VLA 能力范围内选择子任务；为可靠判断子任务完成，又引入策略耦合的任务完成状态检测器，它以 VLA 策略上下文为条件给出候选完成信号。控制层由单个 VLA 承担全部子任务，只用视觉感知、只输出原生键鼠动作。HiSTEVE 在 MineStudio Bench 上原子任务平均 85.0%，OpenHA 上平均成功率 37.4%，并能在长程任务上完成诸如从零制作铁镐这样的目标。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·智能体+游戏（English）

原文发布：2026-10-22

本期推送：2026-10-26

HiSTEVE 1.0: Harnessing Human-Interface VLA
Agents for Open-World Games

Abstract

Building virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games like human players is a long-standing goal requiring both long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying the integration of these capabilities. Existing agents typically provide either native visuomotor control without long-horizon autonomy or high-level planning executed through environment APIs or predefined skills. To bridge this gap, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness. At the orchestration level, we equip the harness with structured memory for tracking progress and a VLM planner for selecting subtasks within the VLA’s capabilities. To reliably determine subtask completion, we further introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. At the control level, a single VLA executes all subtasks with vision-only perception and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. To mitigate interference between heterogeneous GUI and non-GUI interactions, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings. We also train the VLA through world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback to improve reliability and recovery. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance, scoring 85.0% on MineStudio Bench and a 37.4% average success rate on OpenHA, while also completing long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like human players.

1 Introduction

A long-standing goal in embodied intelligence is to build virtual embodied agents [(Fung et al., 2025)] that can operate in open-ended games under the same interaction constraints as human players. Achieving this goal requires two complementary capabilities: long-horizon autonomy to maintain goals and adapt plans; and reliable native-interface control to translate first-person visual observations into keyboard-and-mouse actions. As a procedurally generated open world, Minecraft provides a natural testbed for studying these capabilities by combining partially observable, compositional tasks with diverse visuomotor interactions [(Fan et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023)]. A generally capable Minecraft agent must therefore integrate long-horizon planning with native-interface execution in a closed loop, continually updating its decisions from visual feedback.

Existing Minecraft agents have primarily emphasized one of these two capabilities. On the one hand, visuomotor policies and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models address native-interface control by directly mapping raw first-person observations to keyboard-and-mouse actions [(Baker et al., 2022; Lifshitz et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025)]. However, these models typically lack mechanisms for persistently tracking task state and explicitly reasoning over task dependencies, limiting their long-horizon autonomy. On the other hand, agents driven by large language models (LLMs) or vision-language models (VLMs) support long-horizon reasoning through task decomposition planning [(Wang et al., 2023a; Zhu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024)]. However, many of these methods still rely on environment APIs, predefined skills, or functional actions for low-level execution, which may be unavailable in most games. Although recent work has begun to combine high-level planning with learned policies [(Wang et al., 2025b; Park et al., 2025)], integrating task-state tracking, completion verification, and failure recovery remains an open challenge.

Satisfying both requirements introduces coupled challenges at the planning and action timescales. At the planning timescale, long-horizon autonomy requires tracking the objective, progress, and execution history across subtasks, while ensuring that plans are consistent with Minecraft mechanics and remain within the lower-level policy’s capabilities [(Wang et al., 2023b)]. The agent must also determine when to terminate the current subtask: terminating too early leaves the subtask unfinished, whereas terminating too late wastes actions and may even undo existing progress. At the action timescale, native-interface control requires a single VLA policy to operate reliably across heterogeneous task distributions. In particular, non-GUI control and GUI interaction differ in both visual distributions and mouse-action semantics: mouse movement rotates the camera in the former but displaces the cursor in the latter, making naive joint training susceptible to negative transfer [(He et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026)]. Each VLA invocation must also be reliable, since even small per-subtask failure risks accumulate over repeated invocations in long-horizon tasks.

To address these challenges, we propose HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent that combines a capability-aware harness for long-horizon autonomy and reliable native-interface control. At the slower planning timescale, we design the harness with a structured memory of task progress and a VLM planner that selects the next atomic subtask. To close the planning–execution loop, we introduce a policy-coupled task completion state detector that conditions on VLA policy context to signal candidate completion. The harness then verifies the task state and decides whether to advance, recover, or replan. At the faster action timescale, the VLA predicts native keyboard-and-mouse actions from the subtask instruction and first-person visual observation. To mitigate negative transfer across heterogeneous interaction regimes, we introduce regime-specific RMSNorm branches and separate mouse-movement token embeddings for non-GUI and GUI tasks. Following world knowledge injection and imitation learning, we further finetune the VLA through reinforcement learning (RL) to improve recovery when execution deviates from demonstration trajectories.

We comprehensively evaluate HiSTEVE on atomic and long-horizon benchmarks. Compared with the strongest baseline in our main comparison, HiSTEVE improves average success by 20.0 percentage points on MineStudio Bench and 0.6 points on OpenHA, with family-level gains of up to 28.6 points on LongBench. The largest long-horizon improvements occur in tasks requiring multi-stage resource production or the reuse of information gathered during exploration. Ablations reveal that stronger atomic execution alone does not yield comparable gains in long-horizon performance. With the VLA held fixed, the full harness more than doubles goal success relative to fixed-horizon handoff, highlighting the importance of organizing local execution around a persistent task state. The learned completion detector also outperforms prompted general-purpose VLMs, providing more accurate completion judgments to support this execution loop.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent with a capability-aware agent harness, enabling HiSTEVE to maintain goals and adapt plans throughout long-horizon execution.

  • •

    We enable reliable native-interface control through regime-specific RMSNorm branches, separate mouse-movement token embeddings, and a three-stage training strategy.

  • •

    HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art atomic-task performance and can complete long-horizon tasks such as crafting an iron pickaxe from scratch like a human player.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Agent Harnesses for Execution

    Foundation-model agents often use an agent harness, an external orchestration layer that supports interaction across model calls [(Sumers et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2026)]. Early language agents connect language models to external knowledge and tools and alternate between reasoning and action [(Nakano et al., 2021; Karpas et al., 2022; Yao et al., 2022)]. Later systems added memory, feedback-based reflection, and search-based evaluation, allowing the harness to retain experience and refine subsequent decisions [(Zhou et al., 2023; Packer et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024c; Xu et al., 2026)]. In long-horizon embodied tasks, agent harnesses coordinate high-level planning and low-level execution across multiple steps [(Huang et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2024a; Shah et al., 2025)]. Such harnesses use environmental observations, feasibility assessments, and execution outcomes to continually update subsequent decisions, thereby closing the planning–execution loop [(Huang et al., 2022b; Guo et al., 2024; Zhi et al., 2025)].

    2.2 VLA Models and Systems

    VLA models map visual observations and language instructions to embodied actions [(Ma et al., 2026; Brohan et al., 2023)]. Early language-conditioned policies learned this mapping directly from multi-task demonstrations [(Shridhar et al., 2022; Jang et al., 2022; Brohan et al., 2022)]. As model capacity and robot datasets grew, these policies generalized to a broader range of tasks, environments, and robot embodiments [(Brohan et al., 2023; O’Neill et al., 2024; Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2026; Pertsch et al., 2025)]. To support long-horizon planning, hierarchical systems use a semantic planner to generate policy-compatible subtasks for execution by a low-level policy [(Ma et al., 2026; Ahn et al., 2022; Driess et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2025)]. More recent approaches allow intermediate reasoning or predictive representations to directly guide low-level control [(Belkhale et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b)].

    2.3 Game-Playing Agents in Virtual Worlds

    Games have long served as testbeds for sequential decision making, with research progressing from search-based systems to deep RL agents [(Campbell et al., 2002; Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2016)]. More recently, pretrained models have been used to build agents that follow instructions and reason over observations [(Ma et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025)]. Researchers have also trained unified policies on multi-game data, but such policies often sacrifice control precision and long-horizon reliability [(Raad et al., 2024; Magne et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a)]. Alongside efforts toward cross-game generalization, Minecraft has emerged as a focused testbed for studying embodied interaction within an open world [(Guss et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2022)]. Research in Minecraft includes visuomotor policies learned directly from interaction trajectories [(Baker et al., 2022; Lifshitz et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025)], as well as LLM- or VLM-based agents for autonomous exploration and skill acquisition [(Zhu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2024b)].

    3 Capability-Aware Harness for Long-Horizon Autonomy

    We propose a capability-aware agent harness that coordinates a VLM planner and a VLA policy for long-horizon autonomy. Specifically, we integrate capability-constrained planning, evidence-driven handoff and recovery, and structured memory (Appendix 8).

    3.1 Capability-Constrained Planning

    Long-horizon Minecraft tasks cannot be reliably solved through a single static plan because the environment is partially observable, and local execution failures may change the feasibility of subsequent subtasks. Planning within the harness is reference-free: no predefined subtask sequence or expert task route is provided, and the planner selects the next atomic subtask online from the final objective and current execution context. We constrain the planner to select and instantiate a parameterized atomic subtask schema from a set restricted to the VLA’s execution capabilities. Each schema specifies its applicability, semantic parameters, visually observable progress and completion conditions, recognizable failure conditions, and execution budget.

    Let G denote the long-horizon objective, Oⱼ the current and recent visual observations at the j-th decision step, and hⱼ the structured planning state, which summarizes verified task progress, unresolved requirements, and previous execution outcomes. At each decision step, the harness evaluates schema applicability against hⱼ to construct the currently applicable schema set Sⱼ, while Rⱼ contains contextual memory retrieved according to the current goal and planning state. Given the planning context and admissible schema set constructed by the harness, the VLM planner selects and instantiates the atomic subtask as

    uⱼ=ℙ_VLM(G,Oⱼ,hⱼ,Sⱼ,Rⱼ),

    		(1)

    The structured output uⱼ specifies a semantic objective rather than a callable skill or scripted action sequence. The harness converts it into a fixed natural-language instruction Iⱼ, which the same VLA executes through native keyboard-and-mouse actions within a bounded invocation.

    3.2 Evidence-Driven Handoff and Recovery

    To address the handoff-timing problem between high-level planning and VLA control discussed above, we introduce an evidence-driven handoff-and-recovery protocol. During each bounded VLA invocation, the task-completion state detector estimates a completion probability for the current instruction Iⱼ. When this probability exceeds a confidence threshold, the current invocation ends and returns control to the harness, and exhaustion of the execution budget triggers the same handoff. Our mechanism differs from failure detection: the detector signals candidate completion rather than execution failure, while the harness verifies progress and completion conditions using current and recent visual observations. Based on this reassessment, the execution outcome vⱼ is recorded as success, failure, or interrupted, where interrupted indicates that control has been returned before either success or failure can be verified. Following verification, the harness advances if the completion conditions are satisfied and attempts local recovery if the subtask remains incomplete but recoverable. The harness replans from the updated state if recovery is infeasible or repeatedly fails, the current subtask becomes inapplicable, or the visual state changes substantially.

    3.3 Structured Memory

    Long-horizon execution requires persistent task state, but retaining the full history increases context length and accumulates unverified intermediate information. The harness therefore maintains a compact structured memory centered on verified state transitions. The memory system comprises four stores with distinct roles. Working memory corresponds to the current planning state hⱼ and records the active objective and atomic subtask, verified task progress, unresolved requirements, and recent failures or lack of progress. Episodic memory records the planning states before and after each VLA invocation, together with the selected subtask, the harness-verified outcome, execution cost, and diagnostic information. Procedural memory stores reusable dependencies among parameterized subtasks derived from verified successful executions. World memory stores landmarks and spatial relations inferred from visual observations to support subsequent planning within the current world. At each high-level decision step, the working memory hⱼ is used directly, whereas task-relevant entries are retrieved from the remaining memory categories to form the Rⱼ.

    4 VLA Policy for Native Visuomotor Control

    The lower-level VLA policy maps a subtask instruction with first-person visual observations to native keyboard-and-mouse actions. We describe the policy architecture and action representation, followed by a three-stage training strategy for improving execution reliability.

    4.1 VLA Policy Architecture

    Architecture.

    We initialize the policy from Qwen2.5-VL-7B [(Bai et al., 2025)]. At control step t, the policy takes Iⱼ and the current first-person observation oₜ as input and autoregressively generates the tokenized action aₜ. After executing aₜ, the agent receives a new observation and repeats this process at 20 Hz. Non-GUI and GUI interactions require different visuomotor skills, which can lead to conflicting optimization signals when all parameters are shared. Gradient analysis of a fully shared baseline shows that cross-regime gradients are less aligned than within-regime gradients, with the two RMSNorm modules exhibiting the strongest misalignment among shared components. The complete measurement protocol and results analysis are provided in Appendix 9.1.

    Based on this analysis, we introduce Regime-Specific RMSNorm (RS-Norm), a novel lightweight normalization mechanism for heterogeneous interaction regimes. Specifically, for both the pre-attention and pre-MLP RMSNorms in each decoder layer, we maintain two learnable scale vectors, one for non-GUI interactions and one for GUI interactions. The appropriate scale vector is selected according to the interaction regime of the current subtask. For interaction type c∈{NG,GUI}, the RMSNorm at decoder layer ℓ and module q∈{attn,mlp} is defined as

    RMSNorm_ℓ,q⁽ᶜ⁾(h)=γ_ℓ,q⁽ᶜ⁾⊙(h)/(√1/d∑ᵢ₌₁ᵈhᵢ²+ε),

    		(2)

    where γ_ℓ,q⁽ᶜ⁾∈ℝᵈ is the interaction-specific scale vector, while all other parameters remain shared. For a model with L decoder layers and hidden size d, this design adds only 2Ld parameters relative to the original backbone, resulting in minimal parameter overhead. RS-Norm can also be extended to other heterogeneous task combinations, such as vision-language understanding and visuomotor control, as well as multimodal understanding and generation.

    Action Representation.

    We represent Minecraft’s native keyboard-and-mouse actions as discrete action tokens, allowing supervised action prediction to use the same next-token prediction objective as language modeling. Following the VPT-style action space [(Baker et al., 2022)], we organize each single-step action into multiple categorical action groups. Keyboard and click inputs are represented as discrete choices within predefined action groups, while horizontal and vertical mouse displacements are μ-law transformed and quantized into the same number of bins.

    However, mouse displacement controls camera rotation in non-GUI interactions but cursor movement in GUI interactions, so sharing a single action token set creates an ambiguity. We therefore assign disjoint mouse-displacement token sets: the original mouse tokens are retained for non-GUI interactions, while a separate subset is allocated to GUI interactions. We further insert an interaction-type token at the beginning of the sequence to indicate whether the current interaction is non-GUI or GUI. Because both sets of mouse-displacement tokens decode back to the same physical action codebook, the branching occurs solely at the representation level. We refer to this regime-separated mouse-movement token representation as Dual-Mouse. (Appendix 9.3)

    4.2 Three-Stage Policy Training

    Because per-subtask failures compound over repeated VLA invocations, reliable long-horizon execution requires high reliability. We therefore train the VLA in three stages: world knowledge injection, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with environment feedback.

    Supervised Initialization.

    Before reinforcement learning, we use two supervised stages to establish the semantic knowledge and control capabilities required for reliable native-interface execution. World knowledge injection equips the policy with Minecraft concepts and their visual grounding, while imitation learning teaches it to map subtask instructions and first-person observations to native keyboard-and-mouse actions. Further details on data sources, sample construction and curation, training objectives, and optimization settings are provided in Appendix 10.

    Reinforcement Learning

    After imitation learning, the policy remains less reliable in GUI interactions, because precise cursor positioning and multi-step operations make GUI execution more sensitive to small action errors. We address this imbalance through environment-verified branch comparisons at both trajectory and state-matched segment levels. For each initial condition s₀, we independently sample K trajectories using a behavior policy π_b. Branch outcomes can be scored using either VLMs judge or direct environment feedback. Considering cost and efficiency, we adopt the latter for trainer-side reward construction and state matching. Each trajectory score Rᵢ combines certified completion, maximum verified progress, execution cost, and failure penalties. The resulting trajectories form a same-start branch group, whose scores yield the group-relative advantage:

    B(s₀)={τᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K, τᵢ∼π_b(·|s₀), Aᵢ=(Rᵢ-μ_B)/(σ_B+ε_A),

    		(3)

    where μ_B and σ_B denote the within-group score mean and standard deviation.

    We optimize informative branch groups with clipped GRPO [(Shao et al., 2024)] updates, separating detached behavior-policy importance correction from the current-policy update ratio. However, trajectory-level advantages can penalize correct prefixes in failed rollouts. We therefore construct local preference pairs from successful and failed branches, prioritizing the same rollout origin and matching structured signatures of inventory, GUI, cursor, execution stage, and environment events. The resulting DPO-style pairwise loss targets divergent action segments, using the same completion certificates as group-relative learning. To preserve non-GUI capabilities, we interleave branch updates with world-action replay and regularize against a fixed reference policy π_ref:

    Lₚₒₛₜ=L_branch+λ_worldL_world+λ_refD_KL(π_θ∥π_ref),

    		(4)

    where L_branch is the group-relative loss for informative branch groups or the pairwise loss for matched segments, depending on the available comparisons, and L_world is the world-action replay loss. Reward construction and optimization details are provided in Appendix 10.3.

    5 Task Completion State Detector

    We introduce a novel policy-coupled task completion state detector to support the harness in determining when to pause the VLA invocation. To reduce system overhead, the detector shares the VLA image encoder and additionally conditions on VLA policy context for completion prediction, with Qwen2.5-VL-3B serving as its backbone. At each query, the detector uses the shared image encoder and its self-attention stream to process historical frames sampled at 800, 600, 400, and 200 ms before the query, while the VLA processes the current frame and subtask instruction. The final-layer hidden states of the input prefix preceding the first action token form the policy context Hₜ^π, which is injected through cross-attention after every fourth detector decoder layer. Let Zₜ^(ℓ) denote the detector hidden states at layer ℓ. We apply query-normalized residual cross-attention as

    Z̃ₜ^(ℓ)=Zₜ^(ℓ)+MHA_ℓ(LN_ℓ(Zₜ^(ℓ)),Hₜ^π,Hₜ^π),

    		(5)

    where each cross-attention module has independent projection parameters. To further reduce detector overhead, we use Wanda-inspired activation–weight channel scores to prune the intermediate width of each feed-forward network to approximately one third [(Sun et al., 2024)]. For classification, we map the detector’s final-token hidden state to two logits through a linear classification head and apply a softmax to obtain the completion probability pₜ. We train the detector with the VLA frozen on completion labels derived from VPT human gameplay trajectories [(Baker et al., 2022)]. At deployment, the detector runs before action decoding and raises a candidate completion signal to the harness only when pₜ exceeds τ for two consecutive queries. Details of dataset construction, channel pruning and training are provided in Appendix 11.

    6 Experiments

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    We instantiate HiSTEVE with GPT-4o [(Hurst et al., 2024)] as the upper-level planner and Qwen2.5-VL-7B [(Bai et al., 2025)] as the low-level VLA. We evaluate atomic execution on MineStudio Bench [(Zheng et al., 2023)] and OpenHA [(Wang et al., 2025b)], and long-horizon agency on LongBench. Ablation scores are averaged over repeated independent evaluations for each fixed checkpoint. MineStudio contains 20 tasks with three trials each, OpenHA reports family-wise episode success over Embodied, GUI, and Combat, and LongBench contains 14 goal-only tasks with 49 hidden diagnostic nodes. We compare against prior native-control agents, including VPT [(Baker et al., 2022)], STEVE-1 [(Lifshitz et al., 2023)], ROCKET-1 [(Cai et al., 2025)], and JARVIS-VLA [(Li et al., 2025)], as well as OpenHA variants—LatentHA, MotionHA, GroundingHA, TextVLA, and Text/CoA [(Wang et al., 2025b)]. Complete evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix 12.

    6.2 Main Results

    As shown in Table 1, we evaluate HiSTEVE across atomic and long-horizon tasks.

    Atomic task execution.

    On MineStudio Bench, HiSTEVE achieves strict pass@1 scores of 93.3%, 86.7%, 66.7%, and 93.3% on Mine, Kill, Craft, and Smelt, respectively, corresponding to an overall average of 85.0%. Compared with OpenHA Text/CoA, HiSTEVE improves the four-family average from 65.0% to 85.0%, with gains of 20.0, 13.4, 26.7, and 20.0 percentage points on Mine, Kill, Craft, and Smelt, respectively. The largest absolute gain occurs on Craft, although Craft remains the weakest MineStudio category, indicating that multi-step GUI manipulation remains more challenging than first-person mining and combat.

    On OpenHA, HiSTEVE achieves a 37.4% average success rate, compared with 36.8% for OpenHA Text/CoA. The gain is concentrated in Embodied tasks, where success increases from 37.0% to 46.0%, while GUI and Combat remain slightly below the corresponding baseline scores. Our trajectory analysis shows that failed GUI episodes can reach and interact with the correct interface but break down during multi-step item placement, intermediate-state correction, or result retrieval, indicating that robust multi-step GUI execution remains a key bottleneck.

    Long-horizon execution.

    LongBench evaluates whether atomic native-control capabilities remain effective when they must be repeatedly composed over extended interaction. Unlike atomic benchmarks, success depends not only on executing individual subtasks, but also on maintaining task state across invocations and adapting subsequent decisions to observed outcomes. We evaluate Resource & Crafting, Exploration & Memory, Recovery, and Open-ended tasks using final-goal success as the primary metric, with hidden diagnostic nodes used only for progress analysis.

    HiSTEVE achieves final-goal success rates of 42.9%, 28.6%, 14.3%, and 14.3% on Resource & Crafting, Exploration & Memory, Recovery, and Open-ended tasks, respectively, with the overall Goal SR in Table 3 computed as the macro-average over the four task families. Relative to OpenHA Text/CoA, these correspond to improvements of 28.6, 21.5, 11.4, and 12.9 percentage points. The largest gains appear on Resource & Crafting and Exploration & Memory, where successful execution requires repeated composition of atomic skills and persistent task-state tracking. Recovery and Open-ended tasks remain substantially harder, indicating that robust recovery and weakly structured objectives remain important challenges at longer horizons. Figure 3 complements these results with qualitative examples of atomic and long-horizon execution.

    6.3 Atomic Task Completion Detection Evaluation

    We evaluate completion detection on a class-balanced validation split of 4,674 samples drawn from VPT trajectories [(Baker et al., 2022)] across four task families: mining, killing, crafting, and smelting (details see Appendix 11.1). As baselines, we use a random classifier, the open-source Qwen3.5 VLMs with 9B and 35B parameters [(Team, 2026)], and the closed-source GPT-4o and GPT-5.5 models [(Hurst et al., 2024; Singh et al., 2025)]. These general-purpose models are not trained for task-completion detection. We provide each model with the same history frames, current frame, and subtask instruction, and prompt it to make a binary completion decision. As reported in Table 2, we measure overall accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for the completion class. We additionally report the false-positive rate (FPR) and false-negative rate (FNR), which quantify premature completion predictions and missed completions, respectively.

    As shown in Table 2, our specialized detector consistently outperforms the prompted general-purpose VLM baselines. Qwen3.5 strongly favors the incomplete class, with recalls of only 0.030 and 0.042 at 9B and 35B parameters, respectively. GPT-4o and GPT-5.5 improve F1 to 0.690 and 0.776. In contrast, our detector reaches 0.863 in both accuracy and F1, with precision and recall of 0.861 and 0.865, providing a more accurate and balanced candidate-completion signal for the planning–control interface. The downstream effect of state-dependent handoff within the complete agent is evaluated in Section 6.4, while detector architectural ablations are reported in Appendix 13.

    6.4 Ablation Study

    Table 3 isolates staged policy training, regime-specific representation, and harness orchestration.

    Effect of regime-specific representation.

    RS-Norm and Dual-Mouse provide complementary gains: from a shared-representation baseline of 41.1% on MineStudio All, they individually improve performance to 57.3% and 61.9%, and jointly reach 80.7%. Together, they also improve OpenHA Avg. from 26.6% to 37.7% and LongBench Goal SR from 3.6% to 14.3%. Concurrent gains on both MineStudio World and GUI suggest that regime-specific feature scaling and mouse-action separation mitigate complementary interference between the two interaction regimes.

    Effect of staged policy training.

    World knowledge injection substantially improves the lower-level executor, increasing MineStudio All from 50.4% to 65.1% and OpenHA Avg. from 29.5% to 35.3%, while LongBench Goal SR increases from 7.1% to 14.3%. Environment-feedback RL further raises MineStudio All to 80.7% and OpenHA Avg. to 37.7%, but leaves LongBench Goal SR unchanged at 14.3%. This separation indicates that post-training strengthens local execution reliability, while improving the executor alone is insufficient to solve long-horizon coordination.

    Effect of the agent harness.

    With the lower-level VLA fixed, this ablation evaluates system-level execution, where handoff and verification can still affect atomic success. The complete harness changes atomic performance modestly, from 81.2% to 85.0% on MineStudio All and from 37.8% to 37.4% on OpenHA Avg. In contrast, LongBench Goal SR increases from 10.7% to 25.0%, with diagnostic progress rising from 17.9% to 28.6%. These gains highlight the role of capability-constrained planning and execution handoff and verification in organizing VLA invocations.

    7 Conclusion

    We present HiSTEVE, a hierarchical VLA agent combining a capability-aware agent harness for long-horizon autonomy with native-interface control. The harness enables long-horizon autonomy through capability-constrained planning, evidence-driven handoff and recovery, and structured memory. Regime-specific representations and three-stage training enable a single VLA to reliably handle both non-GUI and GUI interactions. HiSTEVE achieves state-of-the-art performance on MineStudio Bench (85.0%) and OpenHA (37.4%) and can craft an iron pickaxe from scratch using only human-interface. Our work shows that regime-specific representations support reliable control across heterogeneous tasks, while reliable long-horizon execution further requires a harness that combines local control with state-aware orchestration. These results represent a step toward virtual embodied agents that operate in open-ended games human players.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    8 Agent Harness Details

    This section provides additional implementation details for the agent harness introduced in Section 3. We describe the runtime interaction between the VLM planner and the native-control VLA, the capability-constrained atomic interface, evidence-driven verification and recovery, and the structured memory used during long-horizon execution.

    8.1 Harness Runtime

    HiSTEVE executes a long-horizon objective through repeated bounded interactions between a high-level semantic planner and a continuously acting VLA policy. At high-level decision step j, the harness maintains a structured planning state

    hⱼ=(G,pⱼ,rⱼ,v_

    		(6)

    where G denotes the final task objective, pⱼ denotes visually verified progress, rⱼ denotes unresolved requirements, and v_

    Given hⱼ, the harness determines which parameterized atomic subtask schemas are currently applicable and constructs the admissible set

    Sⱼ={s∈S \middle| Applicable(s,hⱼ)=1}.

    		(7)

    Task-relevant information retrieved from episodic, procedural, and world memory is denoted by Rⱼ. The planner then selects and instantiates the next atomic subtask:

    uⱼ=ℙ_VLM(G,Oⱼ,hⱼ,Sⱼ,Rⱼ),

    		(8)

    where Oⱼ denotes the current and recent visual observations.

    The planner output uⱼ specifies a semantic objective rather than an executable Minecraft function or scripted action sequence. The harness converts it into a fixed natural-language instruction Iⱼ, which is executed by the same VLA during one bounded invocation. At control step t within the invocation, the VLA predicts

    aₜ∼π_θ(·|oₜ,Iⱼ),

    		(9)

    where oₜ is the current first-person observation and aₜ is a native keyboard-and-mouse action.

    The instruction Iⱼ remains fixed throughout the invocation, while the visual observation changes after every environment step. This separation yields two interacting timescales: the VLA performs continuous control at the action timescale, whereas the harness updates the task state only at semantic execution boundaries.

    Control is returned to the harness when either the execution budget is exhausted or the completion detector produces a candidate completion signal. Let pₜ denote the detector probability that the current subtask has completed. A detector-triggered handoff is produced when

    pₜ>τ ∧ pₜ₋₁>τ,

    		(10)

    where τ is the detector operating threshold. Requiring two consecutive positive predictions reduces sensitivity to isolated detector errors.

    Importantly, a handoff does not imply successful task completion. It only indicates that the current bounded invocation should stop and return control to the harness for verification.

    8.2 Capability-Constrained Atomic Interface

    Direct free-form decomposition can produce subtasks that are too abstract for reliable execution by the VLA, or conversely, subtasks that are so narrow that they require unnecessarily frequent high-level decisions. HiSTEVE therefore exposes the lower-level VLA to the planner through a parameterized atomic interface.

    Each atomic schema s∈S is represented as

    s=(Aₛ,ℙₛ,ℂₛ,Fₛ,Bₛ),

    		(11)

    where Aₛ denotes the semantic arguments of the subtask, ℙₛ its applicability conditions, ℂₛ its visually observable completion criteria, Fₛ recognizable failure conditions, and Bₛ the execution budget.

    The schema library defines the capability boundary presented to the planner. It does not contain scripted implementations of the corresponding subtasks. Once a schema is instantiated, all physical interactions required to realize the semantic objective are produced by the VLA through native keyboard-and-mouse actions.

    For count-based objectives, the harness does not issue an indefinitely running instruction such as “collect N items.” Instead, it repeatedly invokes bounded acquisition subtasks. After invocation j, the remaining requirement is updated according to the visually verified progress:

    rⱼ₊₁=\max(0,rⱼ-Δⱼ),

    		(12)

    where Δⱼ denotes newly verified progress during the current invocation.

    This decomposition prevents already acquired resources from being repeatedly counted as new progress and avoids continuing a stale local instruction after the corresponding requirement has already been satisfied.

    8.3 Evidence-Driven Verification and Recovery

    HiSTEVE explicitly separates execution handoff from task verification. A detector-triggered handoff only indicates a candidate semantic boundary. After control returns, the harness reassesses the current and recent visual observations and evaluates the completion and failure predicates associated with the active subtask.

    The resulting execution outcome is represented as

    vⱼ∈{success,failure,interrupted},

    		(13)

    where interrupted indicates that control has returned to the harness but neither success nor failure can yet be visually verified.

    The updated planning state is then

    hⱼ₊₁=U(hⱼ,uⱼ,vⱼ,Oⱼ₊₁),

    		(14)

    where U denotes the harness state-update operation and Oⱼ₊₁ contains the visual evidence available after the invocation.

    During deployment, the planner and VLA interact with the environment only through first-person observations and native keyboard-and-mouse actions. Simulator-side state used during training for reward construction or trajectory certification is not provided to the deployed planner or VLA.

    For example, resource acquisition is accepted only after the corresponding inventory change is visually confirmed. Likewise, crafting or smelting is not considered complete merely because an intermediate GUI state is reached; the resulting item must be visually observed in the player inventory.

    After verification, the harness follows three possible transitions:

    Next(vⱼ)=\begincasesadvance,&if the completion condition is verified, recover,&if the subtask remains locally recoverable, replan,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(15)

    Recovery is used for local execution deviations that do not invalidate the high-level objective, such as temporary lack of progress, inconsistent GUI state, target loss, or a produced item that has not yet been collected. If recovery is infeasible or repeatedly fails, the current subtask becomes inapplicable, or the observed state changes substantially, the harness invokes the planner again from the updated task state.

    8.4 Structured Memory

    Long-horizon execution requires persistent task state, but retaining the complete raw interaction history rapidly increases context length and preserves many transient or unverified intermediate states. HiSTEVE instead maintains a compact memory centered on verified subtask-level state transitions.

    The memory system consists of four complementary stores:

  • •

    Working memory records the current objective, active subtask, verified progress, unresolved requirements, and recent failure or no-progress states.

  • •

    Episodic memory records the state transition associated with each bounded VLA invocation, together with the selected subtask, harness-verified outcome, execution cost, and diagnostic information.

  • •

    Procedural memory stores reusable dependencies among parameterized subtasks extracted from verified successful executions.

  • •

    World memory stores visually inferred landmarks and spatial relations that may support later planning within the current world.

    • The episodic record generated by bounded invocation j is represented as

    mⱼ=(hⱼ,uⱼ,vⱼ,hⱼ₊₁,cⱼ),

    		(16)

    where cⱼ contains execution metadata such as execution cost and diagnostic information.
